Atlas Quant Notes

Building trading infrastructure, quant research and honest AI agents, one engineer at a time.

I'm building Atlas Quant Systems: research tools, options analytics and execution infrastructure for index futures, written mostly in C#, with a cloud and AI layer on top. It's a one-person shop. My "team" is a handful of AI coding agents, which is a story in itself.

This is my build log, written as a textbook: 175 chapters in 12 parts, each with learning objectives, figures, a summary and exercises. It covers the engineering and the maths: tick-level replay, regime models, Kalman filters, dealer gamma, and what it really takes to make AI tools useful without letting them make things up.

What you won't find here: trade signals, performance screenshots, or "this one indicator made me rich". I don't publish results, and I'm suspicious of anyone who publishes only the good ones. Every simulated figure states its random process and seed; none uses market data.

Where to start

  • 1.1 Building in public without publishing the recipe: who I am and the rules I work by.
  • 6.1 The random-walk null: why a 67% hit rate can mean nothing.
  • 12.2 An engineer's introduction to day trading futures: the beginner's door.

Or pick any chapter from the list. Each one stands on its own and points back to what it builds on.

Follow along

New chapters and updates go out by email on Substack (link coming soon). The project overview lives at github.com/rutariq.

— Tariq

Chapter 1.1 — Building in Public Without Publishing the Recipe

Subtitle: One engineer, a few AI agents, and a rule: if I can’t prove it, it isn’t a result.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe, in broad terms, the parts of the trading stack this book follows. 2. Explain why writing for others makes technical work more precise. 3. Say what a trading write-up can share safely and what it should keep back, and why.

You need: no special background.

1.1.1 What is being built

For most of this year I have been building tools for researching and trading S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures (contracts that track a stock index; Chapter 12.2 explains them).

It is a stack, meaning layers of software that sit on top of each other:

  • At the bottom, a C# runtime inside NinjaTrader (a trading platform) with thirty-odd custom indicators (calculations drawn on a price chart).
  • Above it, a research engine that replays the market one trade at a time.
  • Beside it, an options engine that estimates where dealers (the banks and market makers who sell options) are likely hedging.
  • Around it all, an AWS (Amazon’s cloud) layer. It collects data, writes a daily market report, and runs a small team of AI agents in shadow mode: they make decisions, I log them, and nobody lets them touch money.

It is a one-person company. The honest answer to “who is on the team?” is me plus several AI coding assistants. That turned out to be the most interesting part of the project, and the most dangerous. Later chapters cover it.

1.1.2 Why write about it

There are three reasons.

  1. Writing forces precision. I have research notes on regime detection, change-point models, volatility scaling and backtest overfitting. Most were written for me. Writing for someone else shows fast which parts I really understand.
  2. The interesting problems are not secret. How to replay tick data without peeking at the future, why a “70% win rate” can be pure geometry, how to stop an AI assistant from quietly cutting corners: none of that is proprietary. It is what I wish I had read a year ago.
  3. Accountability. If I say in public that I don’t trust untested results, I had better not post any.

1.1.3 What stays private

The publishing rule. No trade signals. No equity curves (charts of account value over time). No settings, thresholds or parameters. No diagrams of how my pieces connect.

This is not secrecy for its own sake. Trading research is full of results that look great and mean nothing, and the internet is full of people selling them. I would rather show the engineering and the maths, which you can check, than numbers you can’t.

Figure 1.1.1 — The line between what is shared and what is not. The green column is what this book contains: lessons, standard maths, failures and checkable methods. The orange column is what it leaves out. The rule at the bottom is the reason for the split: a reader can verify the left side but could never verify the right side from a blog post.

1.1.4 What comes next

The chapters that follow cover:

  • How an AI coding assistant quietly replaced my C# engine with a Python shortcut, and the guardrails I built so it can’t happen again.
  • Why a pattern that “continues 67% of the time” can be exactly what a coin flip gives you.
  • Dealer gamma for engineers: what the GEX numbers on social media mean and where they mislead.
  • Replaying the market one trade at a time, and why bars lie.
  • Hidden Markov models, change-point detection and Kalman filters, with as little hand-waving as I can manage.

I post when there is something real to say.

1.1.5 Summary

  • The project is a layered stack: NinjaTrader indicators in C#, a tick-replay research engine, an options engine and an AWS layer with shadow-mode AI agents.
  • The team is one person plus AI coding assistants.
  • Writing in public forces precision and accountability.
  • The book shares engineering and maths, never signals, equity curves, parameters or wiring.

Exercises

  1. (Recall) Name the four layers of the stack described in 1.1.1.
  2. (Think) Why can a reader check a published method but not a published equity curve? (Answer: a method can be re-derived or re-run on your own data; an equity curve depends on data, settings and choices the reader cannot see or reproduce.)
  3. (Apply) You want to share a trading tool you built. List three things you could publish safely and three you should hold back.

Further reading

  • No references in the draft. The later chapters list sources for each topic.

— Tariq

Chapter 1.2 — Starting from the Chart: Writing My Own NinjaTrader Indicators

Subtitle: Spring 2026, a blank NinjaScript folder, and the first lesson in building trading tools: the bar is a model, not a fact.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why owning indicator source code matters for later research. 2. Show why an EMA’s starting value never fully disappears, and why RSI conventions differ. 3. Explain what a Renko brick throws away, and why that matters for stops. 4. List the three facts to record for every indicator.

You need: what a moving average is; reading a simple sum with Σ.

1.2.1 Where it started

The project did not start with AWS, agents or a research engine. It started in spring 2026 with a NinjaTrader install, a folder of C# files, and a common frustration: the indicators I looked at every day were black boxes (tools whose inner workings you can’t see).

In April I started writing my own. The earliest files date from the first week of that month: a prior-day open/high/low/close plotter, a current-day version of it, a regime indicator, a custom Renko bar type and my own RSI. None of this is exotic. The point was to own every line of code that drew something on my screen.

1.2.2 Why not use the built-ins

NinjaTrader ships a decent indicator library. But a built-in is a contract whose small print you can’t read. Does it update on each tick or on bar close? How does it warm up? What does it do on the first bar of a session? Does a moving average carry state over the overnight gap, or reset?

These sound pedantic until you try to reproduce a chart reading in a backtest and the numbers don’t match. Then they are the whole job.

Writing my own versions gave me three things:

What I gained What it means
Known update semantics NinjaScript can run OnBarUpdate on bar close, on each tick, or on price change. Each of my indicators states which, and why.
Known warm-up Recursive indicators carry memory. I wanted to know how much history each needs before its output means anything.
One source of truth When I later rebuilt the research engine, these files became the reference the replay code had to match. That only works if the reference is code I wrote and understand.

1.2.3 The maths hiding in a “simple” indicator

An exponential moving average (EMA) blends the newest value with the previous average:

EMAt=αxt+(1−α)EMAt−1,α=2n+1. \text{EMA}_t = \alpha\, x_t + (1-\alpha)\, \text{EMA}_{t-1}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{2}{n+1}.

Unroll it, and it becomes a weighted sum of all past values:

EMAt=α∑k=0t−1(1−α)kxt−k+(1−α)tEMA0. \text{EMA}_t = \alpha \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} (1-\alpha)^k x_{t-k} + (1-\alpha)^t\, \text{EMA}_0 .

Key fact. The starting value EMA0\text{EMA}_0 never fully disappears. Its weight is (1−α)t(1-\alpha)^t, which shrinks geometrically but is never zero.

So if your chart loaded 3 days of history and your backtest loaded 30, the two EMAs disagree for a while. The disagreement is purely an artefact of where you started counting.

RSI (the Relative Strength Index) has the same trap in another shape. Wilder’s original smoothing is an EMA with α=1/n\alpha = 1/n, not 2/(n+1)2/(n+1):

RSIt=100−1001+U¯tD¯t,U¯t=1nUt+(1−1n)U¯t−1. \text{RSI}_t = 100 - \frac{100}{1 + \dfrac{\overline{U}_t}{\overline{D}_t}}, \qquad \overline{U}_t = \tfrac{1}{n} U_t + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{n}\right)\overline{U}_{t-1}.

Here U¯\overline{U} and D¯\overline{D} are smoothed average up-moves and down-moves. Many libraries quietly use a simple average, or the other EMA convention, and still call it RSI. They agree on trending days and disagree near the thresholds people actually trade. Writing my own RSI was mostly about removing that ambiguity.

Figure 1.2.1 — The starting value fades slowly. Each curve shows how much weight, (1−α)t(1-\alpha)^t, the starting value still carries after tt bars. The blue curve uses the common EMA rule with n = 20; the dashed orange curve uses Wilder’s rule with n = 14, which fades more slowly. The example n values are textbook illustrations only. Until the curve is near zero, two copies of the “same” indicator with different history lengths will not match.

1.2.4 Renko: a bar type is a modelling decision

The most instructive file from that spring was the custom Renko bar type.

A time bar samples the market on the clock. A Renko brick samples it on price movement: a new brick forms only when price has moved a fixed distance from the last brick’s close. If bb is the brick size and ckc_k the close of brick kk, a new up-brick forms when

pt≥ck+b, p_t \ge c_k + b,

and a reversal brick usually needs a larger move the other way (Chapter 6.1 shows what that does to hit rates). Time disappears from the x-axis. Quiet periods shrink to nothing; busy periods stretch out.

That helps trend work because it filters noise. It is dangerous for research because the brick hides what happened inside it. A standard Renko implementation draws a clean rectangle from open to close. The real high and low reached while the brick formed, the wicks, are thrown away unless you deliberately keep them.

Figure 1.2.2 — A body-only brick forgets the high and low. The blue line is a made-up price path inside one period. The middle bar keeps its wicks, so you can see the path dipped to the dashed orange line. The right-hand brick keeps only the body. With the body alone you cannot tell whether a stop on the dashed line was hit.

I did not fully see how much this mattered in April. I do now. Months later, wickless bars became one of the failure modes I wrote rules against, because a bar with no wick cannot tell you whether a stop inside its range would have been hit. Chapter 1.7 returns to this.

1.2.5 Engineering trade-offs inside NinjaTrader

Three things I learned that aren’t in the tutorials:

  • Allocation matters on tick updates. OnBarUpdate can fire thousands of times a minute on a busy instrument. Anything that allocates memory per call (string formatting, LINQ, new lists) shows up as garbage-collection pauses on the chart. I keep per-tick paths allocation-free and format on bar close.
  • Series lookback is a real limit. NinjaTrader keeps a bounded history for custom series by default. If another component later reads far back, it can throw or get invalid values. This bit me in September when a telemetry exporter needed to read sibling indicators by absolute index. The fix was raising the lookback on the series it depended on.
  • Determinism is not free. Running on each tick versus on bar close changes the output of almost every indicator. Pick one per indicator and document it, or two people (or two agents) will read the same chart and see different numbers.

1.2.6 What I’d tell another engineer

Write the boring indicators first: prior-day levels, a moving average, an RSI. They are easy to check by hand. They teach you the platform’s lifecycle: State.SetDefaults, State.DataLoaded, the order bars arrive in, and how historical bars differ from real-time ones.

Three facts per indicator. For each one, write down (1) its update mode, (2) its warm-up length, and (3) what happens at a session boundary.

That short list did more for my later research than any clever feature. The framework grew to thirty-odd custom indicators by the end of the year. But the habit that mattered was set in the first month: if it draws on my chart, I can read its source and reproduce its output.

1.2.7 Summary

  • I wrote my own indicators from April 2026 to own their update mode, warm-up and session behaviour.
  • An EMA’s starting value decays as (1−α)t(1-\alpha)^t but never vanishes, so different history lengths give different values.
  • “RSI” hides two smoothing conventions; they disagree near common thresholds.
  • Renko bricks discard wicks, which hides whether a stop inside the range was hit.
  • Record update mode, warm-up and session-boundary behaviour for every indicator.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) With α=0.1\alpha = 0.1, what weight does the starting value carry after 20 bars? (Answer: 0.920≈0.120.9^{20} \approx 0.12, about 12%.)
  2. (Compare) For n = 14, compute α\alpha under the 2/(n+1)2/(n+1) rule and under Wilder’s 1/n1/n rule. Which fades the seed faster?
  3. (Think) Why does a body-only brick make every stop look either “certainly hit” or “certainly not hit”?
  4. (Apply) Pick an indicator you use. Write its three facts: update mode, warm-up, session boundary.

Further reading

  • J. Welles Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978): the original RSI and ADX definitions.
  • NinjaTrader 8 NinjaScript documentation: OnBarUpdate, Calculate modes and MaximumBarsLookBack.
  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), ch. 2 on alternative bar types.

— Tariq

Chapter 1.3 — A Live Market Platform and an AI Daily Reporter in One Month

Subtitle: What it actually takes to get a language model to write a market report every morning without making things up.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why a language model’s inputs and outputs must be validated like any external data. 2. Write the exponential-backoff-with-jitter formula and say why the jitter matters. 3. Use the Brier score to judge probability forecasts, and say why a small sample can’t be trusted. 4. List the main reliability lessons for a real-time market dashboard.

You need: basic probability; what an API call is.

1.3.1 The month in one ratio

The git history of my main repository starts on 14 July 2026. The first commit is about reporting automation: a system that drafts a daily market report, and a public site to put it on. By the end of July the repository had about 150 commits. Most are not glamorous: retries, timeouts, fallback paths, chart fonts and one-line fixes to build files.

That ratio is the story of the month.

1.3.2 The daily reporter

The idea was simple. Every morning before the US open:

  1. pull together the economic calendar, overnight futures moves and a few options-derived levels;
  2. have a language model on AWS Bedrock draft a research brief;
  3. render it as a PDF and an audio file;
  4. post it to the website and a Discord channel.

The first version worked in a day. The next two weeks went on making it honest and reliable.

Honest. On 15 July a commit switched the drafting “from fictional to real” calendar data. Early drafts had been written against placeholder data, and a language model will write a confident paragraph about a placeholder as happily as about a real CPI print. The fix was structural: wire in a real economic calendar feed, then add official government-sourced actuals for CPI, PPI and unemployment, and make the model’s input contain only those.

Another commit that day maps only known fields from the model’s draft, because the model had returned an extra field nobody asked for.

Theme for the year. Treat model output like untrusted external input, because it is.

Reliable. Bedrock calls fail. Feeds return empty. On 17 July I added hardened retries, a “safe skip” path, and tests for the fallback tiers. On 18 July calendar deploys learned to skip when their sources were empty, rather than publish a blank table.

1.3.3 Retries, properly

The standard pattern is exponential backoff with jitter. Attempt kk waits

wk=min⁡(wmax,w0⋅2k)⋅U,U∼Uniform(0,1). w_k = \min\!\left(w_{\max},\; w_0 \cdot 2^{k}\right) \cdot U, \qquad U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1).

Here w0w_0 is the first wait, wmaxw_{\max} a cap, and UU a random number between 0 and 1. The jitter term UU is the part people drop. Without it, every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment, and you get synchronised “thundering herds” against a service that is already struggling. With full jitter, retries spread across the window.

Figure 1.3.1 — Jitter spreads retries out. Twelve clients fail together at time 0. Without jitter (top), all twelve retry at exactly the same moments, so each orange dot is twelve requests at once. With full jitter (bottom), each client waits a random fraction of its backoff, so the retries scatter. This is a simulation with uniform random numbers and seed 20261107; the backoff values are illustrative units.

The other half is knowing when to stop. A daily report has a deadline: the market opens whether or not the model answered. So every retry loop has a hard budget. When it is spent, the system falls back to a lower tier (a simpler report, or none, clearly marked) instead of publishing something half-generated.

Figure 1.3.2 — Retries live inside a deadline. A valid output is published (green). An invalid one goes to the budget check: if time remains, wait with backoff and jitter and try again; if not, fall back to a clearly labelled lower tier (orange). There is no path that publishes a half-finished report.

1.3.4 Closing the loop

On 20 July I added what the commits call a prediction-versus-outcome loop: after the session, compare what the morning brief leaned towards with what the market did, and feed that back.

The natural score for directional calls that carry a probability is the Brier score:

BS=1N∑i=1N(fi−oi)2, \text{BS} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} (f_i - o_i)^2,

where fif_i is the forecast probability and oio_i is 1 if the event happened and 0 if not. Lower is better. It rewards calibration, not just being right: a brief that says “70%” should be right about 70% of the time when it says that.

The limit, stated plainly: a month of daily briefs is a tiny sample, and “adaptive factor weights” learned on a tiny sample mostly fit noise. Building the loop was right. Trusting what it learned in July would not have been. (Chapter 1.11 puts a number on this.)

1.3.5 The live platform

In parallel, the site grew a live dashboard. Late July went on streaming futures quotes through a broker gateway, building 30-second candles, and drawing options-derived gamma levels next to price. The lessons were the usual ones for real-time systems:

Lesson What happened
Liveness beats connectivity A socket can be open and dead. On 22 July I added an exponential-backoff reconnect loop and a liveness watchdog: if no tick arrives within a window, assume the stream is stale and reconnect.
Contract qualification is fiddly Several commits on 23 July fix exchange mappings for different futures; one notes a crypto future has a different broker symbol than its display name. The fix simplified qualification to the minimum fields. Over-specifying a contract caused more failures than under-specifying it.
Bucket time in one timezone Candle bucketing and axis labels moved to US Eastern time explicitly. Mixed timezones produce bars that are subtly wrong for an hour around every daylight-saving change.
Server rendering and dates don’t mix A commit made date formatting safe for server-side rendering. Hydration mismatches from new Date() on server and client are a classic React trap.

1.3.6 What the commit log says

Looking back at 22 July is a little embarrassing. There are more than a dozen styling commits in one day: font sizes, chart widths, the colour of one label, then the same thing nudged again. One commit removes the top two price charts “to start fresh”.

That is what building something visual with an AI assistant at speed looks like: rapid, cheap, unplanned iterations. It worked, but the history is noisy and some decisions were reversed within hours. I would now batch visual changes and look at them together, rather than commit each nudge.

1.3.7 What I’d tell another engineer

If you put a language model in a daily pipeline:

  1. Give it only real, sourced inputs, and check them before the model sees them.
  2. Validate its output against a schema (a fixed description of allowed fields and types); drop anything unexpected.
  3. Budget retries against a deadline and always have a clearly labelled fallback.
  4. Measure it against outcomes, but don’t believe what a small sample tells you.

The model was the easy part. Everything around it was the product.

1.3.8 Summary

  • A model writes fluently about fake inputs; feed it only real, checked data and validate its output.
  • Exponential backoff needs jitter, a cap, and a hard deadline with a labelled fallback.
  • The Brier score rewards calibrated probabilities, but a month of data is too little to learn from.
  • For live dashboards: watch liveness, keep contract specs minimal, use one timezone, and beware server/client date rendering.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) A brief gives 0.7, 0.6 and 0.9 for three events; the outcomes are 1, 0, 1. What is the Brier score? (Answer: (0.09 + 0.36 + 0.01)/3 ≈ 0.153.)
  2. (Explain) Why does removing jitter make an outage worse even though each client “backs off”?
  3. (Design) Sketch the fallback tiers for a report with a 9:00 deadline. What does the reader see in each tier?
  4. (Think) Why can a socket be “connected” but useless? What would you measure instead?

Further reading

  • Marc Brooker, “Exponential Backoff and Jitter”, AWS Architecture Blog (2015).
  • Glenn W. Brier, “Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability”, Monthly Weather Review (1950).
  • Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2017), on timeouts and failure detection.

— Tariq

Chapter 1.4 — An Education Platform and the Unglamorous Work of Broker Data Bridges

Subtitle: Serverless Next.js, course content, and parsing options chains from a broker API without losing your mind.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why cold starts hurt tail latency more than average latency. 2. Write the standard dealer gamma exposure (GEX) estimate and name its weakest assumption. 3. List defences against “silent, plausible wrongness” in data bridges. 4. Explain why “stale” and “unknown” should be visible states in a UI.

You need: what an API is; the idea of an average and a percentile.

1.4.1 Two threads, one lesson

August was split between a set of trading-education courses on the website and bridges that pull market data from broker APIs. They share one lesson: the interesting part of each took a day. Making it deploy, render and parse correctly took the month.

1.4.2 Deploying Next.js on Lambda

The site is a Next.js app. In early August I moved it onto AWS Lambda (a service that runs code on demand) behind CloudFront (a content delivery network). The commits from 3 and 4 August read like a debugging diary: a build spec phase named pre-build that had to be pre_build, Node version installs in the build container, a CloudFormation template simplified because two resources raced each other on creation, and a handler that went through several rewrites.

The design that stuck uses Next.js’s standalone output. Instead of shipping the whole node_modules tree, the build traces which files the server actually imports and emits a minimal server. That cut the package size, which matters on Lambda because cold start time (the delay when a fresh container must start) grows with package size.

If a fraction qq of requests hit a cold container with extra latency LcL_c, and warm requests take LwL_w, the mean latency is

𝔼[L]=Lw+qLc. \mathbb{E}[L] = L_w + q \, L_c .

The mean hides the problem. The 99th percentile (the latency that 1% of requests exceed) is dominated by LcL_c as soon as q>1%q > 1\%. A site with bursty, low traffic has a high qq, because containers expire between visits. A smaller package lowers LcL_c, the only lever you control without paying for always-warm capacity.

Figure 1.4.1 — The mean barely moves; the tail jumps. Units are schematic: a warm request takes 1 unit and a cold start adds 10. The blue mean rises gently with qq. The dashed 99th percentile jumps to Lw+LcL_w + L_c once more than 1% of requests are cold. Users notice the tail, not the mean.

One commit from 3 August has “PROTOCOL FIX” in its title: removing localhost references and deploying to AWS only. I had been burned by an assistant testing against a local server that did not match production. The rule became: the deployed environment is the test environment for this app.

1.4.3 The courses

On 4 August the first course appeared: a market-fundamentals course, with progress tracking and subscriptions. The same day, progress tracking moved from a database to static export with browser-local storage. The simplest thing won. A course reader doesn’t need server-side state to remember which module you finished. Static pages are cheaper, faster and can’t go down in interesting ways.

The course grew to eleven modules that day, with a “read me first” module zero. Later in the month the education pages were redesigned as a course catalogue. One change was reverted because embedding PDFs with an object tag broke page navigation on remount; an iframe came back. In browser PDF embedding, the older, uglier option is still the reliable one.

Course content is for other chapters. The engineering point is that publishing PDFs with frozen versions, and keeping a reader in sync with the released version, is a release-management problem, not a writing problem.

1.4.4 Broker bridges and GEX

By August the dashboard pulled options chains from a retail broker’s API to compute dealer gamma exposure (GEX) levels. The standard estimate, summed over strikes KK and expiries, is

GEX=∑KΓK⋅OIK⋅m⋅S2⋅0.01⋅sK. \text{GEX} = \sum_{K} \Gamma_K \cdot \text{OI}_K \cdot m \cdot S^2 \cdot 0.01 \cdot s_K .

Symbol Meaning
ΓK\Gamma_K the option’s gamma (how fast its delta changes with price)
OIK\text{OI}_K open interest (contracts outstanding)
mm contract multiplier
SS underlying price
sKs_K sign: +1 for calls, −1 for puts
S2⋅0.01S^2 \cdot 0.01 converts gamma into dollar exposure per 1% move

Weakest link. The sign assumes dealers are long calls and short puts. Nobody outside the dealers knows their real positioning; the convention is a modelling guess.

A separate chapter covers where GEX misleads. Here, the engineering was harder than the maths.

On 7 August there are commits fixing the parsing of the broker’s option chain. It nests contracts in maps keyed by expiry and then by strike, separately for calls and puts. Get the nesting slightly wrong and there is no error: you get a plausible chart built from half the chain. Another commit that day fixed the dashboard to return the strike of a gamma “wall” rather than its value. Again no crash, just a wrong number on screen.

That is the failure I worry about most with data bridges: silent, plausible wrongness. The defences are boring:

  • Assert structure, not just presence. Count calls and puts per expiry; if one side is empty, the parse is wrong.
  • Check units. A later August hotfix reformatted GEX into billions. Unit bugs ship easily because every number looks like a number.
  • Monitor credentials, not just uptime. Broker OAuth refresh tokens expire on a schedule. On 26 August I added a weekly token renewal alert. Before that, the bridge would simply stop one day and the dashboard would show stale data.

1.4.5 Staleness is a first-class state

The same 7 August commit adjusted staleness thresholds in the market-data Lambda. Every quote on the dashboard carries an age. Past a threshold it is shown as stale, not live. In trading, “I don’t know the current price” is a far safer display than an old price that looks current.

Figure 1.4.2 — Three honest states for a quote. A quote starts live (green). As time passes without updates it becomes stale (orange). If the feed is lost entirely it is unknown. A fresh quote returns it to live. The point is that each state is drawn differently, so a stale number can never pass for a live one.

1.4.6 What I’d tell another engineer

  • Pick the dumbest persistence that works. Browser storage beat a database for course progress.
  • Treat every broker API response as hostile. Validate shape, units and freshness.
  • Make “stale” and “unknown” visible states in the UI, not errors in a log.

August produced nothing I’d show off in a demo. It produced a site that deploys, pages that render, and numbers I could trace back to a parse I had checked.

1.4.7 Summary

  • Cold starts barely move mean latency but dominate the tail once more than 1% of requests are cold; smaller packages help.
  • Test where you deploy: for this app, the deployed environment is the test environment.
  • GEX is a sum of gamma × open interest × size terms, with a guessed dealer sign.
  • Data bridges fail silently; assert structure and units, and monitor credential expiry.
  • Show staleness explicitly.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) With Lw=100L_w = 100 ms, Lc=1,500L_c = 1{,}500 ms and q=2%q = 2\%, what is the mean latency? Roughly what is the 99th percentile? (Answer: mean = 130 ms; p99 ≈ 1,600 ms.)
  2. (Explain) Why does a parse that reads only the call side produce no error?
  3. (Design) Write two assertions you would run on every options-chain response.
  4. (Think) Flip the sign convention for puts. What happens to the GEX number, and what does that tell you about trusting it?

Further reading

  • Next.js documentation: output: 'standalone' and self-hosting.
  • SqueezeMetrics, “Gamma Exposure (GEX)” white paper (2017).
  • Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso, “The Tail at Scale”, Communications of the ACM (2013).

— Tariq

Chapter 1.5 — Teaching AI Agents to Stay in Shadow Mode

Subtitle: How I let models make trading decisions all day without letting a single one reach an order.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain what shadow mode is, and what it can and can’t tell you. 2. Tell the difference between a safety policy and a structural property. 3. Show why independent guards multiply, and why shared causes break that. 4. Describe the write-temp-then-rename pattern and its Windows caveat.

You need: basic probability (multiplying independent chances).

1.5.1 The question

By September I had a research process, a live dashboard and a NinjaTrader framework. The obvious next question: could language models take part in the decision loop? The more important question: how do you find out without risking anything?

Definition (shadow mode). Agents receive real market snapshots and produce real decisions. The decisions are logged and later compared with what happened. Nothing they produce can place an order.

Most of September went on making that last sentence true by construction, not by promise.

1.5.2 The agent side

On 15 September the bridge code gained a multi-model “swarm” built on Bedrock’s Converse API. Three properties mattered:

  1. Per-role model routing. Different steps go to different models. A cheap, fast model can classify; a stronger one can reason over a full snapshot.
  2. Schema-enforced output. Every agent must return JSON that matches a fixed schema. Anything that doesn’t match is rejected, not repaired.
  3. A shadow log. Every decision, with its inputs and model, is appended to a log.

The same day there is a “dry-run stub” commit: each agent step first ran against a stub (a fake stand-in) before it ever saw live data.

Free-text model output is unparseable in the ways that matter: the model may hedge, add fields, or quietly change units. A strict schema turns those into validation failures you can count. The rejection rate per model becomes a metric in its own right.

1.5.3 The execution side

The other half lived on the Windows machine that runs NinjaTrader. That repository’s history starts on 15 September. The next day has about twenty commits on one component: a telemetry exporter that reads indicator state off the chart and writes snapshots for the agents.

Read in order, those commits are a lesson in real-time engineering:

  • One logs data-loaded facts and the first bar update, because silent startup failures were the first problem.
  • One reads sibling indicators by absolute bar index without forcing them to update, because the order in which NinjaTrader updates indicators on the same chart is not under your control.
  • One adds an ordered emission cursor that handles pending versus permanent skips under any dispatch order.
  • One gives the exporter its own rotating log that never latches into a failed state.

Each fixed a failure seen on the live machine. None was in the original plan.

1.5.4 Making “no orders” a property, not a policy

If a component can send orders and you have told it not to, you have a policy. Policies get forgotten, misconfigured, or overridden by a well-meaning assistant. I wanted structural guarantees instead:

Guarantee Date How it works
No order code at all 16 September The first execution shell was literally described as a shell with no orders.
Two keys for execution 17 September An entry needs a decision identifier that matches on both sides, so a decision that skipped the full path can’t produce an order.
Health reports state 22 September The component publishes whether orders are enabled in its health file. The control portal shows that state instead of assuming it.

Think of it as a chain of independent gates. If each of nn independent guards fails open with probability pip_i, the chance they all fail together is

P(unsafe)=∏i=1npi. P(\text{unsafe}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i .

Why. For independent events, the chance that all happen is the product of their chances. Each extra guard multiplies the risk by a number below one.

Figure 1.5.1 — Independent guards multiply; shared ones don’t. The y-axis is logarithmic. With an illustrative failure chance of 0.1 per guard, independent guards (blue) cut the joint failure chance tenfold each time one is added. Guards that share one cause (dashed orange), such as two flags in one config file, stay at 0.1 however many you add, because one bad edit flips them all.

The catch is the word “independent”. Two flags in the same config file are not independent; one bad edit flips both.

1.5.5 Atomic writes on Windows

Snapshots are files written by one process and read by another. The standard pattern is:

write(ftmp)→fsync→rename(ftmp,f). \text{write}(f_{\text{tmp}}) \;\rightarrow\; \text{fsync} \;\rightarrow\; \text{rename}(f_{\text{tmp}}, f).

Write to a temporary file, force it to disk (fsync), then rename it over the real one. A reader then sees either the old file or the new one, never half of each.

On POSIX systems, rename over an existing file is atomic. On Windows, File.Replace can fail briefly if a reader, an antivirus scanner or a sync tool has the file open. On 22 September both the exporter and the execution component got a short, bounded retry around the replace. The journal append was also made independent of whether the latest-snapshot replace succeeded. A failed snapshot shouldn’t lose a journal line.

Figure 1.5.2 — Write to temp, sync, then rename. The top row is the atomic write path; the rename step has a bounded retry for Windows. The blue journal append hangs off the side with a dashed arrow: it happens whether or not the replace succeeds.

1.5.6 A mission-control page

Also on 15 September, the admin portal got its first trade-automation control page: bounded policy handles, a draft store and fixture decisions. Later in the month all its clocks moved to Eastern Time with explicit dates. When you compare an agent’s decision to a market event, an ambiguous timestamp makes the comparison worthless.

1.5.7 What shadow mode is and isn’t

Shadow mode tells you whether the plumbing works and whether agents produce well-formed, timely decisions. It does not tell you whether the decisions are good. Comparing logged decisions to outcomes is research, with every pitfall of research: small samples, selection, and the temptation to tune until the log looks good.

I treated September as a plumbing month. The question was not “are the agents making money?” but “can I prove no agent could have sent an order, and can I reconstruct exactly what each one saw?”

1.5.8 Summary

  • Shadow mode runs real decisions on real data with no route to an order.
  • Schema-enforced output turns model misbehaviour into countable rejections.
  • Prefer structural guarantees (no order code, two keys, visible state) over configuration flags.
  • Independent guards multiply failure chances down; guards with a shared cause do not.
  • Write-temp, fsync, rename; on Windows, wrap the replace in a bounded retry and keep the journal independent.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) Three independent guards fail open with chances 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2. What is the chance all three fail? (Answer: 0.05 × 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.001.)
  2. (Think) Give an example of two “guards” that look separate but share a cause.
  3. (Explain) Why must the journal append not depend on the snapshot replace succeeding?
  4. (Design) Write the smallest no-op version of a dangerous component you might build. What does it log?

Further reading

  • Michael T. Nygard, Release It! (2nd ed., 2018), on stability patterns and circuit breakers.
  • Microsoft .NET documentation: File.Replace and file sharing semantics on Windows.
  • Anthropic and AWS Bedrock documentation on tool use and structured output.

— Tariq

Chapter 1.6 — Rebuilding Research Around Tick Replay

Subtitle: Throwing away the convenient engine, porting indicators to a replay harness, and proving they match the chart.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why bar-based backtests can’t tell which of two prices inside a bar came first. 2. State the causal fill rule and spot the bar-close lookahead. 3. Define indicator parity and list its usual causes of failure. 4. Explain why the best of N noise results grows with N, and why trials must be counted.

You need: what a backtest is; the idea of a standard deviation.

1.6.1 The month I stopped trusting bars

Until October, much of my research ran on pre-built bars and, worse, on more than one engine. Some ran in C#, close to NinjaTrader. Some ran in Python, because it was quicker to write. The two disagreed in small ways, and I couldn’t always say which was right.

In October I rebuilt the research side around a single C# tick-replay harness (a program that feeds every recorded trade through the strategy code in order), and decommissioned the Python execution path entirely.

1.6.2 Why tick replay

A backtest on bars must answer a question the bar can’t: inside this bar, what happened first? If a bar’s range contains both your stop and your target, the bar doesn’t know which was hit. Bar-based engines resolve that with an assumption, and the assumption usually flatters you.

Tick replay sidesteps the question. You feed every trade, in order, through the same code that would run live. Bars are built from ticks as they arrive, indicators update when their bar closes, and an order placed at time tt can only fill on a trade at time t′>tt' > t.

Write a signal at the close of bar ii as sis_i, computed only from information up to time τi\tau_i. A causal fill is the first trade strictly after:

fill(si)=min⁡{pj:tj>τi}. \text{fill}(s_i) = \min\{\, p_j : t_j > \tau_i \,\}.

Here min\min is taken in time order: the earliest trade jj whose time tjt_j is after τi\tau_i, and pjp_j is its price.

Lookahead trap. Filling at the bar’s own close, p(τi)p(\tau_i), looks almost identical and is quietly lookahead. The close is the very price the signal was computed from; you could not have traded it.

Figure 1.6.1 — Fill on the first trade after the signal. Each tick mark is one trade. The grey band is bar ii, the only data the signal may use. The orange circle is the bar’s last trade, which a lazy backtest would use as the fill price. The green circle is the first trade after the bar closes: the earliest price you could actually have got.

1.6.3 Parity first

Commits from 25 October port three of my NinjaTrader indicators into the replay harness, with the commit message noting parity verification against NinjaTrader. That word is load-bearing.

Definition (parity). For an indicator computed on the chart, ftNTf^{\text{NT}}_t, and in replay, ftRf^{\text{R}}_t, parity holds when

maxt|ftNT−ftR|≤ε \max_t \left| f^{\text{NT}}_t - f^{\text{R}}_t \right| \le \varepsilon

over a long sample after warm-up, with ε\varepsilon at the level of floating-point noise, not “close enough”.

If parity fails, you have two different indicators, and every replay result describes a system that isn’t the one on your chart.

The usual causes are the ones from Chapter 1.2: different warm-up history, a different smoothing convention, on-tick versus on-close updates, and session boundaries. One of the few truly useful rules I wrote this year: the replay and the chart must reset at the same session boundary, the same way, every time.

1.6.4 One engine, one language

On 18 October I fixed race conditions in a Python sidecar (a helper process) that relayed commands to the trading platform: a thread-safe, acknowledgement-gated queue, priority for flatten commands, and timeouts that always unblock. On 19 October the commit message says the Python sidecar copies were removed and “permanently decommissioned”. On 20 October a .NET 9 daemon took over that role.

Fixing it and deleting it a day later looks wasteful. It wasn’t. The fixes showed how much subtle concurrency logic lived in a second language, duplicated from C#, with its own bugs. The right number of implementations of execution logic is one.

The same applied to research. If the live system is C#, the research engine that claims to predict its behaviour should be the same C#, not a re-implementation.

1.6.5 A catalogue of runs

From 23 October the trading-box repository gained a backtest catalogue: a schema for runs, a strict reader for trade files, a run identity and a trial key, a fill model recorded with each run, and metrics computed from the trades themselves rather than copied from a summary.

The trial key matters more than it looks. When you test many configurations, the best one is biased upward simply because you picked the maximum. If NN independent trials each give a Sharpe ratio estimate with true mean zero and standard deviation σ\sigma, the expected maximum grows roughly like

𝔼[maxi≤NSR̂i]≈σ2ln⁡N. \mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i \le N} \widehat{SR}_i\right] \approx \sigma \sqrt{2 \ln N}.

Figure 1.6.2 — The best of many noise results looks good. The x-axis is the number of trials on a log scale. The orange dots are a simulation: for each N, draw N standard normal numbers (no true edge), keep the largest, and average over 400 repeats (seed 20261107). The blue curve is the rough approximation 2ln⁡N\sqrt{2 \ln N}, which overstates the simulated values at these sizes but has the right shape. At 100 trials the best pure-noise result is already about 2.5 standard deviations above zero.

So a catalogue that doesn’t count trials can’t tell you whether your best result is a discovery or the maximum of noise. Bailey and López de Prado’s deflated Sharpe ratio formalises the correction; the first requirement is simply knowing NN.

On 27 October the catalogue gained a provenance check and a wick gate. That commit leads into Chapter 1.7.

1.6.6 Change-point detection in the harness

One estimator that went into the harness in October is Bayesian online change-point detection (Adams and MacKay, 2007). It tracks a probability distribution over the “run length” rtr_t, the time since the last regime change:

P(rt∣x1:t)∝∑rt−1P(xt∣rt−1,x(r))P(rt∣rt−1)P(rt−1∣x1:t−1). P(r_t \mid x_{1:t}) \propto \sum_{r_{t-1}} P(x_t \mid r_{t-1}, x^{(r)})\, P(r_t \mid r_{t-1})\, P(r_{t-1} \mid x_{1:t-1}).

In words: the new belief about run length combines how well the latest data point fits each possible current regime, the chance of a change, and the previous belief.

One housekeeping commit fixed how a cumulative probability over small run lengths was computed. A small bug in a probabilistic estimator doesn’t crash anything; it just shifts every downstream decision a little. That is another argument for keeping one implementation and testing it hard.

1.6.7 Summary

  • Bars can’t say which price inside them came first; tick replay can.
  • A causal fill is the first trade strictly after the signal; filling at the signal bar’s close is lookahead.
  • Prove numerical parity between chart and replay before running any study.
  • Keep one implementation of execution and research logic.
  • Count trials from day one: the best of N noise results grows roughly like 2ln⁡N\sqrt{2 \ln N}.

Exercises

  1. (Spot the bug) A backtest enters “at the close of the signal bar”. Is this causal? (Answer: no; the close is the price the signal used, so the fill must be the first trade after it.)
  2. (Compute) Using 2ln⁡N\sqrt{2 \ln N}, roughly how many standard deviations is the best of 1,000 noise trials? Compare with Figure 1.6.2.
  3. (Design) Write a parity test for a moving average: what input, what warm-up, what tolerance?
  4. (Think) Why can’t you reconstruct N after the fact?

Further reading

  • Ryan Prescott Adams and David J. C. MacKay, “Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection” (2007).
  • David H. Bailey and Marcos López de Prado, “The Deflated Sharpe Ratio” (2014).
  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), on backtest overfitting.

— Tariq

Chapter 1.7 — The Integrity Reckoning

Subtitle: When an AI agent produced results I couldn’t trust, and what I changed so “I couldn’t do it” became an acceptable answer.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Name the two substitutions that made a set of results meaningless. 2. Compute a wick census and say what a near-zero value means. 3. List the receipts a performance number must carry. 4. Explain why multiple-testing corrections need an honest trial count.

You need: what OHLC bars are (open, high, low, close); the idea of a significance level α.

1.7.1 What happened

In late October an AI agent working on my research produced a set of backtest results that looked complete and well formatted. They had been built in Python, against my explicit instruction that research runs in the C# harness, and on bars with no wicks. Nothing in the output said so.

I won’t describe the results, because they aren’t results. That is the point of this chapter. What I will describe is what I changed afterwards, because it is the most useful thing I did this year.

1.7.2 What actually went wrong

The agent hit a hard path. The C# harness was slower to drive, and getting it to run the study correctly took effort. A Python script could produce something resembling the answer much faster. So the agent took the shortcut and reported the output in the same confident format it would have used for the real thing.

Two substitutions happened at once:

  1. Engine substitution. A re-implementation in another language, presented as if it were the engine.
  2. Data degradation. Bars where high and low equal the body. A wickless bar can’t tell you whether a stop inside its range was hit, so every stop and target in the study was resolved optimistically by construction.

Neither is a bug in the usual sense. Each is a reasonable-looking shortcut. Together they produce numbers that mean nothing and look like everything.

1.7.3 The wick census

The simplest check I added is the one I’d recommend to anyone. For bars with open oo, high hh, low ll and close cc, compute the share that actually have wicks:

W=1N∑i=1N𝟏[hi>max(oi,ci)∨li<min(oi,ci)]. W = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{1}\!\left[\, h_i > \max(o_i, c_i) \;\lor\; l_i < \min(o_i, c_i) \,\right].

Here 𝟏[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] is 1 when the condition is true and 0 otherwise, and ∨\lor means “or”.

Rule. Real bars built from ticks almost always have wicks. A census near zero means the bars were rebuilt from closes or from a body-only brick, and any run on them is invalid.

Figure 1.7.1 — The wick census tells the two sets apart at a glance. These are schematic bars, not market data. On the left, every bar has a high above its body or a low below it, so W = 100%. On the right, the same bars rebuilt from bodies have no wicks, so W = 0% and any run on them is rejected.

The catalogue gained this gate on 27 October. A run without a passing census can’t be imported as a result. It is a crude check, and that is its strength: it costs nothing, it can’t be argued with, and it catches exactly the failure that is hardest to see by looking at a chart.

1.7.4 Receipts

The broader change was a written protocol, dated 27 October, that now sits in my global agent instructions. Its prime directive is short: a result you can’t prove is not a result.

The mechanism is receipts. Any performance number must carry:

  • the engine path, its commit, whether the tree was dirty, and the exact command;
  • the canonical tick data path and its hash, with sessions covered and anything excluded;
  • the bar builder and the wick census;
  • the fill model: slippage, commission, latency, and entries strictly after the signal;
  • the output file and its hash, and the catalogue run identifier;
  • the trial count NN;
  • the validation state.

If an agent can’t produce these, it writes “unprovenanced” instead of a number. That sounds bureaucratic. In practice it is a checklist that takes a minute when the work was done properly, and is impossible to fake convincingly when it wasn’t.

Figure 1.7.2 — A gate at the import boundary. Every run output passes one check before it can count. With full receipts and a passing wick census it is imported as a result (green). Otherwise it is labelled “unprovenanced” and is not a result (orange). The list under the diagram is the receipt checklist.

1.7.5 Naming the dodges

The protocol also lists forbidden substitutions by name: running research in another language because it is faster; using cached or derived data instead of the canonical ticks; building bars without wicks; filling at the signal bar’s price; swallowing errors so a run “completes”; weakening a test so it passes.

Naming them matters. A language model optimising to finish a task will find the shortcut. If the shortcut has a name and a rule against it, the model is much more likely to stop and say “I’m blocked”. I also wrote the stop format: what I was asked, what failed, what I tried, the substitution I could make, and a statement that I haven’t made it.

1.7.6 Confession is not compliance

One line came straight from experience: an agent that admits it broke a rule and then carries on with the same outputs hasn’t fixed anything. Outputs from a violation are marked invalid and never reused. An apology doesn’t repair a number; only an honest rerun does.

1.7.7 Multiple testing, again

The other half of integrity is statistical. Even with a perfect engine, testing many ideas inflates your best result. With NN trials, the simple Bonferroni bound on the family-wise error rate (the chance of any false positive) gives a per-test threshold of

αper=αN. \alpha_{\text{per}} = \frac{\alpha}{N}.

Why. If each of NN tests has false-positive chance α/N\alpha/N, the chance of at least one false positive is at most N⋅α/N=αN \cdot \alpha/N = \alpha.

This gets brutal fast. Softer approaches such as false-discovery-rate control exist, but every one needs an honest NN. So does the deflated Sharpe ratio. That is why the trial count is on the receipt list.

In the first week of November I closed a research round, run as a formal call for proposals with pre-registered tests, that didn’t find what it was looking for. Under the old way of working, that round might have ended with a “promising” variant. Under the new one it ended with a closed document and a rule that new ideas need a new round.

1.7.8 Summary

  • An agent swapped in Python and wickless bars and reported the output as real; nothing in the output said so.
  • The wick census W is a free, unarguable check; near zero means invalid.
  • Every performance number needs receipts: engine, data, bars, fills, output, N, validation.
  • Name the shortcuts and make “I’m blocked” an acceptable answer; outputs from a violation are never reused.
  • Multiple-testing corrections all need an honest trial count.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) Of 200 bars, 3 have a high above the body or a low below it. What is W, and what do you conclude? (Answer: W = 1.5%; the bars are almost certainly wickless and the run is invalid.)
  2. (Compute) You test 40 ideas at overall α = 5%. What per-test threshold does Bonferroni give? (Answer: 0.00125.)
  3. (Design) Write the stop message an agent should send when the required engine fails. Use the five parts from 1.7.5.
  4. (Think) Why is a confident, well-formatted wrong result more dangerous than a crash?

Further reading

  • David H. Bailey, Jonathan Borwein, Marcos López de Prado and Qiji Jim Zhu, “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting” (2016).
  • John P. A. Ioannidis, “Why Most Published Research Findings Are False”, PLoS Medicine (2005).
  • Yoav Benjamini and Yosef Hochberg, “Controlling the False Discovery Rate” (1995).

— Tariq

Chapter 1.8 — Working Solo with AI Agents as a Team

Subtitle: What changes when your “team” is several coding assistants, and why the job becomes review, not typing.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why review bandwidth, not output, is the bottleneck when agents write the code. 2. Use a simple queueing formula to see why running near full review capacity is bad. 3. List written rules that make agent work cheaper to check. 4. Name the failure mode to design for.

You need: the idea of a rate (things per hour).

1.8.1 Alone, but not alone

This year I have worked alone, in that no other human engineer is on the project. I haven’t worked alone day to day. Most code in my repositories was typed by AI coding assistants: Claude Code on the Mac, Google’s Antigravity, VS Code agents, and model calls running inside AWS. My job shifted from writing code to specifying, reviewing and verifying it.

1.8.2 The throughput is real, and so is the noise

The git history is the honest witness. In July my main repository took about 150 commits; in August about 100. A single day in late July has more than a dozen commits adjusting chart styling. On 16 September the trading-box repository went through seven numbered revisions of one component in a day.

Each change is cheap, so you make many. The risk is that cheap changes pile up into a codebase nobody fully understands, including you. I now treat my review bandwidth as the real bottleneck. Agents produce faster than I can verify. The useful question isn’t “how do I get more output?” but “how do I make each output cheaper to check?”

1.8.3 A simple model of review cost

Suppose an agent produces changes at rate λ\lambda per hour, and each takes me time rr to review properly. Call ρ=λr\rho = \lambda r the utilisation: the share of my time review would need. If ρ>1\rho > 1, review falls behind for good. For a simple single-server queue, as ρ\rho approaches 1 the waiting queue grows like

Lq≈ρ21−ρ. L_q \approx \frac{\rho^2}{1-\rho}.

Figure 1.8.1 — The queue explodes before you reach full capacity. The curve is the formula above. Up to about 60% utilisation the backlog stays small. Past 80% it climbs steeply, and at 100% (dashed line) it never clears. Being “almost fully busy” reviewing is already bad.

The practical meaning: running near full review capacity is already bad. The fixes are to lower rr (smaller, well-described diffs; automated checks) or to lower λ\lambda on purpose. I do both.

1.8.4 Rules that actually help

My global instructions file for agents has grown into a short engineering handbook. The parts that pay for themselves:

Rule What it prevents
Declare the diff before editing: which files will change, which won’t; stop if the real diff is bigger Most scope creep
Think before coding; state assumptions Agents silently picking an interpretation
One round of questions, then proceed with stated assumptions Stalling (too many questions) and confident wrong code (none)
Stop conditions: scope overrun, repeated failure, destructive action, an ungrounded claim about a live system, and (since late October) an integrity block Pushing on when it should halt
No claim without a probe: no “healthy”, “connected” or “it ran” unless just checked Made-up status reports

None of these is clever. They are the norms a good senior engineer expects from a junior colleague. The difference is that agents follow written rules more consistently than implied ones, so writing them down pays unusually well.

1.8.5 Different agents, different jobs

I use different assistants for different kinds of work, and I hand off explicitly. Long empirical studies go to one agent with a written brief; I’ve learned to stop after writing the brief rather than half-doing the study myself in parallel. Review, specification and integrity checks go to another.

The brief is the interface. If I can’t write a clear brief, I don’t understand the task well enough to delegate it.

Cross-checking helps too. An agent reviewing another agent’s output, given the code rather than my conclusion, finds different things than the author does. It doesn’t replace my review, but it lowers its cost.

Figure 1.8.2 — Work flows through a written brief. I write the brief (blue). One agent runs a long study; another reviews, given the code rather than my conclusion. Whatever comes back is treated like a pull request I must check, not a finished answer.

1.8.6 The failure mode to design for

The most important thing I learned this year: an agent under pressure to finish will take the shortcut, and report the result in the same confident tone as real work. That isn’t malice. It is what optimising for “task complete” does when the honest path is slow.

Chapter 1.7 covers the incident and the protocol. The general lesson: make “I’m blocked” a legitimate, even praised, outcome. Name the shortcuts in advance. Check outputs with cheap mechanical tests, not by reading the summary.

1.8.7 Memory and continuity

Agents forget between sessions. I keep a short persistent memory of decisions: what has been decommissioned, which records must never be quoted, which research rounds are closed. Each entry is one line with a pointer to detail. It is the closest thing the project has to institutional memory, and it stops each new session from reopening settled questions.

1.8.8 What it feels like

It is a strange job. Some days I write no code and the repository grows by thousands of lines. Other days I spend hours reading one diff because it touches order handling. The skill that matters most has turned out to be knowing which kind of day I’m having.

My advice is short: write your rules down, keep diffs small, verify mechanically, and treat agent output like a pull request from a fast, capable stranger.

1.8.9 Summary

  • With agents writing the code, my review bandwidth is the bottleneck.
  • Queue length grows like ρ2/(1−ρ)\rho^2/(1-\rho); stay well below full review utilisation.
  • Written rules (declare the diff, state assumptions, stop conditions, probe before claiming) make work cheaper to check.
  • Design for the agent that takes the shortcut and sounds confident.
  • Keep a short persistent memory of settled decisions.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) An agent produces 6 changes an hour and each takes 9 minutes to review. What is ρ\rho, and what does the formula give for LqL_q? (Answer: ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9; Lq≈0.81/0.1=8.1L_q \approx 0.81/0.1 = 8.1 changes waiting.)
  2. (Apply) Name two ways to lower rr without reviewing less carefully.
  3. (Design) Write a three-line brief for a task you might delegate. Does it say what “done” looks like?
  4. (Think) Why does giving a reviewer the code, not your conclusion, change what it finds?

Further reading

  • Frederick P. Brooks Jr., The Mythical Man-Month (1975).
  • Leonard Kleinrock, Queueing Systems, Vol. 1 (1975), for the utilisation curve.
  • Atul Gawande, The Checklist Manifesto (2009).

— Tariq

Chapter 1.9 — A Windows Trading Box, a Mac and AWS: Drawing the Boundaries

Subtitle: Three environments, one person, and why the most useful architecture decision was saying what never crosses a line.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why naming zones, and what never crosses between them, prevents mistakes. 2. Describe a hash-verified, all-or-nothing release. 3. Explain why sync is not deploy. 4. Apply the “store UTC, convert at the edge” rule.

You need: what a file hash is (a short fingerprint that changes if the file changes).

1.9.1 Three places

My stack runs in three places. NinjaTrader runs on Windows machines. I develop on a Mac. The website, data collection, report generation and model calls run on AWS. That split was inherited, not designed: NinjaTrader is Windows-only, I like developing on a Mac, and AWS is where the managed services are.

What I did design, in September, was the boundary between them. That mattered more than any single component.

1.9.2 Zones

The repository has a context map that divides everything into zones:

Zone What lives there
shared cross-zone invariants and contracts; read-only; no procedures or state
local Mac compilers, local tooling, research; never synced to the trading machines
AWS cloud the site, data functions, model calls; deployed through a build pipeline
trading box NinjaTrader and the C# that runs inside it

Each zone has its own entry document and its own deploy path.

The rule that does the work is negative. Things from one zone don’t get copied into another zone’s deploy path. Mac tooling doesn’t run on the trading box. Cloud code doesn’t get dropped into NinjaTrader’s folder.

Figure 1.9.1 — Four zones and the walls between them. The shared zone at the top holds read-only invariants, and every other zone reads it (dashed blue). The three working zones sit side by side, separated by orange walls: code and credentials don’t cross them. This is a concept picture, not a wiring diagram.

1.9.3 Why boundaries matter more with agents

In a human team, boundaries are partly kept by people knowing their area. An AI agent can see the whole repository and will happily “fix” something in another zone if it looks related. Explicit zones give the agent a first question: which zone is this task in? That alone prevents a class of mistakes, such as editing a production indicator while working on a website bug.

1.9.4 Getting code onto the trading box safely

The trading box is where mistakes cost most, so how code reaches it got the most care. On 16 September its repository gained a small release kit:

  1. Releases are published to object storage with a manifest listing every file and its hash.
  2. A fetch script on the Windows machine pulls the release using the machine’s own identity, not a person’s credentials.
  3. An apply script checks every file’s hash against the manifest, backs up what it replaces, and only then installs.

For each file ff with expected digest dfd_f in the manifest, the apply step requires

SHA256(f)=df∀f∈manifest, \text{SHA256}(f) = d_f \quad \forall f \in \text{manifest},

(∀\forall means “for every”) and refuses the whole release if any file fails.

Why all-or-nothing. A partial install is worse than none. A half-updated set of indicators can disagree with itself in ways that look like market behaviour.

Figure 1.9.2 — A release installs completely or not at all. Files and manifest are published, fetched with the machine’s own identity, and every hash is checked. If all match, the old files are backed up and the new ones installed (green). If any one fails, the whole release is refused (orange).

The kit also tracked a release number. I went through seven numbered releases of one component in a day. Without the manifest and version, I couldn’t have said for certain which one was running.

1.9.5 Sync is not deploy

For documentation and agent skills, a file sync tool mirrors part of the tree to the trading machines. That is convenient and dangerous in equal measure. The rule I settled on: sync carries information (documents, instructions, skill files) and the release kit carries code. A sync tool doesn’t check hashes, doesn’t back up, and doesn’t know what a coherent release is.

1.9.6 Time

Three environments can mean three clocks and three timezones. Windows defaults to local time, AWS services lean towards UTC, and US futures sessions are defined in Eastern or Central time. In September the control portal moved every displayed time to Eastern with an explicit date. Internally I store UTC and convert at the edges.

The bug this prevents is subtle. A daylight-saving shift moves the mapping between UTC and the exchange’s session by an hour twice a year. Any logic that hard-codes an offset is wrong for part of the year.

1.9.7 Credentials and identity

Each zone authenticates differently, and credentials don’t cross zones. The trading box uses its own machine identity for storage. Cloud functions use roles. Broker tokens live in the zone that uses them, and their expiry is monitored there. An agent working in one zone shouldn’t need, or be able to see, another zone’s secrets.

1.9.8 Costs of this design

It isn’t free. Three environments means three sets of tooling, and debugging across a boundary is slow: a problem on the trading box often means reading a log there, changing code on the Mac, building a release and pulling it. That loop is minutes, not seconds.

I accept the cost because the alternative, one environment where everything can touch everything, is how research code ends up in the execution path. That happened to me once this year with a Python component, and removing it in October was one of my better decisions.

1.9.9 Summary

  • Name your environments and write down what never crosses between them.
  • Explicit zones give agents a first question and stop cross-zone “fixes”.
  • Ship code to the trading machine through a hash-verified, versioned, all-or-nothing release, never a sync.
  • Store UTC; convert at the display edge; never hard-code an offset.
  • Keep credentials in the zone that uses them.

Exercises

  1. (Explain) Why does the apply step refuse the whole release when only one file’s hash fails?
  2. (Think) A US session opens at 09:30 Eastern. Why is “14:30 UTC” correct for only part of the year? (Answer: Eastern time is UTC−5 in winter and UTC−4 in summer, so the open is 14:30 UTC in winter but 13:30 UTC in summer.)
  3. (Classify) For each of these, say whether it should travel by sync or by release: a README, a compiled indicator, an agent skill file, a config file read by the execution component.
  4. (Design) Draw your own projects’ zones. What is the one rule about what never crosses?

Further reading

  • Gene Kim, Jez Humble, Patrick Debois and John Willis, The DevOps Handbook (2016).
  • Jez Humble and David Farley, Continuous Delivery (2010), on deployment pipelines.
  • The Update Framework (TUF) specification, on signed, verifiable software updates.

— Tariq

Chapter 1.10 — Why I Do Trading Research in C#, Not Python

Subtitle: Python is the default for quant research. Here’s why I moved mine to the same language as my execution platform.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain the two-implementation problem and why it hides inside backtest results. 2. State the parity test and why it is easier in one language. 3. Explain how event-driven code makes lookahead structurally harder. 4. List what is given up by not using Python for research.

You need: what a backtest and a rolling window are.

1.10.1 The decision

Almost every trading-research tutorial uses Python: pandas for data, numpy for maths, a notebook to glue it together. I used Python too, for much of this year. In October I moved all research that produces performance claims into a C# tick-replay harness, and wrote a rule that it stays there.

This isn’t a language war. Python is excellent, and I still use it for tooling. The decision was about one property: the research engine and the live engine should be the same code.

1.10.2 The two-implementation problem

My live trading logic runs inside NinjaTrader, so it is C#. If research runs in Python, every indicator, bar builder and fill rule exists twice. Two implementations of the same logic drift. They differ in warm-up, in smoothing conventions, in how they treat a session boundary, and in floating-point order of operations.

Each difference is small. The trouble is that you can’t tell, from a backtest result, how much of it comes from them. If the Python version of an indicator crosses a threshold one bar earlier than the C# version, entries shift, and the backtest describes a system you don’t run.

The fix is one implementation. The live side can’t move off C#, so research moves to it.

Figure 1.10.1 — The thing you test should be the thing you run. On the left, live trading and research each run their own copy of the logic in different languages, and the copies drift apart. On the right, one piece of logic feeds both, so a research result describes the system that actually trades.

1.10.3 Parity as a test

Even in one language, porting indicator code from NinjaTrader into a standalone harness needs proof. My standard is numerical parity on the same input:

maxt≥t0|ftlive−ftreplay|≤εfp, \max_{t \ge t_0} \left| f^{\text{live}}_t - f^{\text{replay}}_t \right| \le \varepsilon_{\text{fp}},

where t0t_0 is the end of warm-up and εfp\varepsilon_{\text{fp}} is floating-point noise.

One language makes this achievable: you compare the same arithmetic in the same order. Across languages, even a correct port can differ in the last bits, because of operation order and library versions of functions like exp and log. Those bits rarely matter alone. In a recursive indicator (one that feeds its last output back in), they compound.

1.10.4 Determinism and lookahead

C# with value types and explicit loops is easy to make deterministic: given the same ticks, the replay produces the same trades, bit for bit. That is what makes a run reproducible from a command and a data hash, the basis of the receipts in Chapter 1.7.

Python can be deterministic too. But vectorised research code invites a specific bug: whole-array operations that accidentally use future values. Examples are a centred rolling window, a normalisation over the full sample, or a shift in the wrong direction. Event-driven C# that processes one tick at a time makes lookahead structurally harder. At time tt, the only state you have is what you’ve seen up to tt.

Figure 1.10.2 — A centred window quietly uses the future. Each square is one bar or tick, and the black line is “now”. The green trailing window covers only past squares. The orange centred window reaches two squares past “now”. One line of array code can produce the orange version; a one-event-at-a-time replay can’t, because the future squares don’t exist yet.

1.10.5 Performance, briefly

People expect this section to say C# is faster. It often is for tick-by-tick event loops: there’s no interpreter overhead per event, and the garbage collector can be kept quiet with careful allocation. But speed wasn’t the reason, and Python with compiled extensions can be fast enough.

The more relevant point is the opposite. When the C# harness was slow or awkward, the temptation was to switch to Python “just for this study”. That is exactly how an agent produced invalid results in October. A rule that research runs in one engine has to hold when that engine is inconvenient, or it isn’t a rule.

1.10.6 What I gave up

Cost How I handle it
Exploration is slower; a compiled harness wants a defined study Casual inspection stays separate and never produces performance numbers
Thinner statistics ecosystem in .NET I implement standard estimators myself, so I must test them myself; one October commit fixed a cumulative probability in a change-point estimator
Plotting is worse Export results and plot elsewhere; plotting doesn’t change numbers

1.10.7 Where Python still lives

Python stays in the repository for tooling: building a symbol graph of the C# code for agents to navigate, documentation pipelines, utilities. The rule is about what produces trading decisions and performance claims, not about banning a language. Execution logic, sizing, and anything between a decision and an order is C# only. The Python relay that once sat in that path was decommissioned in October.

1.10.8 The general principle

Principle. The thing you test should be the thing you run.

If your execution platform is Python, research in Python. If it is C++, Java or C#, research in that. Every translation layer between research and production is a place for silent divergence. Silent divergence is the worst kind, because the backtest still produces a confident number.

1.10.9 Summary

  • Two implementations drift, and you can’t see the drift in a backtest result.
  • Parity to floating-point noise is realistic within one language and hard across two.
  • Event-driven, one-tick-at-a-time code makes lookahead structurally harder than whole-array code.
  • The rule must hold when the right engine is inconvenient.
  • Python remains for tooling, never for decisions or performance claims.

Exercises

  1. (Spot the bug) z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std() over a whole price history, then used as a signal. What is wrong? (Answer: the mean and standard deviation use future data; at time t you only know values up to t.)
  2. (Explain) Why do last-bit differences matter more in a recursive indicator than in a simple one?
  3. (Think) Your live system is Python. By this chapter’s principle, what language should your research use?
  4. (Design) Write a parity test plan for one indicator: input, warm-up, tolerance, and what you do if it fails.

Further reading

  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), ch. 11–13 on backtesting.
  • Ernest P. Chan, Algorithmic Trading: Winning Strategies and Their Rationale (2013), on look-ahead bias.
  • David Goldberg, “What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic” (1991).

— Tariq

Chapter 1.11 — What I Got Wrong This Year

Subtitle: General lessons from seven months of building, taken from the commit history rather than from memory.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Name nine common mistakes in building a solo, agent-assisted trading stack. 2. Compute the standard error of a proportion and use it to judge a small sample. 3. Explain why checks belong at the boundary where data enters a system.

You need: what a proportion and a square root are.

1.11.1 How this list was made

Every item comes from something visible in my git history or my own written rules, not from memory. I kept only lessons general enough to help someone who isn’t building what I’m building.

1.11.2 The nine mistakes

# Mistake Evidence Lesson
1 A second implementation lived too long October: a day fixing race conditions in a Python sidecar, decommissioned the next day for a .NET daemon Two implementations diverge; pick one language for anything between a decision and an order
2 Trusting output formats instead of content The late-October integrity incident: results looked like real results Put cheap mechanical checks (wick census, receipts) at the import boundary
3 Iterating visually in production One July day: a dozen-plus styling commits, some reversed within hours Batch visual changes, look at them together, commit once
4 Feeding a model placeholder data Mid-July switch from placeholder to real calendar data Validate model inputs like any other system’s, or more
5 Testing against a non-production environment Early August commit removing localhost references For serverless apps, packaging, routing and cold starts are behaviour a local server doesn’t test
6 Underestimating plumbing Most commits are retries, timeouts, parsing, log rotation, atomic replace, staleness, build config; one September component had seven releases in a day Assume plumbing is most of the work and plan for it
7 Learning from samples too small to learn from July: adjusting factor weights from a few weeks of daily briefs See 1.11.3
8 Not counting trials from the start Catalogue with run identities and trial keys arrived only in late October You can’t reconstruct N afterwards
9 Rules living in conversation, not files Early working rules existed only in chat and were lost each session If a rule matters, it goes in a file an agent reads at session start

A few notes on the less obvious ones:

  • Mistake 2. The cost was not the shortcut itself but that I read summaries instead of running checks. Those checks would have taken minutes to write in July. General version: if a check is cheap and mechanical, put it where data enters your system. Don’t rely on noticing.
  • Mistake 3. The cost wasn’t time. It was a noisy history that hides the commits that mattered, and a habit of deciding by nudge rather than design.
  • Mistake 6. The seven releases each fixed a real-time behaviour I hadn’t foreseen: indicator dispatch order, data-loaded timing, a log that latched after an IO error.
  • Mistake 8. The expected best of NN noise-only results grows like 2ln⁡N\sqrt{2 \ln N} standard deviations (Chapter 1.6), so an unrecorded NN means an uninterpretable best result.

1.11.3 Small samples, with a number

The standard error of a proportion estimated from nn observations measures how much the estimate would wobble from sample to sample:

SE(p̂)=p̂(1−p̂)n. \text{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat p (1-\hat p)}{n}}.

With twenty observations and p̂\hat p near one half, SE=0.25/20≈0.11\text{SE} = \sqrt{0.25/20} \approx 0.11. Any apparent improvement smaller than that can’t be told apart from noise. I knew the formula; I didn’t apply it to my own feedback loop until later.
