Figure 1.11.1 — Small samples are noisy. The curve is the standard error formula with p̂=0.5\hat p = 0.5. At n = 20 (orange dot) it is about 0.11, so a “60% hit rate” is within one standard error of a coin flip. The curve flattens slowly: halving the error needs four times the data.

1.11.4 What I got right, briefly

To be fair to myself: building shadow mode before any automation, hash-verified releases to the trading box, zoned documentation, and closing a research round that didn’t find anything rather than tuning it until it did. Those were good calls. Most were made after one of the mistakes above.

1.11.5 Summary

  • Keep one implementation of anything between a decision and an order.
  • Put cheap, mechanical checks at the boundary where data enters.
  • Validate model inputs; test where you deploy; plan for plumbing.
  • Use the standard error before trusting a small-sample improvement; count trials from day one.
  • Write rules into files agents read every session.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) A loop is right 12 times in 20. What is p̂\hat p and its standard error? Is it clearly better than 50%? (Answer: p̂=0.6\hat p = 0.6, SE ≈ 0.11; 0.6 is less than one SE above 0.5, so no.)
  2. (Compute) How many observations would you need for SE ≈ 0.05 at p̂=0.5\hat p = 0.5? (Answer: 100.)
  3. (Apply) Pick one of the nine mistakes that applies to your work. What cheap check would have caught it?
  4. (Think) Why does moving a rule from chat into a file change agent behaviour?

Further reading

  • Richard Feynman, “Cargo Cult Science”, Caltech commencement address (1974).
  • Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), on the law of small numbers.
  • Charity Majors, Liz Fong-Jones and George Miranda, Observability Engineering (2022).

— Tariq

Chapter 1.12 — How I Decide What to Build Next

Subtitle: Calls for proposals, pre-registration and kill criteria, applied by one person to their own research.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe a research round: call, pre-registration, frozen spec, run, close. 2. Compute the false-alarm chance from “forking paths”. 3. Explain why every round needs a way to end in “no”. 4. Rank engineering work by cost of delay over job size.

You need: what a significance level α is.

1.12.1 The real constraint is choosing

Working alone with fast AI assistants, the constraint isn’t how much you can build. It is choosing. An agent will start on anything you describe, so the expensive mistake is describing the wrong thing. By autumn I’d settled on a process borrowed mostly from grant funding and clinical research.

1.12.2 Write a call before writing code

For research I open a formal round with a written call for proposals. It states the question, what evidence would answer it, what data and engine must be used, and what counts as failure. Proposals, from me or from an agent asked to propose, are reviewed against the call before anything runs.

A call is a page or two. Its value is that it forces the question to be stated before anyone has seen a result, the only time a question can be stated honestly.

1.12.3 Pre-registration

The idea is from clinical trials: write down your hypothesis, test and decision rule before you look at the outcome data. My reports folder this autumn has several documents titled “pre-registration (draft)”, for things like separation and continuation censuses.

The reason is the garden of forking paths. If, after seeing data, you can choose among kk reasonable analyses, the chance that at least one shows a “significant” effect at level α\alpha under the null is roughly

1−(1−α)k. 1 - (1-\alpha)^k .

Why. Each analysis independently stays quiet with chance 1−α1-\alpha; all kk stay quiet with chance (1−α)k(1-\alpha)^k; at least one fires with the remainder. (Real analyses overlap, so this is approximate.)

Figure 1.12.1 — More choices, more false alarms. The blue curve is 1−(1−α)k1-(1-\alpha)^k with α = 5%. The dashed line is α itself, which you keep only by fixing one analysis in advance. With ten choices, the chance of a spurious “finding” is already about 40%.

Pre-registration fixes k=1k = 1, or at least makes kk visible. It is the cheapest overfitting control there is.

1.12.4 Freeze the spec

Before a sweep runs, its specification is frozen and reviewed. One of my documents is literally a “freeze review” of a sweep spec; another is the frozen spec. Changes after the freeze are a new trial and get counted as one.

Freezing also helps with agents. An agent working from a frozen spec has much less room to “improve” the study mid-run, which is where silent changes creep in.

1.12.5 Kill criteria and closing rounds

Every round needs a way to end with “no”. On 5 November I closed a research round that didn’t find what it was looking for. The note I kept says new ideas need a new round.

That rule is the important part. Without it, a failed round becomes an open-ended search: one more filter, one more variant, until something passes. Each variant raises the effective NN and lowers the meaning of whatever eventually passes. Closing the round preserves the meaning of the next one.

Figure 1.12.2 — A research round from call to close. Each step happens once, left to right. The dashed orange loop shows the one way back: a change after the freeze, which counts as a new trial. The round can close with “no”, and new ideas then start a new round.

1.12.6 Engineering work: cost of delay over effort

Engineering work gets a lighter process. I ask three questions:

  1. What breaks or stays unsafe if I don’t build this? Safety and correctness go first. In September, making “no orders” a structural property came before anything that might one day place one.
  2. What does this unblock? A hash-verified release kit unblocked every later change to the trading box. A backtest catalogue unblocked counting trials. Infrastructure that makes other work verifiable ranks high.
  3. Can I verify it when done? If I can’t describe the check that proves it works, I don’t understand it well enough to delegate it.

A rough ranking is weighted shortest job first:

priority=cost of delayjob size, \text{priority} = \frac{\text{cost of delay}}{\text{job size}},

where cost of delay is a judgement about risk and unblocking value. I don’t compute it precisely. Writing the two terms down for each candidate usually makes the order obvious.

1.12.7 What doesn’t get built

  • Anything that turns a research result into automation without the receipts. The receipts are a prerequisite, not paperwork.
  • A second implementation of anything in the execution path. Decided in October; not revisited.
  • Features driven by a single good-looking chart. A chart is a hypothesis, not evidence.

1.12.8 The role of the end state

I have a long-term picture of where the system is going, and it shapes priorities. Work that produces clean, well-labelled data about decisions and outcomes is valuable whatever happens next: it is guidance now and training material later. Work that only makes sense if some particular result holds up is speculative, and goes through a call.

1.12.9 Summary

  • Write the question down before you see any data.
  • With kk possible analyses, false alarms rise to about 1−(1−α)k1-(1-\alpha)^k; pre-registration fixes kk.
  • Freeze specs; count every change after the freeze as a trial.
  • Give every round a way to end in “no”, and mean it.
  • Rank engineering by cost of delay over size, favouring work that makes other work verifiable.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) With α = 5% and k = 5, what is the chance of at least one false alarm? (Answer: 1 − 0.95⁵ ≈ 22.6%.)
  2. (Apply) Write a one-paragraph call for a question you care about: question, evidence, data, failure condition.
  3. (Rank) Three tasks: A (cost of delay 8, size 4), B (6, 1), C (10, 10). Order them by WSJF.
  4. (Think) Why does “one more variant” after a failed round lower the meaning of any later success?

Further reading

  • Brian A. Nosek et al., “The preregistration revolution”, PNAS (2018).
  • Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken, “The garden of forking paths” (2013).
  • Donald G. Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009), on cost of delay.

— Tariq

Chapter 1.13 — Documentation as an Engineering Tool

Subtitle: Zoned docs, front matter, specs and invariants: writing that AI agents actually read and that keeps a one-person system coherent.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why documentation becomes part of the control system when agents do the work. 2. Describe tiered documentation and useful front-matter fields. 3. Tell invariants from procedures, and say why they must be kept apart. 4. List the three properties of a good spec for agent work.

You need: no special background.

1.13.1 From courtesy to control

I used to think of documentation as something written after the code, for someone else. This year it became something written before the code, mostly for machines. With several AI agents working in one repository, documentation became part of the control system.

1.13.2 Agents read what you give them

An AI coding assistant starts every session knowing nothing about your project except what it can find. If the first thing it finds is a sprawling README, it guesses. If it finds a short routing document that says “declare your zone, then read this one file”, it follows that path.

So in September I restructured the documentation around a master context map: a single entry point with a table of zones (shared invariants, local Mac, AWS cloud, the trading box) and, for each, the runtime environment, the sync or deploy boundary, and the one document to read next.

1.13.3 Front matter that does work

Each document carries a small block of metadata (front matter) at the top: an identifier, a title, a one-line intent, a kind (for example invariant, contract or procedure), the zone, a tier, its inputs and outputs, who consumes it, a confidence state, when it was last verified and by whom, and a token budget.

Two fields deserve a note.

  • Confidence and last-verified. Documentation rots. A field saying when a document was last checked against reality lets an agent (or me) weigh it. A document last verified months ago about a component that has since changed is a hint, not a fact.
  • Token budget. Agents have a finite context window. A budget per document forces top-level documents to stay short and pushes detail down a tier. A document’s cost to an agent is roughly linear in its length; its usefulness usually isn’t:

value per token=V(doc)|doc|. \text{value per token} = \frac{V(\text{doc})}{|\text{doc}|}.

For routing documents, VV saturates quickly. The first paragraph that says where to go next is worth more than the next ten pages.

1.13.4 Tiers

Level 0 is the master map. Level 1 is one map per zone. Below that sit the specifications and procedures. An agent reads top-down and stops as soon as it has what it needs. This is progressive disclosure, a standard interface-design idea, applied to a reader with a context window instead of a screen.

Figure 1.13.1 — Read from the top, stop early. The blue Level 0 map points to one Level 1 map per zone. Each zone map points into the detailed documents at Level 2. An agent follows the arrows only as far as its task needs, so most sessions read a few short pages, not the whole tree.

1.13.5 Invariants versus procedures

Definitions. An invariant is something that must always be true: execution logic is C# only; results need receipts; closed research rounds stay closed. A procedure is how to do something: build a release, run a study, deploy the site.

Invariants live in the shared zone, are read-only to every other zone, and contain no steps. Procedures live in their own zone and change often.

Mixing them causes trouble. If an invariant is buried in step seven of a procedure, an agent editing that procedure can delete it without noticing. Putting invariants in their own documents, with their own kind, makes them hard to remove by accident.

Figure 1.13.2 — Keep invariants out of procedures. The blue box holds rules that must always be true; the grey box holds steps that change often. A procedure may point to an invariant (dashed arrow), but never contains it, so editing the steps can’t silently delete the rule.

1.13.6 Specs before code

For larger work, I write a specification first and have it reviewed (by me, often also by a second agent) before implementation. In late October several commits in the trading-box repository publish architecture specifications alongside the code they describe.

A good spec for agent work has three properties:

  1. it states what done looks like;
  2. it names what is out of scope;
  3. it says how the result will be verified.

The last is the one people skip. If a spec can’t say how you’ll check it, the agent will decide for itself what “working” means.

1.13.7 Generated documentation for code navigation

Some documentation is better generated than written. In September I added a generated symbol graph of the trading box’s C# code: classes, members and references, with skeletons. Agents use it to find callers before changing a function, instead of reading whole files. It is regenerated when the code changes; a late-October commit refreshed it to include the new replay harness.

Rule: generated documentation must say it is generated and how. Hand-editing generated files guarantees drift.

1.13.8 What it costs

Writing this way takes time, and the documents need maintenance. Some of mine are already stale. The last-verified field at least makes that visible. I’d rather have an honest “verified two months ago” than a confident document that is quietly wrong.

1.13.9 Summary

  • With agents, documentation is part of the control system.
  • Give agents one entry point and a routing table; tier the rest and budget tokens.
  • Separate invariants from procedures and make invariants hard to edit by accident.
  • Add a last-verified date to anything describing a live system.
  • Every spec says what done is, what’s out of scope, and how it will be verified.

Exercises

  1. (Classify) Invariant or procedure? (a) “Deploy the site with the pipeline.” (b) “No performance number without receipts.” (c) “Run the study with this command.” (Answer: procedure, invariant, procedure.)
  2. (Design) Write front matter for one document you maintain, including a last-verified date.
  3. (Apply) Take a spec you wrote recently. Does it say how the result will be verified? Add the line.
  4. (Think) Why does a token budget push detail down a tier rather than delete it?

Further reading

  • Daniele Procida, the Diátaxis documentation framework.
  • Michael Nygard, “Documenting Architecture Decisions” (2011), on ADRs.
  • Jakob Nielsen, “Progressive Disclosure”, Nielsen Norman Group (2006).

— Tariq

Chapter 2.2 — Session VWAP, Deviation Bands and the Z-Score

Subtitle: The most-watched line on a futures chart is also one of the easiest to compute wrong.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compute session VWAP and its volume-weighted variance with three running sums. 2. Avoid the two numerical traps: cancellation and a negative variance. 3. Turn VWAP and its spread into a z-score, and say what that number does and does not mean. 4. Explain why VWAP gets “lazy” late in the session and why the anchor matters most.

You need: averages and standard deviation. A little NinjaTrader 8 helps with the last section.

2.2.1 Why I rebuilt VWAP

VWAP was the first level I rebuilt from scratch when I started writing my own NinjaTrader 8 indicators this year. It looks trivial: sum price times volume, divide by volume. Then I put it on a live chart next to the vendor version. The two lines disagreed by a tick or two at the open. They drifted apart after a reconnect. They jumped when the chart reloaded. Each disagreement taught me something.

2.2.2 The definition

Definition (session VWAP). For a session starting at trade ss, with trade prices pip_i and sizes viv_i:

VWAPt=∑i=stpivi∑i=stvi. \text{VWAP}_t = \frac{\sum_{i=s}^{t} p_i v_i}{\sum_{i=s}^{t} v_i}.

In words: the average price paid by everyone who traded since the anchor (the start point). It is a cost benchmark first and a “level” second. Execution desks are judged against it. That is a big part of why price reacts around it.

The textbook bar version replaces pip_i with each bar’s typical price (H+L+C)/3(H+L+C)/3 (high, low, close) and viv_i with the bar’s volume. That is an approximation, and a worse one than people think. On a fast bar the volume is not spread evenly across the range; it clusters. If you have the tick stream (every trade), use it.

2.2.3 Variance and the bands

Definition (volume-weighted variance around VWAP).

σt2=∑i=stvipi2∑i=stvi−VWAPt2. \sigma_t^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=s}^{t} v_i p_i^2}{\sum_{i=s}^{t} v_i} - \text{VWAP}_t^2.

You only need three running sums: ∑v\sum v, ∑pv\sum pv and ∑p2v\sum p^2 v. So each update costs the same small amount (O(1)O(1)) and creates no new objects (allocation-free). The bands are VWAPt±kσt\text{VWAP}_t \pm k\sigma_t for a few multiples kk.

Figure 2.2.1 — VWAP and its bands on a random walk. The grey line is a simulated price; the thick blue line is its VWAP; the dashed lines are one and two standard deviations either side. Look at how quickly VWAP moves early and how flat it becomes later, while the bands stay wide. (Simulation: a seeded Gaussian random walk with random volume per step, seed 2026020201; not market data.)

Two numerical warnings

  1. Catastrophic cancellation. E[p2]−E[p]2E[p^2] - E[p]^2 subtracts two large, nearly equal numbers, and the rounding error can swamp the answer. With index futures in the thousands and a full session of volume, double precision usually survives, but not always gracefully. Two fixes: centre prices on a session reference (subtract the first price before squaring), or use a weighted Welford update, which tracks the mean and the spread directly:

Wt=Wt−1+vt,μt=μt−1+vtWt(pt−μt−1),St=St−1+vt(pt−μt−1)(pt−μt). W_t = W_{t-1} + v_t,\quad \mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \frac{v_t}{W_t}(p_t - \mu_{t-1}),\quad S_t = S_{t-1} + v_t(p_t - \mu_{t-1})(p_t - \mu_t).

Then σt2=St/Wt\sigma_t^2 = S_t / W_t.

  1. Clamp the variance at zero. Rounding can produce a tiny negative number early in the session. Math.Sqrt of that is NaN (not a number), and NaN silently spreads into every plot that touches it.

2.2.4 Z-score distance

Definition (VWAP z-score).

zt=Pt−VWAPtσt. z_t = \frac{P_t - \text{VWAP}_t}{\sigma_t}.

This is the distance of price from VWAP measured in standard deviations. I find it far more useful than the bands. It is one number you can compare across instruments and across days with very different ranges. My VWAP suite publishes a z-score next to the level, plus a slope term (how fast VWAP itself moves per unit of time). “Price is far from VWAP” and “VWAP is trending” are different statements.

Be honest about what zz is not:

  • Intraday prices are not independent random draws around VWAP; they are a path.
  • The distribution of zz is fat-tailed (extreme values are more common than a bell curve suggests).
  • Early in the session, σt\sigma_t comes from very little data, so its scale is unstable. A given zz at 09:35 and at 14:30 do not mean the same thing.

Treat zz as a normalised distance, not a probability.

2.2.5 Why VWAP gets lazy

The textbook calls VWAP “fair value”. In practice it is a running average that responds less and less as the session goes on. Each new trade is a smaller fraction of the cumulative volume. By the afternoon VWAP barely moves. That is not a bug; it is the definition.

Figure 2.2.2 — Each new step counts for less. The line is the newest step’s volume as a share of all volume so far, from the same simulation as Figure 2.2.1. It starts near 100% and falls towards zero. This is why bands from the cumulative variance get wide and slow late in the day, and why a strategy that treats them as fixed-meaning levels will behave differently at the open and at the close.

2.2.6 Anchoring is the real problem

The session anchor decides everything. For CME equity index futures the trading day starts in the evening and runs to the next afternoon (Chapter 2.7). If your anchor uses the chart’s local midnight, or the bar timestamp rule is off by one bar, you get a VWAP that is close but subtly wrong. Nobody notices until two charts disagree.

My fix was to stop computing VWAP inside every chart. One central component reads the tick series once, owns the session anchor, and publishes the level, bands, z-score and slope. Chart indicators are thin consumers that draw what they are given. Every chart on every timeframe agrees, because there is exactly one calculation.

2.2.7 NinjaTrader 8 engineering notes

Topic What to do
Where to update OnBarUpdate with Calculate.OnEachTick sees each tick of the primary series, but only as fast as the chart’s bars allow; historical bars replay bar by bar unless tick replay is on. A secondary 1-tick series (AddDataSeries with BarsPeriodType.Tick, value 1) gives true trade prints historically. OnMarketData gives live last-trade events with bid/ask, but does not run historically without tick replay.
Historical vs realtime seam The most common bug: a jump at State.Realtime because history used bars and live uses ticks. Use the same input in both.
Resets Reset the sums at the session boundary. Guard against the first bar of a session arriving out of order after a reconnect.
Allocation Plain double fields for the sums. No lists of ticks, no LINQ in the hot path.
Rendering AddPlot is fine for the line and bands. SharpDX band fills look nicer, but OnRender runs on the UI thread and must not calculate.

2.2.8 Data quality

The textbook also ignores data quality. One bad print, a reconnect that replays a chunk of ticks twice, or a missing chunk will bias VWAP for the rest of the session, with no way to recover. Check your volume against an independent source when you can.

2.2.9 Summary

  • VWAP and its variance need only three running sums; update them in O(1)O(1) with no allocation.
  • Guard against cancellation (centre prices or use Welford) and clamp the variance at zero.
  • The z-score is a normalised distance, not a probability; its meaning shifts through the session.
  • VWAP becomes slower as volume accumulates, by definition.
  • One owner of the anchor and the calculation keeps every chart consistent.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Three trades: 2 lots at 100, 1 lot at 103, 1 lot at 101. What is VWAP? (Answer: (200 + 103 + 101) / 4 = 101.)
  2. (Compute) For the same trades, compute σ2\sigma^2 with the three-sums formula and with Welford. Do they agree?
  3. (Think) Why does a z-score of 2 at the open carry less information than a z-score of 2 in mid-afternoon?
  4. (Engineering) Describe a test that would catch a step in VWAP at the historical-to-realtime switch.

Further reading

  • Berkowitz, Logue and Noser (1988), “The Total Cost of Transactions on the NYSE”, Journal of Finance.
  • Madhavan (2002), “VWAP Strategies”, Trading (Institutional Investor).
  • Welford (1962), “Note on a method for calculating corrected sums of squares and products”, Technometrics.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.3 — A Kalman Filter on VWAP

Subtitle: A state-space view of a level that every desk watches, and why it is not just another moving average.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Write the local-level state-space model and its Kalman recursion. 2. Show that, in steady state, this filter is an exponential moving average whose weight depends only on Q/R. 3. Use volume-aware noise, the innovation, and a velocity state. 4. Avoid the common pitfalls: tuning by eye, missing resets, fat tails, and a clock mismatch.

You need: Chapter 2.2 (VWAP), basic algebra, and the idea of a variance.

2.3.1 The problem

Once my session VWAP was correct, the next complaint was cosmetic but real. On fast charts the line was noisy in the first part of the session and almost frozen later. I wanted something that tracked the volume-weighted centre of trading with a lag I could control, and that could say how confident it was. That is exactly what a Kalman filter is for: a recursive estimator that blends a model’s prediction with each new noisy measurement.

2.3.2 The state-space model

The simplest useful model treats the true centre of value xtx_t as a random walk, and VWAP (or the last trade) as a noisy measurement of it:

xt=xt−1+wt,wt∼𝒩(0,Q) x_t = x_{t-1} + w_t,\quad w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q) zt=xt+εt,εt∼𝒩(0,R). z_t = x_t + \varepsilon_t,\quad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R).

  • QQ is the process noise: how much the true level may wander per step.
  • RR is the measurement noise: how much we distrust each observation.

2.3.3 The recursion

Predict:

x̂t|t−1=x̂t−1,Pt|t−1=Pt−1+Q. \hat{x}_{t|t-1} = \hat{x}_{t-1},\qquad P_{t|t-1} = P_{t-1} + Q.

Update:

Kt=Pt|t−1Pt|t−1+R,x̂t=x̂t|t−1+Kt(zt−x̂t|t−1),Pt=(1−Kt)Pt|t−1. K_t = \frac{P_{t|t-1}}{P_{t|t-1} + R},\quad \hat{x}_t = \hat{x}_{t|t-1} + K_t (z_t - \hat{x}_{t|t-1}),\quad P_t = (1 - K_t)P_{t|t-1}.

PP is the filter’s uncertainty about its own estimate. KK is the gain: how much of the surprise it accepts.

Result (steady state). For fixed QQ and RR, PtP_t settles to a constant and KtK_t settles to K∞K_\infty. The predicted variance solves P2−QP−QR=0P^2 - QP - QR = 0, so

P∞−=Q+Q2+4QR2,K∞=P∞−P∞−+R. P^{-}_\infty = \frac{Q + \sqrt{Q^2 + 4QR}}{2},\qquad K_\infty = \frac{P^{-}_\infty}{P^{-}_\infty + R}.

This depends only on the ratio λ=Q/R\lambda = Q/R. At that point the filter is exactly an exponential moving average (EMA) with α=K∞\alpha = K_\infty.

Why, in short. In steady state, P∞−=P∞+QP^-_\infty = P_\infty + Q and P∞=(1−K∞)P∞−=P∞−R/(P∞−+R)P_\infty = (1-K_\infty)P^-_\infty = P^-_\infty R/(P^-_\infty + R). Substituting gives the quadratic; its positive root is the formula. Dividing top and bottom by RR shows only Q/RQ/R matters. With a constant gain, the update x̂t=x̂t−1+K(zt−x̂t−1)\hat x_t = \hat x_{t-1} + K(z_t - \hat x_{t-1}) is the EMA rule.

So the first thing to understand: a one-dimensional random-walk Kalman filter with constant noise is an EMA with a principled warm-up. The value is in the warm-up and in what you do with QQ and RR. Pick the ratio, and you have picked the lag.

Figure 2.3.1 — One ratio sets the lag. The curve is the steady-state gain K∞K_\infty as λ=Q/R\lambda = Q/R runs from 0.001 to 100 (log scale). Small ratios give a small gain: heavy smoothing and more lag. Large ratios give a gain near 1: the filter follows each print. This is a plot of the formula above, not data.

Figure 2.3.2 — The warm-up an EMA does not have. After a reset with a large starting PP, the first gain is close to 1, then it falls and settles on the dashed steady-state line within a few updates. The filter locks onto the new level quickly and only then begins to smooth. (Formula recursion with Q/R = 0.05 and starting P = 100R; illustrative values, not tuned settings.)

2.3.4 Where it earns its keep

Volume-aware measurement noise. A one-lot print and a sweep of hundreds of lots are not equally informative. Let RtR_t shrink as the volume of the update grows. The filter then leans on heavy prints and ignores thin ones. That is closer in spirit to VWAP than a time-based EMA ever is.

The innovation as a signal. The innovation is the surprise νt=zt−x̂t|t−1\nu_t = z_t - \hat{x}_{t|t-1}, with variance St=Pt|t−1+RtS_t = P_{t|t-1} + R_t. The standardised surprise is νt/St\nu_t/\sqrt{S_t}. A run of large, same-signed standardised innovations means the random-walk assumption is failing: price is moving away from the level faster than the filter believes it can. That is a cleaner “departure” statistic than eyeballing the gap between two lines.

A velocity state. Extend the state to level and slope:

(xtẋt)=(1Δt01)(xt−1ẋt−1)+wt. \begin{pmatrix} x_t \\ \dot{x}_t \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \Delta t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x_{t-1} \\ \dot{x}_{t-1} \end{pmatrix} + w_t.

Now the filter estimates how fast the volume-weighted centre moves, with an uncertainty attached. I prefer a filtered slope to a finite difference, because differences of a noisy series are mostly noise.

2.3.5 Pitfalls

Pitfall Why it hurts What to do
Tuning by eye Tweaking QQ and RR until yesterday’s chart “looks right” is curve fitting in disguise. Pick the ratio from a property you can defend (a target lag or half-life) and leave it.
No session reset Carrying yesterday’s state pulls the first minutes towards the wrong level. Reset PP to a large value at the session anchor.
Non-Gaussian noise Prints are fat-tailed; one bad tick gives a big innovation and a big correction. Cap the standardised innovation before the update (a Huber-style clip). Document it: it changes the filter.
Calling it “predictive” It is a smoother with an explicit model; it does not see the future. A one-step forecast is just the current estimate plus slope × Δt\Delta t.

2.3.6 NinjaTrader 8 notes

Kalman updates are a handful of multiply-adds, and allocation-free state in fields is easy. The care is in when you update. If you update on every tick live but on every bar historically, the effective gain differs between the two, because the number of updates per minute differs. Either update on the same clock in both (for example a secondary tick series with tick replay), or scale QQ by elapsed time. I prefer the time-scaled version, Qt=q⋅ΔtQ_t = q \cdot \Delta t, so the filter does not depend on how busy the tape was.

2.3.7 Summary

  • The local-level Kalman filter blends a random-walk model with noisy prints using a gain KK.
  • With constant noise it becomes an EMA whose weight depends only on Q/RQ/R.
  • Its real value: a fast warm-up after resets, volume-aware noise, the innovation, and a velocity state.
  • Do not tune by eye, always reset at the session anchor, and keep the update clock the same historically and live.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) With Q=RQ = R, what is K∞K_\infty? (Answer: P−=(1+5)/2≈1.618P^- = (1+\sqrt5)/2 \approx 1.618, so K∞≈1.618/2.618≈0.618K_\infty \approx 1.618/2.618 \approx 0.618.)
  2. (Apply) If you double both QQ and RR, what happens to the lag? Why?
  3. (Think) Why does updating per tick live but per bar historically change the filter’s behaviour after a reload?
  4. (Design) How would you make RtR_t depend on print size without letting one giant print dominate?

Further reading

  • Kalman (1960), “A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems”, Journal of Basic Engineering.
  • Harvey (1989), Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter, Cambridge University Press.
  • Durbin and Koopman (2012), Time Series Analysis by State Space Methods, Oxford University Press.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.4 — Market Profile: POC, Value Area, TPO and Volume

Subtitle: Turning a day of trading into a distribution, and the decisions hiding in the “simple” parts.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Tell a TPO profile from a volume profile and say what each measures. 2. Find the point of control with a deterministic tie-break. 3. Run the standard greedy value-area algorithm and explain where it fails. 4. Build a profile in NinjaTrader 8 without floating-point keys or per-tick rescans.

You need: what a histogram is. Chapter 2.2 helps but is not required.

2.4.1 From folklore to a histogram

Market Profile sounds like folklore until you write it down. Then it becomes a histogram with a handful of well-defined statistics. Every interesting question is about how you build the histogram. I wrote a profile engine for NinjaTrader this year. It computes the auction structure for a session and an acceptance map of where trade actually happened.

2.4.2 Two kinds of profile

Profile How it is built What it measures
TPO (Time Price Opportunity) Split the session into fixed time periods. In each period, mark every price touched. Count periods per price. Time spent at a price
Volume Sum the volume traded at each price. Business done at a price

They often agree. When they disagree, it tells you something. A price visited many times on thin volume is a place the market looked at and rejected. A price with heavy volume in a short time is a place it traded urgently.

2.4.3 The point of control

Definition (POC). For a histogram h(p)h(p) over price bins,

POC=arg⁡maxph(p). \text{POC} = \arg\max_p h(p).

Ties matter more than you would expect. Two bins with equal counts are common in TPO profiles. You need a deterministic tie-break rule (for example, prefer the bin closest to the profile’s centre of mass). Without one, the POC flickers between bars and anything that draws it jumps.

2.4.4 The value area

Definition (value area). The value area is the price range around the POC that holds a fixed fraction ff of the total, by convention about 70%. Its top is VAH (value area high) and its bottom is VAL (value area low).

The 70% comes from a normal distribution: roughly one standard deviation either side of the mean holds about 70%.

The standard algorithm (from the CBOT Market Profile literature):

  1. Start at the POC. Running total T=h(POC)T = h(\text{POC}).
  2. Look at the two bins above and the two bins below the current area.
  3. Add whichever pair has more volume (or TPOs).
  4. Repeat until T≥f⋅∑ph(p)T \geq f \cdot \sum_p h(p).

This is a greedy expansion, not the true narrowest interval holding fraction ff. For one-humped profiles they coincide. For double-distribution days they can differ a lot. The greedy version is what the community means by “value area”, so I implement that and accept it is a convention, not an optimum.

Figure 2.4.1 — The same rule on two shapes. Each bar is the volume at one price; price rises upward. Dark blue is the POC, light blue is the 70% value area found by the greedy rule, grey is outside. On the one-humped day (left) the value area hugs the hump. On the two-humped day (right) it starts at the larger hump and then has to cross the thin valley to collect 70%, so it covers prices where little traded. (Profiles drawn from formulas, not market data.)

2.4.5 Building the histogram from bars

With tick data, each trade goes into its bin. With only bars, you must spread each bar’s volume across its range. The simplest rule is uniform:

vper bin=Vbarnbins(H,L). v_{\text{per bin}} = \frac{V_{\text{bar}}}{n_{\text{bins}}(H, L)}.

My profile module does exactly that: each bar’s volume spread evenly from its low bin to its high bin. It is honest about its ignorance. Fancier schemes (triangular around the close, weighted towards open and close) assume intrabar paths you cannot check. If the shape matters to you, use ticks.

2.4.6 Beyond POC and value area

A useful profile engine also finds auction features:

  • Single prints: prices touched by only one TPO period, often left behind by a fast move. They mark inefficiency the market may come back to.
  • Poor highs and lows: an extreme where several periods traded at the same high (or low) without a tail. It suggests the auction did not finish in that direction.
  • Excess (tails): a run of single prints at the extreme, the opposite of a poor high; a clean rejection.

Once you have the TPO grid, each is a simple scan. Their meaning is interpretive. I keep them as descriptive structure, not signals.

2.4.7 NinjaTrader 8 engineering

  • Bins are tick multiples. Use integer bin indices from a base price: bin = (int)Math.Round((price - basePrice) / binSize). Never use double prices as dictionary keys; floating-point equality will bite you.
  • Preallocate. A session’s range is bounded. Allocate an array for a generous range and grow it rarely, rather than a Dictionary<double,double> that allocates on each new price.
  • Incremental POC. Keep a running maximum as volume arrives. Do not rescan the whole histogram each tick. The value area does need a rescan, but only when the total has changed meaningfully, and it can run on bar close.
  • Rendering. Draw profiles in OnRender with SharpDX. Create brushes in OnRenderTargetChanged and dispose them there too. Build geometry from a snapshot of the histogram, not the live array, because the data thread may write while the UI thread draws.

2.4.8 What textbooks miss

The 70% rule is borrowed from a normal distribution, and intraday volume rarely looks normal. Profiles are often bimodal (two humps), skewed, or flat-topped. On those days the “value area” can span almost the whole range or split a distribution down the middle. Look at the shape before you trust the summary numbers.

2.4.9 Summary

  • TPO profiles measure time at price; volume profiles measure business at price.
  • The POC is the tallest bin; give it a deterministic tie-break.
  • The value area is a greedy 70% expansion from the POC, a convention that misbehaves on two-humped days.
  • From bars, spread volume uniformly; for real shape, use ticks.
  • Use integer bins, preallocated arrays, an incremental POC and snapshot rendering.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Bins (low to high): 2, 5, 9, 6, 3. Total 25, target 70% = 17.5. Run the greedy rule from the POC. (Answer: POC = 9. Up pair = 6 + 3 = 9, down pair = 5 + 2 = 7, so add the up pair: T = 18 ≥ 17.5. Value area = bins 3–5, VAL at the bin with 9.)
  2. (Think) Build a two-humped profile where the greedy value area is much wider than the narrowest 70% interval.
  3. (Engineering) Why is a double price a bad dictionary key? Give an example of two “equal” prices that are not.
  4. (Compare) Describe a session where the TPO POC and the volume POC are far apart. What happened?

Further reading

  • Steidlmayer and Koy (1986), Markets and Market Logic.
  • Dalton, Jones and Dalton (1990/2007), Mind Over Markets.
  • CBOT (1984+), Market Profile and Liquidity Data Bank handbooks.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.5 — Finding Low-Volume Nodes Without Fooling Yourself

Subtitle: Smoothing a volume profile before you look for its valleys.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why valleys in a raw profile are mostly noise. 2. Smooth a profile with a kernel density estimate and choose a bandwidth sensibly. 3. Keep only valleys with real prominence, and check them across scales. 4. Set up a fair test so hindsight does not do your analysis for you.

You need: Chapter 2.4 (volume profiles) and the idea of a weighted average.

2.5.1 What a low-volume node is

A low-volume node (LVN) is a price where little business was done compared with the prices around it. In auction terms, the market moved through it quickly. Traders watch LVNs as possible support or resistance on a revisit. The trouble starts when you try to find them in code.

2.5.2 Why raw profiles are useless for this

A raw volume histogram at tick resolution is jagged. Neighbouring bins can differ wildly because of round-number clustering, iceberg refills (hidden orders that keep reloading), and plain noise. Every one of those dips is a local minimum. A naive valley detector finds dozens of LVNs per session, which is the same as finding none.

The fix: estimate the underlying density first, then look for its valleys.

2.5.3 Kernel density estimation

Definition (weighted kernel density estimate). Treat the profile as samples of a density over price and smooth with a kernel KK of bandwidth (width) hh:

f̂(p)=1Wh∑iviK(p−pih),W=∑ivi. \hat{f}(p) = \frac{1}{W h}\sum_{i} v_i \, K\!\left(\frac{p - p_i}{h}\right),\qquad W = \sum_i v_i.

With a Gaussian kernel this is the histogram convolved with a discretised bell curve. On a regular bin grid it is a cheap 1-D convolution.

The bandwidth is the whole game. Too small and you are back to noise. Too large and real structure melts into one hump. Silverman’s rule of thumb is a starting point:

h=0.9min⁡(σ̂,IQR1.34)n−1/5 h = 0.9 \min\!\left(\hat\sigma, \frac{\text{IQR}}{1.34}\right) n^{-1/5}

(σ̂\hat\sigma is the standard deviation, IQR the interquartile range, nn the sample size). But it assumes roughly normal data and tends to over-smooth multimodal profiles, which are exactly the ones with interesting LVNs. The principle I would defend: tie the bandwidth to the profile’s scale, not to a fixed number of ticks.

Figure 2.5.1 — Thirty-seven valleys or one. Grey bars are a noisy two-humped profile; the orange ticks under the axis mark every raw local minimum (37 of them). The blue curve is the smoothed density, which has a single valley (orange dot). The black arrow is that valley’s prominence: its depth below the lower of the two peaks around it. (Simulation: two Gaussian humps times seeded multiplicative noise, seed 2026020501; smoothing truncated and renormalised at the edges; not market data.)

2.5.4 Detecting valleys

On the smoothed density f̂\hat f:

  1. Find local minima: f̂(pk−1)>f̂(pk)<f̂(pk+1)\hat f(p_{k-1}) > \hat f(p_k) < \hat f(p_{k+1}).
  2. Measure prominence: how far the valley sits below the lower of the two peaks that bound it (the same idea as a mountain’s topographic prominence).
  3. Keep valleys with enough prominence relative to the surrounding peaks, and enough width.

Prominence is the key filter. A shallow dip between two nearly equal humps is not an LVN. A deep trough between two distributions is.

A scale-space view. Valleys of a density are where f̂′=0\hat f' = 0 and f̂″>0\hat f'' > 0. You can compute derivatives of the smoothed density, or convolve with the kernel’s derivative directly. As hh grows, minor valleys vanish and only robust ones survive. Features that persist across a range of bandwidths are worth trusting.

Figure 2.5.2 — Valleys vanish as the kernel widens. The line counts valleys in the same simulated profile as the kernel width grows. Narrow kernels leave dozens; from moderate widths on, one valley remains for a long stretch; far too wide, and even that one melts away. The long flat stretch is what “persists across scales” looks like.

2.5.5 High-volume nodes come for free

The same machinery gives high-volume nodes (the peaks). The POC becomes the global peak of the smoothed density rather than the raw tallest bin. I like the smoothed POC because it does not jump between two adjacent bins on every update.

2.5.6 Engineering in NinjaTrader 8

  • Fixed grid. Work on an integer-indexed bin array. Precompute the kernel weights once per bandwidth into a small array. Convolution is then a tight loop with no allocation.
  • When to recompute. Smoothing a few hundred bins takes microseconds, but there is no point doing it every tick. Recompute on bar close, or when cumulative volume has grown by some fraction since the last pass.
  • Edges. Near the ends of the range, convolution needs a rule: reflect, or truncate and renormalise. Truncate-and-renormalise avoids inventing volume beyond the session’s range.
  • Stability. Valleys appear and disappear as the session develops. Draw only those that have lasted a while, or the chart flickers and you chase ghosts.

2.5.7 What can go wrong

LVNs look wonderful in hindsight. After the session you see the valley and the bounce off it. You do not see the dozen valleys price sliced straight through. If you study them:

  • count every LVN the detector produced in real time, not just the ones you remember;
  • compare revisit behaviour against random price levels at similar distances.

Without that null (the “no-edge” baseline, Chapter 6.1), you are measuring your own pattern recognition.

2.5.8 Summary

  • Raw profiles have many meaningless local minima.
  • Smooth first with a kernel density estimate; tie the bandwidth to the profile’s scale.
  • Keep valleys with real prominence and those that persist across bandwidths.
  • Recompute on bar close, handle edges honestly, and only draw stable valleys.
  • Test against random levels, counting every detection.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Two peaks of height 10 and 6 bound a valley of height 2. What is its prominence? (Answer: 6 − 2 = 4, measured from the lower peak.)
  2. (Apply) Why does Silverman’s rule tend to over-smooth a two-humped profile?
  3. (Simulate) Generate a noisy two-humped profile and count valleys for several bandwidths. Where does the count stabilise?
  4. (Design) Write down a fair test of “price reacts at LVNs”, including the random-level baseline.

Further reading

  • Silverman (1986), Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis, Chapman and Hall.
  • Lindeberg (1994), Scale-Space Theory in Computer Vision, Springer.
  • Dalton, Jones and Dalton, Mind Over Markets.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.6 — Many Anchors, One Chart: Level Maps and Single-Pass Rendering

Subtitle: Drawing prior-day, overnight, VWAP and moving-average levels without turning the chart into spaghetti or the UI thread into a bottleneck.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe any chart level as an anchor (a time window) plus an aggregation. 2. Explain the compute-once, publish, consume design and what it buys. 3. Draw historical levels as stair-steps so the chart does not show lookahead. 4. Merge nearby levels in one sorted pass and render them safely in NinjaTrader 8.

You need: Chapter 2.2 (VWAP). Chapter 2.7 (the CME trading day) is a useful companion.

2.6.1 The problem

Every discretionary futures trader ends up with the same chart: prior-day high, low and close; overnight high and low; session VWAP; a couple of daily moving averages; maybe weekly or monthly boundaries. Each comes from a different anchor in time. Put each in its own indicator and you get a dozen indicators. Each has its own data series, its own session logic, and its own render. That was my chart in the spring. This chapter is about collapsing it into one consumer and one render pass.

2.6.2 What a level actually is

Definition (level). A level is an aggregation gg over the trades inside an anchor window:

L=g({(pi,vi,ti):ti∈[astart,aend)}). L = g\big(\{(p_i, v_i, t_i) : t_i \in [a_{\text{start}}, a_{\text{end}})\}\big).

Level Anchor window Aggregation gg
Prior-day high previous CME trading day max⁡p\max p
Overnight low electronic-only hours of the current trading day min⁡p\min p
VWAP current session start to now ∑pv/∑v\sum pv / \sum v
Daily moving average last nn completed trading days mean of their closes

Seeing levels this way made one thing obvious: the hard part is the anchors, not the aggregations. If every indicator has its own idea of “the previous trading day”, they will disagree around holidays, early closes and the Sunday open.

2.6.3 Compute once, publish, consume

My design separates computing from drawing. A single producer owns the tick and daily series, the trading calendar, and all anchor logic. It computes every level and publishes a snapshot. Chart-side consumers subscribe and draw. A consumer never computes a level; it only decides how to render one.

Figure 2.6.1 — One calculation, many displays. Data is loaded once into the producer, which owns the calendar and anchors. It publishes a snapshot stamped with its trading date. Each chart consumer only draws. This is the general pattern (the Observer pattern), shown at concept level.

This buys three things:

  1. Consistency. All charts show the same numbers because there is one source.
  2. Cost. Expensive series (1-tick for VWAP, daily for moving averages) load once, not once per chart.
  3. Testability. The producer can be checked against a reference on its own.

2.6.4 Historical rendering: stair-steps, not straight lines

A subtle display bug: draw today’s prior-day high as one horizontal line across the whole chart, and you show today’s level over yesterday’s bars. That is visual lookahead: the picture uses information that did not exist at those bars. Anyone reviewing old price action on that chart is misled.

The correct historical rendering is a stair-step: each bar shows the level that was in force at that bar’s time. That needs a history of level values, not just the latest one. I keep a compact time-indexed history and walk it with an index that only moves forward while plotting historical bars. The cost is linear in bars, not bars times history.

Figure 2.6.2 — Draw what was known at each bar. Over three simulated days, the green stair-step shows the prior-day high actually in force: day 1’s high during day 2, day 2’s high during day 3 (no prior day exists for day 1 here). The orange dashed line is the latest value smeared across everything, which puts day 3’s knowledge onto days 1 and 2. (Seeded random walk, seed 2026020601; not market data.)

2.6.5 Single-pass merge rendering

The naive renderer loops over each level type and draws it. With many types, many share a price (the overnight low equals the prior-day low more often than you would think), and you get overlapping lines and labels. A cleaner approach:

  1. Collect all visible levels into one array of (price, kind, style) structs.
  2. Sort by price.
  3. Walk once. Levels within a small price tolerance of each other merge into one drawn line with a combined label.
  4. Draw lines and labels in that single pass, adjusting label positions to avoid collisions.

Figure 2.6.3 — Sort, then merge in one walk. Top: seven levels sorted by price; B and C, and E and F, sit almost on top of each other. Bottom: after one walk, each close pair becomes a single line with a combined label (green). Schematic positions, not real levels.

Sorting a few dozen structs per frame is trivial. The win is visual (no label pile-ups) and in render cost (one geometry batch instead of many).

2.6.6 NinjaTrader 8 specifics

Topic Guidance
Plots vs SharpDX Native AddPlot series are drawn by NinjaTrader, appear in the data box, and stair-step naturally if you set the value per bar. SharpDX gives full control but you own everything, including scaling. I use native plots for levels that change through time and SharpDX for long-horizon boundaries that work better as clean rays.
Y-axis labels Axis price markers are a native plot feature. Reimplementing them in SharpDX is possible but rarely worth it.
Thread safety The producer runs on a data thread; OnRender runs on the UI thread. Copy a snapshot into a local struct at the start of each frame; never read a shared mutable object field by field while drawing.
Struct, not class Per-frame level records as struct in a reused array avoid garbage-collection pauses on the UI thread, which show up as chart stutter.
IsOverlay and auto-scale Levels far from price wreck auto-scale. Override OnCalculateMinMax or exclude distant levels from scaling.

2.6.7 What goes wrong: stale snapshots

The classic failure is a stale snapshot. After a workspace reload or overnight, a consumer may receive yesterday’s levels before the producer has caught up. Every published snapshot should carry the trading date it belongs to, and consumers should refuse to draw a snapshot from the wrong date. It is a one-line check that prevents a very misleading chart.

2.6.8 Summary

  • A level is an anchor window plus an aggregation; the anchors are the hard part.
  • One producer computes, many consumers draw: consistent, cheaper, testable.
  • Draw historical levels as stair-steps to avoid visual lookahead.
  • Sort and merge nearby levels in one pass; snapshot before rendering.
  • Stamp snapshots with their trading date and reject the wrong date.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Write the anchor window and aggregation for “this week’s high”. (Answer: window = from the first trading day of the current week to now; g=max⁡pg = \max p.)
  2. (Think) Why is a flat line for the prior-day high a form of lookahead when you scroll back?
  3. (Design) Sketch the struct you would sort for merge rendering. Which fields decide merging, and which decide drawing?
  4. (Engineering) Describe what a consumer should display while it waits for a snapshot with today’s date.

Further reading

  • Dalton, Jones and Dalton, Mind Over Markets (reference levels in auction theory).
  • NinjaTrader 8 Help Guide: OnRender, OnCalculateMinMax, SharpDX resources.
  • Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides (1994), Design Patterns (Observer).

— Tariq

Chapter 2.7 — What Day Is It? Session Levels and the CME Trading Day

Subtitle: The most boring bug in futures charting is also the most expensive one.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Assign any bar to the correct CME trading day. 2. Define the standard session levels and say which session template each uses. 3. Tell developing levels from frozen ones and draw each correctly. 4. Use NinjaTrader 8’s session tools without the usual traps (templates, time zones, daily bars, rolls).

You need: nothing beyond basic chart reading. Chapter 2.6 (level maps) is a companion.

2.7.1 “Yesterday” is ambiguous

Ask a futures chart “what was yesterday’s high?” and the honest answer is “it depends what you mean by yesterday”. That one ambiguity broke more of my early indicators than any piece of maths.

2.7.2 The CME day is not a calendar day

CME Globex equity index futures trade nearly around the clock. The trading day for a given date starts the previous evening (Central Time, after a daily maintenance break) and ends in the afternoon. So Tuesday’s trading day contains Monday evening’s Asian and European hours plus Tuesday’s US session.

That means:

  • A bar stamped Monday 19:00 Eastern belongs to Tuesday’s trading day.
  • Sunday evening’s bars belong to Monday.
  • Friday afternoon’s close ends the week; there is no Saturday trading day.
  • Holidays and early closes move the boundaries, and some holidays have a Globex session with no US cash session.

Figure 2.7.1 — Trading days start the evening before. The top row is the calendar. The bottom row is the CME trading day: each starts at the evening boundary of the previous calendar day (dashed lines), runs through the overnight Globex-only hours (light blue), and ends after the US cash session (dark blue). The orange arrow shows a Monday-evening bar landing in Tuesday’s trading day. Schematic: no clock times are drawn.

Rule (trading-day assignment). Bars at or after the evening boundary belong to the next business day’s session.

My trading-calendar helper reduces it to exactly that rule. Every component that needs “today” asks the calendar; nobody computes it locally.

2.7.3 The standard session levels

Once you know which trading day a bar belongs to, the usual levels are simple aggregations:

Level Window
Prior-day high, low, close the full previous trading day, or only its regular-hours part (be explicit which)
Overnight high and low from the trading day’s start to the US cash open
Initial balance high and low of the first part of the cash session
Opening range the same idea, shorter window
Developing session high and low running extremes since the anchor

None of these are hard. All of them are wrong if the anchor is wrong.

2.7.4 RTH versus ETH

NinjaTrader charts are bound to a trading hours template. With an RTH (regular trading hours, cash session only) template, “prior day” means the prior cash session. With ETH (extended trading hours), it means the full Globex day.

Prior-day closes are especially messy. The RTH close, the Globex settlement, and the last trade of the ETH session are three different prices. Pick one per level and label it.

A defensible convention: compute every level from a known template on a dedicated data series, whatever the chart’s own template. Then the overnight low is the overnight low whether the chart shows overnight bars or not.

2.7.5 Developing versus historical

Session levels have two lives:

  1. Developing: the current session’s high is a running maximum that can change on any tick.
  2. Historical: once the session closes, it freezes and becomes tomorrow’s “prior-day high”.

The drawing should respect that. A developing high drawn as a solid line from the session start implies it was there all along; really it was being pushed up all morning. I draw developing levels as stair-steps that track their own history, and only extend frozen levels as rays.

Figure 2.7.2 — A level’s two lives. In the left session, the green stair-step is the developing high: it rises each time price makes a new high, then stays flat. At the session close (dotted line) it freezes and is extended into the next session as the blue dashed prior-day high. (Seeded random walk, seed 2026020701; not market data.)

2.7.6 NinjaTrader 8 implementation notes

  • Bars.IsFirstBarOfSession reports the chart’s own session template, not CME’s trading day. Use it only if your template matches the convention you want.
  • SessionIterator gives session begin and end times for a template, including holidays. It is the right tool, but create it once in State.DataLoaded and reuse it; building one per bar is slow.
  • Time zones. Bar timestamps use the platform’s configured time zone. Convert boundaries explicitly. Daylight saving changes on different dates in the US and Europe, which shifts the overnight session against European cash hours for a few weeks each year.
  • Daily series. AddDataSeries(BarsPeriodType.Day, 1) gives settlement-based daily bars on the instrument’s template. Daily bars may not be complete until after the session; do not read the current day’s daily bar as final.
  • Contract rolls. On roll dates, the prior day’s levels may come from the expiring contract. Back-adjusted or not, decide and be consistent; continuous-contract adjustments shift historical prices.

2.7.7 The lesson

Write the calendar first. Test it on:

  • a Sunday open,
  • a US holiday with a Globex session,
  • a half-day,
  • both daylight-saving transitions.

Only then build levels on top. I learned this the slow way, by watching two charts disagree about yesterday.

2.7.8 Summary

  • A CME trading day starts the evening before its date; assign bars with one calendar rule.
  • Session levels are easy aggregations; the anchor makes or breaks them.
  • RTH and ETH give different “prior days” and different closes; label which you use.
  • Draw developing levels as stair-steps and frozen levels as rays.
  • Build and test the calendar before anything else.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A bar is stamped Sunday evening, after the Globex session has opened. Which trading day is it in? (Answer: Monday’s.)
  2. (Apply) Name the three different “prior-day close” prices and when each might be the right choice.
  3. (Think) Why does using Bars.IsFirstBarOfSession on an RTH chart give the wrong overnight low?
  4. (Test design) Write five test cases for a trading-calendar function, one per edge case in Section 2.7.7.

Further reading

  • CME Group, “Trading Hours” and holiday calendar documentation for equity index futures.
  • NinjaTrader 8 Help Guide: SessionIterator, Trading Hours templates.
  • Harris (2003), Trading and Exchanges, Oxford University Press.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.8 — Swing Pivots and Trend Rays Without Hindsight

Subtitle: The classic swing high is a lookahead trap. Here is how to draw it honestly.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define a swing high of strength n and explain why it is only known n bars later. 2. Choose and keep a rule for equal highs. 3. Build a trend ray through two pivots and decide when it breaks and retires. 4. Implement pivots in NinjaTrader 8 without repainting or a historical/realtime mismatch.

You need: equation of a straight line. Chapter 6.1 (null models) is useful background for the pitfalls.

2.8.1 Time is the hard part

Swing highs and lows are the most basic structure on a chart. Drawing support and resistance from them is the oldest trick there is. I built an indicator that marks swing pivots as support and resistance and draws sloped trend lines (“trend cuts”) through them. The interesting part was not the geometry. It was time.

2.8.2 The definition and its hidden delay

Definition (swing high of strength n). Bar tt is a swing high if

Ht>Ht−kandHt≥Ht+k∀k∈{1,…,n}. H_t > H_{t-k} \quad\text{and}\quad H_t \geq H_{t+k}\quad \forall k \in \{1,\dots,n\}.

Look at the right-hand condition. It needs nn bars after tt. You cannot know that bar tt was a swing high until bar t+nt+n closes. The pivot is confirmed nn bars late.

Figure 2.8.1 — Drawn at t, known at t + n. Each vertical line is a bar’s range; the blue bar at tt is the swing high for strength n=3n = 3. The grey zone holds the nn earlier bars, which must be lower. The blue zone holds the nn later bars, which must not exceed it. The marker sits at tt, but the fact only becomes known when bar t+3t+3 closes (green arrow). Schematic bars.

Every indicator that puts the marker at bar tt is drawing in the past. That is fine for reading a chart. It is not fine if anything downstream treats the pivot as known at time tt. In a backtest that is lookahead (using information from the future), and it makes swing-based ideas look much better than they are.

Rule. A pivot exists from bar t+nt+n onward. The marker can sit at tt for display, but the “event” happens at confirmation.

2.8.3 Strict versus non-strict inequalities

Equal highs are common on tick and Renko charts.

Rule Effect on a run of equal highs
Strict on both sides A double top is never a swing high.
Non-strict on both sides Both bars qualify.
Strict on one side, non-strict on the other (usual compromise) Exactly one bar qualifies.

Pick one and keep it. Changing it changes the pivot set.

2.8.4 From pivots to rays

Given two confirmed swing highs (t1,H1)(t_1, H_1) and (t2,H2)(t_2, H_2) with t1<t2t_1 < t_2, the line through them is

y(t)=H1+H2−H1t2−t1(t−t1). y(t) = H_1 + \frac{H_2 - H_1}{t_2 - t_1}(t - t_1).

A descending resistance line uses consecutive lower highs. An ascending support line uses consecutive higher lows. A break happens when price closes beyond the projected line.

Figure 2.8.2 — A ray through two lower highs. The two blue dots are confirmed swing highs; the orange line through them is projected forward with the formula above. When price closes beyond it (green dot) the ray breaks and is retired; the dashed tail shows where it would have continued. Schematic path.

Three decisions shape the result:

  1. Which pivots to connect. Adjacent only, or the most significant pair in a window? The two most extreme pivots give fewer, longer lines. Adjacent pivots give many short ones.
  2. The time axis. On time-based bars, tt is time. On tick, volume or Renko bars, tt is bar index, which is not time. A line on a Renko chart has a slope in “bricks”, which changes meaning whenever activity changes. Neither is wrong, but know which you are using.
  3. Invalidation. A ray should die when price closes through it. Otherwise the chart fills with ancient lines.

2.8.5 Multiple structures at once

Pivots at one strength miss structure at another. Running several strengths together gives a nested picture: minor swings inside major ones. The engineering cost is small (each strength is its own rolling buffer) and the visual payoff is large. But the more structures you draw, the more you will find “something” that explains every move after the fact.

2.8.6 NinjaTrader 8 specifics

  • Rolling buffers. Checking nn bars back and forward each bar costs O(n)O(n). For moderate nn that is fine. For many strengths, keep a monotonic deque (a queue kept in sorted order) of candidate highs, which makes it amortised O(1)O(1).
  • Drawing objects versus SharpDX. Draw.Ray creates a drawing object per call. Thousands of them slow the chart and bloat the workspace. For many lines, render them yourself in OnRender from a list of line structs, and skip lines that are off-screen.
  • Calculate mode. On OnEachTick, the right-hand condition must use closed bars only, or a pivot can appear and vanish within a bar. Detect on IsFirstTickOfBar using [1] indexing, or run on bar close.
  • Historical consistency. If the realtime path confirms pivots one way and the historical path another, the chart looks different after a reload. Use one code path.

2.8.7 Pitfalls I see often

  • Repainting: showing unconfirmed pivots that later disappear. Users love them because they look prescient.
  • Backtesting from the marker: entering at the swing bar’s price when you could not yet have known it was a swing.
  • Survivorship of lines: the lines you remember are the ones that held.

2.8.8 Summary

  • A strength-n swing high is only confirmed n bars after it forms; treat it as an event at t + n.
  • Fix one equal-highs rule and keep it.
  • A trend ray is a line through two confirmed pivots; it breaks on a close beyond it and should then retire.
  • Bar index is not time on tick, volume or Renko charts.
  • Avoid repainting, marker-price backtests and remembering only the lines that held.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With strength n=5n = 5, on which bar can you first act on a swing high formed at bar 100? (Answer: after bar 105 closes.)
  2. (Compute) Pivots at (10,50)(10, 50) and (20,45)(20, 45). Where is the ray at t=30t = 30? (Answer: slope −0.5, so 50 − 0.5 × 20 = 40.)
  3. (Think) Why does a trend line on a Renko chart change meaning when the market gets busier?
  4. (Test design) How would you check that your realtime and historical pivot code produce the same pivots?

Further reading

  • Edwards and Magee, Technical Analysis of Stock Trends (classic treatment of trend lines).
  • Lo, Mamaysky and Wang (2000), “Foundations of Technical Analysis”, Journal of Finance.
  • Bulkowski, Encyclopedia of Chart Patterns.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.9 — Cumulative Volume Delta and the Trade-Classification Problem

Subtitle: “Buyers” and “sellers” are an inference. Here is how the inference works and where it breaks.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define delta and cumulative volume delta (CVD) from signed trades. 2. Apply the quote rule, the tick rule, Lee–Ready, and bulk volume classification. 3. List what goes wrong in futures data, and why classification quality should be tracked. 4. Choose the right NinjaTrader 8 hook and handle resets and reconnects.

You need: bid, ask and last trade. The normal distribution function Φ for one section.

2.9.1 Who started the trade?

Every trade has a buyer and a seller. So “aggressive buying” really means the initiator of the trade was the buyer: someone crossed the spread and lifted the offer. Cumulative volume delta (CVD) adds up initiator-signed volume. It is one of the most popular order-flow tools and one of the most misunderstood, because the sign of each trade is not in the data. You have to infer it.

2.9.2 Delta and CVD

Definition. For trade ii with size viv_i and inferred initiator sign si∈{+1,−1}s_i \in \{+1, -1\}:

Δbar=∑i∈barsivi,CVDt=∑i=atsivi. \Delta_{\text{bar}} = \sum_{i \in \text{bar}} s_i v_i,\qquad \text{CVD}_t = \sum_{i=a}^{t} s_i v_i.

The anchor aa is usually the session start. The interesting quantity is rarely CVD’s level. It is its change compared with price change.

2.9.3 Classifying trades

Quote rule. Compare the trade price with the best bid and ask in force:

si={+1pi≥ask−1pi≤bid?otherwise s_i = \begin{cases} +1 & p_i \geq \text{ask} \\ -1 & p_i \leq \text{bid} \\ \text{?} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

Tick rule. Compare with the previous trade price: an up-tick is a buy, a down-tick a sell, and a zero-tick takes the last non-zero sign.

Lee–Ready. Use the quote rule; fall back to the tick rule for trades inside the spread. Historically the standard in equities research.

Figure 2.9.1 — Quote rule with a tick-rule fallback. If the quote at the moment of the trade is known, compare the price with bid and ask: at or above the ask is a buy (green), at or below the bid is a sell (orange), inside the spread falls through to the tick rule. Without quotes, use the tick rule directly. This is the standard Lee–Ready logic.

Bulk volume classification (BVC). Instead of signing each trade, split each bar’s volume by probability, using the standardised price change:

Vbuy=V⋅Φ(ΔPσΔP),Vsell=V−Vbuy. V^{\text{buy}} = V \cdot \Phi\!\left(\frac{\Delta P}{\sigma_{\Delta P}}\right),\quad V^{\text{sell}} = V - V^{\text{buy}}.

Φ\Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution. BVC needs only bars, which makes it attractive when you have no quotes.

Figure 2.9.2 — BVC turns a price move into a buy share. The curve is Φ(ΔP/σ)\Phi(\Delta P/\sigma). A flat bar splits its volume 50/50. A bar that rose by one standard deviation calls about 84% of its volume “buy”; a bar that fell by one calls about 84% “sell”. A plot of the formula, not data.

2.9.4 What actually goes wrong in futures

  • Timestamp alignment. The quote rule needs the quote in force at the moment of the trade. In NinjaTrader, OnMarketData delivers bid, ask and last events in order; you track the latest bid and ask yourself and compare at each last event. Historically, unless you have tick replay with bid/ask, you only have trades and are forced into the tick rule.
  • Inside-spread trades are rare in liquid index futures (the spread is usually one tick) but common in thinner products.
  • Implied and spread trades can print at odd prices relative to the outright book.
  • Size aggregation. One aggressive order sweeping several price levels shows up as several prints. Summing them is fine for delta, but trade-count statistics are distorted.

Easley, López de Prado and O’Hara argued that in high-frequency markets the tick rule and BVC can be as good as, or better than, Lee–Ready in some settings. I treat classification as a measurement with an error rate, not a truth.

2.9.5 Quality tracking

I think this part is underrated. My CVD engine tracks how each chunk of volume was classified and exposes a quality signal next to the number: which classification mode was active, and how much volume was classified by the preferred method versus a fallback. A CVD built live from quote-rule classification and a CVD rebuilt historically from the tick rule are not the same series. Anything that compares them across the historical/realtime seam should know that.

2.9.6 NinjaTrader 8 engineering

Topic Guidance
OnMarketData vs OnBarUpdate OnMarketData sees every Level 1 event live, in order. OnBarUpdate with OnEachTick sees trades but not quotes. For quote-rule delta, use OnMarketData, and label your historical method (tick replay, or a fallback rule).
Volumetric bars They compute bid/ask volume per price internally. Convenient, but you trust their classification and their historical data source.
Session resets At the CME trading-day boundary, not midnight (Chapter 2.7).
Allocation CVD is a running sum: keep it a double, keep per-bar deltas in a Series<double>, do not store every trade.
Reconnects After a disconnect, NinjaTrader may backfill bars but not the quote stream, leaving a gap in quote-rule delta. Detect it and mark it.

2.9.7 Reading CVD honestly

Rising CVD with flat price is often called absorption (buyers lifting offers that keep refilling). Falling price with rising CVD is called divergence. Both are real descriptions of the tape. Neither is a forecast by itself, and classification noise is big enough that small divergences are often nothing.

2.9.8 Summary

  • Delta signs each trade by its inferred initiator; CVD sums it from an anchor.
  • Quote rule, tick rule, Lee–Ready and BVC are different estimators, each with an error rate.
  • Futures data adds alignment, implied-trade and sweep problems.
  • Track how volume was classified, especially across the historical/realtime seam.
  • Describe the tape with CVD; do not treat small divergences as forecasts.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Bid 100.00, ask 100.25. Trades: 100.25, 100.00, 100.00, 100.25. Using the quote rule, what is delta if each trade is 1 lot? (Answer: +1 −1 −1 +1 = 0.)
  2. (Apply) Classify the same trades with the tick rule, starting from a previous trade at 100.00. Do you get the same delta?
  3. (Compute) A bar’s price change is −0.5σ on 1,000 contracts. Using BVC, roughly how many are “buy”? (Φ(−0.5) ≈ 0.31.)
  4. (Think) Why should a chart that shows CVD across a reload also show which classification method built each part?

Further reading

  • Lee and Ready (1991), “Inferring Trade Direction from Intraday Data”, Journal of Finance.
  • Easley, López de Prado and O’Hara (2012), “Flow Toxicity and Liquidity in a High-Frequency World”, Review of Financial Studies.
  • Easley, López de Prado and O’Hara (2016), “Discerning Information from Trade Data”, Journal of Financial Economics.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.10 — Normalising Order Flow: Delta Z-Scores and a Four-Gauge Panel

Subtitle: Raw delta is not comparable across time. Here is how I turn the tape into bounded, comparable gauges.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why raw delta scales with activity, and normalise it by volume or by its own variability. 2. Compute an exponentially weighted delta z-score in the right order, and bound it for display. 3. Describe event-time estimators and the four gauges: pressure, pace, liquidity imbalance and price-impact efficiency. 4. Build such a panel in NinjaTrader 8 with an allocation-free hot path.

You need: Chapter 2.9 (delta), mean and standard deviation, and the idea of an EMA.

2.10.1 The problem with raw numbers

A bar with a delta of a few hundred contracts is huge at 03:00 Eastern and noise at 09:31. Any order-flow display that shows raw numbers forces you to recalibrate your eyes every hour. This chapter is about normalisation (putting numbers on a common scale), and about a compact panel I built that shows four views of the tape on the same bounded scale.

2.10.2 Why raw delta misleads

Delta scales with activity. If volume per bar is VV and the share started by buyers is bb, then

Δ=(2b−1)V. \Delta = (2b - 1)V.

Doubling activity doubles delta even if the buy/sell balance does not change. Two fixes follow:

  1. Normalise by volume: the imbalance ratio Δ/V∈[−1,1]\Delta / V \in [-1, 1].
  2. Normalise by recent variability: the z-score of delta against its own recent history.

2.10.3 Delta z-score

Definition. With a rolling or exponentially weighted mean μΔ\mu_\Delta and standard deviation σΔ\sigma_\Delta:

zt=Δt−μΔσΔ. z_t = \frac{\Delta_t - \mu_\Delta}{\sigma_\Delta}.

An exponentially weighted estimator is convenient and allocation-free:

μt=μt−1+α(Δt−μt−1),σt2=(1−α)(σt−12+α(Δt−μt−1)2). \mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \alpha(\Delta_t - \mu_{t-1}),\qquad \sigma_t^2 = (1-\alpha)\left(\sigma_{t-1}^2 + \alpha(\Delta_t - \mu_{t-1})^2\right).

Two cautions:

  • Fat tails. Delta has fat tails, so large |z||z| values occur far more often than a normal table suggests.
  • Order of operations. Including the current bar in μ\mu and σ\sigma before computing zz shrinks it. Compute zz against the previous estimates, then update.

Figure 2.10.1 — Same balance, double the activity. Top: raw delta per bar; at the dashed line volume doubles while the buy share stays the same, and the bars roughly double in size. Bottom: the z-score of the same series, computed against the previous estimates; after a brief jump at the change it returns to the same scale. (Simulation: buy share 0.5 plus small seeded noise, seed 2026021001; the first 20 bars are left blank while the estimator warms up; not market data.)

Bounding for display. I squash zz into a fixed range, for example with tanh\tanh, so one extreme bar does not flatten the rest of the panel:

gt=100⋅tanh⁡(zt/c). g_t = 100 \cdot \tanh(z_t / c).

Figure 2.10.2 — Smooth saturation. The blue curve is g=100tanh⁡(z/c)g = 100\tanh(z/c); the dashed line is a straight line clipped at ±100. Near zero they agree. Far out, tanh bends gently towards ±100 instead of hitting a wall, so extremes stay visible without crushing everything else. Plotted against z/cz/c, so no particular scale cc is implied.

2.10.4 Event time instead of clock time

Bars on a time clock mix quiet and busy periods. An alternative is to update estimators in event time: on every classified trade, not every bar. An EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) of signed aggressor volume, decayed per event, has a half-life measured in trades. It responds at the speed of the tape: fast when busy, slow when quiet.

My panel’s first gauge is exactly this kind of volume-pressure imbalance: an event-time EWMA of signed aggressor volume, divided by the EWMA of absolute volume, so it lives in [−1,1][-1, 1].

2.10.5 The other three gauges

Pace. How fast trades arrive is information in its own right. Bursts of activity often come before or with moves. Compare a fast and a slow EMA of the trade rate λ\lambda and z-score the difference:

pacet=λtfast−λtslowσλ, \text{pace}_t = \frac{\lambda^{\text{fast}}_t - \lambda^{\text{slow}}_t}{\sigma_\lambda},

then sign it by the prevailing flow direction. This is a crude cousin of the intensity of a self-exciting (Hawkes) process, where each event raises the chance of more events. A full Hawkes fit is a research project; the fast/slow ratio captures the “excitement” idea cheaply.

Liquidity imbalance. With a depth feed, the size imbalance of the top NN book levels is a classic short-horizon pressure measure:

It=∑k=1NBk−∑k=1NAk∑k=1NBk+∑k=1NAk. I_t = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^N B_k - \sum_{k=1}^N A_k}{\sum_{k=1}^N B_k + \sum_{k=1}^N A_k}.

It is easily spoofed and flickers constantly. Without a depth subscription the gauge should say so (I grey it out) rather than show zero, which looks like “balanced”.

Price-impact efficiency. How much did price move per unit of signed volume? That has its own chapter (2.12), because the volume clock makes it interesting.

Gauge Question it answers Range
Volume pressure How hard is each side hitting? [−1,1][-1, 1]
Pace How fast is the tape, compared with normal? z-score, signed by flow
Liquidity imbalance How is the visible book stacked? [−1,1][-1, 1], greyed out without depth
Price-impact efficiency How much is price giving way? bounded (Chapter 2.12)

2.10.6 Engineering notes for NinjaTrader 8

  • Hooks. Trade classification needs OnMarketData (last, bid, ask events). Depth needs OnMarketDepth. Neither runs historically without tick replay, and depth never does. The panel is a realtime instrument; historically it should stay blank or clearly use a fallback.
  • Allocation-free hot path. OnMarketData can fire thousands of times a second. No new, no strings, no LINQ, no boxing. All state in primitive fields.
  • Rendering cadence. Do not invalidate the chart on every event. Update state on events; let NinjaTrader repaint at its own rate and read a snapshot in OnRender.
  • Threading. Market data and depth callbacks can arrive on different threads from rendering. Copy the four gauge values into locals at the start of OnRender.
  • Autonomy. I built this panel to stand alone, with no shared infrastructure, so it can go on any chart. That is a deliberate trade: a little duplicated classification logic in exchange for zero coupling.

2.10.7 What it is and is not

Four bounded gauges side by side are a description of the tape: how hard each side is hitting, how fast, how the book is stacked, and how much price is giving way. They are not a signal. All four are noisy, and their correlations change with the regime.

2.10.8 Summary

  • Raw delta grows with activity; divide by volume or z-score it against its own history.
  • Compute the z-score against previous estimates, then update; expect fat tails.
  • Bound gauges with tanh so one extreme does not flatten the display.
  • Event-time estimators move at the speed of the tape.
  • Four gauges describe the tape; they are not a trading signal.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A bar has 800 contracts and delta +200. What is the buy share bb? (Answer: 200=(2b−1)⋅800200 = (2b-1)\cdot 800, so b=0.625b = 0.625.)
