  2. (Think) Show with a small example how including the current bar in μ\mu and σ\sigma shrinks the z-score.
  3. (Apply) With c=2c = 2, what gauge value does z=2z = 2 give? (tanh(1) ≈ 0.76.)
  4. (Design) Why should the liquidity gauge be greyed out, not zero, when there is no depth feed?

Further reading

  • Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov (2014), “The Price Impact of Order Book Events”, Journal of Financial Econometrics.
  • Hawkes (1971), “Spectra of some self-exciting and mutually exciting point processes”, Biometrika.
  • Bacry, Mastromatteo and Muzy (2015), “Hawkes Processes in Finance”, Market Microstructure and Liquidity.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.11 — Absorption: When a Lot of Volume Moves Price Very Little

Subtitle: A volume-to-displacement view of the tape, and why the obvious ratio needs care.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define the volume-to-displacement ratio and choose a displacement measure. 2. Handle tiny displacements with a floor and normalise against a baseline in logs. 3. Add direction with the delta share to say who absorbed whom. 4. Explain why detection belongs on closed bars, and how to study it fairly.

You need: Chapter 2.9 (delta) and Chapter 2.10 (z-scores).

2.11.1 Making a word measurable

“Absorption” is an order-flow word that everyone uses and few define. The intuition: aggressive traders hit the market hard, but a large passive participant soaks it up and price barely moves. I wanted a detector that made this measurable on closed bars, so I built a volume-to-displacement anomaly detector. This chapter is about the method family.

2.11.2 The basic ratio

Definition. For a bar with executed volume VV and displacement DD,

R=VD. R = \frac{V}{D}.

High RR means many contracts per unit of price movement. What is DD?

Displacement DD Formula Answers
Range H−LH - L How far did price travel?
Body |C−O|\lvert C - O\rvert Did it get anywhere?
Close-to-close |Ct−Ct−1|\lvert C_t - C_{t-1}\rvert How far did it move bar to bar?

Range is the most natural “how much did price give” measure. Body is better for “did it get anywhere”. They answer different questions. A bar with a big range and a small body is its own pattern: a two-sided fight.

2.11.3 The division-by-zero problem

On tick and Renko-like bars, displacement can be tiny or zero. V/0V/0 is infinite and V/ϵV/\epsilon is enormous. Add a floor: measure DD in ticks and use max⁡(D,1tick)\max(D, 1\ \text{tick}). The floor is a modelling choice, so document it.

2.11.4 Normalise against the instrument’s own behaviour

Volume per unit of range changes by hour, day and regime. A fixed threshold on RR fires constantly in the morning and never overnight. Compare each bar with its own recent baseline instead:

ρt=RtR‾t,zt=log⁡Rt−μlog⁡Rσlog⁡R. \rho_t = \frac{R_t}{\bar R_t},\qquad z_t = \frac{\log R_t - \mu_{\log R}}{\sigma_{\log R}}.

Work in logs. RR is positive and heavily right-skewed (a long tail of big values). log⁡R\log R is much closer to symmetric, so a z-score means something.

Figure 2.11.1 — Take the log before the z-score. Left: a histogram of a positive, skewed ratio, with a long right tail. Right: the same values after taking logs, which gives a near-symmetric bell. A z-score on the right-hand scale behaves the way people expect; on the left it does not. (Simulation: R = exp of a normal draw with σ = 0.8, 20,000 seeded draws, seed 2026021101; not market data.)

A bar is anomalous when it is both a large ratio relative to baseline and a large standardised deviation. Requiring both guards against firing on a quiet baseline, where small absolute changes look large.

2.11.5 Adding direction with delta

Volume-to-displacement says a lot traded for little movement. It does not say who absorbed whom. Bring in the bar’s delta Δ\Delta (signed aggressor volume) as a share:

δt=ΔtVt∈[−1,1]. \delta_t = \frac{\Delta_t}{V_t} \in [-1, 1].

  • δ\delta strongly positive (buyers aggressive) and price did not rise: a passive seller absorbed the buying.
  • δ\delta strongly negative (sellers aggressive) and price did not fall: a passive buyer absorbed the selling.

Figure 2.11.2 — Read the delta share against the move. Columns are which side was aggressive; rows are what price did. Absorption is the blue middle row: lots of one-sided flow, little displacement. The corner cells where flow and price agree are “price gave way”. A concept table, not data.

The detector I use combines executed volume, displacement and bar-aligned cumulative delta, and evaluates only on closed bars.

2.11.6 Closed bars only

This matters. Inside a forming bar, displacement is still growing and volume is incomplete. A detector that fires intrabar will fire and then un-fire, which is useless for review and dangerous for automation. On Calculate.OnEachTick, I evaluate the anomaly on the first tick of a new bar, using the just-closed bar’s values.

2.11.7 Data honesty

  • Level 1 only. The detector uses executed volume and trade classification from Level 1 (best bid, ask and trades). It does not see the book. “Absorption” here is inferred from trades and price, not observed in resting orders.
  • Delta alignment. Delta must be computed on exactly the same bar boundaries as volume and range. If delta comes from a different series with slightly different boundaries, the ratio mixes data from different intervals.
  • Historical classification. As in Chapter 2.9, historical delta usually comes from a cruder classification than realtime. A detector tuned on realtime data will behave differently historically.

2.11.8 NinjaTrader 8 notes

  • Volume on tick bars is not constant: a 1,000-tick bar holds 1,000 trades, not 1,000 contracts. Use Volume[0], not the tick count.
  • Keep the rolling log-ratio statistics as EWMA state; no lists.
  • Draw markers with Draw.* sparingly, or render them in OnRender; thousands of drawing objects slow the chart.

2.11.9 The trap

The cases where absorption “worked” (price reversed afterwards) are vivid. The cases where the absorber got run over are forgettable. If you study this, record every detection in real time and compare what happened next against bars matched on volume and time of day. Without that, you are measuring memory.

2.11.10 Summary

  • Absorption is high volume per unit of displacement; choose range, body or close-to-close on purpose.
  • Floor tiny displacements and compare against a baseline in log space.
  • The delta share tells you which side was absorbed.
  • Evaluate on closed bars only; keep delta aligned to the same bars.
  • Study every detection against matched controls.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A bar trades 2,000 contracts with a range of 4 ticks; another trades 600 with a range of 0 ticks. Using a 1-tick floor, which has the larger RR? (Answer: 2,000/4 = 500 vs 600/1 = 600, so the second.)
  2. (Think) Why can a z-score on raw RR fire too often on a skewed distribution?
  3. (Apply) A bar has δ=−0.6\delta = -0.6 and closes at its open. Which side absorbed which?
  4. (Design) Describe a matched-control study for absorption detections. What would you match on?

Further reading

  • Kyle (1985), “Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading”, Econometrica.
  • Amihud (2002), “Illiquidity and stock returns”, Journal of Financial Markets.
  • Bouchaud, Bonart, Donier and Gould (2018), Trades, Quotes and Prices, Cambridge University Press.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.12 — Price-Impact Efficiency on a Volume Clock

Subtitle: Measuring how much price gives per unit of signed flow, sampled when the market is busy rather than when the clock ticks.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State Kyle’s lambda and what a large or small value means. 2. Explain why clock-time sampling is a poor fit and how a volume clock helps. 3. Compute a per-bucket price-impact efficiency using the microprice, and bound it. 4. Implement the buckets in NinjaTrader 8 and name the method’s limits.

You need: Chapter 2.9 (signed volume), Chapter 2.10 (tanh, EWMA), and linear regression in outline.

2.12.1 The idea

Kyle’s lambda is one of the cleanest ideas in market microstructure. Price moves in proportion to net order flow, and the constant of proportionality measures how illiquid the market is. I wanted a live, bounded version of that idea for my order-flow panel (Chapter 2.10). The twist that made it work was sampling on a volume clock.

2.12.2 Kyle’s lambda

Model (Kyle 1985). Over an interval, the price change is linear in net signed order flow QQ:

ΔP=λQ+ε. \Delta P = \lambda Q + \varepsilon.

Estimated by regression over many intervals, λ̂\hat\lambda is the price impact per contract.

  • Large λ\lambda: a thin market; flow moves price.
  • Small λ\lambda: a deep market; flow gets absorbed.

2.12.3 The problem with clock time

Estimate λ\lambda on one-minute intervals and you mix minutes with a handful of trades and minutes with thousands. The noise in ΔP\Delta P is very different across them, so the regression is heteroskedastic (its error size varies) and is dominated by the busy minutes.

2.12.4 The volume clock

Sample in volume time instead: close a bucket each time a fixed amount of volume has traded. Easley, López de Prado and O’Hara popularised this for flow toxicity (VPIN). Every bucket holds the same amount of business, so per-bucket statistics are more alike. Returns sampled in volume time are also closer to Gaussian than clock-time returns, an observation going back to Clark (1973) and his view of prices as a process running on a business clock (a “subordinated” process).

Figure 2.12.1 — Equal time versus equal business. Top: simulated trade prints, quiet at first, then a burst, then quiet again. Middle: clock buckets cut the timeline into equal lengths, so some hold almost nothing and one holds the whole burst. Bottom: volume buckets close each time the same volume has traded, so they bunch up in the busy stretch. (Simulation: seeded arrivals with a low rate and a burst, seed 2026021201; not market data.)

2.12.5 Price-impact efficiency per bucket

Within each bucket, track:

  • the price at bucket open (I use the microprice; see Section 2.12.6),
  • signed aggressor volume Q=∑siviQ = \sum s_i v_i,
  • absolute aggressor volume |V|=∑vi|V| = \sum v_i.

Definition (price-impact efficiency). At bucket close,

PIE=ΔP/tickQ/|V|, \text{PIE} = \frac{\Delta P / \text{tick}}{Q / |V|},

or, in a bounded form, compare the sign and size of the price move with the sign and size of the imbalance.

  • High efficiency: flow was one-sided and price moved with it. The market is “giving way”.
  • Low or negative efficiency: flow was one-sided but price did not follow, or moved the other way. Something passive is absorbing, or the flow is uninformed.

It has the same spirit as the absorption detector (Chapter 2.11), but it is measured on a volume clock and continuously, rather than as a per-bar anomaly.

2.12.6 Microprice

The mid-price (B+A)/2(B + A)/2 ignores queue sizes. The microprice weights each side’s price by the opposite side’s queue size:

Pμ=A⋅qB+B⋅qAqA+qB, P^{\mu} = \frac{A \cdot q_B + B \cdot q_A}{q_A + q_B},

where qBq_B and qAq_A are the bid and ask sizes. When the bid queue is much larger, the microprice leans towards the ask, reflecting the likely direction of the next mid-price change. Stoikov (2018) formalised a refined version. For impact measurement it is a better reference than the last trade price, which bounces between bid and ask.

Figure 2.12.2 — The microprice leans with the queues. The horizontal axis is the bid’s share of the top-of-book size; the vertical axis runs from the bid to the ask. The blue line is the microprice formula; the dashed line is the mid-price. With balanced queues they agree; a heavy bid pushes the microprice towards the ask, and a heavy ask pushes it towards the bid. A plot of the formula.

2.12.7 Bounded display

Raw efficiency is unbounded and noisy when QQ is near zero. Two safeguards:

  1. Only compute it when the imbalance |Q|/|V||Q|/|V| exceeds a minimum; otherwise report neutral. “Price moved, flow was balanced” is not an efficiency statement.
  2. Squash with tanh\tanh and smooth across buckets with an EWMA.

2.12.8 NinjaTrader 8 implementation

  • Hook. Bucket accumulation lives in OnMarketData on last-trade events, with bid and ask tracked from the same stream. Bucket edges are volume-based, so they never line up with chart bars. The panel shows the latest completed bucket.
  • Splitting a print across buckets. A large print can overflow the current bucket. Either split it proportionally (cleaner statistics) or let buckets overshoot (simpler). Splitting is a few lines and avoids biased last-bucket sizes.
  • State. Bucket open price, signed volume, absolute volume and a bucket-open flag: four primitives. No allocation.
  • Historical. Without tick replay there are no quotes historically, so no microprice. Show nothing rather than a degraded proxy, or label the proxy.

2.12.9 Caveats

  • λ\lambda is not stable. It varies with time of day, volatility and news. One number per bucket is a noisy snapshot.
  • Impact is concave in size in practice (the “square-root law”: impact grows roughly with the square root of size), so a linear λ\lambda is a local approximation at best.

2.12.10 Summary

  • Kyle’s lambda is price change per unit of net signed flow.
  • Clock-time intervals mix very different amounts of business; volume buckets fix that.
  • Per-bucket efficiency compares the price move (from the microprice) with the flow imbalance.
  • Compute only when flow is one-sided enough, then squash and smooth.
  • Lambda drifts and impact is concave; treat the gauge as a noisy local snapshot.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Bid 100.00 with 30 lots, ask 100.25 with 10 lots. What is the microprice? (Answer: (100.25 × 30 + 100.00 × 10) / 40 = 100.1875.)
  2. (Compute) A bucket has Q=+400Q = +400, |V|=1,000|V| = 1{,}000 and the microprice rose 2 ticks. What is the PIE?
  3. (Think) Why does a regression of ΔP\Delta P on QQ over one-minute bars get dominated by busy minutes?
  4. (Design) A 300-lot print arrives with 100 lots left in the current bucket. Show both the “split” and “overshoot” treatments.

Further reading

  • Kyle (1985), “Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading”, Econometrica.
  • Clark (1973), “A Subordinated Stochastic Process Model with Finite Variance for Speculative Prices”, Econometrica.
  • Easley, López de Prado and O’Hara (2012), “Flow Toxicity and Liquidity in a High-Frequency World”, Review of Financial Studies.
  • Stoikov (2018), “The Micro-Price”, Quantitative Finance.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.13 — Daily CVD Across the Historical/Realtime Seam, and CVD at the POC

Subtitle: The hard part of a session CVD is not the sum. It is making yesterday and right now agree.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why historical and realtime CVD are two different estimators of one quantity. 2. Use one producer and epoch numbers so a consumer never draws stale history. 3. Define CVD conditioned on the developing POC without lookahead. 4. Avoid the common NinjaTrader 8 and interpretation pitfalls.

You need: Chapter 2.9 (CVD and classification) and Chapter 2.4 (POC).

2.13.1 A twenty-line indicator that wasn’t

A session cumulative volume delta is a running sum that resets at the start of each trading day. Plotting it in a subpanel sounds like a twenty-line indicator. Mine became a lesson in where state lives, how history is rebuilt, and how a consumer knows the data it draws is still valid.

2.13.2 The quantity

For the trading day starting at anchor aa:

CVDt=∑i=atsivi, \text{CVD}_t = \sum_{i=a}^{t} s_i v_i,

with sis_i the inferred initiator sign. The level is arbitrary; the shape relative to price is what people read.

2.13.3 Two lives of the same number

Historically, you rebuild CVD from whatever data you have: tick bars with a tick rule, volumetric bars, or bars with bulk volume classification. In realtime, you build it from live quote-rule classification. Those are two different estimators of the same quantity.

If one indicator does both, you see a step at the historical-to-realtime switch. My approach: one producer owns the CVD calculation and publishes both a trend history (for historical bars) and a live packet (for realtime). The subpanel consumer plots history on historical bars and the live value in realtime, from one source.

2.13.4 Epochs: knowing your data is current

A consumer that receives published values needs to know whether they are current. After a workspace reload, a data reconnect, or a producer restart, a consumer might hold history from an earlier run.

Definition (epoch). A number that only ever increases, stamped on each published history. The consumer rejects data from an older epoch than the one it expects; when a newer epoch appears, it rebuilds from the new history.

This is a standard idea from distributed systems (fencing tokens, generation numbers). It removed a whole class of “the panel shows yesterday’s line” bugs.

Figure 2.13.1 — Epoch numbers fence off stale data. The producer publishes history under epoch 1, restarts, then publishes under epoch 2. The consumer accepts epoch 1 while it is current, rejects a late copy of epoch-1 data once it expects more (orange), and rebuilds when epoch 2 arrives (green). Concept diagram with generic names.

2.13.5 Reading CVD against the point of control

A common discretionary read pairs the session volume profile’s point of control (POC, Chapter 2.4) with CVD: what is net aggressive flow doing while price trades around the price of greatest acceptance? One way to define it is the delta accumulated while price is within a band bb of the POC:

CVDtPOC=∑i=atsivi⋅𝟏{|pi−POCi|≤b}. \text{CVD}^{\text{POC}}_t = \sum_{i=a}^{t} s_i v_i \cdot \mathbf{1}\{|p_i - \text{POC}_{i}| \leq b\}.

Note the subscript: the POC at time ii, not the final POC. The developing POC moves during the session. Using the end-of-day POC to classify earlier trades is lookahead, and it is an easy mistake when you rebuild from a finished profile.

Figure 2.13.2 — The POC you could have known. The blue stair-step is the developing POC, recomputed after every step of a simulated session. The orange dashed line is the final POC, known only at the close. For much of the session they differ, so classifying early trades against the final POC uses the future. (Seeded random walk, seed 2026021301, unit volume per step; not market data.)

The interpretation is the usual auction one. Heavy one-sided aggression at the POC that fails to move price suggests the other side is defending value. Aggression that pushes price away from the POC and holds suggests value is migrating. These are descriptions, not forecasts.

2.13.6 NinjaTrader 8 notes

  • Calculate mode. The subpanel runs OnEachTick so the live value updates; historical bars still arrive once per bar.
  • Forward-only history walk. For historical bars, walk the published history with an index keyed by time that only moves forward. Searching the full history for each bar is quadratic.
  • Resets. The producer resets at the CME trading-day boundary. The consumer should have no reset logic of its own; two reset rules will eventually disagree.
  • Plot gaps. Before valid data exists, mark the plot as “not set” (Values[0].Reset()) rather than zero. A zero CVD looks like a real value.
  • Threading. The producer may publish from another instrument’s data thread. Published history should be immutable once handed over (a new array per publish, never edited in place), so the consumer can read it without locks.

2.13.7 Pitfalls

  • Comparing today’s CVD level with yesterday’s: different anchors, so the comparison is meaningless.
  • Treating a rebuilt historical CVD as identical to what you would have seen live.
  • Reading divergences into noise. Classification error alone makes small divergences meaningless.

2.13.8 Summary

  • Historical and live CVD come from different classifiers; one producer should own both.
  • Epoch numbers let a consumer reject stale history and rebuild on new history.
  • CVD at the POC must use the developing POC at each trade’s time.
  • Use forward-only walks, consumer-free resets, “not set” plots and immutable published arrays.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A consumer expects epoch 7 and receives history stamped 6. What should it do? (Answer: reject it and keep waiting for epoch 7 or later.)
  2. (Think) Why does rebuilding CVD-at-POC from a finished profile give a better-looking result than you could have had live?
  3. (Engineering) Why is publishing a new array each time safer than editing a shared one?
  4. (Design) Describe what the subpanel should show between a producer restart and the first epoch-2 publish.

Further reading

  • Lee and Ready (1991), “Inferring Trade Direction from Intraday Data”, Journal of Finance.
  • Kleppmann (2017), Designing Data-Intensive Applications, O’Reilly (fencing tokens and generations).
  • Dalton, Jones and Dalton, Mind Over Markets.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.14 — Two Kalman Filters, One Band: A Dual-Speed Adaptive Prediction Filter

Subtitle: What you get when you run a fast and a slow state-space estimator side by side, and why it is not magic.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Build a band from two local-level Kalman filters that share Q and differ in R. 2. Show that, after warm-up, the band is a dual-EMA band, and name what the Kalman form still adds. 3. Describe the adaptive variants and their risks. 4. Avoid the intrabar update bug in NinjaTrader 8.

You need: Chapter 2.3 (the Kalman recursion and its steady state).

2.14.1 A better-behaved crossover

Moving-average crossovers are the oldest trend tool there is: a fast average, a slow average, and the gap between them. I wanted the same picture with better-behaved estimators. So I built a band from two scalar Kalman filters on the same price, one tuned fast and one slow. I call it an adaptive prediction filter, mostly because “two Kalman filters with different noise ratios” does not fit on a chart label.

2.14.2 Each filter

Both use the local-level model:

xt=xt−1+wt,wt∼𝒩(0,Q);zt=xt+εt,εt∼𝒩(0,R). x_t = x_{t-1} + w_t,\ w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,Q);\qquad z_t = x_t + \varepsilon_t,\ \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal N(0,R).

The recursion:

Pt−=Pt−1+Q,Kt=Pt−Pt−+R,x̂t=x̂t−1+Kt(zt−x̂t−1),Pt=(1−Kt)Pt−. P^-_t = P_{t-1} + Q,\quad K_t = \frac{P^-_t}{P^-_t + R},\quad \hat x_t = \hat x_{t-1} + K_t(z_t - \hat x_{t-1}),\quad P_t = (1-K_t)P^-_t.

In my version the process noise QQ is shared, and each line has its own measurement noise RR. A smaller RR means the filter trusts each observation more: higher gain, faster tracking. A larger RR means more smoothing and more lag.

2.14.3 Why share Q?

QQ is a statement about the world: how much the true price level wanders per bar. That should not differ between two observers of the same market. RR is a statement about the observer: how much each distrusts single bars. Sharing QQ and varying RR keeps both filters consistent with one model of the market and two levels of scepticism. It also means one knob moves both lines together.

2.14.4 Steady state and the EMA equivalence

Result. With constant QQ and RR, KtK_t converges to

K∞=P∞−P∞−+R,P∞−=Q+Q2+4QR2, K_\infty = \frac{P^-_\infty}{P^-_\infty + R},\qquad P^-_\infty = \frac{Q + \sqrt{Q^2 + 4QR}}{2},

and after warm-up each line is an EMA with α=K∞\alpha = K_\infty (derivation in Chapter 2.3).

So a dual-speed Kalman band is, in steady state, a dual-EMA band. The honest value-add is threefold:

  1. A principled cold start. A large starting P0P_0 makes the filter lock on quickly, then settle. An EMA started at the first price has a long, biased warm-up.
  2. One parameterisation. Lag is set by the ratio Q/RQ/R, which has a meaning, instead of a period that has none.
  3. Extensibility. Once it is a state-space model, adding a velocity state, time-varying noise or volume-scaled measurement noise is a small change.

If someone says their Kalman indicator “predicts” price, ask what differs from an EMA. Usually nothing, after warm-up.

Figure 2.14.2 — Cold start: EMA versus Kalman. The true level is 0 and the first observation happens to be +3. The orange EMA, seeded with that first print and using the same steady-state weight, takes dozens of bars to forget it. The blue Kalman filter, started with a large PP, averages the first few prints almost equally and is near 0 within about ten bars. (Noise N(0,1), seed 2026021402; first observation set to +3 to show the effect; illustrative Q and R; not market data.)

2.14.5 The band and its states

The band is the region between the fast and slow estimates. Its width comes from their difference, which is a lagged measure of trend. In a steady trend the fast line leads and the gap opens; in a range the two braid.

Figure 2.14.1 — Fast and slow filters on one series. Grey dots are noisy observations of a level that is flat, then drifts up, then flattens. The solid blue line is the fast filter (small R), the dashed line the slow filter (large R), and the shaded area is the band. During the drift the fast line leads and the band opens; in the flat stretches the lines braid. (Seeded simulation, seed 2026021401; shared Q; illustrative values, not tuned settings; not market data.)

The display classifies three states: both filters rising, both falling, or disagreeing/flat. That is deliberately simple. It is a picture of the smoothed state, not a signal.

2.14.6 Adaptive versions

The “adaptive” part can go further, and the literature has many variants:

Variant Idea
Innovation-based noise estimation Scale RR by recent squared innovations, so the filter smooths more in noisy regimes (Mehra, 1970).
Volatility-scaled QQ Let the level wander more when realised volatility is high.
Multiple-model filters (IMM) Run several models and weight them by likelihood.

Each adds parameters and the risk of fitting noise. I kept the core simple and treated adaptation as a separate, testable change.

2.14.7 NinjaTrader 8 engineering

  • State in fields. Two estimates, two covariances. Store the previous bar’s values explicitly. On OnEachTick, recompute the current bar’s update from the previous bar’s posterior each tick, rather than chaining updates within a bar. Otherwise the filter “updates” dozens of times per bar live and once per bar historically.
  • IsFirstTickOfBar. Commit the posterior to the “previous” fields only when a new bar starts.
  • Series for history. Expose both lines as plots so other code and the data box can read them.
  • Band fill. Fill between the two plots in OnRender with SharpDX, building a path geometry from visible bars only. Dispose the geometry each frame or cache it; leaking SharpDX resources slowly kills the chart.

2.14.8 Pitfalls

  • The intrabar update bug is the big one. It makes live behaviour differ from historical behaviour, so everything you see after a reload looks different from what you saw live.
  • Tuning on the chart in front of you. Adjusting QQ and RR until the colours “work” is a parameter search with an uncounted number of trials.

2.14.9 Summary

  • Two local-level filters with shared Q and different R give a fast and a slow line.
  • After warm-up they are two EMAs; the Kalman form adds a clean cold start, one meaningful ratio, and easy extensions.
  • The band is a lagged picture of trend, not a signal.
  • Recompute each tick from the previous bar’s posterior; commit only on a new bar.
  • Do not tune on the visible chart.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) If both filters share Q and the fast one has the smaller R, which has the larger steady-state gain? (Answer: the fast one; smaller R gives larger K∞K_\infty.)
  2. (Compute) With Q = 0.01 and R = 1, compute K∞K_\infty.
  3. (Think) Show why chaining Kalman updates on every tick of a bar changes the effective gain compared with one update per bar.
  4. (Design) How would you test an innovation-based adaptive R without tuning it on the chart you are looking at?

Further reading

  • Kalman (1960), “A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems”.
  • Mehra (1970), “On the identification of variances and adaptive Kalman filtering”, IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control.
  • Harvey (1989), Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.15 — Impulse MACD: SMMA Channels, ZLEMA and Honest Divergence

Subtitle: A popular community indicator rebuilt from its formula, plus the hardest part of any divergence detector.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Write down the Impulse MACD formula and explain its “dead zone”. 2. Show that Wilder’s smoothed average (SMMA) is just an EMA with a different period. 3. Explain what the zero-lag EMA (ZLEMA) gains and what it costs. 4. Time-stamp a divergence at the bar where it became knowable, not at the peak.

You need: what a moving average and an exponential moving average (EMA) are. The idea of a swing high (a local peak in price).

2.15.1 The idea

The Impulse MACD was made popular on TradingView by the author known as LazyBear. It is a variation on MACD.

Plain MACD is the gap between two EMAs. The Impulse MACD measures something else: how far a fast mid-price has escaped a slow channel built from highs and lows. While the mid-price stays inside the channel, the impulse is zero.

I rebuilt it in NinjaTrader 8, added divergence detection, and learned a few things about moving averages along the way.

2.15.2 The formula

Pick a smoothing length NN. Build three lines:

hit=SMMA(H,N),lot=SMMA(L,N),mit=ZLEMA(H+L+C3,N) \text{hi}_t = \text{SMMA}(H, N),\qquad \text{lo}_t = \text{SMMA}(L, N),\qquad \text{mi}_t = \text{ZLEMA}\!\left(\tfrac{H+L+C}{3}, N\right)

Here HH, LL, CC are each bar’s high, low and close. Then the impulse md\text{md} is:

mdt={mit−hitmit>hitmit−lotmit<lot0otherwise \text{md}_t = \begin{cases} \text{mi}_t - \text{hi}_t & \text{mi}_t > \text{hi}_t \\ \text{mi}_t - \text{lo}_t & \text{mi}_t < \text{lo}_t \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

A signal line is a simple moving average of md\text{md}. The histogram is md\text{md} minus the signal.

The channel is slow. The mid is fast. When the mid breaks out of the channel, the market is “impulsing”. When it is inside, momentum is called neutral.

Figure 2.15.1 — A fast mid against a slow channel. The grey band is the channel between the smoothed highs and the smoothed lows. The blue line is the fast mid. Look at where blue leaves the grey band: only those stretches produce an impulse. The data is a simulated random walk with drift segments, not market data.

Figure 2.15.2 — The dead zone in action. The bars show md\text{md} for the same simulation. They are green when the mid is above the channel and orange when it is below. Where the mid is inside the channel, md\text{md} is exactly zero and no bar is drawn. The blue line is the signal line.

That built-in dead zone is the main idea. The indicator refuses to report momentum during compression.

2.15.3 SMMA is an EMA in disguise

Wilder’s smoothed moving average (SMMA) is:

SMMAt=(N−1)SMMAt−1+xtN=SMMAt−1+1N(xt−SMMAt−1). \text{SMMA}_t = \frac{(N-1)\,\text{SMMA}_{t-1} + x_t}{N} = \text{SMMA}_{t-1} + \frac{1}{N}(x_t - \text{SMMA}_{t-1}).

Result. SMMA(NN) is exactly EMA(2N−12N - 1), apart from how it starts.

Why. An EMA moves a fraction α\alpha of the way toward each new value. The right-hand form above is an EMA with α=1/N\alpha = 1/N. A standard EMA of period MM uses α=2/(M+1)\alpha = 2/(M+1). Set 1/N=2/(M+1)1/N = 2/(M+1) and solve: M=2N−1M = 2N - 1.

My implementation uses this identity and says so in its description, because people sometimes think SMMA is a different filter.

2.15.4 ZLEMA: lower lag, more overshoot

The zero-lag EMA (Ehlers and Way) feeds the EMA a “de-lagged” input:

lag=⌊N−12⌋,x̃t=xt+(xt−xt−lag),ZLEMAt=EMA(x̃,N)t. \text{lag} = \left\lfloor \frac{N-1}{2} \right\rfloor,\qquad \tilde x_t = x_t + (x_t - x_{t-\text{lag}}),\qquad \text{ZLEMA}_t = \text{EMA}(\tilde x, N)_t.

The input x̃\tilde x pushes the recent change forward. For a straight-line trend, that cancels much of the EMA’s lag. The price is overshoot at turning points.

“Zero lag” is marketing. It is lower lag with more overshoot.

Average Lag Overshoot at turns
SMMA(NN) = EMA(2N−12N-1) high none
EMA(NN) medium none
ZLEMA(NN) low yes

2.15.5 Divergence detection

A bearish divergence: price makes a higher high while the oscillator makes a lower high. A bullish divergence is the mirror image on lows. It is simple to say and hard to code without cheating.

Step 1: pivots on both series. You need swing highs in price and in the oscillator. A pivot needs some confirmation bars after the extreme (see the swing pivot chapter). So a divergence can only be known some bars after the second peak.

Step 2: pairing. Pair the latest confirmed price pivot with the previous one. Find the oscillator pivot nearest each and compare. The rule for “nearest” (same bar, or within a window) changes the result.

Step 3: filtering. Require the pivots to be a minimum distance apart, and the oscillator to have crossed some reference between them. Otherwise you get divergences between neighbouring wiggles.

The honesty rule. Mark a divergence at the bar where it became knowable, not at the peak. Drawing the line back to the peak is fine for the eye. Time-stamping the event at the peak is lookahead (using information you did not yet have).

Figure 2.15.3 — The event happens at confirmation, not at the peak. The top curve (price) makes a higher second peak; the bottom curve (oscillator) makes a lower one. The dashed orange lines are what you draw for the eye. The dotted line marks the second peak; the solid line marks the bar where the pivot is confirmed. Only from the solid line onward could anyone have known about the divergence. The shapes are schematic.

2.15.6 NinjaTrader 8 notes

  • Use built-in primitives where they are exact. NT8’s EMA and SMA are fine. An SMMA written as EMA(2N-1) reuses a well-tested implementation. NT8’s EMA starts from the first value, so its warm-up differs from some other platforms. Compare only after warm-up.
  • Cache child indicators in State.DataLoaded. Calling EMA(input, n) inside OnBarUpdate with a new input series each time creates new indicator instances.
  • Intermediate series. HLC3 and the de-lagged input should be Series<double> members, created once.
  • Divergence drawing creates objects. On long charts, render lines in OnRender from a list of structs, rather than calling Draw.Line for each divergence.

2.15.7 What to expect

On a trending day, divergences pile up against the trend, one after another. Each one is “wrong” for a while. Divergence detects slowing momentum, and momentum slows all the time. Treat it as context, not as a signal.

2.15.8 Summary

  • The Impulse MACD measures how far a fast mid escapes a slow high/low channel, and reports zero inside it.
  • SMMA(NN) equals EMA(2N−12N-1); it is not a separate filter.
  • ZLEMA trades lag for overshoot. It is not truly zero-lag.
  • A divergence exists only once both pivots are confirmed. Stamp it there.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) What EMA period equals SMMA(14)? (Answer: 27.)
  2. (Apply) For N=20N = 20, what is the ZLEMA lag? Write out x̃t\tilde x_t. (Answer: lag = 9, so x̃t=2xt−xt−9\tilde x_t = 2x_t - x_{t-9}.)
  3. (Think) A pivot needs 3 bars after the peak to confirm. A backtest records the divergence at the peak bar. What has gone wrong, and how many bars of lookahead does it contain?
  4. (Code) Write an md function that returns zero inside the channel. Test it on a series that never leaves the channel.

Further reading

  • G. Appel, Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors (2005), on MACD.
  • J. W. Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978), on smoothed averages.
  • J. Ehlers and R. Way, “Zero Lag (Well, Almost)”, Technical Analysis of Stocks and Commodities (2010).

— Tariq

Chapter 2.16 — MACD Inside Bollinger Bands: A Momentum Regime Band System

Subtitle: Putting a volatility envelope around momentum, not around price.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain MACD as a band-pass filter and why its units are awkward. 2. Build Bollinger-style bands around MACD and read the three things they show. 3. Turn MACD into a unit-free score with the %B transform.

You need: EMA, standard deviation, and the usual Bollinger bands on price.

2.16.1 The idea

Bollinger bands around price are everywhere. Bands around an oscillator are less common. I think they are more useful.

The question changes. Not “is momentum positive?” but “is momentum unusual compared with its own recent behaviour?”

I went through two versions of this indicator this year. The first was a multi-scale experiment that I later deprecated. The second is a simpler, canonical band system. This chapter describes the method.

2.16.2 MACD recap

MACDt=EMAf(P)t−EMAs(P)t,Signalt=EMAg(MACD)t. \text{MACD}_t = \text{EMA}_f(P)_t - \text{EMA}_s(P)_t,\qquad \text{Signal}_t = \text{EMA}_g(\text{MACD})_t.

Here ff, ss and gg are the fast, slow and signal lengths.

MACD is a band-pass filter: a filter that keeps a middle range of speeds. The slow EMA removes the slow trend. The fast EMA removes the fastest noise.

Its units are price. That is awkward. A MACD of a few points means different things on different instruments, and in quiet versus busy markets.

2.16.3 Bands around momentum

Take a moving mean and a standard deviation of MACD itself, over bb bars:

midt=EMAb(MACD)t,σt=1b∑k=0b−1(MACDt−k−MACD¯)2 \text{mid}_t = \text{EMA}_b(\text{MACD})_t,\qquad \sigma_t = \sqrt{\frac{1}{b}\sum_{k=0}^{b-1}(\text{MACD}_{t-k} - \overline{\text{MACD}})^2} Uppert=midt+kσt,Lowert=midt−kσt. \text{Upper}_t = \text{mid}_t + k\sigma_t,\qquad \text{Lower}_t = \text{mid}_t - k\sigma_t.

Three readings. - Inside the band: momentum at its normal pace. - Piercing the upper band: momentum is extreme to the upside compared with recent history. In a trend, that is acceleration. At the end of a move, it can be exhaustion. The band does not tell you which. - Band width: the volatility of momentum. Narrow bands mean momentum is stable. Widening bands mean it is changing fast.

Figure 2.16.1 — Bands that follow momentum. The blue line is MACD on a simulated driftless random walk (fixed seed, textbook settings 12/26 and a 20-bar band at ±2σ). The grey area is the band. Green dots mark bars above the upper band; orange dots mark bars below the lower band. Note how the band widens right after a fast move, so the next move of the same size no longer pierces it. This is pure noise, so no piercing here means anything.

2.16.4 Acceleration

The first difference of MACD is momentum’s acceleration:

at=MACDt−MACDt−1. a_t = \text{MACD}_t - \text{MACD}_{t-1}.

Plotted as a histogram, it shows when momentum is building or fading. It often turns earlier than MACD crossing its signal line. It is also noisier.

2.16.5 A regime score

What made this a “regime” tool is collapsing the readings into one bounded score. The score says where momentum sits relative to its band. Values above a positive threshold read as a bull regime. Values below a negative threshold read as bear. Between them is rotation.

The normalisation is the familiar %B transform, applied to momentum:

%Bt=MACDt−LowertUppert−Lowert. \%B_t = \frac{\text{MACD}_t - \text{Lower}_t}{\text{Upper}_t - \text{Lower}_t}.

Rescale and centre it and you have a unit-free regime score. It compares across instruments. I do not give my exact scaling or thresholds here, but the idea is entirely standard.

Figure 2.16.2 — %B puts momentum on a fixed ruler. The lower band maps to 0, the middle to 0.5, and the upper band to 1. Readings outside the band go below 0 (orange) or above 1 (green). Because both the top and bottom of the fraction are in price units, the units cancel.

2.16.6 What I deprecated and why

The first version ran momentum and bands at several scales at once. It had an alternative smoothing path using the dual-speed Kalman filter, and a squeeze detector built on an RMS-normalised impulse. It was interesting, and too much.

Four scales of anything disagree somewhere on every bar. Every disagreement invites a story. I kept one canonical scale and moved the rest to research.

Lesson. An indicator that can explain everything explains nothing.

2.16.7 NinjaTrader 8 notes

  • Rolling standard deviation. NT8’s StdDev works on any input series. Feed it the MACD series. Do not recompute the sum of squares by hand each bar unless you need a weighted version.
  • Population vs sample. Bollinger’s original uses the population standard deviation (divide by bb, not b−1b-1). NT8’s StdDev does too. Be consistent if you compare with another platform.
  • Plot order. Draw the band fill before the MACD line, so the line stays visible. With SharpDX fills, the order of draw calls in OnRender is the stacking order.
  • Zero-width bands. At the start of the chart, or in a perfectly flat period, σ=0\sigma = 0 and %B divides by zero. Guard it.

2.16.8 Caveats

Bands around an oscillator inherit all of the oscillator’s lag, plus the band’s own. Extremes are relative to a short history. After a long quiet period, an ordinary move will look extreme. The regime score is a smooth description of momentum, not a forecast of it.

2.16.9 Summary

  • Bands around MACD ask whether momentum is unusual for itself, not just whether it is positive.
  • Inside, above and below the band, plus band width, are the four things to read.
  • %B removes price units and gives a score comparable across instruments.
  • More scales give more disagreement, not more insight.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) MACD = 3, Lower = −1, Upper = 5. What is %B? (Answer: (3 − (−1)) / (5 − (−1)) = 4/6 ≈ 0.67.)
  2. (Think) Why does a band that widens after a big move make the next big move look less extreme?
  3. (Code) Add a guard so %B returns a neutral value when Upper equals Lower. What value would you choose, and why?
  4. (Apply) Compute the acceleration ata_t for MACD values 1.0, 1.4, 1.6, 1.5. (Answer: 0.4, 0.2, −0.1.)

Further reading

  • J. Bollinger, Bollinger on Bollinger Bands (2001).
  • G. Appel, Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors (2005).
  • J. Ehlers, Rocket Science for Traders (2001), on oscillators as filters.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.17 — Energy Expansion and the “Dome”

Subtitle: Separating “which way” from “how much is happening” in a single panel.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Separate direction (signed momentum) from energy (unsigned volatility expansion). 2. Describe the five phases that make a momentum histogram look like a dome. 3. Use hysteresis to stop a state from flickering. 4. Compare three ways to estimate the slope of a noisy series.

You need: standard deviation, moving averages, and the idea of a least-squares line.

2.17.1 Two questions, not one

Most momentum indicators answer one question: which way, and how strongly? They do not say whether the market is expanding or compressing.

A small positive momentum reading in a quiet market and the same reading in a violent market are very different situations.

So I built a momentum-plus-energy panel that shows both at once: a directional histogram, an oscillator confirming it, and a separate energy-expansion line. The shape it tends to trace through a move, rising and then rolling over, is what I loosely call a dome.

2.17.2 Direction and energy

Direction is a signed momentum measure mtm_t. For example, the distance of price from a smoothed baseline, scaled by volatility:

mt=Pt−P‾tσt. m_t = \frac{P_t - \bar P_t}{\sigma_t}.

Energy is an unsigned measure of how much the market is moving compared with its baseline. For example, short-horizon volatility over long-horizon volatility:

Et=σtshortσtlong. E_t = \frac{\sigma^{\text{short}}_t}{\sigma^{\text{long}}_t}.

Reading energy. Et>1E_t > 1: volatility is expanding compared with its baseline. Et<1E_t < 1: compression. Energy has no direction on purpose. A market can expand to the downside.

2.17.3 Why the dome appears

A typical impulse goes through five phases:

Phase Energy Momentum histogram
1. Compression low near zero
2. Ignition starts rising turns
3. Expansion rising bars growing
4. Exhaustion flattens may still be high, but bars stop growing
5. Decay falling falling

Figure 2.17.1 — The dome and its phases. Top: a momentum histogram, green while bars grow and grey once they shrink. Bottom: the energy line, with a dashed line at E = 1. Look at the Expansion-to-Exhaustion boundary: energy has already peaked and is falling while the histogram is still near its top. The shapes are drawn from simple formulas, not market data.

The useful information is in the change, not the level: growing bars versus shrinking bars, energy rising versus flattening. Reading the level alone misses the turn.

2.17.4 A momentum state machine

Rather than leave the dome to the eye, I classify it into a small number of states (building, peaking, fading, and so on) with a confidence measure.

The classification uses the sign and slope of the histogram and the slope of energy. The precise rules are mine. The method family is standard: a finite-state machine (a small set of named states with rules for moving between them) over the sign and first difference of two smoothed series, with hysteresis so the state does not flip on every bar.

Hysteresis. If a state changes when xx crosses a threshold θ\theta, noise around θ\theta makes it chatter. Use two thresholds instead: enter at θin\theta_{\text{in}}, leave at θout<θin\theta_{\text{out}} < \theta_{\text{in}}. The gap absorbs the noise.

Figure 2.17.2 — Two thresholds stop the chatter. The blue line is a noisy slow wave (a sine plus Gaussian noise, fixed seed). The first strip uses one threshold and flips many times wherever the line hovers near it. The second strip enters only above the green line and leaves only below the orange line, and changes state far less often. The state counts are printed on the strips.

2.17.5 Estimating slope

Slopes of noisy series are where most of these indicators go wrong. Three options:

  • First difference, xt−xt−1x_t - x_{t-1}. The most noise.
  • Linear regression slope over a window. A least-squares fit; robust to single-bar noise:

β̂=∑k(k−k‾)(xt−k−x‾)∑k(k−k‾)2. \hat\beta = \frac{\sum_k (k - \bar k)(x_{t-k} - \bar x)}{\sum_k (k - \bar k)^2}.

  • Filtered velocity, from a two-state Kalman filter (one state for level, one for slope).

I tried a dedicated slope engine at one point. I rolled it back when it added complexity without making the picture clearer. Regression slopes over short windows were enough.

2.17.6 NinjaTrader 8 engineering

  • Several plots, one panel. Histogram, oscillator and energy have different scales. Either scale all three to a common range, or put energy on its own panel. Mixed scales make the small series invisible.
  • Histogram colouring. Use PlotBrushes[i][0] to colour each bar by state. Do not create brushes per bar. Freeze custom brushes (brush.Freeze()) so they are thread-safe.
  • State as a Series<double>. Exposing the state and confidence as series lets the data box and other code read them, and keeps history for review.
  • Calculate mode. On OnEachTick, the state of the forming bar changes within the bar. Decide whether consumers read the forming bar or only closed bars. I prefer closed bars for anything that is not purely visual.

2.17.7 Caveats

Energy expansion is not a direction signal. It is often largest at climaxes, just before reversals. The dome is easy to see after the fact and much harder in the middle of it. Every state machine has thresholds, and every threshold is a parameter that can be overfit.

2.17.8 Summary

  • Direction and energy are separate questions; show them separately.
  • An impulse runs compression → ignition → expansion → exhaustion → decay, which draws a dome.
  • Read the change in the bars and in energy, not just the level.
  • Hysteresis (two thresholds) stops states flickering.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Short-horizon volatility is 6, long-horizon is 4. Is the market expanding or compressing? (Answer: E = 1.5 > 1, expanding.)
  2. (Think) Why is energy deliberately unsigned? Give a case where a signed energy would mislead.
  3. (Code) Write a two-threshold state update: if(!on && x > in) on = true; else if(on && x < out) on = false;. Test it on a noisy series and count state changes against a one-threshold version.
  4. (Compare) For the series 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 5, compute the first difference at the last bar and the regression slope over all six points. Which is steadier?

Further reading

  • J. Bollinger, Bollinger on Bollinger Bands (2001), on squeeze and expansion.
  • J. Carter, Mastering the Trade (2012), on the squeeze concept.
  • T. Andersen, T. Bollerslev, F. Diebold and P. Labys, “Modeling and Forecasting Realized Volatility”, Econometrica (2003).

— Tariq

Chapter 2.18 — Bull and Bear Strength with Wilder Smoothing, and Robust Scaling

Subtitle: RSI is two averages pretending to be one number. Splitting them back apart is more informative.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Build RSI from two Wilder averages and read it as a proportion. 2. Seed Wilder’s averages correctly and handle the divide-by-zero case. 3. Explain why fixed RSI thresholds do not travel across bar types. 4. Use the median and MAD for robust scaling, and compute a rolling median cheaply.

You need: moving averages, standard deviation, and what a median is.

2.18.1 What RSI really is

The Relative Strength Index is so familiar that people forget what it is: a ratio of two smoothed averages, one of up-moves and one of down-moves.

I built a bull/bear strength oscillator for NinjaTrader on exactly that machinery, with Wilder’s smoothing and a careful seed. Then I spent some time thinking about how to scale it robustly. This chapter is that story.

2.18.2 The construction

For an input xtx_t (usually the close), split each move into its up part and its down part:

Ut=max⁡(xt−xt−1,0),Dt=max⁡(xt−1−xt,0). U_t = \max(x_t - x_{t-1}, 0),\qquad D_t = \max(x_{t-1} - x_t, 0).

Smooth each with Wilder’s average of length NN:

U‾t=(N−1)U‾t−1+UtN,D‾t=(N−1)D‾t−1+DtN. \bar U_t = \frac{(N-1)\bar U_{t-1} + U_t}{N},\qquad \bar D_t = \frac{(N-1)\bar D_{t-1} + D_t}{N}.

Then

RSt=U‾tD‾t,RSIt=100−1001+RSt. \text{RS}_t = \frac{\bar U_t}{\bar D_t},\qquad \text{RSI}_t = 100 - \frac{100}{1 + \text{RS}_t}.

Result. RSIt=100⋅U‾tU‾t+D‾t\text{RSI}_t = 100 \cdot \dfrac{\bar U_t}{\bar U_t + \bar D_t}.

RSI is the share of recent absolute movement that was upward. It is a proportion, not a momentum level.

Why. Substitute RS=U‾/D‾\text{RS} = \bar U/\bar D: 100−100/(1+U‾/D‾)=100−100D‾/(D‾+U‾)=100U‾/(U‾+D‾)100 - 100/(1 + \bar U/\bar D) = 100 - 100\bar D/(\bar D + \bar U) = 100\bar U/(\bar U + \bar D).

2.18.3 Seeding matters

Wilder seeded each average with a simple mean of the first NN values, then switched to the recursive form.

If you instead start the recursion at zero, or at the first value, the first few dozen bars are biased. Your oscillator disagrees with every other platform’s until the bias fades.

My implementation seeds with a simple average at exactly the bar where enough history exists, and holds a neutral value before that. A small thing. It removes a whole category of “why is my RSI different?” questions.

Edge case. When D‾t=0\bar D_t = 0 (no down-moves in the window), RS is infinite and RSI is 100 by convention. Guard the division explicitly.

2.18.4 Splitting bulls and bears

Plotting U‾\bar U and D‾\bar D (suitably normalised) as two lines tells you more than their ratio.

A rising RSI can mean buyers getting stronger or sellers getting weaker. The ratio cannot tell which. Two lines can.

Figure 2.18.1 — Two lines say what one ratio hides. Green is the Wilder average of up-moves, orange of down-moves, on a simulated random walk (fixed seed, N = 14) with an upward drift added in the marked stretch. During the drift, green rises and orange falls; at other times only one of them moves. RSI would show “rising” in every case.

Band fills between the two lines, coloured by which one is on top, make the balance easy to read at a glance. Keep the colouring logic and the plotted state identical, and say so in a code comment. It is very easy for what the chart shows and what a consumer reads to drift apart.

2.18.5 The scaling problem

RSI’s 0–100 scale looks universal. It is not. The spread of RSI values depends on NN, on the bar type, and on how much the instrument’s moves follow each other.

On Renko or range bars, every bar moves a fixed amount. Then UtU_t and DtD_t are nearly on/off, and RSI behaves like a smoothed count of up-bars. On time bars it is continuous. A fixed threshold that “means overbought” cannot mean the same in both.

A common fix is to standardise the oscillator against its own recent values. The textbook way is a z-score with mean and standard deviation. The robust way uses the median and the median absolute deviation (MAD):

MADt=median⁡k|xt−k−median⁡(x)|,ztrob=xt−median⁡(x)1.4826MADt. \text{MAD}_t = \operatorname{median}_k \big|x_{t-k} - \operatorname{median}(x)\big|,\qquad z^{\text{rob}}_t = \frac{x_t - \operatorname{median}(x)}{1.4826\,\text{MAD}_t}.

Why 1.4826? It makes MAD a consistent estimate of σ\sigma when the data are normal.

Why robust? A few extreme bars barely move the median and MAD, but they inflate a standard deviation a lot. The breakdown point (the share of bad data an estimator can take before it can be pushed anywhere) is 50% for the median and zero for the mean.

Figure 2.18.2 — Spikes inflate the standard deviation more than the MAD. Both lines estimate the spread of Gaussian noise with true σ = 1 (dashed), over a rolling 50-bar window, with three large spikes injected (fixed seed). Each spike lifts the orange standard deviation in a block that lasts exactly one window. The blue MAD estimate wanders with ordinary sampling noise but moves much less at the spikes.

Trading data is full of extreme bars, so robust scaling keeps a normalised oscillator stable through news spikes.

I am careful to say this is a hardening I think about, not a claim about every version I run. The core oscillator is classic Wilder.

2.18.6 Computing a rolling median cheaply

Sorting the window every bar costs O(wlog⁡w)O(w \log w) for a window of ww values. That is wasteful. Better options:

Method Cost per update Notes
Sort each bar O(wlog⁡w)O(w \log w) simple, wasteful
Two heaps with lazy deletion O(log⁡w)O(\log w) max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper
Sorted ring buffer, binary-search insert O(w)O(w) worst case very cache-friendly for small ww

For small windows, a sorted array with insertion is usually fastest in practice. Preallocate it.

2.18.7 NinjaTrader 8 notes

  • Child indicators. NT8’s SMA on an internal Series<double> is fine for the seed. Create them once in State.DataLoaded.
  • One owner for thresholds. If several tools read the same oscillator, define its thresholds in exactly one place. Two copies of a threshold will eventually disagree.
  • Minimal variants. I keep a stripped-down variant for fast tick charts that only computes and plots what is needed, without the rendering extras.

2.18.8 Caveats

RSI-type oscillators mean-revert by construction, because they are bounded. “Overbought” in a strong trend can last a long time. Robust scaling changes the units, not the information.

2.18.9 Summary

  • RSI = up-average / (up-average + down-average): a proportion.
  • Seed Wilder averages with a simple mean; guard the zero-down-move case.
  • Two lines (bulls, bears) show what the ratio hides.
  • Median and MAD scale an oscillator without being dragged by spikes.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) U‾=3\bar U = 3, D‾=1\bar D = 1. What is RSI? (Answer: 100 · 3/4 = 75.)
  2. (Apply) For the values 1, 2, 2, 3, 50, find the median and the MAD. Then find the mean and standard deviation. Which pair describes the “typical” value better?
  3. (Think) On a Renko chart, why does RSI behave like a smoothed count of up-bricks?
  4. (Code) Implement a rolling median with a sorted array and binary-search insert/remove. Check it against a sort-every-bar version on random data.

Further reading

  • J. W. Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978).
  • P. Huber and E. Ronchetti, Robust Statistics (2009).
  • P. Rousseeuw and C. Croux, “Alternatives to the Median Absolute Deviation”, JASA (1993).

— Tariq

Chapter 2.19 — Multi-Timeframe ADX/DMI Regime Ribbons in NinjaTrader 8

Subtitle: Wilder’s directional system on several timeframes at once, and the synchronisation traps of AddDataSeries.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compute +DM, −DM, true range, +DI, −DI, DX and ADX. 2. Explain why ADX is slow. 3. Name the five multi-timeframe traps in NinjaTrader 8 and avoid lookahead between timeframes. 4. Render ribbons cheaply and publish their state once.

You need: Wilder’s smoothing (see the previous chapter) and the idea of OHLC bars.

2.19.1 Why ribbons

“Is this market trending?” has a different answer on every timeframe. A one-minute downtrend inside an hourly uptrend is normal.

I wanted a compact way to see trend state on several timeframes stacked together. So I built a ribbon indicator: horizontal bands, one per timeframe, each coloured by a directional-movement regime. The maths is fifty years old. The multi-timeframe plumbing is where the work was.

2.19.2 Wilder’s directional movement

For each bar, with high HH, low LL and close CC:

+DMt={Ht−Ht−1if Ht−Ht−1>Lt−1−Lt and >00otherwise +DM_t = \begin{cases} H_t - H_{t-1} & \text{if } H_t - H_{t-1} > L_{t-1} - L_t \text{ and } > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} −DMt={Lt−1−Ltif Lt−1−Lt>Ht−Ht−1 and >00otherwise -DM_t = \begin{cases} L_{t-1} - L_t & \text{if } L_{t-1} - L_t > H_t - H_{t-1} \text{ and } > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}

In words: +DM is the new ground gained above yesterday’s high, if that beats the ground gained below yesterday’s low. −DM is the mirror.

True range is the bar’s full range including any gap from the previous close:

TRt=max⁡(Ht−Lt,|Ht−Ct−1|,|Lt−Ct−1|). TR_t = \max(H_t - L_t,\ |H_t - C_{t-1}|,\ |L_t - C_{t-1}|).

Smooth all three with Wilder’s average, then:

+DIt=100+DM¯tTR¯t,−DIt=100−DM¯tTR¯t, +DI_t = 100\frac{\overline{+DM}_t}{\overline{TR}_t},\qquad -DI_t = 100\frac{\overline{-DM}_t}{\overline{TR}_t}, DXt=100|+DIt−−DIt|+DIt+−DIt,ADXt=Wilder(DX)t. DX_t = 100\frac{|+DI_t - -DI_t|}{+DI_t + -DI_t},\qquad ADX_t = \text{Wilder}(DX)_t.

Reading it. +DI against −DI gives direction. ADX gives strength, whatever the direction.

Why ADX is slow. It is smoothed twice: DX is built from smoothed inputs, then smoothed again. It often peaks after most of the move is over.

2.19.3 Regime colouring

Each ribbon band encodes a few states: strong up (ADX high, +DI on top), strong down, and weak or transitional. Add rising versus falling ADX and you have a compact regime code per timeframe.

Where “strong” ends and “weak” begins is a judgement call. The usual values in the literature are reasonable starting points, but they behave differently on non-time bars.

2.19.4 The multi-timeframe plumbing

NinjaTrader 8 adds extra timeframes with AddDataSeries in State.Configure. Each added series gets a BarsInProgress index. OnBarUpdate is called once per series per bar update. The traps:

  1. Which series is updating? Always branch on BarsInProgress. Computing the higher-timeframe ADX on the primary series’ updates gives nonsense.
  2. Indicator on a secondary series. ADX(BarsArray[2], n) creates an ADX bound to that series. Create it once in State.DataLoaded.
  3. Reading a higher timeframe from the primary. See Figure 2.19.1.
  4. Historical ordering. Historically, NT8 processes bars in timestamp order across series. Bars with the same timestamp are processed in BarsInProgress order. A 15-minute bar stamped 10:15 and a primary bar stamped 10:15 can arrive in an order that matters. In realtime, the order depends on tick arrival. This is the classic source of “the backtest and live disagree”.
  5. Warm-up. A high timeframe needs many of its own bars for ADX to settle. With only a few days loaded, the slowest ribbon may never warm up. Load enough history, and draw nothing (not a default colour) until the value is valid.

Figure 2.19.1 — What “[0]” means on the higher timeframe. The primary bar closes at 10:07. The 15-minute bar that will close at 10:15 is still forming. With Calculate.OnBarClose, Closes[2][0] is the last completed 15-minute bar (closed 10:00). With OnEachTick on that series, [0] is the forming bar. Know which you want. Mixing them is how lookahead creeps in.

2.19.5 Non-time timeframes

My ribbons are not only minutes. The bands can come from different Renko or tick timeframes, stacked from fastest to slowest.

On Renko bars, the high and low are tied to the brick, so true range is nearly constant. DI then behaves differently than on time bars. That is not wrong, but thresholds borrowed from time-bar literature will not mean the same thing.

2.19.6 Rendering

Four horizontal bands are cheap to draw in OnRender: one rectangle per bar per band, coloured from cached SharpDX brushes. On long charts:

  • draw only visible bars (ChartBars.FromIndex to ToIndex);
  • merge consecutive same-colour bars into one rectangle. That cuts draw calls dramatically.

Figure 2.19.2 — Stacked ribbons, merged runs, honest warm-up. Four bands from fastest (top) to slowest (bottom). Each coloured block is one merged run, drawn as a single rectangle. The dashed boxes on the left are the warm-up stretch, where nothing is drawn; slower bands need longer. The colours come from a seeded random process, not from market data.

2.19.7 Publishing state

A ribbon is a display. If other components want the same regime information, they should read it from a published state, not recompute ADX with their own settings. One computation, many readers. I publish the master timeframe’s ADX/ribbon state for exactly that reason.

2.19.8 Caveats

ADX’s lag means regime changes are confirmed late. Agreement across timeframes looks compelling on a chart, but it is mostly repeated information: higher timeframes contain the lower ones.

2.19.9 Summary

  • +DI vs −DI gives direction; ADX gives strength and is slow because it is smoothed twice.
  • Always branch on BarsInProgress and create secondary-series indicators once.
  • Know whether [0] on a higher timeframe is the completed bar or the forming bar.
  • Draw nothing until warmed up; merge same-colour runs; publish state once.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Today H = 105, L = 99; yesterday H = 103, L = 100, C = 101. Find +DM, −DM and TR. (Answer: up-move 2, down-move 1, so +DM = 2, −DM = 0; TR = max(6, 4, 2) = 6.)
  2. (Think) Why can the same strategy give different results in a historical run and in realtime when two series share a timestamp?
  3. (Apply) On a Renko chart where every bar’s range equals one brick, what happens to true range? What does that do to DI?
  4. (Code) Write OnBarUpdate so the higher-timeframe ADX is only updated when BarsInProgress == 2.

Further reading

  • J. W. Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978).
  • NinjaTrader 8 Help Guide: “Multi-Time Frame & Instruments”.
  • P. Kaufman, Trading Systems and Methods, 5th ed. (2013).

— Tariq

Chapter 2.20 — Trend-Measure Histograms: How Strong Is This Leg?

Subtitle: A directional-strength index, a predictor slope, and colour that means one thing at a time.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compare three families of trend measure: ADX-style, efficiency-style and regression-style. 2. Compute Kaufman’s efficiency ratio by hand. 3. Design a histogram where height and colour carry different information. 4. Avoid the common pitfalls: exhaustion as timing, cross-bar-type comparison, lag stacking.

You need: ADX (previous chapter) and the idea of a least-squares line.

2.20.1 The question

Once regime ribbons tell you whether a timeframe is trending, the next question is how strong the current leg is, and whether it is fading.

I built a trend-measure histogram for that: bar height for strength, colour for direction and momentum state. It is a small indicator. Designing it made me think hard about what each visual channel should carry.

2.20.2 Three families of trend measure

A good trend measure is high when price moves steadily in one direction, and low when it goes back and forth.

ADX-style. Smoothed directional movement relative to true range (see Chapter 2.19). Strength without direction. Slow.

Efficiency-style. Net displacement over path length:

ERt=|Pt−Pt−n|∑k=0n−1|Pt−k−Pt−k−1|∈[0,1]. \text{ER}_t = \frac{|P_t - P_{t-n}|}{\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|P_{t-k} - P_{t-k-1}|} \in [0, 1].

One for a straight line, near zero for noise.

Figure 2.20.1 — Same net move, different paths. Both paths end 6 units above where they start (the green bar). The straight one travels 6 units to get there, so ER = 1. The choppy one travels 14 units, so ER = 6/14 ≈ 0.43. The step sizes are a made-up worked example.

Regression-style. The R2R^2 of a straight-line fit of price on time over a window, or the t-statistic of the slope:

tβ=β̂SE(β̂). t_\beta = \frac{\hat\beta}{\text{SE}(\hat\beta)}.

High |tβ||t_\beta| means a slope that is large compared with the noise around the line. This is the most statistically grounded of the three, and the one most people skip.

Family Signed? Speed Grounding
ADX-style no slow (double-smoothed) heuristic
Efficiency ratio no (can be signed) fast simple geometry
Regression t-stat yes medium statistical

My histogram uses a directional trend-measure index for height, which sits in the ADX family, and a separate predictor slope for direction.

2.20.3 Separating the channels

The design choice I care about most: height and colour carry different information.

  • Height: strength of the current leg, unsigned.
  • Colour: direction (from the sign of a smoothed price slope) and momentum state (whether strength is rising or falling).

So a tall green bar is a strong, still-expanding bull leg. A tall bar that turns to a neutral colour is a strong leg losing momentum.

Taking direction from a separate slope estimator, rather than from the histogram’s sign, avoids a common problem: an unsigned measure with an arbitrary sign stuck on.

Figure 2.20.2 — Height says how much; colour says which way and whether it is still building. A schematic bull leg then a bear leg. Bars are green or orange while strength is rising, and turn grey as soon as it declines, even though the bars are still tall. The dashed reference line is for the eye only. The shapes are drawn from a formula, not data.

2.20.4 The predictor slope

Direction comes from the slope of a smoothed price estimate. A filtered estimate (for example a Kalman level with a slope state, or a least-squares slope over a short window) keeps the colour from flickering bar to bar, unlike a raw difference.

The trade-off is lag: the smoother the slope, the later the colour changes.

2.20.5 Reference lines

A horizontal line at the usual “strong trend” level helps the eye. I keep it purely visual.

Danger. A line on a chart becomes a threshold in someone’s head, and then in someone’s code, without ever having been tested.

2.20.6 NinjaTrader 8 notes

  • Plot style. PlotStyle.Bar gives a histogram natively. Per-bar colour with PlotBrushes[0][0] = brush is cheap if the brushes are created once and frozen.
  • Closed-bar colour. On OnEachTick, the forming bar’s colour can change many times. That is fine visually. Anything that reads the state should read [1].
  • Child indicators. If the measure uses NT8’s ADX or DM, create them once. They are Wilder-smoothed, so warm-up is long. Hide the first part of the output until warmed up.
  • Scale. If the measure is bounded, fix the panel’s scale (override OnCalculateMinMax, or set the min/max behaviour). Auto-scaling a bounded indicator makes weak trends look strong on quiet days.

2.20.7 Pitfalls

  • Exhaustion colour as a timing signal. A falling trend measure often appears mid-trend as the move pauses. “Losing momentum” is not “reversing”.
  • Comparing across bar types. On Renko, path length per bar is constant. That changes the efficiency and ADX distributions entirely.
  • Lag stacking. A smoothed slope on top of a double-smoothed ADX gives a very late indicator. Know the total lag.

2.20.8 Summary

  • Trend measures come in ADX, efficiency and regression families; the regression t-stat is the most grounded.
  • ER = net move / path length, from 0 (noise) to 1 (straight line).
  • Let height carry strength and colour carry direction and momentum state, from separate estimators.
  • Reference lines are visual; read closed bars; know your total lag.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Moves +1, −1, +1, +1, +1. What is ER? (Answer: net 3, path 5, ER = 0.6.)
  2. (Think) Why is attaching a sign to an unsigned measure like ADX a problem? What does a separate slope estimator fix?
  3. (Apply) A slope estimator lags by 4 bars and ADX by about 10. Roughly how late is the colour change on a fresh trend?
  4. (Code) Fit a least-squares line to the last 10 closes and compute tβt_\beta. Compare it with ER on a trending and a choppy simulated series.

Further reading

  • J. W. Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978).
  • P. Kaufman, Trading Systems and Methods (2013), on the efficiency ratio and trend measures.
  • J. Ehlers, Cycle Analytics for Traders (2013).

— Tariq

Chapter 2.21 — A Signed Kaufman Efficiency Ratio on Renko Bricks

Subtitle: Measuring how straight price is moving, on a chart where every bar is the same size.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compute Kaufman’s efficiency ratio (ER) and its signed version. 2. Show that on Renko, ER is just the imbalance between up and down bricks. 3. Explain why the right null for Renko ER is a simulation with the same brick rules, not a coin flip. 4. Update ER in constant time per brick.

You need: the efficiency ratio (Chapter 2.20) and the Renko random-walk null (Chapter 6.1).

2.21.1 The statistic

Kaufman’s efficiency ratio is my favourite simple statistic. It answers “how much of the movement went somewhere?” in one number between zero and one.

On Renko bricks it becomes even simpler and, I think, more interesting, because the brick size removes the noise in the denominator.

I built a Renko-only efficiency ribbon with a signed value on the right scale. Its colours are explicitly descriptive, not permission to trade.

2.21.2 The ratio

Over nn bars:

ERt=|Ct−Ct−n|∑k=0n−1|Ct−k−Ct−k−1|. \text{ER}_t = \frac{|C_t - C_{t-n}|}{\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|C_{t-k} - C_{t-k-1}|}.

The top is net displacement. The bottom is total path length. A straight line scores 1. A perfectly back-and-forth series scores 0.

Kaufman used it to set the speed of his adaptive moving average (KAMA): fast when the market is efficient, slow when it is choppy.

2.21.3 What happens on Renko

On a Renko chart with brick size bb, every close-to-close move is exactly ±b\pm b. (This ignores the reversal-brick convention, where a reversal is drawn as one brick after a larger price move.)

So the path length over nn bricks is just nbnb, and:

Result. On Renko, ERt=|Ct−Ct−n|nb=|#up−#down|n. \text{ER}_t = \frac{|C_t - C_{t-n}|}{nb} = \frac{|\#\text{up} - \#\text{down}|}{n}. The efficiency ratio is simply the absolute imbalance between up-bricks and down-bricks in the window.

That is a much cleaner object: a function of a sequence of ±1\pm 1 steps.

Figure 2.21.1 — ER on Renko is a count. Ten bricks: seven up (green), three down (orange). Each brick moves exactly one brick size, so the path is 10 bricks and the net move is +4. ER = 4/10 = |7 − 3|/10 = 0.4. The sequence is a made-up example.

2.21.4 The null distribution

Because ER is a function of ±1\pm 1 steps, you can write down its distribution under a random walk.

If each brick were independently up with probability pp, then #up∼Binomial(n,p)\#\text{up} \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p) and

ER=|2#upn−1|. \text{ER} = \left|\frac{2\,\#\text{up}}{n} - 1\right|.

But Renko bricks are not independent on a random walk. As Chapter 6.1 showed, the reversal asymmetry makes continuation more likely than reversal by construction. Under the classic rule, the brick sequence is a Markov chain (each brick depends only on the one before) with continuation probability r/(1+r)r/(1+r) for reversal size rr.

Consequence. A high ER on Renko is partly geometry. Any use of it needs a Monte Carlo null: a driftless random walk, rendered with the same brick rules, and ER measured on that.

Figure 2.21.2 — Renko geometry alone pushes ER up. Distribution of ER over 10-brick windows. Grey: independent fair bricks (the binomial model). Blue: bricks drawn with the classic r = 2 rule on a fair random walk. Neither has any edge, yet the Renko version puts much more weight on high ER and has a higher mean (printed in the legend). Both are seeded simulations of 20,000 windows; no market data.

2.21.5 Signing it

The unsigned ratio says “straight” without saying which way. A signed version carries direction:

ERt±=Ct−Ct−n∑k|Ct−k−Ct−k−1|∈[−1,1]. \text{ER}^{\pm}_t = \frac{C_t - C_{t-n}}{\sum_k |C_{t-k} - C_{t-k-1}|} \in [-1, 1].

My display keeps the colour ribbon tied to efficiency (how straight). The signed value on the right scale reflects the latest closed brick direction. Two lookbacks, one short and one long, show whether the current leg is straight compared with the longer context.

2.21.6 Why “not trade permission”

A ribbon that turns a confident colour invites people to treat it as a green light. I state in the description that the colours are not trade permission, because efficiency describes the past window, not the next brick.

Writing that down sounds pedantic. It prevents a surprising amount of misuse.

2.21.7 Shadow logging instead of gating

Efficiency is an obvious candidate for a chop filter: block activity when the market is inefficient. Before letting any such filter affect anything, I log what it would have done next to what actually happened. That is the subject of the next chapter.

2.21.8 NinjaTrader 8 notes

  • Restrict to Renko. The simplification above only holds on Renko-like bars. The indicator is built for Renko only. If you write one, check the bar type in State.DataLoaded and visibly refuse to run on other types, rather than silently computing something different.
  • Constant-time updates. Keep a running count of up and down bricks over the window with a ring buffer. Add the new brick, remove the one falling out. No loop over the window each bar.
  • Closed bricks only. A Renko brick does not exist until it completes. Use OnBarClose, or evaluate on the first tick of the next brick.
  • Ribbon rendering. A thin strip at the bottom of the panel, one rectangle per brick, merged across same-colour runs. Compute widths from the chart’s actual bar spacing, not a constant, so zoom works.

2.21.9 Summary

  • ER = net move / path length; on Renko it is |#up − #down| / n.
  • Renko bricks are not independent even on a random walk, so a coin-flip null is wrong.
  • Use a simulated null with the same brick rules before reading anything into ER.
  • Colours describe the past window; they are not trade permission.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) In a 20-brick window there are 14 up and 6 down. What is ER, and what is the signed ER? (Answer: 8/20 = 0.4 and +0.4.)
  2. (Apply) Under independent fair bricks with n = 4, list the possible ER values and their probabilities.
  3. (Simulate) Repeat Figure 2.21.2 with r = 3. Does the gap between the two distributions grow or shrink? Why?
  4. (Code) Write the ring-buffer update that keeps #up and #down for the last n bricks in O(1) per brick.

Further reading

  • P. Kaufman, Smarter Trading (1995), on the efficiency ratio and KAMA.
  • P. Kaufman, Trading Systems and Methods (2013).
  • W. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1 (1968), on random walks and gambler’s ruin.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.22 — Shadow-Logging a Chop Gate Before Trusting It

Subtitle: The cheapest experiment in trading infrastructure is the one where nothing happens.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe a gate as a binary classifier and say what makes it valuable. 2. Name the two biases that make backtested gates look better than they are. 3. Design a shadow log: what to record, and what not to. 4. Implement a safe shadow logger in NinjaTrader 8.

You need: conditional expectation (“the average of Y given that…”) and basic NinjaScript.

2.22.1 The temptation

Every system builder eventually wants a chop filter: something that says “the market is going nowhere, stand aside”. It is one of the most intuitive ideas in trading, and one of the easiest to fool yourself with.

My rule now: no gate gets to affect anything until it has spent time running in the shadows, writing down what it would have done. This chapter is about that practice and how I implemented it in NinjaTrader.

2.22.2 What a gate is, statistically

A gate is a binary classifier gt∈{0,1}g_t \in \{0, 1\}, evaluated at decision time tt. Its value lies entirely in the two groups it separates:

value(g)∼𝔼[Y∣gt=1]−𝔼[Y∣gt=0], \text{value}(g) \sim \mathbb{E}[Y \mid g_t = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid g_t = 0],

where YY is whatever outcome matters downstream.

The trap. A gate that blocks a random 30% of opportunities looks like it “reduces bad trades”, because it reduces all trades. The real question is whether the blocked set is worse than the allowed set, by enough to matter, out of sample.

Two biases make backtested gates look better than they are:

  1. Selection on the outcome. Gates are usually invented by looking at losing periods and asking what they had in common. That is fitting the gate to the sample.
  2. Lookahead in the inputs. Chop measures built on the current bar’s close, or on a window that includes the bar being decided, leak information. In a backtest that is invisible. In live trading it is impossible.

2.22.3 Shadow mode

Definition. Shadow mode: compute the gate live, exactly as it would run in production, record it with full context, and do not let it affect anything. Later, join the log with what actually happened.

Figure 2.22.1 — The gate runs live but has no effect. Each closed realtime bar triggers the gate, computed exactly as in production. Its decision and inputs go into an append-only log. The dashed orange link shows that nothing flows to downstream decisions. Outcomes come later, from independent data, and are joined only at analysis time. Box names are generic.

This buys things a backtest cannot:

  • Real timing. The gate is computed at the moment it would be used, with the data available then, including the seam between historical and realtime data and any late or missing ticks.
  • Real data. Live-feed quirks, reconnects and session boundaries are all present.
  • Honest sample. The sample is fixed before you look at outcomes. You cannot fit it after the fact.

2.22.4 What to log

One row per closed bar, append-only, with:

  • wall-clock UTC time and bar time (they differ; the gap is latency),
  • instrument and bar configuration,
  • the bar’s OHLC and direction,
  • every input the gate uses, at the values it saw,
  • the gate’s decision,
  • the age of any upstream data the gate depended on.
