The last one is subtle. If an input comes from another component and that component stalled, the gate silently ran on stale data. Recording the age makes that visible in the analysis instead of hiding it in the average.

Do not log outcomes in the same row. Outcomes are joined later from independent data. Mixing them into the logger invites code that peeks.

2.22.5 Implementation in NinjaTrader 8

My shadow logger is a tiny overlay indicator:

Choice Why
Calculate.OnBarClose one row per completed bar, nothing intrabar
returns unless State == State.Realtime historical rows would be a backtest wearing a shadow-log costume
bar-type check runs only on the bar type it was designed for
one CSV per instrument per day, fixed header, in NinjaTrader’s user data directory boring on purpose: any tool can read it, a human can eyeball it
IsSuspendedWhileInactive = false a minimised chart keeps logging
catch I/O exceptions, print once per session, carry on a logger that crashes the chart is worse than one that misses a row; silent failure is worse still
CultureInfo.InvariantCulture for numbers a machine with a comma decimal separator would otherwise write a CSV that parses wrong

File writes can fail (antivirus locks, a full disk). That is why the I/O handling is explicit.

Writing is a synchronous append. At one row per bar, that is negligible. If it ever became a problem, a background writer with a bounded queue would be the next step.

2.22.6 Analysis discipline

When enough rows exist, the analysis is pre-registered: which outcome, which horizon and which comparison are decided before looking.

  • The baseline is the same outcome on bars where the gate was open, and on random subsets of the same size.
  • The number of variants examined is counted. Examining ten gate definitions on the same shadow log is ten trials.

2.22.7 Why bother

A shadow log is slow. You have to wait for the market to produce data. But it is the only test where the gate cannot see the future. It turns “I think this filter helps” into a question with a clean answer. I have retired more ideas through shadow logs than through any backtest.

2.22.8 Summary

  • A gate’s value is the difference between the outcomes it allows and those it blocks, not how many it blocks.
  • Backtested gates suffer from selection on the outcome and lookahead in the inputs.
  • Shadow mode runs the gate live with no effect and logs inputs, decision and data age, but not outcomes.
  • Pre-register the analysis, compare against random subsets, and count every variant.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A gate blocks 40% of bars. Allowed bars and blocked bars have the same average outcome. What is the gate’s value? (Answer: zero; it only reduces activity.)
  2. (Think) Why does logging the age of upstream data matter even when the gate’s logic is correct?
  3. (Design) Write the CSV header for a shadow log following Section 2.22.4. Which column would tempt someone to peek if you added it?
  4. (Apply) You test 12 gate definitions on one shadow log and report the best. How many trials should you report?

Further reading

  • C. Harvey, Y. Liu and H. Zhu, “…and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns”, Review of Financial Studies (2016), on multiple testing.
  • D. Bailey and M. López de Prado, “The Deflated Sharpe Ratio”, Journal of Portfolio Management (2014).
  • R. Kohavi, D. Tang and Y. Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020), on dark launches.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.23 — Realised Versus “Historical” Volatility: Two Estimators and Their Ratio

Subtitle: A short-window RMS and an exponentially weighted variance disagree on purpose. The disagreement is the signal.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compute realised volatility (a short-window RMS) and EWMA “historical” volatility from log returns. 2. Work out an EWMA’s effective window and half-life. 3. Explain the friction ratio and why the annualisation factor cancels. 4. Say when range-based estimators help and when microstructure noise hurts.

You need: logarithms, averages, and the EMA.

2.23.1 Volatility is estimated, not observed

Different estimators answer different questions. Putting two of them side by side tells you something neither tells alone.

I built a small, standalone volatility indicator. It computes a realised volatility, an exponentially weighted “historical” volatility, and the ratio between them, which I call friction.

2.23.2 Log returns

Start from log returns on whatever bar type the chart uses:

rt=ln⁡CtCt−1. r_t = \ln\frac{C_t}{C_{t-1}}.

Log returns add up across time and are roughly symmetric. That is why every estimator below uses them.

2.23.3 Realised volatility: a short-window RMS

RVOLt=1n∑i=0n−1rt−i2⋅A. \text{RVOL}_t = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} r_{t-i}^2}\cdot\sqrt{A}.

No mean is subtracted. At intraday horizons the mean return is tiny next to its spread, and estimating it only adds noise. Using the raw second moment is the realised-variance convention of Andersen, Bollerslev and colleagues.

AA is the annualisation factor: the number of bars per year. On time bars that is bars per day times trading days. On Renko or tick bars, bars per day is not constant, so the factor is an approximation based on a typical count. The level of annualised volatility on those bars is therefore only roughly comparable to quoted volatility. The ratio below does not care, because AA cancels.

2.23.4 Historical volatility: EWMA

σt2=αrt2+(1−α)σt−12,HVOLt=σtA. \sigma_t^2 = \alpha r_t^2 + (1-\alpha)\sigma_{t-1}^2,\qquad \text{HVOL}_t = \sigma_t\sqrt{A}.

This is the RiskMetrics estimator (J.P. Morgan, 1996). In model terms it is an IGARCH(1,1) without a constant.

Memory of an EWMA. The effective window is about 2/α−12/\alpha - 1 bars. The half-life (bars until a shock’s weight halves) is ln⁡2/−ln⁡(1−α)\ln 2 \,/\, {-\ln(1-\alpha)}.

Figure 2.23.1 — Short memory reacts first; long memory catches up. Simulated Gaussian returns whose true σ (dashed) jumps from 1 to 2.5 and back (fixed seed). Blue is a 20-bar RMS; orange is an EWMA with α = 0.01, both per bar (A = 1). After each jump, blue reaches the new level within about 20 bars, while orange takes much longer. Settings are for illustration only.

2.23.5 Friction: the ratio

Ft=RVOLtHVOLt. F_t = \frac{\text{RVOL}_t}{\text{HVOL}_t}.

With a short realised window and a long-memory EWMA, FF compares “how much is price moving right now” with “how much has it been moving”.

Reading friction. Above 1: expansion. Below 1: compression. Both estimators use the same returns, so A\sqrt{A} cancels and FF has no units. It is comparable across instruments.

Figure 2.23.2 — The ratio flags the change, then fades. The friction ratio for the same simulation. When true σ rises (between the dotted lines), F jumps above 1, then drifts back toward 1 as the EWMA catches up. When σ drops back, F falls well below 1 for a long stretch. F measures change in volatility, not its level.

I describe regimes as ranges of FF (compression, normal, expansion). Those cut-offs are judgement, and I treat them as descriptive labels.

2.23.6 Why not a fancier estimator?

Range-based estimators use more of each bar’s information:

Estimator Uses Note
Parkinson (1980) high, low σ̂2=14ln⁡2(ln⁡H/L)2\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{4\ln 2}(\ln H/L)^2
Garman–Klass (1980) adds open and close more efficient
Rogers–Satchell (1991) OHLC robust to drift
Yang–Zhang (2000) OHLC + previous close handles opening jumps

On time bars they are more efficient, often several times so. On Renko bars they are nearly useless: high and low are tied to the brick construction, so the range carries little beyond the brick size.

For an indicator meant to run on Renko and tick charts as well as time charts, close-to-close estimators are the honest choice. On time bars alone, I would use a range estimator.

2.23.7 Microstructure noise

At very high sampling frequency, realised variance is biased upward by bid-ask bounce. The observed price is the true price plus noise, and squared returns pick up that noise twice.

That is why realised-volatility research samples at intervals like five minutes, or uses kernel or two-scale estimators (Zhang, Mykland and Aït-Sahalia, 2005). On Renko bars, the brick size acts as a crude noise filter. On fast tick charts the bias is real, and a ratio of two biased estimators is only partly protected.

2.23.8 NinjaTrader 8 engineering

  • Standalone. The indicator depends on nothing else, so it can go on any chart.
  • Rolling sum of squares. Keep a ring buffer of r2r^2 and a running sum. Add the new value, subtract the outgoing one. Recompute the sum from scratch now and then to stop floating-point drift.
  • EWMA start. Seed σ2\sigma^2 from the mean square of the first few returns, not zero. Otherwise HVOL starts near zero and FF explodes during warm-up.
  • Plot scaling. Volatility and the ratio live on different scales. A display-only scale factor can line them up visually. Keep it out of any computed value.
  • Zero or missing closes. Guard the log against non-positive prices (bad prints, unadjusted spreads).

2.23.9 Summary

  • RVOL is a short RMS of log returns with no mean subtracted; HVOL is a long-memory EWMA.
  • An EWMA with weight α remembers about 2/α − 1 bars.
  • Friction F = RVOL / HVOL is unit-free: above 1 means expansion, below 1 compression.
  • Range estimators help on time bars, not on Renko; very fast sampling inflates realised variance.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) For α = 0.05, what is the EWMA’s effective window? (Answer: 2/0.05 − 1 = 39 bars.)
  2. (Apply) Compute the half-life for α = 0.05. (Answer: ln 2 / −ln 0.95 ≈ 13.5 bars.)
  3. (Think) Why does the annualisation factor cancel in F, and why does that matter on Renko charts?
  4. (Simulate) Repeat Figure 2.23.1 with α = 0.1. How do the two lines and the ratio change?

Further reading

  • J.P. Morgan/Reuters, RiskMetrics — Technical Document (1996).
  • T. Andersen, T. Bollerslev, F. Diebold and P. Labys, “Modeling and Forecasting Realized Volatility”, Econometrica (2003).
  • D. Yang and Q. Zhang, “Drift-Independent Volatility Estimation Based on High, Low, Open, and Close Prices”, Journal of Business (2000).
  • L. Zhang, P. Mykland and Y. Aït-Sahalia, “A Tale of Two Time Scales”, JASA (2005).

— Tariq

Chapter 2.24 — Market Breadth Inside NinjaTrader: TICK, ADD, Volume Ratio, TRIN and VIX in One Packet

Subtitle: Index futures move with the stocks underneath them. Bringing that context into the platform is mostly a data-engineering problem.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define the classic breadth measures: TICK, ADD, up/down volume, TRIN and VIX. 2. Explain why TRIN is asymmetric and why its log is not. 3. Explain the one-server, one-packet design and its three benefits. 4. Avoid the session and staleness traps of breadth data.

You need: ratios and logarithms; AddDataSeries from Chapter 2.19.

2.24.1 Why breadth

An index future is a derivative of a basket of stocks. When most stocks in the basket are ticking up, the future tends to have a tailwind. When the future rallies on a handful of names while most stocks fall, the move is narrow.

Breadth indicators measure that internal participation. I wanted them inside NinjaTrader, normalised, and available to any chart, without each chart subscribing to half a dozen extra symbols.

2.24.2 The classic breadth measures

Measure What it counts
NYSE TICK stocks whose last trade was an uptick minus those on a downtick, at each moment: a snapshot of immediate buying vs selling pressure
Advance–decline (ADD) advancing issues minus declining issues since the open; summed over days it is the advance–decline line
Up / down volume volume in advancing stocks divided by volume in declining stocks
TRIN (Arms index) see below
VIX implied volatility of the index; not strictly breadth, but the same kind of context

TRIN=Advancing issues/Declining issuesAdvancing volume/Declining volume. \text{TRIN} = \frac{\text{Advancing issues}/\text{Declining issues}}{\text{Advancing volume}/\text{Declining volume}}.

Below 1: volume is concentrated in advancing stocks (bullish breadth). Above 1: in decliners.

TRIN’s awkward property. It is a ratio of ratios, so it is asymmetric, and it explodes when declining volume is tiny. Many people use its logarithm, which is symmetric around zero.

Figure 2.24.1 — Plain TRIN squeezes one side. Top: TRIN values 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 on a plain scale. The bullish values (green) are crowded into a short stretch, while the bearish ones (orange) spread out. Bottom: the same values on a log scale, evenly spaced and symmetric around TRIN = 1.

2.24.3 Normalising

Raw TICK swings wildly. A single reading is noise. Useful derived values:

  • the current TICK, its session high and low, and a moving average of TICK;
  • the current ADD and its cumulative value;
  • current TRIN and a smoothed TRIN;
  • current VIX.

A smoothed TICK is a sampled estimate of net uptick pressure:

TICK¯t=1n∑k=0n−1TICKt−k. \overline{\text{TICK}}_t = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\text{TICK}_{t-k}.

2.24.4 The architecture

One component subscribes to the breadth symbols, computes these derived values, and publishes a single immutable packet (one that is never changed after it is built) with a timestamp, an RTH flag (regular trading hours) and a staleness flag. Chart indicators read the packet. They never subscribe to the breadth symbols themselves.

Figure 2.24.2 — Subscribe once, read many times. The breadth inputs on the left feed one server, which publishes one immutable packet carrying values, a timestamp, an RTH flag and a stale flag. Any number of charts read that packet. Box names are generic.

Why one server instead of each indicator adding its own series?

  1. Subscription cost. Every AddDataSeries call is a subscription and a historical data request. Ten charts times six symbols is sixty subscriptions for the same data.
  2. Consistency. Every reader sees the same smoothed TICK.
  3. Staleness, decided once. Breadth symbols only update during the cash session. Outside RTH, the last value is hours old. The packet says so explicitly, rather than every consumer guessing.

Breadth symbol names differ between data providers. The server uses provider presets that map logical names to provider symbols. That keeps symbol strings out of the logic.

2.24.5 NinjaTrader 8 specifics

  • Secondary series in an indicator. AddDataSeries("^TICK", BarsPeriodType.Minute, 1) or similar. The exact symbol depends on the provider. Each added series gets its own BarsInProgress.
  • OnEachTick on the server, so values update within the bar. Consumers read at whatever pace they like.
  • Trading hours. Breadth symbols use equity-session templates. Their session boundaries differ from the futures’ CME trading day. TICK’s session high and low must reset on the equity session, not the futures trading day.
  • Live price cache. It is useful to also cache the latest price per symbol in a simple concurrent map, so dashboards can show current values without their own subscriptions.
  • Backfill. On startup, historical bars let the server compute moving averages straight away, instead of waiting for realtime data to build up.

2.24.6 Interpretation caveats

Breadth measures are coincident, not leading. They describe participation in the move happening now. Extreme TICK readings often mark short-term exhaustion rather than continuation.

They only exist during the cash session. Overnight, an index future has no live breadth context at all. A stale packet should be treated as missing, not as last known truth.

2.24.7 Summary

  • TICK, ADD, up/down volume and TRIN measure how broadly stocks join a move; VIX adds volatility context.
  • TRIN is lopsided; use its log for a symmetric scale.
  • One server subscribes once and publishes one immutable, timestamped packet with RTH and stale flags.
  • Reset breadth stats on the equity session, and treat stale packets as missing.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) 2,000 advancers, 1,000 decliners; advancing volume 600M, declining volume 400M. What is TRIN? (Answer: (2,000/1,000)/(600/400) = 2/1.5 ≈ 1.33.)
  2. (Apply) Compute ln TRIN for TRIN = 0.5 and TRIN = 2. What do you notice?
  3. (Think) Why must TICK’s session high and low reset on the equity session rather than the futures trading day?
  4. (Design) List the fields of a breadth packet. Which field lets a consumer decide to treat the data as missing?

Further reading

  • R. Arms, The Arms Index (TRIN) (1989).
  • M. Zweig, Winning on Wall Street (1986), on the breadth thrust.
  • J. Murphy, Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (1999), breadth chapter.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.25 — An Economic Calendar on the Chart, Without Blocking the UI Thread

Subtitle: Fetching, parsing and drawing scheduled news events inside NinjaTrader 8 safely.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. List the failure modes of a public calendar feed and how to show them honestly. 2. Do network I/O in NinjaTrader 8 without blocking the data or UI thread. 3. Convert event times correctly across daylight-saving changes. 4. Draw a HUD with SharpDX without leaking resources.

You need: basic C# (Task, lock), and the idea that NinjaTrader runs code on more than one thread.

2.25.1 The feature

Scheduled macro releases (payrolls, CPI, FOMC decisions) move index futures more than almost anything else.

I wanted the day’s high-impact US events on the chart as a small HUD (heads-up display: an overlay panel) with countdowns and session alerts, so I would stop being surprised by an 08:30 print.

The feature is simple. The engineering is a good case study in doing network I/O inside a trading platform without hurting it.

2.25.2 The data source

I use a public weekly economic-calendar feed in XML, filtered to high-impact USD events. Two feeds, this week and next week, cover the weekend roll. Each event has a title, a country, an impact level, a date and a time.

A public feed has the usual problems:

  • It can be late, change, or disappear.
  • Times are in a stated time zone that you must convert correctly, including across daylight-saving changes, which happen on different dates in different countries.
  • Some events are “tentative” or “all day”, with no time.
  • Titles change wording between weeks.

So the indicator treats the calendar as advisory display data, never as an input to anything automated.

Honest failure. If the feed fails, the HUD says the feed failed. It never shows an empty calendar as if there were no events. “No events today” and “couldn’t fetch events” are very different statements.

2.25.3 Never do I/O on the wrong thread

This is the main engineering point.

NinjaTrader indicators run OnBarUpdate on a data thread and OnRender on the UI thread. A synchronous HTTP call in either can freeze data processing or the chart for seconds. A frozen data thread is not cosmetic: it delays every indicator and strategy on that instrument.

The pattern I use:

  1. Start the fetch on a background task (Task.Run), never on the data or UI thread. Reuse one HttpClient; creating one per request exhausts sockets.
  2. Parse the XML on that background task into a list of small event records.
  3. Publish the result by replacing the shared list inside a short lock.
  4. OnRender takes the same lock only long enough to copy the list into a local snapshot, then draws from the copy.

Figure 2.25.1 — Network work stays off the threads that matter. The background task fetches, parses and builds a new list, then swaps it in under a short lock (blue). The UI thread takes the same lock only to copy a snapshot, then draws from the copy. The data thread keeps processing bar updates and never waits on the network.

The lock is held for microseconds. The UI never sees a half-built list. The data thread never waits on the network.

An immutable list swapped with Volatile.Write would avoid the lock entirely. At one fetch every few minutes, the difference is irrelevant, and the lock is easier to read.

Refresh politely. Use a slow timer, cache the last good result, and back off on failure. The feed does not change minute to minute, and hammering a free public service is bad manners.

2.25.4 Time zones

Calendar times must be converted to the chart’s time zone. Use TimeZoneInfo with explicit zone IDs, not fixed offsets.

The US and Europe change their clocks on different weekends in spring and autumn. For a couple of weeks a year, the offset between, say, London and New York is an hour different from usual. Fixed offsets get those weeks wrong.

Figure 2.25.2 — Two short windows where the usual offset is wrong. A schematic of the gap between London and New York clocks over a year. It is usually 5 hours (blue). In spring the US moves its clocks first, and in autumn the UK moves back first; in those weeks the gap is 4 hours (orange). The dates are drawn roughly; the point is that a fixed offset misses them.

2.25.5 Drawing

The HUD is drawn in OnRender with SharpDX: a small table of the day’s events, a countdown to the next one, and an alert state as an event approaches.

  • Create TextFormat and brushes once in OnRenderTargetChanged, and dispose of them there. Creating DirectWrite text formats every frame is slow and leaks.
  • Measure text with TextLayout to size the panel. Cache layouts when the text does not change.
  • Countdowns need repainting even when no data arrives (a quiet overnight market). A low-frequency timer that calls ForceRefresh() keeps the clock ticking without redrawing on every tick.

2.25.6 Session alerts

Besides news, the HUD marks session transitions: cash open, cash close, and the CME daily break. These come from the trading calendar, not the feed, so they work even when the feed is down.

2.25.7 What not to do

Do not let a calendar feed gate trading logic directly. If your risk process depends on knowing an event is coming, it needs a robust source with a defined fallback (for example, a maintained local schedule), not a public XML feed parsed in a chart indicator. The on-chart calendar is a reminder for a human.

2.25.8 Summary

  • Treat a public calendar feed as advisory; show “feed failed” rather than an empty list.
  • Fetch and parse on a background task; swap the list under a short lock; render from a copy.
  • Convert times with TimeZoneInfo and zone IDs, never fixed offsets.
  • Create SharpDX resources once per render target, and repaint countdowns on a slow timer.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why is “no events today” a dangerous thing to display when the fetch failed?
  2. (Think) What exactly goes wrong if OnRender iterates over the shared list while the background task is still adding to it?
  3. (Code) Rewrite the publish step using an immutable list and Volatile.Write, with no lock. What must readers do?
  4. (Apply) An event is at 08:30 New York time. In which weeks of the year would a fixed London offset of +5 hours show it at the wrong London time? (Answer: the weeks when only one of the two countries has changed its clocks, in spring and autumn.)

Further reading

  • T. Andersen, T. Bollerslev, F. Diebold and C. Vega, “Micro Effects of Macro Announcements”, American Economic Review (2003).
  • Microsoft Docs: HttpClient guidelines and TimeZoneInfo.
  • NinjaTrader 8 Help Guide: OnRender, OnRenderTargetChanged, SharpDX.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.26 — Building an In-Process Level Bus for NinjaTrader 8 Indicators

Subtitle: One producer computes, many consumers draw. Immutable packets, concurrent maps, and the bugs this pattern prevents.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why NinjaTrader 8 indicators need a sharing mechanism, and why a static store works. 2. Choose between a queue and a blackboard, and justify a blackboard for chart levels. 3. Explain torn reads and how immutable packets prevent them. 4. Handle lifecycle, staleness and recompile hazards.

You need: basic C# (static classes, dictionaries) and the idea of threads.

2.26.1 The problem

Most earlier chapters end with the same idea: compute a thing once, publish it, let charts consume it. This chapter is about the mechanism.

I built a small in-process “bus” that NinjaTrader indicators use to share computed levels, profiles, order-flow snapshots and context packets. It is less a message bus than a blackboard: a shared store of the latest value per key. That distinction turned out to matter.

2.26.2 Why NinjaTrader needs this

NinjaTrader 8 indicators are isolated by default. If two charts both need session VWAP, each indicator loads its own data series and computes its own VWAP. You pay twice, and you risk two slightly different answers.

The platform’s sanctioned sharing method, calling one indicator from another, works inside a single chart or strategy, but not across charts.

The hook. All NinjaScript runs in the same process and the same AppDomain. A static class is visible to every indicator.

2.26.3 Blackboard, not queue

Two classic patterns:

  • Message queue / event stream: every published message is delivered to every subscriber, in order.
  • Blackboard / latest-value cache: producers overwrite the current value for a key; consumers read the current value when they need it.

Figure 2.26.1 — Every message, or the latest one. Left: a queue holds a backlog of messages that the reader must work through, with back-pressure and unbounded growth. Right: a blackboard holds one latest packet per key, overwritten by the producer and read by any number of readers whenever they need it. Box names are generic.

For chart levels, the blackboard is right. A consumer drawing a frame needs the current VWAP, not every VWAP since the last frame. Queues bring back-pressure, delivery guarantees and unbounded growth, and none of them help here.

Where history is needed (a consumer plotting historical bars), the producer puts a history array inside the packet, rather than consumers replaying a stream.

2.26.4 Keys

Values are keyed by what makes them unique. For levels, that is the instrument’s master name plus the trading-hours template, because VWAP on an RTH template and on an ETH template are different numbers. Keying by master instrument (not the specific contract) also keeps consumers working across contract rolls.

Keys are small immutable types with proper equality and hash code. Strings glued together on the fly work, but allocate memory on every lookup.

2.26.5 Immutable packets

The most important rule. A published packet is never mutated. Producers build a new packet with every field set in the constructor (readonly fields or get-only properties) and swap it into the store.

Consumers can read a packet reference once and then read its fields without any locking, because nothing can change underneath them.

The alternative, a mutable shared object updated field by field, produces torn reads: a consumer reads the new VWAP and the old upper band from the same object. Those bugs are rare, hard to reproduce, and look like bad data.

Figure 2.26.2 — How a torn read happens, and how immutability prevents it. Left: the writer updates one field, the reader reads both, then the writer updates the second field, so the reader saw half-new, half-old data. Right: the writer builds a complete new packet and swaps the reference in one step; a reader holding the old reference still sees one whole, consistent packet. Time runs downward.

2.26.6 Concurrency

The store is a set of ConcurrentDictionary instances, one per packet family. ConcurrentDictionary gives lock-free reads and fine-grained locking on writes, which suits many readers and few writers. Replacing a value is an atomic reference swap.

Ordering metadata uses Interlocked:

  • a sequence number, incremented on every publish, lets a consumer cheaply check “has anything changed since I last looked?”;
  • an epoch, incremented when a producer restarts or rebuilds history, lets consumers detect that cached state from a previous run is invalid.

2.26.7 Lifecycle and staleness

A static store outlives the indicators that use it. After closing a workspace and opening another, or after an overnight reload, the store still holds yesterday’s packets. Two defences:

  1. Clear on workspace close, from a lifecycle add-on, so packets do not survive into a new workspace.
  2. Stamp every packet with timestamps and trading date, and have consumers reject packets that are stale or from the wrong session.

The second is the real protection. The first is hygiene.

2.26.8 What consumers must not do

  • Compute. If a consumer starts deriving values from packets, you have two sources of truth again.
  • Mutate. Ever.
  • Assume presence. A consumer may start before the producer. Use TryGetValue, and draw nothing (with a status message) until a packet appears.

2.26.9 NinjaTrader-specific hazards

Hazard What happens Defence
Recompiles compiling NinjaScript reloads the assembly; static state is reset producers republish; consumers cope with an empty store
Type identity across reloads old indicator instances from the previous assembly may briefly coexist with new ones keep packet types simple; never store delegates or indicator references in the store
Thread affinity producers publish from data threads; consumers read from data and UI threads fine with immutable packets and concurrent maps, not with anything else
No cross-process sharing the store is in-process anything outside NinjaTrader needs a separate, explicit export

2.26.10 Summary

  • A static class is shared by all NinjaScript in the process; that makes cross-chart sharing possible.
  • Use a blackboard (latest value per key), not a queue, for chart levels.
  • Never mutate a published packet; swap whole packets so readers never see torn data.
  • Stamp packets, reject stale ones, and expect the store to be empty after a recompile.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why does a chart drawing VWAP not need every intermediate VWAP value since its last frame?
  2. (Think) A consumer sees the sequence number unchanged since its last read. What can it skip?
  3. (Code) Write an immutable LevelPacket class with a constructor that sets every field, and get-only properties. Why must there be no setters?
  4. (Apply) After a recompile, a consumer finds no packet for its key. What should it draw, and what should it say? (Answer: nothing, with a status message that it is waiting for the producer.)

Further reading

  • F. Buschmann et al., Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture, Vol. 1 (1996), on the Blackboard pattern.
  • J. Duffy, Concurrent Programming on Windows (2008).
  • Microsoft Docs: ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue> and Interlocked.

— Tariq

Chapter 2.27 — Custom Renko Bar Types and Renderers in NinjaTrader 8

Subtitle: Building a percentage-based, wick-preserving Renko variant, and drawing it so you can see what actually happened.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State the classic Renko rule and its two hidden problems. 2. Describe the “universal Renko” family with separate trend and reversal steps, and its random-walk null. 3. Explain why a bar builder must keep the real wicks. 4. Write a deterministic BarsType and a matching ChartStyle in NinjaTrader 8.

You need: the Renko random-walk null (Chapter 6.1) and basic NinjaScript.

2.27.1 Why build my own

Renko charts throw away time and keep only movement. That makes them popular for trend-following and for cleaner charts.

It also makes them easy to get subtly wrong. The brick-building rules are a modelling choice, and most implementations hide what they throw away.

I built my own Renko bar type and a matching chart style. This chapter explains the design family, not my settings.

2.27.2 Classic Renko

With brick size bb and last brick close cc:

  • if price reaches c+bc + b, close an up-brick at c+bc + b;
  • if price reaches c−2bc - 2b after an up-brick (or c−bc - b after a down-brick in the same direction), close a reversal brick.

Classic Renko has two problems:

  1. Synthetic opens and closes. Brick opens and closes are grid values, not traded prices. A brick “closes” at a price that may never have printed.
  2. Lost extremes. Moves that do not complete a brick vanish. The chart looks smooth because it deleted the noise, and some of that noise was where your stop would have been.

2.27.3 The “universal Renko” family

The community “UniRenko” design (and its descendants) splits the brick logic into three parameters:

  • a trend step: how far price must move to continue;
  • a reversal step: how far against the brick to reverse;
  • an open offset: where the new brick visually opens.

My bar type comes from that family, with continuation and reversal expressed as percentages of a base height in ticks. Formally, with height hh, trend fraction τ\tau and reversal fraction ρ\rho:

continue up if P≥c+τh,reverse down if P≤c−ρh. \text{continue up if } P \geq c + \tau h,\qquad \text{reverse down if } P \leq c - \rho h.

Null for any geometry. Unequal τ\tau and ρ\rho change the brick statistics. Under a driftless random walk, the gambler’s-ruin result of Chapter 6.1 gives a continuation probability of p0=ρτ+ρ, p_0 = \frac{\rho}{\tau + \rho}, not one-half. That null must be computed for whatever geometry you use.

2.27.4 Keep the wicks

The most important design decision: record the true high and low of each brick.

While a brick is forming, track the actual highest and lowest traded prices. When it closes, those become its high and low. The brick’s open and close may be grid values, but the wicks are real prints.

Figure 2.27.1 — The body is the grid; the wick is what really traded. Left: simulated ticks while one up-brick forms. Price dips well below the grid open before climbing to the grid close. Right: the brick as drawn. The green body runs from grid open to grid close; the black wick below it records the real low. Without the wick, that dip would vanish. The ticks are a seeded Gaussian walk with a dip then a rise; the brick height is schematic.

Wicks matter because:

  • they show where price actually went, including failed attempts in the other direction;
  • any fill simulation that ignores them assumes price never traded beyond the brick, which makes the market look gentler than it was;
  • a quick wick census (how often bricks have wicks at all) is a sanity check that the bar builder is not silently discarding extremes. If almost no bricks have wicks, something is wrong.

2.27.5 Writing a BarsType in NinjaTrader 8

A custom bar type subclasses BarsType:

Member Job
OnStateChange / SetDefaults name, a custom BarsPeriodType enum value (outside the built-in range), default parameters, and which built-in period type supplies the base data (usually tick)
ApplyDefaultBasePeriodValue / ApplyDefaultValue map UI fields to BarsPeriod.BaseBarsPeriodValue, Value and Value2; those three integers are all the parameter space you get, so design around them
OnDataPoint called for every underlying data point; update the forming bar (UpdateBar) or close it and start a new one (AddBar)
GetPercentComplete, ChartLabel UI support

One data point can complete several bricks. A single large tick (a gap or a fast print) can cross several brick levels. Loop until the remaining move is smaller than a brick.

Figure 2.27.2 — One tick, three bricks. The last tick sits at the brick close c. The next tick jumps past c + 3h in one step. The builder must call AddBar three times, once per completed level, rather than drawing one tall brick or dropping two. Schematic, no data.

Mid-session load. When the data series starts mid-session, there is no previous brick. The first bar needs a defined anchor rule, or the grid will differ depending on when you loaded the chart.

Determinism is the goal. The same ticks must always produce the same bricks. The session reset rule, the anchor rule and the handling of large gaps must all be explicit. My Renko series reset at each CME session boundary, so each day’s bricks are reproducible however far back the chart loads.

2.27.6 A matching chart style

The default candlestick style draws bodies and wicks, but it does not know which parts of a Renko brick are synthetic. A custom ChartStyle subclass lets you show that visually.

Mine draws up-bricks filled and down-bricks hollow, both outlined, with wicks in the outline colour, and a doji as a horizontal line. The aim is that the eye can separate the brick body (the grid) from the wicks (real prices).

ChartStyle.OnRender gets the chart scale and bar range:

  • iterate visible bars only;
  • convert prices with chartScale.GetYByValue;
  • reuse brushes;
  • make it look right zoomed far out, where bricks are a pixel wide: below a width threshold, fall back to simple lines.

2.27.7 Pitfalls

  • Backtests on synthetic closes. Filling at a brick close is filling at a price that may not have traded. Use the next real tick.
  • Repainting forming bricks. The last brick is provisional. Anything reading it within the bar is reading a moving target.
  • Comparing settings by chart appearance. Every geometry looks trendier than a random walk “should”. Compare against the geometry’s own null.

2.27.8 Summary

  • Classic Renko invents its opens and closes and deletes moves that do not complete a brick.
  • Separate trend and reversal steps change the null: p0=ρ/(τ+ρ)p_0 = \rho/(\tau + \rho) on a random walk.
  • Keep the true high and low of each brick, and run a wick census as a sanity check.
  • Make the bar type deterministic: loop over multi-brick ticks, define the anchor, reset per session.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Trend fraction τ = 1, reversal fraction ρ = 2. What continuation rate does a random walk give? (Answer: 2/3.)
  2. (Apply) With τ = 0.5 and ρ = 1.5, what is p0p_0? (Answer: 1.5/2 = 75%.)
  3. (Think) Why does a backtest that fills at brick closes overstate how good the fills were?
  4. (Code) Write the OnDataPoint loop that adds one brick per completed level when a single tick crosses several levels. Test it with a tick that jumps 3.4 brick heights.

Further reading

  • S. Nison, Beyond Candlesticks (1994), on Renko, kagi and line-break origins.
  • NinjaTrader 8 Help Guide: BarsType, ChartStyle.
  • W. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1 (1968).

— Tariq

Chapter 3.2 — Two Keys to Fire: Independent Confirmation for Order Entry

Subtitle: An idea from missile silos and bank vaults, applied to a strategy that sends real orders.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe the two-key pattern: permission, trigger and vetoes. 2. Show why two keys only help when their failures are independent. 3. Explain why every key needs a freshness check and must be used only once.

You need: basic probability (multiplying chances of independent events). No calculus.

3.2.1 The idea

Some mistakes are catastrophic. Wherever that is true, an old safety rule shows up: two people, two keys, turned at the same time. Neither key alone can launch anything.

The point is not that either keyholder is untrustworthy. The point is that two independent failures must line up before something irreversible happens.

An order sent to the exchange is the most irreversible thing my code does. Everything before it can be wrong: the data, the models, the indicators, my own reasoning. So I built order entry around two keys.

3.2.2 The shape of the pattern

An entry needs two things at once:

  1. Permission. A slower, higher-level process has decided the current context allows trading in a given direction. Think of it as “the environment is acceptable”.
  2. A trigger. A fast, local process, running right next to the order router, sees a concrete event on its own data feed that says “now”.

Neither is enough alone. Permission without a trigger does nothing; it sits there and expires. A trigger without permission is ignored.

On top of both sits a third layer. It is not a key; it is a padlock. These are absolute vetoes: checks that nothing upstream can ever override (Chapter 3.3).

Definition (entry rule). enter=P∧T∧¬V \text{enter} = P \land T \land \neg V where P is permission, T is the trigger and V is true if any veto is tripped. (∧ means “and”; ¬ means “not”.)

Figure 3.2.1 — Two keys and a padlock. Permission (slow) and trigger (fast) both feed the AND gate. The vetoes feed it through a NOT: one tripped veto is enough to block. Only when all three conditions hold does the order go out. The notes on the right preview the two rules in Sections 3.2.4 and 3.2.5.

The formula is the easy part. The real engineering is making P and T genuinely independent.

3.2.3 Why independence matters

Say the permission process gives a wrong “yes” with probability p, and the trigger gives a wrong “now” with probability q.

Result. If the two fail independently, Pr⁡(bad entry)=p⋅q, \Pr(\text{bad entry}) = p \cdot q, which is much smaller than either. If they fail together (fully correlated), in the worst case Pr⁡(bad entry)→min⁡(p,q). \Pr(\text{bad entry}) \to \min(p, q).

Why. Independent events multiply. If both keys read the same stale file, run on the same thread or depend on the same broken indicator, one failure drags the other with it. Then the second key adds almost nothing, and you have paid for extra complexity.

Figure 3.2.2 — Correlation eats the benefit. The blue line is the chance of a bad entry for two keys that each fail 10% of the time (illustrative numbers, not measurements). With independent failures (green dot) it is 1%. As the failures become correlated it climbs, and with fully shared failures (orange dot) it reaches 10%, the same as one key. The curve uses the standard formula for two correlated yes/no events.

So most of the design work goes into breaking correlation:

Lever How the two keys differ
Different processes They share no memory. They talk through small files on disk.
Different data paths The trigger reads its own live feed inside the trading platform. It does not trust a number the permission side computed.
Different time scales Permission changes slowly; the trigger works tick by tick. A glitch in one rarely hits the other in the same instant.

3.2.4 Freshness is part of the key

A key turned an hour ago is not turned.

An early bug in any two-process design is acting on a stale (out-of-date) message. The upstream process crashes. Its last output file is still on disk saying “yes”. The downstream side keeps trading on it.

So every message carries a timestamp. The consumer checks the age before it reads the content. If either side’s latest output is older than a configured limit, entries are blocked.

Note the default: when in doubt, no. Staleness counts as a veto, never as “keep doing what you were doing”.

3.2.5 Consume once

The second classic bug is double-firing. The trigger side polls a file. The file has not changed. The poll fires again on the next tick. Now there are two orders.

The fix is boring and essential:

  • Every permission decision has an identity. The consumer keeps a set of decisions it has already acted on. Once a decision has produced an order it is consumed; seeing it again does nothing.
  • Commands that arrive through a control file carry a sequence number that only goes up. The consumer ignores any number it has already processed.

Definition (idempotency). An action is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. The message may arrive more than once; the effect must happen at most once.

This is the same idea used in payment APIs. In my case the “network” that repeats messages is the file system plus the polling loop.

3.2.6 Where the pattern bites back

Two keys are not free.

  • Latency. Every extra check costs microseconds to milliseconds, and the permission side runs on a slower clock. Sometimes the trigger fires and is blocked because permission has not refreshed yet. I accept that. A missed entry costs an opportunity; a wrong entry costs money.
  • Silent disagreement. If the keys disagree all the time, the system never trades, and you will not notice unless you log why each candidate was rejected. Every rejection in my setup records a reason string. A histogram (count per reason) of rejections is the fastest way to find a broken side.
  • False comfort. The pattern guards against independent errors. It does nothing about a shared upstream error, such as a bad contract roll or a wrong instrument mapping that feeds both sides. That is why vetoes and an instrument registry exist as separate layers.

3.2.7 Advice to another engineer

Write down, explicitly, which failures each key protects against, and which failures could hit both keys at once. If the second list is long, you do not have two keys. You have one key with extra steps.

Log everything at the decision point: both key states, every veto, and the reason for the outcome. When something breaks at 3 a.m., that log line is the difference between understanding it in a minute and guessing for a week.

3.2.8 Summary

  • Entry requires permission AND trigger AND no veto: enter = P ∧ T ∧ ¬V.
  • Two keys cut the risk to p·q only if their failures are independent; shared inputs push it back toward min(p, q).
  • Separate processes, data paths and time scales keep the keys independent.
  • A stale key counts as “no”, and each permission is consumed at most once.
  • Log a reason for every rejection, or a broken key stays invisible.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Permission is wrong 5% of the time and the trigger 2% of the time, independently. What is the chance of a bad entry? (Answer: 0.05 × 0.02 = 0.1%.)
  2. (Apply) Both keys read the same indicator value from one shared file. Which row of the table in Section 3.2.3 is violated, and what happens to the risk?
  3. (Design) Write pseudocode for a consumer that polls a file every tick but sends at most one order per permission decision.
  4. (Think) Why should a stale message block entries rather than leave the last decision in force?

Further reading

  • James Reason, Human Error (1990), the “Swiss cheese” model of layered defences.
  • Nancy Leveson, Engineering a Safer World (2011), on system-theoretic safety.
  • Pat Helland, “Idempotence Is Not a Medical Condition”, ACM Queue (2012).

— Tariq

Chapter 3.3 — Hard Vetoes and Kill Switches

Subtitle: Most of a strategy is negotiable. A small, boring layer must not be.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State the four properties of a hard veto: local, non-overridable, fail-closed, explained. 2. Name the common veto families and what each protects against. 3. Explain why a veto should be simpler than the logic it protects. 4. Decide in advance what a kill switch does to an open position.

You need: Chapter 3.2 (two-key entry) helps but is not required. Basic probability.

3.3.1 Opinions and walls

Every automated strategy is a pile of opinions. Models have opinions, filters have opinions, and the person who tuned them has the loudest opinion of all. That is fine for deciding whether a trade looks good. It is not fine for deciding whether trading should be possible at all.

So under everything I keep a thin layer of absolute vetoes. They sit right next to the order call. They are checked last. Nothing upstream can turn them off.

Key idea. A veto is only useful if it is dumber, simpler and more local than the thing it protects against.

3.3.2 What a hard veto is

Definition (hard veto). A hard veto is a true/false check ViV_i. If it is true, no new entries are allowed, whatever else is happening: allowed=⋀i¬Vi \text{allowed} = \bigwedge_i \neg V_i (read: allowed only if no veto is true).

Four properties I insist on:

Property Meaning
Local Computed by the process that sends orders, from data that process sees directly. It does not trust a remote verdict.
Non-overridable No config flag, message field or upstream decision can bypass it. To bypass it you change the code and redeploy, on purpose.
Fail-closed If it cannot be evaluated (missing file, parse error, unknown state), it counts as tripped.
Explained Each veto emits a named reason, so logs say which wall you hit.

Figure 3.3.1 — The veto chain fails closed. An entry request passes through each check in turn. Any tripped check sends it down an orange arrow to “blocked”, with the reason logged. Only a request that passes every check reaches “send”. The boxes are the generic families from Section 3.3.3, not a real configuration, and the order shown is arbitrary.

3.3.3 The families

I will not list my exact set, but the families are standard and worth having in any system.

  • A kill file. The simplest kill switch there is: if a file with a particular name exists in a particular folder, no new entries. Anyone can create a file: me on a phone over remote desktop, a monitoring script, an operator. It needs no working network API, no running daemon, no UI that might be frozen. Checking whether a file exists is about as hard to break as code gets.
  • A daily loss limit. Once the session’s realised loss (loss on closed trades) crosses a limit, no new positions for the rest of the session. It is measured in risk units, not dollars, so it scales with position size.
  • A flatten window. Before the daily maintenance break, positions are closed and no new ones open. Futures markets halt daily. Holding through the halt with an automated system that may not reconnect cleanly is risk with no upside.
  • Context floors. Some market conditions are outside what the strategy was designed for. A cheap, robust measurement of that condition can act as a veto. It must be hard to get wrong, not a fancy model.
  • A margin buffer. If available margin is close to the requirement, do not add exposure.

3.3.4 Why “dumber” matters

It is tempting to make vetoes clever. Resist it. A veto that depends on a model inherits the model’s failure modes. A veto that depends on network state inherits the network’s failure modes. The point is a layer whose failures are unrelated to everything above it.

Result (residual risk). If the strategy fails dangerously with probability psp_s and the veto layer misses it with probability pvp_v, the leftover risk is about ps⋅pv, p_s \cdot p_v, but only if the two are independent.

Why. It is the same multiplication as in Chapter 3.2. If the veto uses the same inputs as the strategy, pvp_v quietly becomes a function of psp_s: when the strategy is fooled, the veto is fooled too.

3.3.5 Kill switches stop entries, not necessarily positions

What should a kill switch do to a position that is already open?

My answer: the kill file blocks new entries, and the open position keeps being managed by its protective orders (stop and target). An abrupt market exit can be worse than letting a working stop do its job, especially in a fast market. There is a separate, deliberate flatten path for “get me out now”.

Others disagree. The right answer depends on your instrument and how much you trust your stops. What matters is that the behaviour is decided in advance and written down, not improvised under stress.

3.3.6 Orphans

Definition (orphan). The platform reports a position, but the strategy does not believe it owns one.

Orphans come from a restart, a manual click or a missed callback. The safe response: refuse new entries until the mismatch is resolved, and raise it loudly. An automated system that “adopts” positions it does not understand is how small mistakes become big ones.

3.3.7 Pitfalls

Pitfall What goes wrong Fix
Vetoes that log but don’t block A warning is written and the return is forgotten. Test that a tripped veto really prevents the order call.
Vetoes checked too early Checks pass, slow work follows, the world changes before the send. Evaluate as close to the send as possible.
Reset ambiguity When does a daily loss limit reset: local midnight or session boundary? Use the exchange session, consistently.
Silent config A threshold in an editable config file is not non-overridable; someone edits it at the worst moment. Keep the critical ones in code and review changes.

3.3.8 Advice to another engineer

Write the veto layer first, before the strategy, and test it alone. If your kill switch needs your strategy to be healthy to work, it is not a kill switch.

3.3.9 Summary

  • Hard vetoes are local, non-overridable, fail-closed and explained.
  • Standard families: kill file, daily loss limit, flatten window, context floors, margin buffer.
  • Keep vetoes simpler than the strategy so their failures stay independent (risk ≈ p_s · p_v).
  • Decide in advance what the kill switch does to open positions; here it blocks entries and leaves stops working.
  • Treat orphan positions as a reason to block entries and alert.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) The veto code cannot read its state file because of a parse error. Should entries be allowed? (Answer: no. Fail-closed means an unevaluable veto counts as tripped.)
  2. (Apply) A context veto reads the same indicator the strategy uses to enter. Explain, with psp_s and pvp_v, why this weakens it.
  3. (Design) Write a unit test that proves a tripped kill file prevents the order call, not just that it logs a warning.
  4. (Think) Give one argument for and one against flattening open positions when the kill switch is used.

Further reading

  • Nancy Leveson, Engineering a Safer World (2011).
  • SEC, Findings Regarding the Market Events of May 6, 2010 (the Flash Crash report).
  • SEC administrative proceeding on Knight Capital Americas LLC (2013), a hard lesson in deployment and kill switches.

— Tariq

Chapter 3.4 — When the Stop Is Already Behind You: Fail-Safe Exits

Subtitle: You can’t place a sell stop above the market. What your code does next decides how bad the day gets.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why a “crossed stop” is a routine event, not a rare one. 2. List the failure modes when a stop change is rejected. 3. Apply the fail-safe rule: if the market is already through the stop, exit at market. 4. Route every stop change through one testable function.

You need: what a stop order, bid and ask are. No maths beyond an inequality.

3.4.1 The bug everyone meets

Your strategy is long. It wants to move its protective stop up, perhaps to lock in a smaller loss or breakeven. It computes the new stop price and submits the change.

But in the milliseconds between computing and submitting, price falls through that level. The exchange (or your platform) rejects the order, because a sell stop above the current price makes no sense.

What happens next depends on code you probably did not think hard about.

3.4.2 Why it happens often

Futures move in ticks (the smallest price step) and can move several ticks between your decision and the exchange’s acknowledgment. You decide on the last print you saw. The order arrives after network and processing latency (delay).

Condition (crossed stop). Let ℓ be the latency, Δ(ℓ) how far the market moves during it, and d the distance from the market to your stop. The stop is crossed whenever Δ(ℓ)>d. \Delta(\ell) > d.

A ratchet (a stop that only moves in your favour, Chapter 3.5) that pulls the stop close to price, near breakeven or a tight trail, makes d small on purpose. In a fast market Δ can be large. So the event is routine.

Figure 3.4.1 — How a stop gets crossed. At the blue dot the stop is computed, with price a distance d above the intended stop s (orange dashed line). During the latency (arrow at the bottom) price falls further than d. By the time the order arrives (orange dot) the bid is already below s. The path is a schematic, not market data.

3.4.3 The failure modes

Roughly from worst to least bad:

# What happens Result
1 Change rejected and old stop cancelled No stop at all. Happens if “move stop” is “cancel old, submit new” without checking the new one was accepted.
2 Change rejected, old stop remains Protected, but at the old, wider level, not the one you thought.
3 Platform errors and the strategy halts Some platforms disable a strategy on a rejected order. A live position with nothing managing it.

None of these is acceptable to discover in production.

3.4.4 The fail-safe rule

Rule. Before submitting a protective stop at price s, check it against the current market. If the market has already traded through s, do not submit a stop. Close the position with a market order instead.

  • Long position, bid b: crossed if b≤sb \le s.
  • Short position, ask a: crossed if a≥sa \ge s.

Use the side of the book you would actually exit into, not the last trade. The last trade can be on the other side.

Why it is right. The stop’s purpose was to get you out if price reached s. Price has reached s. The stop’s job is done; you just carry it out yourself.

3.4.5 Don’t loosen the stop instead

Two tempting alternatives, which I do not use for ratchets:

  • Keep the old stop. Your risk is then larger than your logic intended, at exactly the moment the market moves against you.
  • Clamp the new stop to one tick from the market. That places a stop at a level you never chose, set only by how fast the market moved.

Both silently override the risk decision. The market exit has a cost (you cross the spread, the gap between bid and ask, and may slip), but it executes the decision you already made. That is the right default.

3.4.6 One function for every stop change

The structural fix: never move a stop from more than one place. Every protective stop change goes through a single “safe apply” function that:

  1. Computes the intended stop.
  2. Refuses to move the stop backwards (looser) unless a separate, explicit path asks for that.
  3. Checks the intended stop against the current bid/ask.
  4. Either submits the stop change or, if crossed, submits a market exit.
  5. Logs which branch it took, with prices.

Figure 3.4.2 — One function for every stop change. Follow the boxes from the top left. A looser stop is refused (orange, top right). Otherwise the function asks whether the market is already through s: if not, it submits the stop change (green); if so, it exits at market and cancels the old stop (orange). Both paths end in a log line.

One choke point means you can test the behaviour alone and cannot forget it in a new code path.

3.4.7 Races on the way out

Even the market exit can race. The original stop might fill at the same moment you send the market order, leaving you flat and then short. Defences:

  • Track working orders by identity and cancel the old stop as part of the exit.
  • On every execution callback, recompute the position from the platform’s own numbers, not your internal counters.
  • Treat an unexpected opposite position as an orphan (Chapter 3.3): block entries and alert.

3.4.8 Testing it

You cannot wait for a fast market to test this. In replay I inject the condition directly: set the intended stop to a price the market has already passed, and assert that a market exit is issued and no stop is submitted. It is a small test, and one of the most valuable in the whole suite.

3.4.9 Advice to another engineer

Search your codebase for every place that changes a stop. If there is more than one, you probably have a path that ignores the crossed case. Collapse them into one function, then write the test where the stop is already behind the market.

3.4.10 Summary

  • A stop is crossed whenever the market moves more than d during the latency; tight ratchets make this routine.
  • A rejected stop change can leave you with no stop, a wider stop, or a halted strategy.
  • Fail-safe rule: long and bid ≤ s, or short and ask ≥ s, means exit at market instead of placing the stop.
  • Never keep the old stop or clamp the new one as a silent fallback.
  • Route every stop change through one logged, tested function.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) You are short. The intended buy stop is at 101.00; the ask is 101.25. Is the stop crossed? (Answer: yes, because ask ≥ s.)
  2. (Apply) Why check against the bid for a long exit rather than the last trade price?
  3. (Design) Write the replay test from Section 3.4.8 as pseudocode with explicit asserts.
  4. (Think) If you implement “move stop” as “cancel, then submit”, which failure mode in Section 3.4.3 are you exposed to, and how would you order the steps to avoid it?

Further reading

  • Larry Harris, Trading and Exchanges: Market Microstructure for Practitioners (2003), on order types and stop behaviour.
  • CME Group documentation on stop orders and price banding on Globex.

— Tariq

Chapter 3.5 — Stop Ratchets: The One-Way Valve in Trade Management

Subtitle: A stop that only moves in your favour sounds trivial. The details are where accounts get hurt.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State the ratchet rule for long and short positions as one line of maths. 2. Name the common families of rules that propose a new stop. 3. Explain why a tighter trail gets shaken out much sooner, not just a little sooner. 4. List the engineering traps: unconfirmed fills, phantom stop-outs, crossed stops, tick rounding and order spam.

You need: what a stop order is, and what “long” and “short” mean.

3.5.1 What a ratchet is

A ratchet is a mechanism that turns one way and locks the other. A stop ratchet is the same idea in trade management. The protective stop (the order that closes a losing trade) may move toward profit. It may never move back toward more risk.

It is one of the oldest ideas in trading, and it is easy to build badly. This chapter covers ratchets in general: the maths, the variants and the engineering traps. I do not describe how or when my own systems move stops. That is strategy. The mechanics are universal.

3.5.2 The invariant

An invariant is a rule that must always be true. For a long position, let sts_t be the stop at time tt and s̃t\tilde{s}_t the stop that your rule proposes.

Definition (stop ratchet). Long: st=max⁡(st−1,s̃t) s_t = \max(s_{t-1}, \tilde{s}_t) Short: st=min⁡(st−1,s̃t) s_t = \min(s_{t-1}, \tilde{s}_t) Any proposal that would loosen the stop is ignored.

That is all of it. The whole value of the ratchet is in that rule. So the first thing I do in code is enforce it in one place, the function that applies stops. I do not trust every rule to respect it.

Figure 3.5.1 — The applied stop only moves one way. The blue line is price on a long trade. The dashed orange line is what the proposal rule suggests at each step; it often drops. The green step line is the stop actually applied, the running maximum of the proposals. Every drop in the orange line is simply ignored. (Illustration: a seeded random walk, seed 20261107, with a toy “highest price minus a distance” proposal plus random dips. Not market data.)

3.5.3 Families of proposal rules

The ratchet is the valve. The proposal rule is what pushes on it. Common families:

Family What it proposes (for a long) Cost
Breakeven move Once the trade is far enough in profit, a stop at entry, often plus a small offset to cover costs. Turns “can lose” into “roughly can’t lose”. Stopped out by ordinary noise more often.
Fixed-distance trail s̃t=Ht−k\tilde{s}_t = H_t - k, where HtH_t is the highest price since entry and kk a fixed distance. Ignores how volatile the market is.
Volatility-scaled trail s̃t=Ht−c⋅ATRt\tilde{s}_t = H_t - c \cdot \text{ATR}_t, where ATR (average true range) estimates typical bar size. This is the “chandelier” exit family. Stop distance changes with volatility.
Structure-based trail Just beyond the most recent swing low. Moves in steps as new structure forms. Depends on how swings are defined.
Time-based tightening Tighter stops as the trade ages, on the theory that a trade that has not worked yet is less likely to. Can cut trades that were just slow.

3.5.4 The trade-off nobody escapes

Every ratchet trades two things against each other: giving back open profit and getting shaken out by noise.

A toy model shows it. Let price be a driftless random walk (no trend) with per-step volatility σ\sigma. The expected time τ\tau until price first moves a distance kk against you scales like

𝔼[τ]∝(kσ)2. \mathbb{E}[\tau] \propto \left(\frac{k}{\sigma}\right)^2.

Why, in brief. A random walk’s typical distance from its start after nn steps grows like σn\sigma\sqrt{n}. Setting σn≈k\sigma\sqrt{n} \approx k gives n≈(k/σ)2n \approx (k/\sigma)^2.

Figure 3.5.2 — Tight trails die quadratically faster. The curve is the formula above, scaled so the reference distance gives 1. Halving the trail distance (blue dot to orange dot) does not halve the survival time. It cuts it to about a quarter. That is why “just tighten the trail” so often makes things worse.

Real markets are not driftless random walks, and the whole point of a strategy is that there is something non-random to capture. But the scaling is a good sanity check on any rule you design.

3.5.5 Engineering traps

Ratcheting on unconfirmed fills. Suppose the ratchet depends on a partial exit: take part of the position off at a target, then move the rest to breakeven. Only ratchet when the platform confirms the partial fill. If you ratchet when the target order is merely placed, or when price merely touches it, you can end up with a breakeven stop on a position whose partial exit never filled. In my code the breakeven-style move is triggered from the execution callback (the platform’s “this order filled” event), not from a price check.

Phantom stop-outs in backtests. A backtest that evaluates the trail on bar closes but fills the stop inside the bar can produce exits that could never have happened. The proposal must use only information available at that moment, and the stop must be in the order book before the price that would hit it.

Crossed stops. If the market has already passed the proposed stop when you submit it, you cannot place it. You need a fail-safe path for that (covered in a separate chapter).

Tick rounding. Prices must be whole multiples of the instrument’s tick size. Round in the conservative direction: for a long stop, round down so it stays at or below the proposed level. Then apply the max again, so rounding can never loosen the stop below the previous one.

Order spam. A trail that proposes a new level on every tick sends a modification on every tick. Exchanges and brokers do not like that, and each modify is a chance for a race. Only submit when the change is at least one tick.

3.5.6 Testing ratchets

The tests that have earned their keep:

Scenario Assert
Proposals go up, down, up again Applied stop is monotone (never moves back)
Target order is cancelled instead of filled No breakeven move happens
Proposal is already crossed A market exit, not a stop
Rounding near a tick boundary Stop never loosens

3.5.7 Summary

  • The ratchet is one line: max for longs, min for shorts. Enforce it in one function.
  • Keep the proposal (strategy, tunable, debatable) separate from the ratchet (invariant, not debatable).
  • Survival time against noise scales with the square of the trail distance.
  • Ratchet only on confirmed fills, round conservatively, and only send changes of at least one tick.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A short position has stop 105. The rule proposes 107, then 103. What is the applied stop after each? (Answer: 105, then 103.)
  2. (Apply) Using 𝔼[τ]∝(k/σ)2\mathbb{E}[\tau] \propto (k/\sigma)^2, how does survival time change if you triple the trail distance?
  3. (Code) Write a applyStop function for longs that rounds to tick size and keeps the invariant. Test it with the four scenarios in Section 3.5.6.
  4. (Think) Why is triggering a breakeven move from a price touch dangerous when the partial exit is a limit order?

Further reading

  • Charles LeBeau and David Lucas, Technical Traders Guide to Computer Analysis of the Futures Market (1992), origin of the chandelier exit.
  • J. Welles Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978), average true range and the parabolic stop.
  • Ralph Vince, The Mathematics of Money Management (1992).

— Tariq

Chapter 3.6 — Fill Telemetry: Measuring What Actually Happened to Your Orders

Subtitle: Slippage, time-to-fill, rest depth and excursion in R units. The numbers your backtest assumed and your broker never tells you.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define slippage in ticks with a sign that always means “worse for me”. 2. Read time-to-fill and rest depth for signs of adverse selection. 3. Compute MFE and MAE in R units. 4. Explain why statistics on filled orders alone are biased.

You need: market and limit orders, tick size, and the idea of a trade’s initial risk.

3.6.1 Why measure fills

A backtest makes assumptions about fills. A live system either confirms them or does not. The only way to find out is to measure every fill, every time, in a format you can compare against those assumptions.

I added a fill telemetry layer to my execution code for exactly that reason. Telemetry here means recorded measurements. It decides nothing. It records, per trade, a handful of numbers that show how reality differed from the plan.

3.6.2 Slippage, in ticks, against intent

Slippage is the difference between the price you intended and the price you got.

Definition (signed slippage). slipticks=σ⋅(pfill−pintent)tickSize \text{slip}_{\text{ticks}} = \frac{\sigma \cdot (p_{\text{fill}} - p_{\text{intent}})}{\text{tickSize}} with σ=+1\sigma = +1 for buys and −1-1 for sells, so that positive always means “worse for me”.

Figure 3.6.1 — Positive slippage always means worse. On each line the blue dot is the intended price. For a buy, a higher fill is worse; for a sell, a lower fill is worse. The sign σ\sigma flips the sell case so orange (worse) is always positive.

The subtle part is pintentp_{\text{intent}}. Against what? Options include the last trade at decision time, the best bid/ask at decision time, or the limit price. I record against the price the strategy intended at the moment it decided, because that is the price the backtest would have used. Measuring against the touch (best bid or ask) at send time instead hides the latency part.

Ticks, not dollars, because ticks compare across instruments and position sizes.

3.6.3 Time to fill

This is the wall-clock time from order submission to fill confirmation. For market orders it is mostly latency. For limit orders it is latency plus waiting in the queue. Its distribution tells you a lot:

Pattern What it usually means
Long tail of long waits You often fill on trades that reverse back to you (adverse selection: you get filled mainly when it is bad for you).
Cluster at very short times Your limits are often marketable on arrival, so they behave like market orders.

I record it in seconds as a floating-point number and never round it.

3.6.4 Rest depth

For limit orders: how far from the touch was the order resting when placed, in ticks? A limit at the touch behaves very differently from one several ticks away. Recording rest depth lets you split fill statistics by how passive the order was. That is the only way to make sense of them.

3.6.5 Excursion in R units

MFE and MAE are maximum favourable and maximum adverse excursion: how far the trade went for you and against you while open. For a long entered at p0p_0:

MFE=maxt∈trade(pt−p0),MAE=maxt∈trade(p0−pt). \text{MFE} = \max_{t \in \text{trade}} (p_t - p_0), \qquad \text{MAE} = \max_{t \in \text{trade}} (p_0 - p_t).

I express both in R, where 1R is the initial risk of the trade: entry to initial stop, times size qq, times point value. So

MFER=MFE⋅pointValue⋅qR$. \text{MFE}_R = \frac{\text{MFE} \cdot \text{pointValue} \cdot q}{R_{\$}}.

Figure 3.6.2 — MFE and MAE measured against 1R. The blue line is price during one long trade. The green arrow is how far it went in favour (MFE); the orange arrow how far it went against (MAE). The grey bar is 1R, entry to stop. Here the MAE is a large fraction of 1R: the stop nearly got hit. (Illustration: seeded random walk, seed 20261108. Not a real trade.)

R units make every trade comparable whatever its size or instrument. An MAE near −1R on a winner says the stop almost got hit. An MFE well above the final exit says the exit gave a lot back. John Sweeney popularised MAE analysis for stop placement decades ago, and it is still one of the most useful post-trade tools there is.

3.6.6 Fills are conditional

One field I always set: a flag saying that every statistic in the record is conditional on the order having filled. That sounds pedantic. It is not.

Limit orders that do not fill vanish from naive statistics. The ones that do fill are not a random sample. They are disproportionately the ones where price came to you and kept going. Analyse fills without the unfilled orders and you are looking at a biased sample, and you will overestimate your edge.

Figure 3.6.3 — Filled orders are not a random sample. Every limit order sent splits into filled and unfilled. Naive statistics see only the top row. Honest statistics use both rows. So the telemetry also records unfilled and cancelled orders, with the same intent fields and empty fill fields.

3.6.7 Where the numbers come from

On some platforms the strategy does not see every execution directly. For example, if exits are handled by a platform-managed bracket (a stop and target pair the platform manages), the strategy may only see realised P&L, not the exit fill. Then I back-solve an estimated exit price from realised P&L and size, and the record says it is an estimate. Never let an estimate pass as a measured fill.

3.6.8 Format and plumbing

  • Each trade becomes one JSON record with stable field names.
  • Records are written atomically (write a temp file, then replace), so a reader never sees half a record.
  • A downstream process aggregates them. The execution process never does analysis inline.
  • Telemetry must never slow down or crash the order path, so all of it sits behind error handling that logs and moves on.

3.6.9 Summary

  • Measure slippage in ticks, signed so positive is worse, against the price the strategy intended.
  • Time to fill and rest depth reveal adverse selection and how passive your orders really are.
  • MFE and MAE in R make every trade comparable.
  • Record unfilled orders too; filled-only statistics are biased.
  • Build this before going live, not after the first bad week.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A sell order intends 100.00 and fills at 99.75 with tick size 0.25. What is the slippage in ticks? (Answer: σ = −1, so −1 × (−0.25)/0.25 = +1 tick, i.e. one tick worse.)
  2. (Apply) A long is entered at 50 with a stop at 48 on one contract. Price reaches 55 and dips to 49 before exit. Give MFE and MAE in R.
  3. (Think) Why does measuring slippage against the touch at send time hide latency?
  4. (Design) List the fields you would keep for an unfilled limit order so it can sit next to filled ones in analysis.

Further reading

  • John Sweeney, Maximum Adverse Excursion: Analyzing Price Fluctuations for Trading Management (1997).
  • André Perold, “The Implementation Shortfall: Paper versus Reality”, Journal of Portfolio Management (1988).
  • Robert Almgren and Neil Chriss, “Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions”, Journal of Risk (2000).

— Tariq

Chapter 3.7 — Waking Up Mid-Trade: State Recovery After a Restart

Subtitle: Your strategy will restart with a live position. Decide now what it should believe.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Say which source of truth wins after a restart, and for what. 2. List the minimum state a strategy must persist, and when to write it. 3. Walk through the five-step recovery procedure and the four reconciliation cases. 4. Explain how historical warm-up and repeated commands can cause wrong trades after a restart.

You need: what a position and a working order are. Chapter 3.8 (atomic file writes) helps but is not required.

3.7.1 The problem

Trading platforms restart. Windows updates, the connection drops and the platform reconnects, someone recompiles, the machine reboots. If the strategy is flat (holding nothing) when that happens, nothing interesting occurs. If it holds a position with a stop and a target, the restart is one of the most dangerous moments in the system’s life.

After a restart the strategy’s in-memory state is gone, but the world is not. There is a position at the broker. There are working orders. There may be a half-finished management step. The strategy has to rebuild a belief about all of that before it does anything.

3.7.2 Two sources of truth

State can come from two places:

  1. The broker/platform. It knows the position and working orders with authority.
  2. The strategy’s own persisted state (saved to disk). It knows why: the original entry price, the initial risk, which management phase the trade was in, which decisions it already used.

Rule. The broker is authoritative for what exists. Persisted state is authoritative for why it exists. If they disagree about what exists, the broker wins, and the disagreement is an alarm, not something to paper over.

3.7.3 What to persist

Persist the minimum needed to resume correctly, and nothing that can be recomputed:

  • Position direction and quantity as the strategy believes it.
  • Average entry price.
  • Initial risk (1R), because you cannot recompute it once the stop has moved.
  • Current management phase (for example, before or after a partial exit).
  • Current intended stop.
  • Identifiers of the last processed command or decision (for idempotency, Section 3.7.7).
  • A schema version (a number saying which file layout this is).

Write on every state transition, not on a timer. A timer leaves windows where the file is stale.

3.7.4 Write it atomically

A crash in the middle of writing must never leave a half-written file. The standard technique is write-to-temp-then-rename: write the whole new state to a temporary file in the same directory, flush it, then atomically replace the old file. On Windows that is File.Replace; on POSIX it is rename. A reader sees either the old complete file or the new complete file, never a mix. Chapter 3.8 covers the Windows sharp edges.

3.7.5 The recovery procedure

On startup, before the strategy is allowed to submit anything:

  1. Read the broker position. Size and direction.
  2. Read persisted state. Check the schema version and that it parses.
  3. Reconcile (Figure 3.7.1).
  4. Re-verify protection. For a resumed position, make sure a protective stop is really working at the broker. If not, place one through the same fail-safe path used everywhere else. That means a market exit if the intended stop has already been crossed.
  5. Only then enable entries.

Figure 3.7.2 — Recovery order on startup. The five steps run strictly left to right, and nothing may be submitted before the last one. Step 4 is the one people skip. A restart is exactly when you can lose a working order without noticing.

Figure 3.7.1 — The four reconciliation cases. Columns are what the file says; rows are what the broker says. Green cells are safe to handle automatically. The blue cell resumes management only when broker and file agree on direction and size. The orange cell, a position the file knows nothing about, is an orphan: block new entries, alert, and do not guess.

Broker File Action
Flat Flat Clean start.
Flat Positioned Position closed while we were down (stop or target hit). Clear the file, record it.
Positioned Agrees on direction and size Resume management from the persisted phase.
Positioned Flat or disagrees Orphan. Block new entries, alert, do not guess.

3.7.6 Historical replay on startup
