Many platforms “warm up” a strategy by running it over historical data before going live. If the strategy is allowed to act during warm-up, it can create virtual trades that put its internal state out of step with reality.

Two fixes: suppress position-changing logic during historical processing, or make the live transition explicitly discard any virtual position and reload from the reconciled state. In my code, persisted state is loaded at the transition to real-time, not before.

3.7.7 Idempotency across restarts

Idempotent means doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once. If the strategy consumes commands or decisions from an outside source, the “already consumed” set must survive a restart. Otherwise the first thing a freshly restarted strategy does is re-run the last command it saw. If that command was “enter”, that is a duplicate order. Persist the last processed sequence number alongside position state.

3.7.8 Testing it

Test Assert
Kill the process mid-trade and restart Resumes with the right phase and stop
Corrupt the state file Refuses to trade and alarms, rather than starting fresh
Close the position externally while down File is cleared on restart
Replay the last command after restart No duplicate order

3.7.9 Summary

  • Broker decides what exists; the persisted file explains why.
  • Persist a small, versioned state on every transition, written atomically.
  • Recover in a fixed order: read, read, reconcile, re-verify the stop, then enable entries.
  • Ignore warm-up trades and persist the last processed command to avoid duplicates.
  • Design so the worst case is “blocked and alarming”, never “trading on a wrong belief”.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) The broker shows flat; the file says long 2. What should the strategy do? (Answer: the position closed while it was down; clear the file and record it.)
  2. (Apply) Why must initial risk (1R) be persisted rather than recomputed from the current stop?
  3. (Think) Assume a crash happens between “order filled” and “state written”. Which reconciliation case do you land in, and is the outcome safe?
  4. (Design) Sketch a test harness that kills the process at a random point in a trade and checks the four assertions in Section 3.7.8.

Further reading

  • Jim Gray and Andreas Reuter, Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques (1992).
  • Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2017), chapters on durability and idempotency.

— Tariq

Chapter 3.8 — Atomic File Writes on Windows: File.Replace, Sharing Violations and Bounded Retries

Subtitle: The textbook trick is “write a temp file, then rename”. On Windows, the rename is where it gets interesting.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe the write-temp-then-rename pattern and why the temp file must be in the same directory. 2. Explain how a harmless reader can make File.Replace fail on Windows. 3. Write a bounded retry with exponential backoff and work out its worst-case wait. 4. Tell apart “atomic” and “durable”.

You need: basic file I/O and exceptions. The code is C#, but the ideas carry over.

3.8.1 Why it matters

When two processes talk through files, the most important property is that a reader never sees a half-written file. My trading stack leans on small JSON files for health, decisions and state, so I care about this a lot. The textbook answer is simple. The Windows reality has a few teeth.

3.8.2 The textbook pattern

  1. Write the full content to a temporary file in the same directory as the target.
  2. Flush it.
  3. Atomically (in one indivisible step) rename the temp file over the target.

Readers that open the target get either the old file or the new file, never a torn one. Same directory matters: a rename is only atomic within one volume (disk partition). Across volumes it becomes copy-and-delete.

On POSIX, rename(2) does step 3 atomically and does not much care who has the target open. On Windows the equivalent is File.Replace in .NET (backed by ReplaceFile in Win32), or File.Move when the target does not exist yet.

3.8.3 The sharing-violation problem

Windows file handles carry share modes. A process opening a file says what it lets others do at the same time: read, write, delete. Replacing a file counts as deleting the old one. If any reader has the target open without allowing delete sharing, File.Replace fails with a sharing violation.

Which readers do that? A surprising number of ordinary ones. Many command-line tools that tail or read a file, and many language runtimes’ default open(), do not grant delete sharing. So a monitoring script that reads your health file once a second can, with perfectly innocent code, make your writer fail now and then.

I found this the hard way: a directory slowly filling with orphaned temp files. Each one was a write whose final replace had failed. The writer threw, the caller logged it, and nobody cleaned up the temp file.

3.8.4 Bounded retry with backoff

Sharing violations are transient: the reader finishes and closes its handle. So the right response is to retry, briefly. The pattern I use:

string tmp = path + "." + Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N") + ".tmp";
File.WriteAllText(tmp, text, new UTF8Encoding(false));
int delay = initialDelayMs;
for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++)
{
    try
    {
        if (File.Exists(path)) File.Replace(tmp, path, null);
        else File.Move(tmp, path);
        return;
    }
    catch (IOException)
    {
        if (attempt >= maxAttempts)
        {
            try { if (File.Exists(tmp)) File.Delete(tmp); } catch { }
            throw;
        }
        Thread.Sleep(delay);
        delay *= 2;
    }
}

Figure 3.8.1 — Atomic replace with a bounded retry. The top row is the happy path: write temp, replace, done. A sharing violation drops to the bottom row. If attempts remain, sleep, double the delay and try the replace again. If not, delete the temp file and rethrow so the caller decides.

The important bits:

  • Unique temp names. If two writers (or two calls) share a temp name, they clobber each other. A short GUID suffix fixes that.
  • Bounded. A fixed number of attempts with exponential backoff (each wait doubles).
  • Clean up on give-up. Delete the temp file before rethrowing so the directory does not fill with litter.
  • Rethrow. The caller decides what failure means. A missed health write is a warning; a missed state write might be a reason to stop trading.
  • No BOM. Write UTF-8 without a byte-order mark (a hidden marker at the start of some text files). Some JSON parsers choke on it.

3.8.5 The worst-case wait

Result (geometric sum). With first delay dd, doubling each time, and nn sleeps, the total worst-case wait is ∑k=0n−1d⋅2k=d(2n−1). \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} d \cdot 2^k = d\,(2^n - 1).

Why. Call the sum S=d(1+2+…+2n−1)S = d(1 + 2 + \dots + 2^{n-1}). Then 2S−S=d(2n−1)2S - S = d(2^n - 1), because every middle term cancels.

Figure 3.8.2 — The backoff budget grows geometrically. Each bar is the total sleep after nn waits, in units of the first delay dd. Every extra attempt roughly doubles the worst case. Compute this number and make sure it is acceptable on the thread doing the writing.

3.8.6 Fix the readers too

Retries treat the symptom. The cure is readers that open with permissive sharing. In .NET that means opening a FileStream with FileShare.ReadWrite | FileShare.Delete. Other languages may need platform-specific flags. Where I control the reader, I do this. Where I do not, the retry protects me.

Readers should also tolerate the brief window where the file does not exist (between a delete and a move on some code paths). Treat “not found” as “no update yet”, not as an error.

3.8.7 Atomic is not durable

Property Meaning Given by File.Replace?
Atomic No torn reads: old or new, never a mix Yes
Durable Data survives a power loss No; you must flush the temp file to disk before replacing

For health and telemetry files I accept atomic-but-not-durable. For files whose loss would cause a wrong trade after a crash, the extra flush is worth its cost.

3.8.8 Keep it off the hot path

Every retry sleeps the calling thread. In a trading platform, the thread that processes market data is the last place you want a sleep. Write files from a code path that can tolerate a short stall, or hand them to a background writer.

3.8.9 Summary

  • Write a uniquely named temp file in the same directory, then replace.
  • On Windows, any reader without delete sharing can make the replace fail.
  • Retry a bounded number of times with doubling delays; worst case is d(2n−1)d(2^n - 1).
  • On give-up, delete the temp file and rethrow. Fix the readers where you can.
  • Atomic is not durable, and none of this belongs on the market-data thread.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) First delay 10 ms, 5 sleeps, doubling. What is the worst-case total wait? (Answer: 10 × (2⁵ − 1) = 310 ms.)
  2. (Apply) Why does a temp file on a different drive break atomicity?
  3. (Investigate) Search a directory your system writes to for orphaned .tmp files. What would finding some tell you?
  4. (Think) A missed write to a state file versus a health file: how should the caller react to each?

Further reading

  • Microsoft Docs, ReplaceFile function (Win32) and File.Replace (.NET).
  • Microsoft Docs, “Creating and Opening Files”, on share modes.
  • Dan Luu, “Files are hard” (2015), a tour of what file systems actually guarantee.

— Tariq

Chapter 3.9 — Non-Latching Log Rotation

Subtitle: A size cap that fails once and then never tries again is worse than no cap at all.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe simple size-based log rotation and the disk bound it gives. 2. Explain what a latching failure is and why it turns a short error into a permanent one. 3. Write a rotation check that always tries again, and spot the same bug in other maintenance loops.

You need: basic programming (try/catch, files). A little familiarity with state machines helps.

3.9.1 The problem

Logging feels like the dullest part of a trading system, until a log file becomes the problem. I had one component whose log grew to well over a gigabyte. It did not log too much. Its rotation logic had quietly stopped working, and nothing ever made it try again. The failure had latched: it got stuck and stayed stuck.

This chapter is about that word, and about rotation that recovers on its own.

3.9.2 What rotation is supposed to do

Rotation means swapping a full log file for a fresh one. The simplest scheme is size-based with one backup copy:

  1. Before appending, check the file size.
  2. If it is over a cap, rename app.log to app.log.1 (replacing any older .1).
  3. Start a fresh app.log.

Result. With one backup, disk use stays at roughly twice the cap: one full old file plus one growing new file.

That is all most systems need.

3.9.3 How it latches

The bug goes like this. The rotation step sits inside a try. Something goes wrong once: another process has the file open, an antivirus scanner holds it, or a rename hits a sharing violation (Windows refusing because another handle has the file). The catch sets a flag like rotationFailed = true or loggingDisabled = true, or simply turns off the rotation check “to avoid spamming errors”. From then on, rotation is never tried again for the life of the process.

The file keeps growing. Appends get slower as it gets larger. Tools that read the log choke on it. In the end disk space or I/O becomes a real problem for the trading process itself.

Key point. A latching failure turns a short error into a permanent one. The cause lasted a millisecond; the effect lasts until restart.

Figure 3.9.1 — Latching versus non-latching. On the left, one failure moves the rotator into “rotation off”, and the only arrow out of that box points back into it. On the right, a failure costs one message, and the next check leads straight back to healthy. Same failure, very different future.

3.9.4 The non-latching rule

Rule. A short-lived failure in a maintenance step must not prevent the next attempt.

In practice:

  • No sticky failure flags. If rotation fails, log the failure (to the existing file, or stderr) and keep appending. Try again on the next check.
  • Rate-limit, don’t disable. If you worry about error spam, limit how often the error message is printed, not how often the attempt is made. Check at most every so often, but always check again.
  • Keep the cap meaningful. If rotation keeps failing and the file keeps growing, at some multiple of the cap you need a harder response, such as truncating or switching to a new file name. A bound you cannot enforce is not a bound.

Figure 3.9.2 — File size over time. Both rotators behave the same at first, so the green line is hidden under the orange one. After one rotation fails, the latching version (orange) climbs without limit. The non-latching version (green) keeps returning to zero each time it reaches the cap. Schematic shapes only, no real data.

3.9.5 The same idea everywhere

Once I had seen this in logging, I found it elsewhere:

  • A reconnect loop that gives up after N failures and never tries again.
  • A cache that marks itself “broken” on a parse error and stops refreshing.
  • A writer that disables itself after one I/O error.

Each is a small state machine with an absorbing failure state: a state you can enter but never leave. The fix is to ask: is this state absorbing, and should it be?

Component Should failure be absorbing? Why
Kill switch Yes It must stay tripped until a human resets it.
Log rotator No It should always be one attempt from healthy.
Cache refresh No Same: the next refresh may succeed.

In Markov-chain language (a model of states and moves between them), you want maintenance processes to be recurrent: from every state there is a path back to healthy. An absorbing failure state in a maintenance loop is almost always a bug.

3.9.6 Making rotation robust on Windows

On Windows, rotation fails for the same reasons atomic writes do (Chapter 3.8): sharing violations from readers that did not allow delete or rename. Mitigations:

  • Open your own log with permissive sharing, so readers are not blocked by you, and you do not block yourself if several handles exist.
  • Close the handle before renaming. Rotating with a handle open is a common self-inflicted failure.
  • Retry the rename briefly with backoff (waiting a little longer each time). If it still fails, keep appending and try again later.

3.9.7 Watch the logger too

Monitor the monitor. I now include log file sizes in the health output the system writes anyway. A log far past its cap is a visible, checkable symptom. Before that, the first sign was a slow, bloated file nobody was looking at.

3.9.8 A sketch of the shape

on each append:
    if now - lastRotationCheck < checkInterval: append; return
    lastRotationCheck = now
    if size(log) > cap:
        try rotate()
        except IOError as e:
            maybeReport(e)   # rate-limited message, no state change
    append

No flag disables future checks. A failure costs one message and one more check later. The only state that persists is a timestamp used for rate-limiting, and it only moves forward, so the next attempt is always coming.

Rotation also runs on the writer’s own schedule, not from a separate timer thread. That avoids a second class of bugs where a background rotator and the writer fight over the same handle.

3.9.9 Summary

  • Size-based rotation with one backup keeps disk use near twice the cap.
  • A failure flag set in a catch and never cleared turns one brief error into permanent growth.
  • Rate-limit the error message, never the attempt.
  • Maintenance loops should be recurrent; only safety latches like a kill switch should stick.
  • Put log sizes in the health output so growth is visible.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With a cap of 100 MB and one backup, about how much disk can the logs use? (Answer: about 200 MB.)
  2. (Find it) Search a codebase you know for flags set inside catch blocks. Which ones are never cleared? Should any of them be permanent?
  3. (Design) Rotation has failed many times in a row and the file is now ten times the cap. What harder response would you choose, and what do you lose with it?
  4. (Think) Why is it safer to rotate on the writer’s own schedule than from a timer thread?

Further reading

  • Michael Nygard, Release It! (2nd ed., 2018), on stability patterns and failure modes.
  • Betsy Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (2016), chapters on monitoring and handling overload.

— Tariq

Chapter 3.10 — Canonical JSON and SHA-256

Subtitle: If two machines can disagree about whether a message changed, you can’t audit anything.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why hashing plain JSON text does not give a stable fingerprint. 2. List the rules of a canonical JSON form and apply them. 3. Name what a content hash buys you (deduplication, tamper evidence, replay checks) and the common ways it goes wrong.

You need: what JSON is, and the idea of a hash function (a function that turns any input into a short fixed-size fingerprint).

3.10.1 The goal

My trading stack passes decisions between processes as small JSON messages. I wanted one simple property: from a decision message I can compute a fingerprint, and anyone else (another process, a later audit, a replay) computes the same fingerprint from the same content. That needed more care than I expected, because JSON has no single byte form.

3.10.2 Why plain JSON is not enough

These two documents hold the same data:

{"side":"long","qty":1}
{ "qty": 1, "side": "long" }

Hash them and you get two different SHA-256 digests. Key order, whitespace, number format (1 vs 1.0 vs 1e0), string escaping (a literal é vs its \u escape), and line endings all change the bytes without changing the meaning. Different serializers (the code that prints data as JSON) make different choices, and one serializer can change its choices between versions.

Key point. If the fingerprint depends on any of that, it is a fingerprint of whichever library printed the message, not of the decision.

3.10.3 Canonicalisation

Canonicalisation means defining one standard byte form and always hashing that. My rules follow the spirit of RFC 8785, the JSON Canonicalization Scheme:

Definition (canonical form). 1. Object keys sorted by ordinal (byte-wise / code-unit) comparison. Not culture-aware sorting, which can differ between machines with different locale settings. 2. No insignificant whitespace. 3. Numbers in one fixed format. Integers as integers. Floats in a shortest round-trip form (the shortest text that reads back as the same value), printed with the invariant culture so a decimal comma never appears. 4. Strings with one escaping policy. 5. UTF-8, no byte-order mark. 6. Applied recursively to nested objects and arrays. Array order is kept, since arrays are ordered by definition.

Then the message identity is id=SHA256(canonical(m)), \text{id} = \text{SHA256}(\text{canonical}(m)), written as a hex string.

Figure 3.10.1 — Two spellings, one identity. On the left are two texts of the same data. Both pass through the blue canonicalise step and come out as the same bytes, which hash to one id (green). Hashing the raw text instead, as the orange note says, would give two different ids for one decision.

3.10.4 The culture trap

In .NET, the most common source of non-determinism I have hit is culture (the machine’s locale settings). Format 1234.5 on a machine set to a European locale and you can get 1234,5. Sort strings with a culture-aware comparer and the order can differ between machines. Canonical code must use ordinal comparisons and invariant formatting everywhere. I treat any culture-sensitive call inside canonicalisation code as a bug.

3.10.5 Floats deserve suspicion

Two processes computing the “same” float with a slightly different order of operations can get values that differ in the last bit. Canonical formatting keeps that difference, so the hashes differ. That is correct (the values are different), but it surprises people.

My approach: anything that is part of a decision identity is either an integer (ticks, counts, timestamps in integer units) or a float rounded to a stated precision before canonicalisation. The rounding policy is part of the message spec.

3.10.6 What the hash buys you

Property What it means
Idempotency A consumer keeps a set of hashes it already acted on. The same decision arriving twice is recognised and ignored.
Tamper evidence If a message is edited later, its hash no longer matches the log. Not security against an attacker (anyone can recompute SHA-256), but strong protection against accidental edits and confusion.
Audit and replay Logs record the hash. A replay that regenerates the decision can check it produced byte-identical output. If not, something in the pipeline is non-deterministic, and you have found it.
Cross-language parity A canonicaliser in another language can be tested against the C# one with shared fixtures: same input, same bytes, same hash.

3.10.7 Test it with golden fixtures

I keep a small set of golden fixtures: sample messages with their expected canonical bytes and digests. They include awkward cases: nested objects, unicode, negative zero, very small and very large numbers, empty arrays. Any change to the canonicaliser must reproduce every fixture exactly. If a fixture changes, that is a breaking change to every stored identity, and it is treated like one.

3.10.8 Where it goes wrong in practice

  • Serialising, then canonicalising text. Do not parse a string, reformat it and hope. Canonicalise from the in-memory structure, with explicit rules for each type.
  • Duplicate keys. JSON technically allows them, and parsers disagree about which one wins. Reject messages with duplicate keys before hashing.
  • Integers that overflow doubles. Some parsers read every number as a double, which silently loses precision above 2532^{53}. Large integer identifiers should be strings, or parsed with a type that keeps them exact.
  • Hashing the envelope. Decide whether the hash covers only the payload or also the timestamp and sequence number. If it covers the timestamp, two otherwise identical decisions get different identities. That may be what you want, or it may break deduplication. Either way, write it in the spec.
  • Two canonicalisers. If another language must compute the same hash, it must pass the same fixtures. Otherwise you have two definitions of identity.

3.10.9 Summary

  • The same JSON data can be printed as many different byte strings, so raw text hashes are unstable.
  • Define one canonical form (sorted keys, no whitespace, fixed number and string formats, UTF-8) and hash that.
  • Use ordinal comparison and invariant culture; round or avoid floats in identities.
  • Protect the definition with golden fixtures; a changed fixture is a breaking change.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Write the canonical form of { "b": 2, "a": [3, 1] }. (Answer: {"a":[3,1],"b":2} — keys sorted, array order kept.)
  2. (Spot the bug) A canonicaliser sorts keys with the default string comparer. Why might two machines produce different hashes?
  3. (Design) Should a decision’s hash include its timestamp? Give one case where yes is right and one where no is right.
  4. (Test) List five awkward fixture cases you would add for your own canonicaliser.

Further reading

  • RFC 8785, JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) (2020).
  • RFC 8259, The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format (2017).
  • NIST FIPS 180-4, Secure Hash Standard.

— Tariq

Chapter 3.11 — What Day Is It? CME Trading Calendars, Sessions and Contract Rolls

Subtitle: A futures “day” starts the evening before, contracts expire every quarter, and almost every bug I’ve had with dates came from forgetting one of those.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Map any timestamp to its futures trading date with a single function. 2. Handle time zones, daylight saving, holidays and early closes safely. 3. Explain contract rolls and the two standard ways to build a continuous price series. 4. Describe why one instrument registry keyed on the root symbol prevents a class of bugs.

You need: basic idea of a futures contract and of UTC versus local time.

3.11.1 Why calendar days are wrong

Equity people think of a trading day as a calendar day. Futures do not work that way. Build a futures system on calendar-day assumptions and your daily statistics, resets and loss limits will all be quietly wrong.

This chapter covers the two time ideas that took me longest to get right, the trading date and the contract roll, and the dull but critical piece that ties them together: a single instrument registry.

3.11.2 The trading date

CME Globex equity index futures trade almost around the clock. The session for a trading day opens in the evening of the previous calendar day (US Central/Eastern time) and runs to the next afternoon, with a short daily maintenance halt between sessions. So a trade at 7 p.m. Eastern on a Tuesday belongs to Wednesday’s trading date.

Definition (trading date). For a timestamp tt in exchange-local time and a session cutoff cc: D(t)={date(t)+1if time(t)≥cdate(t)otherwise D(t) = \begin{cases} \text{date}(t) + 1 & \text{if } \text{time}(t) \ge c \\ \text{date}(t) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Then skip weekends and exchange holidays: a Friday-evening print belongs to the next Monday’s session (or later, if Monday is a holiday).

Figure 3.11.1 — The trading date runs ahead of the calendar. The grey lines mark calendar midnights; the coloured bars are trading sessions. A print on Monday evening (black dot) is after the orange cutoff, so it belongs to the Tuesday session. The cutoff position is schematic and the maintenance halt is not drawn.

Every per-day thing in my system goes through one function that implements D(t)D(t): daily loss limits, session resets, per-session statistics, file names. If two parts of the code compute “today” differently, resets happen twice or not at all.

3.11.3 Time zones

Always store timestamps in UTC. Convert to exchange-local time only to compute D(t)D(t) and session boundaries, using a real time-zone database so daylight-saving (DST) changes are handled. Two traps:

  • Platform differences. Time-zone names differ between Windows and other systems. Code that runs on both must resolve the zone portably.
  • DST weeks. The US and Europe change clocks on different dates. For a few weeks each year the gap between US exchange time and European wall-clock time is not the usual one. Hard-coded offsets break here.

3.11.4 Holidays and early closes

Exchanges publish holiday calendars, including partial days that close early. These change every year. A calendar module that knows the holidays is part of the system, not an afterthought, and needs updating at least once a year. Get it wrong and the system expects a session that does not exist, or treats a half-day as a normal day.

3.11.5 Contract rolls

Equity index futures are quarterly contracts expiring in March, June, September and December. In the days before expiry, trading volume moves from the expiring (front) contract to the next one. Traders roll: they switch to the new contract. For an automated system the roll raises three problems.

Which contract am I trading? On any date there must be exactly one answer, and every component must agree on it.

Continuous price series. Research over many months needs one series across contracts. There are two standard methods:

Method What it does Keeps Distorts
Back-adjustment Shift older contracts by the price gap at each roll Point differences (good if your logic is in ticks or points) Absolute price levels
Ratio adjustment Scale older contracts by the price ratio at each roll Percentage returns Absolute price levels

Both distort levels, so any logic that refers to absolute prices must be careful which series it uses.

Figure 3.11.2 — Back-adjustment closes the roll gap. The orange line is the old contract and the solid blue line the new one; at the roll date there is a gap between them. The dashed blue line is the old contract shifted up by that gap, so the joined series has no artificial jump. Its shape is unchanged, but its levels are no longer the prices that actually traded. Schematic shapes only.

Do not mix contracts silently. A data set that splices front and back months without saying so contains artificial gaps or jumps at the roll. Those can look like enormous moves.

3.11.6 The master instrument registry

What saved me from most of this was a single registry keyed on the master instrument (the root symbol, the product itself) rather than a specific contract month. It holds the facts that do not change across contracts: tick size, point value, trading-hours template, and which calendar applies.

Keying by root symbol makes the registry roll-safe: when the active contract changes, nothing in the registry changes. The contract-specific part (which month is active) lives in one place and is computed from the calendar.

Everything else looks up the registry. Nobody hard-codes a tick size in a strategy. A tick-size constant typed into strategy code is a future bug: the day you add an instrument with a different tick size, half the code uses the wrong one.

3.11.7 Pitfalls

  • Daily resets keyed on calendar midnight instead of the session boundary.
  • Comparing timestamps from sources in different time zones without converting.
  • Session statistics that span the maintenance halt as if trading were continuous.
  • Research data that drops the evening session, or the roll week, without saying so.
  • Using the platform’s “default” contract in one component and an explicit contract in another.

3.11.8 Summary

  • A futures trading date starts the evening before; compute it with one function D(t)D(t) and ban every other way.
  • Store UTC; convert with a real time-zone database; keep holidays and early closes up to date.
  • Rolls need one agreed active contract and an explicit choice of back- or ratio-adjustment.
  • Keep instrument facts in one registry keyed on the root symbol, never as constants in strategy code.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A trade prints at 7 p.m. Eastern on a Tuesday. Which trading date does it belong to? (Answer: Wednesday.)
  2. (Edge cases) Write test cases for TradingDate(timestamp) covering: a weekend, a holiday, a DST change, and one second before and after the cutoff.
  3. (Compare) Your logic measures moves in ticks. Which continuous series should you use, and why?
  4. (Think) Why does keying the registry on a specific contract month make every roll a code change?

Further reading

  • CME Group, Globex trading hours and holiday calendar documentation.
  • CME Group, “Understanding Futures Expiration and Contract Roll”.
  • John Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, chapters on futures mechanics.

— Tariq

Chapter 3.12 — Release Kits: Hash Manifests and Golden Fixtures

Subtitle: “Which version is running?” should have a provable answer, not a best guess.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. List what goes into a release kit and its manifest. 2. Walk through a strict apply procedure and say what each check catches. 3. Explain why a hash is evidence while a version number is only a claim. 4. Use golden fixtures to check behaviour, not just bytes.

You need: what a hash function and SHA-256 are (Chapter 3.10), and basic git.

3.12.1 The problem

My trading code lives in one place (a development machine with git) and runs in another (a Windows server running the trading platform). Moving code from the first to the second sounds trivial: copy files, recompile. In practice this is where a lot of quiet damage happens: a file copied from the wrong branch, a half-applied update, a hand edit on the server nobody committed, a recompile that picked up a stale file.

I now ship every change as a release kit: a bundle of files, a manifest that fingerprints each one, and a short procedure that refuses to apply anything that does not match.

3.12.2 What is in a kit

Definition (release kit). - The files. Exactly the source files that changed, at their target paths. - A manifest. A JSON document with: a release identifier (a dated, sequential name); the source commit hash the files came from; for every file its relative path, byte count and SHA-256 digest; a status (draft, validated, superseded); and a schema version for the manifest itself. - A checksum list for the kit. A plain text file with the SHA-256 of every file in the kit, including the manifest, so the whole kit can be checked after transfer. - Apply and fetch scripts. Small, readable scripts that do the mechanical work.

3.12.3 The apply procedure

The apply script is strict on purpose:

  1. Verify every file in the kit against the checksum list. Any mismatch: stop.
  2. Verify every artifact against its manifest entry (bytes and digest). Any mismatch: stop.
  3. Back up the files about to be replaced.
  4. Copy files into place.
  5. Re-hash the installed files and compare with the manifest. Any mismatch: stop and restore the backups.
  6. Record which release is now installed.

Figure 3.12.1 — Six steps, three exits to STOP. Read the grey boxes left to right; only a run that passes every check reaches the green “record release”. Failures in steps 1 or 2 stop before anything is installed. A failure in step 5 stops and puts the old files back. No check can let a bad file through; it can only stop the apply.

Step 5 catches the sneaky failures: an editor or sync tool that rewrote line endings, a copy that silently truncated, or a file locked by the running platform that was never actually replaced.

3.12.4 Why hashes, not version numbers

Key point. A version string is a claim. A hash is evidence.

If someone edits a file on the server after a release, its version string does not change, but its hash does. Running the verification step against the installed tree at any time tells you exactly which files match a known release and which do not.

SHA-256 is more than enough to detect accidental corruption, but it is everywhere, fast enough, and ends any argument about collisions (two different files with the same hash).

Result (birthday bound). For nn files, the chance that any two collide by accident is about n22257, \frac{n^2}{2^{257}}, which is zero for all practical purposes.

Why: there are about n2/2n^2/2 pairs of files, and each pair collides with chance 1/22561/2^{256}. Multiply them.

3.12.5 Golden fixtures

Hashes prove the bytes are right. They do not prove the behaviour is right. For that, kits that change logic come with golden fixtures: small, fixed inputs and the exact outputs the code must produce from them.

For example, a canonical-JSON module ships with fixture messages and their expected canonical bytes and digests. A calculation module ships with a short input series and its expected outputs. After applying the kit and recompiling, a check runs the fixtures and compares outputs byte for byte (or within a stated numeric tolerance for floating point).

Golden fixtures are frozen. If a change rightly alters an output, the fixture is updated in the same release, the manifest records it, and the change is called out. A fixture that changes silently defeats the purpose.

Check Proves Does not prove
Hash manifest The installed bytes are exactly the released bytes The code does the right thing
Golden fixtures The code gives the expected outputs on known inputs Every other input is handled correctly

3.12.6 Releases are append-only

Old manifests are never edited. A release that turns out wrong is superseded by a new release, not changed. That gives a complete history: for any date, you can say which release was installed and exactly which bytes it held.

3.12.7 Local-first

The source of truth is a local git repository; each kit is built from a specific commit. There is no “edit on the server and copy back” path. If something must change on the server, it becomes a commit, then a kit, then an apply. That is slower for tiny changes, and worth every second.

3.12.8 Pitfalls

  • Line endings. Git’s newline conversion can change bytes between machines. Decide whether manifests hash files as stored in the repo or as checked out on Windows, and be consistent.
  • Encoding. A file saved with a byte-order mark has a different hash. Pick one encoding.
  • Partial kits. A kit that updates one file of a pair that must change together. The manifest should list everything that belongs to a logical change, even unchanged files, if they are coupled.
  • Compile without verify. The platform will happily compile whatever is on disk. Always verify before compiling.

3.12.9 Summary

  • Ship every change as a kit: files, a hash manifest tied to a commit, a kit checksum list, and apply scripts.
  • Apply strictly: verify, back up, copy, re-hash the installed files, record. Any mismatch stops the apply.
  • Hashes prove bytes; golden fixtures prove behaviour on known inputs.
  • Manifests are append-only, and the local repo is the only source of truth.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Someone hand-edits a file on the server but leaves its version comment unchanged. Which step of a later verification catches it? (Answer: re-hashing the installed files against the manifest; the digest no longer matches.)
  2. (Think) Why must step 5 re-hash the installed files rather than trust that step 4 succeeded?
  3. (Design) Two files must always change together. How should the manifest reflect that when only one of them changed in this release?
  4. (Apply) Your Windows checkout converts line endings. Write down the rule you would adopt so manifests stay consistent across machines.

Further reading

  • The Reproducible Builds project, reproducible-builds.org.
  • Jez Humble and David Farley, Continuous Delivery (2010).
  • Santiago Torres-Arias et al., “in-toto: Providing farm-to-table guarantees for bits and bytes”, USENIX Security (2019).

— Tariq

Chapter 3.13 — Talking to a Trading Platform: IPC Between NinjaTrader and a .NET Daemon

Subtitle: Keep the platform thin, push work out to a separate process, and make the channel between them boring.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compare the four common ways two processes talk on one Windows machine. 2. Explain why small, atomically written files are a good channel for slow messages. 3. Design a message envelope with version, timestamp and sequence number, and a reader loop that never acts on a partial message. 4. State the one-writer-per-file rule and why it removes a class of race conditions.

You need: what a process and a file are; a rough idea of JSON. Chapter 3.8 (atomic file writes) helps.

3.13.1 Why move work out of the platform

Trading platforms like NinjaTrader are good at their job: market data, charts, order routing. They are a poor home for heavy computation, long-lived services, or anything that might block (stop and wait).

Code inside the platform shares threads with market-data processing. A slow calculation can delay everything else.

So in my setup the platform side is kept fairly thin. Heavier work runs in a separate .NET process, a daemon (a background program with no window). The two talk through a deliberately simple channel. This chapter is about that channel. IPC means inter-process communication: how two separate programs pass messages.

3.13.2 The options on Windows

Channel What it is Strength Weakness
Files on disk One side writes, the other polls (checks again and again) Easy to inspect; survives restarts Slow: up to one poll interval of delay
Named pipes A stream between processes on one machine Low latency A connection to manage
Local sockets TCP/UDP on the loopback address Low latency, familiar A connection to manage
Shared memory Memory-mapped files both sides see Fastest Hardest to debug

Each trades off latency (delay), robustness, and debuggability.

3.13.3 Why I lean on files

Most of my messages change on a scale of seconds: decisions, health beats, state snapshots. For those I use small JSON files written atomically (the new file replaces the old in one step). The reasons:

  • Inspectable. I can open the file and see exactly what the other side sees. No packet capture, no debugger.
  • Decoupled lifecycles. Either process can restart without the other noticing, except possibly a stale file. There is no connection to re-establish.
  • Crash-tolerant. With atomic replace, a crashing writer leaves either the old or the new file, never a torn (half-written) one.
  • Durable by default. The last message is still there after a restart. That helps recovery, with staleness checks so it cannot be acted on blindly.

The cost is latency. Polling adds up to one poll interval of delay. File-system notifications on Windows are not fully reliable, so I do not depend on them. For anything that needs sub-millisecond latency, files are the wrong tool.

3.13.4 One writer per file

Figure 3.13.1 — Each side owns its own outbox. Process A writes only the top file; process B writes only the bottom file. Each side reads the other’s file by polling (dashed arrows). No file ever has two writers.

Rule (ownership). Every file has exactly one writer. If both sides need to speak, each gets its own outbox.

That rule alone removes a whole class of race conditions: two writers can never overwrite each other’s message.

3.13.5 The message envelope

Every message carries the same envelope (the wrapper around the content):

  • Schema identifier and version. The reader refuses an unknown version rather than guessing.
  • Timestamp in UTC, set by the writer.
  • Sequence number that only increases, per writer.
  • Content hash of the canonical form, where identity matters (see Chapter 3.10).
  • Payload, the content itself.

3.13.6 The reader loop

Figure 3.13.2 — Every check must pass before the reader acts. The reader asks, in order: has the file’s last-write time changed? Can it read (with permissive sharing) and parse it? Is the version known? Is the timestamp fresh? Is the sequence number new? Any failure drops to the orange bar: “no new message”, never “act on a partial one”.

3.13.7 Sequence numbers and idempotency

Polling means the reader can see the same file many times. Without a guard, a command could run on every poll.

The sequence number is the guard. The reader saves the last sequence it processed and ignores anything not strictly greater.

Definition. An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.

For stronger guarantees, the reader writes an acknowledgment file holding the last sequence it processed. Then the writer can tell whether a command was consumed. That gives at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing, which is effectively an exactly-once effect.

3.13.8 Threading inside the platform

Polling and file I/O are arranged so they do not block market-data processing. Reads are short, and parsing is light because messages are small. Writes from inside the platform go through the bounded-retry atomic writer. That writer can sleep briefly, so it is kept off the critical path.

3.13.9 What files are bad at

  • High-frequency streams. Do not push tick data through files.
  • Tight request/response. Use a pipe or socket.
  • Many-to-many messaging. Files are great point-to-point and awkward beyond that.

For those cases a named pipe is the natural next step on Windows, with the same envelope (version, timestamp, sequence) on each message.

3.13.10 Pitfalls

  • Clock skew. If writer and reader are on different machines, their clocks can disagree. Same-machine IPC avoids this; cross-machine needs a time-sync plan.
  • Last-write-time granularity. File timestamps have limited resolution, so two quick writes can share one. Use the sequence number as the real change detector.
  • Antivirus and indexers. They open files too and can cause sharing violations. Exclude the IPC folder if you can.

3.13.11 Summary

  • Keep the platform thin; move heavy work to a separate daemon.
  • For slow messages, small atomically written JSON files are inspectable, decoupled and crash-tolerant. The price is poll latency.
  • Put a version, a UTC timestamp and a sequence number on every message.
  • Any failed check means “no new message”. One writer per file, always.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A reader polls every 500 ms. What is the worst-case extra delay a file message adds? (Answer: about one poll interval, 500 ms, plus the read time.)
  2. (Apply) Two writes land within the file system’s timestamp resolution. Which envelope field still tells the reader there is a new message, and why?
  3. (Design) Sketch the acknowledgment file for a command channel. Which process writes it? What does the original writer do if the acknowledgment never advances?
  4. (Think) Why is “two processes write the same status file” dangerous even if each write is atomic?

Further reading

  • Microsoft Docs, “Interprocess Communications” (Windows) and “Pipe Operations in .NET”.
  • G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003), especially the idempotent receiver and message sequence patterns.

— Tariq

Chapter 3.14 — Is It Alive? Heartbeat Files and Stale-Node Detection

Subtitle: A process that has stopped working rarely says so. You have to notice the silence.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. List what a useful health file contains, and why it needs two timestamps and a counter. 2. Write the staleness rule and explain the trade-off in choosing its threshold. 3. Explain why staleness is a veto, and why an outside monitor is still needed. 4. Tell a crashed process, a stalled feed and a zombie loop apart.

You need: Chapter 3.13 (file-based IPC). Basic inequalities.

3.14.1 The silent failure

The most common failure in a multi-process trading setup is not a crash with a stack trace. It is silence. A process hangs on a lock, a data feed stops, a loop exits without an error. Everything downstream keeps reading the last thing it said, as if it were still true.

The defence is old and simple: heartbeats. Each process regularly writes a small health file. Everyone who depends on it checks how old that file is. If it is too old, the node (process) is presumed dead.

3.14.2 What goes in a health file

A heartbeat that only says “I’m alive” tells you little. Mine carry a compact snapshot:

  • Timestamp (UTC) of the write.
  • Process identity and version: which release is running.
  • Input liveness: the time of the last market-data event the process saw, not just when it wrote the file.
  • Key state flags: whether a kill switch is engaged, whether the process thinks it has a position, the reason for its latest decision.
  • Counters that should grow over time (events processed, decisions consumed).

The gap between “I wrote this file” and “I saw fresh data” matters. A process can be alive and writing heartbeats while its data feed has silently stalled. Two timestamps catch that.

3.14.3 The staleness rule

Definition (stale). With tbeatt_{\text{beat}} the time inside the newest heartbeat and τ\tau a threshold,

stale⇔tnow−tbeat>τ. \text{stale} \iff t_{\text{now}} - t_{\text{beat}} > \tau.

Figure 3.14.1 — Age climbs between beats and resets at each one. The blue saw-tooth is the age of the newest heartbeat; green dots are writes, spaced about one interval h apart with some jitter. After the last beat the writer goes silent and age climbs without reset. Once it crosses the dashed threshold τ, the node is stale. The beat times are schematic, not measurements.

Choosing τ is a trade-off. If beats come every hh seconds with some jitter (random variation), then τ\tau must clearly exceed hh plus worst-case jitter, or you get false alarms. But every second of τ\tau is a second in which a dead node is believed alive.

A rule of thumb from distributed systems: set τ\tau to a small multiple of hh. Then measure the real distribution of gaps between beats in production, and check the false-alarm chance is acceptable.

The phi-accrual failure detector (Hayashibara et al.) formalises this. Instead of a fixed threshold, it estimates how surprising the current silence is, given the gaps seen so far, and raises suspicion smoothly.

3.14.4 Staleness is a veto

If the trading process depends on another node’s output and that node is stale, new entries are blocked. Existing positions keep their protective orders. The process does not guess what the stale node would have said.

This is the fail-closed principle: when unsure, do the safe thing. The alternative, acting on the last known message, is how a crashed upstream process can keep a downstream one trading for hours on stale permission.

3.14.5 Monitoring from outside

Heartbeats are read by the processes that depend on them, and also by an independent monitor. The monitor takes no part in trading. It reads every node’s health file, checks ages and counters, and alerts if anything is stale or a counter has stopped growing.

Why both? The dependent process blocks entries, which is safe but silent. Without an outside alert, a system can sit safely blocked for a whole session and nobody notices it is not trading.

3.14.6 Counters catch zombies

A zombie keeps writing heartbeats but has stopped doing useful work, for example a loop that writes health while its main work is stuck. Timestamps miss it. A monotonic counter (one that should only go up) does not: if “events processed” has not grown across several beats in market hours, the process is a zombie, however fresh its heartbeat.

Figure 3.14.2 — Each failure shows up in a different signal. Read across a row to see which signals turn orange. A crash ages everything. A stalled feed keeps the heartbeat fresh but ages the last-data time. A zombie keeps both timestamps fresh, and only the flat counter gives it away.

3.14.7 Clock and file-system details

  • Use the writer’s UTC timestamp inside the file for age, not the file system’s last-write time. File times can change with copying, sync tools and resolution limits.
  • If checker and writer are on different machines, clock skew adds straight to apparent age. Keep clocks synchronised or measure age on the writer’s machine.
  • Write heartbeats atomically. A torn health file that fails to parse counts as stale, not as an exception that crashes the reader.

3.14.8 Market hours

A data feed that is silent at 2 a.m. on a Saturday is fine. Input-liveness checks should know the trading calendar (Chapter 3.11). Otherwise you get alerts every weekend and learn to ignore them, which is worse than no alert.

3.14.9 Summary

  • The usual failure is silence, not a crash. Heartbeats make silence visible.
  • Carry at least two timestamps (write time, last data time) and one counter.
  • Stale means tnow−tbeat>τt_{\text{now}} - t_{\text{beat}} > \tau; pick τ\tau from the measured beat gaps.
  • Staleness is a veto on new entries; an outside monitor makes the veto visible.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Beats arrive every 5 s and jitter never exceeds 2 s. Is τ = 6 s safe from false alarms? (Answer: no. A gap can reach 7 s, which exceeds 6 s; τ must be above 7 s with margin.)
  2. (Apply) A process’s heartbeat is fresh and its counter is rising, but the last-data time is ten minutes old on a weekday morning. What failure is this, and what should the consumer do?
  3. (Think) Why does a torn health file have to count as stale rather than be skipped until the next read?
  4. (Design) Describe how the monitor should treat input-liveness over a weekend without simply turning itself off.

Further reading

  • N. Hayashibara et al., “The φ Accrual Failure Detector”, IEEE SRDS (2004).
  • T. Chandra and S. Toueg, “Unreliable Failure Detectors for Reliable Distributed Systems”, JACM (1996).
  • B. Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (2016), chapter on monitoring distributed systems.

— Tariq

Chapter 3.15 — Two Clocks, One Decision: The Dual-Chart Architecture

Subtitle: Higher-timeframe context on one chart, tick-level execution on another. A general pattern, and its traps.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Give four reasons to split context and execution into separate components. 2. Write the causality rule that links the two clocks. 3. Recognise the common traps: lookahead via the slow chart, clock misalignment, session mismatch, stale context, over-coupling. 4. Describe a replay test that makes cross-timeframe lookahead impossible.

You need: what a bar and a tick are; Chapter 3.14 (staleness).

3.15.1 The idea

Discretionary traders have always done this: look at a slower chart to decide what kind of market it is, then drop to a faster chart to time the entry. When I started automating, I kept that split and made it explicit in the architecture: two separate components, two separate clocks, and a narrow, well-defined interface between them.

This chapter describes the pattern in general terms. It does not say what either side computes in my system. The architectural lessons do not depend on that.

3.15.2 Why separate them

Reason What it means
Different time scales Context (trend, regime, key levels) changes slowly; entry timing is about the next few ticks. One clock forces one of them to the wrong resolution.
Different noise tolerance Context should ignore tick noise; execution should react to it. A filter right for one is wrong for the other.
Fault isolation A bug on one side leaves the other producing correct output. Two small parts are easier to test than one big one.
Independent confirmation Context and trigger come from separate computations on separate series, so they act as two keys (Chapter 3.2).

3.15.3 The two sides

The context side runs on an aggregated series: time bars, range bars, Renko bricks or similar. It updates when its own bar closes, not on every tick. Its output is a small, slowly changing state: direction allowed or not, relevant levels, a regime label.

Its key property: its output at time tt depends only on bars that have closed by tt. If it sees the forming bar, its state flickers every tick and the execution side reacts to noise that will never be confirmed.

The execution side runs on every trade print. It takes the context state as an input and looks for a concrete local event to act on. It also owns everything that must be fast: order submission, stop management, fail-safes.

Figure 3.15.1 — The two sides meet only through a snapshot. The context side, on the slow clock, decides whether. The execution side, on the fast clock, decides when. Between them sits one small message with a timestamp and a version; the execution side checks its age before using it.

3.15.4 The interface

Most bugs live in the interface, so it stays narrow:

  • The context side publishes a snapshot: a small structured message with a timestamp and a version.
  • The execution side reads the latest snapshot and checks its age before use.
  • The execution side never reaches into the context side’s internals.

Causality rule. The execution decision at tick time tt is

at=f(x≤t,cτ(t)), a_t = f\big(x_{\le t},\; c_{\tau(t)}\big),

where x≤tx_{\le t} are the ticks up to and including tt, and cτ(t)c_{\tau(t)} is the latest context snapshot whose bar closed at time τ(t)≤t\tau(t) \le t.

The constraint τ(t)≤t\tau(t) \le t, meaning strictly the last closed bar, is the whole causality story for this architecture.

Figure 3.15.2 — At tick t, only closed bars count. Bars 1 and 2 have closed; bar 3 is still forming when tick t arrives. The green dot marks τ(t), the last close before t, so the execution side uses the bar 2 snapshot. Reading bar 3’s values before it closes is lookahead and is blocked.

3.15.5 Traps

  • Lookahead via the slow chart. The most common backtest bug in multi-timeframe systems: using the higher-timeframe bar’s final values while it is still forming. In a backtest the full bar sits in an array, so it is easy. Live, you do not have it yet. The result: a backtest that looks great and a live system that does not match. A replay engine that only shows closed bars to the context side prevents this by construction.
  • Clock alignment. Both sides must agree on the time. If the context side stamps by bar open and the execution side by trade time, you can use a snapshot “from the future” by one bar.
  • Session boundaries. Both sides must reset at the same session boundary. If one carries state across the daily break and the other does not, they disagree every morning.
  • Stale context. If the context side stops updating, the execution side must notice. Snapshot age is a veto (Chapter 3.14).
  • Over-coupling. It is tempting to keep adding fields “just in case”. Each field is a new dependency and a new way to disagree. Keep it minimal.

3.15.6 Testing the pair

I test each side alone with fixed inputs, then test the pair in tick replay (feeding recorded ticks back in order). In replay, the context side gets closed bars as they complete. The execution side gets every tick plus whatever snapshot was current at that tick.

A guard throws an error if anything asks for a bar that has not closed. That one guard has caught more bugs than any other test I have.

3.15.7 Summary

  • Split context (slow clock, decides whether) from execution (fast clock, decides when).
  • Join them with a small, versioned, timestamped snapshot, not shared memory.
  • Causality: at tick tt, use only the snapshot from the last bar closed at τ(t)≤t\tau(t) \le t.
  • Build a replay where lookahead across the two clocks is impossible, not just unlikely.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Context bars close at 10:00, 10:05 and 10:10. A tick arrives at 10:07:30. Which bar’s snapshot may the execution side use? (Answer: the bar that closed at 10:05.)
  2. (Apply) The context side stamps snapshots with bar open time. Show how this can lead the execution side to use information one bar early.
  3. (Design) Write pseudocode for the replay guard that throws when a forming bar is requested.
  4. (Think) Name one field you might be tempted to add to the snapshot, and the new way it could make the two sides disagree.

Further reading

  • A. Elder, Trading for a Living (1993), the “triple screen” multi-timeframe idea.
  • M. López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), on information-driven bars.
  • L. Harris, Trading and Exchanges (2003).

— Tariq

Chapter 4.2 — Why Bars Lie, and Why I Replay Every Tick

Subtitle: A bar is a summary. Summaries throw away the order in which things happened, and order is exactly what a stop and a target care about.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Say what information a bar (open, high, low, close, volume) keeps and what it throws away. 2. Explain the intrabar sequencing problem and why every bar-based fix is a guess. 3. Run a wick census and say why a census near zero makes a result invalid. 4. Describe how tick-by-tick replay removes the problem, and what it costs.

You need: what a price chart and a stop or target order are. No maths beyond max and min.

4.2.1 The claim

Charting tools, backtesting tutorials and most data vendors give you bars: open, high, low, close and volume. A bar is compact and fine for looking at a market. For simulating trades it is quietly dangerous.

My research engine replays every trade print (one reported trade: time, price, size), in order, from the canonical tick record. This chapter explains why I think anything less is a guess dressed up as a measurement.

4.2.2 What a bar throws away

A bar squeezes a sequence of trades {(ti,pi,vi)}i=1n\{(t_i, p_i, v_i)\}_{i=1}^{n} (time, price, volume) into five numbers:

O=p1,H=maxipi,L=minipi,C=pn,V=∑ivi O = p_1,\quad H = \max_i p_i,\quad L = \min_i p_i,\quad C = p_n,\quad V = \sum_i v_i

Three things are lost:

  • the order in which the high and the low happened;
  • everything that happened between them;
  • the timing of each trade.

For many questions that does no harm. For a trade with a stop below and a target above, the order is the only thing that matters.

4.2.3 The intrabar sequencing problem

You are long. Your stop is at ss and your target is at gg. A bar arrives with L≤sL \le s and H≥gH \ge g. Which filled first? The bar cannot tell you.

Figure 4.2.1 — The same bar can hide two opposite outcomes. Both blue paths start at the same entry and give exactly the same open, high, low and close. In path A the price reaches the green target line first. In path B it reaches the orange stop line first. A bar-only backtest sees the two as identical, so it has to guess.

A bar-based backtester must pick a rule:

Rule What it assumes Effect
Optimistic the target hit first inflates results
Pessimistic the stop hit first deflates results
Heuristic guess from the open (open nearer the high means the high came first) sometimes right, often not

Whatever rule you choose, you have swapped a fact for an assumption. And the error is not random. It is tied to volatility. The bars where both levels are touched are the fast, wide bars, which are exactly where your strategy’s behaviour matters most.

4.2.4 The wickless-bar trap

There is a worse failure: bars that have lost their wicks (the thin lines above and below the body). On a wickless bar

H=max⁡(O,C),L=min⁡(O,C). H = \max(O, C), \qquad L = \min(O, C).

This happens when bars are rebuilt from closes, resampled carelessly, or made by a “brick” construction that only records body prices.

Figure 4.2.2 — Without wicks, levels inside the bar’s true range are never touched. The left bar has wicks: its high is above the body and its low is below it. The right bar is wickless: high and low sit on the body. A target or stop just beyond the body (dashed lines) can never be hit on that bar unless the close crosses it. Stops then look as if they almost never trigger, and the strategy looks far better than it is.

Definition (wick census). The wick census of a bar set is the share of bars where H>max⁡(O,C)H > \max(O, C) or L<min⁡(O,C)L < \min(O, C).

I run a wick census on any bar set before I trust it. In real liquid futures data, most time bars have wicks. A census near zero means the bars are synthetic, and any result computed on them is invalid.

4.2.5 Renko and other price-based bars

Price-based bars such as Renko are especially prone to this. A textbook Renko brick has its open and close exactly one brick height apart, and the usual chart shows no wicks. But price obviously went beyond the brick’s close before reversing, or overshot before the brick printed. If a simulation uses brick prices as if they were trade prices, it fills at prices that may never have traded at that moment.

My rule:

The brick is a decision clock, not a price source. Decisions are made when a brick closes. Fills are simulated against the real tick tape after that moment.

4.2.6 Tick-by-tick replay

The replay engine handles every print in timestamp order. At each print it:

  1. updates any bar builders (time, range, brick) with that print;
  2. if a bar closed on this print, shows the newly closed bar to the decision logic;
  3. runs the matching engine for working orders against this print.

Stops and targets are checked against real trade prices in real order. The sequencing question disappears, because there is no “inside the bar” any more. There is only the sequence that actually happened.

4.2.7 The costs

Tick replay is not free:

  • Data volume. Liquid futures produce huge numbers of prints per session. Storage, disk reads and memory all grow with it.
  • Speed. Processing every print is orders of magnitude slower than processing bars. This is a big part of why my engine is in C#: tight loops over arrays of value types, with no memory allocation per tick.
  • Data quality. Ticks have their own problems: out-of-order timestamps, duplicate prints, bad prints at the open. You need a cleaning policy, written down and applied the same way everywhere.

4.2.8 What textbooks get wrong

Most introductory backtesting material treats OHLC bars as the data. That is understandable, because bars are what is freely available. But it produces strategies whose edge lives entirely inside the bar, where the backtest cannot see. If your stop or target is within one bar’s typical range of the entry, a bar backtest is answering a different question from the one you are asking.

Before trusting any backtest, ask two questions:

  1. If the stop and the target are both inside the same bar, what does the engine assume?
  2. Do these bars have real wicks?

If you cannot answer both, the result is a hypothesis, not a measurement.

4.2.9 Summary

  • A bar keeps open, high, low, close and volume, and loses the order of events inside it.
  • With a stop and target inside one bar, any bar-based rule is a guess, and its error grows with volatility.
  • Wickless bars hide stops and targets; a wick census near zero makes a result invalid.
  • Use bricks and bars as decision clocks; fill against the real tick sequence.
  • Tick replay costs data volume, speed and a written cleaning policy.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A bar has O = 100, H = 104, L = 97, C = 101. You are long from 100 with a stop at 98 and a target at 103. Can a bar backtest know which filled first? (Answer: No. Both levels lie inside the bar’s range, so the order is lost.)
  2. (Apply) Out of 1,000 bars, 3 have a high above the body or a low below it. What is the wick census, and what should you conclude?
  3. (Think) Why are the bars that touch both stop and target more likely to be high-volatility bars? What does that do to the size of the optimistic rule’s error?
  4. (Build) Write a function that takes a list of bars and returns the wick census.

Further reading

  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), chapter 2 on bar types.
  • Ernest Chan, Algorithmic Trading: Winning Strategies and Their Rationale (2013), on backtesting pitfalls.
  • Larry Harris, Trading and Exchanges (2003).

— Tariq

Chapter 4.3 — Making Lookahead Impossible: Causality Guards That Throw

Subtitle: Code review won’t reliably catch a peek at the future. A guard that crashes the run will.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State what a causal decision rule is, using the idea of “information available at time t”. 2. Build a view object that throws when code asks for a bar that has not closed. 3. List the kinds of lookahead a guard cannot catch, and the defence for each.

You need: basic programming (arrays, exceptions). The probability notation is explained as it appears.

4.3.1 The problem

Lookahead bias is the most common way backtests lie. Somewhere, a decision at time tt uses information that only existed after tt. It is rarely deliberate. It is an off-by-one error, a centred rolling window, a bar’s close used before the bar closed, or a normalisation over the whole sample. It is almost invisible in review, because the code looks reasonable.

I stopped trying to catch lookahead by reading code. I made it structurally impossible instead. In my research engine, a strategy cannot see the future because the object it is given physically cannot return it. Ask for a bar that has not closed and the engine throws an exception.

4.3.2 The formal requirement

Let ℱt\mathcal{F}_t be the information available at time tt. (Probability texts call this the filtration.) A decision rule is causal when the action ata_t depends only on that information:

at=f(Xs:s≤t) a_t = f(X_s : s \le t)

Definition (causal bar access). If bar kk closes at time τk\tau_k, then at decision time tt the strategy may use the bars {k:τk≤t}\{k : \tau_k \le t\} and nothing else.

Note the wording. It is not “bars whose index is less than the current index” in some array where future bars already sit. It is closed bars.

4.3.3 The guard

The decision logic never gets the bar array. It gets a view object that wraps the arrays and knows the current closed index. Every accessor checks it:

public Bar Bar(int index)
{
    if (index > _currentIndex)
        throw new InvalidOperationException(
            $"causality breach: bar {index} beyond closed index {_currentIndex}");
    return _bars[index];
}

Figure 4.3.1 — The view only hands out closed bars. Blue boxes are bars that have closed; dashed boxes have not. The black line marks “now”, where the current closed index is 6. A request for bar 2 succeeds (green). A request for bar 8 throws and stops the run (orange).

The same check guards indicator values, cross-asset series and anything else the strategy can read. The strategy interface has one entry point: “here is the closed view; a bar just closed; what do you want to do?” It returns an intent (enter, exit or nothing) with a decision timestamp. It does not return a fill price. Fills are another component’s job.

4.3.4 Why throw instead of clamp

Another design silently clamps: ask for a future bar and you get the current one. That is worse. It hides the bug and changes the strategy’s behaviour in a way nobody intended. Throwing is loud. The run dies, the stack trace names the line, and you fix it.

Rule. A causality breach should never be recoverable.

4.3.5 Testing the guard itself

A guard that does not actually guard is worse than none, because it gives false confidence. So the test suite contains a test that deliberately reaches one bar into the future and asserts that an exception is thrown. If that call ever succeeds without an exception, the suite fails. Testing the negative case is the only way to know the wall is real.

4.3.6 Lookahead a view guard does not catch

A view guard catches indexing into the future. It does not catch everything.

Leak How it happens Defence
Precomputed indicators an indicator computed over all bars in advance, e.g. a centred moving average or a full-sample z-score precompute only with causal formulas; test their fidelity separately
Normalisation and scaling mean and variance taken over the whole data set expanding or rolling windows that end at tt
Session totals today’s total volume or today’s high used before the session ends only use values that are final at tt
Labels in features in machine-learning pipelines, a feature built from the outcome window keep label code separate
Fill prices filling at the decision bar’s close, the very price that triggered the decision earliest fill = first trade strictly after the decision, plus latency

Precomputing is fine only if value kk was computed from bars up to kk.

Figure 4.3.2 — A centred window leaks the future. Both rows show the bars feeding one indicator value at decision time t (black line). The trailing window (green) ends at t. The centred window (orange) reaches past t, so every value it produces contains information that did not yet exist. An index guard cannot see this, because the leak happened when the value was computed.

4.3.7 Parameter lookahead

There is a second-order version: choosing parameters after seeing test results, then reporting those results as out-of-sample. No code guard catches that. The defences are procedural:

  • a ledger that records every trial, so the number of configurations tried is part of the result;
  • holding out data that genuinely has not been looked at.

4.3.8 Costs

The guard adds a bounds check on every access. In a tight loop that is measurable but small: the processor’s branch predictor handles a branch that is never taken very well. I have never had a case where it mattered compared with the cost of the rest of the replay. Correctness comes first.

4.3.9 Summary

  • A causal rule uses only information available at decision time: closed bars, not “earlier array slots”.
  • Give strategy code a view that knows the closed index and throws on anything later.
  • Throw, never clamp; and test that the guard throws.
  • Guards miss precomputed leaks, full-sample scaling, session totals, label leaks and fill-price leaks; handle each on its own.
  • Parameter lookahead needs a trial ledger and true hold-out data.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) The current closed index is 40. Which of these calls should throw: Bar(39), Bar(40), Bar(41)? (Answer: only Bar(41).)
  2. (Apply) A feature is “price minus the mean price of the whole data set”. Explain the leak and rewrite it causally.
  3. (Build) Write the negative test for your own view object. What should happen if someone removes the check?
  4. (Think) Why is clamping a future request to the current bar more dangerous than throwing?

Further reading

  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), chapters 7 and 11 on leakage and backtest overfitting.
  • David Bailey, Jonathan Borwein, Marcos López de Prado and Qiji Zhu, “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting”, Journal of Computational Finance (2017).
  • Shaun Kaufman et al., “Leakage in Data Mining: Formulation, Detection, and Avoidance”, ACM TKDD (2012).

— Tariq

Chapter 4.4 — Where Am I in the Queue? FIFO Fill Simulation for CME Globex

Subtitle: A resting limit order doesn’t fill because price touched it. It fills when everyone ahead of it has been filled.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain price-time (FIFO) priority and why a “touch fill” is optimistic. 2. Simulate queue position from trade prints, with queue exhaustion and trade-through fills. 3. Explain adverse selection and why fills should be split by how they happened.

You need: what a limit order and a market order are. Summation notation.

4.4.1 The touch-fill problem

The most flattering thing a backtest can assume about limit orders is the touch fill: if the market trades at your limit price, you are filled. On a central limit order book with price-time priority, that is often false. You were in a queue. If the market touched your price, traded some volume and bounced, the people ahead of you were filled and you were not.

This matters most for the trades that look best in a backtest: price came to your level and immediately turned in your favour. Those are exactly the ones where you were least likely to be filled.

4.4.2 How the matching engine works

CME Globex matches most outright futures by price-time priority, often called FIFO (first in, first out). At each price level, resting orders form a queue in arrival order. An incoming aggressive order eats the queue from the front.

You are filled only when the volume traded at your price exceeds the volume that was ahead of you when you arrived. Cancellations ahead of you would move you forward, but you cannot see them without full order-by-order data.

Figure 4.4.1 — A queue at one price. White boxes are orders that arrived before mine; mine is blue, at the back. Their total size is Q₀, the volume ahead of me. Trades at this price consume the queue from the left. I am filled only after Q₀ is used up, or if a trade prints through my price.

4.4.3 A simple queue model

With trade prints but no history of the full book, you have to model the queue. A conservative model:

  1. When your limit order arrives at price ℓ\ell, set Q0Q_0, the volume ahead of you. Without book data, a conservative stand-in is the size seen at that price on arrival.
  2. For each later trade at exactly ℓ\ell with size viv_i, count down: Qi=Qi−1−viQ_i = Q_{i-1} - v_i.
  3. You are filled when either
    • queue exhaustion: Qi≤0Q_i \le 0, or
    • trade-through: a trade prints at a price strictly beyond ℓ\ell (below a buy limit, above a sell limit). If the market traded through your price, every order at ℓ\ell must have been filled first.

Fill time for a buy limit at ℓ. Counting only trades after your order arrives,

τ=min⁡{ti:pi<ℓor∑j≤i,pj=ℓvj≥Q0}\tau = \min\Big\{ t_i : p_i < \ell \;\;\text{or}\;\; \sum_{j \le i,\; p_j = \ell} v_j \ge Q_0 \Big\}

Figure 4.4.2 — The queue counts down in steps. The blue line is the volume still ahead of me, as a share of Q₀. Each step down is a trade at my price. The fill (green dot) happens only when the line reaches zero. The trade sizes are illustrative; the shape is the point.

4.4.4 Why conservative

The model ignores cancellations ahead of you, which would move you forward. So it tends to underestimate fills. That is deliberate. In research I would rather understate an edge than overstate it. A strategy that only works under optimistic fill assumptions is not a strategy.

Trade-through is the strongest evidence of a fill that prints alone can give. In a pessimistic setting you can require it exclusively: count only fills where price traded through. That is a useful lower bound to report next to the queue model.

4.4.5 Arrival time and market orders

Your order does not arrive when you decide. It arrives after latency. In my engine, an order decided at print kk can at the earliest interact with prints after kk and after the decision time plus a modelled latency. Anything that traded before your order arrived is irrelevant to your queue position.

Market orders do not queue, but they still cannot fill at a price that traded before they arrived. They fill at the first eligible print after arrival, plus a slippage allowance per side. In a thin moment a real market order can walk the book; a single-print fill model understates that, so the slippage allowance has to be honest.

4.4.6 Adverse selection

Condition on your limit order being filled. Fills are more likely when lots of aggressive volume is hitting your side, which tends to happen when price is moving through your level. So, given a fill, the short-term expected move afterwards is worse than average:

𝔼[Δp∣filled]<𝔼[Δp] \mathbb{E}[\Delta p \mid \text{filled}] < \mathbb{E}[\Delta p]

A touch-fill backtest computes the right-hand side. Reality pays the left-hand side. This is called adverse selection.

4.4.7 What the model cannot do

  • Without order-by-order (market-by-order) data, you cannot see cancellations ahead of you or iceberg orders refilling.
  • Implied liquidity from spreads can change the book in ways prints do not show.
  • Your own order would have changed others’ behaviour. With small size this is negligible, not zero.

Name these limits in every report that uses the model.

4.4.8 Reporting fills honestly

Every simulated fill in my engine records how it filled: trade-through or queue exhaustion. Results can then be split by fill type.

Results depend mostly on… Rests on Trust
queue-exhaustion fills the weakest part of the model, the initial queue estimate most scepticism
trade-through fills the strongest evidence prints can give more confidence

Unfilled limit orders are recorded too, with the price path after they were placed. The orders you did not get are half the story of a passive strategy.

4.4.9 Summary

  • Under FIFO you fill when the queue ahead of you is consumed, not when price touches.
  • Model Q₀ conservatively, count it down with trades at your price, and treat trade-through as a fill.
  • Only trades after your order arrives (after latency) count.
  • Fills are adversely selected; touch fills ignore that.
  • Tag every fill by type and record unfilled orders.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Q₀ = 50 contracts. Trades at your price: 20, 15, 10. Are you filled? (Answer: No. 45 < 50, and no trade printed through your price.)
  2. (Apply) Same as above, then a trade prints one tick below your buy limit. Are you filled now, and why?
  3. (Think) Rerun a touch-fill backtest with trade-through only. What does a large change tell you?
  4. (Think) Why does ignoring cancellations make the model conservative rather than optimistic?

Further reading

  • CME Group, “Matching Algorithms” documentation (FIFO and pro-rata).
