  • Jean-Philippe Bouchaud, Julius Bonart, Jonathan Donier and Martin Gould, Trades, Quotes and Prices (2018).
  • Álvaro Cartea, Sebastian Jaimungal and José Penalva, Algorithmic and High-Frequency Trading (2015).
  • Rama Cont and Adrien de Larrard, “Price Dynamics in a Markovian Limit Order Market”, SIAM J. Financial Mathematics (2013).

— Tariq

Chapter 4.5 — The First Trade Strictly After the Signal

Subtitle: The price that triggered your decision is the one price you can be sure you didn’t get.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State the “first trade strictly after the signal” fill rule, including latency. 2. Explain why filling at the signal bar’s close is biased, and which way. 3. Handle prints that share a timestamp, and separate bar-close decisions from resting orders.

You need: what a bar close and a market order are. Expected value, informally.

4.5.1 The impossible fill

Many backtests hide this assumption: the strategy decides on a bar close and is filled at that close. The bar closed at 100, the signal fired at 100, you bought at 100.

It is impossible. The close is the last trade of the bar. By the time your code knows the bar closed, that trade has already happened. Your order can only meet trades that happen after you send it.

4.5.2 The rule

Let tdt_d be the decision time: the timestamp of the print that closed the decision bar. Let ℓ\ell be the latency, the time from decision to the order reaching the exchange.

Rule (market order fill). The fill is the first print ii with

ti>tdandti≥td+ℓ,t_i > t_d \quad\text{and}\quad t_i \ge t_d + \ell,

at price pip_i, adjusted by a slippage allowance per side.

The first condition is a strict inequality. Prints at exactly tdt_d (there can be several with the same timestamp) are excluded. In index terms, a decision at print kk can fill at print k+1k+1 at the earliest.

The strategy’s intent carries the decision timestamp and, for reference only, the decision price. The fill engine never uses that decision price as a fill price.

Figure 4.5.1 — Where the earliest fill can be. Dots are prints in sequence. Print k (black) closes the bar and triggers the decision. Orange prints come after k but inside the latency window, so the order has not arrived yet. The first green print is the earliest legal fill. Print k+1 may even share k’s timestamp; it is still after k in the sequence.

4.5.3 Why it matters so much

Take a breakout signal: “buy when the bar closes above a level”. The bar that closes above the level is, by construction, a bar that ended with buying pressure. The next trades are more likely to be higher, because the aggressive flow that pushed it there is still arriving. Fill at the close and you capture a move you could not have captured.

Bias of filling at the signal price.

bias=𝔼[pfirst after−psignal∣signal]\text{bias} = \mathbb{E}\big[p_{\text{first after}} - p_{\text{signal}} \mid \text{signal}\big]

Signal type Sign of the bias Effect of filling at the close
Momentum (breakout) systematically positive, i.e. against the buyer backtest looks better than reality
Mean reversion can flip, but not zero still a price you did not earn

This small, steady difference is exactly the kind that turns a losing strategy into a winning backtest.

4.5.4 Timestamps and ties

Tick data often has many prints with the same timestamp, especially in fast moves. So the rule must work on sequence, not only time. My engine uses each print’s position in the canonical stream: a decision triggered by print kk can only see fills from k+1k+1 onward, even if k+1k+1 shares a timestamp with kk. Latency then pushes the earliest fill further.

If your data source does not keep the order of same-timestamp prints, you have an ambiguity you cannot resolve. Be pessimistic about it.

4.5.5 Latency and slippage

Even “the next print” is optimistic if it comes microseconds after the signal and your real system takes longer to react. The modelled latency ℓ\ell should cover the whole path: bar-close detection, decision logic, order construction and the network to the exchange. Measure it from live telemetry, then use a conservative value in research.

The first print after arrival tells you a price at which a trade happened. It does not promise your order got that price. If the book was thin, a market order might have walked to a worse price. A per-side slippage allowance covers that. Like latency, calibrate it against live fills, and use the same value in every run you compare. Changing the fill model between two runs makes the comparison meaningless.

4.5.6 Exits too

Exits decided on a bar close follow the same rule: they fill on the first eligible print after the decision. Protective stops and targets resting in the book are different. They are working orders that fill when price trades through them (with queue modelling for limits, Chapter 4.4). The difference is between decisions made at a bar close and orders already sitting at the exchange.

4.5.7 A quick self-check

Search your backtester for any line where a fill price is set from the bar’s close, open, high or low. Each one is a candidate violation. The only legitimate source of a fill price is a print that happened after the order arrived.

4.5.8 Summary

  • The signal bar’s close has already traded; you cannot get it.
  • Fill at the first print strictly after the decision print, and no earlier than decision time plus latency.
  • Use sequence order, not timestamps alone; be pessimistic when ties are ambiguous.
  • Add per-side slippage, calibrated from live fills, and keep the fill model fixed across compared runs.
  • Run once filling at the close and once with the strict rule; the gap measures unearned information.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A decision is made at print 500. Latency is longer than the time to print 503 but shorter than to print 504. What is the earliest fill print? (Answer: print 504.)
  2. (Apply) Print 501 has the same timestamp as print 500. Is it excluded by the strict-after rule? Is it excluded by latency?
  3. (Think) Why does the bias of filling at the close tend to favour momentum strategies?
  4. (Build) Run any simple strategy both ways (close fill vs. strict rule). Report the difference, not just the better number.

Further reading

  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018).
  • Larry Harris, Trading and Exchanges (2003), on latency and execution.
  • Joel Hasbrouck, Empirical Market Microstructure (2007).

— Tariq

Chapter 4.6 — Fidelity Testing: Does the Offline Port Compute What the Live Indicator Computes?

Subtitle: Two implementations of “the same” indicator are two different indicators until you prove otherwise.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. List the common ways a port of an indicator drifts from the original. 2. Run the three levels of test: golden, component fidelity and decision fidelity. 3. Choose a tolerance before looking, and read an error-over-time plot to find the cause.

You need: what an indicator is (for example a moving average). Absolute value and maximum.

4.6.1 Two implementations, one question

My live trading runs inside a trading platform, using indicators written for that platform. My research runs in a separate C# replay engine. Some indicators must exist in both places: the live version the strategy really uses, and an offline port the research engine uses to study it.

Once you have two implementations you have a question that never goes away: do they agree? If they do not, every research result about the port says nothing about the live version. I call answering that question fidelity testing.

4.6.2 Where ports drift

Source of drift What goes wrong
Initialisation the first values are seeded differently: zero, the first price, or a simple average of the first nn. An exponential smoother started differently converges eventually, but “eventually” can be longer than a session.
Bar update semantics one side recomputes on every tick for the forming bar, the other only on bar close, so intermediate values differ
Rounding and tick snapping live code may round to the instrument’s tick size at some step; the port may not
Floating-point order summing in a different order changes the last bits; usually harmless, sometimes crosses a threshold
Session resets one version resets at the session boundary, the other does not
Data differences the live side sees the platform’s bars, the port sees the research engine’s bars; if the bar builders differ, so do the indicators, even with identical formulas

4.6.3 Three levels of test

Figure 4.6.1 — Three levels, three kinds of error. Golden tests check the formula on tiny hand-made inputs. Component fidelity feeds the same bars to both sides and compares every value. Decision fidelity compares what each side would do. A port can pass one level and fail the next.

Golden unit tests. Small hand-built inputs whose correct outputs come from hand calculation or a published definition. They test the formula alone (Chapter 4.7).

Component fidelity. Feed the same bar series to both implementations and compare outputs value by value. In practice the live side exports its values from the platform on historical data, and the port computes on the same bars.

Definition (component fidelity). For each bar kk,

errk=|xklive−xkport|,pass⇔maxkerrk≤ε,\text{err}_k = |x^{\text{live}}_k - x^{\text{port}}_k|, \qquad \text{pass} \iff \max_k \text{err}_k \le \varepsilon,

with the tolerance ε\varepsilon stated in advance.

For discrete outputs (a state, a signal, a direction) the measure is the exact agreement rate, and anything short of full agreement gets every disagreement listed.

Decision fidelity. Even when indicators match within tolerance, a decision that compares an indicator with a threshold can flip when the value sits near the threshold. So I also compare the decisions each side would make: same bar, same decision? Disagreements are listed one by one with both values, so I can see whether they are near-threshold noise or a real bug.

4.6.4 Choose the tolerance before you look

It is tempting to run the comparison, see the largest error, and declare a tolerance just above it. That is not a test; it is a description. The tolerance should come from the problem: how big a difference would change a decision? Set it first, then run.

4.6.5 Which side is the reference?

For my purposes the live indicator is the reference, because it is what actually drives orders. If the port disagrees, the port is wrong, even if the port is arguably more “correct” mathematically. Fidelity means matching what runs, not what is ideal.

When neither side has a clear claim (both are new), golden tests against a published definition become the reference for both.

4.6.6 Record the run

A fidelity run produces a report with a run identifier, the code version, the data used, and pass or fail per component with the worst error and where it happened. That report lets me say “the offline engine reproduces the live indicator on this data” with evidence rather than hope. When something changes later, rerunning the same suite tells me whether parity still holds.

4.6.7 Pitfalls

  • Comparing during the indicator’s warm-up. Exclude a warm-up window, and say so.
  • Testing one instrument and assuming the other is fine. Different tick sizes and price scales expose different rounding bugs.
  • Checking only averages. A mean error near zero can hide occasional large errors. Look at the maximum and the distribution.
  • Accepting “close enough” for discrete outputs. One flipped state can change a whole trade.

4.6.8 Diagnostic: error over time

When a component fails, plot errk\text{err}_k against kk. The shape usually points at the cause.

Figure 4.6.2 — The shape of the error names the bug. Each panel plots the error between live and port (up) against bar index (across). A curve that starts large and decays points to initialisation. Regular jumps point to session resets. A flat line points to an offset or unit bug. Tiny error with rare spikes points to rounding, tick snapping or a bar-builder disagreement on particular bars. The shapes are schematic.

Spending a minute on that plot has saved me hours of reading code.

4.6.9 Summary

  • Two implementations are two indicators until a test proves they agree.
  • Drift comes from initialisation, update timing, rounding, summation order, session resets and different bars.
  • Test at three levels: golden, component (max error ≤ ε) and decision.
  • Fix the tolerance in advance; the live version is the reference.
  • Plot error over time; its shape points to the cause.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Live values 10.00, 10.02, 10.05; port values 10.00, 10.03, 10.05; ε = 0.005. Pass or fail? (Answer: fail. The maximum error is 0.01.)
  2. (Apply) The error is large for the first 30 bars of every session and tiny afterwards. Name two likely causes.
  3. (Think) Why can two indicators that pass component fidelity still fail decision fidelity?
  4. (Think) Why is “set the tolerance just above the observed maximum” not a test?

Further reading

  • Michael Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004), on characterisation tests.
  • David Goldberg, “What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic”, ACM Computing Surveys (1991).
  • Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns (2007).

— Tariq

Chapter 4.7 — Golden Unit Tests: Pinning Numerical Code to Known Answers

Subtitle: For maths code, “it runs” means nothing. “It produces exactly these numbers from exactly these inputs” means a lot.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Say where a trustworthy expected value can come from, and rank the sources. 2. Design inputs (constants, ramps, steps, invariances) that make wrong code fail. 3. Write a tolerance that works for both large and near-zero values.

You need: basic unit testing. A moving average and a least-squares line, in outline.

4.7.1 Why numerical code needs something different

Most unit-testing advice is written for business logic: given this input, assert this behaviour. An indicator, a filter, a geometry routine or a statistical estimator does not have “behaviour” so much as outputs. Those outputs are floating-point numbers, and they are easy to get almost right.

My answer is golden tests: small, frozen inputs paired with outputs known to be correct by some independent route, checked to a stated tolerance.

4.7.2 What makes an output “golden”

The expected output must come from somewhere other than the code under test.

Figure 4.7.1 — Where an expected value comes from, strongest first. The four blue rungs give independent answers and can be called golden. The orange rung, the code’s own earlier output, only proves that nothing changed, not that anything is right.

  1. Closed form. The input is designed so the answer can be derived on paper. A linear ramp into a moving average; a constant series into a variance estimator (answer: zero); a step into an exponential smoother (answer: 1−(1−α)n1 - (1-\alpha)^n after nn steps).
  2. Hand calculation. A short input worked by hand or in a spreadsheet, with the working kept beside the test.
  3. Published reference values. Some methods have certified reference datasets. NIST’s Statistical Reference Datasets are the classic example for regression and summary statistics.
  4. A trusted independent implementation. Another library, or the live platform’s version.
  5. The code’s own previous output. This is a regression fixture, not a golden one.

I label every fixture with its source. A test called “golden” that is really source 5 is misleading.

4.7.3 Inputs that discriminate

A good golden input makes wrong implementations fail.

Input What it exposes
Constant series bugs in variance, range or slope (output should be zero)
Linear ramp lag errors; the lag is known exactly
Step initialisation and warm-up behaviour
Alternating series sign errors and off-by-one indexing
Edge values very large, very small, negative, zero, exactly on a tick boundary
Geometry points placed so the right intersection or slope is obvious

Result (moving-average lag on a ramp). A simple moving average of length nn on a ramp of slope mm lags the input by m(n−1)/2m(n-1)/2.

Why: the average of the last nn points of a straight line is the line’s value at the middle of the window, which is (n−1)/2(n-1)/2 steps back, i.e. m(n−1)/2m(n-1)/2 lower.

Figure 4.7.2 — A golden test you can draw. The grey line is a ramp with slope 1. The blue line is its 5-point simple moving average. The gap between them (orange) is exactly 1 × (5 − 1)/2 = 2 at every point after warm-up. A test can assert that number without ever running the code first.

4.7.4 Tolerances

Floating-point results rarely match to the last bit across platforms and compiler settings. The assertion is

|xactual−xexpected|≤εabs+εrel⋅|xexpected| |x_{\text{actual}} - x_{\text{expected}}| \le \varepsilon_{\text{abs}} + \varepsilon_{\text{rel}} \cdot |x_{\text{expected}}|

with both tolerances written in the test. A purely absolute tolerance fails for large values; a purely relative one fails near zero. Use both.

For integer or discrete outputs (states, counts, signals, tick-rounded prices) the tolerance is zero. Exact match or fail.

4.7.5 Negative tests

Some of my most important golden tests check that something fails. For example, a test reads a bar beyond the current closed index and asserts an exception (Chapter 4.3). If that call ever succeeds, a causality guard has broken. A suite that only tests the happy path cannot notice a safety mechanism quietly disappearing.

4.7.6 Frozen, versioned, hashed

Golden fixtures are frozen. They live in version control, and when shipped with a release their hashes are in the manifest. Changing a fixture is a deliberate act with a written reason, never a way to make a failing test pass.

Warning. Editing expected values until tests go green turns a detected bug into an accepted one.

4.7.7 Run them every time

Golden tests are cheap: milliseconds on tiny inputs. So they run before every research job. A research run that starts with a failing golden test does not start. There is no point spending an hour of compute on a replay that uses a broken indicator.

4.7.8 What they do not do

Golden tests prove the formula on chosen inputs. They do not prove it is the right formula for the job, and they do not prove it behaves the same on real data as on toy data. That is what fidelity testing (Chapter 4.6) and real-data validation are for. Each layer catches a different class of error.

4.7.9 A worked example

A function returns the slope of the least-squares line through the last nn points. Golden input: the points (i,3i+7)(i,\, 3i + 7) for i=0,…,n−1i = 0, \dots, n-1.

  1. The slope must be exactly 3 and the intercept 7, for any nn. (Catches a wrong formula.)
  2. Add a constant to every yy: the slope must not change. (Catches wrong centring.)
  3. Flip the sign of every yy: the slope must become exactly −3. (Catches sign bugs.)

Three tests, each derived without running the code. Geometry works the same way: build points with a known intersection, rotate or translate them, and assert the answer moves exactly as geometry says. Invariance tests like these are among the cheapest, strongest checks you can write.

4.7.10 Summary

  • A golden value comes from outside the code: closed form, hand working, reference data or an independent implementation.
  • The code’s own past output is a regression fixture, and must be labelled as one.
  • Use constants, ramps, steps, alternations, edge values and invariances to make bugs show.
  • Tolerance = absolute + relative for floats; zero for discrete outputs.
  • Freeze fixtures, include negative tests, and run them before every research job.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A 9-point simple moving average runs on a ramp of slope 0.5. What is the lag? (Answer: 0.5 × 8 / 2 = 2.)
  2. (Apply) An exponential smoother with α = 0.5 starts at 0 and receives a step to 1. What should its output be after 3 steps?
  3. (Build) Write the three slope tests from §4.7.9 for your own regression function.
  4. (Think) Why does a purely relative tolerance fail when the expected value is zero?

Further reading

  • NIST, Statistical Reference Datasets (StRD).
  • Nicholas Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms (2nd ed., 2002).
  • Kent Beck, Test-Driven Development: By Example (2002).

— Tariq

Chapter 4.8 — Ablation Studies: What a 4-Way Ablation Actually Tells You

Subtitle: If a system has two parts, you can’t know what either contributes until you’ve run it without each one.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Set up a 2×2 ablation with a precise definition of “off”. 2. Compute the two main effects and the interaction, and read their signs. 3. Explain why every cell counts as a trial and how to put uncertainty on the effects.

You need: averages and differences. The idea of a bootstrap is explained briefly.

4.8.1 The idea

Ablation comes from surgery and neuroscience: remove a part and see what stops working. In machine learning it became the standard way to show which parts of a model matter. In trading research it is just as useful and much less used. Most strategy write-ups show the full system’s results and never ask what would have happened without each piece.

This chapter covers the simplest serious version: the 4-way (2×2) ablation. I reach for it first whenever a system combines two components.

4.8.2 The setup

Take a system with two components, AA and BB. Each is on or off, giving four configurations:

BB off BB on
AA off baseline y00y_{00} BB only y01y_{01}
AA on AA only y10y_{10} full y11y_{11}

Here yy is your outcome measure, computed the same way in every cell: same data, same fill model, same costs, same period.

“Off” must mean something precise. For a filter, off usually means “always passes”. For an exit component, off may mean “replaced by the simplest reasonable alternative”. Write the definition down before running anything.

4.8.3 Reading the four cells

This is a two-factor factorial design, and the standard decomposition applies.

Main effect of A (average change from turning A on): MEA=12[(y10−y00)+(y11−y01)]\text{ME}_A = \tfrac{1}{2}\big[(y_{10} - y_{00}) + (y_{11} - y_{01})\big]

Main effect of B: MEB=12[(y01−y00)+(y11−y10)]\text{ME}_B = \tfrac{1}{2}\big[(y_{01} - y_{00}) + (y_{11} - y_{10})\big]

Interaction (does A’s effect depend on B?): IAB=(y11−y01)−(y10−y00)I_{AB} = (y_{11} - y_{01}) - (y_{10} - y_{00})

Figure 4.8.1 — The 2×2 and where each effect lives. Green arrows are A’s effect, once with B off and once with B on; their average is A’s main effect. Blue arrows do the same for B. The interaction is the difference between the two green arrows: how much more (or less) A helps when B is present.

Interaction Meaning
IAB≈0I_{AB} \approx 0 roughly additive: each part adds the same whatever the other does
large and positive synergy: each helps more when the other is present
negative overlap: they partly do the same job; the full system gains less than the sum of its parts

Figure 4.8.2 — Three kinds of interaction. Each panel plots the outcome with A off and on, for B off (grey dashed) and B on (blue). Parallel lines mean no interaction. Lines that spread apart mean synergy. Lines that close together mean overlap. The values are illustrative only.

4.8.4 Why you need all four cells

People often run only two cells:

  • Baseline and full. This shows the combination does something, but not which part.
  • Full and “full minus A”. This shows A’s contribution given B, which can be very different from its contribution alone if there is an interaction.

A common surprise: a component that looks essential in “full minus A” does nothing on its own, because it only matters as a partner to B. Or the reverse: a component that looks useless in the full system has a strong main effect, but B already captures most of it. Only the full 2×2 shows this.

4.8.5 Ablation and multiple testing

Four configurations are four trials, and they count. Run a 2×2, tweak something, run another, and you have tried eight. The trial count goes into the record, because the chance that the best of NN configurations looks good by luck grows with NN.

Bailey and López de Prado’s deflated Sharpe ratio is one formal correction. The simplest discipline is to report NN honestly and show every cell, not only the best.

4.8.6 Uncertainty

With trading outcomes, differences between cells are often small compared with noise. A difference means little until you know how much it varies from sample to sample. Options:

  • Bootstrap (resample with replacement) trades or, better, whole sessions, because trades within a day are dependent. Recompute the decomposition on each resample.
  • Use paired comparisons: the same sessions in every cell, so session-level noise partly cancels.
  • Report intervals on main effects and interaction, not single numbers.

If the interval on a main effect includes zero, you have not shown that the component matters.

4.8.7 Beyond two factors

With kk components, a full factorial needs 2k2^k runs. That grows fast and multiplies trial counts. Fractional factorial designs estimate main effects with fewer runs, at the cost of mixing up (confounding) some interactions. I prefer to keep systems small enough for a full factorial. If a system needs a fractional design just to be understood, it may be too complicated.

4.8.8 Pitfalls

  • Changing anything else between cells (period, data cleaning, fill model, costs). Then you measure that change, not the component.
  • Defining “off” in a way that is secretly a different component.
  • Looking at the cells, adjusting a component, and rerunning without counting the trials.
  • Reporting the best cell as “the result”.

4.8.9 Summary

  • Run all four cells of a 2×2 under identical conditions, with “off” defined in advance.
  • Main effects average a component’s contribution over the other’s states; the interaction shows synergy or overlap.
  • Two-cell shortcuts can make a component look essential or useless when it is neither.
  • Every cell is a trial; report N and every cell.
  • Put intervals on effects, preferably by session bootstrap with paired cells.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) y00=0y_{00} = 0, y01=2y_{01} = 2, y10=3y_{10} = 3, y11=5y_{11} = 5. Compute MEA\text{ME}_A, MEB\text{ME}_B and IABI_{AB}. (Answer: 3, 2 and 0: additive.)
  2. (Apply) Change y11y_{11} to 9 and recompute. What kind of interaction is it?
  3. (Think) A colleague shows only “full” and “full minus B” and says B is useless. What else would you ask to see?
  4. (Think) How many runs does a full factorial with five components need? What does that do to the trial count?

Further reading

  • George Box, J. Stuart Hunter and William Hunter, Statistics for Experimenters (2nd ed., 2005).
  • Douglas Montgomery, Design and Analysis of Experiments.
  • David Bailey and Marcos López de Prado, “The Deflated Sharpe Ratio”, Journal of Portfolio Management (2014).

— Tariq

Chapter 4.9 — Leave-One-Out Probes: Finding Out Which Filter Is Doing the Work

Subtitle: When a decision requires several conditions to pass, remove them one at a time and watch what changes.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Run a leave-one-out (LOO) probe on a rule made of several gates, and compute each gate’s marginal effects. 2. Read the four typical outcomes. 3. Explain the overlap problem and fix it with pairwise probes or a gate census.

You need: Chapter 4.8 (ablation). Logical AND; “n choose 2”.

4.9.1 The problem

Many trading rules have the shape “act only if conditions g1,g2,…,gkg_1, g_2, \dots, g_k all pass”. I call each condition a gate. Each gate was added for a reason. Over time you lose track of which ones still pull their weight. Some are redundant with others. Some do almost all the filtering. Some have quietly stopped mattering because the market changed.

Leave-one-out (LOO) probing is the cheapest way I know to find out. It is the many-component cousin of the 2×2 ablation, and its cost grows linearly, not exponentially.

4.9.2 The procedure

For kk gates combined with AND:

  1. Run the full system with all gates on. Record the outcome yfully_{\text{full}} and the number of decisions nfulln_{\text{full}}.
  2. For each gate jj, run with every gate except gjg_j. Record y−jy_{-j} and n−jn_{-j}.

That is k+1k + 1 runs.

Figure 4.9.1 — One full run plus one run per removed gate. The top row passes a candidate through all gates. The bottom row is the probe for gate 2: the same chain with that gate switched off (orange). Comparing the two rows gives gate 2’s marginal effects. Gate names here are generic placeholders.

Marginal effects of gate j.

Δnj=n−j−nfull(extra decisions without it)\Delta n_j = n_{-j} - n_{\text{full}} \qquad \text{(extra decisions without it)}

Δyj=y−j−yfull(change in the outcome without it)\Delta y_j = y_{-j} - y_{\text{full}} \qquad \text{(change in the outcome without it)}

4.9.3 How to read it

Result Meaning
Δnj≈0\Delta n_j \approx 0 Removing the gate changes almost nothing about which decisions happen. Given the others, it is redundant. It may still be worth keeping as a safety net, but it is not selecting.
Δnj\Delta n_j large, Δyj\Delta y_j strongly worse The gate filters out many bad decisions. It is doing real work.
Δnj\Delta n_j large, Δyj≈0\Delta y_j \approx 0 It removes many decisions that are, on average, no different from the ones kept. It filters but does not select for quality; it mainly reduces activity.
Δyj\Delta y_j better without it It removes decisions that were on average good. A red flag worth investigating.

4.9.4 The overlap problem

LOO measures a gate’s unique contribution given all the others. If two gates block the same decisions, removing either one alone changes nothing, because the other still blocks them. Both look redundant in LOO, yet removing both would change a lot.

Figure 4.9.2 — Why two overlapping gates can both look useless. The blue circle is what gate 1 blocks; the orange circle is what gate 2 blocks. Remove gate 1 and the shared middle is still blocked by gate 2, so LOO sees only the small “only g₁” area. When most of each circle is shared, both gates look redundant even though together they do a lot.

This weakness is general (feature importance in machine learning has the same issue). Two remedies:

  • Pairwise LOO for suspected overlapping pairs: remove two at a time. That is (k2)\binom{k}{2} extra runs, so do it selectively.
  • A gate census. For each candidate decision, record which gates passed and which failed. Then you can see how often each gate is the sole blocker versus one of several. A gate that is never the sole blocker is redundant given the others; a gate that is often the sole blocker is critical.

The census is cheap, a single run with extra logging, and it answers questions LOO cannot.

4.9.5 Counting trials

LOO runs are trials: k+1k + 1 of them, plus any pairwise ones. If the results lead you to remove a gate and rerun, that is another trial, and the final result must be reported with all of them.

Warning. Using LOO as an optimisation loop (“drop whichever gate makes the metric look best, repeat”) is greedy backward selection on the test data. It overfits exactly as you would expect. Use LOO to understand a system, and validate any change on data not used to choose it.

4.9.6 Uncertainty

Δyj\Delta y_j is the difference between two noisy estimates computed on overlapping samples. The decisions in the full run are a subset of those in the −j-j run, so the two are not independent. The cleanest interval comes from bootstrapping sessions, recomputing both runs’ metrics on each resample, and taking the distribution of the difference.

4.9.7 Relation to other methods

LOO probing is close to permutation and drop-column feature importance in machine learning, and to Shapley values, which average a component’s contribution over all subsets of the others. Shapley values solve the overlap problem properly but need 2k2^k evaluations, or approximations. For small kk and expensive runs, LOO plus a census gives most of the insight for a fraction of the cost.

4.9.8 Keeping the probe honest

  • Keep everything except the removed gate identical: data, fill model, costs, session handling.
  • Record the probe’s design before running it: which gates, which metric, which period. It is easy to look at the first results and change the metric, at which point the probe has quietly become a search.

Every few months, run a LOO probe and a gate census on any multi-condition rule you depend on. Gates pile up. Their reasons fade. The probe tells you which ones still earn their place.

4.9.9 Summary

  • k gates need k + 1 runs; compute Δn and Δy for each gate.
  • Small Δn means redundant; large Δn with worse Δy means real work; better Δy without a gate is a red flag.
  • Overlapping gates hide each other in LOO; use pairwise probes or a sole-blocker census.
  • Every probe run is a trial; never use LOO as a search loop on test data.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A rule has 6 gates. How many runs does a LOO probe need, and how many extra for all pairwise removals? (Answer: 7, plus 15.)
  2. (Apply) Removing gate 3 raises decisions from 200 to 420 and leaves the outcome measure unchanged. Which row of the table in §4.9.3 is this?
  3. (Think) Two gates each show Δn ≈ 0. Describe the census result that would prove they overlap.
  4. (Think) Why are the full run and the −j run not independent samples?

Further reading

  • Leo Breiman, “Random Forests”, Machine Learning (2001), on permutation importance.
  • Scott Lundberg and Su-In Lee, “A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions”, NeurIPS (2017).
  • Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani and Jerome Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning (2nd ed., 2009), on cross-validation and model selection.

— Tariq

Chapter 4.10 — Ground-Truth Outcome Labelling on Renko Bricks

Subtitle: Before you can ask “was this signal good?”, you need a definition of “good” that doesn’t depend on the signal.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe three families of outcome labels: fixed-horizon, triple-barrier and structural. 2. Explain why labels must be computed from ticks and kept apart from features. 3. Explain why neighbouring labels are dependent, and three ways to handle it.

You need: how a Renko brick is drawn (Chapter 6.1 helps). Chapter 4.3 on lookahead.

4.10.1 Why labels matter

Most trading research questions come down to: at this moment, what happened next? To answer that at scale you need labels: outcome tags attached to points in time. How you define the label decides what every later analysis can conclude. Get it wrong and you will find patterns in your labelling scheme, not in the market.

I do much of my structural research on Renko bricks. This chapter describes how I think about labelling outcomes on them. It describes the method family, not my specific label definitions.

4.10.2 Why Renko for labelling

A Renko brick forms when price moves a fixed distance from the previous brick’s close. Time does not matter; only net movement does. That gives a natural vocabulary: “how many bricks did price move this way before reversing by a brick?” is a clean, scale-free question.

If brick kk closes at price ckc_k with direction dk∈{−1,+1}d_k \in \{-1, +1\}, the bricks sit on a lattice where consecutive closes differ by a fixed height hh (or 2h2h on a reversal, in the classic construction).

Definition (run). A run is a maximal sequence of same-direction bricks. Its length is a natural whole-number outcome.

4.10.3 Labels use the future, and must come from ticks

A label at brick kk describes what happens after kk. This is the one place where using future information is not just allowed but required. The danger is labels leaking back into features. So label computation is separate code with a separate output, joined to features only for analysis.

Labels must also be computed from the real tick sequence, not from brick prices alone. Bricks hide moves inside a brick. If a label says “price reached two bricks up before one brick down”, it must be checked against the actual ticks, because a brick-only view can get the order wrong when price whipsaws inside a brick.

4.10.4 Three families of labels

Fixed-horizon labels. What was the move after nn bricks (or nn minutes)? Simple, but the horizon is arbitrary and the path is ignored.

Triple-barrier labels. From López de Prado: set an upper barrier, a lower barrier and a time limit. The label is whichever is hit first. This path-dependent definition matches how trades really end: by target, stop or time.

yk={+1upper barrier hit first−1lower barrier hit first0time limit first y_k = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{upper barrier hit first} \\ -1 & \text{lower barrier hit first} \\ 0 & \text{time limit first} \end{cases}

The first hit is found by walking the tick tape forward from the decision time.

Figure 4.10.1 — A triple-barrier label on a simulated path. The black dot is the decision at brick k. The blue line is the price path walked forward tick by tick; it reaches the orange lower barrier first, so the label is −1. Everything after that (grey) is irrelevant to this label. The right edge is the time limit. Simulation: a fair ±1 random walk, barriers 12 steps away, time limit 180 steps, fixed seed 20261107. Not market data.

Structural labels. Labels tied to the brick structure itself: was this the start of a run that grew beyond some length? Did a reversal here become a new trend? These are the ones I use most for understanding structure, and their definitions are where most of the care goes.

Family Captures path? Main weakness
Fixed-horizon no arbitrary horizon
Triple-barrier yes barrier and time choices must be frozen
Structural yes, in brick terms definitions need the most care

4.10.5 Independence from the thing being tested

The cardinal rule. The label definition must not depend on the signal you are evaluating.

If you define “a good entry” with the same indicator that generates the entries, you will find that the indicator generates good entries, by construction. Define labels once, from price alone, and freeze them before any signal is tested against them. Changing a label definition after looking at signal results is a hidden trial, and should be counted as one.

4.10.6 Overlap and dependence

Labels at neighbouring bricks look at overlapping futures.

Figure 4.10.2 — Neighbouring labels share their future. Each blue bar is the stretch of future that one brick’s label looks at. The windows for bricks k, k+1 and k+2 cover almost the same bricks. Their labels are therefore strongly correlated, not independent coin flips.

Because labels are heavily autocorrelated, naive statistics that treat each label as independent overstate confidence. Remedies:

  • sample decisions sparsely (only at signal times, not every brick);
  • use uniqueness weighting (López de Prado’s average uniqueness);
  • bootstrap by session rather than by label.

4.10.7 Session boundaries

A label should not look across the daily maintenance halt into the next session, at least not without saying so. My brick construction resets at the session boundary, and labels are cut at session end with an explicit “censored” outcome, rather than silently continuing into the next day (Chapter 4.12).

4.10.8 Checking the labels

Labels are code, and code has bugs. I check them two ways:

  • aggregate sanity: label distributions over long periods should look boring and stable;
  • human review of a random sample, plotted with the ticks, to confirm each label says what actually happened (Chapter 4.11).

Write the label definition in plain words before writing code. Compute it from ticks. Freeze it before you test anything against it. Treat every change as a new experiment.

4.10.9 Summary

  • Labels look forward by design; keep them in separate code, away from features.
  • Compute labels from ticks, because bricks hide the order of moves.
  • Triple-barrier labels follow the path; structural labels describe brick runs and reversals.
  • Never define a label with the signal under test; freeze it first.
  • Neighbouring labels overlap: sample sparsely, weight by uniqueness, bootstrap by session; censor at session end.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) On a triple-barrier label, the time limit arrives before either barrier is touched. What is the label? (Answer: 0.)
  2. (Apply) Brick prices alone say “up barrier first”, but the ticks dipped to the lower barrier inside the first brick. Which label is correct, and why?
  3. (Think) You compute 10,000 labels, one per brick, each looking 20 bricks ahead. Why is “10,000 independent observations” wrong?
  4. (Simulate) Reproduce Figure 4.10.1 with a different seed and record how often each label occurs over 10,000 paths.

Further reading

  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), chapters 3 and 4 on labelling and sample weights.
  • Steve Nison, Beyond Candlesticks (1994), on Renko and other price-based charts.

— Tariq

Chapter 4.11 — Rally Catalogs and Human-Labelled Review Samples

Subtitle: Before measuring whether a system catches the big moves, write down which big moves there were. Then look at a sample with your own eyes.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why a strategy-independent catalog of moves gives the denominators signal-based research lacks. 2. Define a move mechanically and say what to record about it. 3. Size a human review sample with the rule of three, and run the review without bias.

You need: basic probability; what a swing high and swing low are.

4.11.1 Start from the market, not the strategy

One of my most useful research artefacts is not a model or an indicator. It is a catalog: a list of every significant directional move (rally or decline) in the data, defined by a rule that has nothing to do with any strategy. Each entry has a start, an end, an extent and a few descriptive fields.

Once the catalog exists, a whole class of questions becomes easy and honest. And the catalog only becomes trustworthy after a human has looked at a random sample of it.

Strategy research usually starts from the strategy: here are its signals, how did they do? That framing has a blind spot. It tells you about the moves the strategy saw, and nothing about the ones it missed. A catalog flips the frame. Start from all the moves that met a strategy-independent definition, then ask for each one: did the system take part? When? How much of the move did it capture? If not, why not?

Definition (coverage).

coverage=#{catalogued moves with participation}#{catalogued moves}\text{coverage} = \frac{\#\{\text{catalogued moves with participation}\}}{\#\{\text{catalogued moves}\}}

Separately, measure the share of the system’s activity that happened outside any catalogued move. That is where false starts live.

Figure 4.11.1 — Coverage and false starts. The top row is the catalog: four moves found by a rule that knows nothing about the system. The bottom row is the system’s activity. Two moves have green activity inside them, so coverage is 2/4. The orange blocks fall outside every move: those are the false starts. Positions are schematic.

4.11.2 Defining a move

The definition must be mechanical, independent of anything you will test, and it may look forward, because it describes history rather than making decisions. Common families:

Family A move is…
Zigzag / swing from a swing low to the next swing high, where swings are separated by a reversal of at least some size
Brick-run on price-based bricks, a run of consecutive same-direction bricks of at least some length
Drawdown-from-peak a rally that ends when price falls back from its peak by some fraction of the rally’s extent

Each family has parameters. They are part of the catalog’s definition and are frozen with it. Changing them creates a different catalog; results against the old one do not carry over.

4.11.3 What to record per move

For each move I record what is needed to analyse it without recomputing: start and end timestamps (from ticks), start and end prices, extent, duration, the session it belongs to, and the sequence of structure within it. How each system under study interacted with the move goes in separate joined tables. The catalog itself contains no strategy information, which keeps it reusable across every study.

4.11.4 Human review

Mechanical definitions have edge cases that aggregate statistics will not show:

  • a move that starts in one session and ends in the next;
  • a spike that is really a bad print;
  • two moves merged because the reversal between them fell just short of the threshold.

Eyes will show them. So for any catalog or labelled data set I draw a random sample and review each item against a chart of the actual ticks, asking:

  1. Is this a real move, or an artefact (bad print, roll gap, session boundary)?
  2. Do the start and end look right?
  3. Is anything obviously missing nearby that should have been catalogued?

4.11.5 Sampling properly

The sample must be random: not “the first twenty”, not “the ones I remember”. A stratified sample is better: some items from each size bucket and each period, so rare but important categories are not missed.

How big? If the true error rate is pp, a sample of nn items contains no errors with probability (1−p)n(1-p)^n.

Result (rule of three). If you see zero errors in nn items, an approximate 95% upper bound on the error rate is

pupper≈3n.p_{\text{upper}} \approx \frac{3}{n}.

Why: set (1−p)n=0.05(1-p)^n = 0.05. Then nln⁡(1−p)=ln⁡0.05≈−3n \ln(1-p) = \ln 0.05 \approx -3. For small pp, ln⁡(1−p)≈−p\ln(1-p) \approx -p, so p≈3/np \approx 3/n.

Figure 4.11.2 — Finding nothing proves little when n is small. The blue line is the rule of three, 3/n. The orange dashed line is the exact 95% bound, 1 − 0.05^(1/n). After reviewing 10 clean items, the error rate could still be about 26–30%. To bound it near a few percent you need many tens of clean items. The two lines agree closely beyond about n = 30.

That is sobering. Reviewing a handful of items and finding no problems tells you very little.

4.11.6 Recording the review

Each reviewed item gets a verdict and a note, stored with the catalog version it reviewed. If the definition changes, old reviews do not automatically transfer. Errors found in review are fixed in the definition or the data cleaning, never by hand-editing catalog entries. Hand edits do not survive regeneration and cannot be audited.

4.11.7 Where the human is weak

Human review has biases: we see what we expect, we are drawn to dramatic examples, and we get tired. Mitigations:

  • review blind to which system took part in each move;
  • randomise the order;
  • keep review sessions short;
  • where possible, have the reviewer label before seeing the mechanical label, then compare.

It is slow and unglamorous, and it has caught more data problems for me than any automated check.

4.11.8 Summary

  • Build a strategy-independent catalog of moves first; it supplies coverage and false-start denominators.
  • Define moves mechanically and freeze the parameters with the catalog.
  • Keep strategy interaction in separate tables.
  • Review a random, stratified sample against ticks; zero errors in n items bounds the rate only at about 3/n.
  • Fix problems in the definition or cleaning, never by hand-editing entries; review blind.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) You review 50 catalog items and find no errors. What is the approximate 95% upper bound on the error rate? (Answer: 3/50 = 6%.)
  2. (Apply) A catalog has 120 moves. The system took part in 78. What is the coverage?
  3. (Think) Why must the catalog contain no strategy information?
  4. (Think) You find a bad-print “move” in review. Why should you fix the cleaning rule rather than delete that entry?

Further reading

  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), on labelling.
  • J. A. Hanley and A. Lippman-Hand, “If nothing goes wrong, is everything all right?”, JAMA (1983), the rule of three.
  • Andrew Lo, Harry Mamaysky and Jiang Wang, “Foundations of Technical Analysis”, Journal of Finance (2000), on algorithmic pattern definitions.

— Tariq

Chapter 4.12 — Session Resets: Why Bars and Indicators Start Fresh Every Trading Day

Subtitle: Carrying state across the daily halt sounds harmless. It quietly makes your research and your live system disagree.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain how continuous construction creates phantom bricks and distorted indicators after a gap. 2. List what “reset” must mean for bar builders, indicators, structure, labels and risk counters. 3. Compute how long an exponential smoother needs to forget its seed.

You need: what a Renko brick and an exponential moving average are. Logarithms.

4.12.1 The daily gap

CME equity index futures stop trading for a short maintenance break every day. Price on the other side of the break can open somewhere quite different. Yet much charting and backtesting code treats the series as continuous, carrying bars, indicators and structure straight across the gap.

I decided to reset at the session boundary everywhere: in the live platform, in the research engine, and in every derived data set.

4.12.2 The problem with continuity

Take a price-based bar such as a Renko brick, which forms when price moves a fixed distance from the previous brick. If the session closes mid-brick and reopens with a gap, a continuous construction treats the gap as a move. It may print several bricks instantly at the open, none of which match any trading that happened. Those phantom bricks then feed indicators, signals and labels.

Figure 4.12.1 — A gap becomes fake bricks unless you reset. Left: the continuous builder fills the gap between the last brick and the reopen with dashed orange bricks that no trade produced. Right: the builder resets at the halt, anchors on the first trade of the new session (blue line), and passes the gap in as a separate named value. Sizes are schematic.

Time-based indicators have a subtler version. An exponential moving average carries the previous session’s value into the next. If the open gaps, the average is far from price and takes a while to catch up. Anything that depends on “price relative to the average” then behaves differently early in the session than later, for reasons unrelated to the market.

4.12.3 Two systems, one answer

The real reason I care: if the live platform builds bars one way across sessions and the research engine another, the two see different bars. Every research result then describes a system that is not the one running. Parity (agreement between the two) needs both sides to agree on what happens at the boundary, and the simplest thing to agree on is a reset.

4.12.4 What “reset” means

At the session boundary, defined by the trading-date function, not calendar midnight:

Component At the boundary
Bar builders discard any partial bar; the first bar of the new session anchors on its first trade
Stateful indicators reinitialise: exponential smoothers re-seed, rolling windows empty, cumulative values (session volume, cumulative delta) restart at zero
Structural state swing points, ranges and session levels clear, or move to an explicit “previous session” slot
Labels and outcome windows cut at session end and marked censored, not continued into tomorrow
Risk counters daily loss and similar counters reset

Earlier sessions are not forbidden. Their information must be carried explicitly: the previous session’s high, low and close as named inputs, not as leftovers inside a smoother.

4.12.5 The warm-up cost

Resetting has a price: every session starts with indicators that have not warmed up.

Result (seed weight). For an exponential smoother with factor α\alpha, the weight left on the initial seed after nn updates is (1−α)n(1-\alpha)^n. To push it below a small ϵ\epsilon you need

n≥ln⁡ϵln⁡(1−α)n \ge \frac{\ln \epsilon}{\ln(1-\alpha)}

updates.

Why: each update keeps a fraction (1−α)(1-\alpha) of the old value, so after nn updates the seed’s share is (1−α)n(1-\alpha)^n. Take logs of (1−α)n≤ϵ(1-\alpha)^n \le \epsilon; since ln⁡(1−α)<0\ln(1-\alpha) < 0, dividing flips the inequality.

Figure 4.12.2 — How fast a smoother forgets its seed. Each curve is (1 − α)^n, the share of the output still coming from the seed after n updates. A larger α (blue) forgets in a few dozen updates; a smaller α (orange, dashed) takes far longer. The α values are examples only, chosen to show the shape.

During that window, decisions that rely on the indicator should be either suppressed or treated as a different regime. This is a design choice that must be made explicitly and identically in live and research.

4.12.6 Where the boundary is

For futures, the boundary is the start of the daily maintenance halt; the new session begins at the reopen. Holidays and early closes move it. A weekend spans two calendar days but is one boundary. All of this goes through a single trading-calendar function, so there is exactly one definition of “the session ended”.

4.12.7 Testing it

  • A session that closes mid-brick and reopens with a gap: assert no bricks come from the gap.
  • Indicator values on the first bar of a session: assert they equal freshly seeded values, not a continuation.
  • A label whose outcome window crosses the boundary: assert it is censored.
  • The same data replayed through live-style and research-style builders: assert identical bar sequences.

4.12.8 The counter-argument, and gaps as information

Some traders argue that overnight structure matters and resetting throws it away. Sometimes it does. My answer: if previous-session information matters, carry it explicitly as an input you can test, not implicitly as state no one is watching.

Resetting does not mean ignoring the gap. The opening gap (new session’s first trade minus previous session’s last trade) is a perfectly good input. It is computed once, explicitly, and passed in as a named value, instead of leaking into a dozen stateful calculations as an unexplained jump.

4.12.9 Summary

  • Carrying state across the daily halt creates phantom bricks and indicators far from price.
  • Live and research must agree at the boundary; a reset is the simplest agreement.
  • Reset bars, indicators, structure, labels (censored) and risk counters; carry old information only as named inputs.
  • A smoother needs about ln ε / ln(1 − α) updates to forget its seed; treat that window deliberately.
  • One trading-calendar function defines the boundary; test gaps, first bars, censoring and live/research parity.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) α = 0.5. What share of the seed remains after 4 updates? (Answer: 0.5⁴ = 6.25%.)
  2. (Apply) With α = 0.1, how many updates until the seed weight is below 1%? (Use ln 0.01 ≈ −4.61 and ln 0.9 ≈ −0.105.)
  3. (Think) Why is “previous close as a named input” safer than letting a smoother carry over?
  4. (Build) Write the gap test from §4.12.7 for your own brick builder.

Further reading

  • CME Group, Globex trading hours documentation.
  • Steve Nison, Beyond Candlesticks (1994), on Renko construction.
  • Robert Brown, Smoothing, Forecasting and Prediction of Discrete Time Series (1963), on exponential smoothing initialisation.

— Tariq

Chapter 4.13 — Staged Study Runners: Research as a Pipeline with Gates Between Steps

Subtitle: Don’t run the expensive experiment until the cheap checks have passed. And make every stage leave a receipt.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Lay out a research study as stages with defined inputs, outputs and gates. 2. Name the main kinds of gate and explain why a gate stops rather than skips. 3. Use content fingerprints for safe caching, a ledger for trial counts, and receipts for audit.

You need: what a file hash is (a short fingerprint that changes if any byte changes). Basic version control.

4.13.1 From one big script to stages

Early on, my research runs were one monolithic command: load data, build bars, compute everything, simulate trades, print a table. When something looked wrong I could not tell which step had failed, and rerunning meant redoing everything.

Now every study is a sequence of stages. Each stage has defined inputs and outputs, writes its outputs to files with fingerprints, and has a pass/fail check that must succeed before the next stage starts. It is slower to set up and dramatically faster to trust.

4.13.2 The general shape

In method terms, a typical study pipeline is:

  1. Preflight. Is the working tree clean? Is the engine commit recorded? Do golden tests pass? If not, stop.
  2. Data. Load the canonical tick source for the period. Record its hash, the sessions covered, and anything excluded.
  3. Bars. Build bars from ticks. Run a wick census (Chapter 4.2). If wicks are missing, stop: the data is invalid.
  4. Features. Compute indicators and features through the causality-guarded view (Chapter 4.3).
  5. Fidelity. Where a live counterpart exists, check parity on a sample (Chapter 4.6).
  6. Simulation. Replay with the fill engine.
  7. Report. Write results with every receipt attached, and add the trial to the ledger.

Each stage’s output is a file. Each file’s hash goes into the next stage’s metadata. The final report can trace every number back to the exact data and code that produced it.

Figure 4.13.1 — A study as seven gated stages. Each blue box is a stage; the grey line under it names its gate. Data only moves along an arrow after that gate passes. If any gate fails, the run stops with a named reason (orange box) instead of carrying on.

4.13.3 Gates between stages

The checks between stages are what make the pipeline more than a script. General kinds of gate:

Gate type Examples
Integrity hash matches, file counts, no missing sessions unless declared
Sanity bar counts per session in a plausible range; wick census above a floor; timestamps never go backwards
Parity offline indicator matches the live export within tolerance
Procedural clean working tree; trial recorded in the ledger before results are shown

Rule. A gate failure stops the pipeline with a named reason. It never silently skips the stage or substitutes a cheaper method.

“Stopped at stage 3: wick census failed” is a perfectly good outcome. It means you found a data problem before it contaminated a result.

4.13.4 Why stages are cheaper overall

Stages make reruns cheap. If I change only the simulation settings, stages 1 to 5 need no recomputing: their outputs are on disk, fingerprinted, and the pipeline can check they are still valid. This content-addressed caching is what build systems do, and research benefits in exactly the same way.

Warning. A cached output is reusable only if its fingerprint proves it came from the same inputs and code. A cache keyed on a file name rather than content hashes is a trap: it will happily serve stale results after the code changes.

4.13.5 The ledger

Every run, successful or not, gets a ledger entry: run identifier, engine commit, data fingerprint, configuration, stage reached, outcome. The ledger refuses entries from a dirty working tree, because a result you cannot tie to a commit cannot be reproduced.

The ledger is also where the trial count comes from. When I report a result, the number of configurations tried in that line of research is a query against the ledger, not my memory.

4.13.6 Splitting large studies

Big studies are broken into numbered steps that build on each other, each a separate runner. Step nn reads step n−1n-1’s outputs and checks their fingerprints. I can inspect intermediate outputs, and a bug found in step 3 only invalidates step 3 onward, not the whole chain.

4.13.7 Stage receipts

Every stage writes a small metadata record, a receipt, next to its output: stage name, input fingerprints, code commit, configuration hash, output fingerprint, wall-clock start and end, and its gate result. The next stage refuses to start if the fingerprints it expects do not match what is on disk.

Figure 4.13.2 — Receipts form a chain you can walk backwards. Each box records what it consumed and what it produced. Starting from the report, you can follow the chain stage by stage to the exact tick files and commit. If any link is missing, the number is reported as unprovenanced rather than quietly included.

The chain also makes failure analysis fast. When a result looks odd, I do not rerun the whole study; I open the receipts and look for the first one whose numbers surprise me.

4.13.8 Failure is information

The most important cultural point: a stage that stops is not a failed run; it is a successful detection. The worst outcome is not a pipeline that halts at stage 2. It is one that carries on past a problem and produces a confident-looking table built on bad data.

Draw your research as a pipeline. For each arrow between boxes, write the check that must pass before data crosses it. Then make the code refuse to cross without it.

4.13.9 Summary

  • Split studies into stages with file outputs, fingerprints and gates.
  • Gates check integrity, sanity, parity and procedure; failure stops the run with a named reason.
  • Cache by content hash, never by file name.
  • A ledger records every run and supplies the trial count; it refuses dirty trees.
  • Receipts chain every number back to its tick files and commit.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) You change only the fill model. Which stages must rerun? (Answer: Simulation and Report; earlier outputs can be reused if their fingerprints still match.)
  2. (Apply) A cache is keyed on “bars_2026-05.bin”. The bar builder code changes. What goes wrong, and how does a content key fix it?
  3. (Think) Why should the ledger refuse a run from a dirty working tree?
  4. (Design) Write the gate for a “Data” stage of your own: what three checks would you make?

Further reading

  • Jez Humble and David Farley, Continuous Delivery (2010), on deployment pipelines.
  • Johannes Köster and Sven Rahmann, “Snakemake: a scalable bioinformatics workflow engine”, Bioinformatics (2012).
  • Roger Peng, “Reproducible Research in Computational Science”, Science (2011).

— Tariq

Chapter 4.14 — Frozen, Hash-Pinned Message Specs

Subtitle: When two programs agree on a message format, write the agreement down, freeze it, and fingerprint it so nobody can change it by accident.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. List what a message spec must define, including units and a canonical form. 2. Explain freezing and hash-pinning, and the failure each prevents. 3. Plan a version upgrade in the safe order: readers first, then writers.

You need: what JSON or a similar message format is; what a hash such as SHA-256 is.

4.14.1 Contracts that lived in people’s heads

My research engine, my live platform code and a few supporting processes exchange structured messages: decisions, snapshots, health records, study outputs. Each message type is a contract between a writer and one or more readers. For a while those contracts lived in people’s heads and in whichever code happened to write the message. That worked until it didn’t.

Now each message type has a written spec, frozen at a version, with a hash that writer and reader can both check.

4.14.2 What goes in a spec

A message spec is a short document plus a machine-readable schema. It defines:

Part Content
Identity a name and an integer version
Fields for each: name, type, unit, whether it can be null, and its meaning in plain words
Units and precision prices in points or ticks? times in UTC, at what resolution? floats rounded to what precision before hashing?
Canonical form how the message is serialised for hashing: key order, number format, encoding
Semantics when the message is written, who writes it, what a reader does if it is stale or invalid
Fixtures a few example messages with their canonical bytes and hashes

Units deserve special mention. A field called stop that is in points for one writer and ticks for another is a disaster type systems do not catch. Units go in the field definition and, where practical, in the field name.

4.14.3 Freezing

Once a spec version is in use, it is frozen. Not “mostly stable”: frozen. Any change, even adding an optional field, makes a new version. The old version’s document and fixtures stay exactly as they were.

Why so strict? Because messages get stored. Research outputs, decision logs and telemetry from months ago were written under some version of the spec. To read them correctly you need that version’s exact definition. If specs change in place, old data silently changes meaning.

4.14.4 Pinning with a hash

Each frozen spec has a SHA-256 hash over its canonical content (schema plus fixtures). Code that writes or reads the message declares which spec hash it implements. At startup or in tests it checks:

H(spec on disk)=Hdeclared H(\text{spec on disk}) = H_{\text{declared}}

Figure 4.14.1 — Writer and reader prove they share one spec. Both programs declare the hash of the frozen spec they implement and check it against the file on disk. Each message carries the spec’s name and version. If the spec file was edited, the hashes differ and the check fails; if a reader sees a version it does not know, it refuses.

This catches the most common failure: someone edits the spec document to match a code change without bumping the version. It also gives a compact way to say “these two programs agree”: they declare the same spec hash.

4.14.5 Readers check the version

Every message carries its spec name and version. A reader that receives a version it does not know refuses it. It does not guess, and it does not read “the fields it recognises”. Refusing is loud and safe; guessing is quiet and dangerous.

That can feel rigid, and it means upgrades need coordination: deploy readers that understand the new version first, then writers. That order is standard for schema evolution in any distributed system.

4.14.6 Backward and forward compatibility

Definitions. Backward compatible: new readers can read old messages. Forward compatible: old readers can read new messages.

Formats such as Protocol Buffers and Avro build rules around these. For my small message set I take the simplest route: readers can explicitly support several versions, each with its own frozen spec, and nothing is implicitly compatible. More code, less ambiguity.

4.14.7 Where specs meet research

For research outputs, the spec is part of reproducibility. A study’s result file declares its spec hash. A later analysis that reads it checks the hash before trusting any field. If someone changed what a column means between studies, the mismatch is caught at load time, not discovered later as a mysterious shift in results.

4.14.8 Pitfalls

  • Specs that describe the code’s current behaviour rather than the intended contract. Write the spec first, then make the code match.
  • Hashing the spec with environment-dependent line endings. Canonicalise before hashing.
  • Version bumps without new fixtures. Every version needs its own examples.
  • Readers that log a version mismatch and carry on anyway.

4.14.9 A spec change, step by step

Figure 4.14.2 — The safe order for a version change. Write the new spec with fixtures and its hash. Teach readers to accept both versions and deploy them. Only then switch writers to the new version and verify. Reader support for the old version can go last, but the old spec document stays in the repository.

  1. Write the new spec version as a new document beside the old one. Add fixtures. Compute its hash.
  2. Update readers to accept both versions; deploy and verify.
  3. Update writers to emit the new version.
  4. Only once nothing emits the old version can reader support for it be removed. Even then, the old spec document stays so archived data remains readable.

It is slower than editing a field in place. It is also the only way I have found to make month-old outputs mean exactly what they meant on the day they were written.

4.14.10 Summary

  • A message format between two programs is an API: write it down with fields, units, canonical form, semantics and fixtures.
  • Freeze each version; any change makes a new version.
  • Pin specs by hash; writers and readers declare and check it.
  • Readers refuse unknown versions; upgrade readers first, then writers.
  • Keep every old spec so stored data keeps its meaning.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Adding one optional field to a frozen spec: same version or new version? (Answer: new version.)
  2. (Apply) A writer deploys v3 before any reader understands it. What happens under the “refuse unknown versions” rule, and why is that better than guessing?
  3. (Think) Why must line endings be canonicalised before hashing a spec file?
  4. (Design) Write a spec entry for a field holding a stop price. What must it say about units?

Further reading

  • Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2017), chapter 4 on encoding and evolution.
  • RFC 8785, JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) (2020).
  • JSON Schema specification, json-schema.org.

— Tariq

Chapter 4.15 — Two Languages, One Answer: Reconciling Python and C# Implementations

Subtitle: When the same calculation exists in two languages, the interesting part isn’t writing the second one. It’s proving they agree.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. List the convention differences that make Python and C# ports disagree without any “bug”. 2. Run a stage-by-stage reconciliation on hash-identical input. 3. Decide which side is right by appeal to a written specification.

You need: some familiarity with pandas/NumPy or C#; exponential smoothing; sample vs. population variance.

4.15.1 Background

For a while, parts of my research existed in both Python and C#. Python was where ideas were sketched quickly; C# was where the replay engine and live code lived. The same calculation ended up written twice, and the two disagreed.

I have since moved research execution entirely to C# (Chapter 4.16). But the reconciliation process I used while both existed taught me a lot about where cross-language ports go wrong.

4.15.2 Why they disagree

Most disagreements are not bugs in the usual sense. They are different conventions under the same name.

Area Python (NumPy / pandas) C# (hand-written)
Rolling windows defaults for minimum periods, centring and missing values whatever the author wrote. A centred window on one side and trailing on the other is also a lookahead bug in the centred one.
Exponential smoothing pandas ewm has an adjust flag. adjust=True: early values are a weighted average normalised by the sum of weights. adjust=False: the recursive form yt=αxt+(1−α)yt−1y_t = \alpha x_t + (1-\alpha) y_{t-1}. They converge but differ in warm-up. usually the recursive form
Variance NumPy std divides by nn (population); pandas divides by n−1n-1 (sample). Same name, different number. whatever was written
Missing values pandas often skips NaN in aggregations a loop over doubles propagates NaN unless told otherwise
Rounding Python round uses banker’s rounding (half to even) Math.Round also defaults to banker’s rounding, but many hand-written tick-snapping routines round away from zero. Pick one and use it in both.
Timestamps nanosecond resolution, optional time zones DateTime ticks are 100-nanosecond units with a Kind. Careless conversion shifts events across session boundaries.
Summation order vectorised sums may use pairwise summation a simple loop sums in sequence. Differences are in the last bits, which matter only near thresholds, but there they matter a lot.

4.15.3 A worked convention clash

Take a simple exponential smoother on a short series. In the recursive form, the first output equals the first input and each later value moves a fraction α\alpha toward the new input. In the adjusted, weight-normalised form, the output at step tt is

yt=∑i=0t(1−α)ixt−i∑i=0t(1−α)i y_t = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{t} (1-\alpha)^i x_{t-i}}{\sum_{i=0}^{t} (1-\alpha)^i}

which, during warm-up, gives relatively more weight to early observations than the recursive form gives the seed.

Figure 4.15.1 — Same name, different numbers during warm-up. The grey line is an input that steps from 0 to 1. The blue line is the recursive smoother; the orange dashed line is the adjusted one, both with the same α (0.2, an example value). They separate clearly in the first updates after the step and only meet later. Right after a session reset, that gap is enough to flip a comparison against a threshold.

Both are legitimate. Neither has a bug; they implement different definitions with the same name. Only a written spec settles it.

4.15.4 The reconciliation procedure

  1. Fix the input. Both sides read the exact same file, verified by hash. Not “the same data”: the same bytes.
  2. Compare stage by stage. Do not compare the final output first. Compare bars, then each indicator, then each derived feature, then decisions, then trades. The first stage that disagrees is where the bug is.
  3. Use explicit tolerances. Absolute plus relative for floats; exact for integers and discrete states.
  4. List every disagreement. Not a summary statistic: a list of index, timestamp, both values and the difference. For discrete outputs, every flip.
  5. Classify each disagreement: convention difference (decide which is correct and change the other), genuine bug, or floating-point noise near a threshold.
  6. Rerun until clean. Then freeze the comparison as a regression test.

Stage pass rule. For stage ss and element kk,

δs,k=|xs,kpy−xs,kcs|,stage passes⇔maxkδs,k≤εs.\delta_{s,k} = |x^{\text{py}}_{s,k} - x^{\text{cs}}_{s,k}|, \qquad \text{stage passes} \iff \max_k \delta_{s,k} \le \varepsilon_s.

Figure 4.15.2 — Find the first stage that disagrees. Both sides read one hash-verified file. Bars and indicators pass (green). Features is the first stage to fail (orange), so the bug is there. Decisions and trades are not trusted yet, because they depend on a failing stage; comparing them first would only show that “something” differs.

4.15.5 Which side is right?

Neither, automatically. The reference is the specification: a written definition of the calculation, ideally with golden test cases (Chapter 4.7). Both implementations are tested against it. If there is no spec, writing one is the first step of reconciliation; otherwise you are just picking a winner.

When one side drives live trading, though, that side’s behaviour is what matters in practice, and the spec should describe it.

4.15.6 What reconciliation taught me

Maintaining two implementations has a permanent cost. Every change must be made twice and reconciled again. Each reconciliation finds new disagreements. Over months, keeping them in sync cost more than the convenience of writing ideas quickly in Python.

That is a big part of why research execution now lives in one language. Python is still fine for reading results and plotting. It does not compute anything a result depends on.

4.15.7 Summary

  • Ports disagree mostly through conventions: windows, smoothing, variance denominators, NaN, rounding, timestamps, summation order.
  • Reconcile on byte-identical input, stage by stage, with stated tolerances.
  • List and classify every disagreement; freeze the clean comparison as a regression test.
  • A written spec decides who is right; if one side drives live trading, the spec describes it.
  • Ask seriously whether you need two implementations at all.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) The values 2 and 4: what are the population and sample standard deviations? (Answer: 1 and about 1.414.)
  2. (Apply) With α = 0.5 and inputs 0, 1, compute the recursive and adjusted smoother outputs at the second step.
  3. (Think) Why compare bars before trades, rather than trades first?
  4. (Think) Python rounds 2.5 to 2. A C# tick-snapper rounds it to 3. Which is “right”? What decides it?

Further reading

  • pandas documentation, “Windowing operations” and DataFrame.ewm.
  • David Goldberg, “What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic”, ACM Computing Surveys (1991).
  • Nicholas Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms (2002), on summation.

— Tariq

Chapter 4.16 — Why My Research Engine Is in C#, Not Python

Subtitle: Python is the default language of quant research. For my situation, it was the wrong one. Here’s the reasoning, with the trade-offs.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why “research and execution in one language” can matter more than research speed. 2. Describe the determinism, speed and type-safety arguments, and their limits. 3. State the costs of giving up Python and where Python is still allowed.

You need: general familiarity with Python and a compiled language such as C# or Java.

4.16.1 The surprise

When people hear that my backtesting and research engine is in C#, the reaction is somewhere between surprise and pity. Python is the common language of quantitative research. It has pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, Jupyter and a giant community. Why give that up?

Because, for my situation, the most important property of a research engine is not how fast I can write a new idea. It is whether the research describes the system that actually trades. Everything else follows from that.

4.16.2 One codebase

My live trading runs inside a C# platform. Indicators, bar logic, order handling and risk checks there are C#. If research were in Python, every piece of logic that matters would exist twice. As Chapter 4.15 showed, two implementations of one calculation are two calculations until proven otherwise, and the proof must be repeated after every change.

With research in C#, logic can be shared at the source level or ported with minimal translation: same language, same numeric types, same rounding functions, same date-time library. Parity testing still matters, but the space of possible disagreements shrinks dramatically.

Figure 4.16.1 — Two implementations versus one. On the left, live and research logic are separate (orange link): after every change you must prove again that they agree. On the right, both sides draw on the same logic (blue arrows). Parity is still tested, but there are far fewer ways for the two to differ.

4.16.3 Determinism

I want a research run to be exactly reproducible: same commit, same data, same output bytes. C# makes that straightforward with discipline:

  • value types and fixed-layout structs for ticks and bars;
  • explicit control of iteration order (ordered structures where order matters, so no dictionary-order surprises);
  • culture-invariant formatting everywhere;
  • no hidden parallelism unless you add it, and then with a deterministic reduction.

Python can be deterministic too, but it is easier to slip. Dictionary order is now stable, but the order of a set of strings is not stable across runs (hash randomisation). Library defaults change between versions. Vectorised operations can change summation order between NumPy builds. Each is solvable; together they are a constant tax.

4.16.4 Speed where it counts

Tick-by-tick replay (Chapter 4.2) processes every trade print in order, with branching logic per print: fill checks, queue updates, bar building. That workload is sequential and branchy, exactly what vectorised NumPy is bad at and a compiled language is good at.
