In Python you either write a slow loop or contort the logic into vectorised form that hides it and is easy to get subtly wrong.

In C#, a plain loop over a struct array is fast, readable and allocation-free on the hot path. I do not have to choose between clear and fast.

Roughly: in an interpreted loop, the cost per print is dominated by interpreter overhead, a constant factor many times larger than the work itself. With very many prints per session and many sessions, that constant is the difference between minutes and hours.

4.16.5 Type safety and refactoring

A research engine changes constantly. Static types catch whole categories of mistakes at compile time: passing ticks where points were expected (if you use distinct types), a renamed field one caller missed, a nullable value used without a check. In a large Python research codebase these show up as runtime errors halfway through a long run or, worse, as silent wrong answers.

4.16.6 What I gave up

Cost What it means
Exploration speed notebooks are wonderful for poking at data; I miss that
Libraries Python’s statistics and ML ecosystem is far richer; some things I must implement and test myself
Community most published quant code, tutorials and examples are Python
Plotting still easiest in Python

My compromise is a strict, one-way boundary.

Figure 4.16.2 — The one-way language boundary. The C# engine computes features, fills and metrics and writes fingerprinted output files. Python may read those files and draw charts. It computes nothing a conclusion depends on, because the moment it “just quickly” recomputes something, there are two implementations again.

4.16.7 The AI-agent angle

There is a newer reason too. I use AI coding agents heavily. When a C# run is slow or awkward, an agent’s easiest path is to reimplement the study in Python and present the result. A hard rule (“research runs in the C# engine, full stop”) makes that substitution an explicit violation rather than a judgement call. One language is easier to enforce than a policy about when each language is appropriate.

4.16.8 When Python is the right choice

If your execution platform is Python, or your research never needs to match a live implementation exactly (macro work, cross-sectional factor research on daily data), Python’s advantages probably win. My argument is not “C# is better”. It is:

Research and execution in the same language, with one implementation of each piece of logic, is better. For me that language is C#.

Choose your research language by where your production logic lives, not by what is popular. The cost of keeping two implementations in sync is paid forever.

4.16.9 Summary

  • The key property of a research engine is that it describes the system that trades.
  • One language lets live and research share logic, shrinking the parity problem.
  • C# helps determinism, branchy per-tick speed and safe refactoring.
  • The costs are real: exploration, libraries, community, plotting.
  • Python may read fingerprinted outputs and plot; it may not compute results.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Name two sources of run-to-run nondeterminism in Python mentioned in this chapter. (Answer: string-set ordering under hash randomisation; library default changes; summation order between NumPy builds; any two.)
  2. (Apply) Your live system runs in Python. Which of this chapter’s arguments now point toward Python for research?
  3. (Think) Why is tick replay hard to vectorise well?
  4. (Think) Why is a blanket language rule easier to enforce on an AI agent than a case-by-case policy?

Further reading

  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), on research infrastructure.
  • Roger Peng, “Reproducible Research in Computational Science”, Science (2011).
  • Microsoft Docs, “Performance best practices” and Span<T> / struct guidance for .NET.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.1 — Dealer Gamma for Engineers: What GEX Is, and What It Isn’t

Subtitle: The most-quoted options number on market Twitter rests on a big assumption. Here is the maths and the fine print.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why dealers’ hedging depends on the gamma of the options they hold. 2. Compute gamma exposure (GEX) for one strike and add it up into a profile. 3. List the five assumptions hidden inside every GEX chart.

You need: what a call and a put are, and the idea of a derivative (“rate of change”). Black–Scholes is used but derived in Chapter 5.2.

5.1.1 Why I built it

Over the summer I built an options engine. It pulls live option chains, computes the Greeks (the sensitivities of an option’s price) and adds them up into “dealer exposure”.

GEX (gamma exposure) is everywhere now: charts of gamma walls, zero-gamma levels, “the market is pinned”. Building it from scratch taught me how much those charts assume.

5.1.2 The idea in one paragraph

Market makers (dealers) who sell options usually hedge them: they trade the underlying asset so that small price moves do not hurt them. How much they must re-hedge when price moves depends on the option’s gamma, the rate at which its delta (price sensitivity) changes.

  • If dealers as a group are long gamma, they sell into rallies and buy dips. That tends to dampen moves.
  • If they are short gamma, they chase price. That tends to amplify moves.

GEX tries to estimate which world we are in, and at which price levels.

5.1.3 The maths

For each option, under Black–Scholes with dividend yield q:

d1=ln⁡(S/K)+(r−q+12σ2)TσT,Γ=e−qTφ(d1)SσT d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r - q + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \qquad \Gamma = \frac{e^{-qT}\,\varphi(d_1)}{S\,\sigma\sqrt{T}}

Here S is spot, K the strike, T the time to expiry in years, r the interest rate, and φ the standard normal density (the bell curve). The implied volatility σ is the volatility that makes the model price match the market price. It has to be solved numerically. I use Newton–Raphson, with vega as the derivative (Chapter 5.4).

Figure 5.1.1 — Gamma lives near the strike. One option with strike 100, σ = 20%, 30 days to expiry, r = q = 0 (illustrative values). Gamma peaks when spot sits at the strike and fades to almost nothing 15–20% away. This is why a strike’s contribution to GEX depends so much on where spot is today.

Gamma per contract is turned into dollars per 1% move and summed over strikes:

Definition (GEX at one strike). GEXK=ΓK⋅OIK⋅100⋅S2⋅0.01 \mathrm{GEX}_K = \Gamma_K \cdot OI_K \cdot 100 \cdot S^2 \cdot 0.01 with calls counted positive and puts negative. OI is open interest (contracts outstanding) and 100 is the contract multiplier.

Where the units come from. Γ·S is the change in delta for a 1-unit move, scaled to a move of 1% of S (×0.01·S). Multiplying by S again turns shares into dollars. So the result is “dollars of hedge to trade per 1% move”.

Summing across strikes gives a profile. The price where the total crosses zero is the famous zero-gamma level (Chapter 5.9). Strikes with large concentrations are the gamma walls (Chapter 5.10).

Figure 5.1.2 — A GEX profile is a sign convention plus a bell curve. A made-up chain: call open interest bunched around 110, put open interest around 90 (toy shapes, stated in the generator), spot 100, σ = 20%, 30 days. Green bars are call strikes, counted positive; orange bars are put strikes, counted negative. Note that the colours come from the assumption about who holds what, not from the data.

The same approach gives delta exposure (Chapter 5.8), vanna (how delta changes with volatility, Chapter 5.6) and charm (how delta drifts as time passes, Chapter 5.7). Charm matters a lot for same-day options.

5.1.4 The fine print nobody puts on the chart

# Assumption Why it can fail
1 Sign convention. Calls +, puts −. It assumes customers buy puts and sell calls to dealers. Often roughly true, sometimes badly wrong. Open interest does not say who is long and who is short.
2 Open interest is current. OI updates once a day. Same-day (0DTE) options can open and close within hours and never show up in OI.
3 The model is right. Black–Scholes gamma at the wrong volatility gives the wrong profile. The volatility surface matters, especially near expiry.
4 Hedging is instant and complete. Dealers hedge in bands, across products, and net against other books. GEX is a map of pressure, not a list of orders.
5 It is a signal. It is a context variable. A big positive GEX says moves may be absorbed more easily. It does not say which way the next one goes.

Because of point 2, I keep two views side by side: same-day options weighted by volume, and longer-dated ones weighted by open interest (Chapter 5.11).

5.1.5 How I use it

As context. Dealer positioning feeds the rest of my research as one input among many. I test any claimed effect with event studies against what would have happened anyway (Chapter 5.14). That is the same null-model discipline as the Renko chapter (Chapter 6.1).

If you build your own, compute the Greeks yourself at least once. You will trust the pretty charts a little less afterwards, and that is healthy.

5.1.6 Summary

  • Dealers hedge; gamma sets how much the hedge must change when price moves.
  • GEX per strike = Γ · OI · 100 · S² · 0.01, calls positive, puts negative; summed it gives a profile, a zero-gamma level and walls.
  • The sign convention, stale open interest, model choice and imperfect hedging are all assumptions, not facts.
  • Treat GEX as context and test any story against a null.

Exercises

  1. (Units) Spot is 5,000, one strike has Γ = 0.002 and OI = 10,000. What is its GEX in dollars per 1% move? (Answer: 0.002 × 10,000 × 100 × 5,000² × 0.01 = $500 million.)
  2. (Sign) Suppose customers mostly sell calls for income at a strike. Under the usual convention that strike shows positive GEX. What is the dealer’s real gamma there?
  3. (Think) Why can a same-day option with heavy trading show zero contribution to an OI-weighted profile?
  4. (Build) Using Figure 5.1.1’s formula, plot gamma against spot for 30 days and for 1 day. What happens to the height and width?

Further reading

  • J. C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, chapter on the Greek letters.
  • N. N. Taleb, Dynamic Hedging: Managing Vanilla and Exotic Options (1997).

— Tariq

Chapter 5.2 — Black–Scholes with a Dividend Yield, Derived Properly

Subtitle: Every Greek in an options engine sits on one formula. Here is where the e−qTe^{-qT} terms come from, and why index options need them.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Derive the Black–Scholes equation for an asset that pays a continuous dividend yield q. 2. Write the call and put prices in spot form and in forward (Black 1976) form. 3. Use put–call parity to check quotes and to infer the forward. 4. Explain why a deep in-the-money call on a dividend payer has delta below one.

You need: the normal distribution, basic calculus, and the idea of Itô’s lemma (the chain rule for random processes). Chapter 5.1 for context.

5.2.1 The bug that started it

When I started building my options engine this year, I copied the Black–Scholes formula from a textbook and plugged in index option prices. The implied volatilities came out slightly but consistently off from what my broker showed.

The culprit was the dividend yield. An index like the S&P 500 pays a steady trickle of dividends. So its forward price (the fair price today for delivery later) sits below what the interest rate alone would imply. Leave out q and every Greek downstream is quietly biased.

This chapter derives the generalised formula (Merton’s 1973 extension) from scratch. If you build anything on option chains, own this derivation rather than trust it.

5.2.2 The model

Assume the price follows geometric Brownian motion (random percentage moves) in the real world:

dSt=μStdt+σStdWt dS_t = \mu S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t

Here μ is the drift, σ the volatility and WtW_t a Brownian motion (pure noise). The asset also pays a continuous dividend yield q: holding one share for a short time dt pays qStdtqS_t\,dt in cash on top of the price change.

A continuous yield is a modelling convenience. For a broad index with hundreds of payers it is a decent approximation. For a single stock with one quarterly dividend it is not; use discrete dividends there.

5.2.3 The hedging argument

Let V(S,t)V(S,t) be the option value. Build a portfolio: long the option, short Δ shares.

Π=V−ΔS \Pi = V - \Delta S

Over dt, the change in value includes the dividend we owe on the short shares:

dΠ=dV−ΔdS−ΔqSdt d\Pi = dV - \Delta\,dS - \Delta q S\,dt

Itô’s lemma gives

dV=(Vt+μSVS+12σ2S2VSS)dt+σSVSdWt dV = \left(V_t + \mu S V_S + \tfrac12 \sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS}\right)dt + \sigma S V_S\,dW_t

where subscripts mean partial derivatives. Now choose Δ=VS\Delta = V_S. The dW terms cancel, and so does μ. That is the miracle of the construction: the drift of the asset vanishes from the price. The portfolio is riskless over dt, so it must earn the risk-free rate:

Vt+12σ2S2VSS−qSVS=r(V−SVS) V_t + \tfrac12\sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS} - qSV_S = r\,(V - SV_S)

Rearranging:

Result (Black–Scholes PDE with dividend yield). Vt+12σ2S2VSS+(r−q)SVS−rV=0 V_t + \tfrac12\sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS} + (r-q)SV_S - rV = 0

The only change from the textbook version is r→r−qr \to r - q in the drift term. In plain words: under the risk-neutral measure (the pricing world where every asset earns the risk-free rate), a dividend payer’s price grows at r − q, because part of its return arrives as cash, not price.

5.2.4 Solving it

You can solve the PDE by turning it into the heat equation. The risk-neutral route is shorter. Under the risk-neutral measure ℚ\mathbb{Q}:

ST=S0exp⁡((r−q−12σ2)T+σTZ),Z∼N(0,1) S_T = S_0 \exp\!\left((r - q - \tfrac12\sigma^2)T + \sigma\sqrt{T}\,Z\right), \quad Z\sim N(0,1)

The call price is the discounted expected payoff, C=e−rT𝔼ℚ[(ST−K)+]C = e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[(S_T - K)^+]. Split the expectation over the region where the option finishes in the money and do the Gaussian integrals:

Result (Merton 1973). C=Se−qTN(d1)−Ke−rTN(d2),P=Ke−rTN(−d2)−Se−qTN(−d1) C = S e^{-qT} N(d_1) - K e^{-rT} N(d_2), \qquad P = K e^{-rT} N(-d_2) - S e^{-qT} N(-d_1) d1=ln⁡(S/K)+(r−q+12σ2)TσT,d2=d1−σT d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r - q + \tfrac12\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}

N is the standard normal cumulative distribution.

A cleaner reading. Define the forward F=Se(r−q)TF = S e^{(r-q)T}. Then

C=e−rT[FN(d1)−KN(d2)],d1=ln⁡(F/K)+12σ2TσT C = e^{-rT}\left[F N(d_1) - K N(d_2)\right], \qquad d_1 = \frac{\ln(F/K) + \tfrac12\sigma^2 T}{\sigma\sqrt T}

This is Black’s 1976 form. Everything about dividends and rates collapses into the forward. I find this far more useful in code: if you can estimate the forward directly from the chain, you do not need to know q separately at all.

Figure 5.2.2 — Rates and dividends only matter through the forward. Spot, rate, dividend and time feed one number, F. The Black form then needs only F, K, σ and the discount factor. Put–call parity on near-the-money quotes gives F directly, so q never has to be looked up.

5.2.5 Put–call parity as a sanity check

Subtract the put from the call:

Result (put–call parity). C−P=Se−qT−Ke−rT C - P = S e^{-qT} - K e^{-rT}

This is model-free: it holds for any distribution of STS_T. That makes it the best diagnostic you have. My engine uses it two ways:

  1. To infer the implied forward from near-the-money call/put pairs.
  2. To flag quotes that break it by more than the bid–ask spread allows.

A chain that violates parity is telling you something is stale, not that you have found free money.

5.2.6 The Greeks it implies

Differentiating gives the familiar set, each now carrying a dividend discount:

ΔC=e−qTN(d1),ΔP=−e−qTN(−d1) \Delta_C = e^{-qT}N(d_1), \qquad \Delta_P = -e^{-qT}N(-d_1)

Γ=e−qTφ(d1)SσT,𝒱=Se−qTφ(d1)T \Gamma = \frac{e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)}{S\sigma\sqrt T}, \qquad \mathcal{V} = S e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)\sqrt T

Note the call delta is e−qTN(d1)e^{-qT}N(d_1), not N(d1)N(d_1). A deep in-the-money call on a dividend payer has delta below one, because the option holder misses the dividends the stock owner receives.

Figure 5.2.1 — Dividends put a ceiling on call delta. Strike 100, one year, σ = 20%, r = 3% (illustrative). The dashed curve has no dividend and climbs to 1. The blue curve has q = 3% and levels off at e−qT≈0.970e^{-qT} \approx 0.970. For short-dated index options the factor is close to one, but not one; summed over thousands of contracts, small biases stack up.

5.2.7 What goes wrong in practice

Textbook input Real-world problem What I do
q known Published yields are trailing; the market prices expected dividends over the option’s life. Lean on parity-implied forwards when the chain is liquid enough.
r is one number The right rate is the funding rate for the option’s tenor. Barely matters for same-day options; for long-dated ones a curve beats a constant.
σ constant The market shows a skew: each strike has its own implied volatility. Fine per contract, as long as the “model” is treated as a quoting convention, not a description of the world.
Continuous hedging Real dealers hedge discretely and pay costs. This is exactly why gamma matters to them, and to anyone modelling their flows.

5.2.8 Engineering notes

  • Compute d1d_1 and d2d_2 once per contract and reuse them for all the Greeks.
  • The normal CDF is the hot path. A good rational approximation of the error function is accurate to near machine precision and allocation-free.
  • Guard T→0T \to 0 and σ→0\sigma \to 0 explicitly, because d1d_1 divides by σT\sigma\sqrt{T}. Expiring contracts are exactly where people get sloppy (Chapters 5.3 and 5.5).

If you take one thing from this chapter: write the forward-form formula, check it with put–call parity on real quotes, and only then trust anything built on top.

5.2.9 Summary

  • With a dividend yield, the Black–Scholes PDE changes only by r→r−qr \to r - q in the drift term.
  • Prices carry e−qTe^{-qT} on the spot leg; in forward form, rates and dividends disappear into F.
  • Put–call parity is model-free: use it to infer F and to catch stale quotes.
  • Call delta tops out at e−qTe^{-qT}, not 1.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) With q = 2% and T = 0.5, what is the largest possible call delta? (Answer: e−0.01≈0.990e^{-0.01} \approx 0.990.)
  2. (Derive) Starting from the call formula and put–call parity, derive the put formula.
  3. (Apply) A call and a put at the same strike K = 100, T = 0.25, r = 4% trade at 5.10 and 4.30. What forward does parity imply?
  4. (Think) Why does the asset’s real drift μ not appear in the price?

Further reading

  • R. C. Merton (1973), “Theory of Rational Option Pricing,” Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science.
  • F. Black (1976), “The Pricing of Commodity Contracts,” Journal of Financial Economics.
  • J. C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, chapters on Black–Scholes–Merton.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.3 — Implementing Greeks Numerically Without Shooting Yourself in the Foot

Subtitle: Closed forms, finite differences, and the floating-point traps that live between them.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Use finite differences as a test harness for analytic Greeks, with a sensible step size. 2. Handle the three regimes where the closed forms break: T→0T \to 0, σ→0\sigma \to 0, and deep in or out of the money. 3. Keep units consistent and stop one bad contract from poisoning a chain-wide aggregate.

You need: Chapter 5.2’s formulas, and the idea of floating-point rounding (computers store numbers with about 16 significant digits).

5.3.1 Why the “easy part” is not easy

Analytic Greeks look like the easy part of an options engine. You write five formulas and you are done.

Then you feed them a contract expiring in eleven minutes with a strike far out of the money. You get NaN, or infinity, or a gamma a hundred times bigger than every neighbouring strike. Add that up across a chain and one bad contract dominates the whole profile.

This chapter is about Greeks that behave at the edges. Real chains spend more time there than you would think.

5.3.2 The closed forms

Under Black–Scholes–Merton with dividend yield q:

d1=ln⁡(S/K)+(r−q+12σ2)TσT,d2=d1−σT d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r-q+\tfrac12\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T}, \quad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt T

ΔC=e−qTN(d1),Γ=e−qTφ(d1)SσT,𝒱=Se−qTφ(d1)T \Delta_C = e^{-qT}N(d_1), \quad \Gamma = \frac{e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)}{S\sigma\sqrt T}, \quad \mathcal V = Se^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)\sqrt T

ΘC=−Se−qTφ(d1)σ2T−rKe−rTN(d2)+qSe−qTN(d1) \Theta_C = -\frac{Se^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)\sigma}{2\sqrt T} - rKe^{-rT}N(d_2) + qSe^{-qT}N(d_1)

Theta (Θ) is the change in value as time passes. The second-order cross Greeks, vanna and charm, come from differentiating delta by σ and by t. They get their own chapters (5.6 and 5.7).

5.3.3 Rule 1: prefer analytic, verify with finite differences

Analytic Greeks are exact (up to rounding) and cheap. Finite differences (approximating a derivative from nearby function values) are the test harness.

For any Greek G=∂V/∂xG = \partial V/\partial x, the central difference is

G≈V(x+h)−V(x−h)2h G \approx \frac{V(x+h) - V(x-h)}{2h}

Two errors fight each other:

  • Truncation error from the approximation itself, of order h2h^2. It shrinks as h shrinks.
  • Rounding error of about ε|V|/h\varepsilon |V| / h, where ε is machine epsilon (about 2.2×10−162.2\times10^{-16} for doubles). It grows as h shrinks.

Result (best step). Balancing h2h^2 against ε/h\varepsilon/h gives h∼ε1/3h \sim \varepsilon^{1/3} times the scale of x. For a second derivative such as gamma, Γ≈V(S+h)−2V(S)+V(S−h)h2 \Gamma \approx \frac{V(S+h) - 2V(S) + V(S-h)}{h^2} the rounding error is ε|V|/h2\varepsilon|V|/h^2, so the best step is larger, about ε1/4\varepsilon^{1/4} relative.

Figure 5.3.1 — Too small a step is as bad as too big a step. Errors of central differences for the simple test function f(x)=exf(x)=e^x at x = 1, computed in ordinary double precision (a textbook stand-in for an option price). On the right, truncation error falls as h shrinks. On the left, rounding error takes over and the error climbs again. The minima sit near ε1/3\varepsilon^{1/3} (first derivative) and ε1/4\varepsilon^{1/4} (second derivative). The second-derivative curve is cut off below h = 1e-8, where it is pure noise.

Use a relative step, not an absolute one. A fixed step that is fine for an index at several thousand is absurd for a stock at five dollars.

My unit tests compute every analytic Greek and compare it with a central difference across a grid of moneyness, volatility and time, including the ugly corners. When they disagree, the analytic formula is usually right and the test step is wrong. But not always. That is the point of having both.

5.3.4 Rule 2: the boundaries are not optional

Three regimes break the closed forms.

T→0T \to 0. σT→0\sigma\sqrt T \to 0 and d1→±∞d_1 \to \pm\infty, depending on moneyness. At the money, gamma behaves like 1/T1/\sqrt T and blows up. Away from the money it collapses to zero faster than any power. The honest answer at expiry is a step function for delta and a spike (a Dirac delta) for gamma.

I handle two cases separately: - I clamp T below at a small positive floor. - A contract at or past expiry gets intrinsic value and zero time Greeks.

They are different cases. Mixing them is a classic bug.

Figure 5.3.2 — Near expiry, gamma either explodes or vanishes. Spot 100, σ = 20%, r = q = 0 (illustrative). The blue at-the-money gamma climbs like 1/T1/\sqrt T in the last hours. The orange option, only 1% out of the money, sees its gamma drop to zero. Two strikes one point apart behave in opposite ways, which is why naive code at expiry produces wild numbers.

σ→0\sigma \to 0. Same algebra, same blow-up. A zero implied volatility usually means the solver failed or the quote was garbage. Reject it upstream; do not silently price it.

Deep in or out of the money. φ(d1)\varphi(d_1) underflows to zero for large |d1||d_1|, which is correct. N(d1)N(d_1) saturates at 0 or 1. The danger is the CDF code: computing N(x)N(x) as 1−N(−x)1 - N(-x) for large positive x loses all precision. Use erfc (the complementary error function) for the tails:

N(x)=12erfc(−x/2) N(x) = \tfrac12\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\left(-x/\sqrt2\right)

which stays accurate deep in the tail.

5.3.5 Rule 3: work in log space where you can

ln⁡(S/K)\ln(S/K) is better computed as log(S) - log(K) only if both logs are cached; otherwise log(S/K) is fine.

The real gain is in the density. φ(d1)=exp⁡(−d12/2)/2π\varphi(d_1) = \exp(-d_1^2/2)/\sqrt{2\pi} is safe, but a product like Sφ(d1)S\varphi(d_1) with huge S and tiny φ is better computed as exp⁡(ln⁡S−d12/2)\exp(\ln S - d_1^2/2). For index options this rarely bites. For crypto-style strikes it does.

5.3.6 Rule 4: units are half the bugs

Greek Raw unit What screens usually show
Vega per 1.00 of volatility (100 vol points) per 1 vol point
Theta per year per day (calendar or trading day)
Gamma per 1 unit of underlying exposure reports scale it per 1% move

Pick one internal convention, document it at the top of the module, and convert only at the display boundary. I keep everything in raw annualised units internally.

5.3.7 Rule 5: don’t let one contract poison an aggregate

When you sum gamma across a chain, one contract with a corrupt implied volatility can dominate. Robust aggregation means validating each contract’s inputs before it contributes:

  • positive price,
  • inside a sane bid–ask,
  • implied volatility within a plausible band,
  • time to expiry positive.

I would rather drop a contract and log it than include it and corrupt the profile. And I count what was dropped: a silent drop rate that drifts upward is itself a data problem.

5.3.8 Performance

Greeks for a full index chain is a few thousand contracts. That is trivial once. But the work multiplies when you build a profile by re-evaluating everything across a grid of hypothetical spot prices. Practical choices:

  • Compute d1d_1, d2d_2, φ(d1)\varphi(d_1), N(d1)N(d_1), N(d2)N(d_2) once per contract per spot, and derive every Greek from them.
  • Keep arrays flat and contiguous; do not allocate per contract.
  • Make it deterministic: same inputs, same outputs, bit for bit. That makes regression tests meaningful.

5.3.9 What the textbook leaves out

The textbook treats Greeks as properties of an option. In a live system they are properties of an option plus your data pipeline: your time-to-expiry clock, your implied volatility solver, your rate and dividend, your quote filter. Most of the “weird gamma” I have chased this year turned out to be one of those, not the formula.

5.3.10 Summary

  • Use analytic Greeks in production and central differences as tests, with a relative step near ε1/3\varepsilon^{1/3} (first derivatives) or ε1/4\varepsilon^{1/4} (second).
  • Treat T→0T \to 0 (floor) and expired contracts (intrinsic only) as two separate cases; reject σ = 0 upstream; use erfc in the tails.
  • Keep one internal unit convention and convert only for display.
  • Validate each contract before it enters an aggregate, and count what you drop.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) Machine epsilon is about 2.2×10−162.2\times10^{-16}. What relative step does the ε1/3\varepsilon^{1/3} rule suggest? (Answer: about 6×10−66\times10^{-6}.)
  2. (Reproduce) Recreate Figure 5.3.1 for a Black–Scholes call’s delta instead of exe^x. Where is the minimum error?
  3. (Bug hunt) Why does 1 - N(-x) lose precision for x = 10, while 0.5*erfc(-x/√2) does not?
  4. (Design) List the checks you would run on a contract before letting it into a chain-wide gamma sum.

Further reading

  • E. G. Haug, The Complete Guide to Option Pricing Formulas.
  • W. H. Press et al., Numerical Recipes, chapter on numerical derivatives.
  • D. Goldberg (1991), “What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic,” ACM Computing Surveys.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.4 — Implied Volatility with Newton–Raphson: Convergence, Bad Quotes, and Vega Near Zero

Subtitle: Inverting Black–Scholes is a one-dimensional root search. It still finds creative ways to fail.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State when an implied volatility exists and why it is unique. 2. Explain how Newton–Raphson fails when vega is near zero, and build a safeguarded solver that cannot diverge. 3. Estimate how uncertain an implied volatility is from the bid–ask spread and vega.

You need: Chapter 5.2 (prices and vega), and the idea of finding a root of a function.

5.4.1 Why the solver matters most

Every Greek I compute depends on an implied volatility, and every implied volatility comes out of a solver. If the solver is wrong, quietly, everything downstream is wrong, quietly. So I spent more time on this small function than on anything else in the options engine.

5.4.2 The problem

Given an observed option price CmktC^{\text{mkt}}, find σ such that

f(σ)=CBS(S,K,T,r,q,σ)−Cmkt=0 f(\sigma) = C_{BS}(S, K, T, r, q, \sigma) - C^{\text{mkt}} = 0

Result (uniqueness). There is at most one solution, because the Black–Scholes price strictly increases with σ. Its derivative is vega: ∂C∂σ=𝒱=Se−qTφ(d1)T>0 \frac{\partial C}{\partial \sigma} = \mathcal V = S e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)\sqrt T > 0

Result (existence). A solution exists only if the price lies inside the no-arbitrage bounds: max⁡(Se−qT−Ke−rT,0)<Cmkt<Se−qT \max\!\left(Se^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT},\, 0\right) \;<\; C^{\text{mkt}} \;<\; Se^{-qT}

Check the bounds first. A large share of “solver failures” are not solver failures at all. They are quotes that no volatility can produce.

5.4.3 Newton–Raphson

Newton’s method follows the tangent line to the root:

σn+1=σn−f(σn)𝒱(σn) \sigma_{n+1} = \sigma_n - \frac{f(\sigma_n)}{\mathcal V(\sigma_n)}

When it works, it converges quadratically: the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step. From a decent starting guess, at-the-money options converge in three or four iterations.

5.4.4 Where it breaks

Vega near zero. Far out of the money, or very close to expiry, vega is tiny. Dividing by something tiny throws the update to an absurd σ, sometimes negative, after which d1d_1 is undefined. This is the single biggest failure mode.

Bad starting point. Newton only converges locally. The price as a function of σ is convex for low σ and concave for high σ: it has an inflection point. From the wrong side Newton can overshoot.

Figure 5.4.1 — The price curve bends one way, then the other. An out-of-the-money call, S = 100, K = 110, T = 0.25 years, r = q = 0 (illustrative). Below the orange dot the curve is convex, above it concave. The flat start near σ = 0 is where vega is tiny and Newton steps explode. Started at the inflection point (about 87% here), Newton converges monotonically (Manaster and Koehler).

Prices at the bounds. A deep in-the-money option trading at intrinsic value implies σ→0\sigma \to 0. An option trading at Se−qTSe^{-qT} implies σ→∞\sigma \to \infty. Neither belongs in a gamma profile.

5.4.5 A safer solver

My engine grew two solvers. One is plain bisection (halve the interval each step): slow, but it cannot diverge. The other is a short Newton loop that bails out when vega drops below a floor and clamps the volatility from below. Writing both made the trade-off obvious. The textbook answer is to combine them into a safeguarded Newton:

  1. Validate the quote. Positive bid and ask, ask above bid, mid inside the arbitrage bounds. Otherwise reject.
  2. Bracket. Keep a lower and upper bound on σ with f changing sign between them. Because f is monotone, bracketing is easy.
  3. Start well. A closed-form approximation such as Brenner–Subrahmanyam for near-the-money options, σ0≈2πTCS \sigma_0 \approx \sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{T}}\,\frac{C}{S} or the Corrado–Miller refinement, gets you close. The inflection point of C(σ)C(\sigma) is also a known safe start.
  4. Step with Newton, fall back to bisection. If the Newton step leaves the bracket, or vega is below a floor, take a bisection step instead. Update the bracket with every evaluation.
  5. Stop on both criteria. Price error below a tolerance and step size below a tolerance. A tiny price error with a large step means you are on a flat part of the curve and σ is poorly determined.

This is Brent-style safety around Newton speed. It never diverges, because it never leaves a sign-changing bracket.

Figure 5.4.2 — Newton when it is safe, bisection when it is not. Green arrows are the normal path. At step 4 the solver asks whether the Newton step stays inside the bracket and vega is above a floor; if not (orange), it bisects instead. Either way the bracket shrinks, so the loop must end. Quotes that fail validation are rejected and logged, never solved.

5.4.6 Bad quotes are a data problem, not a maths problem

Real chains have:

  • Zero bids on far out-of-the-money strikes. The mid is then half the ask, often a meaningless price.
  • Wide spreads, where the mid can imply any volatility you like.
  • Stale quotes after a fast move: the option price lags the underlying.
  • Asynchronous snapshots: the underlying and the option were sampled at different instants.

No root finder fixes these. What helps is deciding, explicitly, which quotes are informative. I prefer out-of-the-money options on both sides (calls above the forward, puts below). They are more liquid, and their prices are mostly time value. In-the-money options are mostly intrinsic value, so their implied volatility reacts wildly to tiny price errors.

Result (implied volatility uncertainty). δσ≈δC𝒱 \delta\sigma \approx \frac{\delta C}{\mathcal V} Price noise (say half a spread) divided by vega is your implied volatility uncertainty.

When vega is tiny, the implied volatility is effectively unknown, even if the solver converges perfectly. A converged answer is not an informative answer.

5.4.7 What I record

For each contract I keep:

  • whether the solve succeeded,
  • how many iterations it took,
  • why it failed if it did (outside bounds, no bid, vega floor, max iterations).

Summed over a chain, those counts are an excellent health check on the feed. A sudden rise in “outside bounds” usually means the underlying price and the chain are out of sync.

5.4.8 Determinism and speed

The solver runs thousands of times per chain snapshot. Each iteration costs one price and one vega, which share d1d_1 and φ(d1)\varphi(d_1), so compute them together. Fix the iteration cap and tolerances so results are reproducible. Do not warm-start from the previous snapshot’s answer without a bracket check: after a gap, that answer can be far away.

For heavy use, Jäckel’s “Let’s Be Rational” reaches machine precision in two iterations using carefully chosen rational approximations. It is excellent. I still keep the simple safeguarded version as a reference implementation, because I can read every line of it.

5.4.9 Summary

  • Implied volatility is unique (price rises with σ) but exists only inside the arbitrage bounds; check bounds first.
  • Plain Newton is fast but blows up when vega is near zero or the start is poor.
  • Safeguarded Newton keeps a sign-changing bracket and falls back to bisection, so it cannot diverge.
  • δσ≈δC/𝒱\delta\sigma \approx \delta C/\mathcal V: low-vega quotes give uninformative volatilities even when the solve converges.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) An option has vega 0.02 (per 1.00 of σ) and a bid–ask spread of 0.10. Roughly how uncertain is its implied volatility? (Answer: half-spread 0.05 / 0.02 = 2.5, i.e. 250 vol points: useless.)
  2. (Bounds) S = 100, K = 90, r = q = 0, and a call trades at 9.50. Can any σ produce this price? Why?
  3. (Build) Implement the five-step safeguarded solver and test it on the option in Figure 5.4.1 from a start of σ = 0.01.
  4. (Think) Why are out-of-the-money options preferred for implied volatility on both sides of the forward?

Further reading

  • S. Manaster and G. Koehler (1982), “The Calculation of Implied Variances from the Black–Scholes Model: A Note,” Journal of Finance.
  • M. Brenner and M. Subrahmanyam (1988), “A Simple Formula to Compute the Implied Standard Deviation,” Financial Analysts Journal.
  • P. Jäckel (2015), “Let’s Be Rational,” Wilmott.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.5 — Exact Time-to-Expiry for 0DTE Options

Subtitle: When an option has hours to live, “T” stops being a rounding detail and becomes the dominant input.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why errors in T distort every Greek of a same-day option, even when the price still fits. 2. Compute T to the second, with the right settlement instant, time zone and clock source. 3. Tell a numerical floor apart from expiry, and calendar time apart from variance time.

You need: Chapters 5.2–5.4.

5.5.1 Why T suddenly matters

For a three-month option, nobody cares whether you count calendar days or trading days, or whether the clock reads 10:00 or 14:00. The change in T is a fraction of a percent.

For a same-day (0DTE) option, the same choice can change T by a factor of three before lunch. Gamma near the money scales like 1/T1/\sqrt{T}. So that is not a rounding detail. It is the whole answer.

5.5.2 Why T matters so much at the end

At the money, d1≈0d_1 \approx 0, and

ΓATM≈e−qTSσ2πT,𝒱ATM≈Se−qTT2π \Gamma_{ATM} \approx \frac{e^{-qT}}{S\sigma\sqrt{2\pi T}}, \qquad \mathcal V_{ATM} \approx \frac{S e^{-qT}\sqrt{T}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}

Gamma explodes as T→0T \to 0 and vega vanishes.

Figure 5.5.1 — In the last day, gamma and vega move in opposite directions. Both curves are shown relative to their value with 24 hours left, using the at-the-money formulas above with σ held fixed. With 2 hours left, gamma is about 3.5 times its 24-hour value and vega is less than a third. Small errors in T therefore move these numbers a lot.

The model only ever sees the total variance σ2T\sigma^2 T. Suppose you overstate T by using “one day” for an option with two hours left. The implied volatility solver compensates by returning a much smaller σ, so the price still matches. You get the right price with the wrong decomposition. Every Greek built on it is distorted: gamma too spread out, charm too small, the profile smeared across strikes.

5.5.3 Calendar time, to the second

The first fix is obvious: measure the actual time left, to the second, until the settlement instant.

T=texpiry−tnowseconds per year T = \frac{t_{\text{expiry}} - t_{\text{now}}}{\text{seconds per year}}

My calculators do exactly that: a timestamp for the settlement time on the expiry date, minus the current UTC time, divided by 365.25×86400365.25 \times 86400.

Three details hide in that one line.

What is the settlement instant? For PM-settled index and ETF options, trading stops at the close, 16:00 New York time. AM-settled contracts (the traditional monthly index options) settle on an opening print, so their effective T ends at the open, not the close. Using the wrong one is an error of most of a trading day.

Time zones and daylight saving. New York is UTC−5 in winter and UTC−4 in summer. A hard-coded offset is right for about half the year and an hour wrong for the other half. One of my calculators did exactly that early on: it computed expiry with a fixed summer offset. On a 0DTE contract, an hour late in the session is a large fraction of the remaining life. The fix: build the expiry in the exchange’s own time zone with a proper time-zone database, then convert to UTC. Never hard-code the offset.

Clock source. “Now” should be the timestamp of the quote, not the wall clock of the machine processing it. If a snapshot arrives ten seconds late, pricing it at the current time adds a systematic error that grows as expiry approaches.

5.5.4 The floor

As T→0T \to 0, d1→±∞d_1 \to \pm\infty and the formulas become numerically unstable. Every implementation needs a floor: a minimum T below which you stop pretending the continuous model is meaningful. My calculators clamp the remaining time to a small minimum. Two warnings:

  1. A floor is a modelling decision, not a numerical trick. Inside the floor, Greeks are computed for an option that is effectively older than reality. Report that.
  2. A floor is not expiry. Once the option has expired it has intrinsic value only. Clamping an expired contract to a positive T gives it phantom time value.

5.5.5 Calendar time or trading time?

Black–Scholes assumes variance builds up evenly in calendar time. Markets disagree. Overnight and weekends carry less variance per hour than the regular session. Within the session, variance bunches around the open, the close and scheduled announcements.

The standard refinement is to measure time in variance time instead of clock time:

Definition (variance time). Tvar=∫tnowtexpiryw(u)du T_{\text{var}} = \int_{t_{\text{now}}}^{t_{\text{expiry}}} w(u)\,du where w(u)w(u) is proportional to the expected instantaneous variance at time u.

  • With w constant you get calendar time.
  • With w zero outside trading hours you get trading time.
  • With an intraday profile (the familiar U-shape) you get something better still.

Figure 5.5.2 — The last hour can hold far more than its share of variance. A toy U-shape, w(u)∝1+3((u−12:45)/3.25 h)2w(u) \propto 1 + 3\,((u - 12{:}45)/3.25\text{ h})^2 over a 09:30–16:00 session, compared with a flat calendar clock. Both average to 1. The shaded area after 15:00 is 15% of the session’s clock time but 24% of its variance under this toy weight. The shape is an illustration, not a measured profile.

For 0DTE this matters. At 15:00 there is an hour left on the clock, but that hour contains the closing auction and often a disproportionate share of the day’s variance. Calendar time treats it like any other hour; a variance clock does not.

I keep calendar seconds as the base measure, because it is unambiguous and easy to audit, and treat variance-time weighting as an explicit, separate layer. Mixing the two silently is how you end up with numbers no one can reproduce.

5.5.6 Annualisation conventions

Be consistent between the implied volatility solve and the Greeks:

  • If T is in calendar years (365.25 days), the implied volatility is a calendar-time volatility.
  • If you then quote theta per trading day, you must convert.
  • If you compare your implied volatility with a broker’s, check their convention first; many use trading days.

5.5.7 Testing it

The tests I found most useful:

  • Fixed timestamps on both sides of each daylight-saving change, checking T against hand-computed values.
  • A synthetic chain priced at a known σ and T, then solved back with a T off by an hour, to see the size of the implied volatility error. It is a sobering experiment late in the session.
  • Expired contracts, contracts at exactly the settlement instant, and contracts one second before it.

5.5.8 The broader lesson

The Black–Scholes inputs we treat as “known” are not equally known.

Input How well known?
Strike exact
Spot close
Rates barely matter for short options
Time, for 0DTE the input with the largest leverage on the output, and the one most often computed carelessly

5.5.9 Summary

  • Near expiry, Γ∝1/T\Gamma \propto 1/\sqrt T and 𝒱∝T\mathcal V \propto \sqrt T; a wrong T gives the right price with wrong Greeks.
  • Compute T in seconds to the true settlement instant (PM close or AM open), in the exchange’s time zone, using the quote’s timestamp.
  • A floor is a stated modelling choice; an expired option is intrinsic only.
  • Keep calendar seconds as the base; add variance-time weighting as a separate, explicit layer.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) An option has 2 hours left but is priced with T = 1 day. By what factor is T\sqrt T overstated? (Answer: 24/2≈3.46\sqrt{24/2} \approx 3.46.)
  2. (Time zones) Expiry is 16:00 New York time on a summer day. What UTC time is that? What goes wrong if the same offset is used in January?
  3. (Simulate) Price a call at σ = 20% with 1 hour left, then solve for σ using T = 2 hours. What implied volatility do you get?
  4. (Think) Why keep calendar seconds as the base measure even if you believe in a variance clock?

Further reading

  • T. G. Andersen and T. Bollerslev (1997), “Intraday Periodicity and Volatility Persistence in Financial Markets,” Journal of Empirical Finance.
  • J. Gatheral, The Volatility Surface: A Practitioner’s Guide.
  • J. C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, discussion of trading days versus calendar days.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.6 — Vanna, Explained from the Derivative Up

Subtitle: How a change in implied volatility moves a hedger’s delta, and why that shows up as flow.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define vanna and derive its Black–Scholes–Merton formula. 2. Read its sign across strikes and explain why calls and puts share the same vanna. 3. Turn vanna into a “vol-crush” hedging-flow story, and list what that story assumes.

You need: Chapters 5.1–5.3.

5.6.1 What else moves delta?

Gamma gets all the attention. But once my engine was computing gamma, the next question was: what else changes a dealer’s delta? Price is one answer. Implied volatility is another. That second sensitivity is vanna. It sits behind much of the “vol crush rally” folklore around big events.

5.6.2 Definition

Definition (vanna). The mixed second derivative of option value with respect to spot and volatility: Vanna=∂2V∂S∂σ=∂Δ∂σ=∂𝒱∂S \text{Vanna} = \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S\,\partial\sigma} = \frac{\partial \Delta}{\partial \sigma} = \frac{\partial \mathcal V}{\partial S}

The symmetry is worth a pause. Vanna is both “how much delta moves when volatility moves” and “how much vega moves when spot moves”. Same number, two readings.

5.6.3 Deriving it under Black–Scholes–Merton

Start from call delta, ΔC=e−qTN(d1)\Delta_C = e^{-qT}N(d_1), and differentiate with respect to σ:

∂ΔC∂σ=e−qTφ(d1)∂d1∂σ \frac{\partial \Delta_C}{\partial\sigma} = e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)\frac{\partial d_1}{\partial\sigma}

Write d1=ln⁡(S/K)+(r−q)TσT+12σTd_1 = \dfrac{\ln(S/K) + (r-q)T}{\sigma\sqrt T} + \tfrac12\sigma\sqrt T. Then

∂d1∂σ=−ln⁡(S/K)+(r−q)Tσ2T+12T=−d2σ \frac{\partial d_1}{\partial\sigma} = -\frac{\ln(S/K)+(r-q)T}{\sigma^2\sqrt T} + \tfrac12\sqrt T = -\frac{d_2}{\sigma}

Result. Vanna=−e−qTφ(d1)d2σ \text{Vanna} = -e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)\frac{d_2}{\sigma}

Put delta differs from call delta by a constant (e−qTe^{-qT}), so put vanna equals call vanna for the same strike and expiry. That surprised me the first time I wrote the test.

5.6.4 Reading the sign

The sign is the sign of −d2-d_2:

  • Out-of-the-money call (S<KS < K, so roughly d2<0d_2 < 0): vanna positive. Raise volatility and the call’s delta rises, because reaching the strike becomes more plausible.
  • Out-of-the-money put (S>KS > K, d2>0d_2 > 0): vanna negative, so the put’s (negative) delta becomes more negative as volatility rises. Same idea: more volatility, more chance of finishing in the money.
  • At the money: d2≈0d_2 \approx 0, vanna near zero. Delta already sits near its midpoint, and extra volatility hardly shifts it.

Figure 5.6.1 — Vanna is the shape of a bell curve’s slope. Spot 100, σ = 20%, r = q = 0, for 30 days (blue) and 7 days (orange) to expiry; illustrative values. Strikes above spot (the out-of-the-money call side) have positive vanna; strikes below spot (the out-of-the-money put side) negative. It is near zero at the money and largest in a band about one standard deviation away. Shorter expiry pulls that band closer to spot.

5.6.5 Vanna as flow

Here is the step from Greek to market story. Suppose dealers are short out-of-the-money puts that customers bought as protection. That is the usual assumption, with all the caveats of Chapter 5.1. Each short put leaves the dealer with positive delta, which they hedge by being short the underlying.

Now implied volatility falls, say after an event passes quietly. The puts’ deltas shrink in size (vanna at work). The dealer is now less long delta than before, so the short hedge is too big, and they buy back underlying. A fall in volatility mechanically creates buying. Rising volatility does the opposite.

Aggregate that across the chain with the usual per-contract scaling:

VEXK=VannaK⋅wK⋅100⋅S \text{VEX}_K = \text{Vanna}_K \cdot w_K \cdot 100 \cdot S

where wKw_K is open interest or volume and the sign follows the dealer-position assumption. The result is a dollar-delta change per unit of volatility. My engine tracks it alongside gamma and delta exposure.

5.6.6 What can go wrong

Implied volatility does not move uniformly. Vanna measures sensitivity to a parallel shift in one contract’s σ. Real surfaces twist: short-dated volatility moves more than long-dated, and the skew steepens or flattens. One “vanna exposure” number assumes every strike’s volatility moves by the same amount. It never does.

Spot and volatility are correlated. In equity indices, volatility tends to rise as spot falls. So the “vanna effect” and the “gamma effect” are not independent shocks you can add up. A realistic scenario moves both, and the combined delta change is a total derivative:

dΔ≈ΓdS+Vannadσ+Charmdt d\Delta \approx \Gamma\,dS + \text{Vanna}\,d\sigma + \text{Charm}\,dt

with dσd\sigma itself a function of dSdS.

Units. Vanna per unit of volatility (per 100 vol points) is a big number; per 1 vol point it is a hundred times smaller. I keep raw units internally and scale only for display. Mixing the two between a calculator and a dashboard is an easy way to be off by two orders of magnitude.

Positioning is unknown. As always, the sign of the aggregate depends on who is long and who is short, which open interest does not tell you.

5.6.7 Engineering notes

  • Vanna reuses d1d_1, d2d_2 and φ(d1)\varphi(d_1), which you already have for gamma, so it costs almost nothing extra.
  • Check it with a central difference on delta with respect to σ. This catches sign errors immediately.
  • Beware very short expiries. φ(d1)/σ\varphi(d_1)/\sigma can be large near the money while d2d_2 swings sign within one strike interval. The 0DTE vanna profile is jagged, and that jaggedness is real, not a bug.

5.6.8 How I think about it

Vanna is useful as a scenario lens: “if implied volatility drops after this event, what hedging flow would the textbook dealer generate?” It is not a forecast. I treat it as context and test any claimed effect against a null, the same way I treat gamma.

5.6.9 Summary

  • Vanna = ∂Δ/∂σ = ∂vega/∂S = −e−qTφ(d1)d2/σ-e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)d_2/\sigma; calls and puts share it.
  • Positive on the out-of-the-money call side, negative on the put side, near zero at the money.
  • Under the usual dealer-short-puts assumption, falling volatility implies dealer buying.
  • The story assumes parallel volatility shifts, ignores spot–vol correlation, and depends on unknown positioning.

Exercises

  1. (Derive) Show that ∂d1/∂σ=−d2/σ\partial d_1/\partial\sigma = -d_2/\sigma.
  2. (Sign) S = 100, K = 110, short expiry. Is vanna positive or negative? What happens to the call’s delta if volatility rises? (Answer: positive; delta rises.)
  3. (Check) Compute vanna for one option analytically and by central difference of delta in σ. Do they match?
  4. (Think) Why does the spot–vol correlation in equity indices make “gamma flow + vanna flow” an over-simplification?

Further reading

  • N. N. Taleb (1997), Dynamic Hedging: Managing Vanilla and Exotic Options.
  • E. G. Haug, The Complete Guide to Option Pricing Formulas, section on second-order Greeks.
  • J. Gatheral, The Volatility Surface, on skew dynamics.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.7 — Charm: Why Delta Drifts with the Clock, and Why It Matters Near Expiry

Subtitle: Nothing has to happen in the market for a hedger’s delta to change. Time alone does it.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define charm and state its Black–Scholes–Merton formula for calls and puts. 2. Explain, with a picture, why charm grows like 1/T1/T near expiry. 3. Turn charm into a “clock-driven” hedging flow and list its pitfalls.

You need: Chapters 5.2, 5.5 and 5.6.

5.7.1 The Greek that wakes up

The first time I plotted charm for same-day options, I thought the code was broken. A Greek that is a footnote for monthly options was suddenly the largest number on the screen.

It was not broken. Charm is exactly the Greek that wakes up as expiry approaches. With a large share of index option volume now expiring the same day, it deserves its own chapter.

5.7.2 Definition

Definition (charm, or delta decay). The rate of change of delta as time passes: Charm=∂Δ∂t=−∂Δ∂T \text{Charm} = \frac{\partial\Delta}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial\Delta}{\partial T} where t is calendar time and T is time to expiry.

Sign conventions vary between sources, so always check which one a reference uses. I report the change in delta as time moves forward.

5.7.3 Deriving it

Call delta is ΔC=e−qTN(d1)\Delta_C = e^{-qT}N(d_1). Differentiate with respect to T:

∂ΔC∂T=−qe−qTN(d1)+e−qTφ(d1)∂d1∂T \frac{\partial\Delta_C}{\partial T} = -q e^{-qT}N(d_1) + e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)\frac{\partial d_1}{\partial T}

with

∂d1∂T=2(r−q)T−d2σT2TσT \frac{\partial d_1}{\partial T} = \frac{2(r-q)T - d_2\sigma\sqrt T}{2T\sigma\sqrt T}

Result (charm, annualised). CharmC=qe−qTN(d1)−e−qTφ(d1)2(r−q)T−d2σT2TσT \text{Charm}_C = q e^{-qT}N(d_1) - e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)\,\frac{2(r-q)T - d_2\sigma\sqrt T}{2T\sigma\sqrt T} CharmP=−qe−qTN(−d1)−e−qTφ(d1)2(r−q)T−d2σT2TσT \text{Charm}_P = -q e^{-qT}N(-d_1) - e^{-qT}\varphi(d_1)\,\frac{2(r-q)T - d_2\sigma\sqrt T}{2T\sigma\sqrt T}

These are per year. To get delta change per day, divide by the days-per-year convention you used for T. My engine reports it per calendar day.

5.7.4 The intuition

At expiry, delta is a step: one if in the money, zero if out. Before expiry it is a smooth S-curve. Time pulls the S-curve towards the step.

Figure 5.7.1 — Time turns the delta S-curve into a step. A call with strike 100, σ = 20%, r = q = 0, at 30 days, 1 day and 2 hours to expiry (illustrative). All three cross 0.5 at the strike. As time runs out, deltas to the left fall towards 0 and deltas to the right rise towards 1. Charm is the speed of that squeeze.

  • An out-of-the-money option’s delta drifts towards zero: less time left to get in the money.
  • An in-the-money option’s delta drifts towards one (minus one for puts).
  • At the money, the curve pivots around its midpoint and the drift is small.

Ignoring the small rate and dividend terms, for short expiries:

Charm≈φ(d1)d22T \text{Charm} \approx \varphi(d_1)\,\frac{d_2}{2T}

That 1/T1/T is the story. As T shrinks, charm grows without bound for strikes near but not at the money. For a monthly option, a day’s passage barely moves delta. For an option expiring in two hours, an hour moves it a lot.

Figure 5.7.2 — Charm concentrates and grows as expiry nears. Call charm per calendar day across strikes, spot 100, σ = 20%, r = q = 0. With 1 day left (blue) it is small and spread out. With 2 hours left (orange) its peak is more than ten times higher and squeezed into strikes within about one point of spot. It is zero exactly at the money and changes sign across it.

5.7.5 From Greek to flow

Dealer hedges are sized to delta. If delta changes because time passed, the hedge must change, even if spot and volatility stood perfectly still. Aggregated across the chain:

Charm flowK=−CharmK⋅wK⋅100⋅S \text{Charm flow}_K = -\text{Charm}_K \cdot w_K \cdot 100 \cdot S

This is the dollar amount of underlying a delta-neutral dealer would need to trade per day to stay hedged, under the usual assumptions about who holds what. The leading minus turns “the dealer’s delta changes by x” into “the dealer trades −x to offset it”.

The classic narrative. Dealers are short out-of-the-money puts. As the day passes, those puts’ deltas decay towards zero. The dealers’ long delta from the short puts shrinks, so their short hedge is too large, and they buy it back. That is buying that needs no news, only the clock. Whether it is visible in prices is an empirical question, and I treat it as one.

5.7.6 Why near expiry is different

Three things compound for same-day options:

  1. The 1/T1/T term. Charm scales roughly as 1/T1/T, so the last hours carry most of the effect.
  2. Concentration. Gamma, and so charm, sits on a narrow band of strikes around spot. A few strikes dominate the total.
  3. Sign flips with spot. Charm’s sign depends on d2d_2. A modest spot move can carry a big strike from one side of the money to the other, flipping its contribution. The total can change sign intraday without anyone trading.

So a single charm number at 10:00 tells you little about 15:00. Recompute it as spot and time move.

5.7.7 Pitfalls

Pitfall Why it matters
Time measurement Charm is a derivative with respect to time, so it is hypersensitive to how you measure time. A sloppy T (wrong time zone, daily granularity) gives a wrong charm (Chapter 5.5).
Holding volatility fixed Textbook charm assumes implied volatility stays constant. Short-dated implied volatility drifts through the day, so the real delta change mixes charm and vanna.
The floor With a minimum-T clamp, charm stops growing inside the floor. That is necessary, but the reported charm is capped near the end of the day. Know where your floor is.
Weekends Friday afternoon to Monday morning passes calendar time without trading. Calendar or trading time are both defensible; using one in the solver and the other in the Greek is not.

5.7.8 Testing

As with every Greek, I check the closed form against a finite difference: compute delta at T and at T − h, and compare. Near expiry the step must be small relative to T, so use a relative step. The test grid includes options minutes from expiry, because that is exactly where charm matters and where bugs hide.

5.7.9 Summary

  • Charm is the change in delta as time passes; I report it per calendar day, as time moves forward.
  • Time pulls delta towards a step: OTM deltas decay to 0, ITM deltas rise to 1.
  • Near expiry charm ≈ φ(d1)d2/(2T)\varphi(d_1)d_2/(2T), so it grows like 1/T1/T, concentrates near spot and flips sign with spot.
  • The “clock-driven buying” story is a hypothesis to test, built on the usual positioning assumption.

Exercises

  1. (Sign) With r = q = 0, show that charm for an out-of-the-money call (K > S) is negative.
  2. (Scale) If T falls from 4 hours to 1 hour at a fixed d2d_2, by roughly what factor does charm grow? (Answer: about 4, from the 1/T1/T term, ignoring changes in φ and d2d_2.)
  3. (Units) Your code computes charm per year using 365.25-day years. How do you report it per calendar day?
  4. (Think) Why can the aggregate charm of a chain change sign during the day without any trades?

Further reading

  • E. G. Haug, The Complete Guide to Option Pricing Formulas.
  • N. N. Taleb, Dynamic Hedging, on time decay of delta.
  • J. C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, chapter on the Greek letters.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.8 — Delta Exposure (DEX): The First-Order View of Dealer Positioning

Subtitle: Gamma tells you how hedges change. Delta exposure tells you how big the hedge already is.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compute DEX per strike and in total, and say what each term in the formula does. 2. Explain the relation between DEX and GEX (level versus slope). 3. Name the two sign conventions and the four ways DEX is commonly misread.

You need: Chapters 5.1 and 5.2.

5.8.1 The afterthought that turned out intuitive

Most dealer-positioning charts lead with gamma. When I built my own, I added delta exposure (DEX) almost as an afterthought, because the inputs were already there. It turned out to be the most intuitive of the lot, and also the easiest to misread.

5.8.2 The definition

For one contract, delta is the change in option value per unit change in the underlying. DEX adds that up into dollars across the chain.

Definition (delta exposure). DEX=∑K,typesKΔKwK⋅m⋅S \text{DEX} = \sum_{K,\,\text{type}} s_{K}\;\Delta_{K}\; w_K \cdot m \cdot S - ΔK\Delta_K: Black–Scholes–Merton delta (e−qTN(d1)e^{-qT}N(d_1) for calls, −e−qTN(−d1)-e^{-qT}N(-d_1) for puts), - wKw_K: weight, either open interest or traded volume, - m: contract multiplier (100 for standard US equity and ETF options), - S: converts share-equivalent delta into dollars, - sKs_K: the sign that encodes the positioning assumption.

Δ⋅w⋅m\Delta \cdot w \cdot m is the number of share-equivalents; times S gives notional dollars. My engine computes this per strike (a DEX profile) and sums it for a total.

5.8.3 What it represents

If customers hold the options and dealers hold the other side, the dealers’ option book has delta −DEXcustomer-\text{DEX}_{\text{customer}}. A delta-neutral dealer then holds an offsetting hedge in the underlying. So DEX estimates the size and direction of that standing hedge.

Gamma is the derivative of DEX with respect to spot:

∂DEX∂S≈∑sKΓKwKmS+DEXS \frac{\partial\,\text{DEX}}{\partial S} \approx \sum s_K\,\Gamma_K\, w_K\, m\, S + \frac{\text{DEX}}{S}

The second term comes from the S multiplier in the dollar conversion. So the GEX profile of Chapter 5.1 is essentially the slope of the DEX profile. DEX is the level; GEX is how fast it changes.

5.8.4 The sign question, again

Two conventions are in common use:

Convention What it does What it means
Raw customer delta Calls add positive delta, puts negative, no assumption about who is long. “The delta of open interest.”
Dealer-signed delta Flip the sign to represent the dealer’s book. Valid only under some assumption about who sold what.

Open interest counts open contracts. Every contract has a long and a short. Summing raw delta over open interest gives the delta of the longs, which is exactly cancelled by the delta of the shorts. Without knowing who the longs are, the number describes the chain, not any participant.

I keep the sign convention explicit in the code and on every display. A DEX number without a stated convention cannot be interpreted.

5.8.5 Why DEX is easy to misread

It is dominated by deep in-the-money options. Deep in-the-money calls have delta near one and can carry large open interest from old positions. They add huge DEX but almost no gamma. They are often held in structures (covered calls, conversions, box spreads) that are already hedged. Their contribution says little about future flows.

It mixes expiries. A long-dated option and a same-day option with the same delta add equally to DEX, but their hedges behave very differently. Separate expiries, or at least separate same-day from the rest. I keep a same-day view weighted by volume and a multi-expiry view weighted by open interest.

It is a stock, not a flow. DEX gives the size of the standing hedge, not what will trade next. Flows come from changes in DEX:

dDEX≈∂DEX∂SdS+∂DEX∂σdσ+∂DEX∂tdt+(new positions) d\,\text{DEX} \approx \frac{\partial\,\text{DEX}}{\partial S}dS + \frac{\partial\,\text{DEX}}{\partial\sigma}d\sigma + \frac{\partial\,\text{DEX}}{\partial t}dt + (\text{new positions})

through spot (gamma), volatility (vanna) and time (charm). The last term, positions opening and closing, is invisible in open interest until the next day.

It ignores the rest of the book. Dealers hedge across products: futures, other options, other underlyings, inventory from other clients. The option chain is one slice of their exposure.

5.8.6 A useful way to look at it

DEX is most helpful as a profile across hypothetical spot prices. Recompute every contract’s delta on a grid of spot levels, holding implied volatility and time fixed, and plot total DEX against spot.

Figure 5.8.1 — DEX is the level; its slope is the gamma side. A toy chain (call open interest centred at 108, put open interest at 92, Gaussian shapes stated in the generator), 7 days to expiry, σ = 20%, raw customer convention. The blue curve is DEX recomputed at each hypothetical spot; the dashed orange curve is its slope. Each is scaled to its own maximum. Read off where DEX changes sign, how steeply it changes, and where it flattens far from the money.

That curve shows:

  • where the aggregate hedge changes sign,
  • how steeply it changes (that is gamma),
  • where it flattens out, because far from the money the deltas saturate.

This uses the same grid machinery as the zero-gamma search (Chapter 5.9), so it costs almost nothing extra.

5.8.7 Engineering notes

DEX is cheap: it reuses d1d_1 and N(d1)N(d_1). The risk is in the inputs, not the computation.

  • A bad implied volatility on a deep in-the-money contract barely changes its delta (it is near one regardless). Reassuring.
  • A bad implied volatility near the money changes it a lot. The quote-validation rules that protect gamma also protect DEX.
  • Keep units consistent: dollars of underlying notional, per whatever multiplier the product uses. Futures options use different multipliers from ETF options; summing them without conversion is meaningless.

5.8.8 The takeaway

DEX is the simplest dealer-positioning number and the one with the most hidden assumptions per digit. It is a decent description of the chain’s delta, a weak description of dealer inventory, and not a forecast. I treat it as context and test any story built on it against what would have happened anyway.

5.8.9 Summary

  • DEX = Σ s·Δ·w·m·S: the dollar size of the standing hedge implied by the chain.
  • GEX is (essentially) the slope of DEX against spot.
  • Always state the sign convention; raw OI delta describes the chain, not a participant.
  • Deep ITM options, mixed expiries, unseen new positions and other books all distort the reading.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) A call strike has Δ = 0.6, OI = 2,000, multiplier 100, spot 400. What is its raw DEX? (Answer: 0.6 × 2,000 × 100 × 400 = $48 million.)
  2. (Derive) Differentiate sΔwmSs\,\Delta\,w\,m\,S with respect to S and confirm the two terms in the slope formula.
  3. (Think) Why might a strike with huge DEX contribute nothing to future hedging flow?
  4. (Build) Recreate Figure 5.8.1 with your own toy chain. Move the put open interest closer to spot. What happens to the sign change?

Further reading

  • J. C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, on delta hedging.
  • S. X. Ni, N. D. Pearson and A. M. Poteshman (2005), “Stock Price Clustering on Option Expiration Dates,” Journal of Financial Economics.
  • N. Garleanu, L. H. Pedersen and A. M. Poteshman (2009), “Demand-Based Option Pricing,” Review of Financial Studies.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.9 — Finding the Zero-Gamma Level: Root Search Versus Interpolation

Subtitle: Two ways to compute the most-quoted level in options analytics, and why they give different answers.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compute a zero-gamma level by interpolating a cumulative strike profile. 2. Compute it properly by a root search over hypothetical spot, using a grid scan and Brent’s method. 3. Explain why the two methods answer different questions, and what their disagreement tells you.

You need: Chapters 5.1 and 5.8, and the idea of a root (where a function equals zero).

5.9.1 One name, two numbers

Zero gamma (or the “gamma flip”) is the spot price at which total dealer gamma changes sign. Above it, the story goes, dealers are long gamma and dampen moves; below it, they are short gamma and amplify them.

I have written two calculators that compute it, with two different methods, and they do not agree. This chapter explains both and why the disagreement is informative.

5.9.2 Method 1: interpolate the strike profile

The common approach on public dashboards:

  1. For each strike K, compute signed gamma exposure at the current spot S0S_0: GEXK=sKΓK(S0)wK⋅m⋅S02⋅0.01 \text{GEX}_K = s_K\,\Gamma_K(S_0)\,w_K\cdot m \cdot S_0^2 \cdot 0.01
  2. Sort by strike and accumulate: C(Kj)=∑i≤jGEXKiC(K_j) = \sum_{i \le j}\text{GEX}_{K_i}.
  3. Find adjacent strikes where the running sum changes sign, and interpolate linearly: K*=Kj+(Kj+1−Kj)−C(Kj)C(Kj+1)−C(Kj) K^* = K_j + (K_{j+1} - K_j)\,\frac{-C(K_j)}{C(K_{j+1}) - C(K_j)}

One of my calculators does exactly this. It is fast, simple, and needs one pass over the chain.

But look at what it finds: the strike where the cumulative sum of gamma, evaluated at today’s spot, crosses zero. That describes how gamma is spread across strikes. It does not say what total gamma would be if spot moved there. Strikes far from today’s spot add almost nothing, because their gamma at today’s spot is tiny. The running sum is dominated by strikes near the money.

5.9.3 Method 2: root search over hypothetical spot

The more faithful definition asks: at what spot S*S^* would total gamma exposure be zero?

Definition (zero-gamma level, root form). G(S)=∑contractsscΓc(S)wc⋅m⋅S2⋅0.01,G(S*)=0 G(S) = \sum_{\text{contracts}} s_c\,\Gamma_c(S)\,w_c\cdot m\cdot S^2\cdot 0.01, \qquad G(S^*) = 0

Every contract’s gamma is recomputed at the hypothetical spot, holding implied volatility and time fixed. As S moves, different strikes come near the money and take over the gamma. This matches the “dealers flip from long to short gamma here” story.

My other calculator does it in two stages:

  1. Scan. Evaluate G(S)G(S) on a grid of spot prices around the current level and look for sign changes.
  2. Refine. Once a bracket [Sa,Sb][S_a, S_b] with G(Sa)G(Sb)<0G(S_a)G(S_b) < 0 is found, solve for the root with Brent’s method.

Figure 5.9.1 — Two definitions on one toy chain. A made-up chain (call open interest centred at 108, put open interest at 92, 7 days, σ = 20%; dealer convention calls +, puts −). Blue: total G(S) recomputed at each hypothetical spot, with open circles marking a coarse scan grid. Orange: the cumulative strike sum at today’s spot of 100. Each curve is scaled to its own maximum. On this tidy, symmetric toy the two crossings land close together (about 98.9 and 98.8). On real chains, with gamma spread out, they can be far apart.

5.9.4 Why Brent’s method

Brent’s method mixes bisection, the secant method and inverse quadratic interpolation. It keeps a sign-changing bracket at every step, so like bisection it is guaranteed to converge. When the function is smooth it converges superlinearly, like the secant method. For a function like G(S)G(S), smooth but with no cheap analytic derivative across thousands of contracts, it is the standard choice.

Newton would need G′(S)G'(S), which involves the derivative of gamma with respect to spot (called speed). That is computable, but Brent gets there without it and without the risk of diverging.

5.9.5 Pitfalls of the root search

Multiple roots. G(S)G(S) can cross zero more than once, especially with large positions at a few strikes. A grid scan finds all sign changes in range; you must decide which to report. The one nearest spot is the usual choice, but it should be a stated rule, not an accident of loop order.

No root at all. If gamma has one sign across the whole grid, there is no flip in range. The honest output is “none in range”, not the grid edge.

Grid resolution. Too coarse a grid can step over a pair of nearby roots (two sign changes cancel). A finer grid costs more evaluations, each a full pass over the chain. That cost is the main engineering trade-off.

Frozen inputs. Holding implied volatility fixed while moving spot ignores skew dynamics: in reality, implied volatility rises as spot falls. A sticky strike assumption (each strike keeps its volatility) and a sticky moneyness assumption (volatility moves with spot) give different profiles. Neither is right; both are assumptions.

5.9.6 Comparing the two

Interpolation Root search
Question answered where cumulative gamma at today’s spot changes sign spot level where total gamma would be zero
Cost one pass grid passes + a few refinement passes
Sensitivity dominated by near-the-money strikes captures strikes coming into play as spot moves
Failure mode can report a “flip” that is really just the put/call boundary multiple roots, or none

The interpolated version often lands near where call-dominated strikes give way to put-dominated strikes, which is a different concept. When the two methods disagree a lot, gamma is usually spread out and the “level” is fuzzy, not sharp. I treat the disagreement itself as information about how much weight the level deserves.

5.9.7 Engineering notes

  • Vectorise the gamma computation across contracts and evaluate the grid with flat arrays; no per-contract object allocation inside the loop.
  • Cache what does not depend on spot: ln⁡K\ln K, σT\sigma\sqrt T, e−qTe^{-qT}, the weights.
  • Make it deterministic: fixed grid, fixed tolerance, fixed tie-breaking rule. Then a regression test can compare outputs exactly.
  • Record which method produced a level. A dashboard showing “zero gamma” without saying how it was computed hides the most important caveat.

5.9.8 Summary

  • Interpolation finds where the cumulative strike sum at today’s spot crosses zero: cheap, one pass.
  • Root search finds the spot where recomputed total gamma is zero: grid scan plus Brent’s method.
  • Report a stated rule for multiple roots, and “none in range” when there is no root.
  • Large disagreement between methods means the level is fuzzy.

Exercises

  1. (Interpolate) Cumulative GEX is −30 at K = 95 and +20 at K = 100. Where is the interpolated flip? (Answer: 95 + 5 × 30/50 = 98.)
  2. (Grid) Why can a coarse grid miss two roots that sit close together?
  3. (Build) Implement the scan-then-Brent search on the toy chain of Figure 5.9.1. Move the call open interest further from spot. Do the methods drift apart?
  4. (Think) How would a sticky-moneyness assumption change G(S)G(S) compared with sticky strike?

Further reading

  • R. P. Brent (1973), Algorithms for Minimization without Derivatives.
  • W. H. Press et al., Numerical Recipes, chapter on root finding and bracketing.
  • E. Derman (1999), “Regimes of Volatility,” Risk (sticky strike versus sticky delta).

— Tariq

Chapter 5.10 — Gamma Walls: What They Are, How to Find Them, and Why They Move

Subtitle: The strikes with the most gamma get treated like concrete. They are closer to sandbags.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Find the positive and negative gamma walls in a GEX profile. 2. Explain why gamma concentrates at some strikes and how time and volatility reshape that concentration. 3. List the pitfalls that make walls fragile, and describe a better mental model.

You need: Chapters 5.1 and 5.9.

5.10.1 Simple maths, heavy interpretation

A gamma wall is the strike with the largest concentration of gamma exposure. People draw walls on charts as support and resistance. When I wrote the code that finds them, I was struck by how simple the computation is and how much interpretation gets stacked on top.

5.10.2 The computation

Given a per-strike profile,

GEXK=∑typesK,typeΓK,typewK,type⋅m⋅S2⋅0.01 \text{GEX}_K = \sum_{\text{type}} s_{K,\text{type}}\,\Gamma_{K,\text{type}}\,w_{K,\text{type}}\cdot m\cdot S^2\cdot 0.01

the walls are just the extremes:

Definition (walls). - Positive wall: arg⁡max⁡KGEXK\arg\max_K \text{GEX}_K, the strike with the largest positive (call-side, under the usual convention) exposure. - Negative wall: arg⁡min⁡KGEXK\arg\min_K \text{GEX}_K, the strike with the largest negative (put-side) exposure.

(arg⁡max\arg\max means “the strike at which the maximum occurs”.) My calculators report both, plus the zero-gamma level between them. That is the whole algorithm. Everything interesting is in the inputs and the interpretation.

5.10.3 Why gamma concentrates

One option’s gamma peaks near the money and decays like a Gaussian (bell curve) in log-moneyness, with width proportional to σT\sigma\sqrt{T}:

Γ∝φ(d1)SσT,d1≈ln⁡(S/K)σT \Gamma \propto \frac{\varphi(d_1)}{S\sigma\sqrt T}, \qquad d_1 \approx \frac{\ln(S/K)}{\sigma\sqrt T}

So a strike’s gamma exposure is roughly “how much open interest sits there” times “how close it is to spot, in standard deviations”. Two forces create walls:

  1. Open interest clusters at round numbers. Strikes at multiples of 25, 50 or 100 index points attract more interest. They are focal points for hedgers and structured products.
  2. Short-dated options have narrow, tall gamma. As T shrinks, the bell narrows and its peak rises. Near expiry, a big strike close to spot can dominate the whole profile.

Figure 5.10.1 — Near expiry, gamma is a spike. Gamma of one contract at each strike, spot 100, σ = 20%, r = q = 0, at 30 days, 5 days and 6 hours (illustrative). At 30 days, strikes ±10 points away still matter. At 6 hours, only strikes within about a point of spot carry gamma, and their peak is about ten times the 30-day peak.

5.10.4 The mechanical story

If dealers are long gamma at a strike (the usual assumption for call-heavy strikes above spot): as spot approaches the strike their delta rises and they sell to rebalance; as it falls away, they buy. That is mean-reverting hedging concentrated near the strike, the basis of “pinning”.

If they are short gamma at a strike (put-heavy strikes below spot, under the usual assumption), hedging amplifies moves: they sell as price falls towards it.

Hence the folklore: positive walls act as magnets or ceilings, negative walls as accelerants.

5.10.5 Why walls move

A wall is not a fixed object. It depends on:

Input How it moves the wall
Spot Recompute gamma at another spot and the same open interest gives a different profile. Strikes far away gain gamma as price approaches.
Time As expiry nears, the profile sharpens. Same-day walls in the morning can look very different by the afternoon.
Implied volatility Higher volatility widens every strike’s bell and lowers its peak. A volatility spike can make a sharp wall disappear without one contract changing hands.
Positions Open interest updates once a day. Same-day options trade intraday and may never appear in OI. A wall built on yesterday’s OI misses everything opened today; hence my separate same-day view weighted by volume.

Figure 5.10.2 — A volatility rise flattens a wall without any trading. One block of open interest at strike 105, 5 days to expiry, its GEX plotted against spot at 15% (blue) and 30% (orange) implied volatility. Doubling volatility halves the peak and doubles the width. The contracts are identical; only the input changed.

5.10.6 Pitfalls

Strike selection. Most calculators, mine included, request a window of strikes centred on spot to keep data requests manageable. A wall outside that window is invisible. If the window is too narrow, the “largest” wall is just the edge of what you fetched. Check whether a reported wall is an interior maximum or a boundary artefact.

Single-strike noise. One stale quote with a wrong implied volatility can create a spike at one strike. Quote validation matters more for walls than for totals, because walls are argmax operations, and argmax is fragile.

Calls and puts at the same strike. Under the signed convention, call and put gamma at the same strike partly cancel. A strike with huge activity on both sides can show a small net. Look at gross and net separately.

The sign assumption. If customers are selling calls (for income) rather than buying them, the call-side “positive wall” is really a dealer short-gamma zone. The algorithm cannot tell.

5.10.7 A better mental model

I think of walls less as levels and more as regions of concentrated hedging sensitivity. Width matters as much as location. A wall one strike tall and isolated is different from a broad plateau of exposure. Plotting the full profile, not just the argmax, makes that obvious.

It also helps to ask a counterfactual: how often does price behave the same way at a strike that is not a wall?
