Round-number strikes attract open interest and order flow for reasons unrelated to hedging. Separating those effects needs an event study with a proper null (Chapter 5.14), not a chart with a horizontal line.

5.10.8 Engineering notes

  • Finding walls from a profile is O(n)O(n) in strikes; the cost is all in building the profile.
  • Break ties deterministically (for example, the strike nearest spot wins).
  • Store the profile, not just the walls. When someone asks “why did the wall jump?”, the profile answers it.

5.10.9 Summary

  • Walls are the argmax and argmin of the per-strike GEX profile.
  • Gamma concentrates where open interest clusters and where short-dated strikes sit near spot.
  • Walls move with spot, time, implied volatility and new positions, and are fragile to bad quotes and window edges.
  • Treat them as regions, plot the full profile, and test any wall story against a null.

Exercises

  1. (Scale) By the σT\sigma\sqrt T rule, how much narrower is a strike’s gamma bell at 1 day than at 25 days, same volatility? (Answer: 25=5\sqrt{25} = 5 times narrower.)
  2. (Fragility) Why is an argmax more sensitive to one bad quote than a sum?
  3. (Think) A strike has heavy call and put open interest. Why might its net GEX be small, and what would a gross view show?
  4. (Design) How would you detect that a reported wall sits at the edge of your fetched strike window?

Further reading

  • S. X. Ni, N. D. Pearson and A. M. Poteshman (2005), “Stock Price Clustering on Option Expiration Dates,” Journal of Financial Economics.
  • M. Avellaneda and M. D. Lipkin (2003), “A Market-Induced Mechanism for Stock Pinning,” Quantitative Finance.
  • N. N. Taleb, Dynamic Hedging.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.11 — 0DTE: Volume-Weighted Versus Open-Interest-Weighted Views

Subtitle: Open interest cannot see same-day options. Volume can, but it cannot see direction. Here is how I keep both honest.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain exactly what open interest and volume count, and what each misses. 2. Build a volume-weighted same-day profile and an OI-weighted multi-expiry profile, and say why they must stay separate. 3. Explain why assigning a dealer sign to volume is a stronger assumption than assigning it to open interest.

You need: Chapters 5.1 and 5.5.

5.11.1 Why two views

Every dealer-exposure calculation multiplies a Greek by a quantity. For years the quantity was open interest, and that was fine when most index options lived for weeks.

Same-day options (0DTE) broke that assumption. A large share of index option volume now opens and closes within a single session, and open interest never records it. So my options engine computes two views side by side: same-day options weighted by volume, and the longer-dated complex weighted by open interest. This chapter explains why, and what each view gets wrong.

5.11.2 How open interest works

Definition (open interest). The number of contracts outstanding at the end of the previous day, as reported by the clearing house.

It changes only when:

  • a trade opens a new position on both sides: +1,
  • a trade closes positions on both sides: −1,
  • one side opens and the other closes: unchanged.

Two consequences:

  1. It is a daily snapshot. Intraday, you are looking at yesterday’s number.
  2. A contract listed today starts with zero open interest. Same-day options listed this morning, or opened and closed today, contribute nothing.

So for a same-day option, an OI-weighted gamma profile measures only positions carried over from earlier days, which may be a small fraction of the day’s activity.

5.11.3 What volume measures

Definition (volume). The number of contracts traded today.

It sees same-day activity immediately. But:

  • No direction. Bought to open, sold to close, sold to open: each adds one. Volume is gross activity, not net position.
  • Round trips count twice. A position opened at 10:00 and closed at 11:00 adds two to volume and zero to end-of-day positioning.
  • No memory. It resets every day.

Figure 5.11.1 — Volume counts activity; open interest counts what is left. Three example trades in one same-day contract. Trade A opens and closes within the hour: volume +2, open interest unchanged. Trade B opens and is held: +1 to both. Trade C has one side opening and one side closing: volume +1, open interest unchanged. The day ends with volume 4 and open interest up 1, and even that +1 is only published for the next day.

So weighting gamma by volume answers a different question: “where is today’s activity concentrated, in gamma terms?”, not “how much gamma is outstanding?”

5.11.4 The two views

For the nearest expiry, my engine computes

GEXKvol=∑typesΓKVK⋅m⋅S2⋅0.01 \text{GEX}^{\text{vol}}_K = \sum_{\text{type}} s\,\Gamma_K\,V_K\cdot m\cdot S^2\cdot 0.01

with VKV_K the day’s volume, and for a window of longer expiries,

GEXKOI=∑expiries∑typesΓK,eOIK,e⋅m⋅S2⋅0.01 \text{GEX}^{\text{OI}}_K = \sum_{\text{expiries}}\sum_{\text{type}} s\,\Gamma_{K,e}\,OI_{K,e}\cdot m\cdot S^2\cdot 0.01

They are kept separate on purpose. Adding them would mix a gross flow measure with a net stock measure, and the sum would mean nothing.

5.11.5 Why the same-day view is so different

Same-day gamma is extreme. With T measured in hours,

ΓATM≈1Sσ2πT \Gamma_{ATM} \approx \frac{1}{S\sigma\sqrt{2\pi T}}

so near-the-money same-day options carry far more gamma per contract than longer-dated ones. Modest volume at one strike can produce an exposure larger than the whole open-interest complex. The profile is also narrow: a few strikes around spot carry nearly all of it.

So the same-day view is highly sensitive to:

  • Time to expiry, to the minute. A sloppy T distorts it badly (Chapter 5.5).
  • Spot. A small move changes which strikes are near the money and reshapes the profile.
  • Quote quality at the handful of strikes that matter.

5.11.6 The sign problem gets worse

With open interest, the standard assumption (customers long puts, short calls, dealers on the other side) is crude but at least rests on a long-run pattern. With same-day volume, the population is different: retail and systematic traders buying cheap wings, market makers trading with each other, spreads and condors where both sides appear at once. Assigning a dealer sign to volume is a stronger assumption than assigning one to open interest.

Some data vendors classify each trade as buyer- or seller-initiated by comparing the trade price with the bid and ask (the Lee–Ready approach and its descendants). That helps, but classification at the quote is noisy for options with wide spreads and for multi-leg trades. Without trade-level classification, the honest label for a volume-weighted profile is “activity-weighted”, not “dealer positioning”.

5.11.7 Practical guidance

  1. Never mix the two in one number. Show them side by side with clear labels.
  2. State the time of the snapshot. A volume profile at 10:00 and one at 15:00 effectively describe different days.
  3. Record cumulative volume, not differences between snapshots, unless you have built a differencing pipeline on purpose. Vendors report cumulative daily volume; differencing it is error-prone around resets and missing snapshots.
  4. Track what you dropped. Same-day chains have many zero-bid wings. Excluding them is right, but count them.
  5. Expect disagreement. The two views often point at different strikes. That is not a bug; they measure different things.

5.11.8 What I’d tell another engineer

Answers Lag Direction
Open interest “What is outstanding?” one day none
Volume “What is active?” real time none

Neither answers “who must hedge, and how much?”, which is the question everyone actually wants answered. Build both, label both, treat both as context, and test any claim against a null before believing it.

5.11.9 Summary

  • Open interest is yesterday’s net count and cannot see same-day positions.
  • Volume sees today’s activity but has no direction and double-counts round trips.
  • Keep a volume-weighted same-day view and an OI-weighted longer-dated view, never summed.
  • Without trade signing, a volume profile is “activity-weighted”, not dealer positioning.

Exercises

  1. (Count) A trader buys 10 same-day calls to open at 10:00 from a market maker who is also opening, and sells them at 14:00 to another trader who is opening. What are the day’s volume and open-interest change? (Answer: volume 20; open interest +10, since the second trade is a close on one side and an open on the other.)
  2. (Units) Why is GEXvol+GEXOI\text{GEX}^{\text{vol}} + \text{GEX}^{\text{OI}} meaningless?
  3. (Think) Why does Lee–Ready classification struggle with multi-leg option trades?
  4. (Design) Your vendor sends cumulative volume every minute, but two snapshots are missing. What goes wrong if you difference them?

Further reading

  • C. M. C. Lee and M. J. Ready (1991), “Inferring Trade Direction from Intraday Data,” Journal of Finance.
  • F. M. Bandi, N. Fusari and R. Renò (2023), “0DTE Option Pricing,” working paper.
  • J. Pan and A. M. Poteshman (2006), “The Information in Option Volume for Future Stock Prices,” Review of Financial Studies.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.12 — The Put/Call Ratio and Its Pitfalls

Subtitle: The oldest sentiment indicator in options is a ratio of two counts. Almost every choice in computing it changes what it means.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Write down four different put/call ratios and say which question each answers. 2. Recognise eight pitfalls, from universe choice to small denominators. 3. Work with the ratio in logs and shrink small-sample ratios sensibly.

You need: Chapters 5.2 (delta) and 5.11 (volume and open interest).

5.12.1 One name, many numbers

The put/call ratio (PCR) is the first options statistic most people meet. Divide put activity by call activity: a high ratio means fear, a low one greed, and the contrarian reading flips both.

My options engine computes one as a side product of every chain snapshot. Building it showed me how many different numbers hide behind that one name.

5.12.2 The definitions

Definitions. With V = volume, OI = open interest, p = option price, superscripts P and C for puts and calls: PCRvol=∑KVKP∑KVKC,PCROI=∑KOIKP∑KOIKC \text{PCR}_{\text{vol}} = \frac{\sum_K V^{P}_K}{\sum_K V^{C}_K}, \qquad \text{PCR}_{\text{OI}} = \frac{\sum_K OI^{P}_K}{\sum_K OI^{C}_K} PCR$=∑KVKPpKP∑KVKCpKC,PCRΔ=∑KVKP|ΔKP|∑KVKCΔKC \text{PCR}_{\$} = \frac{\sum_K V^{P}_K\,p^{P}_K}{\sum_K V^{C}_K\,p^{C}_K}, \qquad \text{PCR}_{\Delta} = \frac{\sum_K V^{P}_K\,|\Delta^{P}_K|}{\sum_K V^{C}_K\,\Delta^{C}_K}

Ratio Question it answers
Volume how many contracts traded
Open interest how much open exposure
Dollar-weighted how much premium
Delta-weighted how much directional exposure

They can move in opposite directions on the same day.

5.12.3 Pitfall 1: universe

Equity-only, index-only and total ratios behave differently. Index options are dominated by hedgers who buy puts routinely, so their ratio sits structurally higher than equity options, which have more speculative call buying. Comparing ratios across universes, or across time when the mix changes, mixes regimes.

The same applies within a chain. A ratio over a narrow strike window around spot (what a calculator that fetches only nearby strikes produces) is not the same statistic as one over the whole chain. The far wings are full of cheap puts bought as crash protection.

5.12.4 Pitfall 2: counting contracts ignores size

A far out-of-the-money put costing a few cents and an at-the-money call costing several dollars each count as one. The contract-count ratio is dominated by cheap wings. Dollar- or delta-weighting fixes that, at the price of model inputs: a delta-weighted ratio depends on your implied volatility and time to expiry, with all the fragility of Chapters 5.3–5.5.

5.12.5 Pitfall 3: direction is unknown

Volume counts trades, not buyers. A put bought for protection and a put sold for income both add to put volume. A high ratio could mean investors are buying puts (fearful) or selling them (confident enough to write insurance). Without signing each trade, a ratio of volumes is a ratio of activity, not sentiment.

5.12.6 Pitfall 4: spreads and multi-leg trades

A put spread is two put trades. A risk reversal is one put and one call. A collar is a long put and a short call against stock. Multi-leg strategies inflate both sides in ways that reflect structure, not sentiment. Same-day options are especially heavy in spreads and condors.

5.12.7 Pitfall 5: 0DTE changes the base rate

As same-day options have grown into a large share of index volume, the mix of activity has shifted. A long history of daily put/call ratios now straddles a structural break. A level that meant “extreme” in one era may be ordinary in another. Any statistical use must handle that non-stationarity: for example, measure the ratio against a rolling distribution instead of a fixed level, and check whether the break shows up in your sample.

5.12.8 Pitfall 6: bounded below, unbounded above

A ratio of two positive numbers is skewed. Going from 0.5 to 1 is the same proportional change as going from 1 to 2, but on a linear chart the second looks twice as big. Work in logs:

ln⁡PCR=ln⁡∑VP−ln⁡∑VC \ln \text{PCR} = \ln \sum V^P - \ln \sum V^C

This is symmetric, adds across components and averages well. Averaging raw ratios over time is biased upward by Jensen’s inequality (the average of a convex function exceeds the function of the average); averaging log ratios is not.

Figure 5.12.1 — On a log scale, equal proportional moves look equal. Top: a linear axis, where 0.5→1 (blue) looks half the size of 1→2 (orange). Bottom: a log axis, where both doublings have the same length. Fear and greed of equal size should look equal; only the log scale draws them that way.

5.12.9 Pitfall 7: division by small numbers

Early in the session, or in thin chains, the denominator can be tiny. A handful of call trades makes the ratio swing wildly. Report the counts alongside the ratio, and either require a minimum denominator or use a smoothed estimator:

PCR̂=∑VP+α∑VC+α \widehat{\text{PCR}} = \frac{\sum V^P + \alpha}{\sum V^C + \alpha}

which shrinks small-sample ratios towards one (α is a small positive constant you choose and document).

Whatever you do, document it. A ratio that silently returns a default when the denominator is zero will one day mislead you. One of my calculators returns a neutral value on failure, and the snapshot carries an error field next to it. That field matters more than the number: anything reading the ratio must check it first.

5.12.10 Pitfall 8: the contrarian story is a hypothesis

“Extreme fear is bullish” is a testable claim, and the evidence is mixed and period-dependent. Treat it as a hypothesis, specify it before looking, and test it with an event study against a proper baseline (Chapter 5.14). Most apparent predictability in sentiment ratios disappears once you account for overlapping windows and the number of thresholds tried.

5.12.11 What I keep

  • Contract-count ratios for both volume and open interest, per expiry group, from the same snapshots that feed the Greek calculations, so they agree with everything else.
  • The raw sums, not just the ratio.
  • The result as one descriptive statistic among many, not a signal.

5.12.12 Summary

  • “Put/call ratio” names at least four statistics: volume, open interest, dollar and delta weighted.
  • Universe, wing-heavy counting, unknown direction, multi-leg trades and the 0DTE break all change its meaning.
  • Use logs; guard small denominators and expose failures explicitly.
  • The contrarian reading is a hypothesis to test, not a rule.

Exercises

  1. (Logs) Ratios on three days are 0.5, 1 and 2. Compare the plain average with the average in logs. (Answer: plain 1.17; log average 0, i.e. a geometric mean of 1.)
  2. (Shrink) With 3 puts, 1 call and α = 5, what is the smoothed ratio? What is the raw one?
  3. (Think) Why can a heavy day of put selling raise the volume put/call ratio?
  4. (Design) How would you test whether the 0DTE era changed the distribution of your ratio?

Further reading

  • J. Pan and A. M. Poteshman (2006), “The Information in Option Volume for Future Stock Prices,” Review of Financial Studies.
  • R. S. Billingsley and D. M. Chance (1988), “Put–Call Ratios and Market Timing Effectiveness,” Journal of Portfolio Management.
  • D. Easley, M. O’Hara and P. S. Srinivas (1998), “Option Volume and Stock Prices: Evidence on Where Informed Traders Trade,” Journal of Finance.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.13 — The Volatility Complex: VIX, VVIX, VXN and SKEW

Subtitle: Four indices, four different questions about the options market. What each one actually computes.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain how VIX turns a strip of option prices into a “model-free” 30-day implied variance, and why it weights strikes by 1/K21/K^2. 2. Say what VXN, VVIX and SKEW change in that recipe. 3. List the engineering traps in collecting and comparing these indices.

You need: Chapter 5.2 (forwards, risk-neutral pricing), and the idea of moments of a distribution (variance, skewness).

5.13.1 Why look inside

Next to the chains, my data pipeline streams a handful of volatility indices. They are cheap to collect and often quoted. Before treating any of them as context, I wanted to know exactly what each one measures. This chapter builds each from first principles.

5.13.2 VIX: model-free implied variance

VIX is not the implied volatility of any one option. It estimates the 30-day risk-neutral expected variance of the S&P 500, computed from a strip of out-of-the-money options.

The theory (Demeterfi, Derman, Kamal and Zou; Britten-Jones and Neuberger) says the fair strike of a variance swap can be replicated by a continuum of options weighted by 1/K21/K^2:

Result (variance from option prices). σ2=2T∫0∞erTQ(K)K2dK−1T(FK0−1)2 \sigma^2 = \frac{2}{T}\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{rT}\,Q(K)}{K^2}\,dK - \frac{1}{T}\left(\frac{F}{K_0}-1\right)^2 Q(K)Q(K) is the out-of-the-money option price at strike K (puts below the forward, calls above), F is the forward and K0K_0 the first strike below it.

The published methodology turns the integral into a sum:

σ2=2T∑iΔKiKi2erTQ(Ki)−1T(FK0−1)2 \sigma^2 = \frac{2}{T}\sum_i \frac{\Delta K_i}{K_i^2}e^{rT}Q(K_i) - \frac{1}{T}\left(\frac{F}{K_0}-1\right)^2

computes it for two expiries bracketing 30 days, interpolates to exactly 30 days in variance, and reports 100σ2100\sqrt{\sigma^2}.

Why 1/K21/K^2? The payoff of a log contract, ln⁡(ST/F)\ln(S_T/F), can be built from options with exactly that weighting. The expected log return under the risk-neutral measure is linked to expected variance. That is what makes VIX “model-free”: no Black–Scholes assumption, only option prices.

Figure 5.13.1 — The 1/K21/K^2 weight leans on low strikes. Weight per unit strike relative to the weight at the forward (F = 100, illustrative). Puts are used below F (left shading), calls above (right). A put at 60 counts about 2.8 times as much per dollar of price as an option at the forward; a call at 140 about half as much.

Two practical consequences:

  • Wing sensitivity. The weight puts heavy emphasis on low-strike puts. Their prices drive a lot of VIX.
  • Truncation. The sum stops where consecutive zero bids appear. When the wings get cheaper or wider, the strip changes length, and VIX changes for partly mechanical reasons.

5.13.3 VXN: the same recipe on the Nasdaq-100

VXN applies the same method to Nasdaq-100 options. The Nasdaq-100 is more concentrated and historically more volatile, so VXN generally sits above VIX. The spread between them is a crude measure of how much extra risk the market prices into large technology names relative to the broad index. As with any spread of two indices, check that both come from matching timestamps before subtracting.

5.13.4 VVIX: the volatility of volatility

VVIX applies the VIX method to options on VIX itself. It estimates the 30-day expected volatility of the VIX index: the market price of uncertainty about future uncertainty.

Two subtleties:

  • The underlying is a forward. VIX options are priced off VIX futures, not spot VIX, because spot VIX cannot be traded. Each VIX option expiry has its own forward.
  • Different dynamics. VIX is mean-reverting and right-skewed. The VIX options surface usually has an upward skew (calls richer than puts), the opposite of equity indices. VVIX rising means the market is paying more for protection against volatility spikes.

5.13.5 SKEW: the price of tail risk

SKEW tries to measure the risk-neutral skewness of 30-day S&P 500 returns. Following Bakshi, Kapadia and Madan, the risk-neutral moments of the log return can be computed from option prices with different weighting functions, just as VIX computes the second moment.

Definition. 𝒮=𝔼ℚ[(R−μ)3](𝔼ℚ[(R−μ)2])3/2,SKEW=100−10𝒮 \mathcal S = \frac{\mathbb E^{\mathbb Q}[(R - \mu)^3]}{\left(\mathbb E^{\mathbb Q}[(R-\mu)^2]\right)^{3/2}}, \qquad \text{SKEW} = 100 - 10\,\mathcal S

Equity index skewness is negative, so SKEW sits above 100. Higher values mean more negative skew: far out-of-the-money puts are expensive relative to the rest of the distribution.

SKEW is noisy. Third moments depend heavily on the far wings, which are thinly traded and wide. It also has a well-known weak relationship with later crashes, which argues for treating it as a description of option prices, not a forecast.

5.13.6 Reading them together

Index Underlying Moment
VIX S&P 500 options 2nd (variance)
VXN Nasdaq-100 options 2nd (variance)
VVIX VIX options 2nd moment of VIX
SKEW S&P 500 options 3rd (skewness)

None of them measures realised volatility. All are risk-neutral, so they embed risk premia. Implied variance usually exceeds later realised variance on average (the variance risk premium), so VIX is a biased forecast of realised volatility by construction.

5.13.7 Engineering notes

  • Timestamps. These indices are calculated and published on their own schedule. Aligning them with tick data needs care about publication latency, and about the fact that some are only calculated during certain hours.
  • Gaps and stale values. A feed that stops updating often keeps serving the last value. Track the age of each value, not just the value.
  • Don’t recompute and call it the index. Reimplementing the VIX formula on your own chain snapshot is a good exercise, but the result is “my VIX-style estimate”, not VIX. Strike selection, quote filters and interpolation rules all differ.

5.13.8 Summary

  • VIX is 30-day risk-neutral variance from a 1/K21/K^2-weighted strip of OTM options, reported as 100σ2100\sqrt{\sigma^2}.
  • VXN repeats it on the Nasdaq-100; VVIX on VIX options (priced off futures); SKEW estimates the third moment.
  • All are risk-neutral and carry risk premia; none measures realised volatility.
  • Track timestamps and value age; a home-made VIX-style number is not VIX.

Exercises

  1. (Weights) Relative to the forward F = 100, what weight does a strike at 80 get? (Answer: (100/80)2≈1.56(100/80)^2 \approx 1.56.)
  2. (Units) A 30-day variance of 0.04 is reported as what VIX value? (Answer: 1000.04=20100\sqrt{0.04} = 20.)
  3. (Think) Why does the VIX option surface usually skew upward while S&P 500 options skew downward?
  4. (Compute) If 𝒮=−2.5\mathcal S = -2.5, what is SKEW?

Further reading

  • Cboe, VIX White Paper (methodology document).
  • K. Demeterfi, E. Derman, M. Kamal and J. Zou (1999), “More Than You Ever Wanted to Know About Volatility Swaps,” Goldman Sachs Quantitative Strategies.
  • G. Bakshi, N. Kapadia and D. Madan (2003), “Stock Return Characteristics, Skew Laws, and the Differential Pricing of Individual Equity Options,” Review of Financial Studies.
  • P. Carr and L. Wu (2009), “Variance Risk Premiums,” Review of Financial Studies.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.14 — Event Studies for Dealer Positioning: Testing the Stories

Subtitle: “Price stalls at the gamma wall” is a claim. Here is the statistical machinery for checking it.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Set up an event study: a causal event, a window, an outcome and a counterfactual. 2. Build counterfactuals for intraday positioning events (matched controls, placebos, null simulation). 3. Correct for volatility, overlapping windows, multiple testing and publication lags.

You need: Chapters 5.1–5.10, a t-statistic, and the null-model idea from Chapter 6.1.

5.14.1 Stories are cheap

Every metric in this part (gamma exposure, walls, zero gamma, vanna, charm) comes with a story about what price should do. Stories are cheap.

The event study is the standard tool for asking whether price really behaves differently around a defined event than it would have anyway. I use it as the default test for anything dealer-positioning related. This chapter explains the method and the ways it lies to you if you are careless.

5.14.2 The classic setup

The event study comes from corporate finance (Fama, Fisher, Jensen and Roll, 1969), where the event is an earnings announcement or a stock split. The structure carries over directly:

  1. Define the event precisely and causally: knowable at time t0t_0 using only information available at t0t_0. For example: “price comes within some distance of the largest positive-gamma strike, computed from the most recent snapshot published before t0t_0”.
  2. Define the window: a pre-event and a post-event window, measured in time, trades or volume.
  3. Define the outcome: return, absolute return, realised variance, time to reach a level, whatever the story predicts.
  4. Define the counterfactual: what the outcome would have been without the event.

Definition (abnormal outcome and test statistic). ARi=Yi−𝔼[Yi∣no event] AR_i = Y_i - \mathbb E[Y_i \mid \text{no event}] AR¯=1N∑i=1NARi,t=AR¯ŝ/N \overline{AR} = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N AR_i, \qquad t = \frac{\overline{AR}}{\hat s/\sqrt N}

The whole difficulty is in step 4 and in the assumptions behind ŝ\hat s (the estimated standard deviation).

Figure 5.14.1 — An event study is a pipeline, and step 4 is the hard part. Steps 1–4 define what is measured and what it is compared with; step 5 computes the abnormal outcome with day-clustered errors. The green box lists what must hold before a result is believed. This is a generic method diagram, not a description of any specific study.

5.14.3 The counterfactual is everything

For stock events, the counterfactual is usually a market model. For intraday positioning events it must be built from the same instrument at comparable times. Reasonable choices:

  • Matched controls. For each event, pick non-event moments with the same time of day, similar recent volatility and similar distance to some round-number strike. Compare outcomes.
  • Placebo levels. Re-run the study with the event defined on a level that should mean nothing: the wall shifted by a random offset, or a strike chosen by a rule unrelated to positioning. If the “effect” shows up at placebo levels too, it is not about gamma.
  • Null-model simulation. Generate price paths from a model without the mechanism (for instance, a random walk matched to realised volatility) and run the identical pipeline on them. This is the discipline of the Renko random-walk chapter: the null shows what the method produces when there is nothing to find.

Round numbers are the trap. Walls tend to sit at round strikes, and round numbers attract order flow, stop orders and limit orders for reasons unrelated to options. A study comparing “near a wall” with “anywhere” will find an effect that is really a round-number effect. Matching on round-number proximity is mandatory.

5.14.4 Volatility conditioning

Absolute returns and realised variance depend strongly on time of day (the intraday U-shape) and persist strongly. An event that tends to happen in quiet afternoons will show smaller post-event moves for that reason alone.

  • Normalise outcomes by a causal volatility estimate available at t0t_0, and match on time of day.
  • Never normalise with a volatility estimate that includes the post-event window.

5.14.5 Overlapping windows inflate significance

If events occur close together, their post-event windows overlap and the ARiAR_i are not independent. The naive standard error ŝ/N\hat s/\sqrt N is then far too small. Options:

  • Thin events so windows do not overlap (and say how many were dropped).
  • Cluster standard errors by day, since events on the same day share a regime.
  • Use a block bootstrap over days.

Day-level clustering is the default I trust most for intraday studies. A study with many events on a few days has an effective sample size close to the number of days, not the number of events.

Figure 5.14.2 — Many events on few days is a small sample. A schematic: 12 events (blue dots) with their post-event windows (orange bars) spread over 4 days. Events on the same day share conditions and their windows overlap, so the study holds closer to 4 independent observations than to 12.

5.14.6 Multiple testing

There are many ways to define a wall event: distances, windows, outcomes, expiry groups, open interest or volume weighting. Try twenty combinations and one will clear a usual significance threshold by chance. The defences:

  • Specify the hypothesis and the event definition before looking at outcomes.
  • Count every variant you tried, and report that count.
  • Adjust for it: Bonferroni is conservative; Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate; for strategy-like searches, the deflated Sharpe ratio of Bailey and López de Prado is built for exactly this.
  • Hold out a period you never touch until the definition is frozen.

5.14.7 Lookahead hides in the data

Positioning data has publication lags. Open interest is published after the close and applies to the next day. A gamma profile built with today’s open interest is not knowable this morning. The event definition must use the snapshot that was actually available at t0t_0, with its real timestamp. This is the single most common way dealer-positioning backtests overstate what was knowable.

5.14.8 What a good result looks like

A credible event-study result has:

  • an event definition fixed in advance and computable causally,
  • a matched or simulated null that the effect clearly exceeds,
  • placebo tests that show no effect,
  • standard errors robust to clustering and overlap,
  • an honest count of variants tried,
  • stability across sub-periods.

Most stories fail at least one of those. That is not a failure of the method; it is the method doing its job.

5.14.9 Summary

  • Event, window, outcome, counterfactual: the counterfactual decides everything.
  • Use matched controls (including round-number proximity), placebo levels and null simulations.
  • Normalise by causal volatility; cluster by day; count and correct for every variant.
  • Use only data that was published before t0t_0.

Exercises

  1. (Effective N) 300 events fall on 15 days, highly correlated within each day. Roughly what effective sample size should you assume? (Answer: closer to 15 than to 300.)
  2. (Placebo) Design a placebo test for “price stalls near the largest positive-gamma strike”.
  3. (Multiple testing) You tried 20 variants. Under Bonferroni, what per-test significance level keeps the overall level at 5%?
  4. (Lookahead) Why is a gamma profile using today’s end-of-day open interest a lookahead error for a morning event?

Further reading

  • E. F. Fama, L. Fisher, M. C. Jensen and R. Roll (1969), “The Adjustment of Stock Prices to New Information,” International Economic Review.
  • A. C. MacKinlay (1997), “Event Studies in Economics and Finance,” Journal of Economic Literature.
  • D. H. Bailey and M. López de Prado (2014), “The Deflated Sharpe Ratio,” Journal of Portfolio Management.
  • C. R. Harvey, Y. Liu and H. Zhu (2016), “…and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns,” Review of Financial Studies.

— Tariq

Chapter 5.15 — Data Plumbing for Option Chains: What Broker APIs Give You and What They Don’t

Subtitle: The maths of the Greeks fits on a page. Getting clean, synchronised chain data into it took most of the work.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compare streaming-socket and REST-snapshot broker APIs and how each fails. 2. Recognise seven failure modes between “the broker has the data” and “my calculator has trustworthy inputs”. 3. Apply a five-question checklist to every chain snapshot.

You need: Chapters 5.3–5.5. No API experience required.

5.15.1 The real work

I have pulled option chains from two retail-broker APIs this year: Interactive Brokers through its socket API, and Schwab through its REST API. The Greek formulas were done in an afternoon. The plumbing took weeks.

This chapter is a general guide to what goes wrong in between. No credentials or endpoints here, just the patterns.

5.15.2 Two API styles

Style How it works Example
Streaming socket A locally running gateway. You qualify each contract (turn symbol, expiry, strike and right into a unique contract ID), then subscribe to its market data. Quotes arrive asynchronously as ticks. Broker-computed Greeks and implied volatilities can arrive as separate tick types. Interactive Brokers
REST snapshot One request returns a whole chain: strikes, bids, asks, volume, open interest and often the broker’s own Greeks. Authentication is OAuth with short-lived access tokens and longer-lived refresh tokens. Schwab

Both work. They fail differently.

Figure 5.15.1 — Every stage should leave a trace. A generic chain pipeline: raw data from a broker API, parsing and validation, an in-house implied volatility solve, Greeks, and a timestamped snapshot. The dashed orange arrows show each stage writing to an audit log: what was requested, returned, dropped (and why), synthesised, and which solves failed. The boxes are generic stages, not a system wiring diagram.

5.15.3 Failure mode 1: rate limits and pacing

Socket APIs cap the number of simultaneous market-data subscriptions and the rate of requests. A full index chain across several expiries can exceed those limits. On the streaming side I select a window of strikes centred on spot for each expiry and request them in batches, pausing between batches so bids and asks have time to fill in.

The trade-off is direct: bigger batches and shorter pauses give fresher snapshots but more missing fields; smaller batches give complete data that is older by the time the last batch arrives.

REST APIs have per-minute request limits. One chain request is cheap, but polling many symbols often adds up. Back off on rate-limit responses instead of retrying immediately.

5.15.4 Failure mode 2: snapshot asynchrony

A chain “snapshot” assembled over several seconds is not a snapshot. If the underlying moves while you collect quotes, early strikes are priced against a different spot from late strikes. For implied volatility this matters: the solver assumes the option price and spot are simultaneous.

Mitigations:

  • Record the underlying price with each option quote, not once per chain.
  • Record the timestamp of each quote, and the spread between the earliest and latest.
  • In fast markets, prefer a REST-style single-request snapshot if the vendor builds it atomically on their side (check whether it does).

5.15.5 Failure mode 3: missing and placeholder values

Chains are full of holes: zero bids on far wings, missing open interest early in the day, NaN Greeks when the vendor’s own solver fails, sentinel values such as −1 for “not available”. Every field needs a parse-and-validate step that turns sentinels into explicit missing values. My calculators have a small numeric coercion function that returns “missing” for anything non-numeric or non-finite, and every downstream step checks for it.

Be careful with fallbacks. When a bid or ask is missing, it is tempting to make one up around the last trade or the mark. That keeps the pipeline running, but the implied volatility is then a function of a synthetic spread. If you do it, flag the row so it can be excluded from anything sensitive, and count how often it happens.

5.15.6 Failure mode 4: whose Greeks?

REST chains often include the broker’s own delta, gamma and implied volatility. They are convenient and usually reasonable, but you do not know the rate, dividend, time convention or quote behind them. Mixing broker Greeks for some contracts with your own for others creates silent inconsistencies.

I compute every Greek myself from the raw quotes and use vendor Greeks only as a cross-check. Large disagreements are a useful alarm for bad inputs on one side or the other.

5.15.7 Failure mode 5: expiries and symbology

Index products have several roots (AM-settled monthlies, PM-settled weeklies and dailies), sometimes on the same underlying with different symbols. ETF options use one root. Futures options have their own multipliers and expiry calendars. Getting “today’s expiry” right means knowing the listing calendar, including holidays.

If today’s expiry is missing from the list the API returns, log it loudly instead of silently falling back to the next one. A profile built on tomorrow’s options but labelled “0DTE” is worse than no profile.

5.15.8 Failure mode 6: authentication lifecycles

OAuth refresh tokens expire. Gateways disconnect overnight and need a re-login. A daemon that runs for weeks must refresh tokens before expiry, detect a dead session, and alert instead of serving stale data.

The worst failure is the quiet one: the process stays up, the last snapshot stays in memory, and dashboards keep showing it. Store the snapshot time with every result and make consumers check its age.

5.15.9 Failure mode 7: the clock

Every timestamp should be UTC internally, converted to exchange time only at the boundaries, using a proper time-zone database. Expiry instants, session boundaries and daylight-saving changes are all places where hard-coded offsets break. Chapter 5.5 covers the time-to-expiry consequences.

5.15.10 A minimal checklist

For every chain snapshot, I want to be able to answer:

  1. When was each quote sampled, and what was spot at that moment?
  2. Which contracts were requested, which were returned, which were dropped, and why?
  3. Which values were synthesised or defaulted?
  4. Which implied volatility solves failed, and for what reason?
  5. How old is this snapshot right now?

If any of those cannot be answered, the Greeks built on the snapshot are unverifiable, however carefully the formulas are written.

5.15.11 Summary

  • Socket APIs stream per-contract ticks under subscription limits; REST APIs return whole chains under request limits and OAuth lifecycles.
  • Record spot and a timestamp with every quote; a slowly assembled chain is not a snapshot.
  • Turn sentinels into explicit missing values; flag and count anything synthesised.
  • Compute Greeks yourself; use vendor Greeks only as a cross-check.
  • Never silently substitute another expiry; make every consumer check snapshot age.

Exercises

  1. (Asynchrony) A chain takes 8 seconds to collect and spot moves 0.1% during that time. Why does this bias implied volatility more for deep in-the-money strikes than for out-of-the-money ones? (Hint: Chapter 5.4’s δσ≈δC/𝒱\delta\sigma \approx \delta C/\mathcal V.)
  2. (Sentinels) List three placeholder values a vendor might send for “no data”, and how you would detect each.
  3. (Design) Write the fields of an audit-log record that answers the five checklist questions.
  4. (Think) Why is a stale snapshot that keeps being served worse than a crash? (Answer: a crash is visible; a stale snapshot looks valid and silently misleads every consumer.)

Further reading

  • Interactive Brokers, TWS API documentation (market data and pacing limitations).
  • Schwab, Trader API documentation (market data and OAuth).
  • IETF RFC 6749, The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework.
  • M. Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, on clocks and time in distributed systems.

— Tariq

Chapter 6.1 — The Random-Walk Null: Why a 67% Renko Hit Rate Can Mean Nothing

Subtitle: Before you celebrate a hit rate, ask what a coin flip would have scored.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain how a Renko chart decides when to draw a new brick. 2. Show, with the gambler’s ruin result, why bricks “continue” about two-thirds of the time even in a market with no edge. 3. Work out the right baseline (the null) for any hit rate before you trust it.

You need: basic probability (what “probability” and “fair coin” mean). No calculus.

6.1.1 The claim

A common forum claim: “After a green Renko brick, the next brick is green about two-thirds of the time.”

It sounds like an edge. This chapter shows it is exactly what you get from pure chance. The reason is not the market. It is the way the bricks are drawn.

6.1.2 How a Renko brick is drawn

A Renko chart ignores time. It only draws a brick when price has moved far enough. Call the brick size b.

The classic rule is not symmetric:

  • To draw another brick in the same direction, price must move one brick (b).
  • To draw a brick in the other direction, price must move two bricks (2b).

Figure 6.1.1 — The brick rule is lopsided. The last brick was green and price sits at its top, P. Price only needs to climb to the green dashed line (one brick up) to print another green brick. To print a red brick it must fall all the way to the orange dashed line, two bricks down. The target above is half as far away as the target below.

Key point: the next brick is a race between a near finish line and a far one. The near one wins more often, even if price moves at random.

6.1.3 Turning it into a probability question

Assume price is a random walk: every small step is up or down with equal chance, like a fair coin. There is no trend and no edge.

Put the current price at 0. Now there are two “finish lines”:

  • +b (one brick up): the next brick is a continuation.
  • −2b (two bricks down): the next brick is a reversal.

Whichever line price touches first decides the brick. Mathematicians call this the gambler’s ruin problem: a gambler with a fair coin stops when they either win a set amount or lose a set amount.

Figure 6.1.2 — Two finish lines, fair steps. Price starts at 0 (blue dot) and takes fair up-or-down steps. The green bar is the continuation line, one brick away. The orange bar is the reversal line, two bricks away. The bottom line gives the chance of reaching the green bar first.

6.1.4 The result

Result (gambler’s ruin, fair walk). If the up line is a distance a away and the down line is a distance c away, the chance of hitting the up line first is

P(up first)=ca+c. P(\text{up first}) = \frac{c}{a + c}.

Why it is true, in one paragraph. With fair steps, the price you expect to end at equals where you start (0). Price ends at either +a or −c. If p is the chance of ending at +a, then the expected end is p·a − (1 − p)·c. Set that equal to 0 and solve: p = c / (a + c).

Apply it to Renko. Here a = b and c = 2b, so

p0=2bb+2b=23≈67%. p_0 = \frac{2b}{b + 2b} = \frac{2}{3} \approx 67\%.

More generally, if a reversal needs r bricks:

p0=r1+r. p_0 = \frac{r}{1 + r}.

We call p₀ the null rate: the continuation rate you get with no edge at all.

6.1.5 Checking the formula by simulation

A formula is easier to trust when you can see it. I simulated a fair random walk, drew Renko bricks on it for reversal sizes r = 1 to 6, and counted how often each brick continued.

Figure 6.1.3 — Theory and simulation agree. The blue line is the formula p₀ = r / (1 + r). The orange dots are the simulated continuation rates, 40,000 bricks for each r. The dashed line at 50% is the “coin flip” benchmark people usually compare against. Every dot sits on the blue line, and only r = 1 (a symmetric rule) gives 50%. Classic Renko (r = 2) gives two-thirds.

Reversal size r Formula r/(1+r) Simulated
1 50.0% 49.8%
2 66.7% 66.7%
3 75.0% 74.6%
4 80.0% 79.9%
5 83.3% 83.3%
6 85.7% 85.6%

Simulation notes: a fair ±1 step walk, brick size 10 steps, fixed random seeds; the generator script is kept with the figures. This is a pure random walk, not market data.

6.1.6 What this means in practice

The useful question is never “is the continuation rate high?” It is: “is it higher than p₀?” And by enough to survive trading costs and a fair number of samples.

In my own research every continuation statistic is tested against p₀, not against 50%. That one change removes a whole family of patterns that only looked meaningful.

The lesson reaches far beyond Renko:

Every trading statistic needs a null model: a clear answer to “what would this number be if there were no edge at all?”

Three everyday examples:

Situation What it looks like What chance alone gives
1-point target, 3-point stop “75% win rate” about 75% on a random walk (same formula: 3/(1+3))
Breakouts on big-range days “breakouts run further” big days move further anyway
Testing 200 settings “the best one is great” the best of 200 looks great by luck; count every trial

6.1.7 Summary

  • Renko continues more easily than it reverses: one brick against two.
  • On a fair random walk that alone gives a continuation rate of r / (1 + r), which is 2/3 for classic Renko.
  • Compare any hit rate with its null, not with 50%.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A Renko variant needs 3 bricks to reverse. What continuation rate does pure chance give? (Answer: 75%.)
  2. (Apply) A strategy uses a 2-point target and a 6-point stop. What win rate would a coin flip give?
  3. (Simulate) Write a short program that flips a fair coin, draws bricks with r = 2, and counts continuations. Do you get close to 2/3 after 10,000 bricks? After 100?
  4. (Think) Why does testing many settings make the best one look better than it is? What would you record to correct for it?

Further reading

  • W. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1, chapter on random walks and ruin problems.
  • D. Bailey and M. López de Prado, “The Deflated Sharpe Ratio” (2014), on correcting for many trials.

— Tariq

Chapter 6.2 — The Kalman Filter from Scratch

Subtitle: Five equations, one idea: blend a prediction with a measurement in proportion to how much you trust each.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Write down the linear Gaussian state-space model and say what each symbol means. 2. Run the predict and update steps of a Kalman filter by hand. 3. Explain the Kalman gain as “the fraction of the surprise you believe”. 4. Name the numerical habits that keep a filter stable in production code.

You need: basic probability (mean, variance, the normal distribution) and matrix multiplication.

6.2.1 Why a filter

A large part of my research engine this year is state estimation: working out a hidden quantity from noisy observations, one tick at a time. The hidden quantity might be a “true” price level, its velocity, or a coefficient that changes over time.

The workhorse for this is the Kalman filter. I had used library versions for years. Writing one from scratch in C#, with no memory allocation in the loop and fully deterministic output, was the first time I really understood it.

6.2.2 The model

The filter assumes a linear Gaussian state-space model: the hidden state moves by a linear rule plus normal (Gaussian) noise, and we see a linear view of it plus more normal noise.

xk=Fxk−1+wk,wk∼𝒩(0,Q) x_k = F x_{k-1} + w_k, \qquad w_k \sim \mathcal N(0, Q)

zk=Hxk+vk,vk∼𝒩(0,R) z_k = H x_k + v_k, \qquad v_k \sim \mathcal N(0, R)

Symbol Meaning
xkx_k the hidden state (say, level and velocity)
FF the transition matrix: how the state evolves
QQ process noise covariance: how much the state can change unexpectedly
zkz_k the observation (a price)
HH maps the state to what we observe
RR measurement noise covariance

The goal is the posterior p(xk∣z1:k)p(x_k \mid z_{1:k}): what we believe about the state after seeing every measurement so far. Under these assumptions it is Gaussian. So it is fully described by a mean x̂k|k\hat x_{k|k} and a covariance Pk|kP_{k|k}.

6.2.3 The two steps

Predict. Push the previous estimate through the dynamics:

x̂k|k−1=Fx̂k−1|k−1,Pk|k−1=FPk−1|k−1F⊤+Q \hat x_{k|k-1} = F\hat x_{k-1|k-1}, \qquad P_{k|k-1} = F P_{k-1|k-1} F^\top + Q

The covariance grows. The transition spreads the uncertainty, and QQ adds fresh uncertainty.

Update. Compare the prediction with the measurement. The innovation (the surprise, also called the residual) and its covariance are

yk=zk−Hx̂k|k−1,Sk=HPk|k−1H⊤+R y_k = z_k - H\hat x_{k|k-1}, \qquad S_k = H P_{k|k-1} H^\top + R

The Kalman gain decides how much of the innovation to accept:

Kk=Pk|k−1H⊤Sk−1 K_k = P_{k|k-1} H^\top S_k^{-1}

and the posterior is

x̂k|k=x̂k|k−1+Kkyk,Pk|k=(I−KkH)Pk|k−1 \hat x_{k|k} = \hat x_{k|k-1} + K_k y_k, \qquad P_{k|k} = (I - K_k H) P_{k|k-1}

That is the entire algorithm.

Figure 6.2.1 — The filter is a two-step loop. The blue box (predict) moves the estimate forward and makes it less certain. The green box (update) takes in a new measurement and makes it more certain. The arrow back to the left shows the loop runs once per observation.

6.2.4 Where the gain comes from

There are several derivations. The most intuitive is the scalar case. The state is one number with prior variance PP. The measurement has variance RR. Two independent Gaussian estimates of the same thing combine by inverse-variance weighting (each is weighted by one over its variance):

x̂+=RP+Rx̂−+PP+Rz=x̂−+PP+R⏟K(z−x̂−) \hat x^+ = \frac{R}{P+R}\hat x^- + \frac{P}{P+R} z = \hat x^- + \underbrace{\frac{P}{P+R}}_{K}(z - \hat x^-)

1P+=1P+1R⇒P+=(1−K)P \frac{1}{P^+} = \frac1P + \frac1R \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P^+ = (1-K)P

Key idea. The gain is the fraction of the surprise you believe. If the prior is uncertain (P≫RP \gg R), K→1K \to 1 and you follow the measurement. If the measurement is noisy (R≫PR \gg P), K→0K \to 0 and you trust the model. The matrix formulas are this, generalised.

More formally, the gain minimises the trace of the posterior covariance (the sum of the state error variances). For Gaussian noise the result is the exact Bayesian posterior.

Figure 6.2.2 — The gain slides between “trust the model” and “trust the data”. The horizontal axis is the ratio P/R on a log scale. When the prior is much tighter than the measurement (left), K is near 0. When it is much looser (right), K is near 1. At P = R the filter splits the difference.

Figure 6.2.3 — A scalar filter on a simulated random walk. The green line is a hidden random walk. The grey dots are noisy measurements of it. The blue line is the Kalman estimate. It follows the green line far more closely than the dots do, but it lags slightly after sharp moves. Simulation: hidden walk with step variance 1, measurement noise variance 25, 150 steps, fixed seed 6002. Not market data.

6.2.5 The steady state

For a model that does not change over time, Pk|k−1P_{k|k-1} settles to a fixed point of the discrete algebraic Riccati equation:

P=FPF⊤−FPH⊤(HPH⊤+R)−1HPF⊤+Q P = F P F^\top - F P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1} H P F^\top + Q

Then the gain becomes constant. For a constant-velocity model with scalar observations, that steady-state filter is equivalent to a fixed alpha–beta filter (a simple tracker with two fixed blending weights).

This helps debugging. If your filter’s gain does not settle, something is changing over time that you did not intend.

6.2.6 What the filter really depends on: Q/R

Scale both QQ and RR by the same constant and the state estimate does not change. Only the reported covariance changes. The ratio controls responsiveness:

Q relative to R Behaviour
large nimble filter that tracks noise
small smooth filter that lags

Choosing that ratio is the real modelling decision. Most later chapters in this part are about choosing it well, or adapting it online.

6.2.7 Numerical engineering

The textbook equations are not the best way to compute.

  • Joseph form. P=(I−KH)PP = (I-KH)P can lose symmetry and positive definiteness through rounding. The Joseph stabilised form, Pk|k=(I−KH)Pk|k−1(I−KH)⊤+KRK⊤, P_{k|k} = (I - K H) P_{k|k-1} (I - KH)^\top + K R K^\top, is valid for any gain and keeps PP positive semi-definite. It costs a little more and is worth it.
  • Don’t invert. Solve SkK⊤=HP⊤S_k K^\top = H P^\top rather than forming Sk−1S_k^{-1}. For small states (two or three numbers), closed-form solves are fine and fastest.
  • Symmetrise. After each update, set P←12(P+P⊤)P \leftarrow \tfrac12(P + P^\top). Cheap insurance.
  • No allocation in the loop. Tick-by-tick processing means millions of updates a day. Every allocation adds garbage-collector pressure. I keep fixed-size state in structs and write the 2×2 and 3×3 algebra out by hand.
  • Determinism. Same inputs, same outputs, bit for bit, across runs. That makes regression tests and replay comparisons meaningful.

6.2.8 What the textbook gets wrong about markets

Each market fact below breaks one assumption. Each has a standard remedy, covered in later chapters.

Market fact Assumption broken Standard remedy
Price noise is heavy-tailed, with jumps Gaussian noise robust or gated updates
Volatility clusters constant process noise adaptive noise estimation
Observations arrive at irregular times regular clock time-varying discretisation
Behaviour switches between regimes one fixed model multiple-model filters

6.2.9 Summary

  • The Kalman filter alternates predict (uncertainty grows) and update (uncertainty shrinks).
  • The gain is the fraction of the surprise you believe: P/(P+R)P/(P+R) in the scalar case.
  • Only the ratio Q/R changes the estimate; choosing it is the real modelling decision.
  • Use the Joseph form, avoid explicit inverses, symmetrise, avoid allocation and keep runs deterministic.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A scalar filter has prior variance P = 4 and measurement variance R = 12. What is K, and what is the posterior variance? (Answer: K = 4/16 = 0.25; P⁺ = 0.75 × 4 = 3.)
  2. (Apply) Multiply both Q and R by 10 in a scalar filter. Show that the gain and the estimate do not change.
  3. (Simulate) Simulate a random walk with noisy measurements and run a scalar filter. Plot the estimate for Q/R = 0.01, 0.1 and 1. Which one lags most?
  4. (Think) Why does the plain update P=(I−KH)PP = (I-KH)P sometimes produce a covariance with a negative variance after many steps?

Further reading

  • R. E. Kalman, “A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems,” Journal of Basic Engineering (1960).
  • Y. Bar-Shalom, X. R. Li and T. Kirubarajan, Estimation with Applications to Tracking and Navigation (2001).
  • D. Simon, Optimal State Estimation (2006).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.3 — Constant-Velocity Models and Van Loan Discretisation

Subtitle: When observations arrive at irregular times, you need F and Q as functions of the gap. Here is how to get them exactly.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Write the continuous-time constant-velocity model and say why “constant” is a slight misnomer. 2. Derive the exact discrete F and Q for any gap Δt. 3. Use Van Loan’s method to discretise any linear model with one matrix exponential. 4. Explain why the choice of clock (seconds, trades, volume) is an explicit modelling decision.

You need: Chapter 6.2 (the Kalman filter), matrix multiplication, and simple integrals of powers of s.

6.3.1 The problem: markets have no clock

Market data does not arrive on a clock. Trades come in bursts and droughts: hundreds in a second, then nothing for a while. A Kalman filter that assumes a fixed time step between observations is wrong at almost every update.

The fix: write the model in continuous time, then discretise it (turn it into a step-by-step model) for whatever gap actually elapsed. This chapter does that for the constant-velocity model, then introduces the Van Loan method that does it for any linear model.

6.3.2 The continuous-time constant-velocity model

Let the state be position and velocity, x=[p,v]⊤x = [p, v]^\top. Velocity is a random walk, and position integrates velocity:

ẋ(t)=Ax(t)+Gw(t),A=[0100],G=[01] \dot x(t) = A x(t) + G\,w(t), \qquad A = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1\\0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\quad G = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}

Here w(t)w(t) is white noise (noise with no memory) of spectral density qq (its strength per unit time). This is the “white-noise acceleration” model.

“Constant velocity” is a slight misnomer. Velocity is constant in expectation, but it diffuses.

6.3.3 Discretising F

The solution of the linear differential equation over an interval Δt\Delta t is

x(t+Δt)=eAΔtx(t)+∫0ΔteA(Δt−s)Gw(t+s)ds x(t+\Delta t) = e^{A\Delta t}x(t) + \int_0^{\Delta t} e^{A(\Delta t - s)}G\,w(t+s)\,ds

so F=eAΔtF = e^{A\Delta t}. The matrix AA is nilpotent: A2=0A^2 = 0. So the exponential series stops after two terms:

F=I+AΔt=[1Δt01] F = I + A\Delta t = \begin{bmatrix}1 & \Delta t\\0 & 1\end{bmatrix}

6.3.4 Discretising Q

The discrete noise is the integral term. Its covariance is

Q=∫0ΔteAsGqG⊤eA⊤sds Q = \int_0^{\Delta t} e^{As}G\,q\,G^\top e^{A^\top s}\,ds

Since eAsG=[s,1]⊤e^{As}G = [s, 1]^\top:

Result (exact process noise, white-noise acceleration). Q=q∫0Δt[s2ss1]ds=q[Δt3/3Δt2/2Δt2/2Δt] Q = q\int_0^{\Delta t}\begin{bmatrix}s^2 & s\\ s & 1\end{bmatrix}ds = q\begin{bmatrix}\Delta t^3/3 & \Delta t^2/2\\ \Delta t^2/2 & \Delta t\end{bmatrix}

Notice the scaling. Velocity variance grows linearly with the gap. Position variance grows with its cube. A long gap creates a lot of position uncertainty. That is exactly right: if you have not seen a price for a while, you should be much less sure where it is.

Figure 6.3.1 — Long gaps add a lot of position uncertainty. Each curve is one entry of Q with q = 1. The green velocity term grows in a straight line. The blue position term starts slowly but grows as the cube of the gap, overtaking the others. This is the formula above, plotted; no data is involved.

A common shortcut. The “piecewise constant acceleration” model uses

Q′=q′[Δt4/4Δt3/2Δt3/2Δt2] Q' = q'\begin{bmatrix}\Delta t^4/4 & \Delta t^3/2\\ \Delta t^3/2 & \Delta t^2\end{bmatrix}

It assumes acceleration is constant within each step. It is rank one (all its noise points in one direction) and scales differently with Δt.

Model Position term Velocity term Rank
White-noise acceleration (exact) qΔt3/3q\,\Delta t^3/3 qΔtq\,\Delta t 2
Piecewise constant acceleration q′Δt4/4q'\,\Delta t^4/4 q′Δt2q'\,\Delta t^2 1

Both appear in textbooks. They are different models. Mixing them up changes how the filter reacts to irregular gaps.

6.3.5 Van Loan’s method

For richer models (constant acceleration, Singer, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck), deriving Q by hand gets tedious. Van Loan (1978) showed that F and Q both come out of one matrix exponential.

Method (Van Loan). Build the block matrix M=[−AGqG⊤0A⊤]Δt,eM=[⋅B120B22]. M = \begin{bmatrix} -A & GqG^\top \\ 0 & A^\top \end{bmatrix}\Delta t, \qquad e^{M} = \begin{bmatrix} \cdot & B_{12} \\ 0 & B_{22} \end{bmatrix}. Then F=B22⊤F = B_{22}^\top and Q=FB12Q = F\,B_{12}.

That is it. One exponential of a matrix twice the state size gives the exact discretisation for any linear time-invariant model (the matrices do not change over time) driven by white noise.

Figure 6.3.2 — Van Loan in three steps. Build the blue block matrix from A, G and q, scaled by the gap. Take one matrix exponential. The two green blocks of the result give F and Q directly.

6.3.6 Computing the matrix exponential

The standard algorithm is scaling and squaring with a Padé approximant (Moler and Van Loan, “Nineteen Dubious Ways to Compute the Exponential of a Matrix”). For the small matrices in tracking models (4×4 or 6×6 blocks), some practical points:

  • Closed form when you can. For constant-velocity and constant-acceleration models, the exact F and Q are polynomials in Δt. Hard-code them. They are faster and exactly symmetric.
  • Van Loan for everything else, or as a test oracle for your closed forms. I use it to check the hand-derived formulas to near machine precision over a range of gaps.
  • Watch tiny and huge Δt. Tiny gaps make Q near zero, which can make the predicted covariance nearly singular. Huge gaps (overnight) blow up the position variance. Both are honest outputs of the model, but downstream code must be ready for them.

6.3.7 What clock?

Engineering choices matter more than maths here. Δt does not have to be wall-clock time.

Clock One unit of “time” is “Constant velocity” means
Seconds one second drift per second (the model above, literally)
Trade count one trade drift per trade
Volume one contract traded drift per unit of traded volume

Changing the clock changes what “constant velocity” means. The volume clock has its own chapter (6.10). The point here: the discretisation formulas do not care which clock you pick, as long as you pick it explicitly.

6.3.8 Practical notes

  • Compute Δt from timestamps, not from assumed spacing. Clamp only at a documented minimum to avoid zero-length steps.
  • Simultaneous events (several trades with the same timestamp) give Δt = 0. The predict step is then the identity with zero added noise. Make sure your code handles that cleanly rather than dividing by zero somewhere.
  • Keep q in the units of the clock. A spectral density per second and one per contract are different numbers.

6.3.9 Summary

  • Irregular data needs F and Q computed for each actual gap.
  • For the constant-velocity model, F is [1,Δt;0,1][1, \Delta t; 0, 1] and Q has Δt3/3\Delta t^3/3, Δt2/2\Delta t^2/2 and Δt\Delta t terms.
  • The piecewise-constant-acceleration Q is a different model; do not mix them up.
  • Van Loan gives exact F and Q for any linear time-invariant model from one matrix exponential.
  • The clock is a modelling choice; make it explicit and keep q in its units.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With q = 2 and Δt = 3, what is the position variance term of the exact Q? (Answer: 2 × 27 / 3 = 18.)
  2. (Derive) Repeat the Q integral for a constant-acceleration model with state [p, v, a] and white-noise jerk.
  3. (Code) Implement Van Loan with any matrix-exponential routine and check it against the closed-form CV result for Δt = 0.01, 1 and 100.
  4. (Think) A filter runs in volume time. What happens to Δt during a very busy minute compared with a quiet one?

Further reading

  • C. F. Van Loan, “Computing Integrals Involving the Matrix Exponential,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control (1978).
  • C. Moler and C. Van Loan, “Nineteen Dubious Ways to Compute the Exponential of a Matrix, Twenty-Five Years Later,” SIAM Review (2003).
  • Y. Bar-Shalom, X. R. Li and T. Kirubarajan, Estimation with Applications to Tracking and Navigation, chapter 6.

— Tariq

Chapter 6.4 — NIS: Testing Whether Your Kalman Filter Believes Its Own Story

Subtitle: A filter reports both an estimate and its uncertainty. The normalised innovation squared checks whether the uncertainty is honest.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compute the normalised innovation squared (NIS) and state its distribution under a correct model. 2. Read NIS that is too high, too low, or bursty as a diagnosis of the filter. 3. Run the time-average and whiteness tests. 4. Use NIS as an outlier gate without falling into the “death spiral”.

You need: Chapter 6.2 (the Kalman filter) and the idea of a chi-squared distribution (a sum of squared standard normals).

6.4.1 Why a filter needs a self-check

A Kalman filter always produces an answer. It never throws an exception because the model is wrong. It just produces confident nonsense.

The first diagnostic I add to any filter is the normalised innovation squared (NIS). It is the cheapest way to catch a filter that is lying about how sure it is.

6.4.2 The idea

At each update the filter predicts the next measurement and its uncertainty:

ẑk|k−1=Hx̂k|k−1,Sk=HPk|k−1H⊤+R \hat z_{k|k-1} = H\hat x_{k|k-1}, \qquad S_k = H P_{k|k-1}H^\top + R

If the model is right (correct F, Q, H, R, and Gaussian noise), the innovation yk=zk−ẑk|k−1y_k = z_k - \hat z_{k|k-1} is zero-mean Gaussian with covariance exactly SkS_k.

Definition (NIS). ϵk=yk⊤Sk−1yk\epsilon_k = y_k^\top S_k^{-1} y_k.

Result. Under a correct model, ϵk\epsilon_k is chi-squared with mm degrees of freedom, where mm is the measurement dimension.

For scalar price observations, m=1m = 1 and ϵk=yk2/Sk\epsilon_k = y_k^2/S_k: the squared z-score of the surprise. Its expected value is mm.

Figure 6.4.1 — What NIS should look like. The blue curve is the chi-squared density with one degree of freedom, the law NIS follows when the model is right. Most values are small and the mean is 1 (dashed line). The orange line marks a high quantile used as a gate; values beyond it (shaded) are rare if the model is correct. This is a formula plot, not data.

6.4.3 What it diagnoses

What NIS does What it means Typical cause
Too large on average innovations bigger than the filter expects: overconfident Q or R too small, or wrong dynamics (e.g. a constant-velocity model during an acceleration)
Too small on average filter is underconfident; sluggish and over-smooth noise covariances too large
Fine on average but in bursts model adequate most of the time, badly wrong some of the time regime changes; the motivation for multiple-model filters

Figure 6.4.2 — Average NIS tells you which way the noise is wrong. Three filters run on the same simulated random walk with noisy measurements. The blue filter uses the true noise levels and its running NIS mean settles near 1. The orange filter’s Q and R are three times too small, so its NIS sits near 3. The green filter’s are three times too large, so it sits near 1/3. Simulation: random-walk state with step variance 1, measurement variance 4, 400 steps, fixed seed 6004. Not market data.

6.4.4 Formal tests

Time-average test. Over a window of NN updates,

ϵ‾=1N∑k=1Nϵk,Nϵ‾∼χNm2 \bar\epsilon = \frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N \epsilon_k, \qquad N\bar\epsilon \sim \chi^2_{Nm}

This holds if the innovations are independent. Under the model they are: the innovation sequence of an optimal filter is white (uncorrelated over time). A two-sided acceptance region at confidence 1−α1-\alpha is

[χNm2(α/2)N,χNm2(1−α/2)N] \left[\frac{\chi^2_{Nm}(\alpha/2)}{N},\; \frac{\chi^2_{Nm}(1-\alpha/2)}{N}\right]

For large NN this is about m±z1−α/22m/Nm \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{2m/N}.

Whiteness test. The innovations of a correct filter are uncorrelated over time. The normalised sample autocorrelation at lag jj,

ρ̂j=∑kykyk+j∑kyk2∑kyk+j2, \hat\rho_j = \frac{\sum_k y_k y_{k+j}}{\sqrt{\sum_k y_k^2 \sum_k y_{k+j}^2}},

should be about 𝒩(0,1/N)\mathcal N(0, 1/N). Significant autocorrelation means the filter leaves predictable structure in the residuals. Typically that is a lag: the dynamics are too sluggish.

NEES. If you know the true state (in simulation), the normalised estimation error squared, (xk−x̂k|k)⊤Pk|k−1(xk−x̂k|k)(x_k - \hat x_{k|k})^\top P_{k|k}^{-1}(x_k - \hat x_{k|k}), tests the state covariance directly. In real markets there is no true state. NIS is the test you can run live.

6.4.5 Using NIS as a gate

The same statistic doubles as an outlier gate. One observation with ϵk\epsilon_k beyond a high chi-squared quantile is very unlikely under the model. You can:

  • Reject it (skip the update). This protects the state from bad ticks.
  • Down-weight it by inflating R for that update. This is a simple robust filter.
  • Treat it as evidence that the model has changed.

Each option has a failure mode. Rejecting outliers blindly means that when the market really jumps, the filter refuses to follow. Its covariance keeps shrinking, and every later tick looks like an outlier too.

Pitfall (the death spiral). A gate that only rejects can lock the filter out of reality for good. Any gate needs a recovery path: after repeated rejections, inflate the covariance or reset.

6.4.6 What markets do to NIS

On real tick data, NIS is almost never well-behaved with a fixed-noise model:

  • Heavy tails. Price changes have far more large moves than a Gaussian. NIS shows excess large values even when the average looks fine. A Student-t check, or looking at quantiles rather than the mean, tells you more.
  • Volatility clustering. Quiet periods show NIS far below its expectation; busy periods far above. The time average can look fine while being wrong almost everywhere.
  • Microstructure noise. Bid–ask bounce (trades alternating between bid and ask prices) creates negative autocorrelation in tick-level innovations. The whiteness test flags it immediately.
  • Discreteness. Prices move in ticks. With very small Δt, many innovations are exactly zero, which the continuous Gaussian model does not predict.

None of these means the filter is useless. They mean NIS is doing its job: telling you which assumption is failing.

6.4.7 Engineering notes

  • Compute ϵk\epsilon_k from quantities you already have (yky_k and SkS_k). It costs almost nothing.
  • Keep running statistics (mean, quantile sketches, a short autocorrelation) rather than storing every value, if memory matters.
  • Log NIS per regime, per time of day and per clock type. Aggregate NIS hides structure.
  • In replay, make sure NIS uses only the prediction made before the measurement. Computing it after the update gives a trivially small number and a false sense of consistency.

6.4.8 Summary

  • NIS is the squared, normalised surprise; under a correct model it is chi-squared with mean m.
  • Too high means overconfident, too low means underconfident, bursty means regime changes.
  • The time-average and whiteness tests turn this into formal checks; NEES needs the true state, so it is for simulation only.
  • As a gate, NIS needs a recovery path or it causes a death spiral.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A scalar filter predicts S = 4 and the innovation is y = 3. What is the NIS? Is it beyond the 99% chi-squared(1) quantile of about 6.63? (Answer: 9/4 = 2.25; no.)
  2. (Apply) Using the large-N approximation, what is the 95% acceptance band for the average NIS with m = 1 and N = 200?
  3. (Simulate) Reproduce Figure 6.4.2, then add a sudden jump in the true state halfway through. What does a reject-only gate do?
  4. (Think) Why does computing NIS after the update give a “trivially small number”?

Further reading

  • Y. Bar-Shalom, X. R. Li and T. Kirubarajan, Estimation with Applications to Tracking and Navigation, chapter 5 (filter consistency).
  • R. K. Mehra and J. Peschon, “An Innovations Approach to Fault Detection and Diagnosis in Dynamic Systems,” Automatica (1971).
  • D. Simon, Optimal State Estimation.

— Tariq

Chapter 6.5 — Adaptive Noise Estimation: Letting the Filter Learn Q and R

Subtitle: Mehra’s innovation-based ideas, and the practical recursive versions that keep a Kalman filter honest when volatility changes.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why a filter’s innovations carry information about wrong Q and R. 2. Outline Mehra’s correlation method and its least-squares successor. 3. Write the recursive covariance-matching estimators for R and Q. 4. List the failure modes of adaptation and the guard rails for each.

You need: Chapter 6.2 (Kalman filter), Chapter 6.4 (NIS and innovation whiteness), and the idea of an exponentially weighted average.

6.5.1 The problem

The Kalman filter’s behaviour is controlled by two covariance matrices, Q and R. The textbook treats them as known. In markets they are neither known nor constant:

  • volatility clusters,
  • microstructure noise (the jitter from how trades hit bid and ask) varies with liquidity,
  • a filter tuned on a quiet morning is miscalibrated by the afternoon.

Adaptive noise estimation lets the filter estimate Q and R from its own residuals. This chapter covers the classical theory and the practical recursive versions.

6.5.2 Why the innovations carry the information

For a correctly specified filter, the innovation yk=zk−Hx̂k|k−1y_k = z_k - H\hat x_{k|k-1} has covariance

𝔼[ykyk⊤]=Sk=HPk|k−1H⊤+R \mathbb E[y_k y_k^\top] = S_k = H P_{k|k-1}H^\top + R

  • If R is wrong, the observed innovation covariance will not match SkS_k.
  • If Q is wrong, the innovations will also be autocorrelated (correlated with their own past). The gain is no longer optimal, so predictable error leaks into the residuals.

Mehra (1970, 1972) turned this into an estimation method: use the sample autocorrelation of the innovations to solve for the noise covariances.

6.5.3 Mehra’s correlation method, in outline

Take a steady-state filter with a fixed (possibly suboptimal) gain KK. The innovation autocovariances (covariance between the innovation now and jj steps ago)

Cj=𝔼[ykyk−j⊤] C_j = \mathbb E[y_k y_{k-j}^\top]

satisfy

C0=HMH⊤+R,Cj=H(F(I−KH))j−1F(MH⊤−KC0),j≥1 C_0 = HMH^\top + R, \qquad C_j = H\big(F(I - KH)\big)^{j-1}F\,(MH^\top - KC_0), \quad j \ge 1

where MM is the steady-state predicted covariance. From sample estimates of C0,C1,…C_0, C_1, \dots you can solve for MH⊤MH^\top, then for R, and then (under identifiability conditions) for Q. The optimal gain follows.

Odelson, Rajamani and Rawlings (2006) later recast this as an autocovariance least-squares problem. It is better conditioned and guarantees positive semi-definite estimates.

This batch approach is elegant, but it assumes stationarity (the statistics do not change) over the estimation window. Markets violate that. So in practice one uses recursive versions with a forgetting factor, which weights recent data more.

6.5.4 Covariance matching, recursively

The simplest adaptive scheme matches the observed innovation covariance to its theoretical value. Keep an exponentially weighted estimate:

Ĉk=(1−λ)Ĉk−1+λykyk⊤ \hat C_k = (1-\lambda)\hat C_{k-1} + \lambda\,y_k y_k^\top

Estimators (covariance matching). The implied measurement noise is R̂k=Ĉk−HPk|k−1H⊤. \hat R_k = \hat C_k - H P_{k|k-1} H^\top. For process noise, a related estimate uses the state corrections: Q̂k=(1−λ)Q̂k−1+λ(Kkykyk⊤Kk⊤+Pk|k−FPk−1|k−1F⊤). \hat Q_k = (1-\lambda)\hat Q_{k-1} + \lambda\left(K_k y_k y_k^\top K_k^\top + P_{k|k} - F P_{k-1|k-1} F^\top\right).

These belong to the Sage–Husa family of estimators, and to Mohamed and Schwarz’s adaptive filter for navigation. The forgetting factor λ\lambda sets the memory: larger reacts faster but is noisier.

Figure 6.5.1 — Adaptation closes a loop. The filter (top left) produces innovations. The noise estimator turns them into new Q and R. Those pass through guard rails (green) before going back into the filter. Because the loop feeds itself, the guard rails are what keep it stable.

Figure 6.5.2 — Faster forgetting reacts sooner but wobbles more. The true measurement noise (dashed) jumps from 1 to 4 halfway through. The orange estimate forgets quickly: it catches the jump within a few dozen steps but is noisy throughout. The blue estimate forgets slowly: it is smooth but takes hundreds of steps to catch up. Simulation: scalar random-walk state with step variance 0.05, Gaussian measurement noise, 1,000 steps, fixed seed 6005; the λ values are illustration choices only. Not market data.

6.5.5 What goes wrong

Failure What happens Guard rail
Negative or indefinite estimates Ĉk−HPH⊤\hat C_k - HPH^\top goes negative when the filter is briefly overconfident project back onto valid covariances: floor variances or clip eigenvalues
Identifiability with a scalar observation and a 2–3 number state, one innovation stream cannot recover every element of Q and R fix or structure something, e.g. keep Q’s shape from the continuous-time model (the Δt3/3\Delta t^3/3, Δt2/2\Delta t^2/2, Δt\Delta t structure of Chapter 6.3) and adapt only its scale
Feedback overestimated R makes innovations look small, which shrinks R… or the reverse; the loop can run away bounds on adapted quantities; adapt more slowly than the state dynamics
Outliers one bad tick adds yy⊤yy^\top and can inflate R for a long time Huber-weighted or median-based updates, or skip updates that fail an NIS gate
Confusing Q and R a burst of large innovations could mean the state moved (large Q) or the measurements got noisier (large R) use their signatures: process noise gives autocorrelated innovations and lasting state changes; measurement noise gives uncorrelated jitter. Separating them on short windows is hard, so be humble about which one you adapt

6.5.6 An alternative view: variational Bayes

Särkkä and Nummenmaa (2009) treat R as an unknown with an inverse-gamma (or inverse-Wishart) prior: a standard distribution for an unknown variance. They alternate between updating the state and updating the belief about the noise.

The result looks like covariance matching, but it has a principled forgetting mechanism and never goes negative. It is a nice bridge between the adaptive-filter literature and Bayesian online learning.

6.5.7 Engineering notes

  • Keep adaptive state separate from filter state, so you can freeze adaptation for testing.
  • Log the adapted Q and R over time. They are often easier to interpret than the filtered state: an adapted measurement noise is a running estimate of microstructure noise.
  • Initialise conservatively and allow a warm-up period before trusting outputs.
  • Make it causal: adaptation uses only past innovations. In replay this is easy to violate by computing statistics over a whole session first.

6.5.8 Summary

  • Wrong R shows up as innovation variance that does not match S; wrong Q also shows up as autocorrelation.
  • Mehra’s method solves for the noises from innovation autocovariances; it assumes stationarity, so practice uses recursive forgetting versions.
  • Covariance matching replaces two hand-tuned constants with two estimators, each with its own tuning (forgetting rate, bounds, robustness).
  • That is still progress: the filter now tracks changing conditions. But it adds a feedback loop, and feedback loops need guard rails.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) The smoothed innovation variance is Ĉ=5\hat C = 5 and the predicted state variance seen through H is HPH⊤=2HPH^\top = 2. What is R̂\hat R? (Answer: 3.)
  2. (Apply) In the same setting, Ĉ\hat C drops to 1.5. What does the raw formula give, and what should the code do?
  3. (Simulate) Reproduce Figure 6.5.2, then add one huge outlier at step 300. How long does each estimate stay inflated? Try a median-based update.
  4. (Think) Why must adaptation run more slowly than the state dynamics?

Further reading

  • R. K. Mehra, “On the Identification of Variances and Adaptive Kalman Filtering,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control (1970).
  • R. K. Mehra, “Approaches to Adaptive Filtering,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control (1972).
  • B. J. Odelson, M. R. Rajamani and J. B. Rawlings, “A New Autocovariance Least-Squares Method for Estimating Noise Covariances,” Automatica (2006).
  • S. Särkkä and A. Nummenmaa, “Recursive Noise Adaptive Kalman Filtering by Variational Bayesian Approximations,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control (2009).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.6 — IMM Filtering: Running Several Motion Models at Once

Subtitle: Blom and Bar-Shalom’s interacting multiple model filter, and the CV, CA, Singer and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck models it is usually built from.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe four standard motion models (CV, CA, Singer, OU) and when each fits. 2. Run the five steps of the IMM recursion. 3. Say what IMM model probabilities do and do not mean. 4. Avoid the common implementation traps: underflow, zero probabilities, heavy tails.
