You need: Chapter 6.2 (Kalman filter), Chapter 6.3 (discretisation), and the idea of a Markov chain (a process whose next state depends only on the current one).

6.6.1 Why more than one model

A single Kalman filter commits to one model of how the state evolves. Markets switch: quiet drift, sustained trends, sharp accelerations, mean-reverting chop. Tuning one filter for all of them gives you something mediocre at each.

The interacting multiple model (IMM) estimator, from Blom and Bar-Shalom (1988), runs a small bank of filters in parallel. It blends them according to how well each explains the data. It is one of the most useful ideas I have borrowed from target tracking. This chapter explains the algorithm and the standard model families, generically.

6.6.2 The model families

Each is a linear Gaussian model, written in continuous time and discretised with the methods of Chapter 6.3.

Model State Equations Good for
Constant velocity (CV) [p,v][p, v] ṗ=v,v̇=w\dot p = v,\ \dot v = w steady drift
Constant acceleration (CA) [p,v,a][p, v, a] ṗ=v,v̇=a,ȧ=w\dot p = v,\ \dot v = a,\ \dot a = w changes in velocity, at the cost of more noise
Singer [p,v,a][p, v, a] ȧ=−1τa+w\dot a = -\frac{1}{\tau}a + w real but temporary accelerations
Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) pp dp=κ(μ−p)dt+σdWdp = \kappa(\mu - p)\,dt + \sigma\,dW range-bound behaviour

Singer. Acceleration is a first-order Gauss–Markov (mean-reverting) process with time constant τ\tau. As τ→0\tau \to 0 it behaves like CV; as τ→∞\tau \to \infty, like CA. Singer (1970) designed it for manoeuvring targets whose accelerations are real but temporary. The discrete F involves terms like e−Δt/τe^{-\Delta t/\tau}, and Q is messy enough that Van Loan’s method is the sane way to get it.

Ornstein–Uhlenbeck. The level itself pulls back toward a long-run value μ\mu at rate κ\kappa. Its exact discretisation is

pk=μ+e−κΔt(pk−1−μ)+εk,Var(εk)=σ22κ(1−e−2κΔt) p_{k} = \mu + e^{-\kappa\Delta t}(p_{k-1}-\mu) + \varepsilon_k,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_k) = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\left(1 - e^{-2\kappa\Delta t}\right)

Mixing different sizes. These models have different state dimensions. To mix them, embed all of them in a common state (pad with zeros and suitable covariances), or mix only the shared components. This bookkeeping is where most implementation bugs live.

6.6.3 The IMM recursion

Suppose there are rr models, and a Markov chain decides which is active, with transition matrix Πij=P(Mk=j∣Mk−1=i)\Pi_{ij} = P(M_k = j \mid M_{k-1} = i). The exact answer is a mixture whose size grows exponentially. The IMM approximates it with rr Gaussians, one per model, at every step.

Step 1. Mixing probabilities. With model probabilities μk−1i\mu_{k-1}^i:

c‾j=∑iΠijμk−1i,μi|j=Πijμk−1ic‾j \bar c_j = \sum_i \Pi_{ij}\mu_{k-1}^i, \qquad \mu^{i|j} = \frac{\Pi_{ij}\mu_{k-1}^i}{\bar c_j}

Step 2. Mixed starting point for each filter jj:

x̂0j=∑iμi|jx̂i,P0j=∑iμi|j[Pi+(x̂i−x̂0j)(x̂i−x̂0j)⊤] \hat x^{0j} = \sum_i \mu^{i|j}\hat x^i, \qquad P^{0j} = \sum_i \mu^{i|j}\left[P^i + (\hat x^i - \hat x^{0j})(\hat x^i - \hat x^{0j})^\top\right]

The second term is the spread-of-means correction. Forgetting it makes the mixture overconfident.

Step 3. Model-matched filtering. Run each Kalman filter’s predict and update from its mixed starting point. Record the innovation yjy_j and covariance SjS_j.

Step 4. Likelihoods and probability update.

Λj=𝒩(yj;0,Sj),μkj=Λjc‾j∑lΛlc‾l \Lambda_j = \mathcal N(y_j; 0, S_j), \qquad \mu_k^j = \frac{\Lambda_j\,\bar c_j}{\sum_l \Lambda_l\,\bar c_l}

Step 5. Combined output (for reporting only, not fed back):

x̂=∑jμkjx̂j,P=∑jμkj[Pj+(x̂j−x̂)(x̂j−x̂)⊤] \hat x = \sum_j \mu_k^j\hat x^j, \qquad P = \sum_j \mu_k^j\left[P^j + (\hat x^j - \hat x)(\hat x^j - \hat x)^\top\right]

The cost is rr Kalman filters plus O(r2)O(r^2) mixing: essentially constant per update.

Figure 6.6.1 — One IMM cycle. Model probabilities are mixed through the transition matrix Π (steps 1–2). Each blue filter then runs on its own mixed starting point (step 3). Their likelihoods update the probabilities (step 4, green), which feed the next cycle. The combined output (step 5) is only reported, never fed back.

6.6.4 What the model probabilities mean

The probabilities μkj\mu_k^j are the interesting by-product. They are a posterior belief about which motion regime best explains recent data, under the assumptions. They respond quickly when one model’s innovations become much more likely than another’s.

Figure 6.6.2 — Model probability follows a simulated regime switch, with lag and noise. A two-model IMM (a slow and a fast random walk) runs on data that is truly “fast” only in the grey bands. The blue probability of the fast model rises inside the bands and falls outside them. It lags at the edges and spikes on false alarms in between. Simulation: scalar random walk with step variance 0.02 (slow) or 1 (fast), measurement variance 1, 600 steps, fixed seed 6006; transition matrix chosen for illustration. Not market data.

Caution. Model probabilities are only as meaningful as the model set. If none of the models is right, the IMM picks the least wrong one, confidently. They are relative, not absolute: a high probability for CA means “more consistent than the others”, not “the market is accelerating”.

6.6.5 Practical issues

Issue What goes wrong Fix
The transition matrix Π encodes how sticky regimes are: large diagonal entries make switching slow; small ones make it jittery treat it as a modelling choice; it matters as much as the filters
Likelihood underflow Gaussian likelihoods for large innovations underflow to zero work in log space; normalise with the log-sum-exp trick
Probability floors a model at exactly zero probability can never recover keep a small floor so every model stays alive
Heavy tails one jump gives a huge innovation to every model; the one with the largest S wins by default. That is a covariance-size contest, not regime detection robust (Student-t) likelihoods or gating
Clock choice discretisation depends on Δt; in a volume or trade clock, “velocity” and “mean-reversion rate” change meaning pick the clock explicitly; expect probabilities to change with it

6.6.6 Summary

  • An IMM runs a bank of Kalman filters and blends them by how well each explains the data.
  • CV, CA, Singer and OU cover drift, acceleration, temporary manoeuvres and mean reversion.
  • The five steps are mix, mixed start, filter, likelihood update, combine; remember the spread-of-means term.
  • Model probabilities are relative beliefs, only as good as the model set.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Two models have probabilities 0.9 and 0.1, and Π has 0.95 on the diagonal. What is the predicted probability c‾2\bar c_2 of model 2? (Answer: 0.05 × 0.9 + 0.95 × 0.1 = 0.14.)
  2. (Derive) Show that the OU variance σ22κ(1−e−2κΔt)\frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}(1 - e^{-2\kappa\Delta t}) tends to σ2Δt\sigma^2\Delta t for small Δt.
  3. (Simulate) Reproduce Figure 6.6.2, then change the diagonal of Π from 0.98 to 0.9 and 0.999. How do lag and false alarms change?
  4. (Think) Why is it a mistake to feed the combined output of step 5 back into the filters?

Further reading

  • H. A. P. Blom and Y. Bar-Shalom, “The Interacting Multiple Model Algorithm for Systems with Markovian Switching Coefficients,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control (1988).
  • R. A. Singer, “Estimating Optimal Tracking Filter Performance for Manned Maneuvering Targets,” IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems (1970).
  • X. R. Li and V. P. Jilkov, “Survey of Maneuvering Target Tracking,” Parts I and V, IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems (2003, 2005).
  • G. E. Uhlenbeck and L. S. Ornstein, “On the Theory of the Brownian Motion,” Physical Review (1930).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.7 — Hidden Markov Models and Baum–Welch

Subtitle: Regimes you cannot see, inferred from returns you can. The forward–backward algorithm and EM, derived step by step.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define a hidden Markov model and Rabiner’s three classic problems. 2. Run the forward and backward recursions and combine them into state posteriors. 3. Write the Baum–Welch (EM) updates and the numerical fixes they need. 4. Explain why smoothed regime labels are lookahead.

You need: Chapter 6.6 (Markov chains of models), conditional probability, and the normal distribution.

6.7.1 What a “regime” means

“The market is in a trending regime” is a statement about something you cannot observe. Hidden Markov models (HMMs) make that kind of statement precise. A discrete hidden state follows a Markov chain, and each state emits observations from its own distribution.

I have used HMMs as a research tool this year, mostly to understand what “regime” can and cannot mean statistically. This chapter derives the core algorithms.

6.7.2 The model

Part Symbol Meaning
Hidden states st∈{1,…,N}s_t \in \{1,\dots,N\} the regime at time t
Initial distribution πi=P(s1=i)\pi_i = P(s_1 = i) where the chain starts
Transition matrix Aij=P(st+1=j∣st=i)A_{ij} = P(s_{t+1}=j \mid s_t = i) how regimes switch
Emission densities bj(ot)=p(ot∣st=j)b_j(o_t) = p(o_t \mid s_t = j) what each regime produces; for returns often Gaussian, 𝒩(o;μj,σj2)\mathcal N(o;\mu_j,\sigma_j^2)

The parameters are θ=(π,A,{μj,σj})\theta = (\pi, A, \{\mu_j,\sigma_j\}).

Rabiner’s three classic problems: 1. evaluate the likelihood of a sequence, 2. find the most likely state path, 3. learn θ\theta.

Figure 6.7.1 — The structure of an HMM. The blue circles are hidden states; each moves to the next by the transition matrix A. Each state emits the observation below it (grey box) through its density b. You only ever see the bottom row.

6.7.3 Forward algorithm (likelihood)

Define αt(i)=p(o1,…,ot,st=i)\alpha_t(i) = p(o_1,\dots,o_t, s_t = i): the probability of the data so far and being in state i now. Then

α1(i)=πibi(o1),αt+1(j)=[∑iαt(i)Aij]bj(ot+1) \alpha_1(i) = \pi_i b_i(o_1), \qquad \alpha_{t+1}(j) = \Big[\sum_i \alpha_t(i)A_{ij}\Big] b_j(o_{t+1})

and the likelihood is p(o1:T)=∑iαT(i)p(o_{1:T}) = \sum_i \alpha_T(i). The cost is O(TN2)O(TN^2) instead of O(NT)O(N^T) for brute force.

6.7.4 Backward algorithm and posteriors

Define βt(i)=p(ot+1,…,oT∣st=i)\beta_t(i) = p(o_{t+1},\dots,o_T \mid s_t = i): the probability of the future data given state i now.

βT(i)=1,βt(i)=∑jAijbj(ot+1)βt+1(j) \beta_T(i) = 1, \qquad \beta_t(i) = \sum_j A_{ij}\,b_j(o_{t+1})\,\beta_{t+1}(j)

Result (posteriors). The smoothed state posterior is γt(i)=P(st=i∣o1:T)=αt(i)βt(i)∑jαt(j)βt(j) \gamma_t(i) = P(s_t = i \mid o_{1:T}) = \frac{\alpha_t(i)\beta_t(i)}{\sum_j \alpha_t(j)\beta_t(j)} and the pairwise posterior is ξt(i,j)=P(st=i,st+1=j∣o1:T)=αt(i)Aijbj(ot+1)βt+1(j)p(o1:T). \xi_t(i,j) = P(s_t = i, s_{t+1}=j \mid o_{1:T}) = \frac{\alpha_t(i)A_{ij}b_j(o_{t+1})\beta_{t+1}(j)}{p(o_{1:T})}.

6.7.5 Baum–Welch (EM)

Baum–Welch is expectation–maximisation (EM) for HMMs: alternate between guessing the hidden states (E-step) and re-fitting the parameters to those guesses (M-step).

  • E-step: compute γ\gamma and ξ\xi with forward–backward under the current parameters.
  • M-step: re-estimate in closed form:

π̂i=γ1(i),Âij=∑t=1T−1ξt(i,j)∑t=1T−1γt(i) \hat\pi_i = \gamma_1(i), \qquad \hat A_{ij} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\xi_t(i,j)}{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\gamma_t(i)}

μ̂j=∑tγt(j)ot∑tγt(j),σ̂j2=∑tγt(j)(ot−μ̂j)2∑tγt(j) \hat\mu_j = \frac{\sum_t \gamma_t(j)\,o_t}{\sum_t\gamma_t(j)}, \qquad \hat\sigma_j^2 = \frac{\sum_t\gamma_t(j)(o_t - \hat\mu_j)^2}{\sum_t\gamma_t(j)}

These are weighted versions of the obvious estimators: transition counts and sample moments, weighted by how much each time step belongs to each state. EM guarantees the likelihood never decreases, and it converges to a local maximum.

6.7.6 Numerical engineering

  • Scaling. αt\alpha_t shrinks exponentially with t and underflows after a few hundred steps. Normalise at each step: ct=∑iα̃t(i),α̂t(i)=α̃t(i)/ct,log⁡p(o1:T)=∑tlog⁡ct c_t = \sum_i \tilde\alpha_t(i), \qquad \hat\alpha_t(i) = \tilde\alpha_t(i)/c_t, \qquad \log p(o_{1:T}) = \sum_t \log c_t The backward pass reuses the same ctc_t. Alternatively, work entirely in log space with log-sum-exp.
  • Variance collapse. A Gaussian emission can shrink onto a single observation, sending its variance to zero and the likelihood to infinity. Floor the variances, or put a prior on them (a MAP version of the M-step).
  • Initialisation. EM finds local maxima; different starting parameters give different answers. Run several and keep the best likelihood, and check whether the solutions agree qualitatively.
  • Label switching. States are unlabelled. “State 1” in one run may be “state 2” in another. Sort states by a parameter (variance, say) before comparing runs.

6.7.7 Viterbi

The most likely single path solves

δt+1(j)=maxi[δt(i)Aij]bj(ot+1) \delta_{t+1}(j) = \max_i\left[\delta_t(i)A_{ij}\right]b_j(o_{t+1})

with back-pointers to recover the path. Note: the Viterbi path and the sequence of individually most likely states (arg⁡max⁡iγt(i)\arg\max_i \gamma_t(i)) can differ. They answer different questions.

6.7.8 What the textbook gets wrong about markets

Smoothing is lookahead. γt\gamma_t uses βt\beta_t, which depends on future observations. A regime label from forward–backward at time t is not knowable at time t. Any study that uses smoothed labels as features is contaminated. Use only the filtered probabilities α̂t\hat\alpha_t for anything that must be causal. This is the most common HMM mistake I see; the next chapter is about the online filtering version.

Figure 6.7.2 — Smoothed probabilities look better because they cheat. Grey bands mark when a simulated two-state HMM is truly in state 2. The orange smoothed probability is clean and rises right at each band’s edge, because it sees the future. The blue filtered probability, the only one available in real time, is noisier and later. Simulation: two Gaussian states with means 0 and 1, standard deviation 1, switch probability 0.03 per step, 300 steps, fixed seed 6007; model parameters known. Not market data.

Other gaps between textbook and market:

Problem Why it matters
Parameters fitted on the full sample also lookahead; fit on one period, evaluate on another
Geometric durations an HMM implies each regime’s duration is geometric, so the most likely duration is always one step; real regimes rarely look like that. Hidden semi-Markov models allow explicit durations, at higher cost
Gaussian emissions understate tails, so the model may invent a “high-volatility state” just to explain a few outliers
Number of states likelihood always improves with more states; use BIC or out-of-sample likelihood, and distrust rarely visited states

6.7.9 Summary

  • An HMM is a hidden Markov chain plus per-state emission densities.
  • Forward gives the likelihood; forward plus backward gives smoothed posteriors; Baum–Welch fits parameters by EM.
  • Scale or use logs, floor variances, try several starts, and fix labels before comparing.
  • Smoothed labels and full-sample parameters are lookahead; use filtered probabilities for causal work.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Brute-force likelihood for N = 3 states and T = 20 needs how many paths? How many operations does the forward algorithm roughly need? (Answer: 3²⁰ ≈ 3.5 billion paths; about T·N² = 180.)
  2. (Derive) Show that the M-step for μ̂j\hat\mu_j is the weighted mean by differentiating the expected log-likelihood.
  3. (Simulate) Reproduce Figure 6.7.2 and count how many steps, on average, the filtered probability needs to cross 0.5 after a true switch.
  4. (Think) Why can the Viterbi path disagree with the sequence of most likely individual states?

Further reading

  • L. R. Rabiner, “A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models and Selected Applications in Speech Recognition,” Proceedings of the IEEE (1989).
  • L. E. Baum, T. Petrie, G. Soules and N. Weiss, “A Maximization Technique Occurring in the Statistical Analysis of Probabilistic Functions of Markov Chains,” Annals of Mathematical Statistics (1970).
  • J. D. Hamilton, “A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle,” Econometrica (1989).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.8 — Forward Filtering Online: Regime Probabilities Without Peeking

Subtitle: Turning a hidden Markov model into a causal, streaming estimator, and the traps between batch and online.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Run the HMM forward filter one observation at a time. 2. List the four things that change between a batch HMM and an honest online one. 3. Estimate how long the filter takes to notice a regime switch. 4. Apply a five-question causality checklist to any HMM-based feature.

You need: Chapter 6.7 (HMMs) and the idea of a log-likelihood ratio.

6.8.1 Why online

Chapter 6.7 warned that forward–backward smoothing uses the future. If you want a regime probability you could have acted on at time t, you need the forward filter alone, run one observation at a time.

That sounds like a trivial restriction. In practice, the gap between a batch HMM and a correct online one is where many research results quietly die.

6.8.2 The filtering recursion

We want P(st=i∣o1:t)P(s_t = i \mid o_{1:t}), the filtered probability. Write it as a normalised vector ptp_t. The recursion has two steps, exactly like a Kalman filter.

Predict:

pt|t−1(j)=∑ipt−1(i)Aij p_{t|t-1}(j) = \sum_i p_{t-1}(i)\,A_{ij}

Update:

pt(j)=pt|t−1(j)bj(ot)∑lpt|t−1(l)bl(ot) p_t(j) = \frac{p_{t|t-1}(j)\,b_j(o_t)}{\sum_l p_{t|t-1}(l)\,b_l(o_t)}

The denominator is the one-step predictive likelihood p(ot∣o1:t−1)p(o_t \mid o_{1:t-1}). Its log, summed over time, is the log-likelihood of the stream. A sudden drop in it is a useful alarm that the model no longer explains the data.

That is the whole online algorithm: O(N2)O(N^2) per observation, constant memory, strictly causal. It is the discrete-state cousin of the Kalman filter; the IMM filter of Chapter 6.6 is a hybrid of the two.

6.8.3 Online versus batch: what changes

1. The parameters. A batch HMM fitted with Baum–Welch on the full dataset has seen the future. Running the forward filter with those parameters is still lookahead, just subtler. Honest options:

Option How Trade-off
Fixed parameters from a strictly earlier period fit once on the past simple; honest if the period is truly prior
Rolling refits refit on a trailing window at fixed intervals; use each fit only going forward adapts in steps
Online EM update sufficient statistics recursively with a step size (Cappé and Moulines, 2009) adapts continuously but can drift

Each must be explicit and reproducible. “We fitted the model, then ran it” hides which one you did.

2. Label consistency. With rolling refits, state labels can swap between fits. The “high-volatility state” may be state 1 in one window and state 2 in the next. Map states by a stable property (for instance, sort by emission variance) every time you refit.

3. Initial conditions. At the start of each day or session, what is p0p_0? Using the previous session’s final probability carries information across the gap, which is fine if the gap is modelled. Resetting to the stationary distribution of A is simpler and avoids leakage from a different market state overnight. Either way, write it down.

4. Latency of belief. Filtered probabilities lag regime changes. After a true switch, it takes several observations of evidence before the new state overtakes the old one. The lag depends on how separated the emission distributions are and on how sticky A is. Smoothed probabilities show the switch exactly in the right place. That is precisely why they look so good in charts and are useless in practice.

Figure 6.8.1 — The filter learns of a switch only after the evidence arrives. A simulated two-state process switches at t = 100 (dashed line). The orange smoothed curve starts rising at the switch, using hindsight. The blue filtered curve, the one you could act on, crosses 0.5 about ten steps later. Simulation: Gaussian emissions with means 0 and 1, standard deviation 1, switch probability 0.01 in the model, one forced switch at t = 100, fixed seed 6008. Not market data.

6.8.4 Quantifying the lag

Take two states with Gaussian emissions of equal variance σ2\sigma^2 and means μ1,μ2\mu_1, \mu_2. Each observation from state 2 adds, on average,

𝔼[Δℓ]=(μ2−μ1)22σ2 \mathbb E[\Delta\ell] = \frac{(\mu_2-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma^2}

to the log-likelihood ratio. This is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the two emissions: a measure of how distinguishable they are.

The filter needs enough observations to build a log-odds change equal to the prior log-odds against a switch, which is set by A.

Result (approximate detection delay). delay≈log⁡((1−a)/a)DKL \text{delay} \approx \frac{\log\big((1-a)/a\big)}{D_{KL}} where aa is the switching probability.

Weakly separated regimes plus sticky transitions mean long delays. That is a fundamental limit, not an implementation issue. The same trade-off appears in change-point detection (next chapter) and in Wald’s sequential tests.

Figure 6.8.2 — Faint, sticky regimes take long to detect. Each curve is the delay formula for one switch probability a. Moving left (less separated regimes) makes delays explode. Moving from green to orange (stickier transitions) shifts the whole curve up. This is the formula plotted; no data is involved.

6.8.5 Engineering notes

  • Log space or scaling. Normalising every step (as above) prevents underflow. Keep the log normaliser for the likelihood.
  • Probability floors. A state at exactly zero probability can never come back. Floor tiny probabilities and renormalise.
  • Outlier handling. One extreme observation can swing the filter violently if emissions are Gaussian. Student-t emissions or a robust likelihood make it steadier.
  • Determinism. The recursion is cheap enough to replay over months of data. Make sure the replay produces identical numbers to the live path, including the treatment of session boundaries.

6.8.6 A causality checklist

Before trusting any regime feature built on an HMM, I ask:

  1. Were parameters estimated only from data before the time they are used?
  2. Is the probability filtered (forward only), never smoothed?
  3. Is state labelling stable across refits?
  4. Is the initial condition at each session boundary defined and causal?
  5. Does a replay from raw data reproduce the live numbers exactly?

If any answer is “no” or “not sure”, the feature is suspect.

6.8.7 Summary

  • The forward filter is predict-then-update, O(N²) per step, constant memory, strictly causal.
  • Honest online use needs causal parameters, stable labels and a defined session start.
  • Filtered probabilities lag switches; the delay is roughly log((1−a)/a) divided by the KL divergence.
  • Run the five-question checklist before trusting any HMM feature.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Two regimes have means 0 and 0.5 with σ = 1, and a = 0.01. Estimate the detection delay. (Answer: D_KL = 0.125; log(99) ≈ 4.6; delay ≈ 37 observations.)
  2. (Apply) For the same regimes, how much separation would you need to bring the delay under 10 observations?
  3. (Simulate) Reproduce Figure 6.8.1 over 1,000 seeds and plot the distribution of crossing times. Compare its median with the formula.
  4. (Think) Why does carrying yesterday’s final probability into today’s open risk leakage, and when is it acceptable?

Further reading

  • L. R. Rabiner, “A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models and Selected Applications in Speech Recognition,” Proceedings of the IEEE (1989).
  • O. Cappé and E. Moulines, “On-line Expectation–Maximization Algorithm for Latent Data Models,” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B (2009).
  • J. D. Hamilton, Time Series Analysis (1994), chapter 22.
  • A. Wald, Sequential Analysis (1947).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.9 — Bayesian Online Change-Point Detection with Normal-Inverse-Gamma Priors

Subtitle: Adams and MacKay’s run-length recursion, derived with conjugate updates you can implement allocation-free.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define the run length and write the BOCPD recursion. 2. Do the Normal-Inverse-Gamma conjugate update and its Student-t predictive. 3. Implement the algorithm with bounded memory, in log space. 4. Name the ways market data fools a change-point detector.

You need: Chapters 6.7–6.8 (HMMs, filtering), Bayes’ rule, and the idea of a conjugate prior (a prior whose posterior has the same form).

6.9.1 Change points versus regimes

Regime models like HMMs assume a fixed set of states that the market moves between. Change-point detection makes a weaker assumption: the data-generating process is piecewise stationary, and occasionally it changes to something new.

Bayesian online change-point detection (BOCPD), from Adams and MacKay (2007), answers “how long has the current regime lasted?” with a full posterior, updated one observation at a time. I implemented an exact version this year. It is one of the most elegant algorithms I know.

6.9.2 Run length

Definition. The run length rtr_t is the number of observations since the last change point. At each step either the run continues (rt=rt−1+1r_t = r_{t-1}+1) or a change occurs (rt=0r_t = 0). The goal is the posterior P(rt∣x1:t)P(r_t \mid x_{1:t}).

6.9.3 The recursion

The joint distribution satisfies

P(rt,x1:t)=∑rt−1P(rt∣rt−1)p(xt∣rt−1,x(r))P(rt−1,x1:t−1) P(r_t, x_{1:t}) = \sum_{r_{t-1}} P(r_t \mid r_{t-1})\;p\big(x_t \mid r_{t-1}, x^{(r)}\big)\;P(r_{t-1}, x_{1:t-1})

where x(r)x^{(r)} are the observations in the current run. Three ingredients:

1. Hazard function. P(rt=0∣rt−1)=H(rt−1)P(r_t = 0 \mid r_{t-1}) = H(r_{t-1}): the chance that a change happens now. With a constant hazard H=1/λH = 1/\lambda, the prior on run lengths is geometric with mean λ\lambda.

2. Predictive probability. πt(r)=p(xt∣x(r))\pi_t^{(r)} = p(x_t \mid x^{(r)}): the probability of the new observation under a model fitted only to the current run. With a conjugate prior this is closed form.

3. Growth and change-point probabilities.

P(rt=rt−1+1,x1:t)=P(rt−1,x1:t−1)πt(r)(1−H) P(r_t = r_{t-1}+1, x_{1:t}) = P(r_{t-1}, x_{1:t-1})\,\pi_t^{(r)}\,(1-H)

P(rt=0,x1:t)=∑rt−1P(rt−1,x1:t−1)πt(r)H P(r_t = 0, x_{1:t}) = \sum_{r_{t-1}} P(r_{t-1}, x_{1:t-1})\,\pi_t^{(r)}\,H

Normalise to get P(rt∣x1:t)P(r_t \mid x_{1:t}). That is the entire algorithm.

6.9.4 The Normal-Inverse-Gamma conjugate model

For Gaussian observations with unknown mean and variance, the conjugate prior is Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG):

σ2∼Inv-Gamma(α,β),μ∣σ2∼𝒩(μ0,σ2/κ) \sigma^2 \sim \text{Inv-Gamma}(\alpha, \beta), \qquad \mu \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal N(\mu_0, \sigma^2/\kappa)

with hyperparameters (μ0,κ,α,β)(\mu_0, \kappa, \alpha, \beta).

Result (NIG update). After observing xx, the posterior is again NIG with κ′=κ+1,μ0′=κμ0+xκ+1, \kappa' = \kappa + 1, \qquad \mu_0' = \frac{\kappa\mu_0 + x}{\kappa+1}, α′=α+12,β′=β+κ(x−μ0)22(κ+1). \alpha' = \alpha + \tfrac12, \qquad \beta' = \beta + \frac{\kappa(x-\mu_0)^2}{2(\kappa+1)}. The posterior predictive for the next observation is a Student-t: xnew∼t2α(μ0,β(κ+1)ακ) x_{\text{new}} \sim t_{2\alpha}\!\left(\mu_0,\; \frac{\beta(\kappa+1)}{\alpha\kappa}\right) with 2α2\alpha degrees of freedom, location μ0\mu_0 and the given squared scale. This is the πt(r)\pi_t^{(r)} in the recursion.

The Student-t predictive is a feature, not a nuisance. A short run has few observations, a small α\alpha, and so heavy tails: the model is appropriately unsure. A long run has many observations, and the predictive tightens toward a Gaussian.

6.9.5 Implementation, efficiently

For each possible run length, keep one set of NIG hyperparameters. At each step:

  1. Compute the Student-t predictive for every run length.
  2. Compute growth probabilities (shift every run length up by one).
  3. Compute the change-point probability (the sum, assigned to r=0r=0).
  4. Normalise.
  5. Update every run’s hyperparameters with the new observation; set r=0r=0 to the prior.

Naively the number of run lengths grows by one each step, so the cost is O(t)O(t) per observation and O(t2)O(t^2) in total. Practical fixes:

Fix How Effect
Truncation drop run lengths whose probability falls below a tiny threshold mass is usually concentrated on a few values
Fixed maximum run length ring buffer of size RmaxR_{\max}, aggregating anything older bounds memory and time; loop stays allocation-free
Log space store log probabilities; log-sum-exp for the change-point sum avoids underflow from tiny predictive densities

“Exact” here means “exact under the model, for the run lengths kept”. If you truncate, say so.

6.9.6 Reading the output

Useful summaries of P(rt∣x1:t)P(r_t \mid x_{1:t}):

  • Probability of a recent change: P(rt<k)P(r_t < k) for small kk.
  • MAP run length: the most likely rtr_t.
  • Expected run length: ∑rrP(rt=r)\sum_r r\,P(r_t = r).

A sharp drop in the MAP run length is the classic picture of a detected change.

Figure 6.9.1 — Data with three hidden changes. Simulated observations with a mean shift at t = 80, a mean-and-variance shift at t = 160 and another shift at t = 250 (dashed lines). The detector sees only the dots, one at a time.

Figure 6.9.2 — The run-length posterior drops to zero at each change. Blue shading is the posterior over run length at each time; the orange line is its most likely value. Between changes the run length climbs one step per observation. At each true change (dashed) it falls back to near zero within a few observations. Just after t = 160 it hesitates, because the new segment is noisier and early points are ambiguous. Simulation: piecewise Gaussian segments, constant hazard 1/100, NIG prior (μ₀ = 0, κ = 1, α = 1, β = 1), exact recursion with no truncation, fixed seed 6009. Not market data.

6.9.7 What goes wrong in markets

  • The hazard is a prior and it matters. A high hazard sees changes everywhere; a low one is slow. There is no free lunch: the detection-delay versus false-alarm trade-off from sequential analysis applies.
  • Model misspecification looks like change. Returns are heavy-tailed and volatility clusters. Under an NIG-Gaussian model, one large return looks like evidence of a new regime. The Student-t predictive helps for short runs but not for long ones. Modelling a transformed quantity, or using a richer observation model, reduces false alarms.
  • Autocorrelation. BOCPD assumes observations are independent within a run. Microstructure noise and overlapping returns violate that. Model residuals rather than raw values where possible.
  • Prior hyperparameters. (μ0,κ,α,β)(\mu_0, \kappa, \alpha, \beta) define what a “new regime” looks like at birth. Fitted on the full sample, they leak the future. Set them from a prior period.
  • Clock. As with every method in this part, the result depends on what one “observation” is: a fixed time bar, a trade, a unit of volume. Changing the clock changes the hazard’s meaning.

6.9.8 Summary

  • BOCPD tracks a posterior over “time since the last change”, updated one observation at a time.
  • Each step multiplies by a predictive, splits into growth and change, and normalises.
  • With an NIG prior the update is closed form and the predictive is a Student-t that is wide for short runs.
  • Truncate or cap run lengths and work in logs; say so when you truncate.
  • Hazard, misspecification, autocorrelation, priors and clock all shape what counts as a “change”.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With a constant hazard H = 1/250, what is the prior mean run length? (Answer: 250 observations.)
  2. (Apply) Start from NIG (μ₀ = 0, κ = 1, α = 1, β = 1) and observe x = 2. Compute the new hyperparameters. (Answer: κ = 2, μ₀ = 1, α = 1.5, β = 2.)
  3. (Simulate) Reproduce Figure 6.9.2, then replace the Gaussian data with Student-t data with 3 degrees of freedom and no change points. How many false changes appear?
  4. (Think) Why does fitting the prior hyperparameters on the whole sample count as lookahead?

Further reading

  • R. P. Adams and D. J. C. MacKay, “Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection,” arXiv:0710.3742 (2007).
  • P. Fearnhead and Z. Liu, “On-line Inference for Multiple Changepoint Problems,” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B (2007).
  • K. P. Murphy, “Conjugate Bayesian Analysis of the Gaussian Distribution,” technical note (2007).
  • E. S. Page, “Continuous Inspection Schemes,” Biometrika (1954) (CUSUM).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.10 — Volume Clock versus Time Clock

Subtitle: Markets don’t run on seconds. Measuring time in traded volume changes the statistics of returns, and it changes your models too.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why returns sampled on a clock are heteroskedastic and fat-tailed. 2. State Clark’s subordination idea and what it predicts. 3. Build volume bars or run a filter in volume time, and handle the practical traps. 4. Design a fair test of whether a clock helps on your own data.

You need: Chapter 6.3 (discretisation and the choice of clock), variance and kurtosis (a measure of how fat a distribution’s tails are; 3 for a normal).

6.10.1 Why the clock matters

Every model in this part has a time step Δt\Delta t somewhere. For a long time I took for granted that Δt\Delta t meant seconds. Then I re-ran the same filters with time measured in traded volume, and the residuals looked like a different market. This chapter explains why, the theory behind it, and the engineering it requires.

6.10.2 The problem with clock time

Activity is wildly uneven. The open and close are busy, lunch is quiet, scheduled announcements produce bursts, and overnight is a different world. In clock time, a one-minute return at 09:31 and one at 12:30 come from very different distributions. Returns sampled on a clock are:

  • Heteroskedastic: variance changes with time of day and with news.
  • Heavy-tailed: mixing low- and high-variance periods produces fat tails, even if each period is Gaussian.
  • Hard to model with a single noise level: a Kalman filter’s Q that fits lunch is wrong at the open.

6.10.3 Subordination: the theory

Clark (1973) proposed that prices evolve in a “business time” that runs faster when trading is intense:

P(t)=W(τ(t)) P(t) = W\big(\tau(t)\big)

Here WW is Brownian motion and τ(t)\tau(t) is a random, increasing time change driven by trading activity. This is called subordination.

Prediction. If τ\tau is proportional to cumulative volume, then returns over equal volume increments are closer to independent Gaussian. Returns over equal clock increments are a Gaussian mixture whose mixing is driven by volume, which explains the fat tails.

Ané and Geman (2000) found that the number of trades is an even better subordinator than volume for many assets. The general lesson: choose the clock that makes your increments closest to homogeneous.

Figure 6.10.1 — Volume time stretches busy periods and squeezes quiet ones. The blue curve is cumulative volume through a schematic day with a busy open and close. Where it is steep, volume time runs faster than the clock; where it is flat, slower. The dashed line is what uniform activity would give. The activity shape is a made-up U curve, not market data.

6.10.4 Volume bars and volume time

Two ways to use the idea:

Volume bars. Group trades into bars that each contain the same volume VV. A new bar closes when cumulative volume crosses the next multiple of VV. Easley, López de Prado and O’Hara popularised this for flow-toxicity measures. Bars arrive faster when the market is busy.

Volume time in continuous models. Keep tick-level updates but set the filter’s time step to the trade’s volume:

Δτk=vk \Delta\tau_k = v_k

The Van Loan discretisation of Chapter 6.3 works unchanged; only the meaning of Δt changes. Velocity becomes “price change per contract traded”, and process noise becomes “variance per contract”.

Figure 6.10.2 — Under subordination, sampling by volume removes the fat tails. Price is simulated as Brownian motion in volume time, with a U-shaped intraday activity curve and random day-to-day activity. Returns over equal clock minutes (orange) have fat tails (kurtosis about 4.6). Returns over equal volume (blue) match the normal curve (dashed). The log scale makes the tails visible. Simulation: 60 days of 390 minutes, fixed seed 6010; this shows what the theory predicts when its assumption holds, not what real data does.

6.10.5 Practical complications

Complication What happens What to do
Splitting large trades a bar boundary falls inside one large trade split it across bars (more faithful) or let bars overshoot (simpler); be consistent and document which
Prints that are not real trading block trades, auction prints, spreads and late reports can carry huge volume at one timestamp and jump the clock decide explicitly which trade types advance the clock
Session structure overnight volume is a fraction of daytime; in volume time the night compresses and the open expands often desirable, but a model still sees a structural break at the session boundary
Volume is non-stationary average daily volume trends and jumps (index rolls, holidays, events); a fixed VV gives many more bars on busy days some scale VV to a trailing average of daily volume; if so, compute it from prior days only
Discreteness integer contracts and tick prices give many zero-change steps at small increments account for it in the measurement noise, or aggregate more

6.10.6 Testing that a clock helps

The claim “volume time makes returns more Gaussian” is testable on your own data:

  1. Sample returns at equal clock intervals and at equal volume intervals, matched so the average number of samples per day is the same.
  2. Compare kurtosis, the autocorrelation of squared returns (volatility clustering), and normality tests.
  3. Run the same filter in both clocks and compare NIS behaviour (Chapter 6.4).

The literature (Ané and Geman, among others) reports that a transaction or volume clock moves returns closer to Gaussian. Run the comparison on your own data rather than assuming it. And remember: jumps on news remain jumps in any clock.

6.10.7 The trade-off

The volume clock is not free.

Volume clock Clock time
depends on volume data quality unambiguous
“how long ago” is harder to explain to people aligned with how people think about the day
can be gamed by your own definition of what counts as volume auditable

I keep both available, and treat the choice of clock as an explicit, named model parameter rather than an implicit assumption.

6.10.8 Engineering notes

  • Represent time as a pair: wall-clock timestamp and cumulative volume. Every derived quantity can then be computed in either clock.
  • Volume clocks are cumulative, so they need a reset rule (per session, per day). Make the rule explicit.
  • In replay, make sure the clock advances with the trade being processed, not before it. Advancing the clock on a trade and then using that trade’s price in the “previous” bar is a subtle lookahead.

6.10.9 Summary

  • Clock-time returns mix quiet and busy periods, which makes them heteroskedastic and fat-tailed.
  • Subordination says price is Brownian in business time; sampling by volume or trades undoes the mixing.
  • Volume bars and volume-time filters are two ways to use it; trade splitting, odd prints, sessions and drifting volume all need explicit rules.
  • Test the claim on your own data, and name the clock as a model parameter.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A normal distribution has kurtosis 3. A sample of clock returns has kurtosis 9. What does that say about its tails? (Answer: far fatter than normal: many more large moves than a Gaussian would give.)
  2. (Apply) Mix two zero-mean normals with variances 1 and 4, half and half. Compute the kurtosis of the mixture. (Hint: kurtosis = E[x⁴]/E[x²]², with E[x⁴] = 3σ⁴ for each part.)
  3. (Simulate) Rerun Figure 6.10.2 but give price a jump at a random time each day. Does the volume clock remove the jumps?
  4. (Think) Describe exactly how advancing the clock before processing a trade creates lookahead.

Further reading

  • P. K. Clark, “A Subordinated Stochastic Process Model with Finite Variance for Speculative Prices,” Econometrica (1973).
  • T. Ané and H. Geman, “Order Flow, Transaction Clock, and Normality of Asset Returns,” Journal of Finance (2000).
  • D. Easley, M. López de Prado and M. O’Hara, “The Volume Clock: Insights into the High-Frequency Paradigm,” Journal of Portfolio Management (2012).
  • M. López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), chapter 2.

— Tariq

Chapter 6.11 — Hawkes Processes for Trade Arrival Intensity

Subtitle: Trades cause trades. A self-exciting point process models that clustering, and its recursive form runs in constant time per event.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define a point process’s conditional intensity and the Hawkes self-exciting form. 2. Compute the branching ratio and the stationary mean intensity. 3. Update the exponential-kernel intensity in constant time per event and write its likelihood. 4. Check the fit with time rescaling, and handle seasonality, ties and kernel shape.

You need: the Poisson process (events arriving independently at a constant rate), exponentials and logs, and the idea of maximum likelihood.

6.11.1 Trades come in bursts

Trades do not arrive like a Poisson process. They come in bursts: one aggressive order triggers responses, which trigger more. If you plot the count of trades per second, you see clusters far tighter than independence would allow.

The Hawkes process is the standard model for this self-excitation. This year I use it to measure “how intense is activity right now, relative to its own recent history”. This chapter derives the parts you need to implement it.

6.11.2 Point processes and intensity

A point process is a random set of event times t1<t2<…t_1 < t_2 < \dots. Its conditional intensity is the instantaneous event rate given everything so far:

λ(t)=limh→0P(event in [t,t+h)∣ℋt)h \lambda(t) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{P(\text{event in } [t, t+h) \mid \mathcal H_t)}{h}

where ℋt\mathcal H_t is the history up to tt. A Poisson process has constant λ\lambda.

Definition (Hawkes, 1971). Each past event raises the intensity: λ(t)=μ+∑ti<tϕ(t−ti) \lambda(t) = \mu + \sum_{t_i < t}\phi(t - t_i) with baseline rate μ>0\mu > 0 and a non-negative kernel ϕ\phi.

6.11.3 The exponential kernel

The most common choice is ϕ(s)=αe−βs\phi(s) = \alpha e^{-\beta s}. Each event adds a jump α\alpha to the intensity, which then decays at rate β\beta. Two derived quantities:

  • Branching ratio n=∫0∞ϕ(s)ds=α/βn = \int_0^\infty\phi(s)\,ds = \alpha/\beta: the expected number of “child” events each event triggers.
  • Stationarity requires n<1n < 1. Then the long-run mean intensity is λ‾=μ/(1−n)\bar\lambda = \mu/(1-n).

Why μ/(1−n)\mu/(1-n). In a steady state, the mean rate equals the baseline plus the children of all events: λ‾=μ+nλ‾\bar\lambda = \mu + n\bar\lambda. Solve for λ‾\bar\lambda.

The branching ratio has a nice reading (Filimonov and Sornette): the fraction of events that are endogenous, triggered by earlier events rather than by outside arrivals. Estimates on liquid futures are often close to one, meaning most activity is reactive. Be careful with that reading, though; it is sensitive to the kernel shape and to how simultaneous events are handled.

Figure 6.11.1 — Each event kicks the intensity up; it then decays. The blue line is the intensity of a simulated Hawkes process; orange ticks on the axis are its events. Bursts of events push the intensity far above its long-run mean (grey dashed), and in quiet spells it decays toward the baseline μ (green dashed). Simulation: exponential kernel with μ = 0.5, α = 0.8, β = 1 (branching ratio 0.8), Ogata thinning, fixed seed 6011. Not market data.

Figure 6.11.2 — Same average rate, very different texture. The blue row is a Poisson process at the Hawkes model’s long-run rate. The orange row is the Hawkes path from Figure 6.11.1. The Poisson events are scattered evenly; the Hawkes events cluster into bursts separated by gaps. Seeds 6111 (Poisson) and 6011 (Hawkes); one sample path each, so event counts differ by chance.

6.11.4 The recursion that makes it fast

Naively, evaluating λ(t)\lambda(t) needs a sum over all past events. With an exponential kernel it collapses to a recursion. Define

Ak=∑i<ke−β(tk−ti) A_k = \sum_{i<k} e^{-\beta(t_k - t_i)}

Result (recursive intensity). Ak=e−β(tk−tk−1)(1+Ak−1),λ(tk−)=μ+αAk A_{k} = e^{-\beta(t_k - t_{k-1})}\,(1 + A_{k-1}), \qquad \lambda(t_k^-) = \mu + \alpha A_k

One multiply-add per event, constant memory, no allocation. That is why the exponential kernel dominates practical use.

6.11.5 Maximum likelihood

For events in [0,T][0, T], the log-likelihood of a point process is

ℓ=∑klog⁡λ(tk)−∫0Tλ(s)ds \ell = \sum_k \log\lambda(t_k) - \int_0^T\lambda(s)\,ds

The integral is called the compensator: the expected number of events so far. For the exponential Hawkes process it is closed form:

∫0Tλ(s)ds=μT+αβ∑k(1−e−β(T−tk)) \int_0^T\lambda(s)\,ds = \mu T + \frac{\alpha}{\beta}\sum_k\left(1 - e^{-\beta(T - t_k)}\right)

So the log-likelihood costs O(n)O(n) with the recursion (Ozaki, 1979).

  • Optimise over (μ,α,β)(\mu, \alpha, \beta) with a bounded optimiser: all three must be positive, and α<β\alpha < \beta for stationarity.
  • The likelihood surface is often flat along ridges where α/β\alpha/\beta is constant, so different (α,β)(\alpha, \beta) pairs fit almost equally well. Report the branching ratio and its uncertainty, not just point estimates.

6.11.6 Goodness of fit: time rescaling

Time-rescaling theorem. If the model is correct, the compensator increments τk=∫tk−1tkλ(s)ds \tau_k = \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}\lambda(s)\,ds are independent exponential variables with mean one.

A Q–Q plot of τk\tau_k against the exponential distribution, or a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, checks the fit. This is the point-process cousin of NIS for Kalman filters (Chapter 6.4), and just as informative.

6.11.7 What markets do to Hawkes models

Problem Effect Remedy
Intraday seasonality a constant μ across the day makes the open look like self-excitation model μ(t) as a deterministic seasonal profile estimated from prior days; let the kernel capture the rest
Timestamp resolution many trades share a timestamp (one aggressive order filling against several resting orders); zero gaps break the likelihood aggregate same-timestamp prints into one event (a “meta-order” view) or jitter timestamps; say which
One exponential is too simple empirical kernels decay more like a power law sums of exponentials approximate a power law and keep the recursion
Marks large trades may excite more marked Hawkes scales the jump by a function of trade size
Cross-excitation buys excite sells; one instrument excites another multivariate Hawkes, a natural lead–lag model
Non-stationarity parameters drift across days and regimes rolling estimation on strictly causal windows

6.11.8 Using intensity as a feature

The filtered intensity λ(t)\lambda(t) is a causal, smoothly decaying measure of activity. Its ratio to the long-run mean, λ(t)/λ‾\lambda(t)/\bar\lambda, says how unusually active the market is right now.

It reacts instantly to bursts and decays at a known rate. That makes it better behaved than counting trades in a fixed window, which jumps when old trades fall out. That is the property I value most: no window edges.

6.11.9 Summary

  • A Hawkes process adds a decaying bump to the intensity after each event, so events cluster.
  • Branching ratio n = α/β; stationary if n < 1, with mean intensity μ/(1−n).
  • The exponential kernel gives an O(1) recursion and an O(n) likelihood; report n with its uncertainty.
  • Check fit with time rescaling; handle seasonality, ties, kernel shape and drift explicitly.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With μ = 1, α = 0.6, β = 1, what is the long-run mean intensity? (Answer: n = 0.6; 1/(1 − 0.6) = 2.5 events per unit time.)
  2. (Derive) Prove the recursion for AkA_k from its definition.
  3. (Simulate) Simulate with Ogata thinning, compute the τₖ under the true parameters, and make a Q–Q plot against Exp(1). Then compute them under a Poisson model with the same mean rate and compare.
  4. (Think) Why does a constant baseline make the market open look like strong self-excitation?

Further reading

  • A. G. Hawkes, “Spectra of Some Self-Exciting and Mutually Exciting Point Processes,” Biometrika (1971).
  • T. Ozaki, “Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Hawkes’ Self-Exciting Point Processes,” Annals of the Institute of Statistical Mathematics (1979).
  • E. Bacry, I. Mastromatteo and J.-F. Muzy, “Hawkes Processes in Finance,” Market Microstructure and Liquidity (2015).
  • V. Filimonov and D. Sornette, “Quantifying Reflexivity in Financial Markets,” Physical Review E (2012).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.12 — Kyle’s Lambda and Price Impact

Subtitle: How much does price move per unit of net order flow? The model behind the number, and how to estimate it without fooling yourself.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Set up the Kyle (1985) model and state its equilibrium λ. 2. Explain why λ rises with private information and falls with noise trading. 3. Estimate λ by regression and name the four hidden choices that bias it. 4. Distinguish permanent from transient impact, and linear from square-root impact.

You need: linear regression, conditional expectation, and the idea of signed order flow (buys positive, sells negative).

6.12.1 Price impact

Price impact is the most basic fact of market microstructure: buying pushes price up, selling pushes it down. Kyle’s lambda is the coefficient that measures how much. It appears everywhere from execution-cost models to liquidity measures.

This year I estimate it as a descriptive statistic of market conditions. Getting it right taught me a lot about how fragile simple regressions are on tick data.

6.12.2 The Kyle (1985) model

One risky asset with value v∼𝒩(p0,Σ0)v \sim \mathcal N(p_0, \Sigma_0). Three players:

  • An informed trader who knows vv and submits order xx.
  • Noise traders who submit u∼𝒩(0,σu2)u \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_u^2), independent of vv.
  • A competitive market maker who sees only total order flow y=x+uy = x + u and sets price p=𝔼[v∣y]p = \mathbb E[v \mid y].

Figure 6.12.1 — The market maker sees only the total. The informed order x and the noise order u merge into one flow y. The market maker (green) cannot split it, so it moves price by λ for every unit of y, informed or not.

Result (Kyle’s linear equilibrium). x=β(v−p0),p=p0+λy, x = \beta(v - p_0), \qquad p = p_0 + \lambda y, β=σuΣ0,λ=Σ02σu. \beta = \frac{\sigma_u}{\sqrt{\Sigma_0}}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\sqrt{\Sigma_0}}{2\sigma_u}.

Intuition. The market maker cannot tell informed flow from noise, so prices respond to all flow.

Change Effect on λ
more private information (Σ0\Sigma_0 larger) λ larger: more impact
more noise trading to hide behind (σu\sigma_u larger) λ smaller: less impact

1/λ1/\lambda is the market’s depth: the order flow needed to move the price by one unit.

In equilibrium, half the private information is built into the price in a single-period model. In the continuous-time version, information enters gradually and the price follows a Brownian bridge (a random walk pinned to end at a known value) to vv.

6.12.3 Estimating lambda

The empirical version regresses price changes on signed order flow over intervals:

Δpt=λOFt+εt,OFt=∑trades in tsivi \Delta p_t = \lambda\,\text{OF}_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \text{OF}_t = \sum_{\text{trades in } t} s_i\,v_i

where si=±1s_i = \pm1 is the trade’s direction and viv_i its size. That looks simple. Each piece hides a choice.

Trade direction. Exchanges often report the aggressor side directly for futures. Where they don’t, it must be inferred:

Rule Classifies a trade as a buy when
Tick rule it is an up-tick
Quote rule it is above the midpoint
Lee–Ready quote rule, falling back to tick rule at the midpoint

Each misclassifies some trades. That biases λ toward zero (errors-in-variables attenuation: noise in the regressor shrinks the slope).

Interval length. Over very short intervals, bid–ask bounce adds noise; over long ones, information from other sources dominates. λ is not scale-invariant: estimates at different horizons differ, and the difference tells you how much impact is transient.

Simultaneity. Price changes also cause order flow (momentum traders chase moves, stop orders trigger). Regressing Δp on OF over the same interval mixes impact with reaction. There is no clean fix in a single-equation regression. Vector autoregressions (Hasbrouck, 1991) separate the effects under identifying assumptions.

Concavity. Empirically, impact is concave in size. The square-root law,

Δp≈YσQV, \Delta p \approx Y\,\sigma\sqrt{\frac{Q}{V}},

where QQ is the metaorder size (a large order executed in pieces), VV daily volume and σ\sigma daily volatility, fits remarkably well across markets for completed metaorders. Linear λ is a local approximation that works for small flows.

Figure 6.12.2 — A line fitted to small flows overstates large ones. The blue curve is the square-root law in scaled units. The orange dashed line has the same value at a small order size. It agrees near zero but rises far faster afterwards. Both are formula plots in arbitrary units; no data is involved.

6.12.4 Transient versus permanent impact

Kyle’s model has only permanent impact: the price moves and stays. Real markets show a large transient part that decays after the flow stops, as liquidity providers refill the book. Propagator models (Bouchaud et al., 2004) write

pt=p0+∑s<tG(t−s)ϵsvsδ+noise p_t = p_0 + \sum_{s<t} G(t-s)\,\epsilon_s v_s^{\delta} + \text{noise}

with a decaying kernel GG. A single λ mixes the two components together.

6.12.5 Practical estimation notes

  • Rolling and causal. Estimate λ on trailing windows only. Liquidity changes through the day and across regimes.
  • Robust regression. A handful of large moves on news can dominate least squares. Huber loss or trimming helps; report which you used.
  • Normalise. λ in price-per-contract is not comparable across instruments or volatility regimes. Normalising by volatility and average volume makes it interpretable.
  • Recursive estimation. Recursive least squares with a forgetting factor gives a smoothly updating λ per event without refitting windows (Chapter 6.14).
  • Clock matters. Estimating per fixed time interval and per fixed volume interval gives different quantities. In volume time, the regression is closer to “impact per unit of flow” by construction.

6.12.6 What lambda is useful for

  • Description. λ tells you how thin the market is right now: the same flow moves price more when liquidity is scarce.
  • Costs. It is a component of transaction-cost estimates.
  • Humility. If your own orders move price, any backtest that assumes fills at the observed price without impact is optimistic in proportion to λ and your size.

6.12.7 Summary

  • In Kyle’s model λ = √Σ₀ / (2σᵤ): more information, more impact; more noise, less.
  • The regression estimate depends on trade signing, interval length, simultaneity and size concavity.
  • Real impact is partly transient and roughly square-root in size; a single linear λ is a local summary.
  • Estimate causally, robustly and normalised, and name the clock.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Σ₀ = 4 and σᵤ = 10. What are λ and the depth 1/λ? (Answer: λ = 2/20 = 0.1; depth = 10 units of flow per unit of price.)
  2. (Apply) Noise trading doubles. By what factor does λ change?
  3. (Simulate) Generate order flow and price changes with a true λ, then flip the sign of 20% of trades at random. Re-estimate λ and compare. What does the attenuation look like?
  4. (Think) Why does regressing price change on same-interval order flow mix impact with reaction?

Further reading

  • A. S. Kyle, “Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading,” Econometrica (1985).
  • J. Hasbrouck, “Measuring the Information Content of Stock Trades,” Journal of Finance (1991).
  • J.-P. Bouchaud, Y. Gefen, M. Potters and M. Wyart, “Fluctuations and Response in Financial Markets,” Quantitative Finance (2004).
  • J.-P. Bouchaud, J. Bonart, J. Donier and M. Gould, Trades, Quotes and Prices (2018).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.13 — Order-Flow Imbalance: Measuring Pressure at the Top of the Book

Subtitle: Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov’s OFI, derived from queue changes, and why it explains short-horizon price moves better than trade imbalance.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why most order-book activity never shows up in trades. 2. Compute the OFI contribution of a top-of-book update, case by case. 3. State the linear OFI–price relation and why its slope depends on depth. 4. List the data and interpretation traps of OFI.

You need: Chapter 6.12 (price impact), and the basic limit order book: bids, asks, queues at each price.

6.13.1 Beyond trade imbalance

Trade imbalance (buys minus sells) is the obvious way to measure buying pressure. But most of the action in a limit order book never trades. Orders are placed and cancelled far more often than they are filled.

Order-flow imbalance (OFI) captures that. It counts net changes in supply and demand at the best quotes from every event, not only trades. This chapter derives it and covers the practical problems of computing it from real feeds.

6.13.2 The book at the top

At any moment the best bid is PbP^b with size qbq^b, and the best ask is PaP^a with size qaq^a. Three kinds of events change those queues:

Event Effect on a queue
Limit order adds to it
Cancellation removes from it
Market order consumes it

A buy market order and a cancellation on the ask side both reduce supply. A new bid and a cancelled ask both shift the balance toward buyers. OFI treats them symmetrically.

6.13.3 The definition

Definition (Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov, 2014). For each update nn of the best quotes, en=𝟙{Pnb≥Pn−1b}qnb−𝟙{Pnb≤Pn−1b}qn−1b⏟bid side−(𝟙{Pna≤Pn−1a}qna−𝟙{Pna≥Pn−1a}qn−1a)⏟ask side e_n = \underbrace{\mathbb 1\{P^b_n \ge P^b_{n-1}\}q^b_n - \mathbb 1\{P^b_n \le P^b_{n-1}\}q^b_{n-1}}_{\text{bid side}} \;-\; \underbrace{\left(\mathbb 1\{P^a_n \le P^a_{n-1}\}q^a_n - \mathbb 1\{P^a_n \ge P^a_{n-1}\}q^a_{n-1}\right)}_{\text{ask side}} OFI over an interval is the sum: OFIk=∑n∈interval ken\text{OFI}_k = \sum_{n \in \text{interval } k} e_n.

Read the bid side case by case:

  • Bid price unchanged: contribution is qnb−qn−1bq^b_n - q^b_{n-1}, the change in queue size.
  • Bid price rose: the whole new queue qnbq^b_n is new demand.
  • Bid price fell: the whole old queue qn−1bq^b_{n-1} has vanished (consumed or cancelled).

The ask side mirrors this, with signs flipped, because ask-side supply pushes price down.

Figure 6.13.1 — Three cases on the bid side. Each panel shows the best-bid queue before (grey) and after (coloured) one update, drawn at its price level. Left: same price, queue grew from 5 to 7, so e = +2. Middle: the bid moved up, so the whole new queue of 4 counts as new demand. Right: the bid moved down, so the whole old queue of 5 counts as lost demand. The numbers are made up for illustration.

6.13.4 The linear price-impact relation

The central empirical finding: mid-price changes over short intervals are approximately linear in OFI:

ΔPk=βkOFIk+εk \Delta P_k = \beta_k\,\text{OFI}_k + \varepsilon_k

with a slope inversely proportional to market depth:

β≈cD‾ \beta \approx \frac{c}{\bar D}

where D‾\bar D is the average queue size at the best quotes.

Intuition. If queues are deep, it takes more net flow to deplete one and move the price a tick. A stylised model where queue depletion triggers a price change gives this relation directly.

Measure Sees Typical explanatory power at short horizons
Trade imbalance trades only lower
OFI trades, cancellations and new limit orders much higher
Kyle’s λ regressor signed trade flow poorer regressor; OFI’s β has a direct depth reading

6.13.5 Multi-level OFI

The top of the book is not everything; deeper levels also hold information. Multi-level OFI computes the same quantity at each of the first several levels. It then either combines them (with weights from regression or principal components) or uses them as separate regressors. Xu, Gould and Howison (2019) and Cont, Cucuringu and Zhang (2023) explore this. Deeper levels add explanatory power but also more noise and more choices.

6.13.6 Computing it from real feeds

  • You need book data, not just trades. OFI requires every top-of-book update. A trade-only feed cannot produce it. A quote feed with snapshots at intervals loses intermediate events and underestimates OFI magnitude.
  • Event ordering. A trade and the resulting quote change usually arrive as separate messages. If your feed delivers them out of order, or you merge two feeds with different timestamps, you can count the same depletion twice or miss it. Process events in exchange sequence-number order where possible.
  • Implied liquidity. For futures, some displayed liquidity is implied from spread markets. It can appear and disappear as other markets move, generating OFI that does not reflect outright orders.
  • Normalisation. Raw OFI is in contracts. To compare across times of day or instruments, normalise by depth (D‾\bar D) or by a trailing standard deviation. Any normalisation must be causal.
  • Interval choice. The linear relation holds best at short horizons. As the interval lengthens, other information dominates. The same clock question as always applies: fixed seconds, fixed events, or fixed volume.

6.13.7 Pitfalls

Concurrency is not causality. OFI and price changes over the same interval are mechanically related: a queue depleting is the price changing. A high R2R^2 for same-interval OFI is a description, not a forecast. Predictive use requires lagged OFI, and the predictive power of lagged OFI is much weaker.

  • Spoofing and flicker. Orders placed and cancelled within microseconds inflate OFI without representing real intent. Some practitioners filter orders by lifetime, which requires order-level data.
  • Tick size. For large-tick instruments (spread usually one tick), queue dynamics dominate and OFI works well. For small-tick instruments, prices change more often for reasons OFI captures less cleanly.

6.13.8 Engineering notes

  • OFI is a running sum of simple increments: O(1)O(1) per book update, trivially allocation-free.
  • Keep the previous top-of-book state per instrument. Reset it cleanly at session boundaries and after feed gaps; an increment computed across a gap is meaningless.
  • Store raw OFI and the normalisation separately, so the normalisation can change without recomputing from raw data.

6.13.9 Summary

  • OFI counts net demand changes at the best quotes from every event, not only trades.
  • Each update contributes by one of three cases per side: same price (queue change), better price (whole new queue), worse price (whole old queue).
  • Short-horizon price changes are roughly linear in OFI, with slope inversely proportional to depth.
  • Same-interval fit is description, not forecast; data ordering, implied liquidity and flicker need care.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) The best bid stays at the same price and its queue goes from 12 to 9. The ask does not change. What is e? (Answer: −3.)
  2. (Apply) The ask price falls by one tick and the new ask queue is 6. The bid does not change. What is e, and why is its sign negative?
  3. (Code) Write a function that takes two top-of-book snapshots and returns e. Test it on all nine combinations of bid and ask price moves.
  4. (Think) Why does a high R² between same-interval OFI and price change not show that OFI predicts prices?

Further reading

  • R. Cont, A. Kukanov and S. Stoikov, “The Price Impact of Order Book Events,” Journal of Financial Econometrics (2014).
  • K. Xu, M. D. Gould and S. D. Howison, “Multi-Level Order-Flow Imbalance in a Limit Order Book,” Market Microstructure and Liquidity (2019).
  • R. Cont, M. Cucuringu and C. Zhang, “Cross-Impact of Order Flow Imbalance in Equity Markets,” Quantitative Finance (2023).
  • J.-P. Bouchaud, J. Bonart, J. Donier and M. Gould, Trades, Quotes and Prices (2018).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.14 — Recursive Least Squares and a Cross-Asset Beta That Updates Every Tick

Subtitle: RLS is regression that learns one observation at a time. It is also a Kalman filter in disguise.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Write exponentially weighted least squares and its recursive (RLS) update. 2. Show that RLS is a Kalman filter with a random-walk coefficient. 3. Recognise covariance windup, errors-in-variables bias and the Epps effect. 4. Treat the forgetting factor as a documented bias–variance choice.

You need: ordinary least squares, Chapter 6.2 (Kalman filter), and Chapter 6.4 (innovation checks).

6.14.1 The problem

Two index futures that track overlapping baskets move together, but not one-for-one, and the relationship drifts through the day. To measure that relationship continuously I needed a regression coefficient that:

  • updates with every new observation,
  • forgets the distant past,
  • costs a few multiplications.

Recursive least squares (RLS) is exactly that. This chapter derives it, connects it to the Kalman filter, and lists the ways it misbehaves.

6.14.2 From batch to weighted regression

We observe pairs (xt,yt)(x_t, y_t), for example returns of two instruments, and want

yt=θ⊤ϕt+εt y_t = \theta^\top \phi_t + \varepsilon_t

where ϕt\phi_t is a regressor vector (say [1,xt]⊤[1, x_t]^\top for an intercept and a beta). Ordinary least squares on all data up to tt:

θ̂t=(∑s≤tϕsϕs⊤)−1∑s≤tϕsys \hat\theta_t = \Big(\sum_{s\le t}\phi_s\phi_s^\top\Big)^{-1}\sum_{s\le t}\phi_s y_s

Recomputing this every step is wasteful, and we usually want old data to count less. So minimise the exponentially weighted loss

Jt(θ)=∑s=1tλt−s(ys−θ⊤ϕs)2 J_t(\theta) = \sum_{s=1}^t \lambda^{t-s}\left(y_s - \theta^\top\phi_s\right)^2

with forgetting factor 0<λ≤10 < \lambda \le 1. The effective memory is about 1/(1−λ)1/(1-\lambda) observations.

6.14.3 The RLS recursion

Let Pt=(∑sλt−sϕsϕs⊤)−1P_t = \big(\sum_s \lambda^{t-s}\phi_s\phi_s^\top\big)^{-1}.

Algorithm (RLS). kt=Pt−1ϕtλ+ϕt⊤Pt−1ϕt,et=yt−θ̂t−1⊤ϕt, k_t = \frac{P_{t-1}\phi_t}{\lambda + \phi_t^\top P_{t-1}\phi_t}, \qquad e_t = y_t - \hat\theta_{t-1}^\top\phi_t, θ̂t=θ̂t−1+ktet,Pt=1λ(Pt−1−ktϕt⊤Pt−1). \hat\theta_t = \hat\theta_{t-1} + k_t e_t, \qquad P_t = \frac{1}{\lambda}\left(P_{t-1} - k_t\phi_t^\top P_{t-1}\right).

The update of PP comes from the Sherman–Morrison formula for a rank-one update of an inverse. That is why no matrix inversion is needed. For a two-parameter model this is a handful of multiplications per observation.

6.14.4 RLS is a Kalman filter

Treat θ\theta as a hidden state that does a random walk:

θt=θt−1+wt,yt=ϕt⊤θt+vt \theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad y_t = \phi_t^\top\theta_t + v_t

Run a Kalman filter with F=IF = I and H=ϕt⊤H = \phi_t^\top.

  • With Q=0Q = 0, the update equations are identical to RLS with λ=1\lambda = 1.
  • With forgetting, the predicted covariance becomes Pt−1/λP_{t-1}/\lambda. That equals adding process noise proportional to the current covariance.

Key point. The forgetting factor is a particular, multiplicative choice of Q.

This matters because it gives you the Kalman toolkit for free: innovation statistics, NIS consistency checks, and the option to replace multiplicative forgetting with an explicit Q that reflects how fast you believe beta really drifts.

6.14.5 Initialisation

RLS needs θ̂0\hat\theta_0 and P0P_0. A common choice is θ̂0=0\hat\theta_0 = 0 and P0=δ−1IP_0 = \delta^{-1}I with small δ\delta (large initial uncertainty), so early data dominate quickly. Alternatively, initialise from an OLS fit on a strictly prior window. Either way, the first stretch of estimates reflects the initialisation more than the data; treat it as warm-up.

Figure 6.14.1 — Short memory reacts fast; long memory lags. The dashed line is the true beta of a simulated pair: it drops at t = 600, then drifts up. The orange short-memory estimate catches the drop quickly but is noisy. The blue long-memory estimate is smooth but takes hundreds of steps to follow. In the grey band the regressor goes almost silent; when it returns, the orange estimate jumps. Simulation: y = βₜx + noise, Gaussian x with standard deviation 1 (0.02 in the grey band), noise standard deviation 0.5, 1,500 steps, fixed seed 6014; λ values are illustration choices. Not market data.

6.14.6 Failure modes

Covariance windup. If the regressor stops varying (the other instrument goes quiet), ϕtϕt⊤\phi_t\phi_t^\top adds little information, but forgetting keeps dividing PP by λ\lambda. PP grows exponentially in the directions that get no information. When the next informative observation arrives, the estimate jumps wildly. Fixes:

  • directional forgetting (forget only in directions that receive new information),
  • bounding the trace of PP,
  • using the Kalman form with additive Q.

Figure 6.14.2 — Windup: P explodes while nothing is learned. The same short-memory run as Figure 6.14.1, showing its covariance P on a log scale. In the grey band the regressor is nearly zero, so each step divides P by λ and it grows in a straight line on the log scale. When normal data returns, the inflated P makes the estimate jump.

Loss of symmetry and positive definiteness. As with the Kalman filter, rounding can break PP. Symmetrise after each update; consider a square-root or UD-factorised implementation for long-running filters.

Errors in variables. OLS assumes the regressor is measured without error. If xtx_t is a noisy return (microstructure noise, asynchronous sampling), beta is biased toward zero. This attenuation is a real problem for high-frequency cross-asset betas.

Asynchronous data. Two instruments do not trade at the same instants. Sampling both on a fixed clock with “last price” gives stale prices for the less active one, which biases correlation downward (the Epps effect). Options:

Option Trade-off
sample at a coarser frequency less staleness, less data
refresh-time sampling (wait until both have traded) removes staleness, discards data
estimators built for asynchronous data (Hayashi–Yoshida) more complex

Outliers. One bad tick in either series produces a large ete_t and a big jump in θ̂\hat\theta. Gate on the normalised innovation, or use a robust (Huber) variant of RLS.

6.14.7 Choosing the forgetting factor

This is the bias–variance trade-off in its purest form. A short memory tracks changes quickly but gives noisy betas. A long memory gives smooth betas that lag regime changes. There is no right answer without saying what the beta is for.

I choose it as an explicit, documented modelling decision, and check the innovation statistics for evidence that it is badly wrong. I don’t optimise it against downstream performance without counting that as a trial.

6.14.8 Engineering notes

  • For two parameters, write the algebra by hand: no matrix library, no allocation.
  • Process both instruments’ updates in timestamp order through one event loop, so the regression always uses data known at that instant.
  • Log θ̂\hat\theta, the trace of PP, and the normalised innovation. Windup and drift show up there first.

6.14.9 Summary

  • RLS updates a weighted least-squares fit in O(1) per observation, with no inversion.
  • It is a Kalman filter on a random-walk coefficient; forgetting is a multiplicative Q.
  • Windup, broken covariance, errors in variables, asynchronous data and outliers are the main failure modes.
  • The forgetting factor is a bias–variance choice; document it, check innovations, and count tuning as trials.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) What is the effective memory of λ = 0.99? Of λ = 0.999? (Answer: about 100 and about 1,000 observations.)
  2. (Derive) Use the Sherman–Morrison formula to derive the PtP_t update from the definition of PtP_t.
  3. (Simulate) Reproduce Figure 6.14.2, then cap the trace of P at a fixed value. How large is the jump after the quiet band now?
  4. (Think) Why does noise in the regressor x bias beta toward zero, while noise in y does not?

Further reading

  • S. Haykin, Adaptive Filter Theory (2002), chapters on RLS.
  • L. Ljung and T. Söderström, Theory and Practice of Recursive Identification (1983).
  • T. W. Epps, “Comovements in Stock Prices in the Very Short Run,” Journal of the American Statistical Association (1979).
  • T. Hayashi and N. Yoshida, “On Covariance Estimation of Non-Synchronously Observed Diffusion Processes,” Bernoulli (2005).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.15 — Measuring Lead–Lag Between Instruments Without Fooling Yourself

Subtitle: “Futures lead the ETF” or “one index leads the other” are claims about cross-correlation at nonzero lags. Asynchronous data makes them very easy to get wrong.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compute a cross-correlation function and the lead–lag ratio. 2. Explain four artefacts that create fake lead–lag: stale prices, Epps, bounce, timestamps. 3. Use the Hayashi–Yoshida estimator, refresh-time sampling and event studies. 4. Build a fair null for lead–lag significance and judge whether a real lead is usable.

You need: correlation, Chapter 6.14 (asynchronous data and the Epps effect), and the idea of a bootstrap.

6.15.1 The claim

Every trader has heard that one instrument leads another. Futures lead cash, large caps lead small caps, one index leads its sibling. If true, the leader’s moves tell you something about the follower’s next moves.

Measuring it properly turned out to be much harder than computing a cross-correlation. This chapter is about the reasons.

6.15.2 The naive approach

Sample both prices on a regular grid, compute returns rtXr^X_t and rtYr^Y_t, and estimate the cross-correlation function:

ρXY(ℓ)=Cov(rtX,rt+ℓY)σXσY \rho_{XY}(\ell) = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(r^X_t, r^Y_{t+\ell})}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}

If ρ(ℓ)\rho(\ell) peaks at some ℓ>0\ell > 0, then X leads Y by ℓ\ell. A common summary is the lead–lag ratio (Huth and Abergel, 2014):

LLR=∑ℓ>0ρ2(ℓ)∑ℓ<0ρ2(ℓ) \text{LLR} = \frac{\sum_{\ell>0}\rho^2(\ell)}{\sum_{\ell<0}\rho^2(\ell)}

Greater than one means X tends to lead.

6.15.3 Why the naive approach lies

Stale prices. On a fixed grid, you use the last traded price in each interval. If Y trades less often than X, its “price” at time t is really its price at some earlier time. That staleness creates an apparent lag: Y seems to follow X simply because it updates later. A completely efficient, simultaneous relationship looks like lead–lag when one instrument is less liquid.

Figure 6.15.1 — A fake lead from stale prices alone. Both X and Y follow the same random walk, so there is no true lead–lag. X trades every step; Y trades only 20% of the time, and both are sampled on a grid with “last traded price”. The cross-correlation still shows large orange bars at positive lags, which a naive reading would call “X leads Y”. Simulation: Gaussian random walk, 200,000 steps, grid of 5 steps, fixed seed 6015. Not market data.

The Epps effect. As the sampling interval shrinks, measured correlation between assets drops toward zero. Asynchronous trading means returns in the same small interval often don’t overlap in real time. Lead–lag estimates at very fine resolution are dominated by this artefact.

Microstructure noise. Bid–ask bounce induces negative autocorrelation in each series. Cross-correlations at small lags pick up a mixture of bounce and real dynamics.

Timestamp differences. If two instruments come from different exchanges or feeds, their timestamps may differ systematically by milliseconds. A fixed clock offset produces a fixed apparent lead. Before believing any sub-second lead–lag, check where the timestamps come from and whether they are comparable.

6.15.4 Better estimators

Hayashi–Yoshida. For prices observed at different times, this covariance estimator sums products of returns over all pairs of intervals that overlap in time:

Cov̂=∑i,jriXrjY𝟙{(ti−1X,tiX]∩(tj−1Y,tjY]≠∅} \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}} = \sum_{i,j} r^X_i\, r^Y_j\,\mathbb 1\{(t^X_{i-1}, t^X_i] \cap (t^Y_{j-1}, t^Y_j] \ne \emptyset\}

No interpolation, no stale prices. It is unbiased for the integrated covariance when there is no noise. Shift one series’ timestamps by ℓ\ell and recompute to get a lagged version; the lag that maximises it estimates the lead (Hoffmann, Rosenbaum and Yoshida, 2013).

Method Idea Cost
Hayashi–Yoshida (lagged) overlap-based covariance, shifted in time more computation
Refresh-time sampling sample only when both have traded since the last sample discards data
Event-time conditioning after each event in the leader (say a price change in X), measure the follower’s response vs. its response after random times an event study; needs a null

6.15.5 Statistical significance

Cross-correlations of financial returns are noisy and autocorrelated. The textbook band of ±2/N\pm 2/\sqrt N assumes white noise, which high-frequency returns are not. You also usually scan many lags, so the maximum of many noisy correlations is biased upward. Two practical defences:

  • Shuffle or block-bootstrap tests. Shift one series by a random large offset. That destroys real lead–lag but keeps each series’ own structure. Recompute. The distribution of the statistic under those shifts is your null.
  • Stability. A real lead–lag should appear consistently across days. Compute it per day and look at the distribution, not just a pooled estimate.

6.15.6 Interpretation

Even a genuine, stable lead–lag in returns does not imply a usable forecast:

  • If the lead is shorter than your latency, it is not available to you.
  • If it exists only in mid-prices and disappears once you pay to cross the spread, it is not available either.
  • Price discovery measures (Hasbrouck’s information share, Gonzalo–Granger component shares) tell you which market incorporates information first in a cointegrated system. That is related to, but different from, lagged cross-correlation.

6.15.7 Engineering notes

  • Keep raw, timestamped events for both instruments. Any resampling should be a reversible view, not the stored data.
  • Record the source and precision of every timestamp. Mixing exchange timestamps with receive timestamps invalidates sub-second analysis.
  • Compute everything in one deterministic event loop, merging both streams in timestamp order with a defined tie-break rule.

6.15.8 Summary

  • Lead–lag is a claim about cross-correlation at nonzero lags.
  • Stale prices, the Epps effect, bounce and timestamp offsets all manufacture fake leads.
  • Hayashi–Yoshida, refresh-time sampling and event studies reduce the artefacts.
  • Test against shifted-series nulls, check day-by-day stability, and ask whether the lead survives latency and costs.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) ρ²(ℓ) sums to 0.20 over positive lags and 0.05 over negative lags. What is the LLR, and which way does it point? (Answer: 4; X appears to lead Y.)
  2. (Apply) In Figure 6.15.1, which instrument would you make trade more often to remove the fake lead? Predict the new bar heights.
  3. (Simulate) Reproduce Figure 6.15.1, then add a fixed 2-step timestamp offset to Y. What happens to the peak?
  4. (Think) Why does scanning many lags and reporting the largest correlation need a different null than testing one lag?

Further reading

  • T. Hayashi and N. Yoshida, “On Covariance Estimation of Non-Synchronously Observed Diffusion Processes,” Bernoulli (2005).
