  • M. Hoffmann, M. Rosenbaum and N. Yoshida, “Estimation of the Lead-Lag Parameter from Non-Synchronous Data,” Bernoulli (2013).
  • N. Huth and F. Abergel, “High Frequency Lead/Lag Relationships: Empirical Facts,” Journal of Empirical Finance (2014).
  • J. Hasbrouck, “One Security, Many Markets: Determining the Contributions to Price Discovery,” Journal of Finance (1995).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.16 — Volatility-Scaled Targets: Measuring Distance in Units of Risk

Subtitle: A fixed distance in points means different things on a quiet day and a wild one. Scaling by volatility fixes that, if you estimate volatility causally.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why a fixed price distance is not comparable across volatility regimes. 2. Express a target as a multiple of σ√h and say what that buys. 3. Choose among causal volatility estimators and know what each needs. 4. Avoid the causality traps: current bar, full-sample scaling, seasonality, clock.

You need: Brownian motion (a continuous random walk) and the idea that displacement grows like √time; Chapter 6.10 helps.

6.16.1 The problem

Any research question of the form “did price reach a level before another level?” needs those levels defined. The naive way is a fixed distance in points or ticks.

The trouble: the same distance is trivial on a volatile afternoon and nearly unreachable in a quiet overnight session. Comparing outcomes across those conditions mixes apples and oranges. Volatility scaling expresses distances in units of expected movement instead. This chapter covers the maths, the estimators and the traps.

6.16.2 Why scale

Under a driftless Brownian motion with volatility σ\sigma (per unit time), the typical displacement over a horizon hh is σh\sigma\sqrt h. A target at distance dd is “near” or “far” according to the ratio

z=dσh z = \frac{d}{\sigma\sqrt h}

The probability of touching it, the expected time to touch it, and the distribution of outcomes all depend on dd and σ\sigma only through combinations like this (see Chapter 6.20 on first passage).

Key point. Set d=cσhd = c\,\sigma\sqrt h for a fixed multiple cc, and the statistical problem looks the same in every volatility regime. Outcomes become comparable, and pooled statistics stop being dominated by high-volatility periods.

Figure 6.16.1 — A fixed distance is easy on wild days and nearly impossible on quiet ones. The orange curve is the chance of touching a fixed distance within the horizon, as volatility changes, using the driftless Brownian formula 2(1 − Φ(z)). It runs from almost 0% to over 60%. The blue line is a target scaled with volatility: its touch chance is the same in every regime. Formula plot in relative units; no data.

The same logic underlies volatility-targeted position sizing (risk parity, volatility-managed portfolios): scale exposure inversely to σ so that risk per unit is roughly constant.

6.16.3 Estimating σ causally

Everything hinges on σ̂t\hat\sigma_t, which must use only information available at tt.

Estimator Formula or idea Notes
Rolling standard deviation std. dev. of returns over a trailing window simple; equal weights; old data drops out abruptly
EWMA (RiskMetrics) σ̂t2=λσ̂t−12+(1−λ)rt2\hat\sigma_t^2 = \lambda\hat\sigma_{t-1}^2 + (1-\lambda)r_{t}^2 smooth, recursive, one memory parameter
GARCH(1,1) σt2=ω+αrt−12+βσt−12\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha r_{t-1}^2 + \beta\sigma_{t-1}^2 mean-reverts to ω/(1−α−β)\omega/(1-\alpha-\beta); fit by maximum likelihood on a prior period
Range-based (Parkinson) σ̂2=14ln⁡2(lnHL)2\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{4\ln 2}\left(\ln\frac{H}{L}\right)^2 with Garman–Klass, Rogers–Satchell, Yang–Zhang: several times more efficient; need genuine intrabar highs and lows
Realised volatility sum of squared high-frequency returns in the window most efficient when microstructure noise is controlled (moderate sampling or noise-robust estimators)
Average true range practitioners’ range measure no clean probabilistic meaning, but behaves similarly

Caution. Range estimators need real highs and lows. Bars rebuilt from closes, or “bodies” without wicks, make them meaningless.

6.16.4 The causality traps

Using the current bar. Suppose the target for a decision at time t is scaled with a volatility estimate that includes the bar ending at t (or later), and that bar is not complete at decision time. Then the target leaks information. This is the most common bug I look for. The estimate must come from bars that closed before the decision.

Figure 6.16.2 — Only closed bars may feed the estimate. Blue bars closed before decision time t and may be used. The orange bar is still forming at t; using its range or close would leak the future. The grey bar is the future.

Full-sample normalisation. Scaling by the volatility of the whole dataset, or z-scoring features with full-sample means and variances, imports the future. Every normalisation must be trailing.

Seasonality. Intraday volatility follows a U-shape. A trailing estimate at 09:31 is dominated by the quiet overnight session and understates what is about to happen. Scaling by a deterministic intraday profile (estimated from prior days) times a slowly varying level is more accurate:

σ̂t=ŝ(time of day)×σ̂tlevel \hat\sigma_t = \hat s(\text{time of day})\times\hat\sigma^{\text{level}}_t

Clock choice. In a volume clock, volatility per unit volume is more stable than per unit time, which partly solves the seasonality problem. But the target distances then mean something different, and the horizon h must be in the same clock.

6.16.5 Consequences for evaluation

  • A fixed-multiple target is hit with roughly constant probability across regimes (under the random-walk null). That makes the null easy to state and test against.
  • Payoffs in points still vary with volatility. If you add them up in points, high-volatility periods dominate again. Decide whether you evaluate in units of risk or units of currency, and report both.
  • Costs do not scale. Commissions and the tick-size part of the spread are fixed per contract. In quiet regimes a volatility-scaled target is small relative to costs. Apply costs in absolute terms, after scaling.

6.16.6 Engineering notes

  • Keep volatility estimators recursive and allocation-free; they update every bar or tick.
  • Store the volatility estimate used for each decision alongside the decision. When you audit results later, you need the exact value, not a recomputation.
  • Warm-up: the first stretch of any estimator reflects its initialisation. Exclude it from evaluation or initialise from a prior period.

6.16.7 Summary

  • Distance only means something relative to σ√h; scaled targets make regimes comparable.
  • Many causal σ estimators exist; range-based ones need real wicks.
  • Never use the current, unfinished bar or full-sample statistics; model intraday seasonality.
  • Evaluate in risk units and currency units, and apply costs in absolute terms.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) σ = 2 points per √minute and h = 25 minutes. What distance is a 1.5σ√h target? (Answer: 1.5 × 2 × 5 = 15 points.)
  2. (Apply) Volatility doubles. By what factor must a fixed-multiple target move? What happens to its touch probability?
  3. (Code) Implement EWMA volatility over bars and write a test that fails if the estimate for bar t uses bar t’s own return.
  4. (Think) Why do fixed costs make volatility-scaled targets look worse in quiet regimes, even under a random walk?

Further reading

  • J.P. Morgan/Reuters, RiskMetrics Technical Document (1996).
  • T. Bollerslev, “Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity,” Journal of Econometrics (1986).
  • M. Parkinson, “The Extreme Value Method for Estimating the Variance of the Rate of Return,” Journal of Business (1980).
  • A. Moreira and T. Muir, “Volatility-Managed Portfolios,” Journal of Finance (2017).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.17 — The Stop-Loss as Hypothesis Invalidation

Subtitle: A stop is not a pain threshold. It is the price at which the reason for the trade is no longer true. Thinking of it that way changes where you put it.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Separate “where to exit” (a question about the premise) from “how much to risk” (a sizing question). 2. Use the reflection-principle touch probability to tell noise from invalidation. 3. Describe Wald’s sequential probability ratio test and how a stop fits inside it. 4. Avoid the common traps when testing stop rules.

You need: Chapter 6.16 (volatility units), the normal distribution function Φ, and the idea of type I and type II errors.

6.17.1 Two decisions, not one

Most stop-loss advice is about money: risk no more than some fraction of the account, place the stop where the loss would hurt. That framing mixes two different decisions:

Question Kind of decision
How much to risk sizing
Where to exit the trade’s premise

This chapter argues for treating the stop as a hypothesis test, and walks through the statistics behind that view.

6.17.2 A trade is a hypothesis

Any trade can be written as a claim: “given what I see now, the distribution of future price is shifted in my favour”. The claim rests on a premise: some structure you believe holds. A level that should contain price, a regime that should persist, a flow that should continue.

Definition. The stop-loss is the price at which the premise is falsified: the point where evidence against the hypothesis is strong enough that keeping the position is no longer a bet on the original idea, but a new, unexamined bet.

Seen that way, a stop at an arbitrary distance (a round number of points, a fixed percentage) has nothing to do with the hypothesis. It might sit inside the normal noise of a valid trade, so it gets hit when the idea was fine. Or it might be far beyond the point where the idea died, so you hold a dead trade.

6.17.3 Noise versus invalidation

Under a random-walk null with volatility σ per unit time and zero drift, the reflection principle gives the chance that price touches a level a distance dd below entry within horizon hh:

P(touch)=2Φ(−dσh) P(\text{touch}) = 2\,\Phi\!\left(-\frac{d}{\sigma\sqrt h}\right)

(The drifted version is in Chapter 6.20.) A stop with dd small relative to σh\sigma\sqrt h is touched with high probability whether or not the premise is correct. Hitting it says little about the hypothesis. This is the quantitative version of “my stop was too tight”.

Figure 6.17.1 — Tight stops are hit by noise alone. The blue curve is the chance that pure noise touches a stop within the holding horizon, as a function of the stop’s distance in volatility units. In the shaded zone noise alone hits the stop roughly half the time or more, so a hit carries little information about the premise. Formula plot; no data.

Conversely, an invalidation level is informative when hitting it is much more likely under “the premise is false” than under “the premise is true”. In likelihood-ratio terms, the stop should sit where

P(reach stop∣H1 false)P(reach stop∣H1 true) \frac{P(\text{reach stop} \mid H_1\text{ false})}{P(\text{reach stop} \mid H_1\text{ true})}

is large. That is a property of the setup, not of the account size.

6.17.4 Sequential testing

Holding a position is a sequential decision: at every moment, continue or exit. Wald’s sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) is the classical framework. Accumulate the log-likelihood ratio of observations under the two hypotheses,

Λt=∑s≤tlog⁡p(xs∣H1)p(xs∣H0), \Lambda_t = \sum_{s\le t}\log\frac{p(x_s \mid H_1)}{p(x_s \mid H_0)},

and stop when it crosses a lower boundary aa (reject H1H_1) or an upper boundary bb (accept H1H_1).

Result (Wald’s approximations). a≈log⁡β1−α,b≈log⁡1−βα a \approx \log\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}, \qquad b \approx \log\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha} where α and β are the type I and type II error probabilities.

Figure 6.17.2 — Evidence accumulates until it crosses a boundary. Each line is the log-likelihood ratio of one simulated stream. Green paths come from the “premise true” model and drift up to the accept boundary b. Orange paths come from the “premise false” model and drift down to the exit boundary a. Paths wander before they cross, which is why early exits from noise are possible. Simulation: Gaussian observations with mean 0.25 (true) or 0 (false), standard deviation 1, α = β = 0.05, fixed seed 6017. Not market data.

A price stop is a crude special case where the “evidence” is only the price path. Other evidence that the premise has failed (for example, the structure that justified the trade disappearing) is also legitimate invalidation. In a well-designed system it often comes before price reaches any fixed level.

6.17.5 Separating where from how much

Once the hypothesis sets the invalidation point, sizing follows from risk tolerance:

position size=risk budget per trade|entry−invalidation|+expected costs \text{position size} = \frac{\text{risk budget per trade}}{|\text{entry} - \text{invalidation}| + \text{expected costs}}

  • A trade with a distant invalidation gets a smaller position.
  • A trade with a close invalidation gets a larger position.

Risk per trade is controlled by sizing, not by moving the stop. Moving the stop closer to “fit” a position size is exactly backwards: it destroys the information content of the stop.

6.17.6 Pitfalls in testing stops

Pitfall What goes wrong Fix
Intrabar sequencing on bar data, if a bar’s range covers both stop and target, you do not know which came first; assuming the favourable order makes backtests optimistic use tick data, or assume the unfavourable order, and report which
Gaps and slippage stops execute as market orders after the trigger; in fast markets the fill can be far beyond the stop do not fill stops exactly at the stop price; losses are understated exactly when they matter
Stop placement as a free parameter scanning many stop distances and picking the best fits noise count every variant as a trial; evaluate the chosen rule out of sample
Stop clustering stops at obvious levels (beyond round numbers, recent highs and lows) cluster and, when triggered together, create the very move that triggers them remember your invalidation level is someone else’s liquidity
Survivorship in the narrative “the stop saved me” and “the stop shook me out” are stories told after the fact judge stop rules by their outcome distribution across many trades, against a baseline such as a time-based exit

6.17.7 A practical checklist

  1. State the premise of the trade in one sentence.
  2. Ask: what observation would show it is false? That defines invalidation.
  3. Check: is that level outside the normal noise for the expected holding time, in volatility units?
  4. Size the position from the distance to invalidation plus costs.
  5. Never move the stop to fit a size; reduce the size instead.

6.17.8 Summary

  • Where to exit is a question about the premise; how much to risk is a sizing question.
  • Stops inside the noise (small d/σ√h) are hit whether or not the idea is right, so they carry little information.
  • An SPRT frames holding as sequential testing; price stops are a crude special case, and other evidence can invalidate sooner.
  • Size from the invalidation distance; test stop rules honestly, with trials counted and unfavourable sequencing.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A stop sits at 0.5 σ√h under a driftless null. Roughly how often does noise alone touch it? (Answer: 2Φ(−0.5) ≈ 62%.)
  2. (Apply) With α = β = 0.05, compute Wald’s boundaries a and b. (Answer: a ≈ −2.94, b ≈ +2.94.)
  3. (Apply) Risk budget 1 unit, entry-to-invalidation distance 4 points, expected costs 0.5 points, value per point 1. What size does the formula give?
  4. (Think) Why does moving a stop closer to fit a larger size destroy its information content?

Further reading

  • A. Wald, Sequential Analysis (1947).
  • K. M. Kaminski and A. W. Lo, “When Do Stop-Loss Rules Stop Losses?” Journal of Financial Markets (2014).
  • V. K. Tharp, Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom (on R-multiples and sizing from stop distance).
  • S. E. Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance II, reflection principle.

— Tariq

Chapter 6.18 — Fractional Kelly and Its Dangers

Subtitle: The Kelly criterion maximises long-run growth, if you know your edge exactly. You never do, and that changes everything.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Derive the Kelly fraction for a binary bet and for a continuous asset. 2. Explain why full Kelly has brutal drawdowns, and what fractional Kelly trades away. 3. Show how an overestimated edge turns “safe” fractional Kelly into zero or negative growth. 4. Shrink the bet for parameter uncertainty with the Bayesian formula.

You need: logarithms, expected value, variance, and the Sharpe ratio (mean excess return divided by its standard deviation).

6.18.1 Beautiful and dangerous

The Kelly criterion is one of the most beautiful results in betting theory and one of the most dangerous in practice. It gives the bet size that maximises the long-run growth rate of capital. It also assumes you know the true probabilities.

This chapter derives Kelly, shows why fractional Kelly is the standard practical response, and explains why even fractional Kelly can ruin you when the edge estimate is wrong.

6.18.2 Derivation: the binary bet

A bet wins bb per unit staked with probability pp and loses the stake with probability q=1−pq = 1-p. Bet a fraction ff of capital each time. After nn bets with WW wins,

Xn=X0(1+fb)W(1−f)n−W X_n = X_0(1+fb)^W(1-f)^{n-W}

The long-run growth rate per bet is

G(f)=limn→∞1nlog⁡XnX0=plog⁡(1+fb)+qlog⁡(1−f) G(f) = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log\frac{X_n}{X_0} = p\log(1+fb) + q\log(1-f)

Result (Kelly fraction). Setting G′(f)=0G'(f) = 0: f*=pb−qb=p−qb. f^* = \frac{pb - q}{b} = p - \frac{q}{b}. That is edge divided by odds.

Kelly (1956) derived it in information theory: the maximal growth rate equals the information rate of the side channel.

6.18.3 Continuous version

For an asset with excess-return drift μ and volatility σ, investing fraction ff gives log-wealth drift

g(f)=fμ−12f2σ2 g(f) = f\mu - \tfrac12 f^2\sigma^2

maximised at

f*=μσ2,g(f*)=μ22σ2=12SR2 f^* = \frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}, \qquad g(f^*) = \frac{\mu^2}{2\sigma^2} = \tfrac12 SR^2

where SR=μ/σSR = \mu/\sigma is the Sharpe ratio.

6.18.4 Why full Kelly is brutal

Even with perfect knowledge, full Kelly produces enormous drawdowns. In the continuous model, when betting cc times Kelly, the probability that wealth ever falls to a fraction xx of its current value is

P(drawdown to x)=x2/c−1 P(\text{drawdown to } x) = x^{\,2/c - 1}

At full Kelly (c=1c = 1), P=xP = x: a 50% chance of halving your capital at some point, and a 10% chance of losing 90%. Few people or institutions can sit through that.

Figure 6.18.1 — Smaller fractions make deep drawdowns far rarer. Each curve is the formula x^(2/c − 1) for one Kelly multiple c. At full Kelly (orange) the chance of ever falling to half your wealth is 50%. At half Kelly (blue) it is 12.5%, and at quarter Kelly (green) under 1%. Formula plot; assumes the edge is known exactly.

6.18.5 Fractional Kelly

Betting f=cf*f = c f^* with c<1c < 1 gives growth

g(cf*)=(2c−c2)g(f*) g(cf^*) = (2c - c^2)\,g(f^*)

and variance proportional to c2c^2.

Multiple c Growth (share of max) Variance (relative) P(ever halve)
0.25 44% 1/16 0.5⁷ ≈ 0.8%
0.5 75% 1/4 0.5³ = 12.5%
1 100% 1 50%
2 0% 4 certain eventually

At half Kelly you keep three quarters of the maximum growth with a quarter of the variance, and the drawdown probability becomes x3x^3. This is why practitioners almost always bet a fraction of Kelly.

Figure 6.18.2 — Undershooting costs little; overshooting costs a lot. The blue curve is growth relative to the maximum, 2c − c², against the multiple c of the true Kelly fraction. It is flat near its peak, so half Kelly keeps 75%. Past c = 2 (shaded) growth is negative: you go broke with certainty despite having an edge. Formula plot; no data.

6.18.6 The real danger: estimation error

All of the above assumes μ and σ (or pp and bb) are known. In reality they are estimated, and the estimates are noisy and usually optimistic.

Edge estimates are biased upward. If you pick a strategy because its backtest looked good, its estimated edge is inflated by selection (the winner’s curse). The more variants you tried, the larger the inflation.

Kelly is linear in the edge. f*=μ/σ2f^* = \mu/\sigma^2.

You overestimate μ by Betting “full Kelly” is really Betting “half Kelly” is really
2× 2× true Kelly: zero growth full true Kelly: 50% chance of halving
4× 4× true Kelly: negative growth 2× true Kelly: zero growth

Fractional Kelly is partly a hedge against exactly this. But the margin is smaller than it looks, and selection bias of that size is not unusual.

Parameter uncertainty can be priced in. A Bayesian treatment replaces μ with its posterior. For a normal posterior μ∼𝒩(μ̂,s2)\mu \sim \mathcal N(\hat\mu, s^2), the expected growth is

𝔼[g(f)]=fμ̂−12f2(σ2+s2) \mathbb E[g(f)] = f\hat\mu - \tfrac12 f^2(\sigma^2 + s^2)

Result (Bayesian Kelly). fBayes*=μ̂σ2+s2 f^*_{\text{Bayes}} = \frac{\hat\mu}{\sigma^2 + s^2} Uncertainty in the edge acts like extra variance and shrinks the bet automatically.

When ss is comparable to μ̂\hat\mu (typical for trading strategies with limited history), the shrinkage is large.

Non-stationarity. Even a correctly estimated past edge may not hold. Kelly assumes the same game repeated forever. Markets change.

Fat tails and serial correlation. The derivation assumes Gaussian returns. Fat tails raise the true variance relative to the estimate, and losing streaks cluster more than independence implies. Both push the true optimum below the computed one.

Multiple bets. With several correlated strategies, Kelly becomes f*=Σ−1μf^* = \Sigma^{-1}\mu. Covariance estimation error is severe and the inverse amplifies it. Unconstrained multi-asset Kelly is notoriously unstable.

6.18.7 What I take from this

Kelly is best used as an upper bound and a way of thinking, not as a sizing formula. It says: size grows with edge, shrinks with variance, and is catastrophic when overestimated.

In practice, sizing should be driven by a risk budget a person can actually tolerate. Kelly is a ceiling you should never approach, applied only to an edge that has been validated out of sample, with its uncertainty included.

And if a strategy has not been validated, its Kelly fraction is zero.

6.18.8 Summary

  • Kelly maximises long-run log growth: f* = p − q/b for a binary bet, μ/σ² for a continuous asset.
  • Full Kelly has a 50% chance of halving capital; fractional Kelly trades a little growth for much less risk.
  • Growth is 2c − c² of the maximum: zero at twice Kelly, negative beyond.
  • Edges are overestimated by selection; a 2–4× overestimate turns “safe” fractions into zero growth. Shrink for uncertainty: μ̂/(σ² + s²).

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A bet pays 1:1 (b = 1) and wins 55% of the time. What is the Kelly fraction? (Answer: 0.55 − 0.45 = 0.10.)
  2. (Apply) μ̂ = 0.04, σ = 0.2, and the standard error of μ̂ is s = 0.04. Compare plain Kelly with Bayesian Kelly.
  3. (Derive) Show that g(c f) = (2c − c²) g(f) from g(f) = fμ − ½f²σ².
  4. (Think) You tested 50 variants and picked the best. Why should that make you bet less than the Kelly fraction its backtest suggests?

Further reading

  • J. L. Kelly, “A New Interpretation of Information Rate,” Bell System Technical Journal (1956).
  • E. O. Thorp, “The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market,” Handbook of Asset and Liability Management (2006).
  • L. C. MacLean, E. O. Thorp and W. T. Ziemba, The Kelly Capital Growth Investment Criterion (2011).
  • S. Browne, “Reaching Goals by a Deadline: Digital Options and Continuous-Time Active Portfolio Management,” Advances in Applied Probability (1999).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.19 — CMA-ES Optimisation with Bounds

Subtitle: A derivative-free optimiser that learns the shape of the landscape as it searches, and the practicalities of keeping it inside a box.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe one generation of CMA-ES: sample, rank, recombine, adapt. 2. Explain how the covariance and step-size updates learn the landscape’s shape. 3. Choose a bound-handling method and read a solution pinned at a bound. 4. Explain why a strong optimiser on a backtest objective is an overfitting hazard, and the statistical defences.

You need: the multivariate normal distribution, covariance matrices, and the idea of a local optimum.

6.19.1 When there is no gradient

Many quantities I want to calibrate have no useful gradient:

  • likelihoods of models with discrete components,
  • objectives computed by a replay engine,
  • anything with thresholds or event counts inside.

For those, the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), by Hansen and Ostermeier, is my default. It is robust, nearly parameter-free, and handles ill-conditioned problems (long, narrow, tilted valleys) far better than simple random or grid search. This chapter explains how it works, how to handle bounds, and why an optimiser this good is also a hazard.

6.19.2 The idea

CMA-ES keeps a multivariate Gaussian search distribution

x∼m+σ𝒩(0,C) x \sim m + \sigma\,\mathcal N(0, C)

with mean mm, global step size σ\sigma and covariance CC. Each generation:

  1. Sample λ\lambda candidates xi=m+σyix_i = m + \sigma y_i, yi∼𝒩(0,C)y_i \sim \mathcal N(0, C).
  2. Evaluate and rank them by objective value.
  3. Recombine: move the mean toward a weighted average of the best μ\mu candidates, m←m+cm∑i=1μwi(xi:λ−m) m \leftarrow m + c_m\sum_{i=1}^{\mu} w_i (x_{i:\lambda} - m)
  4. Adapt CC and σ\sigma using the successful steps.

Figure 6.19.1 — One generation of CMA-ES. Candidates are sampled, ranked, and the best pull the mean toward them. Then the green step adapts the shape (C) and size (σ) of the search distribution, and the loop repeats.

Key property. Only ranks are used, never the objective values themselves. So CMA-ES is unchanged by any monotone transformation of the objective: scaling, shifting or taking logs changes nothing.

6.19.3 Covariance adaptation

Two update terms combine.

Rank-μ update. Estimate the covariance of this generation’s successful steps:

Cμ=∑i=1μwiyi:λyi:λ⊤ C_\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{\mu} w_i\,y_{i:\lambda}y_{i:\lambda}^\top

Rank-one update via the evolution path. Track an exponentially smoothed path of mean movements,

pc←(1−cc)pc+cc(2−cc)μeffmnew−moldσ p_c \leftarrow (1-c_c)p_c + \sqrt{c_c(2-c_c)\mu_{\text{eff}}}\;\frac{m_{\text{new}} - m_{\text{old}}}{\sigma}

which captures consistent directions across generations: correlations a single generation cannot see.

Combined:

C←(1−c1−cμ)C+c1pcpc⊤+cμCμ C \leftarrow (1 - c_1 - c_\mu)C + c_1 p_c p_c^\top + c_\mu C_\mu

Over time, CC approximates the inverse Hessian (the inverse of the curvature matrix) of the objective near the optimum, up to scale. That is how CMA-ES handles rotated valleys: it learns a metric in which the problem looks round.

Figure 6.19.2 — The search distribution learns the valley. Grey ellipses are contours of a stretched, rotated quadratic bowl. Blue ellipses show the search distribution at generations 0, 3, 8 and 15: it first widens and moves, then shrinks. By generation 30 (green) it is small and tilted along the valley, centred near the optimum. Simulation: 2-D CMA-ES with population 6 and standard default learning rates on a rotated ellipsoid (axis ratio 5), fixed seed 6019.

6.19.4 Step-size control

The global step size σ is adapted by cumulative step-size adaptation. A second evolution path pσp_\sigma is computed in the coordinates where CC is the identity.

  • If successive steps point the same way (the path is longer than random selection would give), σ grows.
  • If they cancel, σ shrinks.

σ←σexp⁡(cσdσ(∥pσ∥𝔼∥𝒩(0,I)∥−1)) \sigma \leftarrow \sigma\exp\!\left(\frac{c_\sigma}{d_\sigma}\left(\frac{\|p_\sigma\|}{\mathbb E\|\mathcal N(0,I)\|} - 1\right)\right)

All the learning rates (ccc_c, c1c_1, cμc_\mu, cσc_\sigma, dσd_\sigma) have well-tested default formulas that depend only on dimension and population size. In practice you choose an initial mean, an initial step size and, sometimes, a population size. That is close to parameter-free.

6.19.5 Handling bounds

Real problems have bounds: rates must be positive, probabilities in [0, 1], a decay must be slower than some limit. CMA-ES samples from an unbounded Gaussian, so constraints need explicit handling.

Method How Downside
Transformation map an unbounded internal variable to the box (logistic, periodic/reflective, or Hansen’s piecewise quadratic–linear transform that is the identity inside); the optimiser never sees the bounds distortion near the boundaries
Repair and penalty clip infeasible samples to the box for evaluation; add a penalty proportional to the squared distance between original and repaired point (Hansen et al., 2009, describe an adaptive penalty weight) penalty weight to manage
Resampling reject and resample infeasible candidates biases the distribution; very slow when the optimum is on a boundary
Log-scale parameters for strictly positive parameters spanning orders of magnitude (rates, time constants), optimise the logarithm only for positive parameters; but also improves conditioning

Whatever you use, log how often candidates hit bounds. An optimum pinned at a bound is a message: the bound is binding, or the model wants something your parameterisation does not allow.

6.19.6 Restarts and noise

CMA-ES is a local optimiser with a wide basin of attraction. For multimodal problems (many local optima), restart strategies improve global search:

  • IPOP: restart with increasing population.
  • BIPOP: alternate large and small populations.

Noisy objectives (a replay over a sample of days, a likelihood over noisy data) make ranks unreliable. Larger populations average the noise. Uncertainty-handling variants re-evaluate candidates and increase σ when rankings are unstable.

6.19.7 The danger: an optimiser this good will fit noise

The better the optimiser, the more efficiently it finds parameters that exploit the quirks of the sample. On a likelihood with plenty of data, that is fine. On any objective derived from a finite backtest, it is overfitting with excellent convergence.

The defences are statistical, not algorithmic:

  • Count the evaluations. Every candidate evaluated is a trial. Thousands of trials inflate the best result.
  • Separate calibration from evaluation. Optimise on one period, freeze, evaluate on another you have not looked at.
  • Prefer flat optima. A parameter set whose neighbourhood performs similarly is more trustworthy than a sharp peak. Inspect the objective around the solution, or optimise a smoothed objective.
  • Report the distribution. Not just the best run, but the spread across restarts and across data subsets.

6.19.8 Engineering notes

  • Use a well-tested implementation, or port one carefully and test it on standard benchmarks (sphere, ellipsoid, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin) before trusting it on your problem.
  • Seed the random generator and log the seed. Reproducibility of an optimisation run matters as much as reproducibility of the evaluation.
  • Evaluate candidates in parallel; each generation’s evaluations are independent.

6.19.9 Summary

  • CMA-ES samples from a Gaussian, ranks candidates, moves the mean, and adapts covariance and step size.
  • Using only ranks makes it invariant to monotone transforms of the objective; covariance adaptation learns the valley’s shape.
  • Bounds need transformation, repair-plus-penalty, resampling or log scaling; watch for solutions pinned at bounds.
  • A strong optimiser on a backtest overfits efficiently: count evaluations, hold out data, prefer flat optima, report spreads.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) You replace the objective f with log(f) (f > 0). Does CMA-ES behave differently, given the same seed? (Answer: no; the ranks are unchanged.)
  2. (Apply) A rate parameter could lie anywhere from 0.001 to 10. Why is optimising its logarithm better than optimising it directly?
  3. (Code) Run CMA-ES on a 10-dimensional Rosenbrock function with three different seeds. Report all three results, not just the best.
  4. (Think) An optimisation evaluated 5,000 candidates on a backtest. How should that number change how you read the best score?

Further reading

  • N. Hansen and A. Ostermeier, “Completely Derandomized Self-Adaptation in Evolution Strategies,” Evolutionary Computation (2001).
  • N. Hansen, “The CMA Evolution Strategy: A Tutorial,” arXiv:1604.00772 (2016).
  • N. Hansen, A. S. P. Niederberger, L. Guzzella and P. Koumoutsakos, “A Method for Handling Uncertainty in Evolutionary Optimization,” IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation (2009).
  • D. H. Bailey, J. Borwein, M. López de Prado and Q. J. Zhu, “Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism,” Notices of the AMS (2014).

— Tariq

Chapter 6.20 — First-Passage Probabilities: Will Price Touch This Level First?

Subtitle: The reflection principle, two-barrier formulas and the null model every target-versus-stop question should start from.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Use the reflection principle to get one-barrier touch probabilities, with and without drift. 2. Compute the chance of hitting a target before a stop, and the expected exit time. 3. Explain why no target/stop ratio creates an edge under a martingale. 4. Build the right null for any “target before stop” statistic, and know where Brownian motion fails.

You need: Chapter 6.1 (gambler’s ruin), Chapter 6.16 (volatility units), Brownian motion, and the normal distribution function Φ.

6.20.1 One question behind many

A surprising number of trading questions reduce to one: starting here, will price reach level A before level B, and how long will it take?

Before asking whether any signal improves the answer, you need the answer under a model with no signal at all. First-passage theory for Brownian motion gives that baseline in closed form. This chapter derives the key results, and explains why the baseline is not 50/50 even when it looks like it should be.

6.20.2 One barrier, no drift: the reflection principle

Let WtW_t be standard Brownian motion starting at zero, and a>0a > 0 a barrier.

Reflection principle. For every path that touches aa and ends below it, the path reflected after the first touch ends above it, with equal probability. Hence P(maxs≤tWs≥a)=2P(Wt≥a)=2Φ(−at). P\Big(\max_{s\le t}W_s \ge a\Big) = 2P(W_t \ge a) = 2\,\Phi\!\left(-\frac{a}{\sqrt t}\right).

For price with volatility σ, replace aa by a/σa/\sigma.

First lesson: the chance of touching a level within a horizon is twice the chance of ending beyond it. Touching is much easier than closing beyond.

The first-passage time τa\tau_a (the first time the level is reached) has density

f(t)=a2πt3exp⁡(−a22t) f(t) = \frac{a}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{a^2}{2t}\right)

This is the Lévy distribution. It is heavy-tailed: the expected time to touch any level is infinite for driftless Brownian motion, even though the level is touched with probability one eventually.

6.20.3 One barrier with drift

For Xt=μt+σWtX_t = \mu t + \sigma W_t, the first-passage time to a>0a > 0 follows an inverse Gaussian distribution, and

P(τa≤t)=Φ(μt−aσt)+e2μa/σ2Φ(−μt−aσt) P(\tau_a \le t) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu t - a}{\sigma\sqrt t}\right) + e^{2\mu a/\sigma^2}\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{-\mu t - a}{\sigma\sqrt t}\right)

  • With positive drift toward the barrier, 𝔼[τa]=a/μ\mathbb E[\tau_a] = a/\mu.
  • With negative drift, the barrier may never be reached: the probability of ever touching is e2μa/σ2<1e^{2\mu a/\sigma^2} < 1.

6.20.4 Two barriers: target versus stop

The question traders actually ask: starting at 0, with an upper level +u+u (target) and a lower level −d-d (stop), which is hit first?

No drift. Brownian motion is a martingale (a fair game: its expected future value is its current value). By the optional stopping theorem:

Result (gambler’s ruin, continuous). P(hit +u first)=du+d P(\text{hit } +u \text{ first}) = \frac{d}{u + d}

A target twice as far as the stop is hit first one-third of the time. The expected payoff is

u⋅du+d−d⋅uu+d=0, u\cdot\frac{d}{u+d} - d\cdot\frac{u}{u+d} = 0,

whatever the ratio.

Key point. No choice of target and stop creates an edge under a martingale. Better “risk–reward ratios” are paid for exactly by lower hit rates.

With drift. For Xt=μt+σWtX_t = \mu t + \sigma W_t, the process exp⁡(−2μXt/σ2)\exp(-2\mu X_t/\sigma^2) is a martingale (the scale function), which gives

P(hit +u first)=1−e2μd/σ2e−2μu/σ2−e2μd/σ2 P(\text{hit } +u \text{ first}) = \frac{1 - e^{2\mu d/\sigma^2}}{e^{-2\mu u/\sigma^2} - e^{2\mu d/\sigma^2}}

This reduces to d/(u+d)d/(u+d) as μ→0\mu \to 0. The expected time to leave the band, for zero drift, is

𝔼[τ]=udσ2 \mathbb E[\tau] = \frac{u\,d}{\sigma^2}

For finite horizons, the chance that neither barrier is hit by time t, and the joint law of which is hit first and when, are infinite series from the method of images (alternating reflections in both barriers). They converge fast and are easy to compute.

Figure 6.20.1 — Far targets are hit first less often; drift tilts the whole curve. The blue curve is d/(u + d): the chance the target is hit before the stop with no drift. At u = 2d it is one in three. The dashed green and orange curves add a modest drift toward the target or toward the stop, using the scale-function formula. Formula plot; no data.

Figure 6.20.2 — Twelve fair paths between a target and a stop. Each line is a driftless Brownian path from 0, coloured by which barrier it reaches first: target +2 (green) or stop −1 (orange). Four of twelve reach the target first, close to the one-in-three the formula predicts. One green path is still between the barriers at the right edge and reaches the target later. Simulation: time step 0.01, σ = 1, fixed seed 6020. Not market data.

6.20.5 Why this is the right null

When evaluating any rule of the form “after condition X, does price reach the target before the stop?”, the right comparison is not 50%. It is the first-passage probability for the same distances, volatility and horizon under a no-signal model:

excess hit rate=P̂(target first∣X)−P0(target first) \text{excess hit rate} = \hat P(\text{target first}\mid X) - P_0(\text{target first})

where P0P_0 comes from the formulas above, or from simulating a null process that matches the data’s volatility and microstructure. Distances should be measured in volatility units (Chapter 6.16): the hit probability depends on u/σu/\sigma and d/σd/\sigma, not on raw points.

Simulated nulls are often better than closed forms in practice, because real price paths are discrete (they move in ticks), heavy-tailed and have time-varying volatility. Chapter 6.1 applies the same idea to a chart type: generate paths with no signal, run exactly the same pipeline, and see what the method produces by itself.

6.20.6 Where reality departs from Brownian motion

Departure Effect What to do
Discreteness prices move in ticks; for barriers a few ticks away the continuous formulas are off use a discrete random walk and the integer-step gambler’s-ruin formula
Overshoot barriers are often crossed by a jump, not touched exactly; stops fill beyond the stop, limit targets fill only if the queue clears treat touching and filling as different probabilities
Time-varying volatility σ changes through the day apply the formulas with time measured in a volume or variance clock
Bar data if both barriers fall within one bar’s range, the order of touching is unknown never assume the favourable order; that is a common way backtests manufacture hit rates

6.20.7 Engineering notes

  • Implement the closed forms and test them against Monte Carlo with fine time steps. The discretisation bias of simulated barrier-hitting (paths can cross between steps) is itself a useful lesson.
  • Use the Brownian-bridge correction when simulating: given two consecutive simulated points x1,x2x_1, x_2 below barrier aa, the probability the path crossed aa between them is exp⁡(−2(a−x1)(a−x2)/(σ2Δt))\exp(-2(a-x_1)(a-x_2)/(\sigma^2\Delta t)).
  • Always report observed hit rates alongside their null probabilities and confidence intervals.

6.20.8 Summary

  • Touching a level is twice as likely as ending beyond it (reflection principle); driftless touch times have infinite mean.
  • With no drift, P(target before stop) = d/(u + d) and the expected payoff is zero for every ratio.
  • Drift changes the odds through the scale function; expected exit time is ud/σ² with no drift.
  • Compare any target-first statistic with its null, in volatility units, and account for ticks, overshoot, clocks and bar sequencing.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Target 3 points, stop 1 point, no drift. What is P(target first)? (Answer: 1/(3 + 1) = 25%.)
  2. (Apply) For the same barriers with σ = 1 point per √minute, what is the expected time to hit either one? (Answer: 3 × 1 / 1 = 3 minutes.)
  3. (Simulate) Simulate Figure 6.20.2 with 10,000 paths at time steps 0.1 and 0.001. Which gives a hit rate closer to 1/3, and why? Add the Brownian-bridge correction.
  4. (Think) A strategy reports a 30% hit rate with a 3:1 target-to-stop ratio. What is the right baseline, and what else do you need before calling it an edge?

Further reading

  • W. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Volume II (1971).
  • I. Karatzas and S. E. Shreve, Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus (1991).
  • A. N. Borodin and P. Salminen, Handbook of Brownian Motion: Facts and Formulae (2002).
  • S. Redner, A Guide to First-Passage Processes (2001).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.2 — One Payload Shape for Every Model: A Multi-Agent Swarm on Bedrock Converse

Subtitle: Most multi-agent pain is plumbing. Pick a single request shape and a lot of it disappears.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe a “role” as a small, fixed bundle: instructions, output schema and a list of models. 2. Explain why running roles in parallel costs about the slowest call, not the sum of all calls. 3. Lay out a request so that one parser, one fallback path and one log format work for every model.

You need: a rough idea of what an LLM API call is (you send text, you get text back). No maths beyond sums and maxima.

7.2.1 The real problem was plumbing

When I first wired several language-model “roles” together for my trading research stack, I expected the prompts to be the hard part. They were not. The hard part was that every model vendor wanted a slightly different request body. Each had its own way to state a system prompt and its own place to hide the answer.

By September 2026 I had rebuilt the swarm around one rule: every role, on every model, speaks the same request shape. On AWS that shape is the Bedrock Converse API.

This chapter explains why that rule matters more than the choice of model, and what a role-based swarm looks like with the marketing stripped away.

7.2.2 What “multi-agent” means here

Forget autonomous agents negotiating with each other. Here a swarm is a set of narrowly scoped roles. Each role answers one question about the same input snapshot. They run in parallel, and each role’s output is forced into a schema (a fixed, machine-checkable layout for the answer).

Definition (role). A role is a tuple role=(system instructions,output schema,model preference list). \text{role} = (\text{system instructions},\ \text{output schema},\ \text{model preference list}).

The orchestrator (the code that runs the roles) sends one snapshot out to RR roles and collects RR structured verdicts.

Figure 7.2.1 — One snapshot, many independent roles. The orchestrator hands the same snapshot to every role. Each role returns either a verdict that fits its schema (green) or a structured error (orange). The aggregate keeps both. Note that no arrow runs from one role to another.

Latency. Let the role call times be L1,…,LRL_1,\dots,L_R. Run one after another, they cost ∑iLi\sum_i L_i. Run at the same time, they cost roughly max⁡iLi\max_i L_i plus some overhead. LLM calls take seconds, so that difference is the whole user experience.

Figure 7.2.2 — Sum versus maximum. The orange row runs the roles one by one, so the total is the sum of their lengths. The green rows start together (each a little later than the last: the stagger), so the total is set by the slowest role. Bar lengths are illustrative, not measured.

Nothing in this design needs the roles to talk to each other. I think that is the most underrated choice in multi-agent design. If roles do not converse, you can test each one alone, swap its model on its own, and replay it from a log. Conversation between agents is where determinism (getting the same output for the same input) goes to die.

7.2.3 Why Converse

Converse is Bedrock’s model-agnostic chat interface. You send system blocks, a list of messages, an optional toolConfig, and inference settings. You get back a message, a stop reason (why the model stopped writing) and token usage. The same call works for Anthropic models, Amazon Nova and other models hosted on Bedrock.

That sameness buys three concrete things:

Benefit What it means in practice
One extractor One function parses every response. When output is forced through a tool call (Chapter 7.5), it looks for one toolUse block whatever the vendor.
Fallback without translation If the preferred model is down, the orchestrator retries the identical payload on the next model in the list. No prompt rewriting at 9:31am.
Comparable telemetry Usage fields (input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens) come back in the same structure, so every call can be scored across models later.

The cost: you give up vendor-specific features that Converse does not expose, or you accept them only as optional fields. For my use that was an easy trade.

7.2.4 The payload layout

The layout I settled on is deliberately boring:

  • System: a shared prefix used by every role (house rules, output discipline, the domain’s vocabulary), then a cache marker, then the role-specific block.
  • User turn: only the dynamic data, the snapshot for this run.
  • Tool config: one tool whose input schema is the answer schema, with tool choice forced.

Putting all dynamic data in the user turn is not cosmetic. Prompt caches are prefix-anchored: anything that changes invalidates everything after it. Put a timestamp into the system prompt and you have quietly turned off caching for every role. Chapter 7.4 covers this in detail.

7.2.5 Concurrency in practice

The Bedrock SDK client in Python is synchronous (each call blocks until it returns). So the orchestrator pushes each call onto an executor (a pool of worker threads) and awaits them together. Two details mattered more than I expected:

  • Stagger, don’t stampede. Firing every role in the same millisecond is a good way to trip per-model rate limits. A small gap between launches costs almost nothing against multi-second calls.
  • Isolate failures. One role timing out must not cancel the others. Each role returns either a verdict or a structured error, and the aggregate reports both. “Four verdicts and one error” is far more useful than an exception.

7.2.6 Advice and pitfalls

What I’d tell another engineer:

  • Start with the schema, not the persona. “You are a seasoned risk manager” does less than a tight JSON schema with enumerated fields.
  • Don’t use an LLM where a threshold will do. One of my roles started as a model call and is now plain deterministic code by default, because comparing numbers to limits does not need a language model.
  • Log everything with an input hash. Every verdict, live or dry-run, is appended to a log with the model, token usage, cache hits, latency and a hash (fingerprint) of the input. That log later tells you which model is good at which role, from data rather than vibes.
  • Keep a dry-run path. A dry-run that exercises the whole orchestration without calling a model catches most wiring bugs for free.

Pitfalls:

  • Treating “multi-agent” as “more agents = better answers”. More roles means more cost and more places to disagree. Each role must earn its place.
  • Letting roles see each other’s outputs in the same round. That creates order dependence and makes replays meaningless.
  • Assuming every model honours every inference parameter the same way. Test the boundaries per model.

The swarm itself is unglamorous. That is the point. The interesting work happens in what you do with the verdicts, and that only works if the plumbing underneath is predictable.

7.2.7 Summary

  • A role is (instructions, schema, model list); a swarm runs many roles on one snapshot.
  • Parallel roles cost about the slowest call, max⁡iLi\max_i L_i, not the sum.
  • One request shape (Converse) gives one parser, free fallback and comparable logs.
  • Keep roles independent, keep dynamic data in the user turn, and isolate failures.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Five roles take 3, 2, 4, 2 and 1 seconds. Roughly how long does a sequential run take? A concurrent run? (Answer: about 12 s and about 4 s plus overhead.)
  2. (Apply) A colleague adds today’s date to the top of the shared system prompt “for context”. What breaks, and where should the date go instead?
  3. (Design) Why does letting role B read role A’s answer in the same round make replays from a log unreliable?
  4. (Think) Name one check in your own system that is currently an LLM call but could be a plain comparison.

Further reading

  • AWS, Amazon Bedrock User Guide: Carry out a conversation with the Converse API operations.
  • Anthropic, Building effective agents (2024).
  • Wu et al., AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation (2023).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.3 — Per-Role Model Routing with Fallback and Backoff

Subtitle: Your preferred model will be unavailable at the worst possible moment. Design for it on day one.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Give each role an ordered list of models and walk it on failure. 2. Sort errors into route, transient and caller errors, and handle each one differently. 3. Explain capped exponential backoff with jitter, and why a per-model cooldown is a different tool. 4. Test a router without spending anything on model calls.

You need: Chapter 7.2 (roles and the shared Converse payload). Powers of two.

7.3.1 How it started

The first time I wired a reasoning-heavy role to a top-tier model on Bedrock, it failed before it ever answered a question. Not because of the prompt. The account had not yet completed the model provider’s access form, so every call came back with a “resource not found” style error.

That small annoyance led to one of the better design decisions in my stack: every role has an ordered list of models, and the router quietly falls back and backs off.

7.3.2 The routing table

Each role maps to a preference list:

route(r)=[m1,m2,…,mk] \text{route}(r) = [m_1, m_2, \dots, m_k]

Reasoning-heavy roles put a stronger model first. Cheap classification roles may put a smaller, faster model first. The last entry is always a model I know the account can reach. It acts as a floor.

This is not “use the best model everywhere”. Model choice is a per-role cost-versus-quality decision. A role that pulls three fields out of structured text does not need the same model as a role that must weigh conflicting evidence.

7.3.3 Fallback and the three kinds of error

On each call the router walks the list and tries the first model that is not currently backed off. Every role uses the same Converse payload, so the retry is literally the same request with a different modelId. No prompt translation, no special cases.

What counts as “fall through to the next model” is a judgement call. I sort errors into three kinds:

Kind Examples What the router does
Route error model not found, access not granted, not supported in region This model is not available to you. Fall back and back off.
Transient error throttling, timeouts, service unavailable Retry with exponential backoff, maybe on the same model, then fall back.
Caller error validation failure, malformed payload Do not retry. Five models just give five identical failures and five bills.

Figure 7.3.1 — The router’s walk. A call picks the next model not in cooldown and sends the same payload. Success (green) returns a verdict and records which model answered. An error (orange) is classified: route errors cool the model down and loop to the next candidate, transient errors back off first, and caller errors stop at once. If every model is cooled down, the floor model serves.

7.3.4 Backoff as state, not as sleep

The usual advice is “retry with exponential backoff and jitter”. Jitter means adding randomness to the wait so that many clients do not retry at the same instant.

Formula (capped exponential backoff, full jitter). The wait before retry nn is tn=min⁡(tmax,t0⋅2n)⋅U(0,1), t_n = \min\left(t_{\max},\ t_0 \cdot 2^{n}\right) \cdot U(0,1), where t0t_0 is the first wait, tmaxt_{\max} is the cap and U(0,1)U(0,1) is a uniform random number between 0 and 1.

This is the “full jitter” variant from the AWS Architecture Blog. The ceiling doubles each time until it hits the cap. The actual wait is a random point below the ceiling.

Figure 7.3.2 — The ceiling doubles, the waits scatter below it. The blue line is the ceiling min⁡(tmax,t02n)\min(t_{\max}, t_0 2^n), with the cap set at 32t032\,t_0 for the picture. The orange dots are six random waits per retry, drawn uniformly under the ceiling (mulberry32 generator, seed 20261107). Because the waits spread out, a crowd of throttled clients does not come back all at once.

That formula is right for transient errors inside one request. For route errors I wanted something else: a per-model cooldown that lasts across requests. When a model returns a route error, the router records “do not try this model until time TT”. Every later call skips it until the cooldown ends, then probes it again.

The nice result is self-healing. When the access form for the preferred model was finally approved, the reasoning roles began using it on their own the next time the cooldown expired. Nobody edited a config file.

If every model in a role’s list is cooled down, the router serves the floor model rather than failing. That is deliberate: for an advisory system, a slightly weaker answer beats no answer. If the answer gates something important, you may prefer to fail closed (refuse to proceed) instead. Decide which world you are in.

7.3.5 Log which model answered

A fallback router hides failure. That is what you want operationally and exactly what you do not want analytically. So every verdict records the model that actually produced it. Without that, you will one day compare “role X this week vs last week” and not realise half of last week was served by the fallback.

7.3.6 Pitfalls I hit or nearly hit

  • Retrying non-idempotent work. (Idempotent means safe to repeat.) If a call has side effects downstream, a retry can double them. Keep LLM calls pure and do side effects after you have a validated verdict.
  • Synchronised retries. Without jitter, a burst of throttled calls all retry at the same instant and get throttled again.
  • Silent quality drift. If the floor model serves for days, outputs change. Alert when the fallback rate crosses a level you care about.
  • Schema differences across models. Some models are looser with forced tool output. Validate every response against the schema, whichever model produced it.

7.3.7 Testing the router without a model

The router is pure logic over a list, a clock and an error classification. So it is easy to test for free with a fake client that raises scripted errors:

  1. The first model raises a route error: the call should succeed on the second model, and the first should now be in cooldown.
  2. A second call within the cooldown should not even try the first model.
  3. Move the fake clock past the cooldown: the first model should be probed again.
  4. Every model raises a caller error: the router should stop after the first attempt and return a structured error.

These four tests caught two real bugs in my first version. One was a cooldown keyed by role instead of by model, so one role’s failure did not protect the others. The other was a broad except that classified a schema-validation error as a route error and burned through the whole list.

7.3.8 Cost and latency of fallback

Fallback has a price. A failed first attempt adds its latency to the call. A fast failure (an access error returns in milliseconds) barely matters. A timeout, though, has just doubled the call’s latency.

That is why I separate timeouts from route errors and set per-attempt timeouts tighter than the overall budget.

Rule of thumb. With a total time budget BB and kk candidate models, a per-attempt timeout near B/kB/k guarantees you at least get to try the floor model.

7.3.9 What I’d tell another engineer

Treat your model list like a dependency list: explicit, ordered, testable. Write a live probe that sends a tiny request to each candidate model and reports which are reachable. Run it after any account or region change. Most “the AI is broken” incidents I’ve seen were really “the route was broken”, and a probe tells you which in seconds.

7.3.10 Summary

  • Each role has an ordered model list ending in a reachable floor model.
  • Route errors cool a model down across requests; transient errors back off with jitter; caller errors stop.
  • Cooldowns make the router self-healing when access returns.
  • Log the model that answered, and test the router with a fake client and a fake clock.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With t0=1t_0 = 1 s and tmax=16t_{\max} = 16 s, what is the ceiling on the wait before retry 3? Retry 6? (Answer: 8 s; 16 s, because of the cap.)
  2. (Apply) You have a 12-second budget and 3 candidate models. What per-attempt timeout would you start with, and why?
  3. (Debug) Your cooldown is keyed by role. Describe what goes wrong when two roles share a preferred model that has lost access.
  4. (Think) For an advisory role you serve the floor model when all else fails. Name a kind of role where you would fail closed instead.

Further reading

  • Marc Brooker, Exponential Backoff And Jitter, AWS Architecture Blog (2015).
  • Google, Site Reliability Engineering, chapter “Handling Overload”.
  • AWS, Amazon Bedrock User Guide: Model access.

— Tariq

Chapter 7.4 — The Economics of Prefix-Anchored Prompt Caching

Subtitle: Caching only works if the bytes before the cache marker never change. That one rule reshapes how you write prompts.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain what a prompt cache stores and why it only matches on an exact prefix. 2. Derive the break-even number of calls for caching from write and read prices. 3. Lay out a prompt so that the cache is actually used, and measure that it is.

You need: Chapter 7.2 (the shared prompt layout). Simple algebra with inequalities.

7.4.1 Free money that breaks quietly

Prompt caching is the closest thing to free money in LLM engineering. It is also the easiest thing to break without noticing. When I restructured my multi-role swarm in September 2026, the biggest win was not a better model. It was moving a timestamp.

7.4.2 How prefix caching works

Providers that support prompt caching (Anthropic directly, and Bedrock via a cachePoint block in Converse) let you mark a point in the prompt. The provider stores the model’s internal state for everything before that marker. Later, if a request is byte-for-byte identical up to the marker, the provider reuses that state instead of recomputing it.

Two consequences follow:

  1. Prefix-anchored. The cache key is in effect the exact token sequence up to the marker. Change one character early on and everything after it misses.
  2. Write vs read pricing. Writing a cache entry usually costs more than normal input tokens. Reading from the cache costs well below. Entries also expire after a short idle time.

7.4.3 A simple cost model

Setup. A prompt has PP cacheable prefix tokens and DD dynamic tokens. The normal input price is cc per token. A cache write costs αc\alpha c per token and a cache read costs βc\beta c, with α>1>β\alpha > 1 > \beta. Over NN calls that share the prefix within the cache lifetime there is one write and N−1N-1 reads: Ccached=αcP+(N−1)βcP+NcD,Cuncached=Nc(P+D). C_{\text{cached}} = \alpha c P + (N-1)\beta c P + N c D, \qquad C_{\text{uncached}} = N c (P + D).

Result (break-even). Caching is cheaper exactly when α+(N−1)β<N⇔N>α−β1−β. \alpha + (N-1)\beta < N \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N > \frac{\alpha - \beta}{1 - \beta}.

Why. The dynamic part NcDNcD is the same on both sides, so cancel it. Divide what is left by cPcP. That gives α+(N−1)β<N\alpha + (N-1)\beta < N. Move the NN terms to one side: α−β<N(1−β)\alpha - \beta < N(1-\beta). Since 1−β>01-\beta > 0, divide by it.

With typical published multipliers the break-even is a small handful of calls. Beyond it, the saving on the prefix approaches 1−β1-\beta of its cost. Latency follows a similar shape, because the provider skips recomputing the prefix.

Figure 7.4.2 — Cost of the prefix per call, relative to no caching. The blue curve is (α+(N−1)β)/N(\alpha + (N-1)\beta)/N using illustrative values α=1.25\alpha = 1.25 and β=0.1\beta = 0.1 (stand-ins, not any provider’s price list). Above the dashed 1.0 line, caching costs more than not caching. The orange dot marks the break-even. As NN grows the curve sinks toward the floor β\beta.

The practical reading: caching rewards prompts with a large, stable prefix and a small, changing tail, called often enough to stay inside the cache lifetime.

7.4.4 Designing prompts for the cache

In my swarm every role’s system block is laid out as: shared prefix, cache marker, role-specific block. All dynamic data goes into the user turn.

Figure 7.4.1 — Same parts, different order. Top: the stable shared prefix comes first, then the cache marker (dark block), then the role block and the snapshot. Bottom: a changing value such as the current time sits at the very start, so no two calls share a prefix. Every call writes a cache entry and none is ever read.

A few rules came out of that layout:

  • No timestamps, request IDs or counters in the prefix. This is the classic accident. “Current time: …” at the top of a system prompt silently disables caching.
  • Shared before specific. Put text common to all roles first so one cache entry serves every role. Role-specific text goes after the marker, or behind a second marker if your provider supports several.
  • Deterministic serialisation. If you build the prefix from a dictionary, sort the keys. Two logically identical prefixes with different key orders are two cache entries.
  • Tool definitions count. Tool schemas sit in the request too. Keep them stable and ordered.
  • Minimum size. Providers have a minimum cacheable length. A tiny prefix is not cached at all, so measure, don’t assume.

7.4.5 Measure it

Converse returns cache-read and cache-write token counts in its usage block. I log both on every call, next to latency. That turns “I think caching works” into a ratio you can watch:

Definition (hit ratio). h=cache-read tokenscache-read+cache-write+uncached input tokens h = \frac{\text{cache-read tokens}}{\text{cache-read} + \text{cache-write} + \text{uncached input tokens}}

If hh drops after a prompt edit, you broke the prefix. That has happened to me, and the log caught it the same day.

7.4.6 A worked mental example

Picture five roles fanned out over the same snapshot within a second or two. Without caching, each role pays for the shared house rules in full, five times. With the shared block first and the marker after it, the first role writes the cache and the other four read it. The role blocks and the snapshot are paid at the normal rate every time. That is fine: they are the part that actually differs.

Now picture the same swarm with the snapshot’s timestamp put at the top of the system prompt “for context”. Every call has a unique prefix. Every call writes an entry nobody will read. You now pay the write premium on every request, which is worse than not caching at all. So a broken cache is not neutral: it can cost more than no cache.

7.4.7 Interaction with model fallback and traffic shape

Caches are per model. If a role falls back from its preferred model (Chapter 7.3), the fallback model starts cold. During an outage of the preferred model your hit ratio drops and your bill rises, just when you are least likely to be watching the bill. Log the model next to the cache counters so this shows up.

Most write-ups present caching as an on/off switch. In practice it is a design constraint on prompt structure, and it touches everything else:

Factor Effect on caching
Model fallback A different model means a different cache.
A/B tests Two prompt variants means two prefixes.
Bursty traffic Widely spaced bursts let entries expire between them.
Call frequency A role called once an hour may gain little; a swarm fanning one prefix to many roles in seconds gains a lot.

7.4.8 Summary

  • The cache reuses work only for a byte-identical prefix up to the marker.
  • Caching pays once N>(α−β)/(1−β)N > (\alpha-\beta)/(1-\beta); after that the prefix costs close to β\beta of normal.
  • Put stable, shared text first and every changing value after the marker.
  • A broken prefix pays the write premium every time and can cost more than no cache; watch the hit ratio hh.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With α=2\alpha = 2 and β=0\beta = 0, what is the break-even NN? (Answer: N>2N > 2, so three or more calls.)
  2. (Apply) A prompt builder serialises a dictionary without sorting keys. Why can the hit ratio fall even though the content never changed?
  3. (Calculate) Show that as N→∞N \to \infty the prefix cost per call tends to βcP\beta c P.
  4. (Think) Your preferred model has a two-hour outage. What happens to hh and the bill, and what would you log to see it?

Further reading

  • Anthropic, Prompt caching documentation.
  • AWS, Amazon Bedrock User Guide: Prompt caching for faster model inference.
  • Pope et al., Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference (2022), for why prefix state (the KV cache) is reusable at all.

— Tariq

Chapter 7.5 — Forcing JSON-Schema Output Through Tool Calls

Subtitle: If your parser starts with a regex looking for triple backticks, you have a reliability bug waiting to happen.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Use a single forced tool call to get a model’s answer as a structured object. 2. Validate every answer and turn failures into an explicit error value, never a guess. 3. Design small, clear schemas that models fill in reliably.

You need: Chapter 7.2. A basic idea of JSON and of a schema (a description of which fields an object must have).

7.5.1 The problem with “please return JSON”

Early versions of my agent roles returned prose with a JSON block somewhere inside. The parser found the block with a regular expression, stripped the code fences (the triple backticks), and hoped. It worked most of the time. “Most of the time” is not good enough when the output gates anything.

The fix: stop asking for JSON. Instead, give the model a tool whose input schema is the answer, and force the model to call it.

7.5.2 The trick

Tool use (also called function calling) exists so a model can request an action with structured arguments. The model emits a toolUse block holding a JSON object that is meant to match the tool’s input schema.

So define exactly one tool, say submit_verdict, whose JSON Schema describes your answer. Then set tool choice to “must call a tool” (any) or “must call this tool”. The model’s answer now arrives as structured arguments, not free text.

On Bedrock’s Converse API this is toolConfig with a toolSpec (name, description, inputSchema) and toolChoice. The Anthropic API has the same idea. You never run the tool. The tool call is the output.

Why it beats “please return JSON”:

  • The model is trained for it. Providers fine-tune heavily on producing valid tool arguments. That path is better trained than “write JSON in a reply”.
  • No fence scraping. The arguments arrive as a parsed object in their own content block.
  • The schema documents itself. Field descriptions and enums in the schema are instructions the model actually reads.

It is not a guarantee. Unless the provider offers strict, grammar-constrained decoding (generation that is only allowed to produce schema-valid text), the model can still break the schema: a missing required field, or a string where you wanted a number. So the second half of the pattern matters just as much.

7.5.3 Validate, then decide

Every response goes through three steps:

  1. Extract the toolUse block. If there isn’t one (rare when tool choice is forced, but possible), fall back to text extraction and mark the result as degraded.
  2. Validate it against the same JSON Schema with a real validator.
  3. Coerce or reject. I do not “repair” fields that carry meaning. A verdict that fails validation becomes a structured error, not a guess.

Figure 7.5.1 — Two exits, no middle. The answer either passes validation and goes downstream as a valid object (green), or becomes an explicit error that is logged with the raw arguments (orange). The dashed path is the rare case with no tool block at all: text fallback, clearly marked as degraded.

Definition (role as a total function). Treat a role as a function f:X→Y∪{⊥}, f: X \to Y \cup \{\bot\}, where YY is the set of schema-valid objects and ⊥\bot (“bottom”) is an explicit failure value.

Everything downstream handles ⊥\bot on purpose. That is far easier to reason about than a parser that sometimes returns half an object.

7.5.4 Schema design tips

Tip Why
Enums over free strings If a field can be one of five things, say so; the model picks from the list.
Bounded numbers Use minimum/maximum for probabilities and scores, and still validate them.
A reason field, but last A short rationale helps humans and logs. Code should never branch on it.
Small schemas Deeply nested optional structures cause more invalid outputs. Flatten where you can.
Explicit abstain Give the model a legitimate way to say “insufficient information”, or it will invent confidence to fill required fields.

7.5.5 Reasoning before answering

One objection: forced tool output takes away the model’s room to “think out loud” before it commits. Two reasonable answers:

  • Many current models support a separate reasoning (thinking) channel that runs before the tool call. The structured answer still benefits from deliberation.
  • You can put a short analysis field in the schema before the decision fields. The model writes its reasoning first, then the verdict. JSON key order has no meaning to a parser, but generation order matters, and models tend to fill fields in schema order.

What I avoid is the opposite: a verdict field first, then a justification. That invites post-hoc rationalisation: explaining whatever the first token already committed to.

7.5.6 Log the raw block

I log the raw tool arguments, not just the validated object. When validation fails, the raw arguments are the only way to tell whether the model misread the schema, the schema was ambiguous, or the model simply produced junk. Over a few weeks, the pattern of validation failures is a direct readout of where your schema is unclear.

7.5.7 Pitfalls

  • Forcing a tool call and asking for prose in the prompt. The model may try to do both and get worse at each.
  • Assuming every model on a multi-vendor platform handles forced tool choice the same way. Test each model on your schema.
  • Treating “valid JSON” as “correct answer”. Validation checks shape, not truth.

7.5.8 Summary

  • Define one tool whose input schema is the answer, force the model to call it, and never execute it.
  • Forced tools make valid output likely, not certain: always validate.
  • A role returns a valid object or an explicit ⊥\bot, never a half-parsed object.
  • Keep schemas small, use enums and bounds, allow abstain, and put any reasoning field before the decision.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why is “valid against the schema” not the same as “correct”? (Answer: validation only checks the shape and ranges of the fields; it cannot check whether the content is true.)
  2. (Design) Write a small JSON Schema for a verdict with a three-way label, a bounded confidence and an abstain option. Where do you put the rationale field?
  3. (Debug) Your logs show many failures where a numeric field arrives as a string. List two possible causes and how the raw-argument log helps tell them apart.
  4. (Think) Why might putting the verdict field before the analysis field make answers worse?

Further reading

  • Anthropic, Tool use with Claude documentation (including forcing tool use).
  • AWS, Amazon Bedrock User Guide: Use a tool to complete a model response.
  • JSON Schema specification, json-schema.org.
  • Willard & Louf, Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models (2023), on grammar-constrained decoding.

— Tariq

Chapter 7.6 — Deterministic Sensors Before LLM Calls

Subtitle: If the question is “is this number above that number?”, a language model is the most expensive and least reliable way to answer it.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Separate a pipeline into deterministic sensors and model-based judges. 2. Write sensors that are pure, typed, explainable and easy to test. 3. Use robust statistics (median and MAD) without leaking future data.

You need: mean, standard deviation and median. Chapter 7.2 helps but is not required.

7.6.1 A role that was really arithmetic

One role in my agent swarm used to be a language model reading telemetry: data freshness, feed quality, whether the inputs looked sane. It mostly worked. Then I looked at what it was actually doing and saw it was comparing numbers to limits. I replaced it with plain code. The model became an optional override instead of the default.

That swap generalises. Before any LLM call, ask which parts of the question are deterministic, and answer those with code.

7.6.2 Sensors and judges

I think of the pipeline as two layers:

  • Sensors are deterministic functions of the input: staleness, missing fields, out-of-range values, schema violations, counts, simple statistics. Same input, same output, every time, in microseconds.
  • Judges weigh ambiguous, conflicting or unstructured evidence. That is where a language model can add something.

The sensor layer runs first. Its outputs go two places. They can short-circuit the pipeline (no point asking a model to reason about stale data). And they are passed to the judges as structured facts, so the model reasons over verified numbers instead of working them out again.

Figure 7.6.1 — Cheap, certain checks first. Each sensor returns ok, warn or fail. A written-down combine rule decides. A fail stops the pipeline with no model call (orange). Otherwise the judge receives the verified numbers as facts (green).

7.6.3 Why not let the model do it?

Four reasons, in order of how much they bit me:

Reason Sensor LLM
Reliability Never “mostly” right Usually right with numbers, sometimes confidently wrong, especially with many digits, units or near-boundary comparisons
Determinism Recomputable exactly from logs The same input may give a different verdict on replay
Latency Microseconds; can say “stop” and save the whole call Seconds
Cost Free You pay for every token spent re-checking arithmetic

7.6.4 What makes a good sensor

A sensor should be:

  • Pure. No hidden state, no network calls. Input in, structured result out.
  • Typed. Return an enumerated status (ok, warn, fail) plus the measured values, not a sentence.
  • Explainable. Each result names which check fired and the observed value.
  • Cheap to test. Table-driven unit tests with boundary cases: just below, at, and just above the limit.

Pattern (sensor suite). A suite of named checks, each a function sj:X→{ok,warn,fail}×ℝmj, s_j: X \to \{\text{ok}, \text{warn}, \text{fail}\} \times \mathbb{R}^{m_j}, combined by an explicit rule such as “any fail means fail”.

The combine rule matters. Write it down. Do not leave a model to infer it.

7.6.5 Statistical sensors

Not every sensor is a fixed threshold. Some useful ones are standard statistics:

  • A rolling z-score zt=(xt−μ̂t)/σ̂tz_t = (x_t - \hat\mu_t)/\hat\sigma_t flags values far from recent behaviour. Here μ̂t\hat\mu_t and σ̂t\hat\sigma_t are the mean and standard deviation computed only from data before tt.
  • A robust alternative uses the median and the median absolute deviation, MAD=median(|xi−x̃|)\text{MAD} = \text{median}(|x_i - \tilde x|), where x̃\tilde x is the median. It is not dragged around by the very outliers you are trying to detect.
  • Staleness is just tnow−tlast updatet_{\text{now}} - t_{\text{last update}}. It is astonishing how often it is the most important check in a system.

Figure 7.6.2 — One wild value stretches the standard deviation, not the MAD. Nineteen grey points are random draws from a standard normal; the orange point is a single outlier at 9. The blue band (mean ± 1 sd) is pulled right and more than doubles in width. The green band (median ± 1.4826·MAD, scaled so it matches the sd for normal data) stays close to the true spread. Simulated data only: seeded generator, process stated under the chart.

These are still deterministic. The judgement is in choosing them, not in running them.

7.6.6 Keeping the model as an option

I did not delete the model path for the telemetry role. It sits behind a setting, off by default. That lets me run both in shadow (Chapter 7.7) and compare: when would the model have disagreed with the sensors, and was it ever right to? So far the honest answer is that the sensor suite does the job the role exists for. If that ever changes, the evidence will be in the log, not in my intuition.

7.6.7 Pitfalls

  • Sensors that drift into judgement. If a “sensor” has twenty special cases, it has become a rule engine. That may be fine, but call it what it is and test it like one.
  • Passing raw data to the model anyway. If you have a verified number, pass that number. Do not also pass the raw series and ask the model to recompute it. It may disagree with your sensor and you will not know which to trust.
  • Lookahead in statistics. A rolling statistic that includes the current value, or a normalisation over the full sample, leaks future information. Compute strictly from the past.
  • Silent fallthrough. If a sensor itself errors, that is a fail, not an ok.

7.6.8 What I’d tell another engineer

Draw a line through every LLM prompt you have and mark which sentences ask the model to compute something checkable. Move those into code. What remains is the model’s real job, and it is usually smaller and clearer than you expected.

7.6.9 Summary

  • Sensors are deterministic, fast and testable; judges handle what is truly ambiguous.
  • Run sensors first: they can stop the pipeline, and they hand the judge verified facts.
  • Prefer robust statistics (median, MAD) and compute them only from past data.
  • A sensor that errors is a fail.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) The values are 2, 3, 3, 4, 100. What are the median and the MAD? (Answer: median 3; absolute deviations 1, 0, 0, 1, 97, so MAD = 1.)
  2. (Apply) Write three boundary test cases for a staleness check with a limit LL.
