  3. (Spot the bug) A z-score sensor uses the mean and sd of the whole day, including the current value. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
  4. (Think) Take one of your own prompts and list the sentences that ask the model to do checkable arithmetic.

Further reading

  • Sculley et al., Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (NeurIPS 2015).
  • Breck et al., The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness (2017).
  • Rousseeuw & Croux, Alternatives to the Median Absolute Deviation (JASA, 1993).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.7 — Shadow Mode: Letting an AI Decide Without Letting It Decide

Subtitle: Before a model gets any authority, it should spend a long time being right where nobody is listening.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain shadow mode and what each shadow record must contain. 2. Say why language models are hard to backtest honestly. 3. Design a fair comparison built on disagreements, counterfactual labels and per-cell breakdowns. 4. Apply the engineering rules that keep a shadow path from touching live state.

You need: mean and confidence interval; the idea of a bootstrap (resampling your data to estimate uncertainty).

7.7.1 The habit

Every time I add a model to a decision path, I start it in shadow mode. It sees what the live system sees. It produces a verdict. The verdict is written down. Nothing happens.

Weeks later, the log answers a question no benchmark can: would this model have done better than what I actually ran, on my data, under my conditions?

7.7.2 What shadow mode is

Shadow mode (also called dark launching or shadow deployment) runs a candidate decision-maker next to the incumbent, on the same live inputs, without the candidate’s output affecting anything. The incumbent might be a rule engine, a human or an older model.

Definition (shadow record). For each decision point ii, record: - the input (or a hash of it, plus enough to rebuild it); - the incumbent’s action aiinca_i^{\text{inc}}; - the candidate’s action aicanda_i^{\text{cand}}; - metadata: model, latency, token usage, errors.

Later you join those rows to outcomes. In my trading research the candidate is a language-model tier and the incumbent is a deterministic decision tree. The comparison runs nightly, offline, report-only.

Figure 7.7.1 — Only the incumbent touches the world. The green path is live: the incumbent’s action is what actually happens. The dashed candidate path runs asynchronously with weight zero and only writes to the log. Every attempt from both sides lands in an append-only log, which is joined to outcomes nightly and offline to produce a report.

7.7.3 Why not just backtest the model?

Because language models are hard to backtest honestly:

  1. Training-data leakage. A model trained on internet text up to some date may “know” what happened in historical periods. Any backtest on data before its cutoff is contaminated. Shadow mode only ever asks about the present.
  2. Vendors change. The model behind an API name can change. Shadow logs record which model answered, today.
  3. Operational reality. Timeouts, rate limits, malformed outputs and latency are part of the system. A backtest that replays prompts offline skips all of them.

7.7.4 Designing the comparison

The tricky part is what to compare when the two engines agree only sometimes.

Measure Use Watch out for
Agreement rate Easy to compute Least useful: both engines can agree and both be wrong
Disagreement outcomes Where the information is Needs a label for the action you did not take
Counterfactual labels Say what “would have happened” Rule must be fixed and declared in advance
Per-cell results Show where each engine wins An engine can win on average and lose where you care most

A counterfactual label needs a fixed, pre-declared rule. One example is a first-passage rule: from the decision point, which of two pre-defined levels would price have touched first over a fixed horizon? The rule must be declared before you look, use only data after the decision time, and be the same for both engines.

Cells are the contexts in which decisions were made. Break results down by cell, not just in total.

Per-cell summary. For each decision, the paired difference in outcome is di=yicand−yiinc. d_i = y_i^{\text{cand}} - y_i^{\text{inc}}. Report its mean with a confidence interval. Decisions within a day are correlated, so bootstrap by day, not by row: resample whole days.

Why by day? If you resample single rows, you treat correlated decisions as independent. The interval then comes out too narrow and you feel more certain than you should.

7.7.5 Engineering rules I follow

  • Asynchronous and non-blocking. The candidate runs on a worker. The live path never waits for it. If it times out, the row records an error and life goes on.
  • Fail without side effects. Any exception in the shadow path is caught at the boundary, recorded, and leaves live state untouched. That is the one place I deliberately catch broadly.
  • Weight zero. Shadow outputs may be stored next to live features for analysis, but they carry no weight in any live computation.
  • Append-only logs. Shadow rows are never edited. If the scoring rule changes, rescore from the raw rows.
  • Pre-registered promotion criteria. Decide before you look what evidence would justify giving the candidate any authority. Otherwise you will be tempted to move the goalposts after a good week.

7.7.6 Pitfalls

  • Coercing outputs silently. If the candidate’s answer cannot be expressed in the incumbent’s action space, record that. Do not quietly map it to the nearest action.
  • Survivorship in the log. If rows are only written when the call succeeds, you have hidden the failure rate. Write a row for every attempt.
  • Too-short windows. A couple of weeks of shadow data covers a narrow slice of conditions. Say clearly what the window does not cover.

7.7.7 What I’d tell another engineer

Shadow mode feels slow. It is the fastest way I know to avoid deploying something that looked brilliant in a demo and is mediocre in production. Quite often the result is “the candidate is not better”. That is a perfectly good result, and it cost you nothing.

7.7.8 Summary

  • Shadow mode runs a candidate on live inputs with zero effect, and logs both actions every time.
  • It avoids the training-data leakage and operational blind spots of backtesting a language model.
  • The information is in disagreements, scored by a pre-declared counterfactual rule, broken down by cell, bootstrapped by day.
  • Fix promotion criteria in advance and never let the shadow path touch live state.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Two engines agree on 95% of decisions. Why does this tell you almost nothing about which is better? (Answer: the agreed cases score the same for both; only the 5% of disagreements can separate them, and agreement says nothing about whether either is right.)
  2. (Apply) Write down a counterfactual labelling rule for your own domain. Check that it uses only data after the decision time.
  3. (Statistics) Explain in two sentences why bootstrapping by row gives an interval that is too narrow when decisions within a day are correlated.
  4. (Think) Your shadow log only has rows for successful calls. What number have you lost, and why does it matter for promotion?

Further reading

  • Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Cambridge, 2020).
  • Google, Site Reliability Engineering, chapter “Testing for Reliability”.
  • Sculley et al., Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (NeurIPS 2015).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.8 — Bounded LLM Advisory: Models That Can Only Veto or Size Down

Subtitle: If you let a language model add risk, you have to trust it. If it can only remove risk, you only have to bound it.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State the bounded-advisor rule q′=m⋅qq' = m \cdot q with m∈[0,1]m \in [0,1] and say what each value of mm means. 2. Compare the worst case of a bounded advisor with that of an unbounded one. 3. Map every failure mode of an advisor to a safe, written-down default. 4. Describe how to measure whether an advisor earns its place.

You need: Chapter 7.7 (shadow mode). Multiplication and intervals.

7.8.1 A narrow conclusion

There is a lot of excitement about language models as traders. I read the literature carefully in October 2026 before deciding what role, if any, a model should have in my stack. My conclusion was narrow:

Rule. A model may reduce exposure, never create it. It can veto a decision that a deterministic engine has already made, or ask for a smaller size. It cannot start a trade, flip a direction, or ask for more.

This chapter explains why that asymmetry is the right default for any high-stakes decision system, trading or not.

7.8.2 What the evidence actually shows

The published evidence on LLMs forecasting markets is mostly:

  • short-window,
  • focused on equities,
  • at daily frequency,
  • light on transaction costs.

Some of the most-cited results apply to the immediate reaction to news, which cannot be traded. Longer-horizon re-tests found that reported advantages shrink a lot. I found nothing credible on intraday futures. None of that supports trusting a model as a source of edge. At most, it supports a narrowly gated role where the model can flag situations a rule engine might miss.

There is also a structural concern. A model trained on data up to some date may carry knowledge of historical outcomes, which makes historical evaluation hard to trust (see Chapter 7.7).

7.8.3 The asymmetry argument

Think of the model as a function that, given context, adjusts a proposed action. The deterministic engine proposes a size q≥0q \ge 0 in some direction.

Definition (bounded advisor). The advisor returns a multiplier mm and the final size is q′=m⋅q,m∈[0,1]. q' = m \cdot q, \qquad m \in [0, 1]. m=0m = 0 is a veto; 0<m<10 < m < 1 is a size-down; m=1m = 1 is “no objection”. The advisor cannot return m>1m > 1 and cannot change direction.

Figure 7.8.1 — The advisor lives on a short line. The green band from 0 to 1 is everything the advisor is allowed to say. Anything above 1, or any change of direction, is outside the range and is clamped away in code. The two boxes compare the worst outcomes: inside the band, a missed or smaller trade; outside it, a trade nobody approved.

Why does this matter? Look at the worst case. Suppose the model is wrong, manipulated, hallucinating (stating made-up things confidently) or simply down:

  • With m∈[0,1]m \in [0,1], the worst outcome is that you miss or under-size a trade the engine wanted. The loss is opportunity, bounded by what the engine would have made.
  • With unbounded mm or control of direction, the worst outcome is a trade the engine never wanted, at a size it never approved. The loss is unbounded in the ordinary sense.

The bounded design turns “can I trust the model?” into “can I afford what the model might make me miss?” That second question you can measure in shadow mode.

7.8.4 Failure modes, all mapped to safe defaults

Failure Handling
Timeout or error Treat as m=1m = 1 (no objection) or m=0m = 0 (veto), whichever failure is cheaper for your system. Decide explicitly and write it down. I lean towards the engine’s own decision standing, because the engine is the validated component.
Invalid output Schema-invalid responses are errors, never parsed charitably (Chapter 7.5).
Prompt injection via inputs If any input text could be controlled by an attacker (news, social posts), the bounded range limits what an injected instruction can do. It cannot make the system buy.
Overcautious model A model that vetoes everything is safe and useless. It shows up in the shadow log as a high veto rate with no outcome benefit.

Prompt injection means hiding instructions inside data the model reads, hoping it obeys them.

7.8.5 Measuring whether the advisor earns its place

A veto is only valuable if the trades it removes are worse than the ones it keeps. In shadow, for every engine decision, record what the advisor would have done. Then compare the outcomes of vetoed decisions with non-vetoed ones, using day-level bootstrapping and a pre-declared criterion. If vetoed trades are not reliably worse, the advisor is costing you opportunity for nothing.

A veto also changes which trades exist, so its effect spreads into risk metrics: fewer trades, a different drawdown path. Evaluate on the full path, not just per-trade averages.

7.8.6 Engineering notes

  • The bound is enforced in code, after the model returns, by clamping and by ignoring any direction field. The prompt says the same thing, but prompts are requests, not constraints.
  • The advisor sees a curated, structured context, not raw feeds.
  • The decision record stores the engine’s original proposal, the advisor’s raw output and the applied result, so every adjustment can be audited.

7.8.7 What I’d tell another engineer

If you are adding a model to anything that moves money, health or infrastructure, start by asking: what is the worst thing this component can do, and can I make that worst thing cheap? Bounding the action space is the most reliable safety mechanism I know, because it does not depend on the model being good.

7.8.8 Summary

  • The advisor can only multiply the engine’s size by m∈[0,1]m \in [0,1]; it never adds size or picks direction.
  • Its worst case is a missed or smaller trade, which is bounded and measurable.
  • Every failure maps to a default you chose in advance; invalid output is an error.
  • The clamp lives in code, and the advisor must prove in shadow that what it removes is worse than what it keeps.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) The engine proposes size 4 and the advisor returns m=1.5m = 1.5. What size is used after the clamp? (Answer: 4, because mm is clamped to 1.)
  2. (Apply) For your own system, which failure is cheaper on timeout: m=1m = 1 or m=0m = 0? Write down your reasoning in two sentences.
  3. (Measure) Describe the shadow comparison that would show an advisor is “safe and useless”.
  4. (Think) Why is a rule in the prompt (“never increase size”) not enough on its own?

Further reading

  • Lopez-Lira & Tang, Can ChatGPT Forecast Stock Price Movements? (arXiv 2304.07619).
  • Greshake et al., Not what you’ve signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection (2023).
  • Amodei et al., Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.9 — Comparing an LLM Tier Against a Rule Engine, Fairly

Subtitle: The interesting question isn’t “is the model smart?” It’s “is it better than the boring thing I already have?”

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Build a paired sample so both engines answer the same question at the same moments. 2. Write a counterfactual label that is pre-declared, causal and identical for both engines. 3. Choose the right statistics: paired differences, block bootstrap by session, per-cell results and trial counts.

You need: Chapter 7.7 (shadow mode). Mean, confidence interval, bootstrap.

7.9.1 Most of the work is the comparison

Every proposal to put a language model in a decision path should be answered with a comparison against the incumbent (what you already run). In my case the incumbent is a deterministic decision tree written and validated over months. The challenger is a language-model tier that sees the same situation. The comparison runs nightly, offline, and only produces a report.

Getting that comparison right turned out to be most of the work.

7.9.2 Same question, same moments

Rule one: both engines must answer the same question at the same decision points.

That sounds obvious until you notice the engines may be “active” at different times. A rule engine fires when its conditions are met. A model can be asked at any moment. If you compare the model’s calls at every moment with the engine’s calls only when it fired, you are comparing different populations.

My approach is to define the decision window from the incumbent’s side: only while the upstream system has granted permission in a direction. For each step in that window, each engine says GO or WAIT. That gives a paired sample (airule,aillm)(a_i^{\text{rule}}, a_i^{\text{llm}}) at identical points ii.

Figure 7.9.1 — One column, one pair. Inside the window every step ii gets an answer from both engines, so each column is a fair pair. The dashed orange columns are where the rule engine waited but the model said GO: the subset that matters most (Section 7.9.5). The GO/WAIT pattern is drawn by hand for illustration.

If the model’s answer falls outside the action space (for example, it proposes the opposite direction while permission exists only one way), it is coerced to WAIT and the coercion is counted. Coercions are a result in themselves.

7.9.3 Labelling the road not taken

The model’s GO calls often happen where the engine said WAIT, so there is no real trade to score. You need a counterfactual label: a rule for what would have happened. It must be:

  • Pre-declared: fixed before you see any comparison results.
  • Causal: using only data after the decision point.
  • Identical for both engines.

A common choice is a first-passage label. From the decision point, which of two levels (a target and a stop, defined from information available at decision time) is touched first within a fixed horizon? If neither, the label is neutral. WAIT scores zero. Real trades are scored with their realised outcome where they exist.

7.9.4 The statistics

For each decision point you get yiruley_i^{\text{rule}} and yillmy_i^{\text{llm}}.

Quantity of interest. The paired difference di=yillm−yirule, d_i = y_i^{\text{llm}} - y_i^{\text{rule}}, summarised by its mean d‾\bar d and a confidence interval.

Three rules for doing it honestly:

Rule Why
Block bootstrap by session Points in a session share conditions, so they are not independent. Resample whole sessions to get honest intervals on d‾\bar d.
Per-cell results, corrected Report by cell (setup type, context) as well as overall. Correct for how many cells you look at: with many cells, some look great by chance.
Track the trial count Every prompt variant, model swap or threshold change you evaluate is a trial. The more you try, the more you should discount the best one. (The separate article on the deflated Sharpe ratio covers the maths.)

7.9.5 The subset that matters

One subset deserves its own line: moments where the upstream permission is live but the rule engine has not fired. Those are the moments the model would be the main decision-maker if promoted. Its performance there is the real test. It is reported separately, not averaged in.

7.9.6 What the comparison is not

  • Not a measure of “intelligence”. A model can reason beautifully and add nothing over a rule engine in a given domain.
  • Not live evidence. Counterfactual labels ignore queue position, slippage on entries that never happened, and the model’s own latency at the moment of decision. Those are named limitations in the report.
  • Not a promotion decision. Promotion criteria are separate, written down in advance, and need more than one good window.

7.9.7 What surprised me

How much of the engineering was in the join: matching each order the live system actually placed back to the exact decision step in force, aligning clocks across processes, handling rows where the model errored. None of that is “AI”, and all of it decides whether the comparison means anything.

7.9.8 Summary

  • Pair the engines at identical decision points inside a window defined by the incumbent.
  • Score the road not taken with a pre-declared, causal, shared counterfactual label.
  • Use paired differences, session-block bootstrap, corrected per-cell results and an honest trial count.
  • Report the “rule did not fire” subset separately; it is the real test.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why is comparing the model’s calls at every minute with the rule engine’s calls only when it fired unfair? (Answer: the two sets of moments are different populations, so differences may come from when each was asked, not from which is better.)
  2. (Apply) Write a first-passage label for a non-trading problem (for example, whether a queue clears or overflows first). Check it uses only data after the decision.
  3. (Statistics) You test 20 cells and one shows a large gain. What should you do before believing it?
  4. (Think) List three things the counterfactual label cannot capture about a real live decision.

Further reading

  • Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020).
  • Künsch, The Jackknife and the Bootstrap for General Stationary Observations (Annals of Statistics, 1989).
  • López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018), ch. 3 on barrier labels.

— Tariq

Chapter 7.10 — Policy Trees: Let the Model Choose, Never Invent

Subtitle: The safest LLM decision is a pick from a list you wrote, walked through a tree you approved.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Use closed option sets so that any answer outside the list is an error. 2. Explain why a decision tree stored as data beats an if chain for audited decisions. 3. Apply the reject option: pick the top choice only when its score clears a threshold. 4. Avoid the NaN trap in threshold checks.

You need: Chapter 7.5 (validated outputs). What a decision tree is (yes/no questions leading to an answer).

7.10.1 The problem with “anything it can write”

A language model is very good at producing an answer. That is the problem. When the answer is an action, “anything it can write” is a terrifying action space.

One of the most useful constraints I built in 2026 was simple. For operational decisions, the model may only pick from options supplied by the caller. For well-understood decisions it is not consulted at all: those are made by walking an approved, versioned decision tree.

7.10.2 Two ideas, one goal

1. Closed option sets. Every decision request carries the list of allowed options. Whatever engine answers, its output is checked against that list. An answer outside the list is not “close enough”. It is an error, and the request falls back to a safe default, which is also one of the supplied options.

2. Policy trees. Where the logic is known and stable, I write it down as a decision tree in a structured format. Nodes test conditions on the request. Leaves name an action. A deterministic walker (a small program that follows the tree) evaluates it. No model, no sampling, no probability.

The model’s job shrinks to the truly ambiguous cases. Even there it can only choose.

Figure 7.10.1 — Tree first, then a pick from the list, else the safe default. If an approved, enforceable tree exists, its walk decides, with confidence recorded as “not applicable”. Otherwise a model chooses one of the supplied options with a confidence. Only an in-list pick that clears the threshold is used. Errors, off-list answers, low or NaN confidence all go to the safe default (orange).

7.10.3 Why a tree and not code?

You could write the same logic as an if chain. A tree stored as data can be:

Property What it gives you
Linted A validator checks every node is reachable, every leaf names a valid action, there are no cycles, and every condition uses known fields.
Diffed and approved A change is a reviewable diff with provenance: who approved it, when, and a hash of the exact content.
Rendered It can be drawn as a diagram for a human to check, which is much harder with arbitrary code.
Walked identically everywhere One small, portable walker runs every tree, so behaviour does not depend on which process loaded it.

A tree walk returns a compliance outcome, not a probability. I record its confidence as “not applicable” rather than inventing a number. Mixing “the tree says so” with “the model is 87% sure” in one field is how audit trails become fiction.

7.10.4 Loading rules that matter

The registry that loads trees is deliberately strict:

  • Lookup by exact identifier only. No globbing over folders, no substring matches, no absolute paths from requests. Otherwise a caller could point the loader at a file it should never trust.
  • Lint and approval. A tree loads only if it lints clean and carries full approval metadata.
  • Loading is not enforcing. A loaded tree does not act on its own; enforcement needs separate, explicit approval.
  • Some actions are never automated. Some action types can never be enforced by any tree, setting or request. Safety-critical decisions stay with humans or with hard-coded gates.

Everything else runs in shadow: the tree is walked, its result is logged next to what actually happened, and nothing changes. A tree earns enforcement the same way a model would: by being right in the log first.

7.10.5 Where the model fits

The flow for a decision request, in method-family terms:

  1. Is there an approved, enforceable tree for this action type? Walk it.
  2. Otherwise, ask a model to choose from the supplied options, with a confidence.
  3. If the model fails, errors, or is below the caller’s required confidence, return the safe default.

The model never sees an open-ended question. It sees “here are N options, pick one”. That is a classification problem, which is what language models are most reliably good at.

7.10.6 The maths of choosing from a list

Rule (reject option, Chow 1970). If a model scores options o1,…,oNo_1,\dots,o_N with probabilities p1,…,pNp_1,\dots,p_N, choose ô={arg⁡maxipiif maxipi≥τosafeotherwise. \hat o = \begin{cases} \arg\max_i p_i & \text{if } \max_i p_i \ge \tau \\ o_{\text{safe}} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

In words: take the top option only if its score is convincing; otherwise abstain and use the safe option.

Figure 7.10.2 — Abstain below the line, pick above it. The horizontal axis is the top score. Left of the threshold τ the router abstains and returns the safe option (orange). Right of it, the top option is used (green). Calibration may push τ to the right, never to the left, and a NaN score always abstains. The τ shown is a placeholder for the drawing.

Three rules about τ:

  • It is set per action type, higher for higher-stakes actions.
  • It is never lowered by calibration. A calibration step may tighten it, not loosen it.
  • A NaN (“not a number”) confidence must never pass. This sounds pedantic until you notice that NaN >= x is false but not (NaN < x) is true. Write the check the first way.

7.10.7 Pitfalls

  • Options embedded in free text. If the model has to parse options out of prose, it will sometimes invent a new one. Pass options as a structured list.
  • Defaults that aren’t safe. The fallback must be the option that does least harm, chosen by the caller, not by the router.
  • Trees that grow into programs. If a tree needs loops or external lookups, it has outgrown the format. Split the problem.

7.10.8 Summary

  • The model may only pick from a caller-supplied list; anything else is an error and falls to the safe default.
  • Known logic lives in versioned, linted, approved trees that return outcomes, not probabilities.
  • Trees and models both earn enforcement by being right in shadow first; some actions can never be enforced.
  • Use the reject option with a per-action threshold that calibration can only raise, and make NaN fail.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Scores are 0.55, 0.30, 0.15 and τ = 0.6. What does the router return? (Answer: the safe option, because the top score 0.55 is below τ.)
  2. (Code) Write a threshold check in your language that treats NaN as failing. Test it with NaN.
  3. (Design) List three lint checks you would run on a policy tree before loading it.
  4. (Think) Why should the caller, not the router, choose the safe default?

Further reading

  • Chow, On Optimum Recognition Error and Reject Tradeoff (IEEE Trans. Information Theory, 1970).
  • Breiman et al., Classification and Regression Trees (1984).
  • Open Policy Agent documentation, for policy-as-code ideas outside ML.

— Tariq

Chapter 7.11 — Local-First “System 1” Routing That Fails Closed

Subtitle: Most of the decisions my agents ask about are routine. They should be answered on my machine, fast, and if anything goes wrong the answer should be “no”.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe a tiered decision router: hard rules, policy trees, local model, cloud model, safe default. 2. Explain “fail closed” and list what it means at each failure point. 3. Weigh local-first against cloud-first on latency, privacy, cost, availability and quality. 4. Use a decision cache without serving stale or off-list answers.

You need: Chapter 7.10 (closed option sets and thresholds).

7.11.1 Many small questions

Coding agents ask a lot of small questions. Is this command safe? Which of these two tools fits? Does this request need escalation? Sending every one of them to a frontier model in the cloud is slow, expensive, and leaks context.

In 2026 I built a small local service that answers those questions first, escalates only when it should, and fails closed. The name borrows Kahneman’s System 1 and System 2: fast, automatic judgement first; slow, deliberate reasoning only when needed.

7.11.2 The tiers

The router is a tiny HTTP service on localhost. A request holds a question, a list of allowed options, an action type and a required confidence. It answers in tiers:

  1. Hard rules. A deterministic layer catches things a model should never decide, for example a pattern list of obviously destructive shell commands. These are denied before any model is consulted.
  2. Policy trees. If an approved decision tree exists for the action type, its result is used (or logged in shadow).
  3. Local model. A small pretrained classifier on the machine scores the options zero-shot (without task-specific training). No network; latency from milliseconds to low seconds.
  4. Cloud model. Only if the request is critical or local confidence is below threshold, and only if a key is configured. The payload is redacted first (Chapter 7.12).
  5. Safe default. If every tier fails or is unsure, the router returns the first supplied option, which callers are required to make the safe one.

Every failure along the way is reported in the response. The caller can see that the answer came from the default because tier 3 was unsure and tier 4 was unavailable.

Figure 7.11.1 — Ask the cheapest tier that can be sure. A request falls down the tiers until one is sure enough; that tier’s answer goes out with the tier name and any errors (green). If all tiers fail or are unsure, the safe default is returned (orange). The box on the right lists the fail-closed rules.

7.11.3 What “fails closed” means here

Fail closed means that on error the system denies rather than allows. A door with a fail-closed lock stays locked when the power goes out. For a decision router:

Situation Fail-closed response
Model unavailable Safe default, not a guess
Confidence missing or NaN Treated as below threshold
Redaction fails, or a post-redaction secret check flags something Cloud call blocked, not sent unredacted
Malformed request Error, not best effort

There is a cost. A fail-closed router will sometimes say no to a perfectly fine action because a component was flaky. For agent safety that is the right trade. An unnecessary “no” costs a human glance. An unnecessary “yes” can cost a deleted directory.

7.11.4 Why local first

  • Latency. A small local classifier answers in a fraction of a cloud round trip. Inside an agent loop that runs hundreds of times per session, that adds up.
  • Privacy. Most decision context never leaves the machine.
  • Cost. Routine decisions are free at the margin.
  • Availability. The router works on a plane. The cloud tier is an enhancement, not a dependency.

The downside is quality: a small zero-shot model is less capable than a frontier model. The confidence threshold manages that. Escalation is triggered by uncertainty, so the expensive model is spent where the cheap one admits it doesn’t know.

7.11.5 Calibrating the threshold

Escalating “when unsure” only works if confidence means something. A raw softmax score (the classifier’s normalised output) from a zero-shot model is not a calibrated probability. I treat it as a score and set thresholds per action type. Calibration from logged outcomes may raise a threshold but never lower it below the caller’s floor.

For proper probabilities, the standard methods are Platt scaling and isotonic regression (covered in the separate calibration article). The key point here: thresholds should rise with the stakes.

7.11.6 A small cache

Many questions repeat. The router caches decisions keyed on a hash of the normalised request. A cached answer is served only if:

  • it is still one of the options supplied now, and
  • its stored confidence clears the current threshold.

Caches that ignore the current option list are a classic source of “the router approved an action I didn’t offer”.

7.11.7 Pitfalls

  • Treating the router as authoritative. It advises the agent’s harness. It does not replace permission prompts or hard gates.
  • Unbounded escalation. If every request is “critical”, you have built an expensive cloud proxy. Watch the escalation rate.
  • Hidden fallbacks. If a response does not say which tier answered, you can’t debug it. Always include the tier and errors.

7.11.8 Summary

  • Answer routine decisions locally in tiers; escalate to the cloud only when critical or unsure.
  • Fail closed: missing models, NaN confidence, failed redaction and bad requests all lead to “no” or the safe default.
  • Thresholds are per action type and calibration can only raise them.
  • Every response names the tier that answered; cached answers must still fit today’s options and threshold.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Redaction throws an exception just before a cloud call. What should the router do? (Answer: block the cloud call and fall back, never send the unredacted payload.)
  2. (Apply) Your escalation rate jumps from low to most requests after a release. Name two likely causes.
  3. (Design) Write the two conditions a cached decision must meet before it is served.
  4. (Think) Give one decision you would put in the hard-rules tier and explain why no model should make it.

Further reading

  • Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).
  • Chow, On Optimum Recognition Error and Reject Tradeoff (1970).
  • Saltzer & Schroeder, The Protection of Information in Computer Systems (1975), on fail-safe defaults.

— Tariq

Chapter 7.12 — Egress Redaction: Scrubbing Secrets and PII Before a Prompt Leaves the Machine

Subtitle: Every prompt you send to a cloud model is data leaving your network. Treat it like any other egress.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State four design properties of a safe redaction function. 2. List the main families of things to redact and how each is detected. 3. Explain why a self-check must fail closed, and why two passes of the same patterns are not independent.

You need: Chapter 7.11 (the cloud tier). A basic idea of regular expressions and probability.

7.12.1 Agent context attracts secrets

Egress means data leaving your machine or network. PII is personally identifiable information: data that points to a person.

Agent context is a magnet for secrets: environment dumps, config files, stack traces with connection strings, a log line with an account number. An agent will happily paste any of it into a prompt. When I added a cloud tier to my local decision router, the rule was: nothing leaves the machine without passing through a redaction function first, and if that function is unsure, nothing leaves at all.

7.12.2 Design goals

I wrote down four properties before writing code:

  1. Pure. Redaction takes a payload and returns a redacted deep copy. It never changes the input and never raises an exception.
  2. Countable. A variant returns how many substitutions were made, so the log can record “redacted 3 items” without recording what they were.
  3. Bounded. Strings are truncated at a maximum length, total scanned text is capped, and nesting depth is limited. A pathological payload cannot make redaction slow or blow the stack.
  4. Self-checked, failing closed. After redaction, a separate check scans the output for anything that still looks like a secret. If it finds something, or if it errors, the answer is “contains secret” and the call is blocked.

Figure 7.12.1 — Cap, redact, check, then decide. The payload is size-capped, redacted into a copy with typed placeholders, then scanned again. Only a clean result is sent, with counts and types logged (green). A hit or any error blocks the call (orange). A value that cannot be processed becomes a placeholder rather than passing through.

7.12.3 What gets redacted

The method family is pattern-based detection plus key-name context:

Family How it is found
Known token formats Recognisable shapes: cloud access-key prefixes, source-host personal tokens, LLM provider keys, chat-platform tokens, bearer tokens in headers, private-key PEM blocks, JWTs (three base64url segments joined by dots)
Key-name heuristics Values under keys named like password, secret, token or api key are redacted whatever they look like
Credentials in URLs scheme://user:pass@host is a classic leak from connection strings; the user-info part is replaced
Personal data Email addresses, the current OS username wherever it appears, and home-directory paths (/Users/<name>/... turns up in every stack trace)

Matches are replaced with typed placeholders such as <REDACTED:jwt>, so the model still understands the structure of the text.

A layer I chose not to add yet: entropy. Shannon entropy per character,

H=−∑cpclog⁡2pc, H = -\sum_{c} p_c \log_2 p_c,

where pcp_c is the share of character cc in the string, is high for random base64 and low for prose. I have deliberately not added it: it flags every hash and UUID, and an explainable pattern list is easier to audit. It is the obvious next layer if the pattern list starts missing things.

7.12.4 Why fail closed

Redaction is a classifier, and classifiers have false negatives (secrets they miss). The self-check scans every string of the output against the full pattern set and the username matcher. Any hit means “still contains a secret”.

It catches cases where redaction was skipped (a truncation edge, an unexpected type). It does not catch cases where the patterns themselves are blind. That is an honest limitation.

Result (shared blind spots). With two detection passes, P(leak)≈P(miss1)⋅P(miss2∣miss1). P(\text{leak}) \approx P(\text{miss}_1) \cdot P(\text{miss}_2 \mid \text{miss}_1). If the second pass uses the same patterns, a secret the first missed is almost surely missed again, so P(miss2∣miss1)≈1P(\text{miss}_2 \mid \text{miss}_1) \approx 1 and the second pass adds little.

Independence has to be engineered, not assumed.

If either step throws an exception, the system assumes the worst. The self-check returns “contains secret” on any error, and an unprocessable value is replaced with a placeholder. A redactor that silently returns the original payload on error is worse than no redactor, because it gives you false confidence.

7.12.5 Engineering details that mattered

  • Walk structures, not strings. Redact JSON values recursively, including keys. Serialising to a string and running regexes over it misses structure and breaks escaping.
  • Truncate before scanning. Regexes over megabytes can be slow, and some patterns can backtrack catastrophically (take exponential time). Cap first.
  • Never log the secret. The log records counts and types, not matched values.
  • Test with real-shaped fixtures. Unit tests use fake credentials in the correct formats, plus near-misses that should not be redacted.

7.12.6 Pitfalls

  • Relying on the model provider’s data-retention promises instead of not sending the data.
  • Redacting only the user message and forgetting system prompts, tool results and attachments.
  • Over-redaction that destroys meaning. If every hex string becomes a placeholder, the model can’t reason about commit hashes. Tune for your domain.

7.12.7 Summary

  • Redaction is pure, countable, bounded and self-checked.
  • Detect known token shapes, sensitive key names, URL credentials and personal data; replace with typed placeholders.
  • Any self-check hit or any error blocks the call: fail closed.
  • Repeating the same patterns does not give independent protection.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why is a redactor that returns the original payload on error worse than none? (Answer: it fails silently while you believe you are protected, so you stop taking other precautions.)
  2. (Calculate) A string uses 64 symbols equally often. What is its entropy per character? What about a string of one repeated symbol?
  3. (Design) Propose a second detector that is genuinely different from the pattern list. What blind spot would it cover?
  4. (Think) List three parts of a request, other than the user message, that need redaction.

Further reading

  • OWASP, Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications (sensitive information disclosure).
  • NIST SP 800-122, Guide to Protecting the Confidentiality of Personally Identifiable Information.
  • Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.13 — Hybrid RAG with BM25, Vectors and Reciprocal Rank Fusion

Subtitle: Keyword search and vector search fail in different ways. Fusing their rankings, not their scores, gets you most of both.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain how BM25 and cosine-similarity search each rank documents, and where each fails. 2. Say why adding raw scores from the two is fragile. 3. Compute Reciprocal Rank Fusion by hand and measure retrieval with recall@k.

You need: sums and fractions; vectors and the dot product.

7.13.1 Two kinds of miss

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means looking up relevant documents and giving them to the model with the question. My agents spend a lot of time looking things up in my own notes: research write-ups, runbooks, contracts, decisions.

The first retrieval layer I built used vector search alone. It kept missing exact identifiers: an error code, a config key, a precise phrase. Keyword search found those instantly but stumbled on paraphrases. The fix was neither clever nor new: run both and fuse their rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

7.13.2 The two retrievers

Lexical (BM25). BM25 is the classic keyword ranking formula.

BM25(d,q)=∑t∈qIDF(t)f(t,d)(k1+1)f(t,d)+k1(1−b+b|d|avgdl) \text{BM25}(d, q) = \sum_{t \in q} \text{IDF}(t)\,\frac{f(t,d)\,(k_1 + 1)}{f(t,d) + k_1\left(1 - b + b\,\frac{|d|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)}

Here f(t,d)f(t,d) is how often term tt appears in document dd, |d||d| is the document length, avgdl the average length, IDF rewards rare terms, and k1,bk_1, b are the usual saturation and length-normalisation constants. In words: rare query terms that appear in the document score highly, and repeating a term has diminishing returns. I don’t implement it myself. SQLite’s FTS5 full-text index ranks with BM25 out of the box, so lexical search is one SQL query against a local file.

Dense (vectors). Each chunk of text is embedded (turned into a vector of numbers). The query is embedded the same way, and documents are ranked by cosine similarity:

cos⁡(𝒒,𝒅)=𝒒⋅𝒅∥𝒒∥∥𝒅∥. \cos(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}) = \frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{q}\|\,\|\mathbf{d}\|}.

With unit-length vectors that is just a dot product. My embedder is a deterministic, offline hashing embedder (Chapter 7.14).

7.13.3 Why not just add the scores?

BM25 scores are unbounded and depend on the corpus. Cosine similarities live in [−1,1][-1, 1] and depend on the embedder. Adding them needs normalisation and a weight, and both drift every time the corpus or embedder changes. You end up tuning a number that silently stops being right.

7.13.4 Reciprocal Rank Fusion

RRF (Cormack, Clarke & Büttcher, 2009) ignores scores and uses only ranks.

Definition (RRF). For each document dd and each ranked list rr where it appears at position rankr(d)\text{rank}_r(d) (starting at 1): RRF(d)=∑r1k+rankr(d). \text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r} \frac{1}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)}.

The constant kk damps the advantage of the very top positions. The original paper used k=60k = 60, and that conventional value works well in practice.

Figure 7.13.2 — Consensus wins. Two made-up ranked lists of documents A to G, fused with k=60k = 60. A is 1st and 3rd, so it scores 1/61+1/631/61 + 1/63; C is 3rd and 1st and ties with it. B (2nd and 5th) comes next. Documents found by only one list (F, D, G, E) fall below every document found by both, even F, which was 2nd in one list.

Properties I like:

  • Scale-free. Only order matters, so the two retrievers never need to agree on units.
  • Rewards consensus. A document ranked moderately by both lists beats one ranked top by only one list surprisingly often. That is usually what you want.
  • No training. Nothing to fit, so nothing to overfit.

7.13.5 The full pipeline

Figure 7.13.1 — Fast path first, then two retrievers and a fusion. If the query is an exact identifier or title, that document comes straight back (green). Otherwise BM25 and vector search both run, RRF fuses their ranks, and results are deduplicated by document. The dashed box is the optional symbol graph.

A fast path before both. Before any fusion, I check for a direct hit: if the query looks like an exact identifier or title, return that document at once. It is cheaper and more precise than ranking, and covers a large share of agent lookups (“open the runbook called X”).

Optional structure: the graph. The same engine can also consult a symbol graph of the codebase (Chapter 7.15), so a query naming a function can return its compact skeleton alongside related notes. Retrieval isn’t just text similarity; structure is evidence too.

7.13.6 Practical lessons

  • Chunking matters more than the fusion constant. Chunks that cut a definition in half retrieve badly with any method. I chunk on document structure (headings) before length.
  • Tokenisation must match. If the lexical tokenizer drops underscores and your identifiers are snake_case, BM25 can’t find them.
  • Deduplicate by document, not chunk, before showing results, or one long document crowds out everything else.
  • Evaluate with real queries. Keep a small set of questions you actually asked agents, with the documents that should come back, and measure recall@k whenever you change anything.

Definition (recall@k). For a query with relevant set RR and retrieved top-kk list KK, recall@k=|R∩K||R|. \text{recall@}k = \frac{|R \cap K|}{|R|}.

Even twenty labelled queries catch most regressions.

7.13.7 What textbooks underplay

Most RAG tutorials treat retrieval as solved by “embed everything”. For technical corpora full of identifiers, numbers and jargon, lexical search is not a fallback. It is often the main signal. Hybrid retrieval with RRF is one of the rare techniques that is simpler and better than the alternative.

7.13.8 Summary

  • BM25 finds exact terms; vectors find similar wording; each misses what the other catches.
  • Don’t add raw scores: their scales differ and drift.
  • RRF sums 1/(k+rank)1/(k + \text{rank}) over lists, rewards agreement and needs no training.
  • Use an exact-match fast path, chunk by structure, dedupe by document, and track recall@k.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With k=60k = 60, a document is 2nd in one list and missing from the other. Another is 10th in both. Which ranks higher? (Answer: the second: 2/70≈0.02862/70 \approx 0.0286 beats 1/62≈0.01611/62 \approx 0.0161.)
  2. (Calculate) A query has 4 relevant documents; the top 5 results contain 3 of them. What is recall@5?
  3. (Debug) BM25 never finds max_retry_count. What is the first thing you check?
  4. (Think) Why does RRF not need retuning when you swap the embedder, while a weighted score sum does?

Further reading

  • Cormack, Clarke & Büttcher, Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual Rank Learning Methods (SIGIR 2009).
  • Robertson & Zaragoza, The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond (2009).
  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (NeurIPS 2020).
  • SQLite documentation, FTS5 Extension.

— Tariq

Chapter 7.14 — Offline Hashing Embedders: Vector Search with Zero API Keys

Subtitle: Not every embedding needs a neural network. Sometimes deterministic, free and local beats state of the art.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Build a vector from text with the signed hashing trick. 2. Explain why signed hashing makes collisions cancel on average. 3. Say what a hashing embedder can and cannot do compared with a neural embedder. 4. Avoid the unstable-hash bug that silently corrupts an index.

You need: Chapter 7.13 (cosine similarity). The idea of a hash function (a function that turns any input into a fixed-size number).

7.14.1 The constraint

When I built a local retrieval layer for my agents, one constraint ruled out the usual answer. It had to work completely offline: no API keys, no model downloads, and identical results on every machine. That pushed me back to an old idea, feature hashing. I’ve been pleasantly surprised by how far it goes as the dense half of a hybrid search.

7.14.2 The hashing trick

Feature hashing (Weinberger et al., 2009) maps an unbounded vocabulary into a fixed-size vector without storing a vocabulary. For a feature ww (a token or n-gram) and a vector of dimension DD:

  1. Compute a hash h(w)h(w) with a stable hash function.
  2. Choose a bucket j=h(w)mod⁡Dj = h(w) \bmod D.
  3. Choose a sign s(w)∈{−1,+1}s(w) \in \{-1, +1\} from another bit of the hash.
  4. Add s(w)⋅weight(w)s(w) \cdot \text{weight}(w) to component jj.

Finally, normalise to unit length so that cosine similarity is a dot product:

𝒗=∑ws(w)weight(w)𝒆h(w)mod⁡D∥∑ws(w)weight(w)𝒆h(w)mod⁡D∥, \mathbf{v} = \frac{\sum_w s(w)\,\text{weight}(w)\,\mathbf{e}_{h(w) \bmod D}}{\left\|\sum_w s(w)\,\text{weight}(w)\,\mathbf{e}_{h(w) \bmod D}\right\|},

where 𝒆j\mathbf{e}_j is the vector with a 1 in position jj and 0 elsewhere.

Figure 7.14.1 — Each feature lands in one bucket with a sign. Four features are hashed into a vector of 8 buckets. Green arrows add +1, orange arrows add −1. “stop” and the pair “stop loss” happen to share bucket 2 with opposite signs, so their collision cancels. The buckets and signs are made up for the drawing.

Why signs help. For two different features that collide in the same bucket, the signs are independent and equally likely to be + or −. So the expected contribution of the collision to an inner product is zero: collisions cancel on average instead of piling up.

7.14.3 Words and n-grams

Single tokens give a bag of words vector (word counts, order ignored). Adding word n-grams (runs of adjacent words, such as pairs) captures some local order, so “stop loss” and “loss stop” stop being identical.

My embedder hashes single tokens and adjacent word pairs into the same vector, each adding a signed unit count. Character n-grams are another option. They help with typos and word forms, at the cost of more features per document.

7.14.4 What it is and isn’t

A hashing embedder is essentially a randomly projected, n-gram-weighted bag of words. So:

  • It finds lexical and near-lexical overlap, including multi-word phrases, robustly and deterministically.
  • It does not understand synonyms. “Halt” and “stop” are unrelated unless they co-occur in n-grams. A neural embedder would put them close together.
  • It overlaps with BM25. That is the honest weakness in hybrid search: both retrievers see similar signals. In practice it still adds value, because n-gram matching and length normalisation behave differently from BM25. But it is not the semantic complement a neural model would be.

Why use it, then? Because the alternatives had real costs for my use:

Property Hashing embedder Neural embedder
Determinism Same text, same vector, on any machine, forever Vectors change when the model version changes, silently invalidating the index
Network and keys None needed; works in sandboxed agent sessions Usually needs a download or an API key
Speed Microseconds per document; re-indexing is trivial Much slower
Dependencies Uses NumPy if present, falls back to pure Python Heavy
Synonyms No Yes

7.14.5 Collisions and dimension

Result (expected collisions). With nn distinct features hashed into DD buckets, the chance that a given feature shares its bucket with at least one other is 1−(1−1/D)n−11 - (1 - 1/D)^{n-1}. So the expected number of such features is about n(1−(1−1/D)n−1). n\left(1 - (1 - 1/D)^{n-1}\right).

Why. Each of the other n−1n-1 features misses a given bucket with probability 1−1/D1 - 1/D. All of them miss it with probability (1−1/D)n−1(1-1/D)^{n-1}. Subtract from 1, then multiply by nn features.

Figure 7.14.2 — Bigger vectors, fewer shared buckets. The curves plot the formula above for 1,000 (blue) and 10,000 (orange) features as the number of buckets DD grows. The share of features in a shared bucket stays near 100% until DD is comparable to nn, then falls. This is a formula plot, not a measurement.

Larger DD means fewer collisions and bigger vectors. Small corpora tolerate surprisingly small vectors, because only collisions between features that actually co-occur in queries and documents hurt ranking. Choose DD by measuring recall on real queries, not by intuition.

7.14.6 The stable-hashing pitfall

Python’s built-in hash() for strings is randomised per process unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed. Use a cryptographic or explicitly seeded hash. I use a digest from hashlib: cryptographic strength is irrelevant here, stability is the point.

This is the single most common bug in home-made hashing embedders. It produces an index that is silently garbage after a restart.

7.14.7 Where I’d go next

The design leaves room to swap in a neural embedder behind the same interface when meaning starts to matter more than determinism. If I do, the hashing embedder stays as a fallback for offline sessions.

7.14.8 Summary

  • Hash each feature to a bucket and a sign, add, and normalise: no vocabulary, no network.
  • Signed hashing makes collisions cancel on average.
  • It matches words and phrases deterministically but knows no synonyms, and overlaps with BM25.
  • Pick DD by measured recall, and always use a stable hash.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why must the hash be stable across processes? (Answer: otherwise the same text maps to different buckets after a restart, so stored document vectors no longer match new query vectors.)
  2. (Calculate) With n=100n = 100 features and D=1000D = 1000 buckets, estimate the share of features in a shared bucket.
  3. (Apply) Hash “stop loss now” into tokens and word pairs. How many features are there?
  4. (Think) Give one query where a hashing embedder fails and a neural embedder succeeds.

Further reading

  • Weinberger et al., Feature Hashing for Large Scale Multitask Learning (ICML 2009).
  • Shi et al., Hash Kernels for Structured Data (JMLR 2009).
  • scikit-learn documentation, HashingVectorizer.

— Tariq

Chapter 7.15 — Code Symbol Graphs: Giving Agents a Map Instead of a Pile of Files

Subtitle: An agent that reads whole files to find one function is burning context on scenery.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe a code symbol graph as a typed, directed graph and turn agent questions into graph queries. 2. Explain what a skeleton is and why it saves context. 3. Name the ways static call graphs are wrong, and how to use them safely anyway.

You need: what a function, class and import are; the idea of a graph (nodes joined by edges).

7.15.1 Context spent on scenery

Watch a coding agent work on an unfamiliar repository. It opens file after file, scrolling past hundreds of lines to find one definition and its callers. Every one of those lines uses context window (the limited text the model can hold at once) that it can’t use for thinking.

In 2026 I built a small tool that parses my repositories into a symbol graph and writes compact skeletons. Agents navigate structure first and read code bodies only when they need them.

7.15.2 What a symbol graph is

Nodes are code symbols: modules, classes, interfaces, functions, methods. Edges are relationships:

  • contains (a class contains a method),
  • imports (a module imports another),
  • calls (a function calls another),
  • inherits / implements.

Definition. A symbol graph is a directed, typed multigraph G=(V,E)G = (V, E) with E⊆V×V×TE \subseteq V \times V \times T, where TT is the set of edge types.

Agent questions become graph queries:

Question Graph query
Who calls X? The in-neighbours of X along call edges
What breaks if I change X? The reverse transitive closure of X along call and import edges (everything that reaches X)

Figure 7.15.1 — Walk backwards from the thing you want to change. Grey edges show containment, imports and inheritance. Starting at X (blue) and following call edges backwards reaches g(), h() and then A.f() (orange): the code that may break if X changes. The graph is a made-up example.

7.15.3 How it’s built

The builder parses source files in Python, TypeScript/JavaScript and C#. For Python, the standard library’s ast module gives a full syntax tree (a structured form of the code) for free. For the other languages, lighter-weight parsing extracts declarations and call sites.

The output is a single JSON graph plus, for each important symbol, a skeleton: a short text file with the signature, docstring, members and key relationships, capped at a small token budget.

That skeleton is the key product. Instead of reading a 900-line file, an agent reads a 200-token summary of the class it cares about, then asks for the one method body it needs.

7.15.4 Static analysis is approximate

Call graphs from static parsing (reading code without running it) are not exact, especially in dynamic languages:

  • Dynamic dispatch. obj.run() could be any class with a run method. A static builder either links to all candidates (over-approximation) or none (under-approximation).
  • Reflection, decorators, dependency injection hide edges entirely.
  • Name collisions across modules create false edges if resolution is by name.

I treat the graph as a navigation aid, not a proof. For “find the callers before changing a function”, an over-approximate list is fine: false positives cost a glance, false negatives cost a bug. For safety-critical changes, agents still confirm with a language-server reference search.

7.15.5 Why skeletons beat embeddings for code

You can embed code chunks and use vector search. That helps for “where is the code that does something like Y?”. But many agent questions are structural and exact: the definition of this name, the callers of that method, the interface this class implements. A graph answers those exactly and cheaply. Similarity search answers them approximately and expensively.

I use both: the graph is wired into the hybrid retrieval layer (Chapter 7.13), so a query naming a symbol returns its skeleton alongside related notes.

7.15.6 Keeping it fresh

A stale graph is worse than none, because the agent trusts it. The builder is cheap enough to rerun often, a scheduled background refresh keeps it current, and the query tool checks for drift: if source files changed since the graph was built, it says so loudly instead of answering from an old map.

7.15.7 Token economics

Suppose an agent needs to understand a class with mm methods in a file of LL lines.

  • Reading the file costs roughly in proportion to LL.
  • Reading the skeleton costs a fixed cap, plus the bodies of the jj methods actually needed.

For j≪mj \ll m (jj much smaller than mm), the saving is most of the file. Across a session with dozens of lookups, that is the difference between an agent that keeps the whole task in context and one that forgets the start of the conversation.

7.15.8 Pitfalls

  • Graphs that include generated or vendored code drown real symbols in noise. Exclude them.
  • Skeletons that leak secrets from default argument values or constants. Apply the same redaction you’d apply to any egress (Chapter 7.12).
  • Assuming edges are complete. Always say “callers found by static analysis”, not “all callers”.

7.15.9 Summary

  • A symbol graph stores code structure as typed edges; “who calls X” and “what breaks” become graph walks.
  • Skeletons let agents read a capped summary and fetch only the bodies they need.
  • Static edges are approximate: prefer over-approximation and confirm critical changes with a language server.
  • Keep the graph fresh and warn on drift.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) In Figure 7.15.1, which symbols call X directly? (Answer: g() and h().)
  2. (Apply) Write the graph query for “which classes implement interface I?”.
  3. (Think) Why is an over-approximate caller list safer than an under-approximate one when changing a function?
  4. (Estimate) A file has 900 lines and the skeleton cap is 200 tokens. If you need 2 of 30 methods, roughly what share of the file do you avoid reading?

Further reading

  • Ryder, Constructing the Call Graph of a Program (IEEE TSE, 1979).
  • Python documentation, ast — Abstract Syntax Trees.
  • Language Server Protocol specification (Microsoft).
  • Yamaguchi et al., Modeling and Discovering Vulnerabilities with Code Property Graphs (IEEE S&P 2014).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.16 — Context Engineering with Zoned Documents and Token Budgets

Subtitle: The context window is a budget. Documents that don’t declare what they are and how much they cost will eventually blow it.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Write frontmatter that lets a tool decide what to load before reading a document. 2. Use tiers as token budgets for progressive disclosure. 3. Explain how zones and kinds stop agents wandering and trusting stale state. 4. List the checks a document validator should run on every change.

You need: what a token and a context window are (Chapter 7.4 helps).

7.16.1 From prompt engineering to context engineering

Prompt engineering is about the words you write to a model. Context engineering is about everything else that ends up in front of it: rules files, runbooks, specs, retrieved notes, tool output.

By mid-2026 my agents were loading so much documentation that they spent a large fraction of every session reading instead of working. So I put my documents on a diet, with rules a validator can check.

7.16.2 Every document declares itself

Each document starts with a small frontmatter block (a header of key-value metadata) declaring:

Field Meaning
id A stable identifier
kind What sort of document it is: invariant (must always be true), contract (interfaces and schemas), procedure (step-by-step runbook), decision (branching logic, decision records), state (snapshots and manifests)
zone Which part of the system it belongs to, e.g. shared, core, backend, client, infra, api
tier How deep it is, from a tiny index to a full specification
intent One line saying what a reader should get from it

That is enough for an agent, or a retrieval layer, to decide what to load before reading a single body.

7.16.3 Tiers are token budgets

Each tier has a token cap. The smallest tier is a map: a few hundred tokens saying what exists and where. Next is a domain overview. Then detailed contracts and procedures. Then full specifications.

The validator estimates tokens with a rule of thumb and fails any document over its tier’s cap. The estimate is crude, roughly words × a constant around 1.3 for English text. But it is deterministic, fast and good enough to catch documents that have quietly tripled in size. If you need precision, count with the model’s tokenizer. For budgeting, consistency matters more than exactness.

The point of tiers is progressive disclosure: load the map first, then only the overview you need, then only the one relevant contract.

Context cost. C=Cmap+∑i∈neededCi C = C_{\text{map}} + \sum_{i \in \text{needed}} C_i instead of the sum over everything that might be relevant.

Figure 7.16.1 — Load the top, then only what the task needs. Each tier down has a bigger token cap. For this task the agent loads the map (tier 0) and one contract (tier 2), shaded green, and skips the rest. The cost is the map plus the needed pieces, not the whole stack.

7.16.4 Zones are isolation

Documents can link to parents. The validator enforces that a document in one zone cannot hang under a parent in another zone, except the shared zone.

That sounds bureaucratic. In practice it stops a common failure: an agent working on the client follows links into backend internals, loads them, and starts “fixing” things outside its task. Zones make the boundaries visible to tools, not just to humans.

Figure 7.16.2 — Links stay inside a zone or go up to shared. Green arrows are allowed parent links: within one zone, or from a zone up to the shared zone. The dashed orange link tries to hang a client document under a backend one, and the validator rejects it.

7.16.5 Why kinds matter

Kinds tell the agent how to use a document:

  • An invariant is never edited casually and is checked against changes.
  • A procedure is followed step by step.
  • A decision document is evaluated as branching logic.
  • A state document is expected to go stale and should be re-probed, not trusted.

That last one is the most valuable. Many agent mistakes come from treating a snapshot as truth. Labelling it “state” is a standing reminder that live systems must be checked live.

7.16.6 What the validator checks

  1. Frontmatter is present and well-formed, with valid kind, zone and tier.
  2. The token estimate is within the tier cap.
  3. Parent links resolve.
  4. No cross-zone parenting except via shared.

It runs in seconds over a whole corpus, so it can run on every change.

7.16.7 Pitfalls

  • Splitting to dodge the cap. If every document is split into five tier-two parts that are always loaded together, you’ve saved nothing. Budgets need a human eye for cohesion.
  • Indexes that rot. A map that points to deleted documents is worse than no map. Validate links.
  • Over-classifying. Five kinds is enough. Twenty categories become a taxonomy nobody applies consistently.

7.16.8 What I’d tell another engineer

Treat your agent’s context like memory in an embedded system: allocate it on purpose, measure it, and fail the build when something blows its budget.

7.16.9 Summary

  • Frontmatter (id, kind, zone, tier, intent) lets tools choose before reading.
  • Tiers carry token caps; load the map, then only what is needed.
  • Zones stop cross-boundary wandering; kinds say how to use a document, and “state” means re-check live.
  • A fast validator checks frontmatter, budgets, links and zones on every change.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A tier cap is 600 tokens. Using the 1.3 rule, about how many words fit? (Answer: about 460 words, since 600 / 1.3 ≈ 462.)
  2. (Apply) Give each of the five kinds one example from a project you know.
  3. (Design) A client procedure needs a backend fact. How do you share it without breaking zone rules?
  4. (Think) Why can splitting a document into smaller parts fail to save any context?

Further reading

  • Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents (2025).
  • Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL 2024).
  • Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions (2011).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.17 — MCP Tool Servers: Small, Bounded and Boring on Purpose

Subtitle: The Model Context Protocol makes it easy to give an agent tools. It makes it just as easy to give it too many, too powerful, with no limits.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe MCP: JSON-RPC 2.0 over a transport, with tools, resources and prompts. 2. Carry the stdio transport over SSH to reach a remote server. 3. List the client-side guards that treat the server as an untrusted peer. 4. Design narrow, read-only-by-default tools with small outputs.

You need: JSON; the idea of a client and a server; Chapter 7.5 (schemas).

7.17.1 The easy part and the hard part

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become the common way to plug tools into AI agents. One protocol, many clients: the same tool server can serve Claude Code, an IDE assistant, or your own orchestrator.

I use MCP servers throughout my setup, including one that runs on a separate worker machine and is reached over an authenticated SSH channel. Building and calling those taught me that the protocol is the easy part. The hard part is deciding what a tool may do, and making sure a misbehaving peer can’t take your process down with it.

7.17.2 What MCP is, briefly

MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 (a simple remote-call format written in JSON) over a transport (the channel that carries the messages). Common transports are:

  • stdio: the client launches the server as a subprocess and they exchange newline-delimited JSON messages over standard input and output;
  • HTTP.

A server advertises:

Item What it is
tools Callable functions with a name, description and JSON Schema for arguments
resources Readable data, addressed by URI
prompts Reusable prompt templates

The client performs an initialise handshake, lists what the server offers, then calls tools with tools/call. Every request has an id; responses echo it; notifications have no id.

7.17.3 The stdio transport over SSH

Anything that gives you a two-way byte stream can carry the stdio transport. To reach a tool server on another machine, I launch it through SSH. The SSH client is the subprocess, the remote Python process is the server, and messages flow over the encrypted channel. Authentication and network policy become SSH’s job, which is a well-understood job.

7.17.4 Treat the peer as untrusted

Even a server you wrote is, from the client’s side, an external process that can crash, hang or send garbage. My client enforces:

  • Size caps on outgoing requests and incoming lines. An unbounded readline on a stream that never sends a newline is a memory leak waiting to happen.
  • Envelope checks. Every line must parse as JSON, be an object and carry "jsonrpc": "2.0". Anything else is a protocol error, not something to “try to understand”.
  • ID matching. A response must carry the ID of the outstanding request. Server-initiated notifications are skipped, but only a bounded number, so a chatty server can’t keep the client reading forever.
  • Timeouts on connection and liveness, including SSH keep-alive settings, so a dead link is detected instead of hanging.
  • Typed failures. Each failure mode has a named error: request too large, response too large, transport closed, invalid JSON, invalid envelope, unexpected ID, RPC error. Callers handle them precisely, and logs say exactly what happened.
  • Opt-in and finite. Remote calls are off unless explicitly enabled, and each session makes a bounded number of calls. If the remote side is down, the caller gets a clean error, and no fallback silently replaces it.

Figure 7.17.1 — Every reply passes the guards. The agent client talks to the remote server through SSH, but every message in both directions goes through the client-side guards. Replies (orange arrows) are treated as untrusted data until they pass size, envelope and ID checks.

None of this is exotic. It is the same discipline you’d apply to any network client. It is easy to forget because MCP feels like “calling a function”.

7.17.5 Designing tools

On the server side, the rules I follow:

  • Narrow tools beat general ones. A tool that runs arbitrary shell commands is not a tool; it’s a hole. A tool that returns one specific report is easy to reason about.
  • Read-only by default. Anything with side effects gets its own tool, its own name, and ideally a confirmation step in the client.
  • Schemas with enums and bounds. The argument schema is both documentation for the model and validation for the server. Validate on the server anyway.
  • Small outputs. Tool output goes straight into the model’s context. Return summaries and identifiers, and let the agent ask for more.
  • Descriptions are prompts. The model chooses tools by their descriptions. Write them precisely, say when not to use the tool, and keep them stable (they also sit in your cached prompt prefix, Chapter 7.4).

7.17.6 The tool-count problem

Every tool you expose costs context (its schema is in the prompt) and attention (the model must choose among them). More tools means more wrong choices. Many clients now defer loading tool schemas until needed, which helps. The best fix is still fewer, sharper tools.

7.17.7 Security notes

  • Tool output is untrusted input. If a tool returns text from the web, email or documents, it can carry prompt-injection payloads. The agent must treat it as data.
  • Least privilege. The server process should run with the minimum filesystem and network access its tools need.
  • Never pass secrets through tool arguments, where they will be logged or end up in model context.

7.17.8 Summary

  • MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio or HTTP; servers offer tools, resources and prompts.
  • stdio can ride over SSH, leaving authentication to SSH.
  • The client caps sizes, checks envelopes and IDs, times out, types its errors and limits calls.
  • Tools should be narrow, read-only by default, schema-checked, small in output and few in number.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why is an unbounded readline dangerous on a stream from another process? (Answer: if the peer never sends a newline, the client keeps buffering forever and can run out of memory or hang.)
  2. (Apply) Write the list of typed errors your own client would need for one remote tool.
  3. (Design) Replace a “run any shell command” tool with two or three narrow tools for the same job.
  4. (Think) A tool returns a web page that says “ignore previous instructions”. What should the agent do, and why?

Further reading

  • Model Context Protocol specification, modelcontextprotocol.io.
  • JSON-RPC 2.0 specification, jsonrpc.org.
  • Greshake et al., Not what you’ve signed up for (2023), on indirect prompt injection.
  • Saltzer & Schroeder, The Protection of Information in Computer Systems (1975).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.18 — Cutting LLM Costs Without Cutting Corners

Subtitle: The cheapest token is the one you never send. The second cheapest is the one you send to a small model, or from cache.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Write the per-call cost model and name its three levers. 2. Match each cost-saving technique in this part of the book to the lever it pulls. 3. Say which things must never be cut to save money.

You need: Chapters 7.3, 7.4, 7.6 and 7.10–7.16 are referenced; basic algebra.

7.18.1 Where the money went

In October 2026 I sat down to work out where my language-model spend was actually going, across coding agents, research agents and production roles. The answer wasn’t “the expensive model”. It was waste: repeated context, oversized prompts, and questions that never needed a model at all. This is the checklist I ended up with, roughly in order of payoff.

7.18.2 A cost model

Per-call cost. C=pinTinuncached+preadTcache-read+pwriteTcache-write+poutTout, C = p_{\text{in}} T_{\text{in}}^{\text{uncached}} + p_{\text{read}} T_{\text{cache-read}} + p_{\text{write}} T_{\text{cache-write}} + p_{\text{out}} T_{\text{out}}, where each TT is a token count and each pp a price per token. Output tokens are typically priced several times higher than input, cache reads well below input, and cache writes somewhat above.

Total cost. ∑callsC=Ncalls×C‾, \sum_{\text{calls}} C = N_{\text{calls}} \times \bar C, where C‾\bar C is the average cost per call.

So there are exactly three levers: make fewer calls, make each token cheaper, or use fewer tokens per call. Every technique below pulls one of them.

Figure 7.18.1 — Three levers, and what not to touch. Total cost splits into number of calls times average cost. Each green box is a lever with the techniques that pull it underneath. The orange box lists what should not be cut to save money.

7.18.3 Lever 1: don’t call the model

The biggest savings came from removing calls entirely:

  • Deterministic sensors answer threshold questions in code (Chapter 7.6).
  • Policy trees answer well-understood decisions without any model (Chapter 7.10).
  • Exact-match caches answer repeated questions from a local store, keyed by a hash of the normalised request.
  • Fast-path retrieval returns a document by exact identifier before any ranking or generation (Chapter 7.13).

7.18.4 Lever 2: cheaper tokens

Use the smallest model that does the job. Per-role routing lets cheap roles run on cheap models (Chapter 7.3). A local-first router answers routine classifications with a small model on the machine and escalates only when its confidence is low (Chapter 7.11). Watch the escalation rate: if most requests escalate, the local tier isn’t doing its job.

Cache the prefix. Prefix-anchored caching rewards a large stable prefix and a small dynamic tail (Chapter 7.4). Keep timestamps out of system prompts, serialise deterministically, and put shared content before role-specific content. Watch the cache-read ratio; a sudden drop means someone broke the prefix.

Batch what isn’t urgent. Many providers offer batch interfaces at a discount for work that can wait hours. Nightly analysis and offline evaluation are natural candidates.

7.18.5 Lever 3: fewer tokens per call

Input side:

  • Skeletons instead of files (Chapter 7.15).
  • Tiered documents with token budgets: the map first, detail only when needed (Chapter 7.16).
  • Structured facts instead of raw data: pass computed numbers, not the series they came from.
  • Trimmed tool output: summaries and identifiers, not dumps (Chapter 7.17).

Output side, the expensive one: forced tool output with a tight schema removes preamble and prose (Chapter 7.5). Ask for exactly the fields you need, and set sensible maximum output lengths per role.

7.18.6 Measure before and after

Every call in my production paths logs model, input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens, and latency. Without that, “we saved money” is a guess. With it, every change has a before and after on the same metric. I won’t quote numbers here; the point is that you should have your own.

7.18.7 What not to cut

Keep Why
Validation Skipping schema checks to save a millisecond turns cost savings into incident costs.
Shadow logging Those logs are how you know whether a cheaper model is good enough.
Context that prevents mistakes A rule that stops an agent deleting the wrong directory is worth its tokens every time.

7.18.8 Pitfalls

  • Optimising the visible bill and ignoring rework. A cheaper model that produces wrong answers costs more in the end.
  • Caching with stale semantics. A cached decision must still be valid for the current options and thresholds.
  • Over-compressed prompts. Past a point, removing context hurts quality faster than it saves money.

7.18.9 Summary

  • Cost = number of calls × average cost per call; pull the three levers.
  • The biggest win is not calling the model: sensors, trees, caches, fast paths.
  • Then use smaller models and caches, then send and request fewer tokens.
  • Measure every call, and never cut validation, shadow logs or safety rules.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Which lever does an exact-match cache pull? (Answer: fewer calls.)
