  2. (Calculate) Output costs 5× input per token. A call has 2,000 input and 400 output tokens. What share of the cost is output?
  3. (Apply) Pick one workflow you run and list one technique for each lever.
  4. (Think) Give an example where a cheaper model raises total cost.

Further reading

  • Chen, Zaharia & Zou, FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance (2023).
  • Anthropic and AWS Bedrock documentation on prompt caching and batch inference.
  • Ong et al., RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data (2024).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.19 — LLM-Drafted Daily Reports with a Feedback Loop

Subtitle: Let the model write the prose. Never let it write the numbers. Then grade it every evening.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Separate computed numbers (ground truth) from generated prose in a report pipeline. 2. Explain why a quality gate on volume failed, and what a gate on substance would check. 3. Design a causal feedback loop that only adjusts bounded, explicit modes.

You need: Chapter 7.5 (structured output). The idea of a scoring rule (a way to grade a forecast against what happened).

7.19.1 The setup

Since mid-2026 a pipeline drafts a daily market research report for me before the open. A language model writes the narrative. It does not compute a single number in it. And the next morning’s draft is shaped by how well yesterday’s matched what actually happened. This chapter gives the design, without the content.

7.19.2 Numbers are ground truth, prose is generated

The single most effective anti-hallucination rule I know (hallucination: the model stating made-up facts confidently):

Rule. Compute every number deterministically from real data, and put those numbers in the prompt as facts. The model writes around them, explains context and structures the narrative. It is never asked to compute, recall or estimate a figure.

In practice the pipeline:

  1. Fetches live market data and computes all prices, levels and statistics in code.
  2. Builds a prompt containing those values as labelled ground truth.
  3. Asks the model (via Bedrock) for the narrative fields only, in a structured format.
  4. Passes the draft through a quality-gate step before it becomes the day’s content.

Because the figures come from code, the most dangerous kind of hallucination, a wrong price or level stated with confidence, mostly disappears by construction rather than by checking.

Figure 7.19.1 — Draft in the morning, grade in the evening, adjust next morning. Top row: numbers are computed in code, placed in the prompt as ground truth, and the model writes only the narrative. Middle row: after the close, the playbook is compared with what happened and feedback is written. Bottom: the next draft reads only feedback dated before that day and picks a normal or cautious mode.

7.19.3 A quality gate, and the day I turned it off

The pipeline is headless: there is no human approval step. The original design had a blocking quality gate. If the checks passed (required sections present, minimum content in each, schema valid), the draft became the day’s content. If they failed, the draft was saved separately for inspection, an alert went out, and that day’s publish was skipped.

In practice the gate blocked too often on slow, low-data days, when thin sections were the honest state of the market rather than a defect. So the threshold checks were removed and the gate now always passes.

I mention this because it is the real trade-off, not the textbook one. A gate that says no is only useful if its “no” is usually right. A gate tuned on the wrong idea of quality (length, row counts) trains you to ignore it.

What I would build next is a gate on substance, not volume:

  • every figure in the prose appears in the ground-truth set;
  • required disclaimers are present;
  • the narrative’s direction is consistent with the injected data.

Those can fail loudly without punishing a quiet day.

7.19.4 Closing the loop after the close

After the session, a separate job builds a structured feedback artifact comparing the morning’s playbook with what actually happened. Did the levels discussed matter? Did the scenario framing fit the day? It writes:

  • a per-day feedback file,
  • a prompt-ready summary of that feedback,
  • a row appended to a running scorecard.

The next morning, the drafter reads the most recent feedback from before the current date and adjusts its guardrails. If recent accuracy was poor, the draft runs in a more cautious mode: for example, scenario probabilities are capped so the report can’t lean too hard one way after it has recently been wrong. If accuracy was fine, it runs normally.

7.19.5 Why a guardrail and not “learning”

It is tempting to call this self-improvement. It isn’t, in the machine-learning sense. Nothing is trained. The feedback changes a small set of explicit, bounded modes that I designed. That is deliberate:

  • Bounded. The worst the loop can do is make the report more cautious.
  • Explainable. Every draft records which mode it ran in and why.
  • Causal. Only feedback from previous days is read, never the current one. It sounds obvious, but it is an easy lookahead bug (using information from the future) when files are found by globbing a folder.

7.19.6 Scoring the scorer

A feedback loop is only as good as its scoring rule.

Scoring rule Strength Use when
Coarse ordinal score Hard to game, easy to audit The report gives no explicit probabilities
Continuous proper scoring rule (e.g. the Brier score) Rewards honest probabilities The report states explicit probabilities

A proper scoring rule is one where you get the best expected score by reporting your true belief. Either way, the rule must be fixed in advance and not adjusted after a bad week to make it look better.

There is also a reflexivity trap. If the report shapes how its reader trades, outcomes are partly caused by the report. For a research brief that is a minor concern; for a widely read one it matters.

7.19.7 What I’d tell another engineer

  1. Never let the model generate facts it could get wrong. Inject them.
  2. Gate on substance, not volume. A gate that blocks on the wrong signal will end up switched off.
  3. Close the loop with a pre-declared score, and let it adjust bounded, explicit knobs.
  4. Log the mode, the inputs and the score for every day, so the loop itself can be audited.

7.19.8 Summary

  • Numbers come from code and enter the prompt as ground truth; the model writes prose only.
  • A volume-based gate blocked honest quiet days and was switched off; a substance gate is the better design.
  • Feedback is causal (previous days only) and only switches bounded, explicit modes.
  • Fix the scoring rule in advance and log every day’s mode and score.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why does injecting numbers remove a class of hallucination “by construction”? (Answer: the model is never asked to produce figures, so it has no chance to produce wrong ones; any figure in the prose can be checked against the injected set.)
  2. (Design) Write three substance checks for a report in your own domain.
  3. (Debug) A drafter finds its feedback file with a folder glob and picks “the latest”. What lookahead bug can happen, and how do you prevent it?
  4. (Think) Why must the scoring rule be fixed before results come in?

Further reading

  • Ji et al., Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation (ACM Computing Surveys, 2023).
  • Gneiting & Raftery, Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation (JASA, 2007).
  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (2020).

— Tariq

Chapter 7.20 — One Rulebook Across Claude Code, Antigravity, Cursor and VS Code

Subtitle: If every AI coding tool gets its own rules, you don’t have rules. You have four slightly different suggestions.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain how hand-copied agent instruction files drift apart. 2. Set up one source of truth that generates each tool’s instruction file. 3. Split rules into global and workspace rules, and write rules concrete enough to check.

You need: the idea of configuration files and a build step. No maths.

7.20.1 Many tools, many rule files

I use several AI coding environments: Claude Code in the terminal, Google Antigravity, Cursor, and VS Code with its assistants. Each reads instructions from its own place: CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules, editor settings.

For months those files drifted. A rule added after an incident in one tool simply didn’t exist in the others. In 2026 I consolidated them into one canonical rulebook, installed into each tool from a single source.

7.20.2 The drift problem

Agent instruction files are configuration. Like any configuration copied by hand, they diverge:

  • A rule is added to one file during an incident and never propagated.
  • Wording diverges, so the “same” rule means subtly different things.
  • Section numbers and cross-references break in one copy but not another.
  • Nobody can answer “which rules is this agent actually running under?”

The result is inconsistent behaviour. The agent that ran the study didn’t have the rule against substituting the research engine, because that rule lived in a different tool’s file.

7.20.3 Single source, generated copies

The fix is the standard one for configuration drift: one source of truth, rendered into each target format by an installer.

  • A canonical set of tenets lives in one repository.
  • An install script writes the tool-specific files from that source, adding only the small tool-specific parts each needs.
  • Portable skills (packaged instructions for recurring tasks) are installed into each tool’s skills directory, using the common skill format several tools now support.
  • Tool-specific files are treated as build outputs. Changes go to the source.

Figure 7.20.1 — Edit one file, generate the rest. The canonical rulebook feeds an installer, which writes each tool’s instruction file and skills folder (green: build outputs, never edited by hand). On the right, rules are split into global and workspace sets, with a hook that reminds sessions elsewhere that workspace rules exist.

AGENTS.md is increasingly read by several tools as a shared convention. That helps, but not every tool reads it, and some give it different precedence. Generating all formats from one source sidesteps the question.

7.20.4 Global vs workspace rules

Not every rule belongs everywhere:

Rule set Contents Loaded
Global Integrity, honesty, surgical changes, stop conditions, safety Every project
Workspace Domain-specific constraints, e.g. rules for the trading research workspace only Only in that workspace

Keeping domain rules out of the global file matters for two reasons:

  • Context cost. Every token in a global rules file is paid in every session.
  • Precision. A rule that makes sense in one domain can be actively harmful in another.

A small hook reminds sessions started elsewhere that the domain rules exist, without loading them.

7.20.5 Rules that can be checked

A rulebook full of “be careful” is worth little. The rules that changed behaviour were concrete and checkable:

  • Named forbidden substitutions rather than vague principles.
  • A fixed format for reporting a blocked task.
  • Required evidence for any claimed result.
  • Explicit stop conditions with a fixed announcement format.
  • Cross-reference integrity: before editing the rulebook, list every section reference so renumbering can’t leave dangling pointers.

Because they are concrete, hooks can enforce some of them mechanically around agent actions, and a background job watches the rule files themselves so they can’t be quietly weakened.

7.20.6 Keeping it lean

Every rule costs tokens in every session. I periodically review the rulebook for rules that no longer earn their place. Some are kept on purpose even though they are long, because the incident they prevent is expensive. Token trimming is a decision, not a reflex.

7.20.7 What I’d tell another engineer

If you use more than one AI coding tool, pick a source of truth today and generate the rest. Treat instruction files like code: versioned, reviewed, tested where possible, and never edited in only one place.

7.20.8 Summary

  • Hand-copied instruction files drift; drift means different agents follow different rules.
  • Keep one canonical rulebook and generate each tool’s file from it; treat outputs as build artifacts.
  • Split global from workspace rules to save context and avoid misapplied rules.
  • Write rules concrete enough for hooks and reviewers to check, and trim deliberately.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why should a tool’s generated rules file never be edited by hand? (Answer: the next install overwrites it, and until then it silently differs from the source, which is the drift you were trying to remove.)
  2. (Apply) Rewrite “be careful with data” as a rule a reviewer could check.
  3. (Design) Sketch the installer’s inputs and outputs for two tools you use.
  4. (Think) Name one rule that should be global and one that should only load in a single workspace.

Further reading

  • The AGENTS.md open convention (agents.md).
  • Anthropic, Claude Code documentation: memory and CLAUDE.md files.
  • Humble & Farley, Continuous Delivery (2010), on configuration management and single sources of truth.

— Tariq

Chapter 8.2 — Hidden Markov Regimes in Practice

Subtitle: An HMM will always find regimes. Whether they mean anything is a separate, harder question.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe a hidden Markov model (HMM): hidden states, a transition matrix and emissions. 2. Explain the practical fixes that make Baum-Welch training work. 3. Tell filtered from smoothed probabilities, and say why only one is safe in a backtest. 4. Choose the number of states with more than a likelihood score.

You need: basic probability, conditional probability, and the normal (Gaussian) distribution.

8.2.1 Why regime models

Every trader eventually wants a regime model: trend versus chop, calm versus stressed. The textbook answer is the hidden Markov model.

In 2026 I built two of them:

  • one labels the coming session from pre-market information, for a daily research report;
  • one runs on intraday observations, trained offline and used online.

Both taught me more about what HMMs can’t do than about what they can.

8.2.2 The model

An HMM has a hidden state st∈{1,…,K}s_t \in \{1,\dots,K\}. You never see it directly. It moves as a Markov chain: the next state depends only on the current one. The rules for moving are the transition matrix

Aij=P(st=j∣st−1=i), A_{ij} = P(s_t = j \mid s_{t-1} = i),

plus a starting distribution π\pi. At each time you do see an observation xtx_t. It is drawn from a distribution that depends on the state (the emission). With Gaussian emissions:

xt∣st=k∼𝒩(μk,Σk). x_t \mid s_t = k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \Sigma_k).

Figure 8.2.1 — Two hidden states, one visible stream. Each circle is a hidden state. The grey arrows are transition probabilities, including the “stay” loops A11A_{11} and A22A_{22}. The blue arrows show each state producing observations from its own normal distribution. You only see the bottom row; the model must infer the circles.

A common simplification is a diagonal Σk\Sigma_k: within a state, each dimension is treated as independent. That means far fewer parameters and much more stable estimates. The cost is that the model ignores correlation inside a state.

8.2.3 Training: Baum-Welch

The parameters are fitted with Expectation-Maximisation, called Baum-Welch for HMMs.

  • E-step: run the forward-backward algorithm. It gives state posteriors γt(k)=P(st=k∣x1:T)\gamma_t(k) = P(s_t = k \mid x_{1:T}) and pairwise posteriors (the chance of each pair of consecutive states).
  • M-step: re-estimate π\pi, AA, μk\mu_k and Σk\Sigma_k as averages weighted by those posteriors.

Four practical points matter more than the algebra:

Problem What goes wrong Fix
Underflow Forward probabilities shrink towards zero very fast Normalise at each step and keep the scaling constants; their log-sum is the log-likelihood
Collapsing variance A component locks onto a few points; its variance goes to zero and the likelihood to infinity Set a minimum variance (a floor)
Local optima EM finds a local best, not the global one Run several starting points, keep the best likelihood, and check the solutions look alike
Label switching State “2” in one fit may be state “4” in the next Sort or match states by a stable property, such as mean volatility, before comparing

8.2.4 Inference: filtering, not smoothing

This is where most backtests go wrong.

Forward-backward gives smoothed posteriors, P(st∣x1:T)P(s_t \mid x_{1:T}). They use data up to the end of the sample, which includes the future. For a decision at time tt you may only use the filtered posterior:

Definition (filtered posterior). αt(k)∝p(xt∣st=k)∑jαt−1(j)Ajk. \alpha_t(k) \propto p(x_t \mid s_t = k) \sum_j \alpha_{t-1}(j) A_{jk}. It depends only on x1:tx_{1:t}: everything up to now, nothing after.

Smoothed regimes look beautiful on charts because they know where each regime ended. Using them in a backtest is lookahead (using information you would not have had), plain and simple. My online inference is forward-only by construction.

Viterbi decoding, which finds the single most likely path of states, has the same problem. It is an answer about the whole sequence.

Figure 8.2.2 — What each output is allowed to see. The dashed line is the moment you must decide. The filtered probability (top) uses only green data, known at that moment. The smoothed probability and the Viterbi path also use the orange stretch after it. In a backtest that orange stretch is data from the future.

8.2.5 Choosing K

The likelihood always improves when you add states. A penalised criterion helps:

BIC=−2ln⁡L̂+pln⁡T, \text{BIC} = -2 \ln \hat L + p \ln T,

where pp is the number of free parameters and TT the number of observations.

But BIC answers “how many Gaussians fit this cloud?”, not “how many regimes matter for decisions?”. In practice I choose KK by three tests:

  1. Are the states stable across refits?
  2. Do they last long enough to act on? The expected stay in state kk is 1/(1−Akk)1/(1 - A_{kk}) steps.
  3. Do they differ in something I care about downstream?

Example. If Akk=0.9A_{kk} = 0.9, the expected stay is 1/(1−0.9)=101/(1-0.9) = 10 steps.

8.2.6 What textbooks get wrong in markets

  • Stationarity. HMMs assume fixed parameters. Markets drift. Refit on a rolling window, and accept that a state’s meaning drifts too.
  • Geometric durations. A first-order chain implies durations with an exponential (geometric) shape. Real regimes often have a minimum length. Hidden semi-Markov models handle this, at a cost in complexity.
  • Normalisation leakage. Feature scaling computed over the full sample leaks future information into early observations. Scale with past-only statistics.
  • Interpretation. A state you call “trend” because of its mean is a label you assigned. Check, out of sample, that its outcomes really differ before using the name.

8.2.7 Summary

  • An HMM compresses recent behaviour into a few buckets; it is not an oracle.
  • Make training work with scaling, variance floors, restarts and state matching.
  • Use filtered probabilities only. Smoothed and Viterbi outputs are lookahead in a backtest.
  • Keep KK small, and pick it by stability, duration and usefulness, not by likelihood alone.
  • Validate that states predict something out of sample before they influence anything.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A state has Akk=0.95A_{kk} = 0.95. What is its expected duration? (Answer: 1/0.05=201/0.05 = 20 steps.)
  2. (Apply) Your backtest uses Viterbi labels to choose a strategy each day. Explain the leak in one sentence.
  3. (Think) Two refits give states sorted differently. Name a property you could use to match them, and say why it should be stable.
  4. (Simulate) Simulate a two-state chain with Gaussian emissions. Compute both filtered and smoothed posteriors. Where do they disagree most?

Further reading

  • L. Rabiner, “A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models and Selected Applications in Speech Recognition”, Proc. IEEE (1989).
  • J. Hamilton, “A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle”, Econometrica (1989).
  • K. Murphy, Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective (2012), chapter 17.

— Tariq

Chapter 8.3 — Change-Point Detection versus HMMs

Subtitle: HMMs assume a fixed menu of regimes that recur. Change-point models assume each regime is new. Markets are somewhere in between.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Contrast the HMM view (recurring regimes) with the change-point view (new segments). 2. Explain how Bayesian Online Change-Point Detection (BOCPD) tracks the run length. 3. List the engineering steps that keep BOCPD cheap and safe. 4. Use CUSUM as a simple first detector.

You need: Chapter 8.2 (HMMs), and the idea of a posterior distribution.

8.3.1 Two ways to say “something changed”

After building an HMM regime model, I added a second, quite different detector: Bayesian Online Change-Point Detection (BOCPD), run at daily resolution. The two often disagree, and the disagreements are informative.

8.3.2 Two philosophies

  • An HMM says: there are KK regimes, each with fixed parameters, and the market switches among them. Regimes recur. Yesterday’s “calm” is the same calm as last March’s.
  • A change-point model says: the data is piecewise stationary (steady in pieces). At unknown times the parameters jump to new values, and the new piece need not look like any earlier one. Nothing recurs by assumption.

Neither is “right”. Volatility regimes do recur in a loose sense. Structural breaks, such as a policy change or a new market participant, do not.

8.3.3 BOCPD in one page

Adams and MacKay (2007) track the run length rtr_t: the time since the last change point. At each step one of two things happens:

  • the run continues: rt=rt−1+1r_t = r_{t-1} + 1; or
  • a change occurs: rt=0r_t = 0.

The chance of a change is the hazard HH. In the simplest form it is constant, which is a geometric prior on segment lengths.

Figure 8.3.1 — The run length is a sawtooth. The top panel is a simulated series whose mean jumps twice (dashed lines). The bottom panel is the true run length: it climbs by one each step and drops to zero at each change. BOCPD never sees the bottom panel; it keeps a probability for every possible height of the sawtooth. Simulation: independent normal noise with standard deviation 1, mean 0 then 1.5 then −0.5, changes at t = 120 and 220, seed 8003.

The BOCPD update. P(rt,x1:t)=∑rt−1P(rt∣rt−1)p(xt∣rt−1,x(r))P(rt−1,x1:t−1). P(r_t, x_{1:t}) = \sum_{r_{t-1}} P(r_t \mid r_{t-1})\, p(x_t \mid r_{t-1}, x^{(r)})\, P(r_{t-1}, x_{1:t-1}). The middle term is the predictive probability of the new point, given only the data since the last change.

With a conjugate prior (a prior that keeps the same form after updating), that predictive has a closed form. For Gaussian data with unknown mean and variance, the Normal-Inverse-Gamma prior gives a Student-t predictive. Its summary statistics update in O(1)O(1) time per run length.

For several input series, treat each dimension as independent: a product of univariate Normal-Inverse-Gamma models. It ignores correlation, but it is stable and cheap.

The output at each step is a distribution over run lengths. If probability suddenly moves to short run lengths, a change probably just happened.

8.3.4 Practical engineering

  • Truncate run lengths. The posterior gains one entry per step. Drop run lengths with negligible probability so cost stays bounded.
  • Work in logs to avoid underflow, as with any recursive Bayesian filter.
  • Online by construction. BOCPD only uses data up to tt. That is a big advantage over offline segmentation methods (PELT, binary segmentation). They look at the whole series, so they are lookahead if used for decisions.
  • Priors matter. The hazard and the prior on segment parameters strongly change sensitivity. Set them from domain knowledge about plausible segment lengths. Then check sensitivity rather than tuning for the prettiest chart.

8.3.5 HMM and BOCPD side by side

HMM BOCPD
Regimes recur? Yes, by design No, each segment is new
Output Probability of each named state Probability of time since last change
Training EM on history Online, driven by the prior
Lookahead risk High if smoothing is used Low; online by nature
Strength Interpretable recurring states Detecting new breaks quickly
Weakness Fixed menu; geometric durations No memory of past regimes

8.3.6 Using both

I treat them as two sensors that complement each other.

  • An HMM state with low change-point probability: a familiar regime, stable.
  • A spike in change-point probability while the HMM is still confident in its old state: a warning that the HMM’s menu may not fit what is happening.

How such signals are used downstream is a design choice I won’t go into. The general principle: disagreement between models with different assumptions is itself information.

8.3.7 A simpler alternative: CUSUM

CUSUM (Page, 1954) adds up deviations from a reference level and alarms when the sum crosses a limit:

St=max⁡(0,St−1+xt−μ0−κ). S_t = \max(0,\ S_{t-1} + x_t - \mu_0 - \kappa).

Here μ0\mu_0 is the reference mean and κ\kappa is a small allowance that stops ordinary noise from building up.

Figure 8.3.2 — CUSUM catches a mean shift. Before the shift the sum keeps resetting to zero, because each step subtracts the allowance. After the mean moves up, the sum climbs steadily and crosses the alarm limit a few steps later. Simulation: normal noise with standard deviation 1, mean 0 then 1 from t = 100, μ0=0\mu_0 = 0, κ=0.5\kappa = 0.5, limit 5, seed 8031.

CUSUM is cheap, well understood, and often good enough to detect a mean shift in one series. Start there if you don’t need a full posterior.

8.3.8 Summary

  • HMMs assume recurring regimes; change-point models assume each segment is new.
  • BOCPD tracks the run length online, with a closed-form update under conjugate priors.
  • Truncate, work in logs, and set priors from domain knowledge, then check sensitivity.
  • Offline segmentation is lookahead if used for decisions.
  • When two models with different assumptions disagree, pay attention.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With a constant hazard HH, what is the expected segment length? (Answer: 1/H1/H, as for any geometric distribution.)
  2. (Apply) In Figure 8.3.2, what happens to the alarm delay if κ\kappa is raised towards the size of the shift?
  3. (Think) Why is PELT fine for describing history but not for a trading decision?
  4. (Build) Implement BOCPD for a single Gaussian series with a Normal-Inverse-Gamma prior and run-length truncation.

Further reading

  • R. Adams and D. MacKay, “Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection”, arXiv 0710.3742 (2007).
  • E. Page, “Continuous Inspection Schemes”, Biometrika (1954).
  • R. Killick, P. Fearnhead and I. Eckley, “Optimal Detection of Changepoints With a Linear Computational Cost”, JASA (2012).
  • K. Murphy, “Conjugate Bayesian analysis of the Gaussian distribution” (2007).

— Tariq

Chapter 8.4 — Gradient Boosting versus Random Forests for Events

Subtitle: “Will this breakout follow through or fail?” is a small, noisy, imbalanced classification problem. Model choice matters less than you think, and differently than you think.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain how a random forest and gradient boosting combine trees. 2. Say why correlation between trees limits what averaging can do. 3. List the five things that matter more than the algorithm for event studies. 4. Know when to use neither.

You need: what a decision tree is, and the ideas of bias and variance.

8.4.1 The problem

A recurring question in trading research: will an event, say a price breaking out of a range, follow through or turn into a fakeout? It is binary classification on tabular features (a table of numbers per event). The two default answers are random forests and gradient-boosted trees.

In 2026 I reviewed a plan to replace a hand-built filter with a small learned model. This chapter is the general reasoning, independent of any specific feature set.

8.4.2 The two ensembles

An ensemble combines many models into one.

Random forest (Breiman, 2001). Grow many deep trees. Each sees a bootstrap sample of rows (rows drawn at random with replacement) and a random subset of features at each split. Then average their predictions. Deep trees have low bias and high variance; averaging de-correlated trees cuts the variance:

Variance of an average of BB trees. Var⁡(1B∑bTb)=ρσ2+1−ρBσ2, \operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_b T_b\right) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2, where σ2\sigma^2 is one tree’s variance and ρ\rho the correlation between trees.

Why. The second term shrinks as you add trees. The first does not. So ρσ2\rho\sigma^2 is a floor that no number of trees can beat. Random feature subsets lower ρ\rho, which lowers the floor.

Figure 8.4.2 — Correlation sets a floor. Each curve is the formula above, divided by σ2\sigma^2. With independent trees (ρ=0\rho = 0) variance keeps falling. With ρ=0.3\rho = 0.3 or 0.60.6 it flattens at ρ\rho after a few dozen trees. More trees help only until you hit the floor.

Gradient boosting (Friedman, 2001). Grow shallow trees one after another. Each new tree fits the negative gradient of the loss at the current prediction, which roughly means “what the model still gets wrong”. For log-loss:

FM(x)=F0+ν∑m=1Mhm(x),p(x)=σ(FM(x)), F_M(x) = F_0 + \nu \sum_{m=1}^{M} h_m(x), \qquad p(x) = \sigma(F_M(x)),

with learning rate ν\nu, weak learners hmh_m and the sigmoid σ\sigma turning a score into a probability. Boosting cuts bias step by step. Regularisation controls variance: shrinkage, depth limits, subsampling and minimum leaf sizes. XGBoost and LightGBM add second-order gradient information, histogram-based splits and efficient handling of missing values.

Figure 8.4.1 — Parallel versus sequential. On the left, deep trees are built side by side on different samples and averaged; this lowers variance. On the right, each shallow tree corrects the ones before it, and the scaled sum goes through a sigmoid; this lowers bias.

8.4.3 What usually happens on noisy financial events

On large, clean tabular benchmarks, well-tuned boosting usually edges out random forests. Event studies give small, noisy and non-stationary samples (their behaviour changes over time). There the picture changes:

Random forest Gradient boosting
Overfitting with defaults Hard to overfit badly Will memorise noise if allowed
Free validation Out-of-bag error (optimistic when samples are correlated in time) None built in
Number of knobs Few Many; advantage needs careful regularisation and honest validation
Weak signal, noisy labels Finds spurious structure Finds spurious structure

Neither fixes a weak signal.

My working rule: start with a heavily regularised shallow boosting model or a random forest. Compare both under the same purged cross-validation. Count every configuration you try as a trial.

8.4.4 Things that matter more than the algorithm

  1. Labels. How “follow-through” and “fakeout” are defined dominates everything. Barrier-based labels with costs included are a good default (Chapter 8.6).
  2. Validation. Events cluster in time and overlap. Random K-fold leaks information; use purged, embargoed splits (Chapter 8.8).
  3. Class imbalance. If fakeouts dominate, a model can look accurate by always predicting the majority. Evaluate with proper scoring rules and calibration, not accuracy (Chapters 8.11 and 8.12).
  4. Feature leakage. Any feature computed with information from after the event time invalidates the study. This is the most common bug I see, in my work and others’.
  5. Trial count. Every feature-set and hyperparameter combination evaluated is a trial. Report the number and deflate for it (Chapter 8.9).

8.4.5 Interpretability and deployment

Shallow boosted trees are easy to export and evaluate exactly in another language. That matters if the live system isn’t Python (Chapter 8.13). Random forests with deep trees are larger and slower to evaluate, but just as deterministic.

Feature importance from either model is a weak guide. Impurity-based importances are biased towards features with many distinct values. Permutation importance on held-out data, or SHAP values, are more trustworthy. Even they describe the model, not the market.

8.4.6 When to use neither

If the sample is tiny, a logistic regression with a handful of well-motivated inputs, properly calibrated, is often as good and far more honest. A complex model that can’t beat a simple one under purged validation is telling you only that it can fit noise.

8.4.7 Summary

  • Forests average deep trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees to cut bias.
  • Tree correlation sets a variance floor that more trees cannot remove.
  • On small, noisy event samples, labels, validation, imbalance, leakage and trial counts matter more than the algorithm.
  • Compare models under the same purged validation and count every trial.
  • If a simple calibrated model does as well, use it.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With ρ=0.5\rho = 0.5, what fraction of one tree’s variance remains with infinitely many trees? (Answer: 0.5.)
  2. (Apply) 90% of your events are fakeouts. What accuracy does “always predict fakeout” get, and why is that useless?
  3. (Think) Give an example of a feature that leaks information from after the event time.
  4. (Compare) Why is out-of-bag error optimistic when samples are correlated in time?

Further reading

  • L. Breiman, “Random Forests”, Machine Learning (2001).
  • J. Friedman, “Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine”, Annals of Statistics (2001).
  • T. Chen and C. Guestrin, “XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System”, KDD (2016).
  • L. Grinsztajn, E. Oyallon and G. Varoquaux, “Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?”, NeurIPS (2022).

— Tariq

Chapter 8.5 — Transformer Classifiers for Market State: Where They Fit

Subtitle: A pretrained encoder is a superb text classifier. That doesn’t make it a market classifier.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Tell encoder models from decoder models, and explain how an encoder classifies. 2. Describe zero-shot classification. 3. Give four reasons a text encoder is a poor fit for numeric market state. 4. Fine-tune and calibrate an encoder safely on a small labelled set.

You need: what a neural network and a softmax are, at a high level.

8.5.1 Background

ModernBERT arrived in late 2024. It is a refreshed encoder-only transformer: longer context, faster inference, and trained on a modern corpus that includes code. Encoders like it are excellent for classification. I run one locally as a zero-shot classifier for routine agent decisions.

I also evaluated whether that kind of model belonged in my trading decision path. I decided it didn’t. The reasoning generalises.

8.5.2 Encoders versus decoders

  • Decoder models (GPT-style) generate text one token at a time.
  • Encoder models (BERT-style) read the whole input in both directions and produce contextual embeddings: a vector for each token that reflects its surroundings.

To classify, put a small head on a pooled representation, usually the special [CLS] token:

p(y∣x)=softmax⁡(W𝒉[CLS](x)+b). p(y \mid x) = \operatorname{softmax}(W\,\mathbf{h}_{\text{[CLS]}}(x) + b).

For classification, encoders are smaller, faster and cheaper than generative models of similar quality. They give a probability per class directly, with no text parsing.

ModernBERT adds three things that make it practical on a laptop:

  • rotary position embeddings (a way to encode word order);
  • alternating local and global attention, for long inputs;
  • efficient unpadding (no wasted work on padding tokens).

8.5.3 Zero-shot classification

Zero-shot means classifying without fine-tuning. Two ways:

  1. Frame each label as a hypothesis and use a model trained for natural-language inference (does sentence A imply sentence B?).
  2. Embed the input and embed a description of each label; pick the closest.

That is how my local router scores options for routine agent decisions. It is fast, offline, and good enough for “which of these tools fits this request?”. When confidence is low, it escalates.

8.5.4 Where it doesn’t fit: numeric market state

Market state is mostly numbers: prices, volumes, volatility, order flow. Transformers can read numbers written as text, but:

  • Tokenisation mangles numbers. A tokeniser cuts text into sub-word pieces. “4521.25” becomes a few arbitrary pieces. The model has no built-in notion of size.
  • Pretraining knowledge is irrelevant or harmful. Language priors about the words “bullish” or “breakout” are not evidence about the next minutes of a futures contract.
  • Latency and determinism. A deterministic tree evaluator returns in microseconds and gives the same answer every time. A transformer is orders of magnitude slower. Its outputs shift with library versions and hardware unless carefully pinned.
  • Language and runtime. My execution path is C#. A Python transformer would mean a sidecar process in the hot path, which I explicitly avoid (Chapter 8.13).

For numeric tabular features, tree ensembles and linear models remain the sensible defaults. If you want a neural model on time series, there are architectures designed for that. They still need the same purged validation as anything else.

Figure 8.5.1 — Match the model to the data. Text goes well with a pretrained encoder (top row, green). Numeric market state goes well with trees or linear models (bottom, green). Sending numbers through a text encoder (dashed orange) loses magnitude and adds latency and a second runtime.

8.5.5 Where it might fit: text that affects markets

Encoders suit text signals: classifying headlines, central-bank statements or filings by topic or tone. FinBERT-style models fine-tuned on financial text are the standard example. Even there, the honest questions are:

  • Timing: when did the text become public, to the second?
  • Leakage: was the model trained on text from after your test period?
  • Costs: does the signal survive trading costs?

8.5.6 Fine-tuning on small labelled sets

If you fine-tune an encoder on your own labels:

  • Small data overfits fast. Use few epochs, a small learning rate, and early stopping on a validation set separated in time.
  • Calibrate the outputs. Softmax probabilities from fine-tuned transformers are often over-confident.
  • Purge and embargo the splits, as with any financial label (Chapter 8.8).

Temperature scaling. Fit one number TT on validation data so that softmax⁡(z/T)\operatorname{softmax}(z/T) minimises validation log-loss. T>1T > 1 softens over-confident outputs. It is cheap and does not change the ranking of classes.

8.5.7 Summary

  • Encoders read whole inputs and classify cheaply; decoders generate text.
  • Zero-shot classification works well for routing language requests.
  • For numeric market state, text encoders are a weak prior and an operational liability in a latency-sensitive, non-Python path.
  • Use them where the input is text, and route their decisions through the same shadow evaluation as anything else.
  • Fine-tune carefully and calibrate with temperature scaling.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Name two reasons tree models beat text encoders on numeric features. (Answer: e.g. no tokenisation of numbers; microsecond, deterministic evaluation.)
  2. (Apply) Your headline classifier was trained on news up to last month. Your test period is last year. What is the problem?
  3. (Calculate) Logits are z=(2,0)z = (2, 0). Find the class-1 probability with T=1T = 1 and with T=2T = 2.
  4. (Think) Why must the validation set for early stopping be separated in time, not drawn at random?

Further reading

  • B. Warner et al., “Smarter, Better, Faster, Longer: A Modern Bidirectional Encoder” (ModernBERT), arXiv 2412.13663 (2024).
  • J. Devlin et al., “BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding” (2019).
  • D. Araci, “FinBERT: Financial Sentiment Analysis with Pre-trained Language Models” (2019).
  • C. Guo et al., “On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks”, ICML (2017).

— Tariq

Chapter 8.6 — Labelling for Trading ML: the Triple Barrier and Meta-Labelling

Subtitle: Your model can only learn the question your labels ask. Most trading labels ask the wrong one.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain three flaws of fixed-horizon labels. 2. Build triple-barrier labels correctly, without lookahead. 3. Weight overlapping labels by uniqueness. 4. Use meta-labelling and a cost-based threshold to filter a primary signal.

You need: basic probability; the idea of a classifier that outputs a probability.

8.6.1 Why labels come first

People new to machine learning in markets spend weeks on features and minutes on labels. It should be the other way round. In 2026 I spent a good part of my research time on label design. The two ideas I kept returning to both come from Marcos López de Prado: the triple-barrier method and meta-labelling.

8.6.2 What’s wrong with fixed-horizon labels

The naive label is the sign of the return over a fixed horizon hh:

yt=sign⁡(pt+h−pt). y_t = \operatorname{sign}(p_{t+h} - p_t).

It has three problems:

  • It ignores the path. A trade that would have been stopped out before recovering is labelled a win.
  • It ignores volatility. The same horizon means very different things in quiet and wild markets.
  • It ignores costs. A tiny positive move that would not pay commission and slippage is labelled a success.

8.6.3 The triple barrier

For an event at time t0t_0, set three barriers:

  • an upper barrier at pt0(1+ut0)p_{t_0}(1 + u_{t_0}): profit-take;
  • a lower barrier at pt0(1−dt0)p_{t_0}(1 - d_{t_0}): stop;
  • a vertical barrier at t0+ht_0 + h: time-out.

The label is set by whichever barrier price touches first: +1+1 for upper, −1-1 for lower. For the vertical barrier, use either 00 or the sign of the return at expiry, depending on your convention. The widths uu and dd are usually scaled by an estimate of recent volatility known at t0t_0, so a label means the same thing in different conditions.

Definition (first-passage time). τ=inf⁡{t>t0:pt∉(L,U)}∧(t0+h), \tau = \inf\{t > t_0 : p_t \notin (L, U)\} \wedge (t_0 + h), the first time price leaves the band between the lower level LL and upper level UU, capped at the time-out. The label is a function of pτp_\tau.

Figure 8.6.1 — Whichever barrier is hit first sets the label. The path starts at the first trade after the signal (blue dot). It wanders, dips, then touches the green profit-take line before the orange stop or the grey time-out, so the label is +1. A fixed-horizon label would only look at where the path sits at one moment. Simulation: fair ±1 random walk, barriers ±12 steps, time-out 200 steps, seed 8012 (the first seed from 8006 whose path hits the upper barrier after more than 120 steps). Not market data.

8.6.4 Getting barriers right in practice

  • Use tick data or real intrabar paths. With only bar OHLC (open, high, low, close), you don’t know whether the high or the low came first inside a bar. Pretending you do, or using bars without wicks, biases labels systematically. When both barriers sit inside one bar and the order is unknown, the honest options are: resolve it with finer data, or mark it ambiguous.
  • Start after the event. The path begins at the first trade after the signal, not at the signal bar’s close.
  • Include costs. Shift barriers so that “profit-take” means profit after realistic costs.
  • Volatility at t0t_0 only. The volatility estimate must use data up to t0t_0, never a centred window.

8.6.5 Overlap and sample weights

Triple-barrier labels overlap in time: events close together share parts of their paths. That breaks the independence assumption of most learning algorithms and inflates the apparent sample size. Two standard responses:

  • Uniqueness weights. At each time tt in an event’s span, count ctc_t, the number of events alive at once. The event’s average uniqueness is the average of 1/ct1/c_t over its span. Weight samples by it.
  • Purging and embargo in cross-validation (Chapter 8.8).

Figure 8.6.2 — Overlapping events share credit. The blue bars are four event spans. The columns below count how many are alive at each bar; orange marks overlap. Event 4 stands alone and gets uniqueness 1.00. Event 3 lives entirely in the crowded middle, so it gets only 0.39. A toy example with made-up spans.

8.6.6 Meta-labelling

Meta-labelling splits the problem in two:

  1. A primary model decides the side (long or short) and when an opportunity exists. It can be a simple rule, or a human.
  2. A secondary model learns, given the primary signal and its context, the probability that acting on it hits the profit barrier first:

ytmeta=𝟙{primary signal at t hits its profit barrier first}. y^{\text{meta}}_t = \mathbb{1}\{\text{primary signal at } t \text{ hits its profit barrier first}\}.

Why it helps:

  • The primary model can be tuned for recall (catch most opportunities). The secondary model improves precision (fewer bad ones) by filtering.
  • The secondary probability is a natural input to sizing or to a go/no-go decision.
  • The secondary model cannot flip direction. It only filters, which bounds the damage it can do.

Figure 8.6.3 — Two models, two jobs. The primary model picks side and timing. The secondary model turns each signal into a probability. A cost-based threshold then either takes the trade (green) or skips it (orange). Nothing in the chain can reverse the side.

8.6.7 Asymmetric costs

Missing a good trade and taking a bad one rarely cost the same.

Result (cost-minimising threshold). If a false positive costs cFPc_{FP} and a false negative costs cFNc_{FN}, and pp is a calibrated probability, act when p>cFPcFP+cFN. p > \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}.

Why. Acting costs (1−p)cFP(1-p)\,c_{FP} on average; skipping costs pcFNp\,c_{FN}. Act when the first is smaller, and solve for pp.

This works only if pp is calibrated (its numbers match real frequencies). That is the subject of Chapter 8.11.

8.6.8 Pitfalls

  • Labels that use future information through volatility estimates or barrier definitions.
  • Tuning barrier widths on the same data you evaluate on, without counting them as trials.
  • Treating the vertical-barrier class as noise and dropping it. That silently changes what the model learns.

8.6.9 Summary

  • Fixed-horizon labels ignore path, volatility and costs.
  • Triple-barrier labels use the first barrier touched, starting from the first trade after the signal, with past-only volatility and costs built in.
  • Overlapping labels need uniqueness weights and purged validation.
  • Meta-labelling separates “which side” from “is this one worth taking”.
  • A calibrated probability plus asymmetric costs gives the action threshold.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A false positive costs 1 and a false negative costs 3. What is the threshold? (Answer: 1/(1+3) = 0.25.)
  2. (Apply) Both barriers fall inside one 5-minute bar and you have no tick data. What are your honest choices?
  3. (Calculate) An event spans three bars with concurrency 1, 2 and 4. What is its average uniqueness?
  4. (Think) Why does a secondary model that cannot flip side limit possible damage?

Further reading

  • M. López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018), chapters 3 and 4.
  • C. Elkan, “The Foundations of Cost-Sensitive Learning”, IJCAI (2001).
  • Hudson & Thames, mlfinlab documentation on labelling.

— Tariq

Chapter 8.7 — Small, Clustered Samples

Subtitle: Two hundred trades from twenty sessions is not two hundred observations. It might be closer to twenty.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compute the design effect and the effective sample size. 2. Choose cluster-level standard errors, bootstraps and cross-validation. 3. Do a power calculation before a study starts. 4. Compare a directional result with an exact random-walk null.

You need: mean, variance, correlation, and the idea of a confidence interval.

8.7.1 The quiet way research fools itself

The most common way trading research fools itself isn’t dramatic overfitting. It is quieter: treating observations as independent when they are clustered. Trades from the same session share the same news, volatility and liquidity. Treat them as independent and every confidence interval you compute is too narrow.

8.7.2 The design effect

Suppose you have mm clusters (sessions), each with nn observations, and an intra-cluster correlation ρ\rho (how alike two observations from the same session are).

Result (Kish, 1965). The variance of the overall mean is inflated, relative to independent sampling, by the design effect DEFF=1+(n−1)ρ, \text{DEFF} = 1 + (n - 1)\rho, so the effective sample size is Neff=mn1+(n−1)ρ. N_{\text{eff}} = \frac{mn}{1 + (n-1)\rho}.

Worked numbers, with 20 sessions of 10 trades each (200 trades):

ρ\rho DEFF NeffN_{\text{eff}}
0 1.0 200
0.2 2.8 about 71
0.5 5.5 about 36
→ 1 → 10 → 20 (the number of sessions)

Figure 8.7.1 — Correlation eats sample size fast. The curve is the formula for 20 sessions of 10 trades. A modest correlation of 0.2 already cuts 200 trades to about 71. As correlation approaches 1, you are left with the orange floor: one observation per session.

Cluster sizes vary in practice. Use the average size, or better, estimate variance directly at the cluster level.

8.7.3 Practical consequences

  • Standard errors. For a mean or regression coefficient, use cluster-robust standard errors, clustering by session. With few clusters (fewer than roughly 30 to 50), even those are biased downward. Small-sample corrections or the wild cluster bootstrap are more reliable.
  • Bootstraps. Resample whole sessions, not single trades. A trade-level bootstrap on clustered data gives intervals that are far too tight. For serially dependent data in general, block bootstraps keep local dependence intact.
  • Cross-validation. Split by session or by contiguous blocks of sessions, never by row. Then purge and embargo where labels cross boundaries (Chapter 8.8).

8.7.4 Power before you start

Power is the chance a study detects an effect that is really there. Before running a study, ask what effect size your effective sample could detect.

Approximation (two-sided test of a mean). With standard deviation σ\sigma, significance α\alpha and power 1−β1-\beta, detecting an effect δ\delta needs about Neff≈((z1−α/2+z1−β)σδ)2. N_{\text{eff}} \approx \left(\frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})\,\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2.

If your effective sample can only detect effects much larger than anything plausible, the study can’t succeed. Any “significant” result it produces is more likely noise. I now compute a power floor before a study starts, not after it fails.

8.7.5 A useful null: the random walk

For directional questions (“does this pattern continue?”), compute what a pure random walk would give under the same construction. For a driftless walk, the chance of reaching an upper level before a lower one depends only on the distances (the gambler’s ruin result, Chapter 6.1):

P(hit +a before −b)=ba+b. P(\text{hit } +a \text{ before } -b) = \frac{b}{a + b}.

Any claimed continuation edge must beat that null, with the right effective sample size, not just beat 50%. Bar construction can build structure into this. For some bar types the null must be derived for that construction rather than assumed.

8.7.6 Cell-splitting makes it worse

Breaking results down by setup, time of day and regime is natural. But each cell has fewer clusters, and you are running many comparisons. Expect some cells to look great by chance. Correct for multiple comparisons, or better, decide in advance which cells you will look at.

8.7.7 Summary

  • Count sessions, not trades.
  • Bootstrap and cross-validate at the session level.
  • Estimate effective sample size before you trust any interval.
  • Compute power in advance and abandon studies that can’t succeed.
  • Compare against an exact null for the construction you actually use.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) 30 sessions, 8 trades each, ρ=0.3\rho = 0.3. Find NeffN_{\text{eff}}. (Answer: 240 / (1 + 7·0.3) = 240 / 3.1 ≈ 77.)
  2. (Apply) Why does a trade-level bootstrap give intervals that are too tight here?
  3. (Calculate) With α=0.05\alpha = 0.05, power 0.8 (zz values 1.96 and 0.84), σ=1\sigma = 1, δ=0.2\delta = 0.2: what NeffN_{\text{eff}} do you need?
  4. (Think) You split results into 24 cells and one looks excellent. What would convince you it is real?

Further reading

  • L. Kish, Survey Sampling (Wiley, 1965).
  • A. Cameron, J. Gelbach and D. Miller, “Bootstrap-Based Improvements for Inference with Clustered Errors”, REStat (2008).
  • A. Cameron and D. Miller, “A Practitioner’s Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference”, JHR (2015).
  • H. Künsch, “The Jackknife and the Bootstrap for General Stationary Observations” (1989).

— Tariq

Chapter 8.8 — Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation

Subtitle: Standard cross-validation leaks the future into the past in financial data. CPCV plugs the leaks and gives you a distribution instead of a single number.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why ordinary K-fold leaks information with financial labels. 2. Apply purging and embargo. 3. Count CPCV splits and backtest paths. 4. Report the median path, not the best one.

You need: what cross-validation is; combinations (Nk)\binom{N}{k}; Chapter 8.6 (label spans).

8.8.1 One number is not enough

My research pipeline evaluates every candidate with combinatorial purged cross-validation (CPCV), grouped by session. A single train/test split gives one number. One number from noisy financial data can be almost anything. CPCV gives a distribution of out-of-sample results across many paths, without leaking information across folds.

8.8.2 Why K-fold leaks

In ordinary K-fold, rows are put into folds without regard to time. Financial labels span time: a trade opened at tt resolves at t+ht + h. So a training sample can overlap a test sample’s label window. The model then learns from information that is effectively part of the test outcome. Serial correlation in features makes it worse: neighbouring samples on either side of a fold boundary are near-duplicates.

8.8.3 Purging and embargo

Purging. Remove from training any sample whose label interval overlaps the label interval of any test sample. If training sample ii spans [ti0,ti1][t_i^0, t_i^1] and test sample jj spans [tj0,tj1][t_j^0, t_j^1], drop ii when the intervals intersect.

Embargo. Also drop training samples that start within a short period after the test set ends. Features built from lagged data can still carry information about the test period.

Figure 8.8.2 — Purge what overlaps, embargo what follows. Each bar is one sample’s label span. Orange bars are removed from training: three cross into the test block’s label spans, and one starts inside the embargo zone just after it. Green bars, far enough away, are kept. A toy layout, not real data.

Grouping by session is a natural unit. Folds are made of whole sessions, so correlation inside a session can’t straddle a boundary.

8.8.4 The combinatorial part

Split the sessions into NN contiguous groups. Choose kk of them as the test set and train on the rest (after purging and embargo). Do this for every combination:

(Nk) splits. \binom{N}{k} \text{ splits}.

Each group is in the test set in (N−1k−1)\binom{N-1}{k-1} splits. Stitch together test predictions so each group is covered once, and you get

φ=kN(Nk) \varphi = \frac{k}{N}\binom{N}{k} distinct full backtest paths, each an out-of-sample history over the whole period.

Instead of one Sharpe ratio you get φ\varphi of them.

Figure 8.8.1 — Every way to choose the test groups. With N=6N = 6 groups and k=2k = 2, there are 15 splits (columns). Read across a row: each group is blue (tested) in exactly 5 splits. Taking one tested piece per group gives φ=(2/6)⋅15=5\varphi = (2/6)\cdot 15 = 5 complete out-of-sample paths.

8.8.5 Why a distribution matters

A single walk-forward run gives one realisation. If the strategy is fragile, that path may be lucky or unlucky. With many paths you can report:

  • the median across paths, robust to one lucky path;
  • a lower percentile, showing how bad a plausible path looks;
  • the dispersion, telling you how much to trust either.

My validation rules use the median path, not the best one. Reporting the best of many paths is cherry-picking with extra steps.

8.8.6 Practical notes

Issue What to do
Cost (Nk)\binom{N}{k} grows fast. For expensive models pick NN and kk so the number of fits is manageable. Rule-based strategies with no fitting step make CPCV cheap: you only evaluate on different partitions.
Paths aren’t independent They share training data and test groups. Treat the spread as a robustness indicator, not as φ\varphi independent samples.
Purge on label spans You need each sample’s end time. If labels don’t record it, you can’t purge correctly.
Non-stationarity CPCV trains on data before and after the test group. Fine for a stationary world. If you suspect strong regime drift, add pure walk-forward evaluation.

8.8.7 Pitfalls

  • Tuning hyperparameters on the CPCV result and then reporting that same result as out-of-sample. Any choice made after seeing results is a trial and needs deflating (Chapter 8.9).
  • Purging only next to the test set, but forgetting labels that span longer than one group.
  • Mixing row-level and session-level grouping in the same study.

8.8.8 Summary

  • K-fold leaks when labels span time; purge overlaps and embargo what follows.
  • CPCV tests every combination of kk of NN groups and stitches φ\varphi full paths.
  • Report the median path, a low percentile and the spread, never the best path.
  • Paths share data, so their spread is a robustness signal, not independent evidence.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) N=8N = 8, k=2k = 2. How many splits and paths? (Answer: 28 splits; φ = (2/8)·28 = 7 paths.)
  2. (Apply) A training trade opens Monday and resolves Wednesday. The test block is Tuesday. Purge or keep?
  3. (Think) Why does the embargo sit after the test block and not before it?
  4. (Report) Write the three numbers you would report from a CPCV run, and one you never would.

Further reading

  • M. López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018), chapters 7 and 12.
  • D. Bailey, J. Borwein, M. López de Prado and Q. Zhu, “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting”, J. Computational Finance (2017).
  • S. Arlot and A. Celisse, “A survey of cross-validation procedures for model selection”, Statistics Surveys (2010).

— Tariq

Chapter 8.9 — The Deflated Sharpe Ratio and the Trial Ledger

Subtitle: The best of a hundred backtests is not a discovery. It’s the expected maximum of a hundred random draws.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why the best of NN skill-less trials looks good. 2. Compute the probabilistic Sharpe ratio (PSR) and the deflated Sharpe ratio (DSR). 3. Say what counts as a trial, and why the count must be stored honestly.

You need: the Sharpe ratio, the normal distribution and its quantile function Φ−1\Phi^{-1}, skewness and kurtosis.

8.9.1 Counting is the hard part

Try enough strategy variants and one will look excellent by chance. Everyone knows this; almost nobody counts.

In 2026 I built an append-only trial registry into my research pipeline. Every hypothesis and every configuration evaluated adds a row, and the count survives restarts. That count, NN, feeds the deflated Sharpe ratio, which asks whether the best result beats what luck alone would produce.

8.9.2 Selection bias under multiple testing

Suppose NN independent strategies all have true Sharpe ratio zero. Their estimated Sharpe ratios are noisy, roughly normal with some variance VV across trials. The maximum of NN such estimates is not zero.

Approximation (Bailey and López de Prado). 𝔼[maxnSR̂n]≈V((1−γ)Φ−1(1−1N)+γΦ−1(1−1Ne)), \mathbb{E}\left[\max_n \widehat{SR}_n\right] \approx \sqrt{V}\left((1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right) + \gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1 - \frac{1}{N e}\right)\right), where γ≈0.5772\gamma \approx 0.5772 is the Euler-Mascheroni constant and Φ−1\Phi^{-1} the standard normal quantile.

It grows with NN, roughly like 2ln⁡N\sqrt{2 \ln N}. Try more things and the best one looks better, with no skill involved.

Figure 8.9.1 — Luck grows with the number of tries. The blue curve is the approximation with V=1V = 1. The orange dots are a simulation: the best of NN standard normal draws, averaged over 2,000 repeats (seed 8009). They sit on the curve. The dashed line is the rough 2ln⁡N\sqrt{2\ln N} growth, which overstates the level but shows the shape. With 100 skill-less trials the best one is about 2.5 standard deviations above zero.

8.9.3 The probabilistic Sharpe ratio

Before deflating, account for two facts: Sharpe estimates are noisy, and returns are not normal. The probabilistic Sharpe ratio (Bailey and López de Prado, 2012) is the probability that the true Sharpe exceeds a benchmark SR*SR^*:

PSR̂(SR*)=Φ((SR̂−SR*)T−11−γ̂3SR̂+γ̂4−14SR̂2), \widehat{PSR}(SR^*) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{(\widehat{SR} - SR^*)\sqrt{T - 1}}{\sqrt{1 - \hat\gamma_3\,\widehat{SR} + \frac{\hat\gamma_4 - 1}{4}\widehat{SR}^2}}\right),

with TT observations, sample skewness γ̂3\hat\gamma_3 and kurtosis γ̂4\hat\gamma_4. Negative skew and fat tails, common in trading returns, make the denominator larger, which widens the uncertainty.

8.9.4 Deflating

Definition (DSR). Set the PSR benchmark to the expected maximum under the null: DSR=PSR̂(𝔼[maxnSR̂n]). DSR = \widehat{PSR}\left(\mathbb{E}[\max_n \widehat{SR}_n]\right).

Read it as: the probability that the chosen strategy’s true Sharpe beats what the best of NN skill-less trials would show. If it isn’t high, the “discovery” can’t be told apart from selection bias.

8.9.5 Why the ledger is the hard part

The formula is a few lines of code. The hard part is an honest NN.

  • Every configuration counts. Changing a parameter and re-running is a trial. So is changing a filter, a time window or a label definition.
  • Hypotheses count too. Each new idea tested adds to NN, even if abandoned quickly.
  • Peeking counts. Looking at test results and then adjusting is a new trial.
  • Persistence matters. A counter in memory resets when the process does. My registry is an append-only table on disk. The count is defined as rows since the last explicitly human-approved reset.
  • Readers can’t write. The validation stage reads NN and never changes it. The component judging results can’t be the one deciding how many attempts happened.

Figure 8.9.2 — The judge cannot change the count. Research runs only append rows. The validation stage only reads NN. The single way to lower NN is a rare, recorded, human-approved reset. A concept sketch, not a wiring diagram.

Correlated trials. NN near-identical variants are not NN independent ones. The refined approach clusters trials and estimates an effective number of independent trials. Using the raw NN is conservative, and I prefer conservative.

8.9.6 Session-level statistics

I compute Sharpe on session-level returns, not trade-level, for the clustering reasons in Chapter 8.7. That also gives TT the right meaning: the number of roughly independent observations.

8.9.7 Pitfalls

  • Using an annualised Sharpe in the formula with a TT that counts trades. Units must match.
  • Estimating VV from a handful of trials. The variance across trials is itself noisy.
  • Resetting NN informally (“that was a different project”). Resets should be rare, deliberate and recorded.

8.9.8 Summary

  • The best of NN skill-less trials has an expected Sharpe that grows with NN.
  • PSR corrects for noise, skew and fat tails; DSR uses the expected maximum as the benchmark.
  • Every configuration, hypothesis and peek is a trial.
  • Store NN append-only on disk, and keep the judge read-only.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Does trying more variants raise or lower the bar a winner must clear? (Answer: it raises it, roughly like √(2 ln N).)
  2. (Apply) You tweak one filter after seeing the test results. Does NN change?
  3. (Think) Why is it important that the validation stage cannot write to the ledger?
  4. (Calculate) Using Figure 8.9.1, roughly what best Sharpe (in units of V\sqrt V) would 10 skill-less trials produce?

Further reading

  • D. Bailey and M. López de Prado, “The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality”, J. Portfolio Management (2014).
  • D. Bailey and M. López de Prado, “The Sharpe Ratio Efficient Frontier”, J. Risk (2012).
  • C. Harvey, Y. Liu and H. Zhu, “…and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns”, RFS (2016).
  • A. Lo, “The Statistics of Sharpe Ratios”, Financial Analysts Journal (2002).

— Tariq

Chapter 8.10 — Probability of Backtest Overfitting with CSCV

Subtitle: Instead of asking “is my best strategy good?”, ask “how often does the in-sample winner lose out of sample?”

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Build the combinatorially symmetric splits used by CSCV. 2. Compute the logit rank λ\lambda and the probability of backtest overfitting (PBO). 3. Read PBO values and the companion diagnostics. 4. Explain how PBO complements the deflated Sharpe ratio.

You need: Chapter 8.9; combinations; the logit function ln⁡(p/(1−p))\ln(p/(1-p)).

8.10.1 A different question

The deflated Sharpe ratio corrects one number for the number of trials. The probability of backtest overfitting (PBO) asks a complementary question: when you pick the best configuration in-sample, how often is it below the median out of sample?

I came across it while researching how to control overfitting in a parameter search over indicator settings. It changed how I think about any search over configurations.

8.10.2 Setup

You have NN candidate configurations and a performance series for each over TT periods: a T×NT \times N matrix MM. Split the TT rows into SS equal, contiguous blocks, with SS even.

Combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV) takes every combination of S/2S/2 blocks as the in-sample set JJ. The other S/2S/2 blocks form the out-of-sample set J‾\bar J. There are

(SS/2) \binom{S}{S/2}

such splits. Each block is in-sample exactly as often as it is out-of-sample. That is the symmetry.

Figure 8.10.1 — Half in, half out, every way. With S=6S = 6 blocks there are 20 splits; five are shown. In each, the blue blocks are in-sample (IS) and the white blocks out-of-sample (OOS). Across all 20, each block is IS ten times and OOS ten times.

8.10.3 The procedure

For each split:

  1. Compute each configuration’s performance (for example Sharpe) on JJ. Pick the best, n*n^*.
  2. Compute every configuration’s performance on J‾\bar J. Find the relative rank ω∈(0,1)\omega \in (0,1) of n*n^* among them.
  3. Turn it into a logit:

λ=ln⁡ω1−ω. \lambda = \ln\frac{\omega}{1 - \omega}.

λ>0\lambda > 0 means the in-sample winner beat the out-of-sample median. λ<0\lambda < 0 means it fell below.

Definition (PBO). PBO=1(SS/2)∑splits𝟙{λ<0}, \text{PBO} = \frac{1}{\binom{S}{S/2}} \sum_{\text{splits}} \mathbb{1}\{\lambda < 0\}, the fraction of splits in which the winner fell below the median.

8.10.4 Reading it

PBO Meaning
Near 0 Selection reliably picks configurations that also do well out of sample. Selection adds information.
Near 0.5 In-sample ranking says nothing about out-of-sample ranking. Selection is a coin flip.
Above 0.5 In-sample winners tend to be out-of-sample losers: a classic sign of fitting noise.

Plot the whole distribution of λ\lambda, not just the fraction below zero.

Figure 8.10.2 — With no skill, selection is close to a coin flip. All 100 configurations here are pure noise, so the in-sample winner has no real advantage. The logit ranks spread on both sides of zero. This sample gives PBO = 0.40; the expected value for pure noise is about 0.5, and one finite sample wanders around it. Simulation: 100 configurations of independent standard normal returns over 1,200 periods, S = 10 blocks (252 splits), seed 8010.

Two companion diagnostics come from the same splits:

  • Performance degradation: regress the winner’s out-of-sample performance on its in-sample performance. A strongly negative slope means the better it looks in-sample, the worse it does after.
  • Probability of loss: the fraction of splits where the selected configuration loses money out of sample.

8.10.5 Why it complements DSR

DSR asks whether one chosen result beats the luck of NN trials. PBO judges the selection process itself, using the whole matrix of trials. A search can produce a winner with an acceptable DSR and still have a high PBO. That tells you the winner is fragile, and the next search would pick something else.

8.10.6 Practical notes

  • You need the whole matrix: the performance series of every configuration tried, not just the winner. Another reason to log every trial.
  • Block size versus count. More blocks give more splits but noisier per-block estimates. Each half must hold enough sessions for performance to mean something.
  • Contiguous blocks keep serial structure. Don’t shuffle rows.
  • Similar configurations. Near-duplicates make ranks noisy among them. Consider clustering configurations first.
  • Not a significance test. PBO diagnoses the selection process. It is not a p-value for any single strategy.

8.10.7 A note on parameter searches

Searching for “the best indicator settings” is exactly the setting PBO was built for. A search that reports one best setting and hides the surface is the most common form of overfitting I see. A much more honest object is a search reported with its PBO, its DSR at the true trial count, and the shape of the performance surface around the chosen point.

8.10.8 Summary

  • CSCV evaluates every half/half split of contiguous blocks.
  • PBO is how often the in-sample winner lands below the out-of-sample median.
  • Near 0 is good; near 0.5 means selection is a coin flip; above 0.5 means fitting noise.
  • PBO judges the search; DSR judges the winner. Report both, with the true trial count.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) How many splits does CSCV make with S=8S = 8? (Answer: C(8,4) = 70.)
  2. (Apply) The winner ranks 30th of 100 out of sample. Is λ\lambda positive or negative?
  3. (Think) Why must blocks be contiguous rather than random rows?
  4. (Simulate) Repeat Figure 8.10.2 with ten different seeds. How much does PBO vary?

Further reading

  • D. Bailey, J. Borwein, M. López de Prado and Q. Zhu, “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting”, J. Computational Finance (2017).
  • D. Bailey, J. Borwein, M. López de Prado and Q. Zhu, “Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism”, Notices of the AMS (2014).
  • H. White, “A Reality Check for Data Snooping”, Econometrica (2000).

— Tariq

Chapter 8.11 — Calibration, and Logistic Lift over a Null

Subtitle: A score that ranks well but means nothing as a probability will mislead every decision you base on it.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Tell discrimination from calibration. 2. Read reliability tables and the Cox calibration slope and intercept. 3. Choose a recalibration method. 4. Measure lift over a null with an offset logistic model.

You need: logistic regression, the logit function, and the gambler’s-ruin null (Chapter 6.1).

8.11.1 Scores versus probabilities

Most trading signals produce a score. Very few produce a probability you can bet on. In my research pipeline, every scoring model passes a calibration stage that asks two questions:

  1. When the model says 60%, does the event happen about 60% of the time?
  2. Is the model better than a null that knows only the base rate?

8.11.2 Discrimination versus calibration

  • Discrimination: does the score rank positive cases above negative ones? Measured by AUC and similar.
  • Calibration: do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies?

A model can rank perfectly and be badly calibrated. Multiply every probability by 0.5 and the ranking doesn’t change. For decisions with thresholds, sizing or expected values, calibration is what matters.

8.11.3 Reliability tables

Bucket predictions into bins (deciles are common). In each bin, compare the mean predicted probability with the observed frequency. Plot one against the other: a calibrated model sits on the diagonal. Bins with few samples are noisy, so show counts and confidence intervals.

8.11.4 Cox calibration: slope and intercept

Cox (1958) suggested regressing outcomes on the logit of the predicted probability:

logit⁡P(y=1)=a+b⋅logit⁡(p̂). \operatorname{logit} P(y = 1) = a + b \cdot \operatorname{logit}(\hat p).

Result Meaning
b=1,a=0b = 1,\ a = 0 Perfectly calibrated
b<1b < 1 Predictions too extreme (over-confident): the typical result of overfitting
b>1b > 1 Predictions too timid
a≠0a \ne 0 Systematic over- or under-prediction

Two numbers summarise calibration better than any chart, and they are easy to track over time.

Figure 8.11.1 — What the slope looks like. Each curve is observed frequency =σ(b⋅logit⁡p̂)= \sigma(b \cdot \operatorname{logit}\hat p) with a=0a = 0. The blue diagonal is calibrated. The orange curve (b=0.5b = 0.5) is flatter: when the model says 0.95, the event happens far less often, so the model is over-confident. The dashed curve (b=2b = 2) is steeper: the model is too timid.

8.11.5 Recalibration methods

  • Platt scaling: fit a logistic regression on the model’s score, p̂=σ(αs+β)\hat p = \sigma(\alpha s + \beta). Two parameters; robust on small samples.
  • Isotonic regression: fit a non-decreasing step function from score to probability. More flexible; needs more data; overfits small samples.
  • Temperature scaling: for neural classifiers, divide the logits by one learned number TT.

Always fit calibration on data the model wasn’t trained on. Evaluate on yet another slice, with the same purging and embargo as anything else.

8.11.6 Logistic lift over a null

The question I care about most: does the signal add information beyond what a trivial model already knows?

Define a null model: what you’d expect without the signal. The simplest null is the base rate. A better null encodes structure that exists regardless of the signal. For a barrier-style outcome on a random walk, the chance of hitting the target first is fixed by the barrier distances alone (the gambler’s-ruin result). Any signal has to beat that, not 50%.

Then fit a logistic model on top of the null:

logit⁡P(y=1∣x)=logit⁡(pnull)+β⊤x. \operatorname{logit} P(y = 1 \mid x) = \operatorname{logit}(p_{\text{null}}) + \beta^\top x. The null enters as an offset: a term with its coefficient fixed at one.

The fitted β\beta measures lift over the null. If β≈0\beta \approx 0, the signal adds nothing. Compare the log-likelihoods of the null and the full model with a likelihood-ratio test, adjusted for clustering.

Why I like this form:

  • It makes the null explicit and unavoidable.
  • It separates “the setup is favourable by construction” from “the signal has information”.
  • If the model is well specified, its output is directly a calibrated probability.

Example. A target one unit away and a stop two units away give pnull=2/3p_{\text{null}} = 2/3 on a random walk. A model that predicts 2/3 for every trade has β=0\beta = 0: it has learned only the geometry.

8.11.7 Conditioning on fills

A subtle trap. Suppose you calibrate on signals, but only some signals become fills. Limit orders that get filled are disproportionately the ones price moves through. Then the population you trade differs from the one you calibrated on. This adverse selection shows up as a gap between the average predicted probability across signals and across fills. Calibrate on the population you actually trade, and measure that gap explicitly.

8.11.8 Pitfalls

  • Calibrating on the training set.
  • Per-cell calibration with tiny cells. Pool or regularise.
  • Treating a well-calibrated base-rate forecaster as success. It is calibrated and useless. The skill score in Chapter 8.12 exists to catch it.

8.11.9 Summary

  • Ranking well is not the same as giving true probabilities.
  • The Cox slope and intercept summarise calibration in two numbers; b<1b < 1 means over-confident.
  • Recalibrate on held-out data: Platt for small samples, isotonic for large, temperature for neural nets.
  • Put the null in as an offset; the fitted β\beta is the lift.
  • Calibrate on fills, not just signals.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A refit gives b=0.6b = 0.6, a=0a = 0. Over- or under-confident? (Answer: over-confident; predictions are too extreme.)
  2. (Apply) You have 300 labelled cases. Platt or isotonic? Why?
  3. (Calculate) With a target 1 and stop 3 on a random walk, what is pnullp_{\text{null}}?
  4. (Think) Why might signals that become limit fills have lower success rates than all signals?

Further reading

  • D. Cox, “Two Further Applications of a Model for Binary Regression”, Biometrika (1958).
  • J. Platt, “Probabilistic Outputs for Support Vector Machines” (1999).
  • A. Niculescu-Mizil and R. Caruana, “Predicting Good Probabilities with Supervised Learning”, ICML (2005).
  • B. Van Calster et al., “Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics”, BMC Medicine (2019).

— Tariq

Chapter 8.12 — Strictly Proper Scoring Rules and the Brier Skill Score

Subtitle: If your evaluation metric can be gamed by lying about your confidence, your model will learn to lie.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define proper and strictly proper scoring rules. 2. Compute the Brier score and its Murphy decomposition. 3. Compute and read the Brier skill score (BSS). 4. Test that a validation pipeline rejects a base-rate forecaster.

You need: expected value; Chapter 8.11 (calibration).

8.12.1 The metric shapes the model

When a model outputs probabilities, the metric you judge it by decides what “good” means.

  • Accuracy rewards confident guessing.
  • Profit in a backtest rewards luck.
  • Strictly proper scoring rules reward exactly one thing: reporting your true belief.

In my research pipeline, the Brier score, and its skill version against a base-rate reference, is one of the checks every probabilistic model faces.

8.12.2 Proper and strictly proper

A scoring rule S(p,y)S(p, y) scores forecast pp when outcome yy happens. Suppose your true belief is qq.

Definition. The rule is proper if your expected score is best when you report p=qp = q: 𝔼y∼q[S(q,y)]≥𝔼y∼q[S(p,y)]∀p \mathbb{E}_{y \sim q}[S(q, y)] \ \ge\ \mathbb{E}_{y \sim q}[S(p, y)] \quad \forall p (for a score where higher is better). It is strictly proper if p=qp = q is the only best report.

Under a strictly proper rule there is no gain from hedging, exaggerating or shading forecasts.

Accuracy with a 0.5 cut-off is not proper. A forecaster who believes 0.55 and one who believes 0.99 get the same credit.

8.12.3 The Brier score

For binary outcomes:
