BS=1N∑i=1N(pi−yi)2. BS = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} (p_i - y_i)^2.

Lower is better; 0 is perfect. It is strictly proper, bounded, and easy to explain.

Why it is strictly proper. If the event happens with chance qq, your expected penalty for reporting pp is q(1−p)2+(1−q)p2q(1-p)^2 + (1-q)p^2. Its derivative in pp is 2(p−q)2(p - q), which is zero only at p=qp = q. So honesty is the unique best report.

Figure 8.12.1 — Only the honest report wins. Your true belief is 0.7. The blue curve is the expected Brier penalty for each report; it bottoms out exactly at 0.7. The orange dashed line is the error rate with a 0.5 cut-off: every report above 0.5 scores the same, so it cannot tell 0.55 from 0.99.

Its main competitor, log-loss −1N∑[yiln⁡pi+(1−yi)ln⁡(1−pi)]-\frac{1}{N}\sum[y_i \ln p_i + (1-y_i)\ln(1-p_i)], is also strictly proper but punishes confident mistakes without limit. Log-loss is the right training objective for many models. Brier is often the better reporting metric, because one catastrophic forecast doesn’t dominate it.

8.12.4 Murphy’s decomposition

Murphy (1973) split the Brier score into three parts. Group forecasts into bins kk with nkn_k cases, mean forecast p‾k\bar p_k and observed frequency o‾k\bar o_k. Let o‾\bar o be the overall base rate:

BS=1N∑knk(p‾k−o‾k)2⏟reliability−1N∑knk(o‾k−o‾)2⏟resolution+o‾(1−o‾)⏟uncertainty. BS = \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_k n_k(\bar p_k - \bar o_k)^2}_{\text{reliability}} - \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_k n_k(\bar o_k - \bar o)^2}_{\text{resolution}} + \underbrace{\bar o(1 - \bar o)}_{\text{uncertainty}}.

Part Better when Meaning
Reliability Lower Calibration error
Resolution Higher How well forecasts separate cases with different outcomes
Uncertainty (fixed) A property of the data, not the model

8.12.5 The Brier skill score

A raw Brier score is hard to judge: it depends on the base rate. The skill score compares against a reference forecast:

BSS=1−BSmodelBSref. BSS = 1 - \frac{BS_{\text{model}}}{BS_{\text{ref}}}.

With the climatological (base-rate) reference, BSref=o‾(1−o‾)BS_{\text{ref}} = \bar o(1-\bar o).

Figure 8.12.2 — Reading the skill score. Zero means no better than always forecasting the base rate. Negative means worse than that; there is no lower limit. Positive means real skill, up to 1 for a perfect forecaster.

Two refinements I use:

  • Conditional reference. If base rates differ by context, the fair reference is the context-conditional base rate. Otherwise a model gets credit just for knowing which context it is in.
  • The invariant test. A forecaster that only outputs the base rate should score BSS≈0BSS \approx 0 and fail validation. I test that explicitly. If the pipeline would pass a base-rate forecaster, the pipeline is broken.

8.12.6 Practical notes

  • Report BSS across CV paths, not from one split. The median across paths is more honest than any single one.
  • Small samples are noisy. Bootstrap BSS at the session level to get an interval.
  • Rare events. When positives are rare, both Brier and BSS can be dominated by many easy negatives. Look at the decomposition and the reliability table, not just the headline.
  • Proper doesn’t mean useful. A forecast can score well and still not be actionable after costs. Scoring rules judge probabilities. Profitability needs its own separate, honest evaluation.

8.12.7 Summary

  • Strictly proper rules make honest reporting the unique best strategy; accuracy does not.
  • Brier is bounded and strictly proper; log-loss is too, but unbounded.
  • Murphy’s decomposition separates calibration error, resolution and data uncertainty.
  • BSS > 0 means skill over the base rate; a base-rate forecaster must fail.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Base rate 0.3. What is BSrefBS_{\text{ref}}? (Answer: 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.21.)
  2. (Calculate) A model has BS=0.18BS = 0.18 against that reference. Find BSS.
  3. (Prove) Show that the expected Brier penalty is minimised at p=qp = q.
  4. (Think) Why would a context-blind reference flatter a model that only knows the time of day?

Further reading

  • G. Brier, “Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability”, Monthly Weather Review (1950).
  • A. Murphy, “A New Vector Partition of the Probability Score”, J. Applied Meteorology (1973).
  • T. Gneiting and A. Raftery, “Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation”, JASA (2007).
  • D. Wilks, Statistical Methods in the Atmospheric Sciences (Academic Press), chapter on forecast verification.

— Tariq

Chapter 8.13 — Deploying Models Inside C#/.NET Instead of Python Sidecars

Subtitle: Train in Python if you like. But if your execution engine is .NET, the model should live there too.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. List the costs of a Python sidecar in a latency-sensitive decision path. 2. Compare four ways to run a trained model inside .NET. 3. Build a bit-for-bit parity test and name the usual causes of mismatch. 4. State the governance a model needs before it may load.

You need: what a decision tree ensemble is (Chapter 8.4); basic idea of floating-point numbers.

8.13.1 The decision

My execution stack is C#. In 2026 I decided that no execution, sizing or decision logic would live in a Python process beside it. I then reviewed how a small learned model, if one ever earned its place, should be served.

The conclusion: train offline wherever is convenient, then evaluate the model deterministically inside .NET. No Python at run time.

8.13.2 Why not a Python sidecar?

A sidecar is a separate service next to the main application, called over HTTP or a socket. It is convenient. In a latency-sensitive decision path it has real costs:

  • Another failure domain. The sidecar can crash, hang or start slowly. Every decision now depends on two processes and the link between them.
  • Latency and jitter. Serialisation, a network hop and Python’s garbage collector add milliseconds of unpredictable delay.
  • Drift between research and live. If research runs in one language and live in another, the two implementations drift apart. Feature computation is the usual culprit: a rolling window computed slightly differently in each.
  • Deployment friction. Two runtimes, two dependency trees, two sets of updates.

The principle: one engine, one implementation of every number that affects a decision, used by research replay and live alike.

Figure 8.13.1 — Two processes or one. In A, every decision crosses a serialisation step and a network hop to a second runtime (orange). In B, the evaluator lives inside the engine (green): one runtime, one implementation, the same answer in replay and live. A concept sketch only.

8.13.3 The options in .NET

For tree ensembles and small neural networks there are four realistic routes:

Route How it works Strengths Costs
ONNX Runtime Export to ONNX; run with the official .NET package Well supported, fast; tree ensembles via the ML operator set (recent versions add double-precision thresholds and explicit missing-value routing) and neural nets Large native package; a second numeric implementation whose float/double behaviour you must audit
ML.NET Microsoft’s ML library Excellent for models trained in .NET Importing models from Python’s ecosystem is not its sweet spot
Generated code Tools like m2cgen turn a model into source code (C# is a target); trees become nested if statements No runtime dependency at all Large generated files; regenerate on every retrain
Small managed evaluator Load the model’s own JSON or text dump (XGBoost and LightGBM both export one) and walk the trees in a few dozen lines of C# Simple, dependency-free, fully auditable for shallow ensembles You own the code

For small tree ensembles I’d choose the managed evaluator or generated code. Compile it into a library that targets a framework compatible with every host that needs it. ONNX Runtime becomes attractive as models grow or include neural parts.

8.13.4 Bit-for-bit parity

Whatever the route, the critical test is parity with the training environment:

  1. Export a golden set: inputs and the training library’s predictions, stored at full precision.
  2. Evaluate the same inputs in .NET.
  3. Require agreement within a tight tolerance, and investigate any disagreement.

Common causes of mismatch:

  • Float versus double. Training libraries often store thresholds as 32-bit floats. Comparing a 64-bit double feature against a float threshold that was rounded differently flips splits at the boundary.
  • Comparison operators. < versus <= at the split; it varies by library.
  • Missing values. Each library has its own default direction for NaN.
  • Base score and link function. Forgetting the initial score, or the sigmoid at the end.

Figure 8.13.2 — Parity gates every build. A golden set from training is run through the .NET evaluator. If the two agree within tolerance, the versioned artefact may load (green). If not, the build fails and you look at the usual suspects (orange).

Run the parity check on every build, as a test. A model that passes parity once and then silently drifts after a library upgrade is worse than no model.

8.13.5 Determinism and performance

A tree evaluator is a sequence of comparisons: no allocation, no randomness, microseconds per prediction. Keep it allocation-free in the hot path: preallocated feature arrays, no LINQ. It will never be the bottleneck. Determinism also means a research replay and the live engine give identical predictions for identical inputs, which is the whole point.

8.13.6 Governance

A model that enters a decision path must arrive as a versioned artefact with:

  • a hash;
  • a record of the training data and code;
  • its validation results;
  • its parity test.

If any of these is missing, it doesn’t load. That is the same receipts discipline I apply to any research result.

8.13.7 Summary

  • A Python sidecar adds a failure domain, jitter, research/live drift and deployment friction.
  • For small tree ensembles, a managed evaluator or generated code is simplest; ONNX Runtime suits larger or neural models.
  • A golden-set parity test on every build catches float/double, operator, NaN and base-score mismatches.
  • Keep the evaluator allocation-free and deterministic.
  • No hash, data record, validation and parity test: no load.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Name two causes of parity failure. (Answer: any two of float vs double thresholds, < vs <=, NaN direction, base score/link.)
  2. (Apply) A feature equals a split threshold exactly. Which two library details decide the branch?
  3. (Think) Why is a model that drifts after a library upgrade worse than no model?
  4. (Design) Sketch the fields of a model artefact manifest that meets the governance rule.

Further reading

  • ONNX Runtime documentation, Get started with C#.
  • ONNX operator documentation, ai.onnx.ml.TreeEnsemble.
  • m2cgen project documentation (model-to-code generation).
  • D. Sculley et al., “Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems” (2015).

— Tariq

Chapter 9.2 — Running Next.js Server-Side Rendering on AWS Lambda

Subtitle: A standalone build, a tiny adapter, and the cold-start maths nobody puts on the landing page.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compare three ways to run Next.js on Lambda. 2. Explain what the standalone output and a small adapter do. 3. Estimate the share of cold starts from traffic and idle time. 4. Avoid the common traps: binary bodies, cookies, timeouts, build-time variables.

You need: what a web server, an HTTP request and AWS Lambda are; the exponential function.

9.2.1 Why serverless

My public site is a Next.js app. It renders a daily market report, a dashboard, an education centre and an admin area. I didn’t want to run a server for it. I’m one person, and every box I keep alive is a box I must patch at midnight. So the whole thing runs on AWS Lambda behind API Gateway, server-side rendering (SSR) included.

It works well. It also took longer than any tutorial suggested.

9.2.2 The shape of the problem

Next.js expects to be a long-running Node process: boot, warm its route cache, then answer requests for hours. Lambda is the opposite. An execution environment appears, handles requests one at a time, and may vanish whenever AWS decides.

Three common ways to bridge the gap:

Approach What it is
Managed adapter (OpenNext and friends) Splits the app into several functions, a static bucket and an image optimiser
Container image + Lambda Web Adapter Runs the Node server in a container
Standalone output + small handler Starts the bundled server inside Lambda and proxies each event to it over loopback (the machine talking to itself)

I chose the third. It’s the least clever, and that’s why.

9.2.3 Standalone output

Setting output: 'standalone' in the Next config makes the build trace every file the server really needs and copy it into .next/standalone. That includes a pruned node_modules and a server.js entry point.

It is the single most useful flag for serverless Next.js. A raw node_modules folder blows straight through Lambda’s unzipped package limit (250 MB).

My build step copies the standalone folder, adds public/, drops in my handler as the entry point, zips it, and prints the unzipped size. That way I see a creeping dependency before AWS rejects the deploy.

9.2.4 The adapter

The handler does two jobs.

  1. First call in an environment: it requires the standalone server.js, which starts Next listening on a loopback port. It then polls a cheap route until it answers. A flag in module scope records that the server is up, so later calls skip straight to work.
  2. Every call: it turns the API Gateway event into an HTTP request to the loopback server, collects the response, and turns it back into the shape API Gateway expects: status, headers, and a body that is base64-encoded when it is binary.

Figure 9.2.1 — One request through the adapter. The browser’s request reaches API Gateway as an event. Inside the Lambda environment, the handler converts it into an ordinary HTTP call to the bundled Next server over loopback. The response travels back the same way, with cookies and binary bodies handled carefully.

Two details bite people:

  • Binary responses. Images, fonts and PDFs must be base64-encoded and flagged as such, and API Gateway must be told which media types are binary. Get this wrong and your favicon arrives as garbled text.
  • Multi-value headers. Set-Cookie can appear more than once. Collapse it into one header and auth breaks in a way that looks like a Cognito problem.

9.2.5 Cold starts, quantified

A cold start costs: download and unzip the package, start the Node runtime, run module-scope code, and boot the Next server. Call the total CC. A warm request costs WW. If a fraction pp of requests are cold:

𝔼[L]=pC+(1−p)W. \mathbb{E}[L] = p\,C + (1-p)\,W.

For a low-traffic site, pp is not small.

Result (cold share). If requests arrive as a Poisson process (independent random arrivals) at rate λ\lambda, and an idle environment is reclaimed after about τ\tau seconds, the chance the next request finds no warm environment is about p≈e−λτ. p \approx e^{-\lambda \tau}.

Why. The next request is cold if no request arrived in the last τ\tau seconds. For Poisson arrivals, the chance of zero arrivals in time τ\tau is e−λτe^{-\lambda\tau}.

Figure 9.2.2 — Low traffic means many cold starts. The curve is e−λτe^{-\lambda\tau}. Where λτ\lambda\tau is near one, about a third of requests are cold. The share falls fast only once traffic is several times higher. Formula only; no measured data.

The lesson is in the exponent: change your traffic and the cold-start share does not change in proportion; it compounds through the exponential. A personal or niche site lives where λτ\lambda\tau is near one and pp is depressingly large. That is why I care more about shrinking CC than about micro-optimising WW.

What actually shrinks CC:

  • Package size. Fewer bytes to fetch and unzip. Standalone tracing helps; auditing heavy server-only dependencies helps more.
  • Memory setting. Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory. A bigger setting often boots faster and costs about the same, because you pay for GB-seconds.
  • Lazy imports. Don’t import an SDK client at module scope in a route that rarely needs it.

Provisioned concurrency removes cold starts for a fee. For a hobby-scale site I’d rather pay in milliseconds than dollars.

9.2.6 Cost model

Lambda billing is roughly

cost≈N⋅(creq+cGBs⋅M⋅d‾), \text{cost} \approx N \cdot \big(c_{\text{req}} + c_{\text{GBs}} \cdot M \cdot \bar d\big),

where NN is invocations, creqc_{\text{req}} the price per request, cGBsc_{\text{GBs}} the price per GB-second, MM memory in GB and d‾\bar d mean duration in seconds. CPU scales with MM, so d‾\bar d usually falls as MM rises. The product Md‾M\bar d is flatter than intuition says. Measure two or three memory settings before assuming the cheapest one is cheapest.

9.2.7 What the textbooks skip

  • Static assets don’t belong in the function. Every image served through Lambda is a paid invocation. Put static output in S3 behind a CDN; let the function handle only dynamic routes.
  • ISR and on-disk caches assume a persistent disk. Lambda’s /tmp is per-environment and temporary. Incremental regeneration “works”, but every environment has its own cache, so two readers can see different versions. For a daily report I prefer explicit data fetches with sane HTTP cache headers.
  • Timeouts stack. API Gateway has its own integration timeout, separate from Lambda’s. A slow SSR page can be killed by the gateway while the function keeps running and billing.
  • Environment variables are build-time and run-time. NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are baked into the client bundle at build. Change them in the Lambda console and nothing happens until you rebuild. I lost an afternoon to that.

9.2.8 Would I do it again?

Yes, for this kind of site: mostly read-heavy, bursty, one maintainer. With steady traffic and a team, I’d run a container on a managed service and stop thinking about cold starts. The right answer depends on λτ\lambda\tau, not on fashion.

9.2.9 Summary

  • Standalone output plus a small loopback adapter is the simplest way to run Next.js SSR on Lambda.
  • Handle binary bodies and repeated Set-Cookie headers explicitly.
  • The cold share is about e−λτe^{-\lambda\tau}, so low-traffic sites see many cold starts; shrink CC.
  • Serve static files from S3 and a CDN; watch stacked timeouts and build-time variables.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) With λτ=2\lambda\tau = 2, what share of requests is cold? (Answer: e−2≈0.14e^{-2} \approx 0.14.)
  2. (Calculate) C=2C = 2 s, W=0.1W = 0.1 s, p=0.37p = 0.37. Find the mean latency.
  3. (Apply) Login works locally but fails on Lambda after the first cookie. What do you check first?
  4. (Think) Why can a larger memory setting cost about the same or less?

Further reading

  • Next.js documentation, “Output: standalone”.
  • AWS Lambda Developer Guide, “Lambda execution environment lifecycle”.
  • AWS Lambda Web Adapter project documentation.

— Tariq

Chapter 9.3 — SAM and CloudFormation for a Team of One

Subtitle: Infrastructure as code isn’t for big teams. It’s for the person who will forget everything by next month.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain what the SAM transform does to a CloudFormation template. 2. Say why a declared state beats a history of console clicks. 3. Apply five practical template patterns. 4. Plan stacks by blast radius and handle drift honestly.

You need: basic AWS resources (functions, buckets, tables, roles).

9.3.1 The console trap

When you are the only engineer, the console is tempting. Click, create, done. The trouble comes three months later. Something breaks, and you have no idea which of the forty things you clicked matters.

So I keep the core of my AWS footprint in a CloudFormation template written with the AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM) transform. It isn’t every resource I own; I’ll be honest about that below. But it’s enough to reason about the system from a file instead of from memory.

9.3.2 What SAM actually is

SAM is a CloudFormation macro. You write AWS::Serverless::Function, and the transform expands it into the underlying Lambda function, IAM role, permissions and event-source mappings. At deploy time CloudFormation sees only plain resources.

That matters because every SAM problem is really a CloudFormation problem. When a deploy fails, read the expanded template (sam validate, or the processed template in the console), not the short one you wrote.

My template is small on purpose:

  • one serverless function for the web app;
  • a REST API with a proxy resource and a deployment;
  • an execution role;
  • the permission that lets API Gateway call the function;
  • a handful of CloudWatch alarms.

That’s it.

9.3.3 Why a template beats memory

Think of your infrastructure as a state SS. A console click applies an unrecorded change S→S′S \to S'. After nn clicks:

Sn=fn∘fn−1∘…∘f1(S0), S_n = f_n \circ f_{n-1} \circ \dots \circ f_1(S_0),

and you have lost every fif_i. A template replaces that chain with a declaration: “the state should be S*S^*”. CloudFormation works out the difference and applies it. You can read S*S^*, diff it in git, and rebuild it in a new account.

Figure 9.3.1 — Steps versus a target. Top: each click moves the system to a new state, but the changes themselves are not written down. Bottom: the template states the target, and CloudFormation computes how to reach it. Only the bottom can be read, reviewed and replayed.

For a solo builder the real benefit isn’t scale. The template is documentation that can’t go stale, because it is the system.

9.3.4 Practical patterns that helped

Pattern Why
Parameters for anything environment-specific (bucket, domain and stage names) Never hard-coded; the same template renders a test stack
Outputs for anything another tool needs (API URL, function name) Scripts read stack outputs instead of copy-pasted identifiers
Least-privilege roles written by hand Forces the question “does this function really need to delete objects?” Usually it doesn’t.
Alarms next to what they watch Deleting the function deletes its alarm; no orphan alarms paging about ghosts
Change sets before deploys Shows what will be replaced. Replace on a stateful resource means data loss. I read every change set that touches state.

9.3.5 The honest part: drift

Not all my infrastructure is in that template. Scheduled rules, some CodeBuild projects, the data tables and a few buckets were made by scripts or by hand during fast iteration. That is real technical debt, and I’d rather name it than pretend.

CloudFormation has drift detection: it compares live resources with the template, for the resources it manages. It can’t tell you about resources it never knew about. For those I keep a plain operations reference and a script that lists what exists. Not elegant; better than nothing.

If I started again, I’d split stacks by blast radius:

blast radius(stack)=∑r∈stackcost of losing r. \text{blast radius}(\text{stack}) = \sum_{r \in \text{stack}} \text{cost of losing } r. Keep the expensive terms out of the stack you deploy most often.

Figure 9.3.2 — Separate what is costly to lose. Stateful resources (tables, buckets) go in a rarely deployed stack with DeletionPolicy: Retain. Stateless compute goes in a stack you can tear down freely. A bad deploy of the busy stack then cannot destroy data.

9.3.6 Pitfalls

  • Logical ID changes cause replacement. Renaming a resource in the template deletes the old one and creates a new one. For a function, fine. For a table, catastrophic.
  • Circular dependencies via permissions. A function references an API that references the function. Break the loop with an explicit AWS::Lambda::Permission.
  • Stuck rollbacks. A failed rollback leaves UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. Know the “continue update rollback” escape hatch before you need it.
  • Deployments don’t redeploy themselves. An API Gateway deployment is immutable. If its logical ID doesn’t change, new methods may not go live. SAM handles this for implicit APIs; explicit ones need care.

9.3.7 Should a solo developer bother?

Yes, but start small. Put the thing you deploy most often in a template first. Add the rest when it hurts. The goal isn’t purity. It is that future-you can answer “what’s running and why” without archaeology.

9.3.8 Summary

  • SAM expands into plain CloudFormation; debug the expanded template.
  • A declared target state beats an unrecorded chain of clicks.
  • Use parameters, outputs, hand-written roles, co-located alarms and change sets.
  • Split stacks by blast radius and protect stateful resources.
  • Name the drift you have; drift detection only sees what the stack manages.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) You rename a DynamoDB table’s logical ID. What happens on deploy? (Answer: CloudFormation replaces it: a new table, the old one deleted, unless retained.)
  2. (Apply) Which of your resources would you put in a “retain” stack, and why?
  3. (Think) Why can’t drift detection find a bucket you created by hand?
  4. (Design) Write the Outputs you’d want so a deploy script never needs a copy-pasted ID.

Further reading

  • AWS SAM Developer Guide, “AWS SAM template anatomy”.
  • AWS CloudFormation User Guide, “Detecting unmanaged configuration changes (drift)”.
  • K. Morris, Infrastructure as Code (O’Reilly).

— Tariq

Chapter 9.4 — CodeBuild as a General-Purpose Job Runner

Subtitle: Most people use it to compile code. I use it to run the whole daily pipeline, and it’s been a good fit.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Say when CodeBuild beats Lambda for batch jobs. 2. Treat buildspec phases as a contract. 3. Compute end-to-end pipeline reliability and the effect of recovery. 4. Implement retries with full jitter, and handle secrets safely.

You need: basic shell scripting; probability of independent events.

9.4.1 More than CI

AWS CodeBuild is sold as a CI service: check out a repo, build, publish an artifact. That’s how I use it for the website. But most of my CodeBuild projects don’t build software. They fetch market data, draft a report, generate charts and audio, run a post-market review, or diagnose and repair the pipeline itself.

9.4.2 Why not Lambda for everything?

Lambda is great for short, bounded work. A daily report job is not that. It pulls data from several sources, runs Python analysis with heavy scientific libraries, calls a language model, renders charts and synthesises audio. The limits collide:

  • Duration. Lambda caps at 15 minutes. A slow upstream API can push a job past that.
  • Package size. Scientific Python, plotting libraries and SDKs crowd the limit fast.
  • Debuggability. A CodeBuild run has a full log stream per phase and a clear pass/fail state.

CodeBuild gives a fresh container per run, a generous timeout, and phases. You pay per build-minute; for a handful of runs a day, the cost is small.

9.4.3 Anatomy of a buildspec

Every buildspec has the same skeleton: install, pre_build, build, post_build. I treat them as a contract.

Figure 9.4.1 — Each phase has one job. Install only installs. Pre-build only validates, and is where a job should fail fast (orange arrow). Build does the work. Post-build publishes, archives, notifies, and checks the build really produced what it claims.

  • install: pin runtimes and install dependencies. Nothing else.
  • pre_build: validate. Are the credentials there? Is the upstream data reachable? Does the destination exist? Fail here, loudly, before expensive work.
  • build: the actual job.
  • post_build: publish, archive, notify, and verify the output.

The pre-build validation phase turned out to be the most valuable thing I added. A job that fails at minute one with “the source returned nothing” is far better than one that fails at minute twelve with a confusing stack trace, or worse, succeeds with an empty report.

I keep one buildspec per job (buildspec.publish.yml-style naming, one per pipeline stage), not one giant file with conditionals. Each file is boring and readable.

9.4.4 Reliability, roughly

Result. If a pipeline has kk independent stages, each succeeding with probability qiq_i, end-to-end success is Psuccess=∏i=1kqi. P_{\text{success}} = \prod_{i=1}^{k} q_i.

Five stages at 99% each gives about 95%: roughly one failed day in twenty. That’s a lot for something that should run every trading day. Two levers:

  1. Raise each qiq_i with validation and retries on transient failures.
  2. Add recovery. A second attempt that fixes a failure with probability rr lifts each stage to qi+(1−qi)rq_i + (1-q_i)\,r.

Figure 9.4.2 — Reliability multiplies. The orange line is 0.99k0.99^k: each extra stage shaves off about a percent. The green dashed line adds one recovery attempt that fixes half of failures, which lifts each stage to 0.995. Formula only.

The second lever is why I built a self-healing layer on top (Chapter 9.5).

9.4.5 Retries with backoff

Upstream APIs fail transiently. I retry with exponential backoff and jitter:

tn=min⁡(tmax,t0⋅2n)⋅U,U∼Uniform(0,1). t_n = \min\!\big(t_{\max},\; t_0 \cdot 2^{n}\big)\cdot U, \qquad U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1).

The wait doubles each try, up to a cap tmaxt_{\max}, then is multiplied by a random factor UU. This “full jitter” matters more than people think. Without it, every client that failed together retries together, and you hammer the API in synchronised waves.

What I don’t retry: authentication failures and validation errors. Retrying a bad token five times just delays the alert.

9.4.6 Secrets

Credentials come from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, referenced in the buildspec’s env section, never written in the file. CodeBuild injects them at runtime and masks them in logs.

A pitfall: masking is string-based. If your code prints a transformed version of a secret (say, URL-encoded), it won’t be masked. Don’t print secrets, even partially.

9.4.7 Pitfalls I hit

  • Runtime version drift. Managed images update. A job that worked yesterday can fail because the default Node or Python moved. Pin explicitly in install.
  • set -e semantics. Each command line in a phase runs separately, and a failure fails the phase. But in cmd | tee log the exit code is tee’s, not cmd’s. Use set -o pipefail inside multi-command lines.
  • Silent success. A script that catches every exception and exits zero marks the build green. Exit non-zero on real failure. Always.
  • Artifact naming collisions. Two runs writing the same S3 key race. I write a timestamped copy and a “latest” pointer.

9.4.8 The website build

The site pipeline is the one conventional CI job: install, npm ci, next build, assemble the standalone server plus handler into a zip, print the unzipped size, upload to S3, update the function code. Printing the unzipped size on every build is a cheap early warning that a dependency has grown.

9.4.9 Summary

  • CodeBuild fits batch jobs too long or heavy for Lambda but too small for a cluster.
  • Phases are a contract: install, validate, build, publish-and-verify.
  • Reliability multiplies across stages; validation, retries and recovery fight that.
  • Use full jitter; don’t retry auth or validation errors.
  • Never print secrets; pin runtimes; use pipefail; fail honestly.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Eight stages at 98% each. End-to-end success? (Answer: 0.988≈0.850.98^8 \approx 0.85.)
  2. (Calculate) A stage has q=0.97q = 0.97 and a retry fixes 60% of failures. New stage success?
  3. (Apply) Your build log shows the job “succeeded” but the report is empty. Name two checks that would have caught it.
  4. (Think) Why does jitter reduce load on a recovering API?

Further reading

  • AWS CodeBuild User Guide, “Build specification reference”.
  • M. Brooker, “Exponential Backoff And Jitter”, AWS Architecture Blog.
  • B. Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (O’Reilly), chapter on handling overload.

— Tariq

Chapter 9.5 — A Self-Healing Daily Pipeline on AWS

Subtitle: The worst failure isn’t a red build. It’s the report that quietly didn’t appear and nobody noticed for a week.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Detect absence with an outcome check. 2. Describe a four-layer monitoring and repair design. 3. State the rules that keep an automatic repair path safe. 4. Model how a repair rate changes expected downtime.

You need: Chapter 9.4; expected value.

9.5.1 Silent failure

My daily market report is made by a chain of jobs on AWS: fetch data, analyse, draft, render, publish. In the early weeks, when it failed, it failed silently. A schedule didn’t fire, a permission changed, a job never started. There was no red build because there was no build. I found out days later.

In July I built a layered monitoring and repair system around it. The pattern is useful well beyond trading.

9.5.2 Detecting absence

Most monitoring watches for errors. The hard case is absence: nothing happened, so nothing errored. The fix is to stop asking “did something fail?” and ask “does the thing that should exist, exist?”

So the core check is an outcome check. On a schedule after the report should be published, a small Lambda looks for the report in its expected place with today’s date. If it is there and valid, all is well, whatever happened on the way. If not, something is wrong, whether or not any job reported an error.

Principle (dead man’s switch). Assume failure unless you see positive proof of success.

9.5.3 Four layers

  1. Pre-build validation. Each job checks inputs and permissions before working, and fails fast with a clear message.
  2. Infrastructure alerts. Build failures publish to a notification topic.
  3. Scheduled health check. The outcome check, run independently of the pipeline.
  4. Auto-diagnose and repair. When the health check finds the report missing, it starts a separate diagnostic job.

The diagnostic job walks the common causes in order:

  • Is the schedule rule enabled and pointed at the right target?
  • Does the role still have the permissions it needs?
  • Is the destination reachable?
  • Did the last build start, and if so, how did it end?

For a known class of problems (a disabled rule, a missing target) it applies the fix, re-triggers the report, and sends an alert saying what it found and did. For anything else it sends an alert listing what it checked and what needs a human.

Figure 9.5.1 — Check the outcome, then repair or escalate. The pipeline (left) can fail loudly through the alert topic. Independently, a scheduled check looks for the finished report. If it is missing or invalid, a diagnostic job either fixes a known fault and reports it (green) or hands over to a human (orange). A concept sketch.

9.5.4 Why the repair path must be boring

A self-healing system is a program with permission to change production. That deserves suspicion. My rules:

  • Fix only known, enumerated faults. No “try things until it works”.
  • Idempotent actions. Doing it twice equals doing it once. Enabling an enabled rule is a no-op; re-running a report overwrites cleanly.
  • Always report. Every repair sends an alert saying what changed. Silent repair hides the underlying fault, and it will come back.
  • Bounded attempts. One repair attempt, then hand off to a human.

9.5.5 How much does it help?

Model daily failure as probability ff. Without detection, a failure is found after a delay DD that can stretch to days, so each failure costs about DD missing-report days.

With a daily outcome check, detection delay drops below a day. With auto-repair that succeeds with probability rr:

𝔼[missing]≈(1−r)⋅dhuman+r⋅ϵ, \mathbb{E}[\text{missing}] \approx (1-r)\cdot d_{\text{human}} + r \cdot \epsilon, where dhumand_{\text{human}} is how long I take to respond and ϵ\epsilon is the small repair delay.

The point isn’t the exact numbers. The two terms are weighted by 1−r1-r and rr, so even a modest repair rate moves most of the weight onto the tiny term.

Figure 9.5.2 — Repair rate shifts the weight. The line is the formula with an illustrative dhuman=3d_{\text{human}} = 3 days and ϵ=0.1\epsilon = 0.1 day. Every step up in repair rate trades slow human days for a short automatic delay. Illustrative numbers, not measurements.

9.5.6 Pitfalls

  • The monitor can fail too. If the health-check Lambda’s own schedule breaks, you are back to silence. I have a separate heartbeat for the monitors (Chapter 9.11).
  • Repairs can mask real changes. If I disable a rule on purpose, say for a holiday, the repair job will happily re-enable it. Make intent explicit: a market-calendar check decides whether a report is expected at all (Chapter 9.6).
  • Check content, not existence. An empty file exists. A report full of NaN exists. The outcome check validates shape and key fields, not just presence.
  • Alert fatigue. If every repair pages you, you will start ignoring pages. Successful repairs go to a lower-priority channel; failed repairs go to the loud one.

9.5.7 Summary

  • Monitor outcomes, not just processes: assume failure until you see proof of success.
  • Layer validation, failure alerts, an independent outcome check, and a bounded repair job.
  • Repairs fix only known faults, are idempotent, always report, and try once.
  • Even a modest repair rate cuts expected missing days a lot.
  • Process monitoring says which step broke; outcome monitoring says users are affected. If you build only one, build the outcome check.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) dhuman=2d_{\text{human}} = 2 days, ϵ=0.1\epsilon = 0.1, r=0.5r = 0.5. Expected missing days per failure? (Answer: 0.5·2 + 0.5·0.1 = 1.05.)
  2. (Apply) The report file exists but every number is null. Which layer should catch it?
  3. (Think) Why must the repair job be idempotent?
  4. (Design) How would you stop the repair job from “fixing” a deliberately disabled holiday schedule?

Further reading

  • B. Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (O’Reilly), “Monitoring Distributed Systems”.
  • M. Nygard, Release It! (Pragmatic Bookshelf), on stability patterns.
  • AWS Well-Architected Framework, Reliability Pillar.

— Tariq

Chapter 9.6 — Scheduling with EventBridge: Cron, Time Zones and Market Calendars

Subtitle: “Run at 9 every weekday” sounds simple until daylight saving time, holidays and half-days arrive.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Choose between EventBridge scheduled rules and EventBridge Scheduler. 2. Explain why a fixed UTC time drifts in local time, and fix it. 3. Handle holidays, at-least-once delivery and failed invocations.

You need: what UTC and daylight saving time are; basic cron syntax.

9.6.1 Two clocks

Almost everything in my AWS setup runs on a schedule: a pre-market job, a post-market job, a weekly calendar refresh, health checks, heartbeat monitors. For most of the year that’s Amazon EventBridge doing what it does well: firing a target at a time.

The hard part isn’t EventBridge. It’s time itself. Markets run on New York time, observe holidays, and sometimes close early. Cloud schedulers run on UTC unless told otherwise. This chapter is about the gap between those two clocks.

9.6.2 Two schedulers in one service

Scheduled rules EventBridge Scheduler
Where Default event bus A newer, separate service
Expressions Cron or rate Cron, rate, one-off
Time zone UTC only Any, explicit
Extras — Flexible time windows; built-in retries with a dead-letter queue

Older tutorials (and some of my earliest schedules) use rules. If you are starting fresh, use Scheduler with an explicit time zone. Most of the pain below disappears.

9.6.3 The daylight saving trap

New York is UTC−5 in winter and UTC−4 in summer. A rule written as “13:00 UTC” means one local time in January and another in July. For a job that must run before the cash open, being an hour late twice a year is a real failure.

With UTC-only rules you have three options:

  1. Two rules, one per daylight-saving regime, flipped twice a year. Fragile; I’ve forgotten.
  2. Run hourly and gate in code. The job wakes, converts now to local time, and exits unless it is the right local hour. Robust but wasteful, and it spreads logic across two places.
  3. A time-zone-aware scheduler. Correct by construction.

The difference, formally. Let tUTCt_{\text{UTC}} be the fire time and o(t)o(t) the local offset at that instant. Then tlocal=tUTC+o(t). t_{\text{local}} = t_{\text{UTC}} + o(t). A fixed tUTCt_{\text{UTC}} gives a tlocalt_{\text{local}} that jumps whenever oo changes. A time-zone-aware scheduler fixes tlocalt_{\text{local}} and solves for tUTCt_{\text{UTC}} each day.

Figure 9.6.1 — A fixed UTC time moves in local time. The orange line is a rule at 13:00 UTC seen from New York: 08:00 in winter, 09:00 in summer, with jumps at each clock change. The green dashed line is a time-zone-aware schedule, which stays at the same local time all year. Schematic dates.

That is the whole difference, and it is worth migrating for.

9.6.4 Cron syntax gotchas

  • AWS cron has six fields (minutes, hours, day-of-month, month, day-of-week, year), not five.
  • One of day-of-month or day-of-week must be ?.
  • Day-of-week numbering starts with Sunday as 1, unlike Unix cron, where Sunday is 0.

MON-FRI is clearer than numbers, so I always use names.

9.6.5 Holidays and half-days

No cloud scheduler knows the exchange calendar. A job set for weekdays will happily run on Thanksgiving and produce a report about a closed market.

I handle this in the job, not the schedule. The first thing a market job does is ask: “is today a trading session, and what are its hours?”, against a maintained calendar. If not, it exits cleanly and records that it skipped on purpose.

That record matters for monitoring. The health check must tell “skipped because holiday” from “didn’t run”. Otherwise the self-healing layer (Chapter 9.5) will try to repair a holiday.

9.6.6 Delivery semantics

EventBridge delivers at least once. Rarely, a target fires twice. So every scheduled job must be idempotent: running it twice for the same date gives the same result, not two reports or two alerts.

The simplest pattern: key everything on the logical date the job is for, not the wall-clock time it ran. “Write the report for 2026-08-14” is idempotent. “Append today’s report” is not.

9.6.7 Retries and dead letters

If a target call fails (throttling, a permission error), EventBridge retries with backoff for a configurable window and number of attempts. Then it drops the event, or sends it to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) if you set one up. Set one up. A dropped scheduled event is exactly the silent failure of Chapter 9.5.

Result. With nn independent attempts, each failing with probability ff, the event is lost with probability fnf^n.

That is tiny for transient faults and exactly 1 for a permanent one, such as a deleted target. Retries fix the first; only a dead-letter queue and an alarm catch the second.

9.6.8 Permissions

A rule needs permission to invoke its target. For Lambda that is a resource-based policy on the function. For CodeBuild it is an IAM role the rule assumes.

The most common “my schedule didn’t fire” bug I’ve seen is a rule that fires fine but can’t invoke the target. It shows up only as a failed-invocation metric. Alarm on FailedInvocations.

9.6.9 What I’d do differently

Start with EventBridge Scheduler and explicit time zones. Keep the market-calendar logic in one shared function every job calls. Make every job idempotent on the logical date. Alarm on failed invocations and on outcomes. Nothing fancy, and most of my early schedule bugs would never have happened.

9.6.10 Summary

  • Scheduled rules are UTC-only; Scheduler supports explicit time zones. Prefer Scheduler.
  • A fixed UTC time jumps in local time at each daylight-saving change.
  • Check the market calendar inside the job, and record deliberate skips.
  • Delivery is at least once: key work on the logical date.
  • Retries fix transient faults; a DLQ and a FailedInvocations alarm catch permanent ones.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A rule fires at 14:00 UTC. What New York time is that in July? In January? (Answer: 10:00 and 09:00.)
  2. (Calculate) Each attempt fails with probability 0.1. How likely is loss after 3 attempts?
  3. (Apply) Rewrite “append today’s alert to the log” so a duplicate delivery is harmless.
  4. (Think) Why must a deliberate holiday skip be recorded, not just silently exit?

Further reading

  • Amazon EventBridge Scheduler User Guide, “Schedule types”.
  • Amazon EventBridge User Guide, “Cron expressions reference”.
  • CME Group, trading hours and holiday calendar pages.

— Tariq

Chapter 9.7 — S3 as an Archive: Layout, Versioning and Lifecycle Rules

Subtitle: Storage is cheap. Not being able to find or trust what you stored is expensive.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Separate public and private data into buckets with the right settings. 2. Design a key layout that makes uploads idempotent. 3. Pick a storage tier from storage price, retrieval price and read count. 4. Protect integrity and avoid hidden costs.

You need: what an object store and a key are.

9.7.1 What gets kept

Every day my pipeline produces things worth keeping: structured report content, rendered HTML and PDF files, a narrated audio brief, model-ready signal files, and health snapshots from the automation. All of it ends up in S3.

S3 is the obvious choice. Less obvious: how to lay it out so that in a year I can find what I need, prove it wasn’t changed, and not pay to keep junk forever.

9.7.2 Two buckets, two purposes

Public website bucket Private archive bucket
Fronted by A CDN Nothing; never served
Contents Only what visitors should see Everything else
Settings Read through the CDN Public access blocked, server-side encryption on, versioning on

Mixing the two is a common mistake. One misconfigured policy on a shared bucket and your private research is indexed by a search engine. Separate buckets keep the blast radius of a policy mistake small.

9.7.3 Key layout

S3 is a flat key-value store; the slashes are just characters. A consistent prefix scheme still makes it navigable:

  • one prefix per content type (content, audio, reports, signals, health);
  • the logical date in the key;
  • no upload timestamps, unless I genuinely need several versions per day.

Keying on the logical date makes uploads idempotent: re-running yesterday’s archive overwrites yesterday’s objects instead of creating near-duplicates. Versioning keeps the previous copy if I ever need it.

Each run I also rebuild a flat corpus file (one JSON line per day) from every daily content file. Rebuilding from source, rather than appending, means a corrected day shows up everywhere, and a partial run can’t leave the corpus half-updated.

Figure 9.7.1 — Separate buckets, schema-like keys. The public bucket holds only what visitors see. The private archive is locked, encrypted and versioned, with one prefix per content type and the logical date in every key. A layout sketch; no real bucket or key names.

9.7.4 Versioning is your undo button

With versioning on, an overwrite or delete creates a new version (or a delete marker) and keeps the old data. That protects me from my own scripts.

It is also a cost: old versions are billed like current ones until a lifecycle rule removes them.

9.7.5 Lifecycle rules

A lifecycle rule moves or expires objects by age. Typical tiers:

  • Standard for recent, frequently read data.
  • Standard-IA or Glacier Instant Retrieval for older data read occasionally.
  • Glacier Flexible / Deep Archive for data you will almost never read.
  • Expiration of noncurrent versions after a while, and of incomplete multipart uploads.

Cost model. For an object of size ss kept for TT months and read kk times, the cost in tier jj is roughly Cj=s(pjT+rjk)+minimum-duration penaltyj, C_j = s\,\big(p_j\,T + r_j\,k\big) + \text{minimum-duration penalty}_j, where pjp_j is the storage price per GB-month and rjr_j the retrieval price per GB.

Colder tiers lower pjp_j and raise rjr_j. They also charge for a minimum storage duration and a minimum billable object size. So the right tier depends on kk. Data you read often belongs in Standard, even if it is old.

Figure 9.7.2 — The right tier depends on reads. The warm tier (blue) costs the same however often you read. The cold tier (orange) starts cheaper but adds a charge per read. They cross at a break-even read count: below it, go cold; above it, stay warm. Prices are invented to show the shape; they are not AWS prices.

The minimum-object-size rule bites small files. Thousands of tiny JSON files moved to an infrequent-access tier can cost more than leaving them alone. Batch them, or leave them.

Intelligent-Tiering automates the choice for unpredictable access, for a small monitoring fee per object. Good for large objects with unknown patterns; poor for millions of tiny ones.

9.7.6 Integrity

S3 stores checksums and can verify uploads against a checksum you supply. For research data I also keep my own SHA-256 hash alongside anything that might be cited later. A hash lets me say “this is the exact file the analysis used”, which matters a lot for the research-integrity side of my work.

9.7.7 Pitfalls

  • Forgetting multipart cleanup. Failed large uploads leave invisible parts you pay for. One lifecycle rule fixes it forever.
  • Versioning without noncurrent expiration. Your bill grows with every overwrite.
  • Region assumptions in scripts. A script that hard-codes a region breaks the day you copy it. Read region and bucket from configuration.
  • Listing as a database. ListObjects is paginated and slow at scale. If you need queries, keep an index somewhere else.

9.7.8 Summary

  • Treat S3 layout like a schema: prefixes per type, logical dates in keys.
  • Separate public from private; lock, encrypt and version the archive.
  • Pick tiers by read count, not age alone; beware minimum size and duration charges.
  • Hash anything you may cite; clean up multipart uploads and old versions.
  • Write lifecycle rules on day one.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Why does keying on the logical date make re-runs safe? (Answer: a re-run writes the same key, overwriting instead of duplicating; versioning keeps the old copy.)
  2. (Calculate) Using the model, find the break-even kk when pwarmT=10p_{\text{warm}} T = 10, pcoldT=3p_{\text{cold}} T = 3 and rcold=0.8r_{\text{cold}} = 0.8 (per unit size).
  3. (Apply) You have 50,000 files of 2 KB each. Should they move to an infrequent-access tier?
  4. (Think) Why rebuild the corpus file from source instead of appending?

Further reading

  • Amazon S3 User Guide, “Managing your storage lifecycle”.
  • Amazon S3 User Guide, “Using versioning in S3 buckets”.
  • Amazon S3 pricing page, storage class minimums.

— Tariq

Chapter 9.8 — Cognito Auth and SES Email: the Pitfalls Nobody Warns You About

Subtitle: Sign-up looks like a solved problem. Then the verification email doesn’t arrive.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe how a Cognito user pool and SES fit together. 2. Get email delivered: sandbox, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, bounces. 3. Verify a JWT fully, not just decode it. 4. Avoid token-lifetime, enumeration, case and trigger traps.

You need: what a login, a token and DNS are.

9.8.1 The setting

My site has accounts. People register, verify an email, accept the legal terms, and reach parts of the site that anonymous visitors don’t. I used Amazon Cognito user pools for identity and Amazon SES for email. Both are good services. Both have sharp edges that only show up in production.

9.8.2 How the pieces fit

A user pool stores users, handles sign-up and sign-in, issues tokens (ID, access and refresh), and sends verification and password-reset codes. By default it sends those emails itself, with a low daily limit meant for testing. For anything real you point it at SES.

The app then trusts tokens issued by the pool: verify the signature against the pool’s public keys (JWKS), check the issuer, audience and expiry, and read claims such as the user’s groups.

9.8.3 Email pitfalls

Pitfall 1: the default email sender. Fine for a demo, inadequate for users. The cap is low, the sender address is generic, and deliverability is mediocre. Switch to SES early, with a verified domain identity.

Pitfall 2: the SES sandbox. New SES accounts start in a sandbox: you can only send to verified addresses. Everything works in testing because you verified your own. Then a real user registers and nothing arrives. Request production access before launch, and be specific about how you collect consent and handle bounces.

Pitfall 3: deliverability is DNS. Mail in spam is effectively mail that didn’t arrive. Three DNS records decide most of it:

Record What it says
SPF Which servers may send for your domain
DKIM A signature proving the message wasn’t altered and came from your domain
DMARC What receivers should do when SPF/DKIM fail, and where to send reports

SES can generate DKIM records. Use a custom MAIL FROM domain so SPF alignment works. Then set a DMARC policy: start permissive with reporting, tighten once reports look clean.

Pitfall 4: bounces and complaints. SES watches your bounce and complaint rates. Cross its thresholds and sending can be paused, which also stops password resets. Subscribe to bounce and complaint notifications and suppress addresses that hard-bounce. The account-level suppression list helps, but your own code must also stop retrying dead addresses.

9.8.4 Token pitfalls

Pitfall 5: token verification done halfway. The most dangerous bug isn’t email. It is accepting a token you haven’t fully verified. Decoding a JWT is not verifying it. You must:

  1. check the signature with the right key from JWKS (cache the keys; refresh on an unknown kid, the key ID);
  2. check iss matches your pool;
  3. check aud (ID token) or client_id (access token);
  4. check exp, with a small allowance for clock skew;
  5. check token_use is the type you expect.

For admin areas I also check group membership server-side on every request, not just in the UI. Hiding a button is not authorisation.

Figure 9.8.1 — Five checks before trusting a token. Each blue box must pass in turn; any failure drops to the orange bar and the request is rejected. Only after all five does the server look at permissions such as admin group membership.

Pitfall 6: token lifetimes and refresh. Short access tokens limit damage from leaks; refresh tokens keep users signed in.

If the access-token lifetime is LaL_a and a stolen token is used at a uniformly random point in its life, the expected window of misuse is La/2L_a/2.

That is the argument for a short LaL_a. Refresh tokens should be revocable and stored more carefully: HTTP-only, secure cookies rather than local storage.

9.8.5 Account pitfalls

Pitfall 7: user enumeration. Messages like “no account with that email” tell an attacker which emails are registered. Cognito has a setting to prevent user-existence errors. Turn it on, and make your own UI messages equally vague.

Pitfall 8: case and aliases. Is Name@Example.com the same user as name@example.com? Decide at pool creation: username case sensitivity can’t be changed later. I treat emails as case-insensitive and normalise before any lookup.

Pitfall 9: triggers that fail. Cognito Lambda triggers (pre-sign-up, post-confirmation) are handy for recording consent or adding users to groups. If a trigger throws or times out, the user sees a generic failure and the account can end up half-created. Keep triggers small, idempotent and fast, and log enough to reconstruct what happened.

9.8.6 What I’d tell another engineer

Budget a day for email deliverability and a day for token verification before you think auth is done. Test with an address you’ve never verified, on a fresh device, through a spam filter you don’t control. That is the real user’s path.

9.8.7 Summary

  • Move to SES with a verified domain, leave the sandbox, and set SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
  • Handle bounces and complaints, or SES may pause all sending, resets included.
  • Verify signature, issuer, audience, expiry and token use; authorise on the server.
  • Keep access tokens short; store refresh tokens in HTTP-only secure cookies.
  • Block user enumeration, fix email case at creation, keep triggers small and idempotent.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Access tokens last 60 minutes. Expected misuse window for a stolen one? (Answer: 30 minutes.)
  2. (Apply) Testing works but real users get no email. Name the two most likely causes.
  3. (Think) Why is checking admin rights only in the UI unsafe?
  4. (Design) Write a sign-in error message that does not reveal whether an account exists.

Further reading

  • Amazon Cognito Developer Guide, “Verifying a JSON Web Token”.
  • Amazon SES Developer Guide, “Moving out of the Amazon SES sandbox”.
  • RFC 7519 (JWT); RFC 7489 (DMARC).

— Tariq

Chapter 9.9 — DynamoDB for Market Snapshots, and Why NaN Will Ruin Your Day

Subtitle: A number type that refuses floats, a JSON spec that refuses NaN, and the guard layer between them.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Model a “latest snapshot” access pattern in DynamoDB without scans. 2. Convert between floats and Decimal safely. 3. Explain where NaN and infinity come from and why they break storage and JSON. 4. Build one tested guard that maps non-finite values to null.

You need: basic Python; what floating-point numbers and JSON are.

9.9.1 A small, simple use

My dashboard shows a market snapshot: index levels, changes, breadth figures, volatility measures and so on. A scheduled function fetches them, normalises them and writes them to DynamoDB. The site reads the latest snapshot and renders it.

It is a small, simple use of DynamoDB. It still broke, in a way every data engineer should know about: non-finite numbers.

9.9.2 Why DynamoDB for this

The access pattern is trivial: write the latest snapshot, read the latest snapshot, occasionally read a short history. A key-value store with single-digit-millisecond reads, no servers and on-demand pricing fits well.

I key items so that “latest” is a single GetItem, or a Query with a limit of one on a sorted key. Never a Scan (which reads the whole table).

9.9.3 The Decimal problem

DynamoDB’s number type is arbitrary-precision decimal. The Python SDK refuses to write a float and demands decimal.Decimal. So you convert. On the way out the SDK hands you Decimal objects, and the standard JSON encoder refuses those. So you convert back.

That round trip hides two problems:

  • Decimal(0.1) captures the binary float’s exact value: a long, ugly decimal. Convert through a string, Decimal(str(x)), to get what you meant.
  • DynamoDB numbers allow up to 38 significant digits. Fine for prices, but an unrounded computation can exceed it.

9.9.4 The NaN problem

IEEE-754 floats include +∞+\infty, −∞-\infty and NaN (“not a number”). They appear naturally in market data:

  • a percentage change Δ=(pt−pt−1)/pt−1\Delta = (p_t - p_{t-1})/p_{t-1} when pt−1=0p_{t-1} = 0 or is missing;
  • a ratio such as advancers over decliners on a day with no decliners;
  • a rolling statistic over an empty window, which is 0/00/0;
  • an upstream API returning null that pandas turns into NaN.

Then:

  • DynamoDB rejects them. Decimal('NaN') and Decimal('Infinity') aren’t valid number values, so the write fails.
  • JSON rejects them. The JSON specification has no NaN or Infinity. Python’s encoder emits NaN anyway by default, producing invalid JSON that browsers refuse to parse. One bad field and the whole dashboard is blank.

NaN also poisons arithmetic. Any expression containing it is NaN, and every comparison with it is false. So NaN > threshold and NaN <= threshold are both false. Code that branches on comparisons silently takes the “else” path.

9.9.5 The guard

I put a sanitising step at every boundary where numbers leave Python:

  1. Walk the structure recursively.
  2. For each float, check math.isfinite(x). If finite, convert via string to Decimal (for DynamoDB) or keep it (for JSON).
  3. If not finite, replace it with None (stored as null or omitted) and record which field was bad.
  4. On read, convert Decimal back to float or int before serialising.

Figure 9.9.1 — One guard at every boundary. Every number leaving Python passes one test. Finite values are converted safely and continue (green). NaN and infinity become null, and the field name is logged (orange). Nothing else reaches storage or the API.

The key design decision is step 3: null, not zero. Replacing NaN with 0 is a lie. A missing change is not “unchanged”. The UI renders null as a dash, which is honest.

Step 3’s logging matters just as much. If a field is non-finite every day, that’s an upstream bug, not noise. I’d rather know.

9.9.6 Encoding the rule as an invariant

Invariant. For every numeric field xx written to storage, x∈ℝ∨x=null, x \in \mathbb{R} \;\lor\; x = \text{null}, with ±∞\pm\infty and NaN excluded.

Write this as a single function used at every boundary, with a unit test that feeds it NaN, ±∞\pm\infty, nested lists and dictionaries. It is cheap insurance. It has two call sites (the writer and the API reader), which is exactly when a shared helper earns its place.

9.9.7 Other DynamoDB lessons

  • Item size limit is 400 KB. A snapshot with embedded history grows. Keep history in separate items.
  • Empty strings and sets have their own rules; test them.
  • On-demand versus provisioned. For a few writes a minute, on-demand is simpler and cheap.
  • TTL (time to live) gives automatic cleanup of old snapshots, but deletions are lazy, not instant. Never rely on TTL for correctness, only for cost.

9.9.8 Summary

  • Read “latest” with GetItem or a limit-one Query, never a Scan.
  • Convert floats with Decimal(str(x)); watch the 38-digit limit.
  • NaN and infinity break DynamoDB writes and JSON, and make every comparison false.
  • One tested guard at every boundary: finite passes, non-finite becomes null and is logged.
  • Null means missing; zero is a lie.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) What does NaN == NaN return in Python? (Answer: False; every comparison with NaN is false.)
  2. (Apply) Advancers 300, decliners 0. What does the ratio become, and what should the dashboard show?
  3. (Think) Why log the field name and not just replace the value?
  4. (Test) List five inputs your guard’s unit test should include.

Further reading

  • Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, “Supported data types”.
  • IEEE 754-2019, Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic.
  • RFC 8259, The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format.

— Tariq

Chapter 9.10 — Narrating a Daily Report with Amazon Polly

Subtitle: Text-to-speech is easy. Writing text that sounds right when spoken is the actual work.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Build an asynchronous Polly synthesis step with bounded polling. 2. Choose an engine and voice with the support tables in mind. 3. Rewrite text for the ear, keeping numbers deterministic. 4. Estimate duration and cost before synthesising, and use basic SSML safely.

You need: what text-to-speech is; the idea of polling a job until it finishes.

9.10.1 Audio for every report

Every daily report on my site has an audio version: a short spoken brief you can listen to on a walk. Amazon Polly generates it automatically as part of the publishing pipeline.

The API part took an hour. Making it sound like something a person would want to hear took weeks, and almost all of that was about the text, not the speech engine.

9.10.2 The pipeline

  1. The report is produced in two layers: a technical archive and a plain-language narrative. The narrative layer includes an audio-optimised version.
  2. That text is cleaned and marked up.
  3. Polly synthesises it asynchronously into S3.
  4. The pipeline polls for completion, moves the file to its final location, and archives it.
  5. The site’s audio player picks it up.

Figure 9.10.1 — Narration as an asynchronous pipeline. Text is cleaned by deterministic code (green), sent as a synthesis task, polled a bounded number of times, then copied to a stable dated key. If polling runs out or the task fails, the step fails loudly (orange).

9.10.3 Synchronous versus asynchronous

SynthesizeSpeech StartSpeechSynthesisTask
Returns Audio directly A task ID; writes audio to S3
Input length Limited Longer (still has a per-task character limit)
Fits a daily brief? No, too long Yes

With the async call you poll GetSpeechSynthesisTask until it reports completed or failed.

Bound the polling. With interval Δ\Delta and at most nn polls, the job gives up after nΔn\Delta seconds. Pick nΔn\Delta comfortably above the slowest synthesis you have seen, and fail loudly when it is exceeded. Never loop forever in a build that bills by the minute.

Async output lands under a scratch prefix with a task-ID filename. I copy it to a stable, dated key and delete the scratch object, so the archive layout stays predictable.

9.10.4 Engines and voices

Polly offers several engines: standard, neural, long-form and generative. Each has its own voices and features.

  • Neural voices sound far more natural than standard ones.
  • The newer engines go further but support fewer SSML tags and fewer voices.
  • Not every voice supports every engine, and not every SSML tag works on every engine.

Check the support tables before you design your markup around a tag.

9.10.5 Writing for the ear

This is the real work. Text written for reading is often bad for listening:

Problem Fix
Long sentences lose the listener Short sentences, one idea each
“SPX -0.43%” is unreadable aloud Turn it into words with units, sign and context: “down a little under half a percent”
Abbreviations and tickers: engines guess, and guess differently Spell them out, use SSML say-as, or define a lexicon
Nested acronyms and tongue-twisters Rewrite; fine on a page, awful spoken
Parentheticals: readers skip them, listeners can’t Rewrite or remove
Bullets don’t exist in audio Spoken signposts: “first”, “then”, “finally”

I enforce some of this in the narrative generation step and the rest in a deterministic clean-up pass before synthesis. The clean-up must be deterministic. If a model rewrote numbers for speech, I’d need to be sure it didn’t change them. So numeric formatting for speech is done by code, from the structured data, not by a language model.

9.10.6 Pacing and cost

A comfortable narration pace is often quoted at around 150 words per minute.

Duration estimate. For WW words at speaking rate vv, plus the pauses bib_i inserted with SSML <break>: T≈Wv+∑ibi. T \approx \frac{W}{v} + \sum_i b_i.

That estimate keeps the brief near a target length before you spend money synthesising it. Polly bills per character, so a length check up front also controls cost.

Example. 600 words at 150 words per minute, plus ten 1-second breaks: T≈4T \approx 4 minutes +10+ 10 seconds.

9.10.7 SSML basics that helped

SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language) is XML that tells the engine how to speak.

  • <break> for pauses between sections.
  • <prosody rate> sparingly, if at all; neural voices sound odd when pushed far.
  • <say-as interpret-as="date"> and similar for dates and numbers, where supported.
  • Escaping: &, < and > must be escaped inside SSML, or the whole request fails. A single ampersand in a company name broke one of my early runs.

9.10.8 Pitfalls

  • Character limits per task exist even for async. Very long text must be split and the audio joined.
  • SSML validation errors are fatal. Validate before sending.
  • Region and voice availability differ. Don’t assume a voice exists in every region.
  • Accessibility. Audio complements text; it doesn’t replace it. Always publish the transcript.

9.10.9 Summary

  • Use asynchronous synthesis to S3 with bounded polling, then move output to a dated key.
  • Check engine, voice and tag support before relying on a tag.
  • TTS quality is mostly a writing problem: short sentences, spoken numbers, no parentheticals.
  • Format numbers for speech in code, never by a model.
  • Estimate length up front; escape and validate SSML; publish the transcript.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Polls every 10 s, at most 30 polls. When does the job give up? (Answer: after 300 s.)
  2. (Apply) Rewrite “NDX +1.2% (tech-led)” for the ear.
  3. (Calculate) 900 words at 150 wpm with eight 2-second breaks: estimated duration?
  4. (Think) Why is it risky to let a language model rewrite numbers for speech?

Further reading

  • Amazon Polly Developer Guide, “Generating speech from SSML documents”.
  • W3C, Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) Version 1.1.
  • Amazon Polly Developer Guide, “Supported SSML tags” by engine.

— Tariq

Chapter 9.11 — CloudWatch Alarms and Heartbeat Monitors

Subtitle: Alarms tell you something went wrong. Heartbeats tell you something stopped. You need both.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Configure a CloudWatch alarm’s window, missing-data handling and actions. 2. Build a heartbeat monitor that checks existence, freshness and content. 3. Use a per-node state machine to avoid alert spam. 4. Choose a staleness threshold, and watch the watcher.

You need: what a metric and a scheduled function are.

9.11.1 Loud failures and quiet ones

I run several always-on pieces of software: automation on Windows machines, background agents on a Mac, scheduled jobs on AWS. Each can fail loudly, which is easy, or go quiet, which is not. This chapter is about catching the quiet ones.

9.11.2 Alarms: thresholds on metrics

A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric over periods and changes state when a condition holds for some number of datapoints. My web stack has a few: function errors, throttles, and duration approaching the timeout. They are defined in the same template as the function they watch.

Three settings matter more than the threshold:

  • Period and evaluation window. “M of N datapoints breaching” filters single blips. A 1-of-1 alarm is noisy; a 3-of-3 alarm is slow.
  • Missing-data treatment. By default missing data is “missing”, and the alarm can sit in INSUFFICIENT_DATA forever. For an error metric, missing usually means “no errors”: treat it as not breaching. For a liveness metric, missing means “dead”: treat it as breaching.
  • Actions on every transition. Alert on ALARM, but also on OK, so you know when it recovered.

The missing-data setting is the one people get wrong. An alarm on an error count can’t tell you the function stopped running, because a stopped function produces no errors.

9.11.3 Heartbeats: proof of life

A heartbeat inverts the logic. Each component regularly writes “I’m alive, here’s my state” to a known place: in my case, a small JSON file in S3 with a timestamp and a few status fields. A separate monitor function runs on a schedule, reads every heartbeat, and asks:

  1. Does it exist?
  2. Is it fresh, meaning younger than an allowed staleness?
  3. Does its content say healthy (for example, a connection-state field)?

Any “no” is an alert. This catches crashed processes, frozen threads, dead network links, and machines that rebooted into a login screen. None of those produce error metrics.

9.11.4 A state machine for alerts

A naive monitor alerts every time it runs while a node is down. That is spam. So the monitor keeps a tiny state machine per node:

  • healthy → unhealthy: send an alert.
  • unhealthy → unhealthy: stay quiet, unless enough time has passed since the last alert; then re-alert as a reminder.
  • unhealthy → healthy: send one recovery message.

The state lives in a small parameter store entry, so the monitor itself stays stateless and can be redeployed freely.

Figure 9.11.1 — Alert on transitions, not on every check. Going from healthy to unhealthy sends one alert (orange). Staying unhealthy is silent except for occasional reminders. Coming back sends one recovery message (green). Staying healthy is silent.

9.11.5 Choosing staleness

Suppose a component writes a heartbeat every hh seconds, and the monitor checks every mm seconds with staleness threshold ss.

Detection delay. Worst case, about Dmax≈s+m. D_{\max} \approx s + m. False alarms. A false alarm needs a gap between heartbeats longer than ss. Expected false alarms per day ≈ (heartbeats per day) × P(gap>s)P(\text{gap} > s).

You trade detection delay against false alarms through ss. Set ss to a few multiples of hh, then look at real gap data and adjust.

Figure 9.11.2 — Staleness and detection delay. Green dots are heartbeats; the component dies just after the last one. The shaded bar is the staleness window measured from that last beat. The first monitor check (blue tick) after the window closes raises the alert, so the delay is at most about s+ms + m. Schematic timing.

9.11.6 The lesson from a real gap

The most useful change I made came from an incident. One component’s internal messaging thread died, but a different component kept writing the heartbeat the monitor was reading. The node looked alive. Nothing alerted for a while.

The fix: make heartbeats come from the thing they claim to describe, and monitor each critical sub-component separately. A process that is up is not the same as the thread doing the work being up. Measure liveness as close to the work as possible.

9.11.7 Who watches the watcher?

The monitor is itself a scheduled function. If its schedule breaks, there are no alerts at all. I cover that with a CloudWatch alarm on the monitor’s own invocation count, treating missing data as breaching. If the monitor doesn’t run, that alarm fires.

9.11.8 Pitfalls

  • Clock skew. Freshness compares the writer’s timestamp with the monitor’s clock. Use UTC everywhere and keep machine clocks synced.
  • Alerting through the thing that’s down. If alerts travel the same network path that failed, they never arrive. Use an independent path.
  • Alarming on everything. You will learn to ignore it. Alarm on user-visible outcomes and on liveness; put the rest on a dashboard.

9.11.9 Summary

  • Alarms catch errors; heartbeats catch silence. Use both.
  • Set missing data to “not breaching” for error metrics and “breaching” for liveness.
  • Check heartbeats for existence, freshness and content; alert on state transitions.
  • Detection delay is about s+ms + m; tune ss against real heartbeat gaps.
  • Heartbeats must come from the work itself, and the monitor needs its own alarm.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) s=300s = 300 s and m=60m = 60 s. Worst-case detection delay? (Answer: about 360 s.)
  2. (Apply) An error-count alarm stays green while the function is not running at all. Why?
  3. (Think) Why should a heartbeat be written by the worker thread rather than the process supervisor?
  4. (Design) Sketch the alarm that fires if the monitor itself stops running.

Further reading

  • Amazon CloudWatch User Guide, “Configuring how CloudWatch alarms treat missing data”.
  • B. Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering, “Practical Alerting”.
  • U. Joshi, “Heartbeat”, in Patterns of Distributed Systems (also published on martinfowler.com).

— Tariq

Chapter 9.12 — Bedrock Knowledge Bases and RAG Ingestion for a One-Person Research Shop

Subtitle: Retrieval is only as good as what you put in, how you chunk it, and whether it’s still true.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) end to end. 2. Explain cosine similarity, top-k retrieval and hybrid search. 3. Choose a chunking strategy and keep the index fresh and in scope. 4. Measure retrieval with Recall@k.

You need: what a vector and a dot product are; what a language model prompt is.

9.12.1 Too much to remember

I have a lot of documentation: research notes, runbooks, design contracts, operating procedures, AWS architecture references. Too much for any AI agent’s context window, and too much for me to remember. So I built a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) setup on Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases, plus an incremental refresh that keeps it current.

9.12.2 RAG in one paragraph

Split documents into chunks. Embed each chunk as a vector (a list of numbers that captures meaning). Store the vectors in an index. At question time, embed the question, find the nearest chunks, and paste them into the model’s prompt as context. The model answers from that context.

Bedrock knowledge bases manage the chunking, embedding, vector store and retrieval for you. You point them at a data source, such as an S3 prefix, and run ingestion jobs.

Figure 9.12.1 — The two halves of RAG. Ingest (blue) runs on a schedule: curated sources are chunked on headings, embedded and stored with metadata. Query (green) embeds the question, retrieves the best chunks from that index (dashed arrow) with hybrid search, and asks the model to answer with citations. A concept sketch, not my configuration.

9.12.3 The maths of “nearest”

With an embedding function e(⋅)e(\cdot), similarity between a question qq and a chunk cc is usually cosine similarity:

sim⁡(q,c)=e(q)⋅e(c)‖e(q)‖‖e(c)‖. \operatorname{sim}(q, c) = \frac{e(q)\cdot e(c)}{\lVert e(q)\rVert\,\lVert e(c)\rVert}.

It is the cosine of the angle between the two vectors: 1 means “pointing the same way”.

Retrieval returns the top-kk chunks by similarity. Hybrid search adds a lexical score (BM25-style word matching) so exact terms, such as an error code or a function name, aren’t drowned out by semantic neighbours. For technical documentation hybrid is usually better: embeddings are great at paraphrase and poor at exact identifiers.

9.12.4 Chunking is the whole game

Most bad RAG answers I’ve seen trace back to chunking:

Chunk problem What goes wrong
Too small “The threshold is set in the config”, without saying which config
Too large Five topics in one chunk; its embedding is an average and matches nothing well
Split mid-structure A table or list cut in half

Structure-aware chunking (split on headings, keep sections intact) worked better for me than fixed-size windows.

I also give every document front-matter metadata: identifier, title, intent, domain, verification date and validity. And I write titles and intents so that a chunk read alone still makes sense.

9.12.5 Freshness: the problem nobody demos

A knowledge base that confidently answers from last month’s runbook is worse than no knowledge base. Two things helped:

  1. Incremental refresh. A scheduled job detects changed source documents and re-ingests only those. Ingestion jobs are asynchronous and can partly fail; the job checks the result and reports documents that failed.
  2. Verification metadata. Documents carry a “last verified” date and a confidence state. The retrieval prompt tells the model to prefer verified, current documents and to say when its source is stale.

9.12.6 Scope rules

Not everything belongs in the index. I keep explicit scope rules: which kinds of documents are eligible, and what must never be ingested:

  • secrets and credentials;
  • raw personal data;
  • anything known to be false or superseded.

Once a wrong document is in a vector index, it will be retrieved for months. Excluding it at the source is far easier than chasing it out later.

9.12.7 Evaluating retrieval

You can’t improve what you don’t measure. For a set of test questions with known relevant documents:
