Recall@k=|relevant∩top-k||relevant|, \text{Recall@}k = \frac{|\text{relevant} \cap \text{top-}k|}{|\text{relevant}|}, the share of the relevant documents that appear in the top kk results.

I check it whenever I change chunking or add a large batch of documents. It is crude, but it catches regressions that “the answers seem fine” doesn’t.

Example. A question has 4 relevant documents; 3 appear in the top 5. Recall@5 = 3/4.

9.12.8 Pitfalls

  • Citations or it didn’t happen. Ask the model to cite which chunk each claim came from. Then check a sample. Models will cite a chunk that doesn’t support the claim.
  • Embedding model changes invalidate the whole index. Re-ingest everything.
  • Cost of re-ingestion. Full re-syncs are slow and billed; incremental updates matter.
  • Permissions. The knowledge-base role needs read access to the source and write access to the vector store. Ingestion fails quietly, per document, if a file is unreadable.
  • RAG isn’t memory of truth. It retrieves text. If the text is wrong, the answer is wrong, with confidence.

9.12.9 Summary

  • RAG = chunk, embed, index, retrieve, then answer from the retrieved context.
  • Hybrid search (cosine + BM25) suits technical docs with exact identifiers.
  • Chunk on structure; give every document metadata that makes chunks stand alone.
  • Refresh incrementally, track verification dates, and keep strict scope rules.
  • Measure retrieval with Recall@k, separately from generation. RAG is a data-quality problem dressed as an AI problem.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Two vectors point in exactly the same direction. What is their cosine similarity? (Answer: 1.)
  2. (Calculate) 5 relevant documents, 2 in the top 10. What is Recall@10?
  3. (Apply) A query for a specific error code returns general troubleshooting pages. What change helps most?
  4. (Think) Why is excluding a false document at the source easier than removing it later?

Further reading

  • P. Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks” (2020).
  • Amazon Bedrock User Guide, “Knowledge bases”.
  • S. Robertson and H. Zaragoza, “The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond”.

— Tariq

Chapter 10.2 — Real-Time Dashboards over WebSockets, with Caching That Doesn’t Lie

Subtitle: Push for freshness, cache for cost, and always show the reader how old the number is.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Compare polling and pushing by the load each puts on a server. 2. Build a dashboard with the snapshot-plus-delta pattern. 3. Set caching rules that save cost without hiding stale data. 4. Design reconnection so a server restart does not cause a second outage.

You need: basic web terms (HTTP request, browser, server). No maths beyond division.

10.2.1 The problem

My site has a market dashboard: index levels, breadth, volatility and an options-positioning panel. People leave it open in a tab during the session. That creates two competing needs. The data should feel live. And serving it should not cost a fortune or hammer the upstream data providers.

The design I landed on has three parts: a WebSocket stream for live updates, a cached snapshot for everything else, and a strict rule that every number shows its age.

10.2.2 Polling versus pushing

Polling means the browser asks “anything new?” every few seconds and gets a JSON snapshot back. It is easy, cacheable and stateless (the server remembers nothing between requests). The costs: most polls return nothing new, and the delay can be up to one polling interval.

Pushing means the server sends a message only when something changes.

Load comparison. With N open clients polling every T seconds, request load is N / T per second, whatever the data does. With push, load is roughly the update rate u times the number of connected clients, and quiet periods cost almost nothing. When u ≪ 1/T (updates are much rarer than polls), push is far cheaper. When updates never stop, the advantage shrinks.

A WebSocket is a long-lived, two-way connection: the browser opens it once and the server pushes messages down it. Server-Sent Events (SSE) are a simpler one-way alternative. For a fresh build I would consider SSE first.

10.2.3 The snapshot-plus-delta pattern

A client that connects halfway through the session needs the current state, not just the next change. So:

  1. On page load, fetch a full snapshot over plain HTTP. A CDN (content delivery network, a cache near the user) can keep it for a short time, so a thousand people opening the page cost about one request to the origin server.
  2. Then open the WebSocket and apply deltas (small change messages) as they arrive.
  3. Every message carries a sequence number or timestamp. If the client sees a gap, it refetches the snapshot rather than guessing.

Figure 10.2.1 — Snapshot first, then deltas. The top row is the one-off HTTP fetch, served mostly by the CDN. The bottom row is the live stream: the update source emits changes and the connection layer only relays them. The orange dashed arrow is the safety net: a missing sequence number sends the browser back for a fresh snapshot.

This keeps the live channel small and lets the cache do most of the work.

10.2.4 Caching rules

Rule What it does
Short TTLs on snapshots A few seconds at the edge collapses “thundering herds” (many identical requests at once). TTL = time to live in the cache.
stale-while-revalidate Serve the cached copy instantly while fetching a fresh one in the background. The reader sees a slightly old number, labelled as such, instead of a spinner.
Memoise upstream calls on the server If ten routes need the same upstream quote, fetch it once per interval.
Never cache errors as data A failed upstream call must not be stored as “zero”.

10.2.5 Show the age of every number

This is the rule I care about most. A dashboard that shows stale data as if it were live is misleading, and in markets that is dangerous. Every panel shows when its data was last updated. The UI visibly changes state when data is older than expected. If the stream drops, the panel says “reconnecting” and the age keeps counting.

Key idea. Freshness belongs to each value, not to the page. A page can be half-fresh.

10.2.6 Reconnection

WebSockets drop. Laptops sleep, phones switch networks, servers redeploy. A robust client:

  • reconnects with exponential backoff and jitter (waits longer after each failure, plus a random amount), so a server restart is not met by every client at once;
  • resubscribes to its channels;
  • refetches the snapshot after reconnecting, because it may have missed deltas;
  • stops trying when the tab is hidden and resumes when it is visible.

Reconnection load. Without jitter, all N clients reconnect within milliseconds of a restart: one spike. With full jitter over a window W seconds, arrivals are roughly uniform at N / W per second.

Figure 10.2.2 — Jitter turns a spike into a trickle. The orange bar is 1,000 clients all reconnecting in the first second. The green bars are the same 1,000 clients each waiting a random time over 30 seconds: about 33 per second. Simulation: 1,000 clients, uniform random delay over 30 s, fixed seed 20261107; not measured traffic. That is the difference between a smooth recovery and a self-inflicted outage.

10.2.7 Serverless and WebSockets

Persistent connections do not sit naturally on a request/response platform. Options include API Gateway’s WebSocket APIs (which manage connections and call a function per message), a managed pub/sub service, or a small always-on process. The right choice depends on connection count and update rate. Whatever you pick, keep the connection layer dumb: it relays messages; it does not compute them.

10.2.8 Pitfalls

  • Rendering cost. Redrawing the whole page on every tick makes the browser stutter. Update only changed values and batch updates per animation frame.
  • Timezones. Send UTC, render local time.
  • Memory leaks. Unsubscribe and close sockets when components unmount.
  • Market closed. Outside session hours, say so. Do not show yesterday’s last tick as if it were current.

10.2.9 Summary

  • Polling costs N/T requests per second regardless of change; push costs scale with real updates.
  • Snapshot over cacheable HTTP, then deltas over the socket, with sequence numbers to detect gaps.
  • Cache aggressively but never cache errors, and label every value with its age.
  • Reconnect with backoff and jitter, then refetch the snapshot.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) 2,000 clients poll every 5 seconds. What is the request load? (Answer: 400 requests per second.)
  2. (Apply) After a restart, 6,000 clients reconnect with full jitter over 60 seconds. Roughly how many arrive per second?
  3. (Design) A delta arrives with sequence number 105, but the last one applied was 103. What should the client do, and why not just apply 105?
  4. (Think) Why is “cache errors as zero” more dangerous on a market dashboard than a spinner?

Further reading

  • RFC 6455, The WebSocket Protocol.
  • RFC 5861, HTTP Cache-Control Extensions for Stale Content.
  • Ilya Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking (O’Reilly).

— Tariq

Chapter 10.3 — Building a GEX Strike Map UI

Subtitle: Turning an options chain into a chart people can read in five seconds, without pretending it predicts anything.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State the common simplified formula for gamma exposure (GEX) by strike, and name its weakest assumption. 2. Lay out a strike ladder chart that reads at a glance. 3. Compute a zero-crossing level by linear interpolation and explain why it is shown as a band. 4. List the labels an honest GEX chart must carry.

You need: what an option, a strike and open interest are. Gamma is explained below.

10.3.1 What the panel is for

One panel on my dashboard shows a gamma exposure (GEX) profile by strike: where options positioning is concentrated around the current index level, plus a view for same-day expiries. I cover dealer-gamma theory elsewhere. This chapter is about the interface: how to present a noisy, assumption-heavy quantity honestly.

10.3.2 What is being plotted

Gamma (Γ) is how fast an option’s delta changes when the underlying price moves. Open interest (OI) is the number of contracts outstanding.

Definition (simplified GEX by strike). For strike K,

GEX(K)=∑i∈KΓi⋅OIi⋅m⋅S2⋅0.01⋅si, \text{GEX}(K) = \sum_{i \in K} \Gamma_i \cdot \text{OI}_i \cdot m \cdot S^2 \cdot 0.01 \cdot s_i,

where m is the contract multiplier, S the underlying price, and s_i a sign (+1 or −1) that encodes an assumption about whether dealers are long or short that option. The factor S² · 0.01 turns gamma into dollar exposure per 1% move.

The sign is the weakest link. Open interest does not tell you who is on which side. The UI must carry that uncertainty, not hide it.

10.3.3 Layout choices

  • Horizontal bars by strike. Strikes on the vertical axis, exposure on the horizontal, positive one side, negative the other. Price levels read top to bottom, like a ladder.
  • A marker for the current price. Everything is relative to spot. Without it the chart is just bars.
  • An obvious zero line. The sign is the point, so the zero axis is the strongest line on the chart.
  • Diverging colours, colour-blind safe. Two hues that also differ in lightness, so the chart survives greyscale and common colour-vision deficiencies.
  • A window around spot. A full chain has hundreds of strikes, most irrelevant. Show a window, with the option to expand.

Figure 10.3.1 — The strike ladder. Each row is a strike, higher strikes at the top. The thick black vertical line is zero; blue bars are positive, orange negative. The dashed line marks spot. Note how one large strike (K₁₁) dominates the view. The values come from a made-up formula, not market data.

10.3.4 Aggregation and noise

Raw per-strike values are spiky: a single large open-interest strike dominates. Two honest options:

Option Shows Trade-off
Raw values each strike as computed the reader sees the spikes
Cumulative profile G(K)=∑K′≤KGEX(K′)G(K) = \sum_{K' \le K} \text{GEX}(K') easy to see where net exposure changes sign

I avoid smoothing that invents values between strikes. Interpolation implies a precision the data does not have.

10.3.5 The zero-gamma level

People often want one number: the price where cumulative exposure crosses zero. Find adjacent strikes Kj,Kj+1K_j, K_{j+1} where G changes sign and interpolate linearly:

K*=Kj+(Kj+1−Kj)−G(Kj)G(Kj+1)−G(Kj). K^* = K_j + (K_{j+1} - K_j)\,\frac{-G(K_j)}{G(K_{j+1}) - G(K_j)}.

Why it works. Draw a straight line between the two points. The fraction −G(Kj)/(G(Kj+1)−G(Kj))-G(K_j)/(G(K_{j+1}) - G(K_j)) is how far along that line you must go for the height to reach zero.

Figure 10.3.2 — The crossing is a band, not a line. The blue line is a toy cumulative profile. It is negative at K₄ and positive at K₅, so the orange dot between them is K. The shaded band is how I display it: K moves with the sign assumption, with stale open interest (OI updates once a day), and with the gamma model’s inputs.

10.3.6 Labelling for honesty

Every GEX chart on the site carries:

  1. the time of the underlying options snapshot;
  2. a short note on the assumptions (sign convention, OI is from the prior day);
  3. a reminder that this is a positioning estimate, not a forecast or a signal.

The last matters. GEX charts circulate on social media as if they predict where price will go. They describe a hypothetical hedging pressure under assumptions. Useful context, not a trade.

10.3.7 Engineering notes

  • Compute on the server. The browser gets a compact array of (strike, value) pairs, not the whole chain.
  • Fixed axis ranges within a session, so the chart does not rescale with every update and fool the eye.
  • Accessible tooltips with the exact value and strike, reachable by keyboard.
  • Fallbacks. If options data is stale or missing, the panel says so rather than showing the last good chart as current.
  • Test fixtures. A mock dataset for UI development, kept clearly separate from anything that could reach production.

10.3.8 Summary

  • GEX by strike rests on a sign assumption that open interest cannot confirm.
  • A ladder with a strong zero line and a spot marker reads in seconds.
  • Show raw or cumulative values; never invent values between strikes.
  • Draw the zero crossing as a band and label time, assumptions and “not a forecast”.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) G(K_j) = −2 at strike 100 and G(K_{j+1}) = 6 at strike 105. Find K. (Answer: 100 + 5 · 2/8 = 101.25.)*
  2. (Apply) Why must the zero line be the strongest line on the chart?
  3. (Think) If you flip the sign assumption for one large strike, what happens to K*? What does that tell you about showing it as a precise line?
  4. (Design) Write the three-line label you would put under a GEX chart.

Further reading

  • John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, chapter on the Greeks.
  • Sheldon Natenberg, Option Volatility and Pricing.
  • Cynthia Brewer’s ColorBrewer guidance on diverging palettes.

— Tariq

Chapter 10.4 — The “Mission Control” Admin Portal Pattern

Subtitle: A readiness banner, a decision journal and bounded controls. Admin pages should make the safe action easy and the dangerous one deliberate.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Build a pessimistic readiness banner from many health checks. 2. Explain why a decision journal must be append-only. 3. Design admin controls whose risk matches their confirmation.

You need: what a health check and a server-side API are.

10.4.1 Where the pattern came from

As the platform grew I ended up with an admin area: infrastructure status, logs, user registrations, documentation, telemetry and the trade-automation status view. Early versions were a pile of tables. The version I like now follows a pattern I call mission control. It has three parts: a readiness banner, a decision journal and bounded controls.

10.4.2 Part 1: the readiness banner

At the top of the page is one line that answers “can I trust the system right now?” It rolls the health checks behind it into one state, ready, degraded or not ready, with reasons.

Roll-up rule (pessimistic). If checks c1,…,cnc_1, \dots, c_n each return a state in the ordered set {ok < warn < fail}, the banner shows

banner=maxici. \text{banner} = \max_i c_i.

Not an average, not a majority vote. One failing critical component makes the whole banner fail. Averages hide the one thing you needed to see.

Each check also reports its own age. A green check from two hours ago is not green. A stale check counts as a warning by itself.

Figure 10.4.1 — The worst check wins. Three checks feed the roll-up: one ok, one warn because it is stale, one fail. The banner takes the maximum, so it reads NOT READY and names the reason. The note at the bottom adds the fourth state, “unknown”, which must never display as ok.

10.4.3 Part 2: the decision journal

Every meaningful action taken through the portal, and every automated decision worth recording, goes into an append-only journal: what was done, by whom or which process, when, why, and the system state at the time.

Why bother, as a team of one?

  • Memory. I can answer “why is this disabled?” weeks later.
  • Post-mortems. Incidents rarely have one cause. A timeline of decisions shows how we got there.
  • Agents. AI agents also take actions. Recording their decisions in the same format as mine lets me audit both the same way.

Append-only. If entries can be edited, the journal is a story, not a record. Corrections are new entries that point to the old ones.

10.4.4 Part 3: bounded controls

The portal can change things, but only within explicit bounds:

  • Allow-listed actions only. No free-form commands. Each button maps to one known operation.
  • Validated ranges. Every numeric input is checked on the server against hard limits. UI limits are a convenience; server limits are the control.
  • Confirmation proportional to risk. Viewing needs nothing. Pausing needs one click. Anything irreversible needs typed confirmation and lands in the journal.
  • Read-only by default. The page loads in view mode; switching to control mode is explicit.

Figure 10.4.2 — Friction rises with risk. Read the steps from bottom left to top right. Viewing (green) needs no confirmation, pausing needs one click, and an irreversible action (orange) needs typed confirmation plus a journal entry. The whole page starts read-only.

The principle: the portal cannot do anything a careful runbook would not. It just makes the runbook faster.

10.4.5 Authorisation, properly

Admin routes check group membership on the server for every request. Hiding admin links from non-admins is cosmetic. The API behind each control re-verifies the token, the group and the action’s bounds independently.

10.4.6 Lessons learned

Lesson Why
Status pages lie when computed in the browser A failed API call can look like “no problems”. Compute the roll-up on the server and return an explicit “unknown” when a check cannot run.
Unknown is a state Ok, warn, fail and unknown. Never let unknown render as ok.
Fewer numbers, more states A wall of metrics hides the signal. The banner is the product; tables are for drilling in.
Don’t build controls you’ll never use Each control is an attack surface and a maintenance cost. No place in the runbook, no button.

10.4.7 Summary

  • The banner is the maximum (worst) of all checks, and stale checks count as warnings.
  • The journal is append-only; corrections are new entries.
  • Controls are allow-listed, range-checked on the server and confirmed in proportion to risk.
  • Authorisation is enforced on the server for every request.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Checks return ok, ok, warn, ok. What does the banner show? (Answer: warn, i.e. degraded.)
  2. (Apply) A check last ran 3 hours ago and said ok. How should the banner treat it?
  3. (Think) Why is an average of check states a bad roll-up? Give a case where it hides a failure.
  4. (Design) Pick one admin action you use. Which confirmation level does it need, and why?

Further reading

  • Betsy Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering, “Being On-Call” and “Managing Incidents”.
  • Atul Gawande, The Checklist Manifesto.
  • OWASP Top 10, “Broken Access Control”.

— Tariq

Chapter 10.5 — SEO for Daily Generated Content: JSON-LD, Sitemaps and Canonicals

Subtitle: Publishing a new page every day is easy. Getting search engines to understand which page matters is not.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain the duplicate-content problem for templated daily pages. 2. Set canonical URLs, sitemaps and JSON-LD correctly. 3. Use a simple crawl-budget model to decide what to keep out of the index.

You need: what a URL, an HTML <head> and a search crawler are.

10.5.1 The problem

My site publishes a market report every trading day, plus education articles and research pages. That is a lot of near-identical pages: same template, same headings, different numbers. Search engines are wary of that pattern, because it is also what spam looks like.

10.5.2 Duplicate content

Daily reports share most of their boilerplate. If two URLs serve substantially the same content, a search engine picks one as canonical (the official copy) and may ignore the rest. Worse, if your own site exposes the same report under several URLs (with and without a trailing slash, with tracking parameters, an old route and a new one), you split ranking signals across copies.

10.5.3 Canonical URLs

Every page declares one canonical URL with <link rel="canonical">. My site builds it from the cleaned request path: no query strings, no trailing-slash variants, legacy routes mapped to their current home. When I merged the legal pages into one document, the old routes kept working but declared the new page as canonical.

Rules for canonicals. - Absolute URLs with the production origin, never relative. - Self-referencing canonicals on every indexable page. - One canonical per page, rendered on the server so crawlers see it without running JavaScript. - Never canonicalise to a page that redirects or returns an error.

Figure 10.5.1 — Many addresses, one official copy. Four ways of reaching the same report (plain, trailing slash, tracking parameter, legacy route) all declare the same canonical URL. “DATE” stands for any report date. The canonical target itself must return the page, not a redirect or error.

10.5.4 Sitemaps

A sitemap lists the URLs you want crawled, with optional last-modified dates. For a site that grows daily, generate it from the content store. Next.js supports a sitemap.ts route that returns entries at request or build time; a matching robots.ts points crawlers at it and keeps private areas (admin, auth) out.

Two details matter:

  • lastmod must be truthful. If every URL claims to have changed today, crawlers learn to ignore the field. Use the real modification date.
  • Size limits. One sitemap is capped at 50,000 URLs and 50 MB uncompressed. Plan a sitemap index before you need it.

10.5.5 Structured data with JSON-LD

JSON-LD is a <script type="application/ld+json"> block that describes the page using schema.org vocabulary.

Page type Schema.org type
Daily report Article (or NewsArticle if it genuinely is news): headline, dates, author, publisher
Whole site Organization, WebSite
Education page Article, or Course where it fits
Navigation BreadcrumbList

Structured data does not rank you higher by itself. It helps search engines understand the page and makes you eligible for richer results. It must match the visible content: marking up claims the page does not show is a policy violation.

10.5.6 Making daily pages distinct

The honest fix for near-duplication is to make each page genuinely different where it matters:

  • a unique, specific title and meta description built from that day’s content;
  • a narrative summary that differs day to day, not just the numbers;
  • a clear date in the title, URL and visible header;
  • internal links from a dated archive, so each report is reachable in a few clicks.

10.5.7 Crawl budget, roughly

Model. Suppose a crawler gives your site about B fetches per day. You publish n new pages a day and keep M old ones. If new pages are fetched first, the leftover budget is B − n, so each old page is revisited about every

MB−n days. \frac{M}{B - n} \text{ days.}

Figure 10.5.2 — The archive slows its own revisits. Both lines use an illustrative budget of B = 1,000 fetches a day. As the archive M grows, the gap between revisits grows in a straight line. Publishing more new pages a day (orange) makes the slope steeper. These are formula curves, not crawl logs.

That argues for keeping low-value pages out of the sitemap and using noindex for pages that should not compete, so crawl effort goes where it is useful.

10.5.8 Pitfalls

  • Client-only rendering of titles and canonicals. Crawlers may not wait for your JavaScript.
  • Soft 404s: an empty report page that returns 200. Return a real 404, or do not publish.
  • Indexing admin or auth routes by accident. robots.txt is not access control, but it keeps them out of results. Authorisation keeps them private.
  • Financial content and trust. Search engines hold finance pages to a higher standard. Clear authorship, dates, disclaimers and no exaggerated claims help readers and rankings alike.

10.5.9 Summary

  • Templated daily pages look like duplicates; give each one canonical, absolute, server-rendered URL.
  • Generate sitemaps from the content store with truthful lastmod dates.
  • JSON-LD aids understanding, not ranking, and must match visible content.
  • Revisit interval ≈ M/(B − n): keep low-value pages out so the budget goes where it matters.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) B = 2,000, n = 100, M = 38,000. How often is an old page revisited? (Answer: 38,000 / 1,900 = 20 days.)
  2. (Apply) List three URL variants of one report your site might expose by accident.
  3. (Think) Why does setting every lastmod to today hurt you over time?
  4. (Design) Write a title and meta description for a daily report that would differ from the day before.

Further reading

  • Google Search Central, “Consolidate duplicate URLs”.
  • schema.org, Article and BreadcrumbList types.
  • sitemaps.org protocol specification.

— Tariq

Chapter 10.6 — Legal and Consent Flows for a Small Financial Content Site

Subtitle: Terms, privacy, cookies and risk disclaimers aren’t decoration. They’re state you have to store and prove.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Treat legal documents as versioned, immutable artefacts. 2. Record and enforce terms acceptance on the server. 3. Build a cookie-consent flow that actually honours the choice.

You need: what a database record and a cookie are.

10.6.1 Scope and caveat

I am not a lawyer, and this is not legal advice. It is an engineer’s account of the plumbing behind legal pages and consent on a site that publishes market content and has user accounts.

My site has terms of service, a privacy policy, a cookie policy, an end-user licence agreement and a risk disclaimer. Registered users accept the current terms. Visitors choose cookie preferences.

10.6.2 Documents are versioned artefacts

The first mistake is editing legal text in place. If a user accepted the terms in August and you changed them in October, which version did they accept? You must be able to answer that.

Each legal document has: - a version identifier and an effective date; - content that is immutable once published (a new version is a new artefact); - a stable URL for the current version, and retrievable past versions.

I eventually merged the separate legal pages into one continuous document with anchored sections; the old URLs redirect to the matching section. Readers get one place to read, and the canonical URL is unambiguous.

10.6.3 Acceptance is a record, not a checkbox

When a user accepts terms, store a record: user, document, version, timestamp (UTC), and how it was accepted (which flow). Then:

  • Gate on the current version. On sign-in, if the user’s latest accepted version is older than the current required one, show the acceptance flow before continuing.
  • Never pre-tick boxes. Consent must be an affirmative action.
  • Make the text readable before accepting. A link to a 10,000-word document is not much, but a scroll-trapped modal is worse. Show a summary and the full text.

Gate condition. Access to gated features requires

vaccepted(u)≥vrequired, v_{\text{accepted}}(u) \ge v_{\text{required}},

checked on the server. The UI prompt is a convenience; the server check is the rule.

Figure 10.6.1 — The sign-in gate. After sign-in the server compares the user’s accepted version with the required one. Yes (green) opens the features. No (orange) shows the acceptance flow, with no pre-ticked boxes; accepting stores the record and then opens the features.

10.6.4 Cookie consent

Depending on where visitors are, privacy laws (GDPR and the ePrivacy rules in Europe, various US state laws) require consent before non-essential cookies or tracking. The engineering:

  • Categorise cookies. Strictly necessary ones (session, security) need no consent; analytics and marketing do.
  • Default to off for anything non-essential until the visitor chooses.
  • Make “reject” as easy as “accept”. Same prominence, same number of clicks.
  • Store the choice with a version, and ask again when categories change.
  • Actually honour it. Load analytics scripts only after consent. A banner that records “no” while the tag fires anyway is worse than no banner.

Figure 10.6.2 — Consent as three states. Every visitor starts with non-essential cookies off. Accept and reject are equally easy paths. When the cookie categories change, both stored choices lead back (dashed) to “no choice yet”, so the visitor is asked again.

10.6.5 Risk disclaimers for market content

Content about trading carries real risk for readers. The disclaimer should sit where the content is, not buried in a footer: educational purpose, not personalised advice, past performance does not predict future results, leveraged products can lose more than the initial deposit.

I also hold my own content to it. The site does not publish performance claims. I would rather the disclaimer be true by construction than a shield for something misleading.

10.6.6 Data subject requests

Privacy laws give people rights to access and delete their data. Even a small site needs a process: where is this user’s data (identity pool, application tables, logs, email provider), how do I export it, and how do I delete it? Draw that map early; it is painful to rebuild later.

10.6.7 Pitfalls

Pitfall Fix
Editing legal text in place New version, new artefact
Consent stored only in the browser Fine for cookie choices; not for account terms
Third-party scripts setting cookies before the consent manager loads Load them only after consent
Logs full of personal data Log user IDs, not emails

10.6.8 Summary

  • Legal documents are immutable, versioned artefacts with stable URLs.
  • Acceptance is a stored record, enforced on the server at sign-in.
  • Cookie consent defaults to off, makes reject as easy as accept, and is actually honoured.
  • Map where each user’s data lives before someone asks for it.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A user accepted terms version 3; version 4 is now required. What happens at sign-in? (Answer: the acceptance flow is shown before gated features open.)
  2. (Apply) List the five fields of an acceptance record.
  3. (Think) Why is a banner that records “no” but still loads analytics worse than no banner at all?
  4. (Design) Sketch the data map for one user on a site you know: where would their data be?

Further reading

  • Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Articles 6, 7 and 17.
  • UK ICO guidance on cookies and similar technologies.
  • FINRA and CFTC investor education pages on risk disclosure (US context).

— Tariq

Chapter 10.7 — Dual-Layer Reports: A Technical Archive and a Plain-Language Narrative

Subtitle: One report, two readers. The trick is making sure the friendly version can’t drift from the facts.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why two independently written reports drift apart. 2. Describe a two-layer report built from one data source. 3. Write a consistency check between a narrative and its numbers. 4. Use a readability formula as a regression test.

You need: what JSON is, and basic set notation (⊆ means “is contained in”).

10.7.1 Two audiences

My daily market report has two audiences. One wants every figure: levels, changes, breadth, volatility, positioning. The other wants to know, in plain words, what happened and why it might matter, ideally in something they could listen to.

In July I restructured the reports into two layers stored together: a technical archive and a human narrative layer, with an audio-optimised variant.

10.7.2 The layers

  • Layer 1: technical archive. A verbatim copy of every figure and analysis in the technical report, stored under its own key in the report’s JSON. No rounding, no simplification. It is the audit trail.
  • Layer 2: narrative. The same day told as a story: what set the tone, what pushed against it, how it resolved. Short sentences, defined terms. The audio variant goes further: shorter sentences, no nested acronyms, numbers phrased for speech.

Both live in one JSON document per day, so they are published, archived and versioned together.

10.7.3 Why not just write a simpler report?

Because two independently written reports drift. The friendly one gets a number slightly wrong, or says “rallied” on a flat day, and now there are two versions of the truth. Keeping both in one artefact, generated from one data source, with explicit checks between them, is the defence.

10.7.4 How the narrative is built

The narrative is produced by code, not free-written. A transformer step extracts the key metrics from the same data that produced the archive, then builds the story in stages: headline, short deck, lede, a “conflict” section (what pushed against the day’s tone) and a “resolution”. Along the way it translates jargon into plain words and rewrites numbers into readable forms (compressing large figures, phrasing percentages). For the audio variant it also shortens sentences and escapes characters that would break speech markup.

Main consistency guard. Every number in the narrative is rendered from a field in the archive. So the two layers cannot disagree about a figure unless the rendering code is wrong, and rendering code can be unit-tested.

Figure 10.7.1 — Two layers, one source. The day’s figures flow both into the verbatim archive and into metric extraction, which feeds the narrative stages (and then the audio variant). The green check compares the two layers. Because extraction reads the same fields as the archive, the check rarely has anything to catch.

10.7.5 If you let a language model write it

Many people will want a model to draft the friendly layer. Models are good at tone and bad at copying numbers faithfully, so you would need an explicit check.

Containment check. Let A be the set of numeric facts in the archive and N the set of numeric mentions extracted from the narrative. Require

N⊆A(up to an agreed formatting map). N \subseteq A \quad \text{(up to an agreed formatting map)}.

The formatting map covers legitimate changes: rounding for speech, percent versus basis points, “half a percent” for 0.5%. Any narrative number not in A fails. Directional words (“rose”, “fell”) are checked against the sign of the figure they describe. Deterministic rendering makes most of this unnecessary, which is a good argument for it.

10.7.6 Writing for a general reader

  • Define a term the first time you use it, or do not use it.
  • One idea per sentence.
  • Say what a number means, not just what it is.
  • No predictions dressed as observations. “Volatility rose” is an observation. “Volatility will keep rising” is a forecast, and the narrative does not make those.

Flesch–Kincaid grade level.

FKGL=0.39wordssentences+11.8syllableswords−15.59 \text{FKGL} = 0.39\,\frac{\text{words}}{\text{sentences}} + 11.8\,\frac{\text{syllables}}{\text{words}} - 15.59

Readability formulas are blunt, but useful as a regression check: if a change to the drafting step suddenly raises the grade level, something drifted.

10.7.7 Pitfalls

Pitfall Example Guard
Humanised numbers drift 0.48% → “about half a percent” is fine; “nearly one percent” is not Tests for number-phrasing rules
Tone versus data A dramatic story on a quiet day misleads Tone proportional to the size of moves
Schema drift Archive schema changes and a field silently drops out of the story A test asserting the key metrics were found

10.7.8 Summary

  • Store the technical archive and the narrative in one document per day, from one data source.
  • Render narrative numbers from archive fields; that is the main consistency guard.
  • If a model writes text, require N ⊆ A and check direction words against signs.
  • Use readability scores as regression tests, not targets.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A sentence has 20 words and 30 syllables. Compute FKGL. (Answer: 0.39·20 + 11.8·1.5 − 15.59 = 7.8 + 17.7 − 15.59 ≈ 9.9.)
  2. (Apply) The archive says −0.3%. The narrative says “stocks edged higher”. Which check fails?
  3. (Think) Why is deterministic rendering a stronger guard than checking model output afterwards?
  4. (Design) Write three entries for a formatting map (archive form → allowed narrative form).

Further reading

  • Rudolf Flesch, “A New Readability Yardstick” (1948).
  • Plain Language Action and Information Network, Federal Plain Language Guidelines.
  • Ehud Reiter and Robert Dale, Building Natural Language Generation Systems.

— Tariq

Chapter 10.8 — Automated Post-Market Feedback Loops

Subtitle: A morning report that never checks itself is a horoscope. Here’s how mine gets graded every afternoon.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe the six steps of a daily grade-and-constrain loop. 2. Explain why structured output is the prerequisite for grading. 3. Normalise errors by volatility using the average true range. 4. Judge how much a few weeks of grades can tell you.

You need: averages, and the idea of a standard error (how uncertain an estimate is).

10.8.1 Why grade a report

Every trading day my pipeline publishes a pre-market report with context: reference levels, scenarios, the fundamental backdrop. That kind of report is easy to write and hard to evaluate. So after the close, a second job grades the morning report against what actually happened and feeds the grade into the next morning’s draft.

This chapter describes the shape of that loop. It deliberately leaves out how levels are computed and what the grading thresholds are.

10.8.2 The loop

  1. Morning: the report is generated and archived as structured data, not just prose. Every level and scenario is a field.
  2. After the close: a feedback job loads that report and the session’s intraday data, limited to the regular session window.
  3. Grade: it measures how price interacted with each published level, whether key reclaim or break scenarios held, how fast price moved after scheduled events, and whether the morning’s directional lean matched the session.
  4. Summarise: it produces a compact accuracy summary and a short written retrospective, drafted with a language model from the computed results, not instead of them.
  5. Constrain tomorrow: if the grade is poor, the next draft runs in a more cautious mode, with explicit rules about how confidently it may state continuation scenarios.
  6. Aggregate weekly: a digest rolls up the daily grades so trends show through the noise.

Figure 10.8.1 — Grade, then constrain. Steps 1–5 run left to right each day. The blue arrow back to the morning only ever makes wording more cautious. Step 6 collects grades into a weekly digest. The morning report itself is never edited.

10.8.3 Structured output is the prerequisite

You cannot grade prose. “Watch for support near the prior low” cannot be checked. A field holding a level can. The single most important decision was making the morning report emit machine-readable claims alongside the narrative.

10.8.4 Volatility-normalised error

Raw distance between a level and where price turned means little across days: three points on a calm day is not three points on a wild one. So distances are divided by a measure of the day’s typical range, such as the average true range (ATR) over short bars.

Definition. For bar t with high HtH_t, low LtL_t and previous close Ct−1C_{t-1}:

TRt=max⁡(Ht−Lt,|Ht−Ct−1|,|Lt−Ct−1|),ATR=1n∑tTRt. \text{TR}_t = \max\big(H_t - L_t,\; |H_t - C_{t-1}|,\; |L_t - C_{t-1}|\big),\qquad \text{ATR} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_t \text{TR}_t.

An overshoot of d points becomes d / ATR, which is comparable across sessions.

This is the same idea as a z-score: express error in units of the noise.

10.8.5 Guarding against self-deception

A feedback loop can fool you as easily as help you.

  • Grade after the fact; never revise the morning report. The archive is immutable. The grade is a new artefact.
  • Use only data from the session being graded. No peeking at the next day to decide whether a level “really” held.
  • Small samples are noisy. With a daily hit indicator, the standard error of a hit rate over n days is p̂(1−p̂)/n\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}, which is wide for a few weeks of data.
  • The constraint is one-directional. A poor grade makes tomorrow’s language more cautious. A good grade never makes it more aggressive. Recent success is not evidence of an edge.

Figure 10.8.2 — Four weeks of grades is a wide band. The shaded area is the 95% range p̂ ± 1.96·√(p̂(1−p̂)/n), drawn with p̂ = 50% for illustration. At 20 graded days a hit rate is uncertain by about ±22 points; at 250 days, about ±6. This is a formula curve, not my grades. It is why the weekly digest is read for trends with that width in mind.

10.8.6 Is this “learning”?

Not in the machine-learning sense. Nothing is fitted. It is closer to a control loop with a governor: measure, compare, and limit the next output when the last one was poor. That is deliberate. A loop that re-tuned levels automatically from a few days of outcomes would be curve-fitting with extra steps.

10.8.7 Engineering details that mattered

  • Idempotent on the date. Re-running the grader for a date overwrites that date’s grade; it never appends a second one.
  • Hard alerts are separate from grades. A poor grade is information. Certain outcomes also raise an explicit alert, so I read the retrospective that day instead of finding it in the weekly digest.
  • Corpus building. Each graded day is appended to a session corpus, rebuilt from source files rather than patched, so a corrected day propagates.

10.8.8 Pitfalls

Pitfall Effect Fix
Data-source mismatch Different session times or adjustments create fake errors Same source, or reconcile explicitly
Holidays and half-days The grader scores an empty session Skip or handle them
Retrospective model over-explains Confident causes for random outcomes Quote computed results; say “cause unknown” when it is

10.8.9 Summary

  • Grade the morning report every afternoon, and let a poor grade only make tomorrow more cautious.
  • Structured, field-based claims are what make grading possible.
  • Normalise errors by ATR so days are comparable.
  • A few weeks of grades carry wide error bars; read trends, not days.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Price overshot a level by 6 points; ATR was 4. What is the normalised error? (Answer: 1.5 ATR.)
  2. (Apply) Over 25 days the hit rate is 60%. Compute the standard error and a rough 95% range.
  3. (Think) Why should a good grade never make the next report more aggressive?
  4. (Design) Rewrite “watch for support near the prior low” as a checkable field.

Further reading

  • J. Welles Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (ATR).
  • Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner, Superforecasting, on scoring forecasts.
  • Glenn W. Brier, “Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability” (1950).

— Tariq

Chapter 10.9 — Discord Automation: Webhooks, Embeds and Alerts That Expire Gracefully

Subtitle: A chat channel is a surprisingly good operations console, as long as you respect its limits.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Choose webhooks over bots for one-way messages and keep webhook URLs secret. 2. Stay within Discord’s embed and rate limits. 3. Design alerts that fire on transitions, remind rarely and announce recovery. 4. Estimate how much a “k bad checks in a row” rule cuts false alerts.

You need: HTTP POST and status codes; basic probability.

10.9.1 Why Discord

Discord is where my automation talks to me. The daily report announcement, system alerts, heartbeat warnings and recovery notices all land in channels there. It is free, it is on my phone, and it has a decent API. It also has rate limits, payload limits, and a way of turning into noise if you are careless.

10.9.2 Webhooks, not bots, for one-way messages

A webhook is a URL that accepts a POST and posts a message to one channel. No gateway connection, no bot process to keep alive, no permission model to configure. For anything one-way (reports, alerts) it is the right tool.

A webhook URL is a secret. Anyone who has it can post to your channel. I keep webhook URLs as encrypted parameters and fetch them at runtime. They never appear in code, logs or committed config. If one leaks, delete and recreate it.

Separate webhooks per purpose (reports, alerts, automation logs) mean a noisy source cannot drown an important one.

10.9.3 Embeds and their limits

Plain text is fine for alerts. For a daily report summary, embeds are better: a title, description, coloured accent, fields, footer and image. My report post includes a short summary, a handful of fields with key context, and an attached rendered image of the report page.

Limit Value
Field value 1,024 characters
Description 4,096 characters
Total across one embed 6,000 characters
Fields per embed 25
Embeds per message 10

The posting code shortens every field to a safe length with an ellipsis rather than letting Discord reject the whole message. A rejected message is a silently missing report unless you check the response.

10.9.4 Rate limits

Discord returns HTTP 429 with a retry_after value when you exceed a rate limit, plus headers describing the bucket. Respect them: sleep for retry_after, then retry. Do not invent your own schedule. If several jobs post in bursts, serialise them.

10.9.5 Alerts with memory

The design that works best for me has three properties:

  1. Transition-based. Alert when something goes from healthy to unhealthy, not every time a check runs.
  2. Debounced reminders. While a problem lasts, re-alert only after a long interval.
  3. Recovery messages. When it is fixed, say so once.

That needs a little state per alert key, stored outside the function (a parameter or a small table), so the alerting function itself stays stateless.

Figure 10.9.1 — Alerts as a two-state machine. Moving from healthy to unhealthy (orange) sends one alert. Staying unhealthy loops back on itself and only reminds after a long interval. Returning to healthy (green) sends one recovery message. The state lives outside the function.

False-alert rate. If p is the chance a check sees a transient blip, alerting on every bad check sends about p × (number of checks) false alerts a day. Requiring k consecutive bad checks cuts that to about pkp^k per check, if blips are independent.

Figure 10.9.2 — Each extra confirmation multiplies by p. On a log scale, pkp^k falls in a straight line. With p = 0.2 (orange), two checks give 0.04 per check; with p = 0.05 (blue), three checks already give about 1 in 8,000. These are formula values that assume independent blips; real blips often cluster, so the true gain is smaller.

10.9.6 Token-expiry alerts

Some integrations depend on credentials that expire: broker authorisations, API tokens, certificates. The worst way to find out is a failed job, so expiry is monitored like any other health signal. If a token expires at texpt_{\text{exp}} and renewal needs a human (some OAuth flows require an interactive login), warnings go out at several lead times, each sent once:

warn at texp−δk,δ1>δ2>… \text{warn at } t_{\text{exp}} - \delta_k,\qquad \delta_1 > \delta_2 > \dots

The alert says what expires, when, and the exact step to renew. An alert without the fix is just anxiety.

10.9.7 Testing the poster

The posting module has its own tests: field truncation at the limits, missing optional data, formatting of percentages and large numbers, and a failed HTTP response surfacing as an error rather than being swallowed. Notification code is easy to neglect because it “only” sends messages. It is also the code that tells you everything else broke.

10.9.8 Pitfalls

  • Mentions. @everyone in an automated message is a good way to get muted. Use allowed_mentions to control pings.
  • Markdown injection. Escape external text (headlines, error messages), or it will render oddly or mention people.
  • Silent failures. Check the HTTP status of every post, and log failures somewhere that is not Discord.
  • Personal data. Do not post user emails or account identifiers to a chat channel.

10.9.9 Summary

  • Use webhooks for one-way messages and treat their URLs as secrets.
  • Truncate to the embed limits and obey 429 retry_after.
  • Alert on transitions, remind rarely, announce recovery once; keep the state outside the function.
  • Requiring k bad checks cuts independent false alerts to about pkp^k per check.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) p = 0.1 and you require 3 bad checks in a row. False-alert chance per check? (Answer: 0.001.)
  2. (Apply) An embed field holds 1,500 characters. What should the poster do?
  3. (Think) Why does clustering of blips (one network hiccup causing several bad checks) weaken the pkp^k estimate?
  4. (Design) Write the text of a token-expiry alert that includes what, when and how to fix it.

Further reading

  • Discord Developer Documentation, “Webhook Resource” and “Rate Limits”.
  • Discord Developer Documentation, “Embed Limits”.
  • Betsy Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering, “Practical Alerting”.

— Tariq

Chapter 10.10 — Broker OAuth Token Renewal Without Waking Up at 3 a.m.

Subtitle: Access tokens expire in minutes, refresh tokens in days, and the human-in-the-loop step is the one that bites.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Walk through the OAuth 2.0 authorisation code flow. 2. Schedule proactive refreshes with a safety margin. 3. Avoid the rotating-refresh-token race with a single writer. 4. Plan staged warnings for the step that needs a human.

You need: what an API token is; the idea of a probability.

10.10.1 The situation

Several of my data and brokerage integrations use OAuth 2.0. That is good for security and annoying for automation, because tokens expire and some renewals need a person. This chapter covers the pattern I use to keep integrations alive and to fail loudly and early when they cannot be.

Nothing here is specific to one broker. Lifetimes and flows differ by provider, so check their documentation.

10.10.2 The OAuth pieces

In the authorisation code flow:

  1. The user is sent to the provider’s login page and approves access.
  2. The provider redirects back with a short-lived authorisation code.
  3. Your server exchanges the code (plus client credentials, and a PKCE verifier if used) for an access token and usually a refresh token. (PKCE, “proof key for code exchange”, stops a stolen code from being used.)
  4. The access token goes on API calls. When it expires, the refresh token gets a new one.
  5. When the refresh token expires or is revoked, you are back to step 1, with a human.

Typical shape: access tokens last minutes to an hour; refresh tokens last days to months. Some providers rotate the refresh token on every use, invalidating the old one.

10.10.3 Proactive refresh

Do not wait for a 401 (unauthorised) error. Refresh before expiry, with a margin.

Refresh time. If an access token was issued at t0t_0 with lifetime L, refresh at

trefresh=t0+L−m, t_{\text{refresh}} = t_0 + L - m,

with margin m larger than clock skew plus the slowest refresh call you have observed.

Handle the 401 path anyway: tokens can be revoked early.

Figure 10.10.1 — Two clocks. Top: each access token is replaced at the green dashed line, a margin m before it expires, so the next token overlaps the old one. Bottom: the refresh token lives much longer, but when it expires (orange line) a human must log in. The three triangles are staged warnings before that moment. Lengths are schematic.

10.10.4 Single writer

The nastiest bug with rotating refresh tokens is a race. Two processes refresh at once with the same refresh token. The provider accepts the first, rotates it, and rejects the second, or in some implementations treats the reuse as theft and revokes the whole grant.

Fix. Exactly one component owns refreshing. Everything else reads the current access token from a shared store. If you must refresh from several places, use a lock (a conditional write works) so only one refresh happens at a time.

Figure 10.10.2 — Race versus single writer. Left: two processes present the same refresh token; one wins and the other is rejected, or the grant is revoked. Right: one refresher talks to the provider and writes both new tokens to a shared store in one atomic step; every other caller only reads.

10.10.5 Storage

Tokens are credentials. Store them encrypted, restrict read access to the components that need them, never log them, and never put them in URLs. Write the new token pair atomically: if you store the new access token and fail before storing the rotated refresh token, you have locked yourself out.

10.10.6 The human step

When the refresh token itself nears expiry, automation cannot help; a person must log in. The pattern:

  • track refresh-token expiry as a monitored value;
  • alert ahead of time with the renewal steps;
  • make renewal short: one link that starts authorisation, a callback that completes the exchange and stores tokens, and a confirmation message;
  • after renewal, run a health-check call to confirm the new grant works.

10.10.7 How much margin is enough?

Outage probability. Let R be the time until someone acts on an alert. If the first warning goes out δ before expiry, the chance of an outage is

P(R>δ). P(R > \delta).

You cannot make R small at 3 a.m., but you can make δ large. Several staged warnings let the first one be early and ignorable, and the last one loud.

10.10.8 Failure modes to design for

Failure Defence
Clock skew makes a fresh token look expired, or the reverse Use the lifetime in the token response, measured from when you received it
Provider outage at refresh time Retry with backoff; keep using the current access token until it actually expires
Silent scope changes A renewed grant with fewer scopes works until one call fails; check granted scopes after renewal
Redirect URI mismatch after moving hosts The provider must know the exact callback URL

10.10.9 Testing

Simulate expiry. Use a fake clock or a tiny lifetime in a test double and confirm: proactive refresh fires, concurrent callers do not double-refresh, a revoked grant produces an alert, and no token value appears in logs. Expiry bugs only show up at expiry, so make expiry happen on demand.

10.10.10 Summary

  • Refresh at t0+L−mt_0 + L - m, and still handle early revocation.
  • One component refreshes; everyone else reads; write the token pair atomically.
  • The refresh token’s expiry needs a human: monitor it and warn in stages.
  • Make expiry testable with a fake clock.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A token issued at 10:00 lasts 30 minutes; margin 3 minutes. When do you refresh? (Answer: 10:27.)
  2. (Apply) Why must the access token and the rotated refresh token be written in one atomic step?
  3. (Think) If R is often 8 hours overnight, where would you put the first warning?
  4. (Design) List the four tests you would write for a token refresher.

Further reading

  • RFC 6749, The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework.
  • RFC 7636, Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients.
  • RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security.

— Tariq

Chapter 10.11 — Writing a Figma Plugin to Generate Diagrams from Data

Subtitle: When you redraw the same decision diagram for the fifth time, it’s time to make the computer draw it.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe the parts of a Figma plugin. 2. Use nested auto-layout frames instead of computing coordinates. 3. Explain the idea behind the Reingold–Tilford tree layout. 4. Convert a hex colour to Figma’s 0–1 RGB format.

You need: basic JavaScript, including async/await.

10.11.1 Why a plugin

I teach, and teaching needs diagrams: decision trees, order-of-analysis flows, “check this before that” charts. I used to draw them by hand in Figma. Every content change meant nudging boxes and re-aligning arrows. So I wrote a small Figma plugin that builds the diagram from data, using native frames and auto-layout, so the result stays fully editable.

A generated PNG is a dead end; you cannot tweak it. A plugin creates real nodes (frames, text, rectangles, connectors) that I can restyle like anything else. The plugin does the tedious 90% and leaves the taste-driven 10%.

10.11.2 Plugin anatomy

Part Role
manifest.json Names the plugin, points at the main script, declares supported editors (design files, FigJam boards, or both; mine supports both)
Main script Runs in a sandbox with the figma global: create nodes, set properties, read the selection, then call figma.closePlugin()
Optional UI Runs in an iframe and talks to the main script by messages. Mine has none; it builds and exits

10.11.3 Fonts first

Before you can set text, load the font with figma.loadFontAsync. Forget this and text creation throws. Load every weight you will use, once, up front.

10.11.4 Auto-layout does the geometry

Key insight. Do not compute coordinates. Give each card a frame with auto-layout (vertical stack, padding, spacing, hug contents) and put text inside; Figma sizes it. Put cards in a row frame with horizontal auto-layout, and rows in a column frame. The layout engine handles wrapping and alignment, and later edits reflow automatically.

Figure 10.11.1 — Frames inside frames. The grey dashed box is the column frame; it stacks the blue row frames vertically. Each row lays its cards out horizontally, and each card hugs its own text. No x or y value is ever set by the plugin.

For a tree, the structure maps naturally: each level is a row, each node a card.

10.11.5 Laying out trees properly

Laying out a tree so parents sit above children without overlap is a classic problem. The Reingold–Tilford algorithm solves it in O(n) time. It lays out each subtree on its own, then pushes neighbouring subtrees apart by the minimum separation along their facing outlines (contours).

Shift rule. Over shared depths d, with required separation s,

shift(TL,TR)=maxd(rightd(TL)−leftd(TR))+s. \text{shift}(T_L, T_R) = \max_{d}\big(\text{right}_d(T_L) - \text{left}_d(T_R)\big) + s.

Why it works. At each depth, right_d(T_L) − left_d(T_R) is how far the right subtree must move so its leftmost node sits exactly on the left subtree’s rightmost node. Taking the maximum over depths satisfies the tightest depth, and adding s leaves a gap everywhere.

Figure 10.11.2 — The tightest depth decides. Two subtrees face each other. The arrows show the gap at each depth. The bottom pair (green) is closest, so that depth sets how far apart the subtrees must be.

For the small diagrams I make, nested auto-layout frames are a good enough approximation without implementing the algorithm.

10.11.6 Styling as data

Colours, stroke weights and corner radii live in a small palette object, with helpers that turn hex colours into Figma’s 0–1 RGB format. Figma paints are arrays of paint objects, which trips people up the first time; a helper that returns a solid-fill array keeps the code readable. Changing the theme means editing one object.

Hex to RGB. For a 24-bit colour c,

r=⌊c/216⌋mod⁡256255,g=⌊c/28⌋mod⁡256255,b=cmod⁡256255. r = \frac{\lfloor c / 2^{16} \rfloor \bmod 256}{255},\quad g = \frac{\lfloor c / 2^{8} \rfloor \bmod 256}{255},\quad b = \frac{c \bmod 256}{255}.

10.11.7 Connectors

Arrows are the hardest part. FigJam has native connectors that attach to nodes and re-route when you move them. Design files do not, so you either draw vector lines (which do not follow moved nodes) or let layout imply the flow. Check figma.editorType and choose accordingly.

10.11.8 Pitfalls

  • Async everywhere. Font loading and some APIs are async. await them, or nodes appear half-styled.
  • Performance. Creating thousands of nodes is slow. Batch work and avoid reading layout properties in tight loops; each read forces a layout pass.
  • Viewport. Select and zoom to the result with figma.viewport.scrollAndZoomIntoView, or it looks like nothing happened.
  • Sandbox limits. The main thread has no DOM and no general network access; anything like that goes through the UI iframe.

10.11.9 Would I do it again?

Yes. The plugin is small, has no dependencies, and turned a recurring chore into a click. That is the best kind of automation: narrow, boring and used often.

10.11.10 Summary

  • A plugin is a manifest, a sandboxed main script and an optional UI iframe.
  • Load fonts first; let nested auto-layout frames do the geometry.
  • Reingold–Tilford separates subtrees by their tightest depth; auto-layout is enough for small diagrams.
  • Keep styling in one palette object; paints are arrays.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Convert #1BAF7A to Figma RGB. (Answer: r = 27/255 ≈ 0.106, g = 175/255 ≈ 0.686, b = 122/255 ≈ 0.478.)
  2. (Apply) At depths 0, 1, 2 the values right_d(T_L) − left_d(T_R) are −300, −200, −120, and s = 40. What is the shift?
  3. (Think) Why is reading a layout property inside a loop slow?
  4. (Design) Sketch the frame nesting for a three-level decision tree.

Further reading

  • Figma Plugin API documentation, “Plugin Quickstart Guide” and “Auto Layout”.
  • Edward Reingold and John Tilford, “Tidier Drawings of Trees” (1981).
  • Edward Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information.

— Tariq

Chapter 10.12 — macOS LaunchAgents for Background Agents

Subtitle: Cron’s quieter, more capable cousin, and the right home for small always-on helpers on a Mac.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Choose between a LaunchAgent and a LaunchDaemon. 2. Write the essential keys of a launchd plist. 3. Predict how periodic, calendar and keep-alive jobs behave around sleep and crashes. 4. Debug a job that works in Terminal but not under launchd.

You need: basic command-line use on macOS.

10.12.1 Why launchd

My Mac runs a handful of small background jobs: a local router service for AI agent decisions, a periodic refresh of a code graph, a knowledge-base refresh, a tunnel to a local model server, and a guard that watches my rule files for unauthorised changes. None deserves a server. All need to start at login, run on a schedule or stay alive, and log somewhere I can find. On macOS that is what launchd and LaunchAgents are for.

10.12.2 launchd in one paragraph

launchd is the process that starts everything on macOS. You describe a job in a property list (plist): what to run, when, and how.

LaunchDaemon LaunchAgent
Runs as root, system-wide the user, in their session
Starts at boot at login
Use for system services personal tooling that touches your files (~/Library/LaunchAgents)

10.12.3 The plist

Essential keys. - Label: a unique reverse-DNS name; how you refer to the job. - ProgramArguments: the executable and arguments as an array. No shell parsing: no globbing, no ~, no variable expansion. Use absolute paths. - RunAtLoad: start when loaded (at login). - StartInterval (every n seconds) or StartCalendarInterval (cron-like times). - KeepAlive: restart if it exits; can be conditional. - StandardOutPath / StandardErrorPath: where output goes. Without them it vanishes. - Nice and LowPriorityIO: be polite to the foreground.

10.12.4 Job shapes, sleep and drift

Two shapes cover most needs:

  1. Periodic jobs (StartInterval): run, do a bounded amount of work, exit. A drift guard or a refresh works like this. If a run is still going when the next is due, launchd will not start a second copy of the same job.
  2. Long-running services (KeepAlive): a local HTTP router or a tunnel. launchd restarts it if it dies, with throttling, so a crash loop does not spin as fast as it can.

For StartCalendarInterval, if the Mac was asleep at the scheduled time, the job runs on wake, and several missed runs are merged into one. StartInterval is a timer, so periodic jobs drift against the wall clock.

Spacing. If a job takes d seconds and the interval is I, runs are spaced about max(I, d) apart while awake, with gaps during sleep.

Figure 10.12.1 — Three ways a job lives. Top: a periodic job runs about every max(I, d) and simply pauses while the Mac sleeps (grey). Middle: calendar times missed during sleep (orange ×) become a single green catch-up run on wake. Bottom: a keep-alive service crashes and is restarted after a throttle delay. Schematic, not measured.

For “about every ten minutes” a timer is fine. For “at exactly this time”, use a calendar interval and expect a catch-up run after wake.

10.12.5 Managing jobs

Modern launchctl uses domains and service targets:

Command Does
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/<label>.plist load
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/<label> unload
launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/<label> restart now
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/<label> state, last exit code, run count

The older load/unload still work but report errors poorly. print is the single most useful debugging command.

10.12.6 Environment gotchas

LaunchAgents start with a minimal environment: a short PATH, no shell profile, no virtualenv activation. A script that works in Terminal fails under launchd because the interpreter resolves differently or a tool is not on the path. Fixes:

  • call interpreters by absolute path (for a virtualenv, its own binary);
  • set EnvironmentVariables in the plist for anything required;
  • run interpreters in isolated mode where available, so the current directory and user site packages do not leak onto the import path.

Privacy permissions (TCC, macOS’s consent system for protected folders) also apply. A job that reads protected folders may need Full Disk Access for its interpreter, and the prompt does not appear for a background job; it just fails.

10.12.7 Pitfalls

  • Logs that grow forever. Rotate them or keep jobs quiet.
  • Exit codes. A non-zero exit under KeepAlive triggers restarts; a crash loop is throttled but still burns CPU. Check print for the last exit status.
  • Plist syntax. plutil -lint before loading saves confusion.
  • Secrets in plists. Environment variables in a plist are readable by anything running as you. Use the keychain.
  • Watching the watchers. A background guard that silently stopped is worse than none, because you trust it. Have it write a heartbeat, and check it.

10.12.8 Summary

  • Personal background tooling belongs in a LaunchAgent with absolute paths and log files.
  • Periodic jobs drift and pause in sleep; calendar jobs catch up once on wake; keep-alive services restart with throttling.
  • launchctl print is the first debugging step.
  • Assume a bare environment, and give every guard a heartbeat.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) StartInterval is 600 s and a run takes 900 s. Roughly how far apart are runs? (Answer: about 900 s, since max(600, 900) = 900.)
  2. (Apply) A calendar job is due at 02:00 and 03:00; the Mac sleeps from 01:30 to 07:00. How many runs happen on wake?
  3. (Debug) A script works in Terminal but exits with “command not found” under launchd. Name two fixes.
  4. (Think) Why is a silently stopped guard worse than having no guard?

Further reading

  • Apple, Daemons and Services Programming Guide, “Creating Launch Daemons and Agents”.
  • man launchd.plist and man launchctl.
  • Jonathan Levin, *OS Internals, volume on user space.

— Tariq

Chapter 11.1 — My AI Assistant Quietly Swapped My Engine

Subtitle: The most dangerous thing an AI coding agent can do isn’t crash. It’s succeed at the wrong task.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe the “silent substitution” failure mode of AI coding agents. 2. Explain why wickless bars flatter strategies with stops inside the bar. 3. Name five engineering defences that make honesty enforceable.

You need: what a backtest and a price bar (open, high, low, close) are.

11.1.1 What happened

I do most of my building with AI coding agents. They are fast, tireless and good, often better than me at the boring parts. But in October I learned what their worst failure mode looks like, and it is not a crash.

My research engine is written in C#. That is deliberate: the code that runs live in NinjaTrader is C#, and I want research and live trading to share the same logic so they cannot drift apart.

I asked an agent to run a set of studies through that engine. It came back with neat result tables for several variants. Everything looked finished.

It was not. Somewhere along the way the C# run had been slow or awkward, so the agent had rebuilt the study in Python. Worse, the bars it built had no wicks: the highs and lows sat exactly on the open and close, as if price had never moved inside a bar. Any strategy whose stops or targets live inside a bar looks far better on data like that than it ever could in a real market.

Nothing in the output said “I substituted a different engine and different data”. It just said “done”.

Figure 11.1.1 — The honest path and the silent swap. Green is what was asked: the required engine on real ticks, producing a result with receipts. Blue is the honest way out when that path is blocked: stop and report. Orange is what happened: a slow engine led to an other-language rebuild on wickless bars, reported as “done” with no mention of the swap.

11.1.2 Why this is the scary failure

A crash you notice. A wrong answer that looks right gets built on. If I had not looked closely, those tables would have shaped weeks of decisions.

The agent was not malicious. It was optimising for finishing the task. When the honest path was blocked, “finish anyway with something similar” looked like success. Many people work the same way under deadline pressure. The difference is that an agent does it in seconds and never mentions it.

Definition (silent substitution). Replacing a required engine, dataset or method with an easier one, and presenting the output as if it came from the required one.

11.1.3 What I built

I stopped treating “please be honest” as a prompt and started treating it as engineering.

Defence What it does
1. A written list of forbidden substitutions Names specific dodges: running the study in another language; cached or resampled data instead of the real tick source; bars without wicks; filling at the signal price instead of the next real trade; reporting the best run and hiding the rest. An agent cannot argue it did not know.
2. “BLOCKED” as a first-class answer If the required engine or data is unavailable, the agent stops and reports in a fixed format: what failed, what it tried, what it could substitute and what that would change, and that it has not done it.
3. No receipt, no result Every number carries its evidence: engine version, a fingerprint of the exact data, a check that bars have real wicks, the fill model, a hash of the output file, and how many variations were tried. Missing any of these, the number is labelled unproven.
4. Hooks, not hope Hooks run around the agent’s actions and check its final messages. A small background job watches the rule files themselves, so nobody (human or agent) can quietly water them down.
5. Confession is not a fix If an agent discovers it broke a rule, saying sorry does not rescue the output. Everything produced by the violation is marked invalid and never reused.

“I couldn’t do this” is always acceptable. A quietly degraded answer never is. Later chapters in this part cover each defence in detail.

11.1.4 What changed

The agents are a little slower and a lot more trustworthy. More of my sessions now end with “BLOCKED: here’s why” than with a beautiful table, and I have come to like that. I would rather get an honest “I couldn’t” than a fabricated “done”.

The bigger lesson goes beyond trading. If you use AI agents on anything where a wrong answer is expensive (finance, medicine, infrastructure), “the output looks finished” is not evidence. Ask what it would take to prove the answer, then make the agent bring that proof every time.

11.1.5 Summary

  • The worst agent failure is a finished-looking answer built on a silent substitution.
  • Wickless bars hide stops and targets inside the bar, so results look better than they can be.
  • Defences: named forbidden substitutions, BLOCKED as a valid answer, receipts, hooks, and invalidating outputs from violations.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Name two signs that a backtest was run on wickless bars. (Answer: highs equal max(open, close) and lows equal min(open, close) on almost every bar; stops inside the bar are almost never hit.)
  2. (Apply) An agent reports “done” with a results table. List the questions you would ask before reading the numbers.
  3. (Think) Why does an agent under “finish the task” pressure tend to substitute rather than stop?
  4. (Design) Write one forbidden-substitution rule for a domain you work in.

Further reading

  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning, on backtesting pitfalls.
  • Atul Gawande, The Checklist Manifesto, on making the right step hard to skip.

— Tariq

Chapter 11.2 — No Receipt, No Result

Subtitle: A backtest number without its evidence isn’t a weak result. It isn’t a result at all.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. List the seven parts of a backtest receipt and the question each answers. 2. Explain reproducibility as pinning every argument of a function. 3. Explain why the rule is binary: six of seven is still no result.

You need: what a git commit and a file hash are (a hash is a short fingerprint of a file’s exact bytes).

11.2.1 The rule

In my research workflow one rule does more work than all the others: every number about a backtest must arrive with its receipts. If it cannot, it is written as “unprovenanced, not a result”, and nobody, including me, builds on it.

That sounds bureaucratic. In practice it is the cheapest defence I know against fooling myself, and against AI agents that are very good at producing tidy tables.

11.2.2 What a receipt contains

# Item Contents Question it answers
1 Engine harness path, git commit, dirty flag, exact command Would the same code give the same answer? (A dirty tree means the commit describes code that did not run.)
2 Data canonical tick source, SHA-256, sessions (first, last, count), exclusions Was it really that data?
3 Bars bar builder and parameters, plus a wick census Were the bars real?
4 Fills fill model, slippage per side, commission, latency, entry rule (first trade strictly after the signal) How optimistic was execution?
5 Output result file path and hash; catalog run ID once imported Is this the file you are quoting from?
6 Trials how many configurations were tried in this search How hard did you search?
7 Validation passed, failed with named gates, or not evaluated Did it survive the tests designed to kill it?

Notes on why each matters:

  • Data hash. Two files with the same name can differ. If h=SHA256(D)h = \text{SHA256}(D), finding a different D′ with the same h is computationally infeasible, so matching hashes is as close to proof of identity as engineering gets.
  • Wick census. Bars with no wicks make many strategies look far better than they can be (Chapter 11.3).
  • Fill model. Two runs with different fill assumptions are not comparable.
  • Output hash. Stops numbers being copied from a stale or edited file.
  • Trial count. The best of a thousand configurations is expected to look good by luck alone (Chapter 11.4).
  • Validation state. “Not evaluated” is a valid state, but it must be stated.

11.2.3 Reproducibility as a function

Model. Think of a backtest as a function

R=fθ(D;c,m), R = f_{\theta}(D;\, c, m),

where c is the code version, D the data, m the execution model and θ the parameters. A result is reproducible only if every argument is pinned.

Why. Leave one argument out and R is no longer one number. It is a draw from an unknown spread of results over all the values that argument could have taken. The receipt is simply the list of arguments.

Figure 11.2.1 — The receipt pins every input. Five inputs on the left (code, data, bars, execution model, settings) feed the engine run f. Out come the result file with its hash and the validation state. If any input box were blank, the output would be one sample from an unknown spread.

11.2.4 What “no result” means in practice

Without a full receipt, the number does not appear in reports, summaries or decisions. It is not “preliminary”. It is not “promising”. Those words would let it leak into decisions while dodging the rule. The literal text that replaces the number makes the gap visible.

This also changes how I read AI-agent output. An agent that returns a table without receipts has returned prose, not results. The response is to ask for the receipts, not to evaluate the numbers.

11.2.5 Costs

Receipts take effort. Hashing large tick files takes time; recording trial counts means keeping a ledger; listing exclusions means knowing them. The effort pays back the first time a number has to be defended, or the first time it cannot be, and you find that out before acting on it.

11.2.6 Pitfalls

  • Receipts copied, not computed. A hash typed from memory is worthless. Receipts must be produced by the run itself.
  • Partial receipts. Six of seven is still no result. The rule is binary on purpose.
  • Hashing the wrong thing. Hash the exact bytes the engine read, not a sibling file.

11.2.7 Summary

  • Seven receipt items: engine, data, bars, fills, output, trials, validation.
  • A receipt is the list of a backtest’s arguments; leave one out and the number is not reproducible.
  • No full receipt means the literal text “unprovenanced, not a result”, never “preliminary”.
  • Receipts must be computed by the run, on the exact bytes it read.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A run’s commit is recorded but the tree was dirty. Is the engine item satisfied? (Answer: no; the commit does not describe the code that ran.)
  2. (Apply) A table arrives with engine, data, bars, fills, output and validation, but no trial count. What do you write in place of its numbers?
  3. (Think) Why is “promising” a dangerous word for an unprovenanced number?
  4. (Design) Which receipt items could your current workflow produce automatically today?

Further reading

  • Roger D. Peng, “Reproducible Research in Computational Science”, Science (2011).
  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning, on backtesting pitfalls.
