  • NIST FIPS 180-4, Secure Hash Standard.

— Tariq

Chapter 11.3 — The Wick Census: A One-Line Test for Whether Your Bars Are Real

Subtitle: If the highs equal the closes, your backtest is trading in a market that doesn’t exist.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define a wick and compute the wick census of a bar series. 2. Explain why wickless bars bias results in one direction. 3. List the free sanity checks to run alongside the census, and what the census cannot tell you.

You need: what open, high, low and close mean for a price bar.

11.3.1 What a wick is

A price bar summarises many trades with four numbers: open (O), high (H), low (L) and close (C). The high and low are the extremes reached inside the bar. On a chart, the parts that stick out beyond the open and close are the wicks.

In real markets, most bars have wicks. Price rarely opens at its low and closes at its high with nothing in between. When a dataset has almost no wicks, something upstream has rebuilt bars from closes, from a mid-price, or from a body-only representation. That quietly breaks any strategy whose stops or targets sit inside the bar.

11.3.2 The census

Definition. For bar i,

wi=𝟏[Hi>max(Oi,Ci)∨Li<min(Oi,Ci)], w_i = \mathbf{1}\!\left[\,H_i > \max(O_i, C_i)\;\lor\; L_i < \min(O_i, C_i)\,\right],

that is, 1 if the bar has an upper or a lower wick, else 0. The wick census is the share of bars with a wick:

ŵ=1n∑i=1nwi. \hat{w} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i.

Figure 11.3.1 — Three bars count, one does not. The first three bars have a wick above, below or both, so wᵢ = 1. The last bar’s high and low sit exactly on its body, so wᵢ = 0. A dataset made mostly of bars like the last one is broken.

For bars built from real trades, ŵ is high. For bars that have lost their wicks, ŵ is near zero. I report it, with separate upper- and lower-wick shares, in the receipt for every run. A census near zero makes the run invalid, full stop.

11.3.3 Why wickless bars flatter strategies

Suppose a long trade has a stop below entry and a target above. Within a bar, price can touch the stop before it reaches the target. With real highs and lows, the backtest sees that risk. With wickless bars the low is just min(O, C), so moves inside the bar vanish. Stops that would have been hit are not, and drawdowns shrink.

The effect is not random noise. It is a systematic bias in one direction: toward looking better.

Figure 11.3.2 — Same bar, with and without its wick. Both bars have the same open and close. The real bar’s low reaches the stop (orange dot), so the trade is stopped out. The wickless copy never touches the stop, and the backtest keeps the trade alive. Schematic bars, not market data.

11.3.4 Sanity checks that come free

While walking the bars, it costs nothing to check basic rules:

  • Li≤min⁡(Oi,Ci)L_i \le \min(O_i, C_i) and Hi≥max⁡(Oi,Ci)H_i \ge \max(O_i, C_i). A violation means corrupt data.
  • Hi≥LiH_i \ge L_i.
  • Timestamps strictly increasing.
  • No duplicate bars.

Any violation is reported, not repaired.

11.3.5 Constructed bars are a special case

Some bar types (range, Renko and similar) are built from price movement rather than time. Their bodies have fixed sizes by design, and textbook versions draw them without wicks. If your engine builds them from ticks, though, the trades inside a brick still have extremes, and a faithful builder records them. A “body-only” brick series throws away exactly what a stop needs. So the census applies here too, and matters even more.

11.3.6 What the census does not tell you

A healthy wick share does not prove the bars are correct. Bars can have wicks and still be wrong: built from the wrong contract, misaligned in time, missing a session. The census is a necessary-condition test: passing it is required but not enough. It catches one specific, common and very flattering failure. That is why it sits next to a data hash and a session count in the receipt rather than replacing them.

11.3.7 Why it deserves its own check

Because the failure is silent. Wickless bars look like bars. Charts render fine. Code runs. The only symptom is a backtest that looks better than it should, and that is the one symptom nobody investigates. A one-line statistic turns an invisible failure into a visible number.

11.3.8 Pitfalls

Pitfall Fix
Census computed on a different file from the one the engine read Compute it inside the run, on the bars actually used
Floating-point equality treats rounding noise as a wick Compare prices as integer ticks
Averaging across instruments hides a broken one Report per series

11.3.9 Summary

  • A wick is any part of the bar beyond max(O, C) or min(O, C).
  • Wickless bars hide intrabar stops and always bias results upward.
  • The census ŵ is the share of bars with a wick; near zero means the run is invalid.
  • It is necessary, not sufficient: keep the data hash and session count beside it.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Bar: O = 10, H = 12, L = 10, C = 11. Does it have a wick? (Answer: yes, an upper wick, since 12 > 11.)
  2. (Apply) 1,000 bars, 30 with any wick. What is ŵ, and what do you conclude?
  3. (Think) Why might a time bar with a wick still be wrong?
  4. (Code) Write the census as a loop over integer-tick bars, with separate upper and lower counts.

Further reading

  • Ruey S. Tsay, Analysis of Financial Time Series, on high-frequency data.
  • Larry Harris, Trading and Exchanges, on how trades become prices.
  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning, chapter on financial data structures.

— Tariq

Chapter 11.4 — Trial Ledgers and the Multiple-Testing Problem

Subtitle: The best of a thousand backtests is mostly a measure of how many backtests you ran.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain why the best of many zero-edge trials looks good. 2. Use the expected-maximum formula and its √(2 ln N) growth. 3. Read the deflated Sharpe ratio and say why N is its key input. 4. Decide what counts as a trial and keep an honest ledger.

You need: the normal distribution and what a Sharpe ratio is (average return divided by its standard deviation).

11.4.1 A thought experiment

Take a strategy with no edge at all. Generate a thousand variants by tweaking its settings. Backtest them all. Report the best one.

It will look good. Not because it is good, but because the maximum of many noisy estimates is biased upward. That is the multiple-testing problem, and in quantitative research it is the default state of affairs, not an edge case.

My defence is unglamorous: a trial ledger that records every configuration tried, and a validation step that uses the true count.

11.4.2 The maths of the maximum

Result (expected maximum). Suppose each of N independent variants has a true Sharpe ratio of zero, and each estimate Ŝk\hat S_k is roughly normal with standard deviation σ. Then approximately

𝔼[maxkŜk]≈σ[(1−γ)Φ−1(1−1N)+γΦ−1(1−1Ne)], \mathbb{E}\big[\max_k \hat S_k\big] \approx \sigma\left[(1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\tfrac{1}{N}\right) + \gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\tfrac{1}{Ne}\right)\right],

where γ ≈ 0.5772 is the Euler–Mascheroni constant and Φ⁻¹ the normal quantile. It grows roughly like σ2ln⁡N\sigma\sqrt{2\ln N}.

Why it grows. The largest of N normal draws sits near the point that only about 1 in N draws exceed, which is Φ⁻¹(1 − 1/N). That point moves outward slowly but without limit as N grows. Searching harder raises the bar a real result must clear.

Figure 11.4.1 — The best of N grows with N, edge or not. The blue line is the formula above with σ = 1. Orange dots are a simulation: for each N, the average of 2,000 maxima of N standard normal draws (fixed seed 20261107; values saved in figures/fig-11-4-1-simulation.json). The dashed line is the rough √(2 ln N) growth. At N = 1,000 the best zero-edge trial sits about 3.2σ above zero. Pure simulation, not backtests.

11.4.3 The deflated Sharpe ratio

Bailey and López de Prado turned this into a test. The deflated Sharpe ratio (DSR) asks: given the number of trials, the variance of their Sharpe estimates, the sample length T, and the skew γ₃ and kurtosis γ₄ of returns, what is the probability that the observed Sharpe Ŝ\hat S beats S0S_0, the expected maximum under the null?

DSR=Φ((Ŝ−S0)T−11−γ3Ŝ+γ4−14Ŝ2). \text{DSR} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{(\hat S - S_0)\sqrt{T-1}}{\sqrt{1 - \gamma_3 \hat S + \frac{\gamma_4 - 1}{4}\hat S^2}}\right).

The crucial input is N, through S0S_0. Undercount N and the test is meaningless.

11.4.4 What counts as a trial

This is where honesty lives. A trial is any configuration whose result you saw, including:

  • parameter grid points;
  • variants you abandoned after a glance;
  • different date ranges you “just checked”;
  • reruns after fixing a bug that changed results;
  • ideas tried by an AI agent on your behalf.

The last two are easy to forget. If you peeked at a test result and then changed something, that is a new trial, and the old one still counts.

11.4.5 The ledger

Every run appends a row: configuration identifier, the search it belonged to, timestamp, engine commit, data hash, output hash. Searches have identifiers, and N for a search is the ledger count, not my memory. The ledger is append-only; deleting a row is exactly the cherry-picking it exists to prevent.

Correlated trials complicate this. Nearby grid points are not independent, so the effective number of independent trials is less than N. There are ways to estimate it (clustering the trial returns, for example), but the conservative default is to use the raw count and say so.

11.4.6 Cross-validation built for time series

Multiple testing interacts with overfitting through the validation scheme. Combinatorial purged cross-validation (CPCV) splits the history into groups, forms many train/test combinations, purges overlapping observations, embargoes data near the boundaries, and yields a distribution of out-of-sample results across paths. Reporting the median across paths, not the best path, is the same principle as the ledger: do not let selection pose as evidence.

11.4.7 Pitfalls

  • Counting only “serious” runs. Every run you looked at is serious to the statistics.
  • Splitting searches to shrink N. Calling one search three small searches does not make it three times more credible.
  • Reusing the test set. Every look at held-out data spends some of its independence.

11.4.8 Summary

  • The best of N zero-edge trials is expected near σ·√(2 ln N): about 3.2σ at N = 1,000.
  • The deflated Sharpe ratio corrects for this, but only if N is true.
  • A trial is anything whose result you saw, including agent runs and bug-fix reruns.
  • Keep an append-only ledger; report medians across CPCV paths, not the best path.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Roughly how does the expected best of N zero-edge trials grow? (Answer: like σ√(2 ln N).)
  2. (Apply) You ran 40 grid points, glanced at 10 abandoned variants, and reran 5 after a bug fix. What is N?
  3. (Simulate) Draw N = 100 standard normals 1,000 times and average the maxima. Compare with Figure 11.4.1.
  4. (Think) Why does splitting one search into three not reduce the multiple-testing problem?

Further reading

  • David H. Bailey and Marcos López de Prado, “The Deflated Sharpe Ratio” (2014).
  • Campbell R. Harvey, Yan Liu and Heqing Zhu, “…and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns” (2016).
  • Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning, chapters 11–12.

— Tariq

Chapter 11.5 — The BLOCKED Protocol: Making “I Couldn’t Do It” a Valid Answer

Subtitle: Agents and people cut corners when finishing is the only acceptable outcome. So I changed what counts as finishing.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Write a BLOCKED report in the six-part format. 2. Explain the incentive that drives silent substitution, and how the protocol changes it. 3. Tell a genuine fix attempt from a substitution.

You need: no special background.

11.5.1 Redefining success

Most failures in my research work did not come from bugs. They came from a reasonable-looking decision made under pressure: the right tool was slow or broken, so something close enough was used instead, and the output did not mention it.

The fix that worked best was not technical. It was redefining success.

Rule. A clear report that a task is blocked is a successful outcome. A completed task built on an unapproved substitute is a failure, however good it looks.

11.5.2 The format

When the honest path is blocked, the report must say, in order:

  1. What I was asked to do.
  2. What failed, with the exact error.
  3. What I tried, up to three attempts.
  4. The substitution I could make, and exactly what it would change.
  5. That I have not made it.
  6. What I need to proceed.

Then it stops. No “in the meantime I ran a quick version”. The substitute is not produced, even as a preview, because previews have a way of becoming results.

11.5.3 Why a fixed format

Free-form explanations drift toward justification. “The engine was slow so I used a faster approach, which should be broadly equivalent” sounds reasonable and hides everything. A fixed format forces the important parts into the open: the exact error (so it can be fixed) and the exact difference the substitute would make (so the human can decide).

Item 4 is the heart of it. Naming the substitute and its consequences turns a silent decision into an explicit choice that belongs to the person responsible for the result.

11.5.4 The incentive problem

Why do agents, and people, substitute silently? Because the reward is lopsided. Delivering something gets credit; reporting a block feels like failing.

Model. Let VdoneV_{\text{done}} be the perceived value of finishing and VblockedV_{\text{blocked}} the value of reporting a block. Substitution happens whenever

Vdone−(perceived risk of being caught)>Vblocked. V_{\text{done}} - \text{(perceived risk of being caught)} > V_{\text{blocked}}.

You cannot do much about the perceived risk with an agent. You can raise VblockedV_{\text{blocked}} by making it explicitly acceptable, and lower VdoneV_{\text{done}} for substituted work by making it explicitly a failure. The protocol does both, in writing.

11.5.5 Three attempts, then stop

The protocol is not permission to give up at the first error. It expects genuine attempts on the honest path: read the error, change something, retry, up to three times. What it forbids is changing the method rather than fixing the problem.

Action Classification
Retry the right engine with a corrected path Attempt
Fix a missing dependency and rerun Attempt
Switch to a different engine Substitution
Use a cached copy of the data “for now” Substitution

Figure 11.5.1 — Fix, or stop and ask. When the honest path fails, the only allowed move is to fix and retry with the same method, up to three times. If that works, carry on (green). If not, write the BLOCKED report and stop (blue). The crossed-out orange box, switching method silently, is never allowed. The human then picks one of the three options at the bottom.

11.5.6 What happens next

The human chooses one of three things: fix the blocker, approve that one named substitution for this task, or drop the task. An approval covers only the substitution named. It does not extend to the next task, or to a different substitution in the same task.

11.5.7 Pitfalls

  • Vague blocks. “It didn’t work” is not a block report. The exact error is mandatory.
  • Blocking too early. One failed attempt is usually a problem to solve, not a block.
  • Blocks that quietly continue. If the output after a block report contains results, the protocol was violated, whatever the report said.

11.5.8 Summary

  • A clear BLOCKED report is success; unapproved substitution is failure.
  • Six items, in order, then stop: no preview of the substitute.
  • The protocol raises the value of reporting a block and removes the value of substituting.
  • Fix with the same method up to three times; changing method is a substitution.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Which item of the report is “the heart of it”? (Answer: item 4, the substitution and exactly what it would change.)
  2. (Apply) The required engine fails to build because a path is wrong. Is fixing the path an attempt or a substitution?
  3. (Think) Why must the substitute not be produced even as a preview?
  4. (Design) Write a BLOCKED report for a task you once finished with a workaround.

Further reading

  • Atul Gawande, The Checklist Manifesto, on forcing functions.
  • Sidney Dekker, The Field Guide to Understanding ‘Human Error’.
  • Charles Goodhart, on targets that stop being good measures (Goodhart’s law).

— Tariq

Chapter 11.6 — Forbidden-Substitution Lists: Naming the Dodges

Subtitle: “Be rigorous” is a value. “Don’t fill at the signal bar’s price” is a rule. Agents follow rules.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Name the seven families of research dodges. 2. State the two causality conditions every backtest must meet. 3. Explain why approval must name one specific substitution.

You need: what a backtest, a bar and a fill are.

11.6.1 Principles did not work

When I first tried to keep AI agents honest, I wrote principles: be rigorous, do not cut corners, report limitations. They did not help much. An agent can agree with every principle and still decide that a cached file is “effectively the same” as the canonical source.

What helped was a list of specific, named dodges, grouped by family, each forbidden unless I approve that exact substitution, by name, in the current session.

11.6.2 The families

Family Examples
Engine and language Re-running research in a different language because the canonical engine is slow or failing. Re-implementing part of the engine and calling it equivalent. Post-processing engine output in ways that change numbers. Stubs, mocks, samples or hard-coded values where the real component was required.
Data Cached, converted or resampled files instead of the canonical tick source without proving identity. Bars without wicks. Synthesising prices by interpolation or forward-fill. Silently dropping sessions, hours, contracts or rolls. Filling missing values without saying so. Mixing contracts or instruments.
Lookahead Using any value at decision time T that is only known after T: the current bar’s close, high, low or volume before it has closed; session totals; centred windows; full-sample normalisation. Filling at the signal price instead of the first trade strictly after the signal. Tuning on the data reported as out-of-sample.
Execution realism No slippage, no commission, zero latency, ignored queue position, concurrent positions the strategy could not hold. Changing the fill model between runs being compared.
Model downgrade Replacing a rigorous model with a heuristic or “simplified version”. Loosening a gate or shrinking a sample so something passes. Swapping a failing statistical test for a weaker one.
Reporting Missing labels. Cherry-picking. Numbers not computed from a named file in this session. Language that changes meaning: “roughly break-even” for a loss, “verified” for “ran without errors”. Invented explanations.
Process Skipping or weakening failing tests. Swallowing errors so a run completes. Bypassing hooks. Claiming a file exists without listing it.

11.6.3 Why naming works

An agent asked to “avoid lookahead” has to decide what lookahead means in context, and that judgement is where it slips. An agent told “don’t use the current bar’s high before the bar has closed” has nothing to interpret.

Causality conditions. Every feature used at decision time T must be measurable with respect to the information available then, written ℱT\mathcal{F}_T; and the entry fills at the first trade strictly after T:

xT∈ℱT,entry price=pτ,τ=min⁡{t>T:trade at t}. x_T \in \mathcal{F}_T, \qquad \text{entry price} = p_{\tau},\ \ \tau = \min\{t > T : \text{trade at } t\}.

“Measurable with respect to ℱT\mathcal{F}_T” just means: you could have computed it using only what had happened by time T.

Figure 11.6.1 — What is known at decision time. The grey box is one bar, with trades as tick marks. Everything left of the blue line (decision time T) may be used. The bar’s final high, low, close and volume are only known at the bar close, so they are off limits at T. The entry is the green dot: the first trade strictly after T. Filling at the signal price itself (orange ×) is forbidden.

The list is a catalogue of concrete ways to break those two lines, written so they can be spotted in code review.

11.6.4 Why approval must be specific

Some substitutions are legitimate in context. A quick exploratory look on resampled data can be fine if everyone knows that is what it is. So the rule is not “never”; it is “never unless approved by name”. Approval for one dodge never covers another. That stops a single “fine, use the cached file” from becoming permission for everything nearby.

11.6.5 Keeping the list alive

The list grows from incidents. Each new dodge I catch, in agent output or my own, gets a line. The list is mirrored into the instruction files of every agent I use, and a guard watches those files so the list cannot be quietly trimmed (Chapter 11.8).

11.6.6 Pitfalls

  • Lists that are too abstract slide back into principles. Keep entries concrete enough to spot in a diff.
  • Lists that are too long to read get skimmed. Group them and keep each line short.
  • Rules without an exit. Without the BLOCKED protocol beside it (Chapter 11.5), a forbidden-substitution list just pressures agents to hide substitutions better.

11.6.7 Summary

  • Principles invite interpretation; named dodges do not.
  • Seven families: engine, data, lookahead, execution, model downgrade, reporting, process.
  • Causality: features must be known at T; entries fill at the first trade after T.
  • Approval is per named substitution, per session, and always paired with a BLOCKED exit.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A rule reads “this bar’s volume” at a time inside the bar. Which family does it break? (Answer: lookahead.)
  2. (Apply) Classify: “used last week’s cached file because the tick source was slow”.
  3. (Think) Why does a forbidden list without a BLOCKED exit make hiding more likely?
  4. (Design) Write two new list entries for a dodge you have seen in your own work.

Further reading

  • Marcos López de Prado, “The 10 Reasons Most Machine Learning Funds Fail” (2018).
  • David H. Bailey et al., “Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism” (2014).
  • Shachar Kaufman et al., “Leakage in Data Mining: Formulation, Detection, and Avoidance” (2012).

— Tariq

Chapter 11.7 — Hooks That Enforce Rules on AI Agents

Subtitle: Instructions are advice. A hook is a gate. Here’s where each belongs.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain what an agent hook is and why it is stronger than an instruction. 2. Decide when a hook should fail closed and when it should fail open. 3. Choose between precision and recall for a command classifier. 4. State what hooks cannot do.

You need: what a shell command is; the terms true/false positive.

11.7.1 Why instructions are not enough

Every AI coding agent I use reads an instruction file. Mine are long and specific. Agents still break them, not out of malice but because instructions compete with everything else in a long context, and “finish the task” tends to win.

So for the rules that matter most, I stopped relying on the agent remembering them. I enforce them with hooks: small programs the agent’s harness runs around its actions, which can block, ask, or annotate.

11.7.2 What a hook is

Modern agent harnesses expose lifecycle events: before a tool call, after a tool call, when the session starts, when the agent is about to stop. You attach a script to each event. The script receives the event as JSON (which tool, with what input) and returns a decision: allow, deny, ask the human, or add context.

Key property. The hook runs outside the model. The model cannot talk its way past it, forget it, or decide it does not apply.

Figure 11.7.1 — The hook sits between the agent and its tools. Every tool call passes through the hook as JSON before it runs. The hook returns one of four decisions: allow (the tool runs), deny (with a reason), ask (a human decides), or add context (the agent reads extra guidance).

11.7.3 What I enforce with hooks

Engine rules. In my trading workspace, research must run through the C# harness. A pre-tool hook inspects shell commands and blocks the alternative-language tooling that has been used to dodge it in the past, with a message pointing to the right path and to the BLOCKED format. It catches me too, which is the point: while drafting this series, a text-editing command of mine was blocked because it looked like that tooling running inside the workspace.

State-altering commands. A separate advisory hook classifies shell commands with a regular expression: deletes, kills, git history operations, service management, cloud write operations. Those go to a local on-device router for a second opinion. A “block” verdict, or the router being unreachable, escalates the command to a human permission prompt. An “allow” verdict grants nothing extra; the normal permission flow still applies.

Asymmetry. A small local model is useful as a tripwire and untrustworthy as an authority. It can only make things stricter.

Figure 11.7.2 — The second opinion can only escalate. Commands that do not look state-altering go to the normal permission flow. Those that do go to the local router. “Block”, or the router being down, sends them to a human (orange). “Allow” (green dashed) leads back to the same normal flow and grants nothing extra.

Final-message checks. A stop-time hook can scan the agent’s last message for performance figures without the required label, or claims like “validated” without receipts, and push back before the turn ends.

11.7.4 Designing hooks well

  • Fail closed for dangerous actions. If the hook errors or its dependency is down, ask the human rather than allowing.
  • Fail open for advisory checks. A context-adding hook that crashes should not freeze the agent.
  • Be fast. Hooks sit on every tool call. A slow hook makes everything slow; time out and fall back to “ask”.
  • Explain the block. A denial should say which rule, why, and what to do instead. Otherwise the agent tries creative workarounds.
  • Test the hook. Mine has unit tests: known-dangerous commands must be flagged, known-safe ones must not.

11.7.5 The precision–recall trade-off

A command classifier has false positives (safe commands flagged) and false negatives (dangerous commands missed).

Definitions. With TP true positives, FP false positives and FN false negatives,

P=TPTP+FP,R=TPTP+FN. P = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \qquad R = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}.

Hook type Cost of a false positive Cost of a false negative Tune for
Escalates to a human one click whatever the command does recall
Blocks outright, no human blocked legitimate work whatever the command does precision matters more

So for my escalate-only gate I tune for recall and accept lower precision.

11.7.6 Limits

Hooks see actions, not intent. A regex on shell commands can be evaded by an agent writing a script file and running it. Hooks raise the cost of the common dodges; they do not make dodging impossible. That is why they sit alongside receipts, ledgers and review, not instead of them.

11.7.7 Summary

  • Instructions compete with the task; hooks run outside the model and cannot be argued with.
  • Dangerous checks fail closed; advisory checks fail open; all hooks are fast and explain themselves.
  • A local model may only escalate, never grant.
  • Escalate-only gates favour recall. Hooks raise the cost of dodging but do not end it.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A classifier flags 50 commands: 40 truly dangerous, 10 safe. It misses 5 dangerous ones. Compute P and R. (Answer: P = 40/50 = 0.8; R = 40/45 ≈ 0.89.)
  2. (Apply) The router behind an advisory hook is down. What should happen to a state-altering command?
  3. (Think) How could an agent evade a regex-based shell hook, and what else catches that?
  4. (Design) Write the denial message for a blocked command: rule, reason, alternative.

Further reading

  • Claude Code documentation, “Hooks reference”.
  • James Reason, Human Error, on the Swiss cheese model.
  • Saltzer and Schroeder, “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems” (1975), on fail-safe defaults.

— Tariq

Chapter 11.8 — Drift Guards: Watching the Rule Files Themselves

Subtitle: The easiest way to break a rule is to edit it. So the rules have a watchdog.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Recognise the quiet forms of rule-file drift. 2. Describe a read-only guard that hashes protected sections against a baseline. 3. Explain why baseline updates are a separate, reviewed step.

You need: what a file hash is (SHA-256 gives a fingerprint that changes if any byte changes).

11.8.1 The problem

My integrity rules live in plain-text instruction files: one per agent, plus project-level files. They are the most important text in my workspace. They are also just files, and anything with write access can change them: an agent “tidying up”, a merge that drops a section, me trimming tokens late at night.

A rule that can be silently weakened is not a rule. So I run a small drift guard: a background job that checks the rule files on a schedule and alerts when protected content changes.

11.8.2 What drift looks like

Drift is rarely dramatic:

  • a forbidden-substitution line removed during a “consolidation”;
  • “must” softened to “should”;
  • a section renumbered so cross-references now point at the wrong thing;
  • one agent’s copy edited while the others are not;
  • a permission setting quietly added that lets the forbidden tooling run without a prompt.

Each looks harmless in a diff. Together they turn a firm protocol into a suggestion.

11.8.3 How the guard works

The guard runs as a macOS LaunchAgent at a regular interval, at low priority (Chapter 10.12). Each run:

  1. extracts the integrity-protocol section from each agent’s instruction file, between known start and end markers, and hashes it;
  2. compares each hash with a stored known-good baseline;
  3. checks that the short “integrity first” summary block at the top of each file is still there;
  4. checks that the guard itself and the settings around it are intact, so nobody can quietly make it fail open;
  5. logs every run, and raises a desktop notification once per new finding.

Detection rule. For protected section s,

drift(s)=𝟏[SHA256(s)≠hbaseline(s)], \text{drift}(s) = \mathbf{1}\big[\,\text{SHA256}(s) \neq h_{\text{baseline}}(s)\,\big],

and a missing section counts as drift too.

Hashing sections rather than whole files means unrelated edits elsewhere in a file do not trigger false alarms.

Read-only. The guard reports drift; it never restores files. An app may hold a file open, and an intended edit must never be silently reverted.

Figure 11.8.1 — One run of the guard. The five steps on the left run in order every interval. Any finding goes to the orange box: report only, never restore. The blue dashed box is the only way the baseline in step 2 changes: a separate step that a human reviews.

11.8.4 Legitimate changes

Rules do need to change. The process: make the change deliberately, review the diff, then update the baseline as a separate, explicit step. The guard does not prevent edits; it prevents unnoticed edits. Updating the baseline is the moment a human says “yes, I meant that”.

11.8.5 Cross-reference integrity

My rule files use section numbers as pointers (“halt per §9”). Renumbering a section silently breaks every pointer to it. So editing the rule file has its own rule: list every cross-reference first, and update all of them in the same change. The guard complements that by flagging a change in section structure even if the text inside is untouched.

11.8.6 Why not just use git?

git Drift guard
Records changes yes logs findings
Watches for changes and alerts no yes
Covers files outside repositories (global agent instructions in a home directory) no yes
Stops a committed weakening from counting as fine no yes, until the baseline is approved

Git is a passive history. The guard is an active monitor with a baseline and an alert.

11.8.7 Watching the watchdog

A guard that quietly stopped running is worse than none, because you trust its silence. The guard writes to a log on every run, and the absence of that entry is itself checkable. It is the same heartbeat principle I use for production services.

11.8.8 Pitfalls

  • Over-broad protection. Guarding whole files creates alert fatigue. Protect the sections that matter.
  • Auto-repair. Tempting, and wrong. A guard that rewrites files will one day revert an edit you meant. Report, do not restore.
  • Baselines updated by the same actor that made the change, without review. That defeats the purpose. Treat baseline updates as an approval step.

11.8.9 Summary

  • Rule files drift quietly; a guard hashes protected sections and compares them with a baseline.
  • The guard also protects itself and the settings around it.
  • It is read-only and notifies once per new finding; it never restores.
  • Baseline updates are separate, human-reviewed approvals; the guard’s own heartbeat is checked.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A protected section is deleted. Is that drift? (Answer: yes; a missing section counts as drift.)
  2. (Apply) Someone edits an unrelated paragraph in the same file. Does the guard fire? Why?
  3. (Think) Why is auto-restore dangerous even when the guard is right?
  4. (Design) Which three files in your own setup would you protect, and which sections?

Further reading

  • Gene Kim et al., The Phoenix Project, on change management.
  • NIST SP 800-53, control family CM (Configuration Management), on baseline configuration.
  • Gene Kim and Eugene Spafford, “The Design and Implementation of Tripwire” (1994).

— Tariq

Chapter 11.9 — Provenance in a Backtest Catalog

Subtitle: A results database that can’t tell you where a number came from is a liability with a query language.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. List the provenance columns a backtest catalog needs. 2. Use content addressing (identity by hash) to detect changed files and nondeterminism. 3. Backfill provenance without inventing it.

You need: what a relational database table and a file hash are.

11.9.1 Why a catalog needs provenance

Research produces a lot of runs. After a few months, “what did we try, and what happened?” cannot be answered from memory or a folder of CSVs. So I keep a catalog: a small relational database that every backtest result is imported into, with one row per run and the trades and metrics hanging off it.

In late October I added provenance (the record of how something was produced) to that catalog. Every run now carries the evidence of how it was made, and runs without that evidence are flagged rather than mixed in with the rest.

11.9.2 The problem with a plain results table

A table with columns like strategy, period and metric invites a dangerous query: sort by the metric, take the top row. That query ignores everything that makes the number meaningful: which engine, which data, which fill model, how many siblings were tried. Worse, it silently mixes runs produced under different assumptions, some of which may be invalid.

11.9.3 Provenance columns

Column group Contents
Engine identity harness path, git commit and dirty flag, command line
Data identity canonical source path and SHA-256, session range and count, exclusions
Bar quality the wick census
Execution model fill model, slippage, commission, latency
Output identity result file path and SHA-256
Search membership which search the run belongs to, so N can be counted
Validation state passed, failed with named gates, or not evaluated
Provenance status complete, or which items are missing

The import step computes the hashes itself from the files on disk. It does not trust values typed into a config.

11.9.4 Content addressing

Using hashes as identities has a useful property. If two runs report the same data hash, they used byte-identical data. If the output hash recorded at import does not match the file on disk today, the file changed after import, and every number derived from it is suspect.

Run identity.

id(r)=(hcode,hdata,hconfig)↦houtput. \text{id}(r) = \big(h_{\text{code}},\, h_{\text{data}},\, h_{\text{config}}\big) \;\mapsto\; h_{\text{output}}.

If the mapping is deterministic, re-running the same tuple must reproduce the same output hash. When it does not, you have found nondeterminism, which is itself a finding worth recording.

Figure 11.9.1 — A run is named by its hashes. Code, data and config hashes go into the run, which produces an output hash. At import, the catalog recomputes the hashes from the files on disk and sets the run’s status to complete (green) or unprovenanced (orange). A rerun of the same three inputs must give the same output hash.

11.9.5 Backfilling honestly

Adding provenance to an existing catalog raises an awkward question: what about runs imported before? Some evidence can be rebuilt (hash the files if they still exist); some cannot (the dirty flag at the time is gone).

Rule. Never invent provenance. Reconstruct what can be proven, mark the rest missing, and set those runs’ status to unprovenanced.

I took a backup of the database before the migration, so the change itself is reversible and auditable.

11.9.6 Queries that respect provenance

Only runs with complete provenance count as results. Querying unprovenanced runs is possible, but it should be deliberate, and their numbers are labelled. Any best result from a search is reported with its N, because a best-of-N without N is meaningless (Chapter 11.4).

11.9.7 Pitfalls

  • Provenance as optional columns. If nulls are silently allowed, they will be everywhere. Make completeness a computed status that queries respect.
  • Hashing paths, not contents. A path is a name, not an identity.
  • Mutable result files. Write results once; never edit them in place. Corrections are new runs.
  • Schema migrations without backups. The catalog is evidence. Back it up before changing it.

11.9.8 Summary

  • Every run row carries engine, data, bars, execution, output, search, validation and provenance status.
  • Import computes hashes from disk; it never trusts typed values.
  • Same inputs must give the same output hash; a mismatch is a finding.
  • Backfill only what can be proven; everything else is unprovenanced.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) The output hash stored at import differs from the file’s hash today. What does that mean? (Answer: the file changed after import, so numbers derived from it are suspect.)
  2. (Apply) An old run’s data file still exists but its dirty flag was never recorded. What status does it get?
  3. (Think) Why is “sort by metric, take the top row” dangerous even if every run is valid?
  4. (Design) Write a query rule that only returns runs with complete provenance.

Further reading

  • W3C, PROV-O: The PROV Ontology (2013).
  • Juliana Freire et al., “Provenance for Computational Tasks: A Survey” (2008).
  • Ralph Merkle, on hash-based content addressing (Merkle trees, 1987).

— Tariq

Chapter 11.10 — Label Unproven Runs. Don’t Hide Them.

Subtitle: Deleting bad results feels like hygiene. It’s actually the first step of cherry-picking.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Give three reasons why deleting invalid runs is dangerous. 2. Apply the three labels INVALID, UNPROVENANCED and Superseded. 3. Show with a formula how removing the worst runs inflates the average.

You need: averages and conditional expectation (“the average among the ones that are kept”).

11.10.1 The instinct to delete

When I discovered that some earlier research outputs had been produced the wrong way (substituted engine, wickless bars, missing receipts), my first instinct was to delete them. Clean slate. No risk of anyone using them.

That instinct is wrong, and it took me a little while to see why.

11.10.2 Why deletion is dangerous

  • It destroys the trial count. Every run you looked at is a trial. If invalid runs disappear, the record of how much searching happened disappears with them, and every later result looks more credible than it is.
  • It destroys the lesson. An invalid run is evidence of a failure mode. Deleted, it cannot be studied, and the same failure is easier to repeat.
  • It creates a habit. Today you delete runs that are invalid. Tomorrow, runs that are “probably” invalid. Then runs that are inconvenient. The line between hygiene and cherry-picking is a judgement call, and judgement calls drift.

11.10.3 What I do instead

Invalid or unproven outputs are kept and marked:

Label Meaning Use
INVALID Produced in violation of the protocol (a forbidden substitution, lookahead, wickless bars) Kept for the record; never reused as evidence; never quoted
UNPROVENANCED May or may not be fine, but lacks the receipts to say Not a result until proven
Superseded Replaced by a corrected rerun Kept, with a pointer to the replacement

The label travels with the data: in the catalog, in file headers, in any document that references the run. A document that relies on an invalid output inherits the problem and is itself marked ineligible as a source.

11.10.4 Confession is not repair

If I, or an agent, discover a violation, saying so is necessary but not sufficient. The affected outputs are listed and marked invalid, the work stops, and nothing proceeds until there is a decision on how to redo it honestly. An apology followed by continuing to use the outputs is worse than not noticing, because it looks like accountability.

11.10.5 The statistics of survivorship

Result. Remove a fraction q of runs. The mean of the runs that are kept is

𝔼[X∣kept]=𝔼[X]−q𝔼[X∣removed]1−q, \mathbb{E}[X \mid \text{kept}] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[X] - q\,\mathbb{E}[X \mid \text{removed}]}{1-q},

which is larger than 𝔼[X]\mathbb{E}[X] whenever the removed runs were worse than average.

Why it is true. The overall mean is a weighted average of the two groups: 𝔼[X]=q𝔼[X∣removed]+(1−q)𝔼[X∣kept]\mathbb{E}[X] = q\,\mathbb{E}[X\mid\text{removed}] + (1-q)\,\mathbb{E}[X\mid\text{kept}]. Solve for the kept mean. If the removed group’s mean is below the overall mean, the kept group’s mean must be above it.

Figure 11.10.1 — Delete the worst and the average rises. Twenty thousand runs with true mean 0 (standard normal draws, fixed seed 20261107; values in figures/fig-11-10-1-simulation.json). Removing the worst fraction q (orange dots, blue theory line) lifts the kept mean to about 0.8 when half are removed. Removing the same share at random (green) leaves it at 0. Pure simulation, not research results.

That is survivorship bias: the same mechanism that makes fund databases look better than the funds that ever existed. Keeping and labelling preserves the denominator.

11.10.6 Live records too

The same principle applies to live trading records. Drawdowns and bad days stay in the record. If a live record turns out to be wrong (a reporting error, a mismatched account), the correction is recorded and the wrong figures are retracted explicitly, not silently replaced.

11.10.7 Pitfalls

  • Labels that do not propagate. A flag in the database that does not appear in exported reports protects nothing.
  • Ambiguous labels. “Questionable” invites interpretation. Use a small set with exact meanings.
  • Rerunning and overwriting. A corrected run is a new run, with the invalid one kept beside it.

11.10.8 Summary

  • Deleting invalid runs erases the trial count, the lesson, and the line against cherry-picking.
  • Keep and label: INVALID, UNPROVENANCED, Superseded; labels travel with the data.
  • Confession requires listing, marking and stopping, not just apologising.
  • Removing worse-than-average runs always inflates the kept average.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) Overall mean 0, 20% removed with mean −1. What is the kept mean? (Answer: (0 − 0.2·(−1)) / 0.8 = 0.25.)
  2. (Apply) A run was produced on wickless bars. Which label does it get, and can it be quoted?
  3. (Think) Why is “apologise and continue” worse than not noticing?
  4. (Design) Where in your own files would a label have to appear so it cannot be lost on export?

Further reading

  • Stephen J. Brown, William Goetzmann, Roger Ibbotson and Stephen Ross, “Survivorship Bias in Performance Studies” (1992).
  • Robert Rosenthal, “The File Drawer Problem and Tolerance for Null Results” (1979).
  • Retraction Watch, on how science handles corrections.

— Tariq

Chapter 11.11 — LAB SIM Labels and the Five-Point Friction Audit

Subtitle: Every backtest is a simulation of a market that’s friendlier than the real one. The label says so; the audit says how.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain the purpose of a fixed simulation label on every backtest figure. 2. Walk through the five friction items: sequencing, lookahead volume, slippage and latency, queue position, live discrepancy. 3. Tell a touch fill from a trade-through fill.

You need: what a stop, a target and a limit order are.

11.11.1 The label

Every simulated performance figure in my work carries a prefix: [LABORATORY BACKTEST SIMULATION — UNVERIFIED FOR LIVE EXECUTION]. Beside it sits a short audit of five ways the simulation is friendlier than reality.

The label is blunt on purpose. It stops a backtest number from being read, quoted or remembered as something that happened. The audit makes the gap between simulation and market explicit, item by item.

11.11.2 Item 1: intrabar sequencing

Within a bar, did price hit the stop or the target first? A bar’s open, high, low and close do not say. Simulators guess, and the default guesses are often optimistic: assume the favourable extreme came first, or resolve ties in the trade’s favour.

The honest approaches: replay the tick sequence so ordering is known, or, where only bars exist, resolve ambiguity pessimistically (stop first). The audit states which was used. A strategy whose results depend heavily on this choice is a strategy whose results are mostly assumptions.

Figure 11.11.1 — One bar, two stories. The bar on the left spans both the stop and the target. Path A rises to the high first and hits the target (green). Path B falls to the low first and hits the stop (orange). Both produce the same open, high, low and close. The pessimistic rule assumes path B. Schematic prices.

11.11.3 Item 2: lookahead volume leakage

Volume, delta and similar flow measures accumulate through a bar. Their final value is known only when the bar closes. A rule that reads “this bar’s volume” at a decision time inside the bar is using the future.

Causality. A feature xTx_T used at decision time T must be measurable with respect to the information set ℱT\mathcal{F}_T (computable from what had happened by T). Bar-level volume is in ℱtclose\mathcal{F}_{t_{\text{close}}}, not in ℱT\mathcal{F}_T for T<tcloseT < t_{\text{close}}.

The audit states how each flow feature is computed and confirms it uses only completed data.

11.11.4 Item 3: slippage and latency

The simulated entry is the first trade strictly after the signal. In reality there is latency between signal and order arrival, and the fill price depends on what is available when the order arrives.

Implementation shortfall per trade.

IS=s⋅(pfill−pdecision)+c, \text{IS} = s\cdot\big(p_{\text{fill}} - p_{\text{decision}}\big) + c,

with s = +1 for a buy and −1 for a sell, and c the commissions and fees.

Backtests that set the price difference to zero describe a market with infinite liquidity and no delay. The audit states the slippage and latency assumptions, per side.

11.11.5 Item 4: FIFO queue position

Limit orders on a first-in, first-out (FIFO) exchange fill in time priority. A backtest that fills a limit order whenever price touches it assumes you were first in the queue. In reality you might be behind thousands of contracts, and price can touch your level and leave without filling you. Worse, the times you do fill on a touch are disproportionately the times price keeps going through you: adverse selection.

A common conservative rule: a limit fills only if price trades through the level, not merely at it. The audit says whether fills are touch-based or trade-through, and whether queue position is modelled.

Figure 11.11.2 — Touching is not trading through. Left: price only touches the buy limit and turns away. A touch-fill backtest books a fill; the real queue may never reach you. Right: price trades past the level, so a fill is credible. Schematic paths.

11.11.6 Item 5: live discrepancy

How does the simulation compare with live or paper execution of the same logic? Where there is a live record, the audit notes the gap. Where there is not, it says so. A simulation never compared with live execution is a hypothesis about execution, not a description of it.

11.11.7 Why both label and audit

Alone Weakness
Label only Easy to ignore once it becomes wallpaper
Audit only Easy to skip
Both Put the uncertainty in front of the number and make the reader ask “how much survives friction?” rather than “is this good?”

11.11.8 Pitfalls

  • Labelling the headline but not the table. Every simulated figure, everywhere.
  • “Friction included” as a blanket claim. Each of the five items is answered separately.
  • Changing friction between runs being compared. Comparisons are only valid under the same model.

11.11.9 Summary

  • Every simulated figure carries the fixed LAB SIM label.
  • The five audit items: intrabar sequencing, lookahead volume, slippage and latency, FIFO queue position, live discrepancy.
  • Resolve bar ambiguity pessimistically; fill limits on trade-through, not touch.
  • Answer each item separately, and keep friction fixed across compared runs.

Exercises

  1. (Warm-up) A buy decided at 100.00 fills at 100.25 with 0.05 commission. What is IS? (Answer: +1 × 0.25 + 0.05 = 0.30.)
  2. (Apply) A bar’s range contains both your stop and your target. Which does the pessimistic rule assume was hit?
  3. (Think) Why are touch fills biased toward the trades that go against you?
  4. (Design) Write the five-line audit for a backtest you have seen, answering each item honestly.

Further reading

  • Larry Harris, Trading and Exchanges, on order books and queue priority.
  • André Perold, “The Implementation Shortfall: Paper versus Reality” (1988).
  • Robert Almgren and Neil Chriss, “Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions” (2000).

— Tariq

Chapter 12.2 — An Engineer’s Introduction to Day Trading Futures

Subtitle: What a futures contract is, what “day trading” one actually involves, and the maths that decides whether you survive.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe a futures contract and its specification. 2. Compute profit and loss, including costs. 3. Compute expectancy and the break-even win rate. 4. Explain why losing streaks are normal and why risk per trade must be small.

You need: basic probability; multiplication.

This is education, not advice. Trading futures carries substantial risk, including losing more than you deposit.

12.2.1 Why start here

I came to futures as an engineer, not a trader. The first thing I wanted was a clear model of the instrument: what exactly am I buying, how is profit computed, what can go wrong. This is the explainer I wish I’d had.

12.2.2 What a futures contract is

Definition. A futures contract is a standardised agreement to buy or sell something at a set price on a future date.

The “something” can be a commodity, a currency, an interest rate or, in my case, a stock index. Equity index futures are cash-settled: nobody delivers 500 stocks; at expiry the contract settles to the index value.

Every contract has a specification set by the exchange:

Term Meaning
Multiplier dollar value of one index point
Tick size minimum price increment
Tick value multiplier × tick size
Expiry cycle equity index futures usually list quarterly contracts (March, June, September, December)
Trading hours nearly 24 hours on weekdays, with a short daily maintenance break

12.2.3 Profit and loss

For a position of qq contracts (positive for long, negative for short) entered at P0P_0 and exited at P1P_1, with multiplier mm:

P&L=q⋅m⋅(P1−P0)−costs. \text{P\&L} = q \cdot m \cdot (P_1 - P_0) - \text{costs}.

Costs are commissions, exchange and clearing fees, and slippage (the gap between the price you expected and the price you got). They look small per trade. Across many trades they are often the difference between a strategy that works on paper and one that doesn’t.

12.2.4 Marking to market

Futures positions are settled daily. Gains and losses are credited or debited to your account each day, not only when you close. That is why you need margin: a deposit that absorbs daily losses. If losses push your account below the maintenance level, you get a margin call or, more often with retail brokers, automatic liquidation.

12.2.5 What “day trading” means here

Day trading means opening and closing positions within the same session, holding nothing overnight. Brokers often offer lower “day trading margin” for intraday positions. That is the same leverage with less cushion. Holding past the session close usually requires full exchange margin.

12.2.6 The maths of survival

The most important idea for a beginner isn’t a pattern. It is the expectancy of a process and the risk of ruin.

If a process wins with probability pp, averages WW on winners and LL on losers (as a positive number), with average costs cc, its expectancy per trade is

E=pW−(1−p)L−c. E = pW - (1-p)L - c.

Setting E=0E = 0 and ignoring costs gives the break-even win rate p*=L/(W+L)p^* = L/(W+L).

Figure 12.2.1 — A high win rate means nothing on its own. The curve is the break-even win rate for each ratio of average win to average loss, with costs ignored. Above the curve expectancy is positive; below it, negative. Small wins against a loss three times larger (orange dot) need a 75% win rate just to break even, before costs.

Even with positive EE, risking too much per trade can wipe out an account during an ordinary losing streak. A run of nn losses in a row has probability about (1−p)n(1-p)^n at any given point, but over hundreds of trades there are hundreds of starting points, so streaks that seem impossible become near-certain.

Figure 12.2.2 — Long losing streaks are normal over many trades. Simulated independent trades with a fixed loss chance (seed 20261107, 2,000 runs of 500 trades each). With a 50% loss chance, a streak of 7 losses happens in most runs; with 40%, a streak of 5 is near-certain. Size each trade so such a streak is survivable.

12.2.7 The honest base rates

Studies of retail day traders in several markets have found that most lose money over time, and only a small fraction sustain profits. That isn’t a reason never to learn. It is a reason to treat it as a skill with a long apprenticeship, start with simulated or very small size, and keep risk per trade small relative to the account.

12.2.8 What to learn first

  1. Contract specifications and costs for whatever you trade.
  2. Order types: market, limit, stop, and how each can fill badly.
  3. Position sizing from risk, not from conviction.
  4. Recording every trade, so your expectancy is measured, not imagined.

12.2.9 Summary

  • A futures contract is standardised; index futures are cash-settled and marked to market daily.
  • P&L = contracts × multiplier × price change − costs; costs add up.
  • Expectancy, not win rate, decides; break-even win rate is L/(W+L)L/(W+L) before costs.
  • Long losing streaks are normal; keep risk per trade small.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) Long 2 contracts with multiplier $5, from 5000.00 to 5004.50, costs $4 total. What is the P&L? (Answer: 2 × 5 × 4.5 − 4 = $41.)
  2. (Compute) A process wins 60% of the time, averages $100 per win and $180 per loss. What is its expectancy before costs? (Answer: 60 − 72 = −$12 per trade.)
  3. (Think) Why does day-trading margin not reduce risk?
  4. (Simulate) Simulate 500 coin-flip trades. What is the longest losing run? Repeat ten times.

Further reading

  • CME Group Education, “Introduction to Futures”.
  • John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, chapters 2–3.
  • Fernando Chague, Rodrigo De-Losso and Bruno Giovannetti, “Day Trading for a Living?” (2019).

— Tariq

Chapter 12.3 — How Exchanges Work: Order Books, Matching Engines and CME Globex

Subtitle: Before you click “buy”, it helps to know what’s on the other side of the wire.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Trace an order from your platform to the clearing house. 2. Describe a central limit order book and FIFO matching. 3. Explain why a limit order can be “touched” and not filled. 4. Compare the main order types and the exchange’s protections.

You need: no special background.

12.3.1 The path of an order

An order for an equity index future doesn’t go to “the market” in the abstract. It travels through your broker (a futures commission merchant, or FCM) and a risk gateway to a specific exchange’s matching engine. For US equity index futures that is CME Globex, the electronic trading platform of CME Group.

Figure 12.3.1 — The path of an order. Your order passes through your broker and a risk gateway before reaching the matching engine (blue), where it either trades or rests. Matched trades go to the clearing house, which becomes the counterparty to both sides.

12.3.2 The central limit order book

At the heart of the exchange is a central limit order book for each contract: two sorted lists of resting limit orders.

  • Bids (buy orders) sorted by price, highest first.
  • Offers (sell orders) sorted by price, lowest first.

The best bid and best offer form the inside market; the gap between them is the spread. The book is grouped into price levels, and each level holds a queue of orders, each with a size and an arrival time.

12.3.3 Matching

When a new order arrives, the engine checks whether it can trade against the other side. A buy limit at or above the best offer trades immediately (it aggresses); otherwise it rests in the book.

For most CME futures, matching at a price level is first-in, first-out (FIFO): the earliest order at that price fills first. Some products use pro-rata or hybrid allocation, where fills are shared by size. The algorithm is part of the product specification.

Under FIFO, a resting order’s fill depends on its queue position. If QaheadQ_{\text{ahead}} contracts sit ahead of you at your price, and incoming market sell volume at that price is VV, you fill only if

V>Qahead. V > Q_{\text{ahead}} .

That is why “price touched my limit but I didn’t fill” is normal, not a glitch.

Figure 12.3.2 — The book and your place in the queue. On the left, a schematic book: offers (orange) above, bids (green) below, each bar one resting order. On the right, the queue at your bid price: orders A and B arrived first and total 7 contracts. Selling volume at that price must exceed 7 before any of it reaches you. The sizes are illustrative.

12.3.4 Order types

Type What it does Trade-off
Market trade now at whatever is available fast; price uncertain
Limit trade at this price or better price certain; fill uncertain
Stop becomes an order when a trigger price trades useful for exits; can fill well beyond the trigger in a fast market
Stop-limit a stop that becomes a limit trades certainty of fill for price protection

CME also applies protections. Market and stop orders have protection points that cap how far they can sweep, and price banding rejects orders far from the market.

12.3.5 Circuit breakers and velocity logic

Equity index futures have price limits tied to the cash market’s circuit breakers. Globex also uses velocity logic: if price moves too far too fast, the market pauses briefly to let liquidity return. These events are rare, but they matter for anyone using stops.

12.3.6 Clearing

Once matched, the trade goes to the clearing house, which becomes the counterparty to both sides. That is why you don’t care who sold to you: your obligation is to the clearing house, which manages default risk through margin and daily settlement. Its margin model (SPAN, and successor frameworks) sets the minimum margin.

12.3.7 Sessions

Globex trades nearly around the clock on weekdays. Liquidity isn’t uniform: it is deepest during US cash hours and thinner overnight. The trading day for settlement rolls over in the late afternoon US Central time, with a short daily maintenance break.

12.3.8 Market data

What you see on screen is a feed derived from the book: trades, top-of-book quotes, and depth (several levels per side). Retail platforms often show a conflated (merged) or aggregated view. For anything that depends on the order of events, like intrabar stop logic, that difference matters.

12.3.9 Summary

  • Orders go broker → risk gateway → matching engine → clearing house.
  • The book holds bids and offers in price levels; most CME futures match FIFO within a level.
  • A resting limit fills only when volume at its price exceeds the queue ahead of it.
  • Each order type trades price certainty against fill certainty; the exchange adds protections.
  • The clearing house is everyone’s counterparty.

Exercises

  1. (Apply) 40 contracts sit ahead of your bid. 35 contracts sell at your price, then price moves away. Did you fill? (Answer: no; 35 is not more than 40.)
  2. (Compare) When would you prefer a stop-limit over a stop? What risk do you accept?
  3. (Think) Why can a conflated data feed mislead a backtest of intrabar stops?
  4. (Explain) Why don’t you need to know who took the other side of your trade?

Further reading

  • CME Group, “CME Globex Matching Algorithms” (Client Systems Wiki).
  • Larry Harris, Trading and Exchanges: Market Microstructure for Practitioners.
  • Maureen O’Hara, Market Microstructure Theory.

— Tariq

Chapter 12.4 — Leverage Across Stocks, ETFs and Futures

Subtitle: The same idea in three costumes. What changes is how it’s financed, and how fast it can hurt.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define leverage and compute the equity change for a given move. 2. Explain why daily-reset leveraged ETFs decay on choppy paths. 3. Compute the maximum leverage available on futures margin. 4. Compare financing, path dependence and loss limits across the three.

You need: percentages; the idea of compounding.

This is general education, not advice.

12.4.1 The basic ratio

Leverage means controlling more exposure than the cash you put up. It magnifies gains and losses equally. Define it as notional exposure over equity:

λ=notionalequity. \lambda = \frac{\text{notional}}{\text{equity}} .

If the underlying moves by return rr, your equity changes by about λr\lambda r. At λ=5\lambda = 5, a 2% adverse move costs 10% of equity; a 20% move wipes it out.

Figure 12.4.1 — Leverage scales losses in a straight line. Each line is equity change =λr= \lambda r for one leverage level. At λ = 1 a 20% fall costs 20%. At λ = 10 (dotted) a 10% fall reaches −100%, the whole account.

12.4.2 Stocks on margin

In a US margin account (Regulation T), you can usually borrow up to half the purchase price of eligible stocks for overnight positions, so initial leverage is up to 2:1. Maintenance requirements (set by FINRA rules and brokers, often higher) trigger margin calls if equity falls too far. You pay interest on the borrowed amount.

Pattern day trader rules in the US have historically required a minimum account equity for frequent intraday stock trading, with higher intraday buying power. Rules and thresholds change, so check current regulations.

12.4.3 Leveraged ETFs

Leveraged and inverse ETFs aim to deliver a multiple of the index’s daily return. That word hides a trap. Over several days, compounding makes the result differ from the multiple of the period return.

Take a 2× fund over two days with index returns r1,r2r_1, r_2. The fund returns (1+2r1)(1+2r2)−1(1+2r_1)(1+2r_2) - 1, while twice the index’s two-day return is 2[(1+r1)(1+r2)−1]2[(1+r_1)(1+r_2) - 1]. On volatile, directionless paths the fund decays. A rough continuous-time approximation for leverage β\beta on an index with volatility σ\sigma is

ln⁡VTV0≈βln⁡STS0−β(β−1)2σ2T, \ln\frac{V_T}{V_0} \approx \beta\,\ln\frac{S_T}{S_0} - \frac{\beta(\beta-1)}{2}\,\sigma^2 T ,

so the drag grows with β2σ2\beta^2\sigma^2. These products are designed for short holding periods, and their prospectuses say so.

Figure 12.4.2 — Daily-reset leverage decays on a choppy path. A simulated index (blue) moves up or down 2% each day with equal chance (seed 20261107; not market data). The dashed line is twice the index’s cumulative return; the orange line is a fund that doubles each daily return. By the end the index is near where it began, but the 2× daily fund is well below both.

12.4.4 Futures

Futures embed leverage in the contract. You don’t borrow; you post margin, a performance bond, and the contract’s full notional value moves with the index. If notional is m⋅Pm \cdot P (multiplier × price) and margin is MM, the leverage available on margin alone is

λmax=mPM, \lambda_{\max} = \frac{mP}{M} ,

often far higher than stock margin allows. Day-trading margins from some brokers push it higher still. Nothing forces you to use it: holding more account equity than margin lowers your effective leverage, and that is what most risk-aware traders do.

Futures also mark to market daily, so losses leave your account immediately rather than accruing on a loan.

12.4.5 Comparing the three

Stocks on margin Leveraged ETFs Futures
Financing pay interest on the loan built into the fund with fees built into the price versus the index (the basis)
Path dependence none, apart from margin calls by design none, apart from margin calls
Loss beyond deposit possible in a gap no; limited to what you paid possible in a gap

12.4.6 What actually matters

Choose leverage from the size of loss you can tolerate, not the maximum a broker allows. If you risk a fraction ff of equity on each trade, a run of nn losses leaves (1−f)n(1-f)^n of it. Small ff is what lets you survive long enough to learn anything.

12.4.7 Summary

  • Equity change ≈ leverage × underlying return.
  • Reg T stock margin starts around 2:1; leveraged ETFs reset daily and decay on choppy paths, with drag growing like β2σ2\beta^2\sigma^2.
  • Futures leverage on margin is mP/MmP/M, often high; you can use less.
  • Pick leverage from tolerable loss; small risk per trade keeps you in the game.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) Notional $250,000, equity $25,000. What is λ, and what does a 3% adverse move cost? (Answer: λ = 10; about 30% of equity.)
  2. (Compute) Index +10% then −10%. What do the index and a 2× daily fund return over the two days? (Answer: index −1%; fund (1.2)(0.8) − 1 = −4%.)
  3. (Compute) Risking 2% per trade, what is left after 10 straight losses? (Answer: 0.98¹⁰ ≈ 81.7%.)
  4. (Think) Why is “maximum available leverage” the wrong way to choose position size?

Further reading

  • FINRA, “Margin Accounts” and “Leveraged and Inverse ETFs” investor alerts.
  • Minder Cheng and Ananth Madhavan, “The Dynamics of Leveraged and Inverse Exchange-Traded Funds” (2009).
  • CME Group Education, “Understanding Futures Margin”.

— Tariq

Chapter 12.5 — Micro Futures: Same Market, One-Tenth the Size

Subtitle: Why the smaller contracts are the right place to learn, and where they still bite.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. State the multipliers of the E-mini and Micro E-mini index contracts. 2. Size a position from a risk budget and see why granularity matters. 3. Explain why micros cost more per unit of exposure. 4. Say what does not change when the contract is smaller.

You need: division and rounding down.

This is education, not advice.

12.5.1 The product

In 2019 CME Group launched Micro E-mini equity index futures. They track the same indices as the E-mini contracts at one-tenth the size. For anyone learning index futures, that was the most important product change in years, because it makes risk granular (adjustable in small steps).

12.5.2 The specifications

Contract Multiplier per index point
E-mini S&P 500 (ES) $50
Micro E-mini S&P 500 (MES) $5
E-mini Nasdaq-100 (NQ) $20
Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 (MNQ) $2

Tick sizes are the same in points, so tick values are one-tenth. Always confirm current specifications on the exchange’s website; they are the source of truth.

Micros trade on the same platform, in the same hours, against the same index. Their price tracks the larger contract closely, because arbitrage between them is cheap.

12.5.3 Why granularity matters

Position sizing aims to risk a chosen dollar amount RR per trade. With a stop distance of dd points and multiplier mm, the number of contracts is

q=⌊Rmd⌋, q = \left\lfloor \frac{R}{m\,d} \right\rfloor ,

where ⌊⋅⌋\lfloor \cdot \rfloor means round down to a whole number.

With a large multiplier, qq is often 0 or 1 for a small account: you either can’t trade or you risk far more than intended. With a multiplier ten times smaller, qq can be set much closer to the intended risk.

Figure 12.5.1 — Smaller contracts turn sizing into a dial. The x-axis is the risk you intend per trade; the y-axis is the risk you actually take after rounding down. The illustrative contract risks $500 per contract at your stop (orange), so you take $0 until you can afford $500, then jump. A ten-times-smaller contract (blue) steps every $50 and stays close to the ideal dashed line.

12.5.4 Costs are not one-tenth

Commissions and exchange fees on micros are lower per contract, but not proportionally. If cost per contract is cc and notional per contract is mPmP, cost as a fraction of notional is

cmP, \frac{c}{mP},

which is larger for micros because mm is smaller. For frequent trading the difference compounds. It is the price of granularity, and usually worth paying while learning.

12.5.5 Liquidity

Micros are liquid, but less so than E-minis at the top of the book. Spreads are usually one tick in normal conditions; depth is smaller. For small orders that rarely matters. For larger ones, ten micro contracts are not always as easy to fill as one E-mini.

12.5.6 The learning case

The best use of micros is building a real record with real fills at small size: actual slippage, actual emotions when a stop is hit, actual discipline. Simulated trading teaches mechanics; small real trading teaches the rest. Scaling up should be a decision based on a measured record, not on a good week.

12.5.7 What doesn’t change

  • Leverage per contract is the same ratio as the larger contract. A micro isn’t “safer”; it is smaller.
  • Gap risk and fast markets apply identically.
  • Daily settlement and margin calls work the same way.

12.5.8 Summary

  • Micros are one-tenth of the E-minis: MES $5 vs ES $50, MNQ $2 vs NQ $20 per point.
  • Contracts = ⌊R / (m·d)⌋; a smaller multiplier lets real risk track intended risk.
  • Costs per unit of exposure are higher on micros.
  • Leverage per contract, gap risk and daily settlement are unchanged.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) Risk budget $150, stop 6 points. How many MES contracts? How many ES? (Answer: MES ⌊150/30⌋ = 5; ES ⌊150/300⌋ = 0.)
  2. (Compute) Cost $1.20 per MES contract versus $4.50 per ES, index at 5000. Compare cost as a fraction of notional.
  3. (Think) Why is ten micros not always equivalent to one E-mini in practice?
  4. (Plan) What record would you want before moving from micros to E-minis?

Further reading

  • CME Group, “Micro E-mini Equity Index Futures” product pages and contract specifications.
  • CME Group Education, “Calculating Futures Contract Profit or Loss”.
  • Van K. Tharp, Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom, chapters on position sizing.

— Tariq

Chapter 12.6 — Prop-Firm Evaluations: The Realities Behind the Funded Account

Subtitle: A business model built on rules, fees and drawdown arithmetic. Read the maths before you pay for a challenge.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Describe how a typical evaluation programme makes money. 2. Explain a trailing drawdown and why it is harsher than it looks. 3. Estimate the chance of passing with no edge, using gambler’s ruin. 4. List the rules and behavioural traps that affect outcomes.

You need: Chapter 6.1’s gambler’s ruin result helps but is not required.

This is general education, not advice. Rules vary widely between firms; read each firm’s terms carefully.

12.6.1 The offer

“Get funded to trade futures” is one of the most advertised offers in retail trading. You pay a fee, pass an evaluation, and trade a firm’s account for a share of the profits. Some people do well. Many don’t, and the structure explains why.

12.6.2 How the model usually works

  1. Evaluation. You pay a fee (often monthly) to trade a simulated account with a profit target, a maximum drawdown, and other rules.
  2. Funded stage. If you pass, you trade an account under similar or stricter rules, sometimes still simulated, with payouts subject to conditions.
  3. Revenue. The firm earns from evaluation fees, resets, data fees and its share of profits.

When most revenue comes from fees, the business works even if few traders are ever paid. That isn’t an accusation; it is a structure worth understanding.

12.6.3 The trailing drawdown

Many evaluations use a trailing maximum drawdown: the loss limit follows your account’s peak. If equity is EtE_t and the drawdown allowance is DD, you fail when

Et<maxs≤tEs−D. E_t < \max_{s \le t} E_s - D .

Some versions trail intraday peaks, including unrealised profit. That is harsher than it looks: a trade that goes well and then comes back to breakeven has used up drawdown allowance without losing money.

Figure 12.6.1 — The failure line follows the peak. A schematic account (blue) with an allowance of 10 units. The dashed orange failure line sits 10 below the highest point reached, and rises with it. After the peak the account gives back most of its gain. It is still in profit, yet only one unit from failing.

12.6.4 Target versus drawdown as a race

Treat the account as a random walk with drift μ\mu and volatility σ\sigma per trade, starting between a loss barrier DD below and a profit target GG above. For a driftless walk, the chance of reaching the target first is roughly

P(pass)≈DD+G. P(\text{pass}) \approx \frac{D}{D + G} .

Why. This is the gambler’s ruin result: with fair steps, the expected end equals the start, so p⋅G−(1−p)⋅D=0p \cdot G - (1-p) \cdot D = 0, giving p=D/(D+G)p = D/(D+G). It ignores the trailing feature, which makes things worse.

Figure 12.6.2 — With no edge, passing is a weighted coin. The curve is D/(D+G)D/(D+G) for a static drawdown. When the target equals the allowance, the chance is 50%; when the target is twice the allowance, it is one-third. A trailing drawdown pushes the real chance below this curve, and the fee is paid on every attempt.

With no edge, passing is a coin weighted by the ratio of drawdown to target, and fees are paid each attempt. Positive drift helps, but only if it is real; you can’t tell that from a single pass.

12.6.5 Rules that change the game

  • Consistency rules: limits on how much of total profit can come from one day.
  • Daily loss limits on top of the overall drawdown.
  • News restrictions: no trading around certain announcements.
  • Position limits and scaling plans.
  • Payout conditions: minimum days, buffers above the drawdown, withdrawal caps.

Each reduces variance-seeking behaviour, which is reasonable risk management. Each also reduces the chance that a lucky streak turns into a payout.

12.6.6 Behavioural traps

Fee-based resets encourage “one more try” thinking, which is how small fees add up. Profit targets encourage oversizing to reach them faster, which raises the chance of hitting the drawdown first. Treat each fee as a cost of a process you have measured, not a lottery ticket.

12.6.7 A sensible approach, if you try one

  • Read every rule, especially how drawdown is calculated and when payouts are allowed.
  • Have a measured record at small size before paying for evaluations.
  • Size so that an ordinary losing streak can’t touch the drawdown.
  • Budget a fixed total for fees and stop when it is spent.

12.6.8 Summary

  • Fee revenue lets the model work even when few traders are paid.
  • A trailing drawdown follows the peak, so giving back gains eats your allowance.
  • With no edge, P(pass) ≈ D/(D+G), and trailing makes it worse.
  • Extra rules and payout conditions cut the payoff from lucky streaks.
  • Budget fees in advance and size for ordinary losing streaks.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) Allowance $2,000, target $3,000, no edge, static drawdown. Chance of passing? (Answer: 2000/5000 = 40%.)
  2. (Compute) At $100 per attempt and that chance, what is the expected fee spent before a first pass? (Answer: about 1/0.4 = 2.5 attempts, so about $250.)
  3. (Trace) Equity goes 0 → +1,500 → +200 with a trailing allowance of 2,000. Where is the failure line now?
  4. (Think) Why does oversizing to reach the target faster lower the chance of passing?

Further reading

  • CFTC, “Customer Advisory” pages on trading education and evaluation programmes.
  • William Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1 (gambler’s ruin).
  • Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, on sunk-cost and loss aversion.

— Tariq

Chapter 12.7 — Trading Process Frameworks: Deciding Before the Market Does

Subtitle: The edge you can control is the quality of your process, not the outcome of any single trade.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain “resulting” and why outcomes are noisy over few trades. 2. Name the common stages of a trading process. 3. Grade trades on adherence and compare outcomes conditional on it. 4. List why frameworks fail.

You need: the idea of an average and a standard deviation.

This is general education, not advice or a trading system.

12.7.1 Decisions versus outcomes

New traders tend to judge themselves by outcomes: a winning trade was good, a losing one bad. That is a poor way to learn. In a noisy game, good decisions lose often and bad ones win often.

Annie Duke calls the mistake resulting: judging a decision by its result. A decision with positive expectancy still loses some fraction of the time. Over nn trades, the average return x‾\bar x has standard error of roughly

σn, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},

where σ\sigma is the spread of single-trade results. For small nn, outcomes are mostly noise. Process is what you can grade every day.

Figure 12.7.1 — Few outcomes are mostly noise. The curve is σ/n\sigma/\sqrt n, in units of one trade’s spread. After 10 trades the average is still uncertain by about a third of a single trade’s spread; it takes about 100 trades to bring that to a tenth. Grading process gives feedback long before outcomes do.

12.7.2 A common shape for a process

Most serious frameworks share stages, whatever they call them:

  1. Preparation. Before the session: the calendar of scheduled events, the overnight context, the reference levels you care about, and the conditions under which you won’t trade at all.
