  2. Order of analysis. A fixed sequence for reading the market, from broad context to narrow timing, so you don’t jump straight to an entry trigger.
  3. Setup definition. Written criteria for what you are looking for. If you can’t write it down, you can’t test or review it.
  4. Risk definition before entry. Where you are wrong, what that costs, and the position size derived from it.
  5. Execution. Placing orders as planned.
  6. Management. Pre-decided rules for exits and adjustments.
  7. Review. A journal entry for every trade: plan, execution, outcome, and whether you followed the process.

Figure 12.7.2 — A process is a loop, not a line. The seven stages run clockwise. The blue review step feeds back into the next day’s preparation, which is how the process improves. Each stage can be graded on whether it was done, regardless of how the trade turned out.

12.7.3 Grading process

A simple review grades each trade on adherence (did I follow the plan?), independent of P&L. Over time, compare outcomes conditional on adherence:

𝔼[P&L∣followed plan]vs𝔼[P&L∣deviated]. \mathbb{E}[\text{P\&L} \mid \text{followed plan}] \quad \text{vs} \quad \mathbb{E}[\text{P\&L} \mid \text{deviated}] .

If deviations are systematically worse, the fix is discipline. If they are better, the plan is wrong and should be revised deliberately, not by improvisation.

12.7.4 Checklists

Checklists aren’t for beginners; they are for anyone working under pressure. Pilots and surgeons use them because stress narrows attention. A short pre-trade checklist (context checked, risk defined, size computed, no event imminent) catches the predictable mistakes.

12.7.5 Rules for stopping

Good frameworks include rules for not trading: after a set number of losses, after a daily loss limit, around major events, when tired. These protect against the most expensive behaviour, trying to win back losses quickly.

12.7.6 Why frameworks fail

Failure Why it happens
Too complex to follow live ten minutes of analysis per trade won’t happen in a fast market
Not written down a process in your head changes with your mood
No review a framework without review doesn’t improve
Changed after every loss revisions should be scheduled and based on many trades, not the last one

12.7.7 Summary

  • Judge decisions by process, not single outcomes; outcomes are noisy as σ/n\sigma/\sqrt n.
  • A process runs preparation → analysis → setup → risk → execution → management → review.
  • Grade adherence and compare outcomes when you followed the plan versus when you didn’t.
  • Use short checklists and rules for stopping; revise on a schedule.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) Single-trade spread σ\sigma = $200. What is the standard error of the average after 16 trades? After 400? (Answer: $50; $10.)
  2. (Apply) Write a four-item pre-trade checklist for yourself.
  3. (Think) Your deviations score better than your plan over 50 trades. What should you do, and what should you not do?
  4. (Design) Write three stopping rules you would actually follow.

Further reading

  • Annie Duke, Thinking in Bets.
  • Brett N. Steenbarger, The Daily Trading Coach.
  • Atul Gawande, The Checklist Manifesto.

— Tariq

Chapter 12.8 — Reading Market Breadth

Subtitle: The index tells you where the market went. Breadth tells you how many stocks came along.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Define the main breadth measures and the advance–decline line. 2. Compute and read the TRIN, and describe the McClellan indicators and the TICK. 3. Explain divergence and why it is a caution, not a sell signal. 4. Avoid the main data pitfalls in breadth research.

You need: what a cap-weighted index and a moving average are.

This is general education, not advice.

12.8.1 Why breadth

A cap-weighted index like the S&P 500 can rise while most of its members fall, if a handful of very large companies rally. Market breadth measures participation: how broadly a move is shared across stocks. It is a context tool, not a timing signal.

12.8.2 The basic measures

Advance–decline. Count advancing stocks AtA_t and declining stocks DtD_t on an exchange or within an index. The net is At−DtA_t - D_t; the cumulative advance–decline line is

ADLt=∑s≤t(As−Ds). \text{ADL}_t = \sum_{s \le t} (A_s - D_s).

A rising index with a falling ADL means narrowing participation.

Measure What it counts
Up/down volume volume in advancing stocks versus declining stocks
New highs vs new lows stocks at 52-week highs versus 52-week lows
Percent above a moving average share of members above, say, their 50- or 200-day average; bounded 0–100%, so easy to compare across time

Figure 12.8.1 — An index can rise while most stocks fall. A simulation of 500 stocks (seed 20261107; not market data): five very large stocks drift up, the rest drift slightly down. The cap-weighted index (blue) climbs because the large stocks dominate its weight. The advance–decline line (dashed orange), which counts every stock equally, falls. Both are rescaled to start at 100.

12.8.3 Classic composite indicators

The TRIN (Arms Index).

TRIN=A/DVA/VD, \text{TRIN} = \frac{A/D}{V_A/V_D},

where VAV_A and VDV_D are advancing and declining volume. Below one, volume is concentrated in advancers; above one, in decliners. It is noisy intraday and best read as context.

The McClellan Oscillator is the difference between a fast and a slow exponential moving average of net advances. The McClellan Summation Index accumulates it. Both smooth the raw counts into something trend-like.

The TICK is the number of stocks last trading on an uptick minus those on a downtick, updated through the day. Extreme readings show moments of broad, simultaneous buying or selling pressure, often from program activity.

12.8.4 Divergence

The most cited use of breadth is divergence: the index makes a new high while breadth measures don’t. It suggests the move is narrow. But divergences can last a long time, and many resolve with breadth catching up rather than the index falling. Treat them as a reason for caution and smaller size, not a sell signal.

12.8.5 Concentration

When a few mega-cap stocks make up a large share of an index, cap-weighted performance and equal-weighted breadth can diverge for long stretches. Comparing the cap-weighted index with its equal-weight version is a simple way to see concentration directly.

12.8.6 Data pitfalls

  • Universe matters. NYSE breadth includes many non-operating issues (funds, preferreds); index-member breadth is cleaner for index trading.
  • Survivorship. Historical breadth computed from today’s index members is biased. Use point-in-time membership (who was in the index on that date).
  • Intraday vs closing data. Intraday breadth is revised as trades print; closing values are stable.
  • Different vendors, different numbers. Definitions vary. Pick one source and stay with it.

12.8.7 Summary

  • Breadth measures how many stocks join a move; the ADL accumulates net advances.
  • TRIN compares the advance/decline ratio with the volume ratio; McClellan smooths net advances; TICK counts upticks minus downticks.
  • Divergence signals a narrow move and calls for caution, not automatic selling.
  • Use the right universe, point-in-time membership and one consistent vendor.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) 300 advancers, 200 decliners; advancing volume 1.2 billion, declining 0.4 billion. What is the TRIN, and what does it suggest? (Answer: (300/200)/(1.2/0.4) = 1.5/3 = 0.5; volume concentrated in advancers.)
  2. (Compute) Net advances over five days: +50, −120, +30, −80, −10. Starting from 0, what is the ADL each day?
  3. (Think) Why does building historical breadth from today’s index members bias results?
  4. (Explain) Why is percent-above-a-moving-average easier to compare across decades than the raw ADL?

Further reading

  • Gerald Appel, Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors.
  • Sherman and Marian McClellan, Patterns for Profit.
  • Richard W. Arms Jr., The Arms Index (TRIN).

— Tariq

Chapter 12.9 — Fear, Greed and Sentiment Indicators

Subtitle: Measuring the crowd’s mood is easy. Knowing what it implies is much harder than the headlines suggest.

Learning objectives. After this chapter you should be able to: 1. Name the main kinds of sentiment data and their strengths and weaknesses. 2. Describe what the VIX measures and how it is built, in outline. 3. Explain how composite gauges are built and why a trailing window matters. 4. Explain the limits of contrarian readings.

You need: what an option and a z-score are.

This is general education, not advice.

12.9.1 The idea

Sentiment indicators try to measure how optimistic or fearful market participants are. The idea is old: when everyone is already bullish, who is left to buy? The practice is harder, because sentiment can stay extreme far longer than any rule expects.

12.9.2 Kinds of sentiment data

Surveys. Investor polls ask whether people are bullish, bearish or neutral. Direct but slow (weekly), and they capture what people say, not what they do.

Options-based measures.

  • Put/call ratios: volume or open interest of puts divided by calls. High ratios suggest demand for protection.
  • Implied volatility: the VIX estimates the market’s expected 30-day volatility of the S&P 500 from option prices. It is derived from a strip of out-of-the-money options; the variance it represents is, schematically,

σ2=2T∑iΔKiKi2erTQ(Ki)−1T(FK0−1)2, \sigma^2 = \frac{2}{T}\sum_i \frac{\Delta K_i}{K_i^2} e^{rT} Q(K_i) - \frac{1}{T}\left(\frac{F}{K_0} - 1\right)^2 ,

where Q(Ki)Q(K_i) are option mid-prices at strikes KiK_i, ΔKi\Delta K_i the strike spacing, rr the interest rate, FF the forward level and K0K_0 the strike just below it. VIX is the square root, annualised and scaled. - Volatility term structure: whether near-term implied volatility is above or below longer-term. Inversion (near-term higher) often accompanies stress. - Skew: how much more expensive downside puts are than upside calls.

Positioning. Commitments of Traders reports, fund flows, margin debt. Slow, but they reflect actual money.

Composites. “Fear and greed” indices combine several of these, typically by normalising each component and averaging. A common normalisation is a z-score over a trailing window of length ww:

zt=xt−x‾t−w:tst−w:t, z_t = \frac{x_t - \bar x_{t-w:t}}{s_{t-w:t}},

then mapped onto a 0–100 scale.

Note. The window is trailing. A centred window, or a mean and spread over the whole sample, would use future data.

Figure 12.9.1 — Normalise only with the past. Both lines z-score the same simulated random walk (uniform steps, seed 20261107; not market data). The blue line uses a trailing 40-step window and could have been computed live. The dashed orange line uses the mean and spread of the whole series, including values that hadn’t happened yet. The two disagree often, and a backtest using the orange one would be using future information.

Figure 12.9.2 — How a composite gauge is built. Each input is turned into a z-score, the z-scores are averaged, and the result is mapped to 0–100. The orange input is built from price itself (for example momentum), so part of the gauge can simply echo what price already did. Real gauges differ in their exact components.

12.9.3 The contrarian idea, and its limits

The classic reading is contrarian: extreme fear is often near lows, extreme greed near highs. There is some evidence that extreme readings carry information about returns over longer horizons. But:

  • extremes can persist and deepen; “fearful” can become “panicked”;
  • the relationship is weak and unstable over short horizons;
  • composite indices are partly built from price itself (momentum, distance from highs), so they can echo price rather than add information.

12.9.4 How I think about them

As context about conditions, not as triggers. High implied volatility means wider ranges and faster moves, which matters for sizing and stop placement regardless of direction. An inverted volatility term structure says the market is paying up for near-term protection. Those are facts about the environment. What happens next isn’t.

12.9.5 Pitfalls

  • Lookahead in backtests. Many sentiment series are published with a delay or revised later. Use the value that was available at the time.
  • Changing definitions. Composite indices change their components. Long histories may not be comparable.
  • Single-number thinking. One gauge flattens several different signals into one. Read the parts.

12.9.6 Summary

  • Sentiment comes from surveys, options (put/call, VIX, term structure, skew), positioning and composites.
  • VIX is built from a strip of out-of-the-money option prices and estimates 30-day expected volatility.
  • Composites z-score and average their inputs; the window must be trailing.
  • Contrarian readings are weak and unstable short-term; use sentiment as context for sizing and stops.

Exercises

  1. (Compute) A put/call series has trailing mean 0.9 and trailing standard deviation 0.1. Today’s value is 1.15. What is its z-score? (Answer: 2.5.)
  2. (Spot the bug) A study z-scores sentiment using the full 20-year mean. What is wrong?
  3. (Think) Why can a gauge that includes momentum look predictive without adding information?
  4. (Apply) Implied volatility doubles overnight. What would you change about position size and stop distance, regardless of direction?

Further reading

  • Cboe, VIX White Paper.
  • Malcolm Baker and Jeffrey Wurgler, “Investor Sentiment in the Stock Market” (2007).
  • Robert J. Shiller, Irrational Exuberance.

— Tariq
